title: A 1000-hour EEG-EMG-audio dataset of Japanese speech production
expert_take_short: A 1020-hour multimodal EEG-EMG-audio dataset for Japanese overt speech vastly expands data resources, enabling diverse speech decoding and EEG research, though generalization is limited by three participants and no decoding benchmarks are presented.
expert_take_long: This paper releases the JapanEEG dataset, a large-scale multimodal collection of 1020 hours of scalp EEG, facial EMG, and audio recorded during open-vocabulary overt Japanese speech from three participants using three different EEG systems. The dataset substantially exceeds prior public speech EEG datasets in scale and diversity of recording hardware. Rigorous technical validation demonstrates expected physiological EEG spectral profiles and event-related potentials across devices and participants, confirming high data quality. The work's principal contribution is the dataset itself, positioned to enable diverse speech decoding studies and to support broader EEG research on artifact modeling, representation learning, and cross-session/device adaptation. Limitations include a small participant pool limiting generalization and the lack of downstream decoding benchmarks. Overall, this dataset fills a notable gap in publicly available speech EEG resources, particularly for overt speech in Japanese, and offers valuable opportunities for the SSI community to develop and evaluate decoding approaches with large longitudinal multimodal EEG data.
expert_true_value: A large multimodal dataset of high-quality EEG, EMG, and audio for overt Japanese speech with strong technical validation, advancing data availability for non-invasive speech decoding research.
canon_before: Prior public EEG datasets for speech decoding were smaller in scale (hours from single- or few-channel systems), often limited to imagined speech or single devices, and predominantly in languages other than Japanese.
delta_from_canon: Significantly larger scale and multimodal dataset with cross-device, longitudinal recordings in Japanese overt speech, supporting broader research areas beyond speech decoding alone.
position_in_field: significant dataset contribution expanding scale and modality diversity for speech EEG decoding in Japanese overt speech
practical_value: High practical value for research in EEG-based speech decoding, artifact modeling, and cross-device studies; direct application to deployed systems not presented.
axes_moved: scale of available EEG speech datasets dramatically increased with simultaneous multimodal recording and multiple EEG systems across many sessions.
axes_unresolved: Generalization to larger subject populations is unresolved due to only three participants.
axes_regressed: No regression in the axes of modality or evaluation scope was identified from the text.
technical_limits: Small sample size (n=3) limits generalization; lack of downstream decoding evaluations; longitudinal recordings from few participants only; no testing of wearable or mobile suitability reported.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation is limited to basic signal quality and physiological validation analyses, not downstream decoding performance or benchmarking.
deployment_limits: The dataset itself is not a deployed system; no deployment readiness or specific application deployment is described.
scope_limits: Data collected only from three Japanese male participants limits participant diversity; evaluation limited to signal quality checks without decoding experiments.
input_modality: multimodal
sensor_hardware: g.Pangolin (128 ch), g.SCARABEO (62 ch), eego™sports (63 ch); scalp EEG caps with up to 128 channels plus facial EMG electrodes (3 channels) configured around lips and eyes; lavalier microphone for audio recording.
vocabulary_type: open vocabulary
vocabulary_size: open vocabulary
evaluation_mode: quantitative

evidence.statement: We present a multimodal dataset of 1020 hours of simultaneously recorded scalp electroencephalography (EEG), facial electromyography (EMG), and speech audio from three healthy native Japanese speakers during open-vocabulary overt speech.

Three scalp EEG systems were employed across the dataset: g.Pangolin (128 channels), g.SCARABEO (62 channels), and eego™sports (63 channels). Facial EMG was recorded simultaneously with three bipolar channels placed on the upper lip, lower lip, and eye regions.
The dataset is publicly available via OpenNeuro in Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format under a CC0 waiver with approximately 955 GB in size.

Technical validation comprised power spectral density and event-related potential analyses across participants, devices, and tasks, showing the expected 1/f spectral profile, task-related alpha-band attenuation, and time-locked evoked responses consistent with speech-related cortical activity.
The dataset involves only three participants, limiting generalizability across larger populations.

en.summary: A 1020-hour EEG-EMG-audio dataset of Japanese overt speech from three participants, with signal-quality and physiological validation but no decoding benchmarks.
en.sensor: 128/62/63-channel scalp EEG, 3-channel facial EMG, microphone
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Only three Japanese male participants; evaluation limited to signal-quality checks without downstream decoding experiments.

title: A First Exploration of Neuromorphic OT-CFM for Multi-Speaker VSR
venue: Computer Vision – ECCV 2026, Lecture Notes in Computer Science
expert_take_short: Event input and a two-step OT-CFM decoder are standard; the DVS-Lip evaluation is behind: WER on an isolated-word set with no split details or seeds, and baselines that do not match their sources.
expert_take_long: The paper [@chen2026lipsflow] changes two components: event-stream input (M05, standard: DVS-Lip already supplies camera events) and a two-step OT-CFM text decoder (M06, standard: 0.2 WER points over its own diffusion variant, one run). Its evaluation (M12) is behind the field: DVS-Lip is a 100-word isolated-word set with one speaker per clip, scored by word accuracy on a speaker-disjoint split [@tan2022mstp]; the paper cites that protocol (Sec. 5.1) but calls the set multi-speaker and reports WER and VER with no split details, seeds or intervals. The baseline tables do not hold together: Table 2 sets AVA "Clean" equal to the Table 1 DVS-Lip results for six methods, MSTP is listed 2.6 WER points worse than its published accuracy implies (inference), and the SynthVSR row carries the timing of the authors' own 50-step diffusion decoder, so the headline speed claim compares the paper with its own ablation. The low-light claim rests on events converted from the same RGB frames and shows no event-sensor advantage.
expert_true_value: Brings a flow-matching text decoder and event-stream input to lip reading; its value is the in-paper speed comparison of two-step OT-CFM against a 50-step diffusion decoder, not a validated advance on the DVS-Lip benchmark.
canon_before: Event lip reading uses the DVS-Lip camera-event set (100 isolated words, 40 speakers, speaker-disjoint 30/10 split) scored by word accuracy: MSTP 72.10%, later 75.3% and 75.08%. Visual speech recognition mostly decodes with hybrid CTC/attention, LLM decoders or attention encoder-decoders.
delta_from_canon: Adds a learned RGB-to-event conversion for in-the-wild video, a speaker-conditioned OT-CFM text decoder solved in two ODE steps, and BERT/Sentence-BERT semantic supervision; multi-speaker scenes are cut into single-speaker clips by tracking and active-speaker detection.
position_in_field: Standard on event input (M05) and on the decoder (M06): the OT-CFM gain over the authors' diffusion variant is 0.2 WER points in one run. Behind on evaluation (M12): the paper cites the official DVS-Lip protocol but reports WER with no split details or seeds, unlike the word accuracy of earlier DVS-Lip studies.
practical_value: A reference for few-step generative text decoding in lip reading; the DVS-Lip and AVA numbers cannot be placed beside published results without split details, the metric definition and re-run baselines.
axes_moved: Decoder latency inside the paper: two OT-CFM steps at RTF 0.18 and 240 ms against 4.80 and 6000 ms for the authors' 50-step diffusion decoder, at similar WER (22.3 vs 22.5).
axes_unresolved: Word accuracy on the official speaker-disjoint DVS-Lip split; seeds and intervals; robustness with a physical event camera rather than RGB-converted events; overlapping-speaker recognition; LRS3 comparison with other decoders; timing protocol.
axes_regressed: Comparability: baseline rows do not match their sources (MSTP listed at 30.5 WER against its 72.10% accuracy, which shrinks the claimed 8.2-point margin to 5.6; SynthVSR given the timing of the authors' diffusion decoder; AVA Clean values identical to DVS-Lip values for six methods).
technical_limits: Events for AVA are synthesized from RGB frames and add no dynamic range; ten ODE steps give lower WER (22.0) than the two steps called optimal; checkpoints of BERT and Sentence-BERT and any test-time language model are not stated.
evaluation_limits: Official protocol cited without test speakers, sample counts, seeds, run counts, intervals or validation and checkpoint selection; WER/VER normalization undefined; DVS-Lip is an isolated-word set scored here by WER; AVA subset sizes and selection thresholds not given.
deployment_limits: Offline GPU benchmark timing with no stated device, batch size or input duration; no live camera, on-device or power measurement.
scope_limits: Visual speech recognition of voiced speech from video or event streams; offline benchmark study.
task: Visual speech recognition (text) from lip event streams; multi-speaker scenes are reduced to single-speaker clips before recognition.
input_modality: Event streams: recorded by an event camera in DVS-Lip, converted from RGB video for AVA.
sensor_hardware: DVS-Lip event-camera recordings; RGB video for AVA converted by a learned event-generation pipeline.
body_site: Face and lips, recorded at a distance.
output_type: Text transcript with a self-terminating token.
vocabulary_type: DVS-Lip isolated words (100-word vocabulary per the dataset paper); AVA open speech; the paper states no vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: Not stated in the paper; DVS-Lip has 100 words.
metrics: DVS-Lip: WER 22.3, VER 19.8, RTF 0.18, 240 ms, 45.8 M parameters (Table 1); AVA: Clean 22.3, Rapid Motion 24.1, Low Light 22.9, Severe Occlusion 26.5 WER (Table 2); one run each.
evaluation_mode: Offline benchmark comparison on DVS-Lip and AVA subsets with decoder, fusion, step-count and loss ablations on DVS-Lip.

evidence.statement: The authors present LipsFlow as converting RGB video to event streams, segmenting speakers by ByteTrack and TalkNet, and decoding text with OT-CFM and dual-level semantic supervision.
Input is event streams: dataset-provided camera events for DVS-Lip and events converted from RGB for AVA.
Multi-speaker scenes are cut into single-speaker clips by tracking and active-speaker detection before recognition; overlapping speech is not evaluated.
The decoder solves a probability-flow ODE with two deterministic Euler steps (step 0.5) to semantic representations.
Table 1 (DVS-Lip) reports WER 22.3, VER 19.8, RTF 0.18, 240 ms latency and 45.8 M parameters.
The abstract and Sec. 5.2 call 22.3% WER at 240 ms state of the art; DVS-Lip is an isolated-word set whose earlier studies report word accuracy.
Table 2 (AVA) reports Clean 22.3, Rapid Motion 24.1, Low Light 22.9 and Severe Occlusion 26.5 WER; the Clean values equal the DVS-Lip values for all six methods.
Table 4 reports WER 28.5 at one step, 22.3 at two steps and 22.0 at ten steps; the text calls two steps optimal.
Table 3 reports 27.8 WER visual-only, 24.5 with an autoregressive decoder, 22.5 with diffusion and 22.3 with OT-CFM, each from one run.
The new combination is event input, an OT-CFM text decoder and semantic supervision; a concurrent work also decodes VSR text generatively, and no prior ledger study does.
Evaluation covers DVS-Lip and RGB-converted AVA subsets; no physical event-camera test under low light and no LRS3 result.
Within lip reading the paper sits with event-camera studies on DVS-Lip, where the concurrent state of the art is 77.49% word accuracy.
Homophene ambiguity is addressed through BERT and Sentence-BERT supervision; no ambiguity-specific test is reported.
Timing is reported without device, batch size or input duration; the SynthVSR timing equals the authors' own diffusion decoder row; the text gives 26x and Table 4 25.0x.

en.summary: Event input and a two-step OT-CFM decoder are standard; the DVS-Lip evaluation is behind: WER on an isolated-word set with no split details or seeds, and baselines that do not match their sources.
en.sensor: Event streams: event-camera recordings (DVS-Lip) and events converted from RGB video (AVA)
en.task: Visual speech recognition; multi-speaker scenes cut into single-speaker clips
en.vocabulary: Not stated; DVS-Lip has 100 isolated words
en.speaker: Not stated (DVS-Lip has 40 speakers; official protocol cited without split details)
en.key_result: 22.3 WER on DVS-Lip with 2-step OT-CFM vs 22.5 for 50-step diffusion at 25x lower latency; one run
en.limitations: DVS-Lip scored by WER with no split details or seeds; baseline rows do not match their sources; low-light gain uses RGB-converted events; two steps called optimal though ten score better.

title: AESSI: An Around-Ear Silent Speech Interface for Cross-Day Online Reuse without Test-Day Calibration
expert_take_short: 耳周囲cEEGridで25の固定中国語文を認識。テスト日較正なしの別日ホルドアウトで平均92.24%、21日以上後のライブ250試行で98.00%。開語彙会話や患者適用は未実証。
expert_take_long: AESSIはカメラ唇読取やSilentSpellerの口蓋電極、SottoVoceの超音波、Nasovoceの鼻パッドではなく、両側cEEGridによる耳周囲の混合電気生理で無声構音を読む。課題は開語彙会話ではなく、6文字程度の中国語日常文25クラスの文選択である。24人・44セッションから学習し、6人の完全な後日セッションをテスト日較正なしで測ると参加者マクロ平均正解率は92.24%（チャンス4.00%、Table 4では±3.81）。AugとMCRPなしの文監督のみでも74.16%で、最強適応ベースラインATCNetの41.67%を上回る。著者報告のベースライン差50.57ポイントは、元モデルの想定課題やフィルタ境界の変更も踏まえて読む必要がある。前向き評価では、履歴最終収録から少なくとも21日後に5人が電極を再装着し、凍結モデルで各50試行・計250試行を行い245正解（98.00%）。CPU再生の前処理＋文予測中央値は31.70 ms。価値は「付け直した当日に較正コーパスを取らずに履歴モデルを使えるか」を耳周囲レイアウトで具体化した点にある。一方、著者自身が開語彙・自由文入力は未対応、健常者のみ、脳卒中後構音障害への適用は今後と明記する。人口事前学習なしの本人履歴0では68.44%まで落ち、本人履歴が薄いときの人口データの寄与が大きい。したがって92%や98%を、誰でも装着するだけで開語彙会話ができる性能や、顔・頸部EMG・VTPと直接比較できる汎用数字として読むべきではない。
expert_true_value: 皮膚接触の耳周囲SSIについて、電極再装着後もテスト日較正なしで履歴モデルをオンライン再利用できるかを、別日セッション保留と前向きライブで示した点。
canon_before: 耳周囲配列によるオンライン無声発話はInoueらが64語で示した一方、健常者はテスト日に640ラベル試行の個人較正を要した。顔・頸部sEMGやSilentSpeller、SilentWearも別日再利用の証拠を持つが、レイアウトと再装着条件ごとに評価が必要とされていた。
delta_from_canon: 耳周囲SSIで、テスト日の個人較正コーパスやモデル適応を禁止したドメイン汎化設定を前面に出し、完全な後日セッション保留と21日以上後の前向きオンラインを同じ系で示した。
position_in_field: 非侵襲の耳周囲／ウェアラブル電気生理SSIにおける、閉集合文認識と別日・再装着再利用の研究。KimuraらのSilentSpeller（EPG）・SottoVoce（超音波）や、RekimotoらのNasoVoce（鼻パッド）とはセンサ部位が異なる。
practical_value: 耳周辺デバイスで「翌日付け直してすぐ使う」設計を検討するときの、較正コストと閉集合精度の参照になる。会話生成や開語彙入力の完成を示したものではない。
axes_moved: セッション全体を保留する別日評価と、電極再装着後の前向きライブ評価を同じ耳周囲レイアウトで接続し、テスト日較正なしの再利用を主目標に据えた。
axes_unresolved: キーボード依存の開始・正誤ラベル付けの日常代替、瞬き等の非構音ノイズ耐性、より多数の利用者・反復フォローアップ・自然場面での安定性、候補文集合拡大時の収集負担。
axes_regressed: 語彙は固定25文に限定され、開語彙会話は扱わない。健康被験者のみで、脳卒中後構音障害など想定利用者での検証はない。混合信号の筋電・脳波寄与は分離していない。
technical_limits: 混合信号の音源分離なし。緑十字固視で眼球運動を抑えるが非構音寄与を排除できないと著者も認める。ベースラインは元論文の想定と異なる制約下で再実装。
evaluation_limits: オフラインは参加者マクロ平均と3シード。ライブはseed 42のみ。チャンス率4%。クラス不均衡や被験者別オフラインの分散、統計検定の詳細は限定的。P024はスケジュール都合でライブ未実施。
deployment_limits: 開始はスペースキー、正誤は1/0キー。遮へい室または会議室。歩行・騒音・長時間装着・患者利用は未評価。電極装着と信号確認に平均約5分26秒かかるが、較正収集はない。
scope_limits: arXiv v1全文（要旨、方法、Table 1–4、図1–8、Discussion 5.7、Conclusion）と抽出テキストを確認。図表はテキスト抽出と要旨数値を照合。著者コードの実行や実験の独立再現、未公開補足動画の全確認はしていない。
task: 3秒の無声構音窓から、事前定義25の中国語日常文のうちどれかを選ぶ閉集合文認識。開語彙の音声認識や文章生成ではない。
input_modality: 両側耳周囲の非侵襲電気生理（混合；著者は構音関連の顔面・顎筋電や脳波成分を含むとしつつ寄与は分離しない）。3秒窓のlog-STFT。
sensor_hardware: TMSi SAGA 32+、両側cEEGrid計20電極のうち接触不良で18・20を除外し18チャネル、1 kHz、平均参照、左腕接地。インピーダンスは実験前に18チャネルとも20 kΩ未満。
body_site: 両側耳周囲の皮膚（cEEGrid）。口腔は塞がない。左腕に接地電極。
output_type: 25クラスの文ラベル（事前定義の中国語短文）。音声波形や自由テキストは出力しない。
vocabulary_type: 日常行動・社会的やりとり・身体／感情状態をカバーする事前定義の中国語短文。開語彙ではない。
vocabulary_size: 25文（各6漢字）。ライブも同一25クラス。
metrics: クロスデイ（6人・3シード平均）AESSI 92.24±3.81%。Aug/MCRPなし74.16±12.62%。ベースライン例：ATCNet 41.67±12.59%、SpeechNet 35.60±18.33%、InoueNet 30.87±21.70%、チャンス4.00%。ライブ：245/250＝98.00%（参加者別46/50/50/50/49）。CPU再生中央値31.70 ms（95パーセンタイル35.1 ms）。H=0・G=fullのLOPO 68.44%。共有10文事前学習からの転移で全体51.18%→81.56%。著者報告値であり独立再現ではない。
evaluation_mode: 歴史セッションで学習し完全な後日セッションを保留するクロスデイ評価（6人）と、電極再装着後の前向きライブ50試行×5人。テスト日のラベル付き／なし適応なし。ターゲットはRANDOM.ORGで現場生成。

evidence.statement: 課題は事前定義25の中国語短文の閉集合認識であり、開語彙や自由作文の入力ではない。著者もLimitationで開語彙非対応を明記する。
センサはTMSi SAGA 32+と両側cEEGrid（計20電極、実用18チャネル、1 kHz）。カメラ唇、EPG、超音波、鼻パッドではない。
24人から44セッション・11,000試行を収集。各セッションは10ブロック×25文＝250試行。クロスデイ対象は複数セッションの6人。
テスト日較正なしのクロスデイ評価でAESSI平均正解率92.24±3.81%（6人・3シードの参加者マクロ平均）。チャンス率4.00%。
Table 4の適応ベースライン最高はATCNet 41.67%。AESSI完全系との差は著者が50.57ポイントと報告。Aug/MCRPなしのAESSIでも74.16%。
履歴最終収録から≥21日後、5人が電極再装着し凍結モデルで各50試行。245/250正解でオンライン精度98.00%（内訳46/50/50/50/49）。
ライブではモデル・フロントエンド・クラス対応を訪問前に凍結し、テスト日の適応や較正収集は行わない。ターゲットは独立タブレットのRANDOM.ORGで生成。
250本の生ライブ録音を配備CPUで再生した前処理＋文予測時間の中央値は31.70 ms（95パーセンタイル35.1 ms）。全予測はライブログと一致。
MCRPはマスクした時間周波数入力から凍結教師表現を予測する経路で、Augありでは74.16%→92.24%、Augなしでも74.16%→89.67%へ平均精度が上がると報告。
本人履歴なしの厳格LOPO（H=0, G=full）では平均68.44%。H=1で人口データなし13.29%→full 73.62%と、個人履歴が薄いときの人口データの寄与が大きい。
著者は脳卒中後構音障害などへの短文コミュニケーション支援を動機に挙げるが、検証参加者は健常者のみで、想定利用者への適用は今後の課題と明記する。
Limitation: 開語彙・自由文非対応、健常者のみ、開始／確認がキーボード依存、混合信号の筋電・脳波寄与未分離、固視指示だけでは非構音運動の影響を排除できない。
関連研究対比として、Inoueらの耳周囲64語オンラインはテスト日に健常者640ラベル試行の微調整を含む。本論文はその較正を禁じた再利用設定を主眼とする。
対比上、本系はSilentSpellerのEPG、SottoVoceの顎下超音波、カメラVTP、Nasovoce鼻パッドではなく、口腔を塞がない耳周囲皮膚電極である（著者のSSI分類整理と装置記述）。

en.summary: Around-ear cEEGrid system recognizing 25 fixed Mandarin sentences from silent articulation without test-day calibration; 92.24% mean accuracy on held-out later-day sessions and 98.00% in 250 live trials 21+ days later.
en.sensor: Bilateral around-ear cEEGrid electrodes (mixed EMG/EEG), 18 channels
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: 92.24% accuracy, cross-day held-out sessions, no test-day calibration, chance 4%; 98.00% live (245/250)
en.limitations: Closed 25-sentence set only; mixed signal sources not separated; open-vocabulary conversation, walking, noise, long wear and patient use untested; live test used a single seed.

title: Affect Decoding in Phonated and Silent Speech Production from Surface EMG
expert_take_short: Affect decoded from silent-articulation EMG, a design absent from 99 ledger studies (M08, ahead); it works within subject, nears chance across speakers, and is not separated from facial expression.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the output (M08) to an affect label decoded from facial and neck EMG during silent articulation, a design none of the 99 ledger studies on paralinguistic output from production signals has (Appendix); the closest priors decode speaker identity and speaking mode from EMG, analyse emotional articulation without an emotion classifier, or decode emotion in a silent-speech wearable from carotid pulse. The phonated-to-silent test (M04) is standard; the zero-shot BioCodec encoder loses little across modes. The claim that affect is carried by speech-motor activity is not established: the authors name a brow electrode as the most prominent site and concede that facial expression cannot be separated from articulation. Within-subject decoding works (AUC 0.845); unseen-speaker EMG AUC is 0.567 to 0.574, close to chance with no chance-level test, and spontaneous affect is decoded better from audio.
expert_true_value: Shows where silent affect decoding works and fails, with paired articulation modes and lexical-control analyses that expose the gap between personalization and generalization.
canon_before: Facial EMG emotion recognition and EMG speech decoding already exist, but often address passive emotion elicitation or lexical reconstruction separately. This study examines their intersection during speech production.
delta_from_canon: Combines paired-mode speech production with affect classification and explicit sentence/speaker controls, rather than reconstructing words or audio.
position_in_field: Silent paralinguistics: affect-label inference from articulatory and facial signals, complementary to lexical silent speech recognition.
practical_value: Offers baseline designs and evidence for personalized affect sensing; the held-out-speaker and repeated-content results are more useful for system planning than the headline score alone.
axes_moved: Adds affect labels and channel-level analyses to silent articulation; tests sentence-grouped evaluation, held-out speakers, repeated lexical content and cross-mode transfer.
axes_unresolved: Natural silent conversation, independent recording days, patient populations, separation of articulation from facial expression, real-time operation and the exact spontaneous-training protocol.
axes_regressed: EMG discriminability drops sharply for unseen speakers; prompted repeated-content trials are harder than affect-specific sentences. Speech foundation-model features outperform EMG in spontaneous phonated conversation.
technical_limits: Whole-utterance summary features and baseline normalization require trial context. Facial expression and speech motor activity are not causally separated. The structural-feature median-frequency equation integrates half the spectral area rather than specifying the frequency splitting that area; implementation is unclear.
evaluation_limits: Small and demographically imbalanced cohort; affect and mode order are fixed, and silent trials immediately follow phonated counterparts. Sentence grouping reduces direct lexical leakage, but task/order effects remain. Section 5.3 and Section 6.3 disagree on whether training includes spontaneous trials. No independent-day or patient test.
deployment_limits: Laboratory recordings with eight gel electrodes, roughly one hour of preparation, participant-held recording button and offline whole-trial features. No mobile, continuous or clinical evaluation.
scope_limits: English prompted/induced polite and frustrated expression in 12 adults without current neurological or psychiatric diagnoses. Neutral data are collected but excluded from the reported binary comparisons. No clinical cohort or spontaneous silent condition.
input_modality: Eight-channel facial and neck surface EMG; separately evaluated audio baselines for phonated speech.
sensor_hardware: actiCHamp Plus amplifier with eight bipolar Ag/AgCl surface electrodes at infrahyoid, suprahyoid, mylohyoid, mentalis, upper orbicularis oris, depressor supercilii and bilateral zygomaticus major sites; 10 kHz acquisition downsampled to 1 kHz. Gel and skin preparation; separate Rode NT1-A/Focusrite audio acquisition.
vocabulary_type: Affect classes rather than lexical output
vocabulary_size: Not a word-vocabulary task: binary polite/frustrated labels, with neutral trials excluded from the primary reported classification.
metrics: Table 5 prompted pooled EMG: TD-0 within-subject AUC 0.845 +/- 0.058 and BAC 0.762 +/- 0.063; EMG held-out-speaker AUC 0.567-0.574. Table 8 silent-only within-subject structural AUC 0.829 +/- 0.056; phonated-to-silent BioCodec AUC 0.763 +/- 0.094. Table 9 spontaneous phonated held-out-speaker BioCodec AUC 0.630 +/- 0.009, BAC 0.595 +/- 0.014, versus Vox-Profile AUC 0.743 +/- 0.004. Table 9 dispersion is described at trial level and should not be equated with subject-wise SD in Tables 5/8. Results are author-reported, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline binary polite-versus-frustrated classification with neutral trials excluded; 5-fold sentence-grouped within-subject evaluation and nested leave-one-subject-out evaluation. Additional repeated-content, cross-mode, single-electrode and spontaneous-phonated analyses.

evidence.statement: ST-CASE contains 2,780 utterances from 12 participants: 1,588 phonated and 1,192 silent. Task 2 is phonated only; all silent recordings come from prompted Tasks 1 and 3.
The study evaluates affect labels rather than lexical reconstruction, comparing handcrafted/TD EMG features and pretrained BioCodec embeddings with separate acoustic baselines.

Within-subject evaluation groups all repetitions of a sentence in the same fold. Inter-subject evaluation uses an outer leave-one-subject-out loop and sentence-grouped inner folds. Neutral trials are excluded from the binary affect results.
Table 5 reports within-subject TD-0 AUC 0.845 +/- 0.058 and BAC 0.762 +/- 0.063, while the three EMG representations yield only 0.567-0.574 AUC in held-out-speaker evaluation.
Table 8 reports silent-only within-subject structural AUC 0.829 +/- 0.056 and phonated-to-silent BioCodec AUC 0.763 +/- 0.094. Silent-only held-out-speaker AUC ranges from 0.563 to 0.608.

On repeated lexical content, within-subject EMG AUC is 0.720-0.751, whereas Vox-Profile falls from 0.889 on affect-specific sentences to 0.469 on repeated-content sentences. Reviewer assessment: this is useful lexical-confound control, not proof of articulation-specific affect coding.
The eyebrow-region E6 channel has high within-subject discriminability; the paper acknowledges that the design cannot disentangle articulatory modulation from accompanying facial expressions.

Prompted affect conditions occur in a fixed temporal order, and every phonated trial immediately precedes its silent counterpart. Task 3 repeats Task 1 roughly 30 minutes later. Reviewer assessment: order, repetition and within-visit adaptation are not independent-day generalization tests.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 3.2; Figure 3 and Section 6.2; PDF pp. 3 and 6-7

evidence.statement: Section 5.3 says training uses controlled and spontaneous tasks, whereas Section 6.3 describes training on controlled Tasks 1/3 and testing the held-out speaker on spontaneous Task 2. Reviewer assessment: the exact training-domain boundary must be clarified before claiming controlled-to-spontaneous transfer.
Table 9 reports spontaneous phonated BioCodec AUC 0.630 and BAC 0.595, compared with Vox-Profile AUC 0.743 and BAC 0.670. These are phonated affect results, not spontaneous silent-speech decoding.

The protocol requires skin preparation, conductive gel and participant-held button segmentation. The dataset is not publicly released, and no online latency, mobile use or clinical communication evaluation is reported.

en.summary: Affect decoded from silent-articulation EMG, a design absent from 99 ledger studies (M08, ahead); it works within subject, nears chance across speakers, and is not separated from facial expression.
en.sensor: 8-channel bipolar facial/neck surface EMG (gel)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Silent-only within-subject AUC 0.829; held-out-speaker EMG AUC 0.567-0.574
en.limitations: Small imbalanced cohort; facial expression and speech motor activity not separated; fixed task order; no independent-day, mobile or patient testing.

title: Articulatory movements influence electromagnetic wave transmission through the vocal tract
expert_take_short: A useful two-person physical model of contact-RF articulation sensing; qualitative agreement below about 3 GHz does not establish recognition accuracy or general-user robustness.
expert_take_long: This paper is valuable as a physical explanation and simulation study for contact-RF silent speech sensing. It builds MRI-derived head geometries for three sustained vowels in two male participants and compares HFSS simulations with repeated scattering-matrix measurements from cheek-mounted antennas. The clearest result is qualitative agreement in transmission magnitude and some vowel-dependent spectral structure up to roughly 2-3 GHz; measurements above 3 GHz become too noisy to validate the detailed simulated patterns. The observed transmission differences between vowels can reach about 15 dB, whereas repeat variation is typically about 5 dB and sometimes 10 dB. These contrasts support articulation sensitivity, but they are not classification accuracy. In particular, the 99.17% recognition rate in Figure 1 belongs to a cited earlier study and must not be assigned to this paper. The field maps suggest that internal resonances, external scattering and antenna positions jointly shape the spectrum; they do not isolate tongue motion as the sole signal source. Several modeling choices are informed by the experimental response, including replacing unsegmented fat-like tissue with muscle-like properties and selecting a 1 micrometre antenna gap. Thus, agreement is partly calibration rather than an independent prospective prediction. Different MRI protocols, supine-versus-seated posture, missing anatomy, and tissue-property approximations limit precision. The work supplies a useful basis for studying antenna placement and anatomy effects, but further participants, controlled gesture perturbations, quantitative error analysis and an actual model-guided recognition experiment are needed to show practical SSI improvement.
expert_true_value: Makes the RF transmission mechanism inspectable and offers an anatomy-aware basis for future hardware optimization beyond trial-and-error recognition studies.
canon_before: Earlier contact-RF SSI studies demonstrated recognition from transmission spectra and optimized antennas empirically. Distant radar primarily senses external motion; contact antennas aim to improve coupling into tissue.
delta_from_canon: Relates measured vowel-dependent transmission spectra to simulated internal resonances and external scattering patterns instead of treating the RF signal solely as a learned recognition feature.
position_in_field: Physical foundations and sensor design for contact-RF articulatory SSI, rather than a speech-decoding benchmark.
practical_value: Supports hypotheses about antenna location, usable bandwidth, anatomy effects and future controlled simulation studies; demonstrated improvement to recognition remains absent.
axes_moved: Physical interpretability of contact RF sensing, anatomy-specific modeling, and a simulation route for future antenna and frequency-band design.
axes_unresolved: Quantitative predictive error, new-subject prediction, dynamic gestures, independent internal-versus-external motion contributions, and actual recognition gains from model-guided design.
axes_regressed: No matched end-to-end system comparison. Detailed anatomical modeling introduces substantial preparation and simulation complexity.
technical_limits: Model omits cables and balun, approximates unsegmented tissues as muscle, flattens local cheek surfaces and uses a fitted 1 micrometre antenna gap. Missing/cropped anatomy and posture mismatches affect agreement. Minima can depend on both internal and external fields and on moving antenna geometry.
evaluation_limits: Only two male participants and three sustained vowels, with three RF repetitions per condition. Agreement is principally qualitative; no global prediction-error score, uncertainty interval, or held-out anatomy validation is reported. Tissue assignment and antenna gap are adjusted using the measured response. Above 3 GHz, measurement noise prevents useful comparison of spectral minima.
deployment_limits: Two adhesive cheek antennas are connected to laboratory vector network analyzers. No complete wearable recognizer, live communication loop, mobility test, or patient use is evaluated.
scope_limits: Static sustained vowel production and same-person numerical/experimental comparison; not continuous silent speech decoding, speaker identification, or clinical rehabilitation testing.
task: Physical modeling of articulatory RF sensing
input_modality: Contact radio-frequency transmission between cheek-mounted antennas; MRI supplies offline anatomical models.
sensor_hardware: Two bow-tie antennas, conductor dimensions 27 mm by 11.5 mm on 0.8 mm FR4, taped near the mouth corners. Subject 1: Rohde & Schwarz ZVL6 VNA; Subject 2: Keysight M9374A in M9005A chassis. 3T MRI supplies anatomical geometry.
output_type: Reflection/transmission spectra and simulated electric-field distributions; no decoded speech output.
vocabulary_type: Static articulatory configurations, not a recognition vocabulary
vocabulary_size: 3 sustained vowel configurations (/a/, /i/, /u/); no word vocabulary.
metrics: Measurements sweep 1-6 GHz at -10 dBm VNA output. Repetition variation is typically around 5 dB and reaches 10 dB; some between-vowel differences reach 15 dB near 1.5 GHz. Simulated transmission is generally of similar magnitude below 2-3 GHz, except Subject 1 /i/ is about 10 dB lower than measured. No new recognition accuracy, WER, latency or global simulation-error metric is reported. Separate simulations at 0.5 W input report approximately 17-40 W/kg over 10 g and 51-280 W/kg over 1 g across 1-6 GHz; these are model estimates at a different power from the experiments, not device certification.
evaluation_mode: Same-subject comparison of measured and simulated reflection/transmission spectra and inspection of simulated electric fields; numerical RF absorption estimates.

evidence.statement: Two male participants, aged 54 and 33, provide MRI geometries for sustained /a/, /i/ and /u/. RF measurements use the same subjects and three repetitions per vowel, while MRI and RF acquisition differ in posture and institution.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections II-B and II-E; PDF pp. 3-5; Discussion p. 12

evidence.statement: A custom CGAL-based MRI-to-surface-mesh workflow enables HFSS anatomical electromagnetic models, compared with measured scattering matrices and inspected through simulated electric fields.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections II-F and II-G; Figures 4 and 8-10; PDF pp. 5-10

evidence.statement: Two cheek-mounted bow-tie antennas measure 1-6 GHz scattering matrices using vector network analyzers at -10 dBm output. The study does not train a speech recognizer.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections II-D and II-E; PDF pp. 4-5; Results pp. 6-11

evidence.statement: Transmission magnitude is generally comparable below about 2-3 GHz, except the Subject 1 /i/ simulation is about 10 dB below measurement. Repetition variation is typically around 5 dB and can reach 10 dB; vowel differences can reach 15 dB near 1.5 GHz.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III; Figures 6 and 7; PDF pp. 7 and 10

evidence.statement: Above 3 GHz, excessive measurement noise prevents meaningful comparison of the spectral minima. Some measured minima are absent in the corresponding simulations even below this range.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III and Discussion; PDF pp. 10 and 12

evidence.statement: Unsegmented tissue initially modeled as fat was changed to muscle because it better matched measurement magnitude. An antenna-to-head gap of 1 micrometre was selected by parametric analysis to match reflection magnitude. Reviewer assessment: these are measurement-informed calibration choices.

Field maps relate transmission minima and maxima to local fields at antenna locations; internal resonances, external scattering and their combination can all contribute. Reviewer assessment: the results do not isolate tongue motion alone.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III and Discussion; Figures 8-10; PDF pp. 8-13

evidence.statement: The 99.17% command-word recognition rate illustrated in Figure 1 is attributed to Wagner et al. 2022. The present paper validates a physical model and does not supply a new recognition accuracy.
evidence.section_or_location: Figure 1 and Introduction; PDF p. 2; Results and Conclusion pp. 6-14

evidence.statement: Absorption simulations use 0.5 W input, separately from -10 dBm experimental measurements. Reported 10 g averages rise from about 17 to 40 W/kg, and 1 g averages from about 51 to 280 W/kg, over 1-6 GHz. Reviewer assessment: these are model-specific numerical results, not certification of a deployed device.
evidence.section_or_location: Section II-G and Section III; PDF pp. 6 and 11

evidence.statement: The authors identify missing/cropped anatomy, segmentation and tissue-property approximations, antenna-position mismatch, posture and articulation variability as discrepancy sources, and call for a larger and more diverse participant sample.

en.summary: Physical modeling and measurement of contact RF transmission through the vocal tract for three sustained vowels in two participants; simulations qualitatively agree with measurements below about 3 GHz.
en.sensor: Two cheek-mounted bow-tie antennas with lab VNA; MRI models
en.task: Physical modeling of articulatory RF sensing
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Between-vowel transmission differences up to 15 dB near 1.5 GHz; repetition variation ~5-10 dB
en.limitations: Only two participants and three vowels; agreement mainly qualitative with no error metric; no recognition system, wearable device or patient use.

title: AVSRBench: A Multi-Condition AVSR Benchmark
expert_take_short: Zero-shot cross-corpus AVSR testing (M12) and a video-call test set (M11) are standard after WildVSR; each condition mixes several shifts, without repeated runs.
expert_take_long: The paper [@jain2026] changes the evaluation (M12), testing three released AVSR checkpoints zero-shot in three input modes on six datasets, and the reference (M11), an Easy/Hard RoomReader video-call set. Both are standard: testing publicly released checkpoints outside LRS3 was already done in WildVSR [@djilali2023wildvsr], and concurrent work tests the same checkpoints on conversational video [@kwak2026voxmm] and on an LRS3-matched unseen set over five runs [@lin2026mv2lrs3], which shares the target's senior author. The main claim, that broadcast WER overstates generalization, holds, but each condition shifts speaking style, vocabulary, transmission, pose and preprocessing at once, and the design does not separate them. Auto-AVSR visual-only WER on RoomReader-AV exceeds 100% even on Easy clips (Table X), so the collapse lies mainly in the video channel, not only in short turns; Hard clips add 21.6 points (inference). The authors' blame on the LLM decoder for the Llama-AVSR failure (§IV-E, §V) rests on one run per condition, without variance.
expert_true_value: A comparison resource for reading saturated broadcast benchmarks: it reports how three released AVSR checkpoints behave on grammar, Lombard, lipspeaker and video-call corpora, and provides a RoomReader-AV preparation pipeline. Its conditions change several factors at once, so it locates failures rather than explaining them.
canon_before: AVSR evaluation centres on the LRS2 and LRS3 broadcast corpora, where released models reach about 1% audio-visual WER. Testing released checkpoints outside LRS3 already existed (WildVSR, 2023), and concurrent work tests conversational and video-call data.
delta_from_canon: Moves from a single broadcast test set to zero-shot visual-only, audio-only and audio-visual testing of three released checkpoints on six datasets, adds a RoomReader-AV Easy/Hard split, and releases a shared preparation pipeline.
position_in_field: A camera-based AVSR generalization benchmark; adjacent to wearable silent speech interfaces, which it does not test.
practical_value: Shows where visual and audio-visual recognition from released checkpoints degrades (video calls, profile views, non-professional speakers) before a system is designed for those settings.
axes_moved: Visual-only collapse outside broadcast data; audio-visual gain mainly on Lombard speech for one model; acoustic fallback at 90 degree profile; articulation skill mattering more than a 30 degree angle; instability of the LLM-based model out of domain.
axes_unresolved: Which factor drives each drop (transmission, pose, speaking style, vocabulary, preprocessing); variance over runs; latency; wearable or silent articulation; unseen languages.
axes_regressed: No regression in measurement; the paper shows that saturated broadcast scores overstate generalization rather than claiming a new best model.
technical_limits: Evaluation uses released checkpoints with official decoding settings whose values are not stated; no retraining or change of fusion. RoomReader results use individual participant streams, not session audio.
evaluation_limits: No seeds, repeated runs, intervals or chance reference; whole corpora used as test sets outside LRS2/LRS3 without a speaker-overlap audit; scoring normalization not stated; Easy/Hard boundary differs between text (below 2 s) and code (at most 2.0 s).
deployment_limits: Camera and microphone AVSR only; no wearable sensors; no streaming or on-device measurement; GPU memory reported for inference only, latency not measured.
scope_limits: arXiv 2609.10366 v1 read in full with Tables I-XI and the public preparation code; values are taken from the paper's tables; no independent re-run of the checkpoints.
input_modality: RGB face and lip video with audio (audio-visual speech recognition), compared in visual-only, audio-only and audio-visual modes; not a wearable or contactless silent speech sensor.
sensor_hardware: Corpus-dependent RGB cameras and microphones. Preprocessing: RetinaFace with 68-point landmarks, 96x96 mouth ROI, 16 kHz mono audio. No worn electrodes or ultrasound probes.
output_type: Text transcript scored by word error rate (WER); not a command label or speech waveform.
vocabulary_type: Continuous word sequences (open vocabulary), except the fixed GRID grammar.
vocabulary_size: Corpus-dependent: GRID uses a fixed six-word command grammar; LRS, TCD-TIMIT and RoomReader are open-vocabulary continuous speech.
metrics: LRS3 AV WER: Llama-AVSR 0.79%, Auto-AVSR 0.90%, AV-HuBERT 1.47% (Table II). GRID VO: 66.53 / 83.80 / 116.39% (Table III). LombardGrid Auto-AVSR AV 11.73% vs AO 14.02% (difference +2.29; Table V). LombardGrid Auto-AVSR VO 64.88% at 0 degrees, 92.50% at 90 degrees (Table VI). RoomReader-AV Auto-AVSR VO/AO/AV 110.07/25.40/26.39%; Llama-AVSR VO 311.48%, AV penalty about 40.5 points (Table IX). RoomReader-AV: 6.49 h, 10,324 utterances, 118 participants (Table I). Author-reported WER, not an independent reproduction.
evaluation_mode: VO/AO/AV WER on six datasets; LombardGrid at 0 and 90 degrees; TCD-TIMIT lipspeakers, volunteers and matched volunteers at 0 and 30 degrees; RoomReader-AV on individual streams with Easy/Hard subsets; visual-only comparison across training scale.

evidence.statement: The authors evaluate three AVSR systems under six conditions to test whether sub-1% LRS3 WER reflects generalization or broadcast-domain fit, and release RoomReader-AV with a unified preparation pipeline.

The corpora are LRS2, LRS3, GRID, LombardGrid, TCD-TIMIT and RoomReader, covering broadcast, fixed grammar, Lombard speech, professional lipspeakers and volunteers reading, and spontaneous multi-party conversation.
Table I lists RoomReader as 6.49 h, 10,324 utterances and 118 speakers of spontaneous conversation; the prepared set is called RoomReader-AV.
The systems are Auto-AVSR, AV-HuBERT Large and Llama-AVSR, all with official released checkpoints and decoding settings, scored by VO/AO/AV WER.
LRS3 AV WER in Table II is 0.90% for Auto-AVSR, 1.47% for AV-HuBERT and 0.79% for Llama-AVSR; within broadcast data AV is close to AO.
GRID visual-only WER is 66.53% (Auto-AVSR), 83.80% (AV-HuBERT) and 116.39% (Llama-AVSR); for Auto-AVSR and Llama-AVSR, AV is worse than AO (differences -8.90 and -41.88).
On LombardGrid, Auto-AVSR improves from AO 14.02% to AV 11.73% (difference +2.29), the main out-of-domain case where AV fusion helps.
LombardGrid visual-only WER from 0 to 90 degrees: Auto-AVSR 64.88% to 92.50%, AV-HuBERT 87.06% to 102.53%, Llama-AVSR 111.01% to 180.62%; AV stays nearly flat, consistent with acoustic fallback.

On TCD-TIMIT, the 0 versus 30 degree difference is mostly under 3 points, while the visual-only gap between lipspeakers and matched volunteers is about 16.9 (Auto-AVSR), 21.6 (AV-HuBERT) and 44.1 points (Llama-AVSR).
On RoomReader-AV, Auto-AVSR gives VO 110.07%, AO 25.40%, AV 26.39%; Llama-AVSR gives VO 311.48% and AV 128.54%, about 40.5 points worse than AO 88.01%.
The paper diagnoses camera-and-microphone AVSR; it does not evaluate wearable or contactless silent speech sensors.
Sub-1% LRS3 AV WER should be read as a broadcast-domain result, not as readiness for open conversation or silent input.
Training scale alone does not fix the out-of-domain visual-only collapse: raising Auto-AVSR from 1.7k to 3.4k hours leaves RoomReader-AV VO at 110.07% against 113.20%.
The contribution is RoomReader-AV, the six-condition comparison and the shared preparation pipeline compatible with Auto-AVSR and AV-HuBERT; no new fusion architecture or sensor is proposed.

en.summary: Zero-shot cross-corpus AVSR testing (M12) and a video-call test set (M11) are standard after WildVSR; each condition mixes several shifts, without repeated runs.
en.sensor: RGB camera and microphone (audio-visual)
en.vocabulary: Dataset-dependent; continuous open vocabulary (GRID fixed grammar)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: 0.79% AV WER on LRS3 (Llama-AVSR); visual-only WER 110.07% on RoomReader-AV (Auto-AVSR)
en.limitations: Uses fixed public checkpoints without retraining; camera-based AVSR rather than wearable SSI; no real-time or on-device measurement; limited speaker-split and statistical detail.

title: Brain-to-Speech: Prosody Feature Engineering and Transformer-Based Reconstruction
venue: Artificial Intelligence, Data and Robotics (E. Curry et al., eds.)
expert_take_short: Same three parts and same Table 1 values as MiSTR (2025, same first two authors), not cited. Features (M06) and phase vocoder (M08) standard, unablated; no listener test (M12, behind).
expert_take_long: The chapter [@alradhi2026brain] changes the neural features (M06) and the waveform step (M08); both are standard and unablated. MiSTR [@alradhi2025mistr], by the same first two authors, lists the same three parts and reports the same 28 Table 1 values; the chapter's reference list does not include it. The evaluation (M12) is behind: no listener test, against 24 prior listener-test studies (Appendix) and naturalness of 18–29 of 100 on the same dataset [@arthur2024speech]. The claim of highly intelligible speech has no listener measure, Table 1 contradicts the uniformly lower MCD, and two baseline MCDs come from [@arthur2024speech]'s 80/20 split rather than the stated shared protocol.
expert_true_value: Puts multi-scale neural features, prosody conditioning and phase reconstruction into one candidate pipeline; its strongest immediate value is a set of hypotheses for controlled replication.
canon_before: The chapter compares regression, recurrent, convolutional, Seq2Seq and encoder-decoder mappings from intracranial activity to speech representations, with conventional phase recovery described as a limitation.
delta_from_canon: Proposes jointly incorporating multi-scale neural features and explicit prosody-related features before transformer spectrogram prediction, followed by iterative harmonic phase refinement.
position_in_field: Invasive overt-speech reconstruction and proposed prosody-aware neural synthesis; not demonstrated imagined-speech or non-invasive SSI.
practical_value: A research proposal to reproduce with explicit neural-only features, matched ablations and stronger held-out evaluation; current reporting is insufficient for selecting a deployment method.
axes_moved: Reported spectrogram correlation, STOI and harmonic-to-noise ratio; explicit attention to prosodic and phase representations.
axes_unresolved: Neural-only prosody feature extraction, independent train/test protocol, held-out participants and vocabulary, measured human intelligibility, causal inference and component-specific gains.
axes_regressed: Table 1 MCD is slightly worse than Seq2Seq: 3.92 versus 3.90, despite the surrounding claim of superiority across criteria.
technical_limits: Harvest is identified by the cited reference as a speech-signal F0 estimator, yet its direct neural application is not validated. Neural RMS is not automatically acoustic loudness. Duration derivation, Mel-to-linear conversion, harmonic phase updates and inference-time targets need specification. No numerical model-size or latency profile accompanies the deployment discussion.
evaluation_limits: Tenfold cross-validation is stated, but split unit, participant separation, temporal overlap, model-selection protocol, retained sample counts and per-baseline implementation details are not specified. No ablation isolates prosody embedding or the proposed vocoder. MOSA-Net is an automated predictor rather than human assessment; claims of statistical significance lack a reported test procedure.
deployment_limits: Implanted depth electrodes, offline overt-speech recordings and A100 GPU training. Real-time inference and cross-user robustness remain acknowledged challenges, with no numeric latency, online communication or patient speech-restoration trial.
scope_limits: Overt speech recorded during clinical sEEG monitoring in epilepsy participants. No demonstrated silent or imagined speech, spontaneous clinical communication, or validation of the separately mentioned French scalp-EEG corpus.
input_modality: Intracranial stereotactic EEG during overt speech, with synchronized acoustic targets
sensor_hardware: Multi-contact implanted depth electrodes described in STG, sensorimotor cortex and IFG; 1024 Hz neural sampling with synchronized 16 kHz microphone recordings. Exact channel counts and selection are not given in the chapter.
vocabulary_type: Overt speech reconstruction; evaluated word inventory and unseen-word split unspecified
vocabulary_size: Not specified for the evaluated intracranial dataset; the 270-word description belongs to a separate future-work scalp-EEG corpus.
metrics: Table 1 proposed model: PC 0.91, MCD 3.92, STOI 0.73, HNR 12.7 dB. Encoder-decoder: 0.87, 4.34, 0.64, 11.1 dB. Seq2Seq: 0.85, 3.90, 0.59, 10.7 dB; its MCD is lower than the proposed value. MOSA-Net results are plotted without a numeric table and are automated estimates, not listener MOS. No WER, human transcription, direct pitch/duration error or measured end-to-end latency is reported. Results are not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Author-reported tenfold cross-validation with spectrogram Pearson correlation, MCD, STOI, HNR, automated MOSA-Net scores and illustrative spectrograms.

evidence.statement: The evaluated data are described as simultaneous overt speech and intracranial depth-electrode recordings from ten Dutch-speaking epilepsy participants; 1024 Hz neural and 16 kHz audio sampling are reported.

The proposed pipeline combines db4 wavelet features, phase-amplitude coupling, a prosody embedding, autoencoder compression, transformer spectrogram mapping and iterative harmonic phase reconstruction.

Section 3.1.3 says F0 is estimated using Harvest directly from iEEG and describes neural RMS as loudness. Reference 36 identifies Harvest as an estimator from speech signals. Reviewer assessment: the neural-to-acoustic prosody mapping and exact feature source require clarification; this alone does not prove leakage.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 3.1.3 and Reference 36; PDF pp. 8 and 24

evidence.statement: Training uses Adam at 0.001 and a stated tenfold cross-validation protocol. The chapter does not specify split units, sample counts, architecture dimensions or a held-out-participant procedure.
Table 1 reports proposed PC 0.91, MCD 3.92, STOI 0.73 and HNR 12.7 dB; encoder-decoder values are 0.87, 4.34, 0.64 and 11.1 dB.
Table 1 lists Seq2Seq MCD 3.90, lower than proposed 3.92, contrary to the nearby text claiming lower MCD than Seq2Seq and superiority across all criteria.

Perceptual assessment is performed by MOSA-Net, an automated model; no human listening test is reported. Figure 4 uses standard-deviation error bars, whereas Section 5.2 describes medians and interquartile ranges.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 4.3.5 and 5.2; Figure 4; PDF pp. 15 and 18-19

evidence.statement: The chapter attributes gains to prosody and phase reconstruction but supplies no component ablation or direct F0/duration error results to isolate those effects.
Real-time inference, computational complexity and cross-subject variability are acknowledged as unresolved; no numeric end-to-end latency accompanies the discussion.
A 96-channel scalp-EEG corpus from 16 French-speaking healthy participants, with four sessions of 270 spoken words, appears in future directions. It is not the dataset used for Table 1.

en.summary: Same three parts and same Table 1 values as MiSTR (2025, same first two authors), not cited. Features (M06) and phase vocoder (M08) standard, unablated; no listener test (M12, behind).
en.sensor: Implanted sEEG depth electrodes
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: PC 0.91, MCD 3.92, STOI 0.73, HNR 12.7 dB, tenfold cross-validation
en.limitations: Split unit and participant separation unspecified; neural prosody features not validated; no human intelligibility, WER or latency measurement.

title: Brain2Speech-Net: Fast and Intelligible Brain-to-Speech Synthesis Without Text Decoding
expert_take_short: Text-free synthesis is shown, but its real time is throughput, not causal synthesis, unseen-sentence WER is 2.3 times the cascade, and intelligibility rests on ratings and ASR.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the processing (a phoneme bottleneck with deep-HMM alignment into a TTS latent space) and the output (a pretrained VITS decoder). The output interface is standard: its effect rests on one participant and one run. The authors' real time is throughput (RTF 0.532); on causality the processing is behind the field: the alignment uses evidence up to the end of the utterance, whereas causal intracortical synthesis already plays audio within 10 ms. On unseen sentences WER is 0.472 against 0.206 for the 5-gram plus LLM cascade, and seen-data parity is a training-fit result. Intelligibility rests on a 1–5 rating and Whisper WER rather than listener transcription, which 29 text-verified synthesis studies use.
expert_true_value: Shows how phoneme-informed neural features can support direct speech synthesis with limited intracortical training data, while exposing the accuracy cost of removing text-language-model decoding.
canon_before: Cascaded neural-to-text-to-speech systems exploit language models for intelligibility, while direct acoustic-unit synthesis is difficult with limited intracortical data; the paper compares both routes.
delta_from_canon: Uses phoneme posterior representations as an uncertainty-preserving bridge to a TTS latent space; text and synthetic targets supervise training, but text decoding is omitted during synthesis inference.
position_in_field: Invasive attempted-speech BCI synthesis, adjacent to non-invasive articulatory SSI and distinct from imagined speech.
practical_value: A research baseline for investigating lower-latency synthesis without discrete text decoding; current open-set errors remain substantial.
axes_moved: Neural-to-speech representation alignment, removal of explicit inference-time text decoding, and a measured accuracy-throughput tradeoff.
axes_unresolved: Causal streaming, first-audio latency, new-user transfer, spontaneous communication, natural voice identity and prosody, and independent replication.
axes_regressed: Open-set speech WER is higher than the cascaded baselines; the approach retains invasive recording and single-participant calibration.
technical_limits: The deep-HMM forward-backward alignment uses observations up to the end of the utterance and a predicted segment count, so synthesis is not causal; the reported real-time factor is per-utterance throughput, not first-audio latency. Synthetic targets and a pretrained single-speaker VITS decoder do not recover the user's own voice.
evaluation_limits: Table 2 uses 880 training sentences and is a training-fit diagnostic, not a held-out test. Unseen-sentence results come from the official test split of the same participant; session disjointness and prompt overlap are not stated. References and targets are VITS speech. Listeners gave a 1-5 rating only; no listener transcription; whether listeners saw the prompt is not stated. The released Phase 1 configuration selects the encoder checkpoint on the official test split by default, and the released Phase 2 configuration uses lambda_CTC 0.3 where the paper states 0.1.
deployment_limits: Offline evaluation of one implanted participant; RTF alone does not establish closed-loop conversational latency. Hardware for timing, first-audio delay, and everyday reliability are not specified.
scope_limits: Prompted attempted speech from one participant with ALS, synthetic single-speaker audio targets; not spontaneous inner speech, natural-voice restoration, or non-invasive sensing.
input_modality: Intracortical neural recordings; not scalp EEG
sensor_hardware: Four implanted microelectrode arrays; threshold-crossing and spike-band-power features, with 256 motor-cortex feature channels selected for decoding.
vocabulary_type: Closed training-utterance sample and open unseen-utterance evaluation
vocabulary_size: Large-vocabulary utterances; distinct target vocabulary size not specified. The comparison 5-gram language model has 125,000 words, not a verified system vocabulary count.
metrics: Table 1 (unseen sentences): Brain2Speech-Net Whisper WER 0.472, PER 0.373, MCD 5.522 dB, RTF 0.532; 5-gram cascade WER 0.229 (RTF 1.846); 5-gram plus LLM cascade 0.206 (RTF 1.962); direct speech-unit baseline 1.054 (RTF 0.060); VITS reference 0.025. Table 2 (seen training sentences): 0.068 WER. Fig. 2: MOS on a 1-5 intelligibility rating 3.34 +/- 0.11 (95% CI) against 3.85 and 3.90 for the cascades and 1.57 for the speech-unit baseline.
evaluation_mode: Offline: official unseen-sentence test split versus a seen training-set sample; Whisper WER, phoneme-recognizer PER, DTW-aligned MCD, RTF, and a 20-listener 1-5 intelligibility rating.

evidence.statement: One participant with ALS supplies prompted attempted-speech intracortical recordings. Table I lists 8,800 training and 880 test sentences; audio references are synthesized from transcripts with VITS.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III and V-A; Table I; PDF pp. 2-5

evidence.statement: The model uses CTC-supervised phoneme representations and a differentiable HMM to predict TTS contextual phoneme latents; it removes explicit text decoding at inference, not text-derived supervision during training.
evidence.section_or_location: Section IV and Figure 2; PDF pp. 3-4

evidence.statement: The closed-set evaluation uniformly samples 880 utterances from the training set. Reviewer assessment: its 6.8% WER is not an independent held-out generalization result.
evidence.section_or_location: Section V-A; Table II; PDF pp. 4-5

evidence.statement: Open-set speech WER is 47.2% for Brain2Speech-Net, 22.9% for the 5-gram cascade, 20.6% for the LLM-reranked cascade, and 105.4% for the direct-unit baseline.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II, Open WER column; PDF p. 5

evidence.statement: Closed/open RTF is 0.504/0.532 for Brain2Speech-Net. The 5-gram cascade has 1.664/1.846. Reviewer assessment: RTF measures generation throughput and does not establish streaming first-output latency.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II; Section VI-B; PDF pp. 5-6

evidence.statement: HMM forward-backward inference includes future observations until sequence termination; no prospective streaming communication evaluation is reported. This limits interpretation of the real-time claim.
evidence.section_or_location: Section IV-C; Sections V-VII; PDF pp. 4-6

evidence.statement: Twenty English-speaking listeners rated 20 unseen-sentence samples per system on a 1-5 intelligibility scale. Brain2Speech-Net MOS is 3.34 +/- 0.11, with error bars labeled 95% confidence intervals.

The authors acknowledge that synthetic-reference metrics do not measure fidelity to natural recorded speech, the user's voice identity, or paralinguistic content, and that unseen-utterance performance deteriorates.

en.summary: Text-free synthesis is shown, but its real time is throughput, not causal synthesis, unseen-sentence WER is 2.3 times the cascade, and intelligibility rests on ratings and ASR.
en.sensor: Intracortical microelectrode arrays (four recorded); 256 area-6v motor-cortex features (threshold crossings and spike-band power)
en.task: Speech synthesis from attempted speech without text decoding (offline)
en.vocabulary: Large-vocabulary prompted sentences; no lexicon or language model in the proposed model (cascade baselines use a 125k-word 5-gram LM)
en.speaker: One participant with ALS (Willett et al. 2023 dataset)
en.session: Recording sessions of the public dataset; session count not stated in the paper
en.key_result: Unseen-sentence Whisper WER 0.472 and PER 0.373 at RTF 0.532, against 0.206-0.229 WER at RTF above 1.8 for text cascades and 1.054 WER for a direct speech-unit baseline; MOS 3.34 on a 1-5 intelligibility rating; seen training sentences 0.068 WER.
en.limitations: Alignment uses future observations up to the end of the utterance, so synthesis is not causal; RTF without hardware or first-audio latency; intelligibility by rating and ASR, not listener transcription; one participant, one run, no seeds; targets, decoder and MCD reference all come from the same VITS model; released Phase 1 configuration selects on the official test split by default.

title: Comparison of sEMG Encoding Accuracy Across Speech Modes Using Articulatory and Phoneme Features
expert_take_short: Applies an ECoG articulatory-versus-phoneme encoding comparison (Chartier 2018) to sEMG in three speech modes; the gain is small, mode contrasts are confounded, and no decoder is tested.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the predictor space of a forward sEMG encoding model (M06, SPARC articulatory features against phoneme one-hots) and how silent EMG gets its features (M02, features from paired aloud audio, silent EMG warped to the aloud EMG by DTW); both are standard. The same articulatory-versus-phoneme comparison was made on ECoG with session-held-out tests and the same outcome (Chartier et al. 2018), so the contribution is the signal and the speech modes. The only tabulated effect is small (Gaddy single subject: mean r 0.455 against 0.443 voiced, 0.364 against 0.346 mimed), and the 24-participant results are plotted only. Mode contrasts mix 14 aloud features with 12 silent ones and depend on a DTW warp to the aloud trial that the null leaves in place. No decoder is trained, so the claim about better SSI intermediates is untested; folds, seeds and sessions are unstated.
expert_true_value: A comparatively broad within-subject physiological analysis that motivates articulatory intermediate targets without pretending to have demonstrated an end-to-end silent speech decoder.
canon_before: Forward encoding models of speech mostly use acoustic predictors (envelope, spectrogram). Articulatory kinematics inferred from audio had already been compared with phoneme and acoustic (formant) encoding models on ECoG, with the articulatory model better on sentences from separate sessions (Chartier et al., 2018). In the decoding direction, audio-inverted articulatory features had been predicted from 8-electrode surface EMG of one speaker (Lee et al., 2025).
delta_from_canon: Applies the articulatory-versus-phoneme encoding comparison to surface EMG envelopes in aloud, mimed and subvocal speech, with silent EMG warped by DTW to the paired aloud trial and all predictors derived from aloud audio; adds variance partitioning and per-channel weight maps.
position_in_field: Standard on both changed components: the predictor comparison (M06) follows the earlier ECoG result, and aloud-derived targets for silent EMG via DTW (M02) follow established target transfer. Non-invasive articulatory SSI representation research using forward encoding, not a speech decoder.
practical_value: Helps choose candidate intermediate training targets and formulate electrode-placement hypotheses for subsequent sEMG decoding experiments.
axes_moved: Evidence for intermediate representation choice, comparison of muscle-signal predictability across speech modes, and descriptive electrode-to-articulator relationships.
axes_unresolved: Whether the encoding advantage improves inverse speech decoding, unaligned silent inference, unseen-user and cross-mode transfer, and prospective electrode selection.
axes_regressed: No matched decoding or deployment regression established; paired voiced-reference alignment is an analysis requirement rather than a demonstrated deployable advantage.
technical_limits: SPARC kinematics are inferred from voiced audio rather than measured during silent production. Aloud uses 14 features including pitch/loudness, silent modes use 12. DTW may inflate absolute correlations. Squared Pearson correlation is not automatically calibrated predictive R-squared; correlated predictors and normalized absolute weights limit causal anatomical interpretation.
evaluation_limits: All models are evaluated within subjects using sentence-level folds, not held-out users or cross-mode transfer. Silent evaluation depends on paired voiced reference and response-derived DTW alignment. Fold count and exact repeat grouping are not detailed. Primary numeric results are plotted rather than tabulated. The Gaddy replication has one participant and incompletely specified uncertainty aggregation.
deployment_limits: Offline forward encoding uses features derived from paired aloud audio and silently produced EMG warped to the paired aloud envelope. No autonomous silent decoder, latency measurement, wearable implementation, walking test, or patient communication study is provided.
scope_limits: Speech-typical participants and prompted sentences. Subvocal means attempted speech with an occluded vocal tract and no phonation; it should not be treated as unconstrained imagined speech. No clinical communication or end-to-end silent recognition study.
task: Forward encoding of sEMG from speech representations
input_modality: Surface electromyography with paired aloud audio used to derive predictors and timing references
sensor_hardware: Eight surface EMG channels on lower face and neck; band-pass 10-450 Hz and 60 Hz harmonic notches, Hilbert envelopes at 2 kHz downsampled to 50 Hz. Aloud audio is processed at 16 kHz.
output_type: Predicted sEMG envelopes and representation/electrode analyses; no decoded text or speech audio.
vocabulary_type: Prompted sentence encoding; no evaluated recognition vocabulary
vocabulary_size: 50 distinct sentence prompts per participant; phoneme representation has 39 ARPAbet phonemes plus silence, not a 40-word vocabulary.
metrics: Primary 24-participant results report Pearson r by channel/mode in Figure 2, averaged across folds using Fisher z and summarized with SEM across subjects; precise per-channel means are not tabulated. SPARC outperforms phoneme features on most channels, and subvocal prediction is above the permutation threshold. Separate single-participant Gaddy results: voiced r 0.443 ± 0.017 (phoneme) versus 0.455 ± 0.021 (SPARC); mimed 0.346 ± 0.029 versus 0.364 ± 0.032, with gains on 7/8 electrodes in each mode. No WER, decoding accuracy or synthesis-quality result is reported.
evaluation_mode: Within-subject sentence-level cross-validation of forward feature-to-EMG envelope regression, nested regularization selection, Pearson correlation, permutation nulls, paired FDR-controlled comparisons, variance partitioning and normalized weight maps.

evidence.statement: Twenty-four speech-typical participants each produced 50 TIMIT sentences three times per mode. Aloud, mimed and subvocal modes are defined separately; subvocal involves an occluded vocal tract with no phonation. Eight facial/neck EMG channels were recorded.
The analysis compares forward prediction of EMG envelopes from SPARC and phoneme features; it explicitly does not demonstrate end-to-end decoding gains.
evidence.section_or_location: Introduction and Conclusion; PDF pp. 1 and 4

evidence.statement: Features for every mode are extracted from paired aloud audio: 14 SPARC features for aloud, 12 kinematic features for silent modes, and 40 phoneme/silence one-hot indices at 50 Hz.

Silent envelopes are warped to paired aloud EMG with FastDTW. Both predictors use the same trial-specific path. Authors acknowledge possible inflation of absolute correlations; reviewer assessment: results remain conditional on paired-reference alignment.
evidence.section_or_location: Section II-A and Section III-B; PDF pp. 2 and 4

evidence.statement: Evaluation is within subjects using sentence-level outer folds and training-only inner regularization selection; lags span -300 to +300 ms. Pearson correlations are averaged with Fisher z, and comparisons use FDR-controlled Wilcoxon tests.

Figure 2 reports higher SPARC prediction correlation than phoneme features on most channels across modes; subvocal performance remains above the permutation threshold, and upper-lip channel 6 is strongest. Exact primary per-channel means are not tabulated.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III-A and Figure 2; PDF p. 3

evidence.statement: On the separate single-participant Gaddy dataset, voiced correlation increases from 0.443 ± 0.017 to 0.455 ± 0.021, and mimed correlation from 0.346 ± 0.029 to 0.364 ± 0.032. SPARC improves on 7 of 8 electrodes in each mode.

Variance partitioning uses squared correlations from articulatory, phoneme and combined models. Shared contribution dominates, and unique articulatory contribution exceeds unique phoneme contribution; this does not imply absence of shared phonemic information.
evidence.section_or_location: Figure 3; Equations 3-5 and accompanying text; PDF pp. 3-4

evidence.statement: Weight maps sum absolute coefficients over lags, average across participants and normalize within each channel. Anatomical relationships are descriptive; a formal quantitative consistency test is deferred.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III-B and Figure 4; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Downstream decoding evaluation is future work. All reported comparisons are within-subject, and above-chance forward envelope prediction does not establish word recognition or new-user communication performance.
evidence.section_or_location: Section II-C and Conclusion; PDF pp. 3-4

en.summary: Applies an ECoG articulatory-versus-phoneme encoding comparison (Chartier 2018) to sEMG in three speech modes; the gain is small, mode contrasts are confounded, and no decoder is tested.
en.sensor: 8-channel lower-face/neck surface EMG
en.task: Forward encoding of sEMG from speech features
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Gaddy replication voiced r 0.455 (SPARC) vs 0.443 (phoneme); main results plotted, not tabulated
en.limitations: Within-subject only; articulatory features inferred from paired voiced audio; DTW may inflate correlations; no actual decoding or synthesis gains tested.

title: Cross-Modal Masking for Robust Silent Speech Synthesis Using sEMG and Lipreading
review_confidence: High confidence based on extensive full text analysis
expert_take_short: Speech synthesis from fused sEMG and lip video is new to the ledger (M05, ahead); span masking (M03) adds a non-significant clean gain; seen speakers only (M12, behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@delblanco2026xmask] changes the sensors (M05), synthesizing speech from fused surface EMG and lip video, and the training (M03), masking spans of each stream. The sensor pairing is ahead: both earlier fused sEMG-video decoders in the ledger classify words or sentences (Appendix), and here the pair cuts silent-speech WER from 54.5% (best lip-only model) to 40.5% for six laryngeal speakers (Table III). The masking is standard: span masking added to a video dropout of up to 75% (§IV-D), never compared with whole-stream dropout of both streams, with a clean gain of 3.5 points the authors call not statistically significant (§V-B). The strongest confound is capacity: with sEMG zeroed at test, the unmasked multimodal model still reaches 46.9% WER, so 7.6 of its 10.5-point lead over lip-only needs no sEMG (inference). The evaluation (M12) is behind the best comparable work: test speakers are all seen in training (Table I), with no listener test or repeated runs, and for three laryngectomized speakers the gain is not significant (§V-E).
expert_true_value: Speech synthesis from fused sEMG and lip video is new to the ledger: fusion lowers silent-speech WER from 54.5% (best lip-only) to 40.5% for six laryngeal speakers seen in training. Much of that lead remains with sEMG zeroed at test (46.9%), the span-masking gain on clean input is not significant, and for laryngectomized speakers fusion does not significantly beat lip-only.
canon_before: Earlier fused sEMG-video decoders classify digits or a closed set of sentences; silent-speech synthesis uses sEMG or lip video alone; audio-visual models use modality dropout, withholding a whole stream during training.
delta_from_canon: Synthesizes speech from fused 8-channel sEMG and lip video, trained with time-span masking of each stream added to a video dropout of up to 75%; robustness is tested with one stream removed and with reduced video frame rate, not against whole-stream dropout of both streams.
position_in_field: Multimodal silent-speech synthesis between sEMG-to-speech and lip-to-speech work: ahead on sensor pairing (M05), standard on training (M03), behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12, seen speakers only).
practical_value: Shows that lip video carries most of the intelligibility and that adding sEMG helps seen laryngeal speakers; it does not yet show a benefit for laryngectomized users or unseen speakers.
axes_moved: Silent-speech WER with fused sEMG and lip video below either single stream on seen laryngeal speakers; WER with lips removed improved by masking (92.5% to 73.7%); phone-level gains for vowels and affricates.
axes_unresolved: Generalization to unseen speakers beyond the dataset, full speaker-independent operation, efficacy for other languages remain unexplored.
axes_regressed: Adaptation to laryngectomized speakers shows performance challenges; unimodal masking degrades performance especially for sEMG.
technical_limits: The fused model has 101.7M parameters against 55.6M for lip-only, with no size-matched control; masking is not compared with whole-stream dropout of both streams; offline inference only; a surrogate voice is needed for laryngectomized speakers.
evaluation_limits: Six laryngeal speakers, all seen in training (splits are text-disjoint only); Whisper WER, phone accuracy and SSIM without a listener test; no repeated training runs, and bootstrap intervals cover test sampling only; Table IV cohort not stated; bitrate values without units; three laryngectomized speakers adapted by fine-tuning.
deployment_limits: Current study does not evaluate real-time deployment, mobile suitability, or wearable system practicalities; robustness to speaker variability especially post-laryngectomy remains a challenge.
scope_limits: Limited to Spanish language sentence data; limited number of laryngectomized subjects; no spontaneous speech or large vocabulary continuous speech tested.
input_modality: multimodal (sEMG and video lipreading)
sensor_hardware: Surface electromyography 8 bipolar sensors placed on face and neck; video from RGB camera of speaker's lips
vocabulary_type: Phoneme-level labels, sentence-level utterances with limited vocabulary size not quantified extensively
vocabulary_size: Limited to about 30 phoneme classes plus silence token; test sentences phonemically balanced
metrics: Phone Accuracy and Word Error Rate (WER) from Whisper v3, Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) for spectrogram quality; exact metrics provided with confidence intervals.
evaluation_mode: Quantitative evaluation with monomodal baselines and multimodal models under controlled experimental conditions including masking ablations and bitrate/video degradation simulations.

evidence.statement: Main contributions: 1) Demonstrate sEMG and lipreading are complementary, fusion improves WER and phone accuracy; 2) critical role of temporal adaptive masking for robustness and generalization; 3) phone-level multimodal contributions with benefits for vowels and affricates.

Proposes masked multimodal speech synthesis framework integrating sEMG and lipreading with modality masking during training to improve robustness and performance under modality degradation and sensor failure conditions in continuous speech synthesis.

Evaluation on multi-speaker Spanish ReSSInt dataset including audible and silent speech, with 8-channel sEMG and lip video, controlled studio conditions, with data splits ensuring text independence. Includes laryngeal and laryngectomized subjects for silent speech synthesis evaluation.

Performance reported via Word Error Rate (WER), Phone Accuracy, Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) for spectral reconstruction; WER improvements up to 14 absolute points over strongest unimodal baseline.
Adaptation to laryngectomized speakers remains an open challenge due to articulatory variability and lack of paired audible speech; multimodal fusion less beneficial for such speakers.

Robust multimodal fusion with masking promotes resilience to sensor noise, missing or degraded modality data, advancing towards real-world deployments, but real-time and mobile suitability not demonstrated yet.

en.summary: Speech synthesis from fused sEMG and lip video is new to the ledger (M05, ahead); span masking (M03) adds a non-significant clean gain; seen speakers only (M12, behind).
en.sensor: 8 bipolar face/neck sEMG sensors plus RGB lip video
en.task: Speech synthesis from sEMG and video
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: No held-out-speaker test, listener test or repeated runs; masking not compared with whole-stream dropout of both streams; bitrate units unstated.

title: CS-ETS: Chaos-Inspired Samba-Based EMG-To-Speech Synthesis with Nonlinear Chaotic Losses
expert_take_short: A smaller EMG-to-speech model with a modest reported WER gain; large acoustic-metric gains are confounded by reference-based alignment applied asymmetrically.
expert_take_long: CS-ETS is a potentially useful compact EMG-to-speech model, but its strongest numerical claims require careful separation. The reported model size falls from 54.10M to 32.03M parameters, while WER improves only from 42.20% to 41.26%, a 0.94-percentage-point change without reported uncertainty. Within the smaller architecture, adding both temporal losses reduces WER from 50.37% to 41.26%, which is a more informative ablation than the broad chaos-theory framing. The headline acoustic improvements are less secure: Table 1 applies post-vocoder alignment to the proposed method but not to the baselines. Table 3 shows that alignment alone moves STOI from 0.15 to 0.61 and LSD from 1.92 to 1.10 while WER stays 50.37%. This is reference-dependent evaluation processing, not an independent recognition gain or a deployable correction of speech timing. The SI-SDR change from -41.96 to -33.41 dB is an 8.55 dB difference; interpreting the ratio of negative dB values as a 1.25-fold noise-reduction benefit is inappropriate. Human MOS is reported as 4.21 versus 3.98 from ten listeners, distinct from the automated NISQA values, but sampling and uncertainty are not detailed. Results come from one English speaker and one corpus, and the paper does not restate exact train/test counts.
