The contribution should therefore be treated as a promising compression and regularization study awaiting a matched-alignment evaluation, rather than proof that chaotic physics delivers large general speech-quality improvements.
expert_true_value: The compact model and paired-loss ablation warrant reproduction; the alignment ablation also demonstrates how evaluation processing can dominate apparent acoustic improvements.
canon_before: Gaddy-style EMG-to-speech systems use aligned vocalized targets, mel reconstruction and phoneme supervision. The paper compares retrained 2020/2021 models and reports another published streaming baseline.
delta_from_canon: Adds two nonlinear temporal regularizers to a compact hybrid state-space/attention encoder and introduces reference-dependent waveform alignment for evaluation.
position_in_field: Directly relevant EMG-based articulatory SSI synthesis and model-efficiency research, with substantial evaluation qualifications.
practical_value: A compact architecture worth reproducing on a fully specified benchmark with identical evaluation processing across methods.
axes_moved: Model compression and a loss-ablation study on EMG-to-speech; explicit attention to waveform alignment during objective evaluation.
axes_unresolved: Matched alignment for all models, exact held-out protocol, significance across seeds/listeners, cross-speaker transfer, end-to-end real-time operation and field noise.
axes_regressed: Without the added losses, the smaller architecture has worse WER than the comparison baseline. The full model only modestly improves WER and does not improve every quality metric.
technical_limits: Target-dependent evaluation alignment, unspecified timing boundaries and train/test details, weak absolute acoustic metrics, and an unverified chaos-mechanism explanation.
evaluation_limits: One speaker and one dataset, insufficient split details, no reported confidence intervals or repeated seeds. Main acoustic metrics compare aligned proposed output with unaligned baselines. Ten-listener MOS lacks sample-count and uncertainty details. Table 3 single-loss labels conflict with explanatory prose.
deployment_limits: Training and timing use a workstation setting; no prospective wearable interaction, noisy-environment, walking or clinical-user study. Target-audio-dependent post-vocoder alignment is unavailable during ordinary deployment.
scope_limits: Single-speaker offline EMG-to-speech experiments; waveform alignment uses target audio and cannot be assumed available at inference.
input_modality: emg
sensor_hardware: Eight-channel facial EMG from an existing corpus; workstation training on two RTX 4090 GPUs. No new wearable sensing system.
vocabulary_type: open-vocabulary EMG corpus
vocabulary_size: Not specified in this paper.
metrics: Tables 1-3: model parameters 54.10M to 32.03M; WER 42.20% to 41.26%; FLOPs 2.40G to 2.08G; batch inference 5.97 to 5.55 ms for 200 time steps; RTF 0.0057 for both. Alignment-only ablation: STOI 0.15 to 0.61 and LSD 1.92 to 1.10 with WER unchanged at 50.37%. Human MOS: 4.21 versus 3.98 with ten listeners; no confidence intervals. All results author-reported, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Author-retrained baselines, loss/channel/layer ablations, WER, aligned waveform metrics and computational counts; ten-person listening panel.

evidence.statement: The experiments use an eight-channel EMG input and describe a 19-hour open-vocabulary corpus from one English speaker across silent and vocalized speech. Exact train/test counts are not restated.
Table 1 reports 32.03M parameters and 41.26% WER for CS-ETS versus 54.10M and 42.20% for the retrained 2021 baseline. Reviewer calculation: the WER difference is 0.94 percentage points.

Table 1 marks post-vocoder alignment as present only for CS-ETS and absent for the baselines. Reviewer assessment: acoustic-metric comparisons combine model changes with unequal evaluation processing.
In Table 3, adding alignment without either new loss changes LSD from 1.92 to 1.10 and STOI from 0.15 to 0.61, while WER remains 50.37%; adding both losses yields 41.26% WER.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3 rows P1, P2 and P5; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Post-vocoder alignment computes DTW between generated and target audio and reconstructs the aligned signal. Reviewer assessment: reference-dependent alignment is evaluation processing, not an available correction for ordinary unseen-input deployment.

Table 2 reports 2.08G versus 2.40G FLOPs, 5.55 versus 5.97 ms batch inference, and identical RTF 0.0057. Section 3.3 defines the timing input as 200 time steps; full pipeline timing boundaries are not established.

A panel of ten people gives human MOS 4.21 for CS-ETS versus 3.98 for the baseline. This is distinct from Table 1 automated NISQA-MOS 3.31 versus 3.30; listening sample counts and confidence intervals are not reported.
Table 3 assigns 49.45% WER to the configuration without MSDFA and 48.65% to the configuration without LER, while its explanatory prose associates the individual losses in the reverse way.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 4.3(a), Table 3 and following paragraph; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: SI-SDR is reported as -41.96 versus -33.41 dB. Reviewer calculation: the difference is 8.55 dB; dividing those negative dB numbers does not establish a 1.25-fold physical noise-reduction factor.
evidence.section_or_location: Introduction; Section 4.1; Table 1; PDF pp. 1 and 3

en.summary: Smaller chaos-inspired Samba-based EMG-to-speech model with nonlinear losses; WER improves modestly from 42.20% to 41.26% while parameters drop from 54.10M to 32.03M.
en.sensor: Existing 8-channel facial EMG corpus
en.vocabulary: Open-vocabulary EMG corpus; size not specified
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 41.26% WER vs 42.20% baseline; 32.03M parameters
en.limitations: Single speaker and dataset; large acoustic-metric gains confounded by target-audio alignment applied only to the proposed output; insufficient split details and no confidence intervals.

title: Do EEG Foundation Models Transfer to Speech? A Benchmark on Overt and Imagined Speech Decoding
expert_take_short: Benchmark (M03) confirms earlier reports that LaBraM gains nothing on speech EEG; decoders (M06) sit far below same-corpus results; test-subject early stopping (M12).
expert_take_long: The paper [@khanday2026eegfm] fine-tunes the public LaBraM-Base and EEGMamba checkpoints against CNN baselines on UGR-MINDVOICE and BCIC2020-T3 (M03, M06). M03 is standard: earlier work found LaBraM below EEGNet on silent-speech EEG [@zhou2025lblm] and, on BCIC2020-T3, near 25% balanced accuracy within subject with a linear head and chance across subjects [@wang2025neurottt], so the claim of a first benchmark does not hold. The conclusion that general-purpose EEG pretraining does not transfer rests on two checkpoints; CBraMod reached 0.3976 balanced accuracy with a linear head on the competition's per-subject splits [@wang2025neurottt]. M06 is behind the best comparable work: the best within-subject score, 30.2%, is below deep metric learning's 48.10% on the same corpus [@lee2021dml] and the competition winner's 82.6% [@jeong2022bcicomp]. M12 uses the most frequent leave-one-subject-out design but stops training on the test subject (Sec. 2.4).
expert_true_value: A second-corpus confirmation, with overt and covert trials, that public LaBraM and EEGMamba checkpoints give no gain over CNN baselines on closed-set speech EEG; the same pattern for LaBraM had been reported on silent-speech EEG (2025-04) and on BCIC2020-III (2025-09).
canon_before: Before this paper, LaBraM-Base had been fine-tuned on 24-word silent-speech EEG, where it scored 20.6% word-level accuracy against 30.5% for EEGNet (2025-04), and on BCIC2020-III, where it reached 0.2529 balanced accuracy within subject with a linear head and chance across subjects while CBraMod reached 0.3976 (2025-09). Same-corpus within-subject results on BCIC2020-T3 reached 82.6% in the 2020 competition and 48.10% with deep metric learning (2021).
delta_from_canon: Adds EEGMamba and the UGR-MINDVOICE overt/covert corpus, and separates speech-mode, semantic-category and word-identity tasks under one preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol; it does not test CBraMod or a speech-pretrained model.
position_in_field: Standard on training (M03): the usual general-checkpoint fine-tuning, with a result that confirms earlier reports. Behind on decoding (M06): best within-subject BCIC2020-T3 score 30.2% against far higher same-corpus results. Standard leave-one-subject-out evaluation (M12), weakened by early stopping on the test subject.
practical_value: Useful as a caution that public general EEG checkpoints do not by themselves improve closed-set speech EEG decoding; the conclusion should not be extended to other checkpoints or to better-tuned recipes.
axes_moved: foundation-model comparison extended to overt and covert Spanish word production (UGR-MINDVOICE)
axes_unresolved: other general checkpoints (CBraMod) and speech-specific pretraining under one protocol; baselines that reproduce published same-corpus accuracies; selection data separate from test subjects; seed repetition
technical_limits: Low lexical signal, small cohorts and fixed vocabulary; EEGConformer collapses to chance on all UGR tasks under this training configuration. No random-initialization ablation of the same foundation architectures establishes the causal benefit or harm of pretraining.
evaluation_limits: Section 2.4 explicitly uses the held-out test subject for early stopping and restores the best checkpoint; although gradients do not use that subject, model selection is test-informed. BCIC results use the official validation split, not a hidden test set. Multiple training seeds are left to future work. Table 1 lists 3/6/30 classes whereas Table 2 and the word-analysis text use 60 word classes.
deployment_limits: Only offline classification is reported. No online communication interface, assistive-user trial, walking test, latency, power consumption, or mobile execution measurement is provided.
scope_limits: Two EEG datasets, two foundation-model families, and finite-label offline tasks. Spanish lexical tasks combine overt and covert trials; they do not establish a silent-only continuous decoder. No free-form thought reading, audio reconstruction, or open-vocabulary communication is tested.
input_modality: eeg
sensor_hardware: Existing 64-channel scalp EEG recordings. UGR-MINDVOICE uses a 10–20 layout, 1000 Hz acquisition and FCz reference, retaining 62 scalp channels after preprocessing; both datasets are resampled to 200 Hz. No new hardware.
vocabulary_type: closed-set word/phrase and category labels; no open vocabulary
vocabulary_size: UGR results: 60 word classes, six semantic categories, and three speech modes; BCIC: five words/phrases. Table 1 inconsistently lists 30 for the UGR word-class count.
metrics: UGR-MINDVOICE Table 2: speech-mode accuracy EEGNet 61.3% (95% CI 56.5–66.1), LaBraM 57.3% (53.0–61.7), EEGMamba 56.6% (51.8–61.3), versus 33.3% chance; EEGNet semantic-category accuracy 19.9% versus 16.7% chance; 60-word accuracy across models 1.7–2.9% versus 1.7% chance. BCIC2020-T3 Table 3, mean ± SD across 15 participants: within-subject balanced accuracy EEGNet 26.7 ± 3.3%, EEGConformer 30.2 ± 4.4%, LaBraM 27.7 ± 2.7%, EEGMamba 25.7 ± 2.5%; cross-subject range 18.9–20.2%, all p > 0.18 against 20% chance. These are reported results, not independently reproduced measurements.
evaluation_mode: Offline UGR-MINDVOICE leave-one-subject-out evaluation over 14 participants, with test-subject-informed early stopping; semantic and word tasks pool overt and covert examples. BCIC2020-T3 reports within-subject and leave-one-subject-out results over 15 participants. Accuracy or balanced accuracy, weighted F1, Cohen kappa, and Wilcoxon tests are reported.

evidence.statement: UGR-MINDVOICE starts with 15 participants and 22 sessions; excluding subject 15 for ICA errors leaves 14 evaluated participants. BCIC2020-T3 contains 15 healthy participants and five imagined words/phrases.

Table 2 reports speech-mode accuracy of 61.3% for EEGNet, 57.3% for LaBraM, and 56.6% for EEGMamba against 33.3% chance. This task distinguishes overt, covert, and rest states rather than individual words.
The UGR-MINDVOICE 60-word task yields 1.7–2.9% accuracy across the six models against 1.7% chance. EEGNet reaches 2.8%, LaBraM 1.9%, and EEGMamba 2.9%.

BCIC2020-T3 within-subject balanced accuracy is 26.7 ± 3.3% for EEGNet, 30.2 ± 4.4% for EEGConformer, 27.7 ± 2.7% for LaBraM, and 25.7 ± 2.5% for EEGMamba; these are means and standard deviations over 15 participants for five classes.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3, Within-subject columns and caption; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: BCIC2020-T3 cross-subject balanced accuracy ranges from 18.9% to 20.2%; no model significantly exceeds 20% chance, with all reported one-sided Wilcoxon p-values greater than 0.18.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3 and Section 3.1 continuation; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Section 2.4 says the held-out UGR test subject determines early stopping and that the best checkpoint is restored. Reviewer assessment: excluding this subject from gradient updates does not make the evaluation independent, because the test subject informs model selection.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 2.4, first two paragraphs; PDF p. 2

evidence.statement: The authors report BCIC2020-T3 results on the official validation split because official test labels are unavailable. Absence of this dataset from pretraining, as asserted by the authors, does not resolve the separate issue of validation/test separation during model selection.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 2.1 final paragraph; Section 2.4; PDF pp. 2–3

evidence.statement: Table 1 lists UGR classes as 3/6/30, but Table 2 and Figure 1 label word identity as 60 classes. This review reports Table 2 values and preserves the inconsistency for clarification.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1, PDF p. 2; Figure 1, PDF p. 3; Table 2, PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: UGR semantic-category and word models train on pooled overt/covert labels. Their separate overt-only and covert-only evaluation shows no statistically significant difference, all p > 0.11; this is not a silent-only training protocol.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 2.4, PDF p. 2; Section 3.2, PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Multiple-seed experiments and speech-specific pretraining are explicitly future work. Reviewer assessment: speech-specific pretraining is a proposed direction, not an experimentally demonstrated remedy.

The paper compares pretrained LaBraM and EEGMamba with established baselines across speech-mode and lexical tasks on two datasets. Reviewer assessment: its contribution is comparative evidence about transfer, not a new decoder or usable speech interface.
evidence.section_or_location: Abstract; Sections 2.2 and 3; Tables 2–3; PDF pp. 1–4

en.summary: Benchmark (M03) confirms earlier reports that LaBraM gains nothing on speech EEG; decoders (M06) sit far below same-corpus results; test-subject early stopping (M12).
en.sensor: Existing 64-channel scalp EEG
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: BCIC2020-T3 within-subject balanced accuracy 25.7-30.2% (best EEGConformer 30.2%; LaBraM 27.7%; chance 20%); LOSO 18.9-20.2%, all at chance. UGR-MINDVOICE speech mode EEGNet 61.3% vs LaBraM 57.3%, EEGMamba 56.6% (chance 33.3%); 60-word identity at most 2.9% (chance 1.7%).
en.limitations: Findings for LaBraM repeat uncited earlier work; only two foundation models; within-subject scores far below same-corpus results; test subject used for early stopping on UGR-MINDVOICE; no seed repetition; 30 vs 60 word classes inconsistent; offline only.

title: EEG-Based Imagined Speech Decoding Using a Hybrid CNN-SNN Architecture
expert_take_short: CNN-to-LIF decoder (M06) is standard: a 2024 SNN-CNN inner-speech decoder precedes it; 80.13% on the validation subset is not comparable with the 82.6% competition test score (M12); no SNN ablation.
expert_take_long: The paper [@shalhoub2026cnnsnn] changes the decoder (M06): a temporal CNN feeds two leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) layers trained with surrogate gradients. M06 is standard: a 2024 hybrid of a spiking network and a CNN already classified inner-speech EEG [@sun2024smallworld], so that study refutes the authors' first-use claim (Abstract; Section V), and no CNN-only ablation shows that the spiking layers add accuracy (Section IV). Evaluation (M12) is standard in protocol, but the benchmark claim is not shown: 80.13% on the public validation subset is not comparable with the 82.6% that won the 2020 competition on its test trials [@jeong2022bci], a result missing from Table II. The low-power and real-time framing (M13) rests on a GPU timing, with no energy or neuromorphic measurement. Any advantage of spiking computation remains unshown.
expert_true_value: A CNN front end followed by a surrogate-gradient leaky integrate-and-fire classifier for five-class imagined-speech EEG, reporting 80.13% on the public validation subset of the 2020 BCI Competition Track 3 data; not the first spiking decoder of inner-speech EEG (an SNN-CNN hybrid was published in 2024), and the spiking layers are not isolated by an ablation.
canon_before: Imagined-speech EEG classification mostly used CNNs and other non-spiking decoders; a 2024 SNN-CNN hybrid classified four inner-speech words at 27.66% (chance 25%); on the Track 3 data the competition winner reached 82.6% on the released test trials and a 2020 study used the validation subset as test with 5-fold model selection (59.47 +/- 6.86%).
delta_from_canon: Reverses the earlier hybrid's order: a temporal CNN encodes the EEG and two LIF layers trained with surrogate gradients classify by output firing rate, instead of a dense output head.
position_in_field: Standard on the decoder (M06): spiking decoding of inner-speech EEG has a 2024 precedent, and no dense-head control shows a spiking benefit. Standard on evaluation (M12) in protocol, but 80.13% on validation trials is not comparable with the 82.6% competition winner on test trials, so the claimed superiority is not shown. Standard on device (M13): offline only, like most of the field.
practical_value: A candidate spiking classifier head for EEG command decoding whose value depends on a matched ablation, competition test-set scores and measured energy, none of which the paper reports.
axes_moved: decoder head type (spiking LIF classifier after a CNN) for imagined-speech EEG
axes_unresolved: contribution of the spiking layers over a dense head; ranking on the competition test trials; held-out-subject generalization; run-to-run variance; energy or neuromorphic deployment; online closed-loop use
technical_limits: Spike-encoding rule and number of SNN time steps are not specified; no checkpoint or hyperparameter-selection rule for 350 epochs; per-subject versus pooled training not stated.
evaluation_limits: 750 public validation trials serve as the only test data; single run without seeds or variance; no chance level, per-subject scores or F1 averaging rule; Table II lists comparator accuracies without their protocols and omits the competition ranking (winner 82.6%, second 75.5%).
deployment_limits: Offline pre-recorded EEG; 98 +/- 3 ms per trial on a cloud GPU; no energy, operation count, neuromorphic hardware or online feedback.
scope_limits: Five cued imagined words or phrases, 15 healthy participants, 64-channel EEG, subject-dependent classification.
input_modality: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG)
sensor_hardware: Existing 64-channel scalp EEG, international 10-20 placement, reported sampling frequency 256 Hz; amplifier and wearable configuration are not specified here.
vocabulary_type: closed-set prompted words and phrases
vocabulary_size: 5 classes: Hello, Help me, Stop, Thank you, Yes.
metrics: Accuracy 80.13% and F1 80.14% on 750 validation-subset trials; Table II comparators 48.10%, 58.51%, 66.93%, 69.00%, 70.19%; competition winner 82.6% on test trials (organisers' review).
evaluation_mode: Offline, subject-dependent five-class classification; dataset validation subset used as test; one run.

evidence.statement: The abstract claims the first integration of SNNs into EEG-based imagined-speech decoding and a result above literature values up to 70.19%.
A 2024 hybrid of a spiking network and a CNN classified four inner-speech words from 128-channel EEG of 10 participants at 27.66% average accuracy.
The 2020 International BCI Competition Track 3 was won at 82.6% accuracy on the released test trials; second place 75.5%.
The study trains on 4,500 training-subset trials and tests on 750 validation-subset trials because test labels were unavailable to the authors.
The authors concede that the experiment used pre-recorded EEG offline and that real-time validation remains necessary; no ablation isolates the SNN.

en.summary: CNN-to-LIF decoder (M06) is standard: a 2024 SNN-CNN inner-speech decoder precedes it; 80.13% on the validation subset is not comparable with the 82.6% competition test score (M12); no SNN ablation.
en.sensor: Existing 64-channel scalp EEG
en.vocabulary: 5 words/phrases (Hello, Help me, Stop, Thank you, Yes)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 80.13% five-class accuracy and 80.14% F1 on the public validation subset (750 trials, 15 subjects, subject-dependent), one run; competition winner 82.6% on the test trials
en.limitations: Validation subset used as test with no selection set; no dense-head ablation, chance level, per-subject scores or run variance; prior SNN-CNN inner-speech decoder uncited; no energy or online measurement.

title: EMG-to-Speech with Fewer Channels
expert_take_short: Exhaustive subset search shows useful channel complementarity, and full-channel pretraining helps smaller EMG inputs. Single-person evaluation, unclear selection independence and a dropout text/figure conflict limit layout recommendations.
expert_take_long: The useful result is that sensor selection is a joint prediction problem: channel 6 is removed first by greedy elimination yet belongs to the best four-channel subset, while channel 3 appears in nine of the ten highest-ranked subsets. Evaluating all seventy combinations is a meaningful improvement over a partial search, and the paper shows why a ranking of individual channel importance should not be treated as an optimal device layout. The best from-scratch four-channel combination, 1/3/5/6, reaches 47.2% recognizer-derived WER; full-channel pretraining reduces the penalty of using four to six channels, but the plotted reduced-channel results remain above the roughly 35% eight-channel reference. Transfer learning and channel dropout must also be separated: plain pretraining already helps, and the paper does not show that added dropout always improves it. In fact, Section 5.4 says no dropout is best with four channels, whereas Figure 3 places the 0.125-dropout curve lowest there. That discrepancy needs source results before selecting a training policy. The phoneme analysis is valuable as a complementary diagnostic, but category errors and surface-electrode locations do not isolate causal contributions of particular muscles; silence is included in the overall phoneme error, and channel importance differs from the synthesis-WER ranking. Finally, all results come from one existing participant and virtually removed channels. The work offers a credible training and sensor-search baseline, while independent subset validation and a genuinely reduced wearable recording study remain necessary before claiming a practical sensor layout.
expert_true_value: Makes channel interactions and task-dependent sensor utility explicit, rather than equating individually important channels with the best low-channel system.
canon_before: Gaddy-style EMG-to-speech already maps facial/neck muscle signals to acoustic features with phoneme supervision and a vocoder. Reduced-channel subsets and dropout are established ideas; channel information depends on interactions and the downstream objective.
delta_from_canon: Completes the full four-of-eight subset search and compares random initialization with full-channel pretraining at dropout probabilities 0, 0.125 and 0.25.
position_in_field: Single-participant EMG-to-speech benchmark analysis aimed at fewer facial/neck sensors.
practical_value: Useful for selecting candidate electrode combinations and pretraining baselines; current evidence cannot prescribe a universally best four-channel device.
axes_moved: Evaluates all seventy four-channel subsets, demonstrates that greedy channel importance does not determine the best combination, and improves four-to-six-channel WER through fine-tuning.
axes_unresolved: Independent subset-selection/test separation, repeated-seed uncertainty, cross-person/session robustness, exact reduced-input checkpoint adaptation, and actual reduced-electrode hardware usability.
axes_regressed: Reducing sensors still increases synthesis WER relative to the full eight-channel reference. Dropout is not uniformly beneficial relative to ordinary pretraining, and the best four-channel setting is inconsistent between text and figure.
technical_limits: Automatic WER combines encoder, vocoder and recognizer errors. Anatomical assignments are interpretations of broad surface recordings. Paper describes resizing the first convolution for reduced inputs but does not fully specify pretrained weight transfer. Exact checkpoint, optimization schedule and result split are not provided in the paper.
evaluation_limits: One subject, no explicit sample counts or independent split for choosing among seventy subsets versus reporting their final WER. No repeated-run intervals, statistical tests or human listening study. Frame/category phoneme errors are not interchangeable with synthesized-speech WER. Figure 3 conflicts with Section 5.4 about the best dropout setting at four channels.
deployment_limits: Retrospective channel removal from a fixed eight-channel recording setup; no physically redesigned four-channel device, latency, power, comfort or clinical communication trial.
scope_limits: Existing one-person open-vocabulary dataset and offline synthesized-speech evaluation; no new clinical, multi-person, mobile or real-world recording study.
input_modality: Surface electromyography from selected channels of an eight-channel face/neck array; voiced acoustic targets and phoneme labels are training supervision.
sensor_hardware: Eight existing surface-EMG channels distributed across cheeks, chin and throat, with retrospective subsets. Figure 1 lists positions including left cheek, left chin, below chin, throat and right facial sites; physical reduced-channel acquisition is not tested.
vocabulary_type: continuous open-vocabulary corpus speech
vocabulary_size: Not reported for the evaluated open-vocabulary subset.
metrics: Table 1 four-channel WER: subset 1356 47.2%, 2357 47.3%, 1346 47.7%; at least ten combinations outperform greedy 1234. Table 2 inclusion-average WER: channel 3 51.4%, channel 2 52.3%, channel 1 52.6%, channel 5 52.8%. Table 3 total phoneme error 16.0% with eight channels and 17.1% after removing channel 8; silence 4.5% versus 5.8%. Figure 3 places the full-channel WER reference at approximately 35%; exact fine-tuned numeric values are not tabulated. Author-reported, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline channel-ablation study with greedy backward elimination, exhaustive four-channel search, direct phoneme-head category errors, and HiFi-GAN synthesis transcribed by Whisper medium.

evidence.statement: The study evaluates all seventy four-of-eight channel subsets and compares them with greedy backward elimination.
Experiments reuse a single-subject dataset, retaining approximately sixteen hours of open-vocabulary data and excluding the closed-vocabulary portion.
Table 1 reports WER 47.2% for subset 1356, 47.3% for 2357 and 47.7% for 1346; channel 3 appears in nine of the top ten subsets.
Channel 6 is removed first in greedy elimination but appears in the best four-channel subset. Reviewer assessment: individual elimination rank does not determine optimal combinations.
Table 3 total phoneme error is 16.0% for the eight-channel baseline and 17.1% after the worst single-channel removal, channel 8. Silence is included and has 4.5% baseline error.

The phoneme analysis assigns ablation effects to nearby muscles from approximate electrode locations. Reviewer assessment: these observations do not isolate individual-muscle causality or match the synthesis-WER channel ranking.

Fine-tuning is compared with random initialization for selected four-to-seven-channel subsets, using independent training-time channel dropout probabilities 0, 0.125 and 0.25 during full-channel pretraining.

Section 5.4 states that no dropout is best at four channels, but Figure 3 plots the 0.125-dropout green curve lowest at four channels. Reviewer assessment: exact source results are needed before endorsing the stated best setting.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 5.4 and Figure 3; PDF p. 4, rendered and visually inspected

evidence.statement: Dataset and experimental sections do not identify separate final evaluation data for selecting the best among seventy subsets, nor report repeated-seed uncertainty. Reviewer assessment: independence of selection and performance estimation remains unverified.
The reported evaluation removes channels from existing recordings and measures synthesized-speech WER with Whisper medium; no reduced-array hardware or user communication trial is presented.

en.summary: Channel-reduction study for EMG-to-speech using exhaustive subset search and full-channel pretraining; best four-channel subsets reach about 47.2% WER versus roughly 35% with all eight channels.
en.sensor: Subsets of 8-channel face/neck surface EMG
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 47.2% WER, best 4-channel subset (full-channel ~35%)
en.limitations: Single subject; subset selection not clearly independent of reporting; no repeated runs or physically built reduced-channel device.

title: iPhoneme: Brain-to-Text Communication for ALS Using ConformerXL Decoding
expert_take_short: Behind: 26.61% WER is four times the 6.67% holdout baseline on the same recordings; the T15 best-result claim fails, the scoring split is unnamed and the gaze interface is untested.
expert_take_long: iPhoneme changes the decoder (M06) and language model (M07) of the standard phoneme-CTC-plus-LM cascade. On recordings of the same participant its 26.61% WER is four times the 6.67% offline RNN baseline on the Brain-to-Text 2025 holdout, and Card et al. report 2.5% online in their final five sessions, so the claim of the highest performance on T15 does not hold; the 89% attributed to Card et al. names no metric and differs from the 90.2% and 97.5% word accuracies that paper reports. No scoring split is named while validation errors shape the LM and 150 decoder configurations were searched (M12). The lexicon-free phoneme 6-gram plus external LLM departs from the usual word n-gram but is never compared with it, so it is rated standard. The gaze-plus-phoneme confirmation interface (M09) has no user evaluation.
expert_true_value: Connects neural phoneme decoding with a concrete interaction design question, while providing a staged decoder comparison that can be reproduced under cleaner evaluation boundaries.
canon_before: Neural speech decoders already combine sequence models and language-model constraints. Conformer, CTC, n-grams and WFSTs originate in existing sequence-recognition methods; gaze dwell-time is the interaction comparator proposed here.
delta_from_canon: Adapts a Conformer to intracortical feature sequences and adds validation-confusion-informed phoneme correction and beam search; proposes phoneme onset/offset as a gaze gesture confirmation signal.
position_in_field: Intracortical attempted-speech brain-to-text decoding on the Card et al. T15 data with the field's phoneme-CTC-plus-LM cascade; word-level results are behind the 6.67% offline holdout baseline on the same recordings and the online results already reported for that participant.
practical_value: A Conformer and phoneme-WFST variant of the standard cascade and a testable gaze-confirmation idea; at 26.61% WER on an unnamed split it is not yet a better decoder for this participant than the 6.67% Brain-to-Text 2025 holdout baseline or the published 2.5% online system.
axes_moved: Reported within-participant phoneme error reduction across decoder stages and a proposed combination of gaze pointing with phoneme confirmation.
axes_unresolved: Independent final evaluation after validation-informed tuning, actual end-to-end latency, gaze interaction benefits, architecture contribution, and user/session transfer.
axes_regressed: Word error (26.61%) is four times the 6.67% offline baseline on the Brain-to-Text 2025 holdout of the same recordings and well above the 2.5% online WER reported for that participant; latency rises from 45 ms (greedy) to 180 ms (WFST), and full-sequence context plus an external LLM limit the claimed offline interface.
technical_limits: BiGRU and unmasked sequence context are noncausal. Table II reports both 192.9M total parameters and approximately 25M for ConformerXL. Described trial lengths vary from typical 150 frames to 700-1400 frames. The preprocessing claim that 50/60 Hz lies outside a 0.3-300 Hz passband is internally incorrect; raw filtering and already-binned spike features need reconciliation.
evaluation_limits: Validation confusion patterns explicitly inform language-model correction; 150 Optuna decoder configurations are explored without a separately reported untouched final evaluation. Hidden test labels are unavailable. Prior-work comparisons lack matched reruns, while architecture, UI and late-session effects lack controlled ablations.
deployment_limits: Single implanted participant, retrospective decoding, a full-sequence bidirectional GRU and phoneme-to-word conversion by an external commercial LLM. CPU model and timing boundaries are unspecified; no online gaze study or clinical communication trial is reported.
scope_limits: One participant and a retrospectively analyzed subset. The paper calls the task overt speech; the underlying T15 resource includes attempted vocalized and some attempted silent speech, without a separately reported mode-specific result here. No new clinical user trial.
input_modality: Intracortical neural threshold crossings and spike-band power; gaze is a proposed additional interaction input.
sensor_hardware: T15 uses four implanted 64-electrode microelectrode arrays, supplying 512 features from 256 intracortical sites. The paper calls this ECoG/iEEG, which should not be confused with a surface ECoG array or scalp EEG. Primary acquisition context: https://github.com/Neuroprosthetics-Lab/nejm-brain-to-text .
vocabulary_type: Sentence-level phoneme-to-text decoding; word-disjoint evaluation unclear
vocabulary_size: 42 output classes including CTC blank; this is a phoneme inventory, not a 42-word vocabulary. Exact evaluated word vocabulary is not reported.
metrics: Table IV: greedy PER 10.62% / 45 ms; 6-gram rescoring PER 9.98% / 65 ms; WFST PER 7.86% / 180 ms. Reported word error is 26.61%. WFST gives a 2.76 percentage-point PER reduction from greedy. Reported error components are 5.2% substitutions, 1.8% deletions and 0.86% insertions. These are author-reported, not independently reproduced; latency hardware/boundaries and untouched evaluation are unclear.
evaluation_mode: Retrospective single-participant phoneme/word decoding, decoder-stage comparisons and validation confusion matrices; proposed trigger ranking uses corpus frequency and validation precision/recall.

evidence.statement: The study analyzes one T15 participant across 45 sessions, reporting 7,050 training and 1,021 validation trials. Test ground truth is unavailable, and the reported split percentages and total need reconciliation.
ConformerXL combines a dilated-convolution/BiGRU prenet, 8x temporal subsampling and 12 modified Conformer blocks, followed by phoneme language modeling and WFST search.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections V-VII; Table II; PDF pp. 4-9

evidence.statement: A confusion matrix derived from systematic errors on the validation set informs language-model correction weights. Decoder configurations are explored over 150 Optuna trials. Reviewer assessment: independent final evaluation after these choices is not established.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections VI-VII; Table V; PDF pp. 7-8 and 11

evidence.statement: Table IV reports greedy/LM/WFST PER of 10.62%/9.98%/7.86% and respective latencies of 45/65/180 ms; the WFST reduction from greedy is 2.76 percentage points.
evidence.section_or_location: Table IV; Section IX; PDF p. 11

evidence.statement: Reported WER is 26.61%; phoneme-error components are 5.2% substitutions, 1.8% deletions and 0.86% insertions. These do not establish exact-sentence accuracy or human communication performance.

The authors acknowledge that the backward GRU needs the full sequence and propose future 500-1000 ms overlapping windows for deployment. Reviewer assessment: the 180 ms figure is not demonstrated causal acquisition-to-output latency.
Phonemes are converted to words using an external commercial LLM; replacing this dependency to enable fully offline operation is future work. The timing boundary for that stage is not specified.
evidence.section_or_location: Section V and Figure 5; Sections XI; PDF pp. 4-5 and 12-13

evidence.statement: Gaze-plus-phoneme swipes and text dragging are proposed; trigger ranking combines validation precision/recall with corpus frequency. No integrated user study of selection errors, false activations or throughput is reported.
Table II gives 192.9M total parameters but also approximately 25M for ConformerXL. Sequence-length descriptions also differ between typical 150-frame trials and 700-1400-frame architecture examples.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II; Sections III and V; PDF pp. 3-5

evidence.statement: Section IV claims a 0.3-300 Hz bandpass removes 50/60 Hz interference because it is outside the passband. Reviewer assessment: those frequencies are inside the stated interval, and preprocessing details need correction.

The discussion reports roughly 80.8% validation accuracy for 2025 sessions and acknowledges single-participant generalization limits; vocabulary shift and neural change are not isolated in controlled tests.

en.summary: Behind: 26.61% WER is four times the 6.67% holdout baseline on the same recordings; the T15 best-result claim fails, the scoring split is unnamed and the gaze interface is untested.
en.sensor: Four implanted 64-electrode intracortical microelectrode arrays
en.vocabulary: 42 phoneme classes; word vocabulary not reported
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 26.61% WER, 7.86% PER on an unnamed split (offline)
en.limitations: Scoring split unnamed while validation informs LM and decoder tuning; behind the 2.5% online WER on the same participant; single participant; noncausal model; latency protocol missing; gaze interface not user-validated.

title: Lip-Siri: Contactless Open-Sentence Silent Speech with Wi-Fi Backscatter
expert_take_short: Wi-Fi backscatter lip sensing (M05) and subword sentence output (M08) are standard; open-sentence decoding is untested, with no sentence-disjoint split and 36.87% WER.
expert_take_long: The paper [@tian2026lipsiri] changes the sensor (M05), a passive Wi-Fi backscatter tag near the face, and the output (M08), subword sentences instead of class labels. Both are standard: contactless radio-frequency sensing is already usual, Wi-Fi lip reading predates it [@hameed2022rf], and face-worn RFID tags already sense speech by backscatter (Table I). The open-sentence claim is untested: 340 scripted sentences, each read at least twice, are split 80/20 at random, so test sentences very likely also appear in training (inference), and no unseen-sentence test exists. The headline 36.87% WER is worse than the visual baseline's 32.3% in the same room (§VI-B), although the text calls the two comparable. The held-out-user test (M12, standard) is the paper's strongest evidence.
expert_true_value: A working contactless sentence decoder for a fixed 340-sentence corpus using a passive Wi-Fi backscatter tag off the body, with a held-out-user test (three new users, 81.5-85.5% word accuracy); open-sentence decoding itself is not tested.
canon_before: Radio-frequency silent-speech work mostly uses active radar at a distance, with Wi-Fi channel sensing and face-worn RFID backscatter tags as alternatives; outputs are class labels from closed lists of vowels, words or sentences, or token sequences scored by WER on fixed sentence sets.
delta_from_canon: Replaces active radar with a passive frequency-shifted Wi-Fi backscatter tag on a bracket within 50 cm of the user, and outputs variable-length subword sequences from a corpus-built lexicon instead of class labels.
position_in_field: Standard on sensing (M05) and output (M08) against radio-frequency silent speech: contactless sensing is the usual practice and the open-sentence claim lacks a sentence-disjoint test; standard on the held-out-user evaluation (M12).
practical_value: Moderate: nearby-object placement and no on-body sensor are promising for quiet or privacy-sensitive settings, but manual segmentation, 50 cm geometry, SDR hardware, and unmeasured whole-system power limit immediate deployment claims.
axes_moved: Sequence output instead of class labels for radio-frequency silent speech; a passive tag off the body that reflects ambient Wi-Fi (face-worn RFID backscatter tags predate it); three held-out users at 36.3-39.6% WER.
axes_unresolved: Unseen-word recognition; sentence-disjoint evaluation; speaker/session independence; continuous hands-free operation; rejection coverage; tag and receiver cost/power; robustness to violent motion and tag-facing geometry
axes_regressed: Sentence WER of 36.87% is above the 32.3% of the visual lip-reading baseline in the same environment; the prototype uses software-defined radios, a PC, a tag within 50 cm and manual start/end clicks, with no measured whole-system power.
technical_limits: The tag isolates a shifted component but does not remove all non-target paths; contaminated windows are discarded and the rejection rate is not reported. The main cohort uses random sample splitting, leaving possible sentence or repetition overlap unspecified. Lexicon composition is not evidence of unseen-word recognition. Manual start/end clicks prevent a hands-free streaming interpretation of the reported latency. Jumping substantially worsens RF WER, while tag geometry and whole-system power are unmeasured.
evaluation_limits: The 12-user experiment uses a random 80/20 sample split without an explicit sentence-disjoint protocol, while only three users are held out as new users. The lexicon is initialized from a fixed English handbook and its final size is not reported; adding words is only supported when they can be composed from existing subwords. Rejection rate from contamination gating, confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, ablations, exact beam width, optimizer settings, and full power are not reported.
deployment_limits: The demonstrated system is a software-defined radio prototype with an Ethernet-connected PC and a backscatter tag within 50 cm. Users manually click start and end buttons, the tag is fixed on a bracket, and a commercial Wi-Fi implementation is outside the paper's scope. Violent motion such as jumping breaks recognition, and tag-facing geometry is not characterized beyond the tested scenarios.
scope_limits: Fifteen-volunteer SDR prototype evaluation with 340 handbook sentences, 3,398 reported word occurrences, three held-out users, and selected indoor/motion scenarios. No clinical participants, unrestricted vocabulary, sentence-disjoint split for the main cohort, adversarial privacy analysis, or continuous hands-free use.
input_modality: Contactless Wi-Fi frequency-shifted backscatter sensing of lip-motion traces; SDR transmitter/receiver prototype.
sensor_hardware: Frequency-shifted passive backscatter tag on a bracket or nearby object with an antenna; software-defined radio transmitter and receiver controlled from an Ethernet-connected laptop; a camera records lip motion for the visual comparison.
vocabulary_type: Lexicon-guided subword sequence decoding; composable sentence combinations within a scenario lexicon.
vocabulary_size: The base handbook is organized into 340 sentences and 3,398 reported words; unique-word count and final subword lexicon size are not reported.
metrics: Overall average word prediction accuracy 85.61% and continuous sentence WER 36.87%; representative visual SSI WER 32.3% on recorded videos. Three new users range from 81.5% to 85.5% word accuracy and 36.3% to 39.6% WER. The silent-assistant 100-word lexicon case reports 92% accuracy and 90.5% under 50 dB audio interference. Reported latency is 717.5 ms from end-button click to displayed result for a 10-second signal, consisting of no more than 50 ms transmission, 525 ms processing, and 142.5 ms inference. Values are author-reported and not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline word accuracy and continuous-sentence WER on a random 80/20 split plus three held-out users; sentence-length, signal-strength, time-interval, office/library/bedroom, silent-assistant, and eight-condition motion/lighting/mask comparisons; visual-SSI comparison from recorded video; end-button-to-result latency measurement.

evidence.statement: The abstract presents Lip-Siri as a Wi-Fi backscatter SSI supporting open-vocabulary sentence recognition through lexicon-guided subword decoding, with a frequency-shifted tag and Transformer encoder-decoder.
The prototype uses a frequency-shifted passive backscatter tag placed on a stand or monitor, allowing the user to face the tag without attaching or holding it near the chin.

The system extracts a first-order shifted backscatter component, computes phase differences, applies a 0–50 Hz low-pass filter, rejects windows above median plus three MAD, and uses VMD to suppress slower modes.

Lip-motion units are approximately segmented with 0.2 s, 5 s, and 0.1 s windows; 67-dimensional time/frequency/differential features are standardized and clustered with K-means. The signal-processing description separately cites VMD with K=4 as its implementation example.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections V-B1–V-B2 and Algorithm 1; PDF pp. 6-7

evidence.statement: The lexicon starts from characters in a scenario corpus and repeatedly merges frequent adjacent symbols; the decoder predicts variable-length subword sequences with a 12-layer, 12-head encoder, 6-layer, 4-head decoder, and beam search.

The paper defines open-sentence recognition as variable-length decoding over a lexicon and states that adding a word does not require retraining only when it is composable from existing subwords. This does not test recognition of words outside the lexicon or unrestricted open-vocabulary speech.
evidence.section_or_location: Section V-C2 and Table I caption; PDF pp. 8 and 11

evidence.statement: The evaluation recruits 15 volunteers over six months, uses 340 handbook sentences and 3,398 reported words, asks users to repeat base sentences at least twice, and collects 11,700 base samples. Three users are reserved as new users; the remaining data use a random 80/20 training/testing split.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections VI-A–VI-B, Data Collection and evaluation setup; PDF pp. 8–9

evidence.statement: The reported overall result is 85.61% average word accuracy and 36.87% average continuous-sentence WER; a recorded-video visual SSI comparison reports 32.3% WER.
For three new users, average word accuracy ranges from 81.5% to 85.5% and sentence WER ranges from 36.3% to 39.6%.

The paper does not specify sentence-disjoint grouping for the random 80/20 split, unique vocabulary size, final subword lexicon size, beam width, optimizer, epochs, contamination rejection rate, confidence intervals, or component ablations.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections VI-A, V-B, and V-C; PDF pp. 6-9

evidence.statement: The interface requires a user to click start before lip-reading and end afterward. For a 10-second signal, the paper reports no more than 50 ms transmission, 525 ms signal processing, 142.5 ms inference, and 717.5 ms total latency from end click to displayed result.

In eight scenario comparisons with two volunteers, RF WER is 35.8% in normal conditions, 38.5% with head rotation, 83.5% while jumping, 33.4% while typing, 39.0% while walking, and 46.5% with a mask; the prototype uses SDR hardware and the paper does not measure whole-system power.

en.summary: Wi-Fi backscatter lip sensing (M05) and subword sentence output (M08) are standard; open-sentence decoding is untested, with no sentence-disjoint split and 36.87% WER.
en.sensor: Wi-Fi backscatter tag with software-defined radio transceivers
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: 85.61% word accuracy, 36.87% sentence WER, random 80/20 split; new users 81.5-85.5%
en.limitations: Open-sentence decoding untested: random 80/20 split of 340 repeated sentences, no sentence- or word-disjoint test; WER above the visual baseline; power not measured; manual start/end clicks.

title: LipSody: Lip-to-Speech Synthesis with Enhanced Prosody Consistency
expert_take_short: Pitch and energy predicted from lips, face and emotion (M06) is standard: Faces-to-Voices did it in 2025. Prosody metrics improve, WER does not; normalization change unablated.
expert_take_long: LipSody adds pitch and energy predictors, fed by lip content, a face-image speaker embedding and a face-video emotion embedding, to a LipVoicer-style diffusion lip-to-speech model. The design is standard in video-to-speech: VCVTS (2022) and Let There Be Sound (2023) already predict pitch, and energy, from video, and Faces-to-Voices (2025) predicts pitch and energy from facial expressions beside lip and face-identity streams; neither Faces-to-Voices nor ImaginTalk (2025), which aligns speech with content, identity and emotional expression, is cited. Against the reimplemented LipVoicer, global and local F0 deviation and energy consistency improve (28.87 to 25.15, 45.26 to 41.06, 1.2667 to 0.9141) while WER is 22.5% against 22.1% and naturalness 3.47 against 3.36, both not significant; ABX prosody preference is 54.22%. Most of the energy-consistency gain remains without the emotion embedding, and the switch to speaker-wise waveform normalization is never ablated, so the gain cannot be assigned to visual prosody prediction alone. The 21.0% oracle WER uses ground-truth pitch and energy from audio. The evaluation follows the field's usual unseen-speaker LRS3 protocol with listener tests, but intelligibility is compared with LipVoicer only, under one ASR scorer, with no repeated runs and unitless prosody metrics.
expert_true_value: A measured ablation of a face-video emotion embedding inside a pitch-and-energy-conditioned diffusion lip-to-speech model, with oracle headroom; the conditioning design itself follows earlier video-to-speech work.
canon_before: Video-to-speech systems already predict pitch and energy from video (VCVTS 2022, Let There Be Sound 2023), and Faces-to-Voices (2025) predicts both from facial expressions alongside lips and face identity; LipVoicer combines diffusion with lip-reader text and ASR classifier guidance.
delta_from_canon: Adds audio pitch and energy as training conditions and video-predicted pitch and energy at inference to the LipVoicer pipeline, using an EmoCLIP face-video emotion embedding as one predictor input, and replaces clip-wise with speaker-wise waveform normalization.
position_in_field: Diffusion lip-to-speech on LRS3 in the LipVoicer lineage: standard on the decoder (M06), where pitch and energy predictors from facial cues predate it, and standard on evaluation (M12), with unseen speakers and listener tests but no repeated runs.
practical_value: Useful extension when prosodic resemblance matters; content errors and operational cost still need independent validation before communication use.
axes_moved: Lower reported global/local pitch and energy errors and small gains in speaker embedding similarity; modest listener preference for reference-matched prosody.
axes_unresolved: Generalization to genuinely silent articulation, speaker-wise audio normalization at evaluation, contribution of normalization versus prosody inputs, independent pitch-estimator results, perceptual effect size and complete runtime.
axes_regressed: WER is numerically 22.5% versus 22.1% for the reconstructed LipVoicer baseline and 21.9% for the official version. Removing the emotion feature improves WER to 22.0% while worsening prosody metrics.
technical_limits: Unobserved prosody remains ambiguous from vision. Speaker-level normalization changes target energy statistics and lacks an isolated control. Predictor training uses MSE with pretrained encoders; oracle conditioning in generator training differs from estimated inputs at inference. Emotion embeddings are not independently validated emotional labels.
evaluation_limits: Comparison is mainly two LipVoicer variants; other systems excluded on prior WER. Listener tasks each assigned to 100 subjects, but stimulus counts, assignment structure, exact p-values and uncertainty intervals are not reported. Multiple prosody tests, speaker/clip dependence and ABX aggregation require clarification. Alternative pitch-extractor results are asserted but omitted.
deployment_limits: Iterative diffusion plus a lip reader, ASR gradient guidance, emotion/prosody networks and vocoder. No runtime, power, streaming, camera robustness or assistive-user evaluation.
scope_limits: LRS3 unseen-speaker benchmark and online listener ratings; no genuine silent-articulation or clinical deployment study.
input_modality: Facial video: mouth motion for linguistic content, a selected face frame for generator identity and video-derived face/emotion features for prosody prediction. Audio supplies training supervision and reference evaluation, not the proposed inference inputs.
sensor_hardware: Existing RGB facial videos sampled at 25 frames/s with face/mouth crops; no new acquisition apparatus.
vocabulary_type: continuous speech-video corpus
vocabulary_size: No fixed command lexicon; exact evaluated lexical size not reported.
metrics: Table 1 WER 22.5% (LipSody), 22.1% (LipVoicer reconstruction), 21.9% (official); STOI-Net estimate 0.92 versus 0.93 and DNSMOS 3.18 versus 3.17. Table 2 GF0/LF0 errors 25.15/41.06 versus 28.87/45.26, energy error 0.9141 versus 1.2667, Resem 0.6040 versus 0.5974 and time-varying Resem 0.6618 versus 0.6578. Table 3 naturalness 3.47 versus 3.36, ABX preference 54.22% versus 45.78%. Table 4 oracle WER 21.0%, no-emotion WER 22.0%. Author-reported, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline unseen-speaker LRS3 generation with conventional learned quality/intelligibility metrics, reference-based pitch/energy and speaker similarities, crowd-sourced online naturalness/ABX ratings and emotion/oracle ablations.

evidence.statement: Pitch and energy extracted from paired audio condition diffusion training; separately trained predictors estimate them from content, speaker and emotion features at inference. Faces-to-Voices (2025) predicts pitch and energy from facial expressions with lip and identity streams before this paper, so the design is not new to video-to-speech.
LRS3 predefined training/test partitions are used with an unseen-speaker protocol, but no newly recorded silent-articulation cohort is described.
Table 1 gives WER 0.225 for LipSody versus 0.221 for the reconstructed LipVoicer baseline and 0.219 for the official model. The prose reports p greater than 0.05 for conventional-metric comparisons.
Table 2 gives global/local pitch errors 25.15/41.06 versus 28.87/45.26 and energy error 0.9141 versus 1.2667, with small increases in both speaker-similarity measures.

Table 3 reports naturalness 3.47 versus 3.36 and prosody ABX preference 54.22% versus 45.78%; naturalness is not significantly different, whereas preference is reported above chance at p less than 0.05.

Each subjective task is assigned to 100 subjects. Reviewer assessment: stimulus counts, confidence intervals and rater/clip aggregation are not reported, limiting assessment of the modest preference effect.
The oracle condition supplies ground-truth pitch and energy at inference and achieves WER 0.210. Reviewer assessment: it is not a deployable visual-only result.
Removing emotion worsens GF0, LF0 and EC but lowers WER from 0.225 to 0.220. Reviewer assessment: emotion-derived prosody gains do not establish improved word accuracy.

Speaker-wise waveform normalization divides by a maximum across all clips for that speaker. Reviewer assessment: split boundaries and a normalization-only control are needed before attributing energy improvements entirely to visual prediction.
Alternative pitch-extractor comparisons are described as consistent but detailed results are omitted. The system specifies 400 denoising steps without measured end-to-end timing.

en.summary: Pitch and energy predicted from lips, face and emotion (M06) is standard: Faces-to-Voices did it in 2025. Prosody metrics improve, WER does not; normalization change unablated.
en.sensor: Existing RGB facial video
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: 54.22% ABX preference; WER 22.5% vs 22.1% baseline, unseen-speaker LRS3
en.limitations: No WER improvement; oracle audio cues and normalization changes complicate comparisons; limited perceptual study reporting; no runtime evaluation.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Brain-to-Speech Models Across Speech Modes
expert_take_short: Patching shows the decoder depends on donor activations, not that transfer runs through a compact subspace: kept regions score below the unpatched decoder, with no null and no held-out split.
expert_take_long: The paper changes one component: it explains an sEEG Conv1D-BiGRU decoder (Sec. 4.2) by patching activations between vocalized, mimed and imagined speech (M06). Intervening on internal activations is rare (2 of 38 studies, pattern match, Appendix), but one participant and one architecture give no repetition, so by the verdict rules it is standard, not ahead. The central claim, vocalized-to-imagined transfer through a compact subspace, holds only against random blocks: the kept convolutional subspace beats a matched random block (PCC 0.666 against 0.564) but not the unpatched imagined decoder (0.725; Tables 1 and 3). Full patching gives the same PCC 0.954 and MCD 1.63 for imagined and mimed recipients, above the donor's 0.752 (Table 3), so it reflects the donor, not transfer (inference). The field's own transfer test, an overt-trained decoder applied to covert input (M04), is not reported, and no null model backs any effect (M12).
expert_true_value: A candidate toolkit for auditing how a decoder responds to cross-mode activation changes, with useful matched-control and multi-scale intervention ideas.
canon_before: Intervening on a neural network can identify dependencies in that network, but substituting donor activations is distinct from extracting more information from recipient brain signals. Smooth responses to interpolated activations do not by themselves establish a shared biological manifold.
delta_from_canon: Studies where donor-mode activations influence a convolutional/bidirectional recurrent speech decoder through full replacement, temporal/channel subsets and neuron-level ranking.
position_in_field: Offline interpretability analysis of an intracranial neural speech decoder, not a validated assistive communication system.
practical_value: Potentially useful for debugging trained decoders after raw results and interventions are made reproducible; unsuitable as current evidence of reliable imagined-speech transfer.
axes_moved: Provides directional activation interventions, channel/time localization, matched random controls and sentence-level neuron diagnostics beyond ordinary predictive scores.
axes_unresolved: Single shared decoder versus separate mode checkpoints, consistency of baseline/full-patch evaluation, impossible winner counts under the reported layer width, independent subspace selection, signal-quality confounds and biological interpretation.
axes_regressed: No demonstrated improvement to an imagined-only deployable decoder. Restricted scrubbing retains only part of full donor-conditioned performance, and quantitative contradictions prevent accepting strong sufficiency or shared-manifold conclusions.
technical_limits: Whole-layer replacement removes the recipient path at that site. Smooth interpolation is expected from continuous computation and does not identify an intrinsic manifold. Neuron selection uses mean effects across the analyzed dataset. Convolutional winner counts and mode-specific model references conflict with the architectural description; model neurons are not biological neurons.
evaluation_limits: One participant and one architecture; training details, fold counts, target alignment and held-out subspace selection are absent. Figure 5 uses a k=1 reference whereas the method describes an unpatched baseline. Full-patch scores are inconsistent with donor baselines under a shared serial model. Table 5 convolutional winner counts exceed the described 64 channels.
deployment_limits: Diagnostic interventions require paired donor-mode brain recordings or activations for the same content. No deployable imagined-only transfer method, new-user test, intelligibility assessment or real-time demonstration.
scope_limits: One participant, one described model, paired speech-mode sentences and activation diagnostics. No biological intervention, intelligibility, open communication or clinical outcome.
input_modality: Invasive stereotactic EEG for vocalized, mimed and imagined speech; interventions additionally use paired donor-mode hidden activations.
sensor_hardware: Existing stereotactic intracranial EEG electrodes in VOCALMind; acquisition channel counts and preprocessing are not detailed in this paper.
vocabulary_type: paired sentence-level speech-mode tasks
vocabulary_size: Exact unique lexical size unreported; 200 sentence samples per condition in winner analysis.
metrics: Table 2 baseline PCC concat: vocalized 0.7519, imagined 0.7254, mimed 0.5686; MCD 2.7928/2.8830/3.2948. Table 3 full vocalized-to-imagined/mimed patch PCC 0.954 and MCD 1.63; imagined-to-vocalized PCC 0.177. Table 1 imagined-from-vocalized KEEP-Conv/RAND-Conv PCC 0.666/0.564 and KEEP-RNN/RAND-RNN 0.462/0.398. Table 5 reports 96-120 distinct convolutional winners despite a 64-channel architecture. Author-reported values, internally unresolved and not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline intervention analysis of a neural speech decoder, using flattened mel-spectrogram PCC, spectral distortion, baseline pitch measures, donor activation replacement, interpolation and matched random scrubbing controls.

evidence.statement: The study combines full activation patching, convex interpolation, channel/time localization, matched random scrubbing and neuron ranking in a speech decoder.
VOCALMind data come from one participant, and Table 5 reports 200 sentence samples per mode-pair condition; no cross-person experiment is described.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 4.1 and Table 5; PDF pp. 3 and 14

evidence.statement: Equation 1 computes the patched output as the post-layer network applied to donor activation. Reviewer assessment: in the stated serial architecture, complete replacement bypasses the recipient representation rather than improving information extraction from it.

Table 3 lists vocalized baseline PCC 0.752 but full vocalized donor patch PCC 0.954. Methods describe a fixed model, while Appendix E refers to activations from a vocalized model. Reviewer assessment: checkpoint and evaluation semantics need reconciliation.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 5.4 and Appendix B.1/E; Table 3; PDF pp. 6, 11-13

evidence.statement: The convolutional output is described as 64 channels, but Table 5 lists 96-120 unique convolutional winner neurons. Reviewer assessment: these counts exceed the stated channel universe unless an unreported aggregation or different architecture is used.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 4.2/5.2 and Table 5; PDF pp. 3-4 and 14, rendered table inspected

evidence.statement: Table 1 imagined-from-vocalized KEEP-Conv/RAND-Conv PCC is 0.666/0.564, while KEEP-RNN/RAND-RNN is 0.462/0.398; full patch is 0.954. Reviewer assessment: localized control benefits are not full performance recovery.

Figure 7 includes nonmonotonic recurrent MCD curves despite broad prose claims of monotonic interpolation. Reviewer assessment: smooth interpolation through a continuous decoder does not by itself establish a shared biological causal manifold.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 6.1, Appendix C and Figure 7; PDF pp. 7, 12-13, figure rendered

evidence.statement: Top-k neurons are ranked by mean single-neuron effects across the analyzed dataset; a separate held-out selection/evaluation procedure is not specified.

Figure 5 labels delta PCC relative to k=1, whereas methods describe changes relative to an unpatched baseline. Reviewer assessment: reference conditions must be specified consistently before interpreting improvements.

Table 2 baseline PCC is 0.7519 for vocalized, 0.7254 for imagined and 0.5686 for mimed. Reviewer assessment: these baselines do not place mimed speech between the other two modes in decoding performance.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2 and Discussion; PDF pp. 8 and 11

evidence.statement: Evaluation centers on spectrogram correlation/distortion and intervention diagnostics; no word-recognition or listening-comprehension outcome, new participant or live communication test is reported.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 6 and Appendices A-F; PDF pp. 6-14

en.summary: Patching shows the decoder depends on donor activations, not that transfer runs through a compact subspace: kept regions score below the unpatched decoder, with no null and no held-out split.
en.sensor: Stereotactic intracranial EEG (VocalMind dataset), one participant
en.task: Interpretability of a speech-reconstruction decoder across vocalized, mimed and imagined speech (activation patching, interpolation, causal scrubbing)
en.vocabulary: Paired sentences across three speech modes; 200 sentences per condition in the winner analysis; acoustic output, no lexicon or language model
en.speaker: One participant (speaker-dependent)
en.key_result: Unpatched PCC 0.725 imagined, 0.752 vocalized, 0.569 mimed; full vocalized-to-imagined patch 0.954; kept convolutional subspace 0.666 against 0.564 for matched random blocks, below the unpatched imagined decoder
en.limitations: One participant and one architecture; no described train-test split, fold count or seeds; subspaces selected and scored on the same data; full patching replaces the recipient activation; no overt-trained transfer test and no null model; 96 to 120 convolutional winners reported for a 64-channel layer.

title: Multi-Subject Pretraining Enables Short-Calibration Personalization for Closed-Corpus Surface EMG Speech Decoding
expert_take_short: Standard training recipe (M03) at larger scale: pretrain on 26, calibrate 3 min. The closed corpus carries the result: unseen sentences give 99.9% WER (M12, behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@le2026multisubject] changes training (M03): pretraining on the other members of a 27-person cohort, then calibrating on the held-out one. The design is standard: sEMG decoders have been pretrained on other speakers and adapted to a new one since 2008 [@wand2008speakeradaptive; @wu2022picnn; @scheck2024crossspeaker]; cohort size and a 1-to-26 pool sweep combined with minute-level calibration budgets are what it adds. The strongest confound is the closed corpus: other participants' repetitions of the five test sentences stay in pretraining (§3.2), and once those sentences leave all training, CER rises from 21.7% to 78.6% and WER from 31.9% to 99.9% (Table 3). The 3-minute result thus measures how fast a model recognizes sentences already seen from other people. The evaluation (M12) is behind the best comparable work, which reports silent-EMG error on sentences absent from training [@gaddy2021improved; @benster2024monalisa].
expert_true_value: A 27-participant leave-one-subject-out measurement of multi-subject pretraining and calibration budgets for face and neck sEMG character decoding on a closed 50-sentence corpus: 21.7% CER / 31.9% WER after pretraining and full calibration, 3 minutes not significantly different, and 78.6% CER / 99.9% WER once the test sentences are absent from all training.
canon_before: Pretraining an sEMG decoder on other speakers and adapting it to a new one predates this paper: an HMM recognizer with MLLR adaptation and a training-data-amount curve (2008), a 28-subject phrase classifier fine-tuned on new subjects with 1 to 8 sessions (2022), and cross-speaker EMG-to-speech fine-tuned on one session of a leave-out speaker (2024); more training speakers raised cross-speaker phrase accuracy in 2023. Open-vocabulary silent-EMG tests on unseen sentences reached 42.2% WER (2021) and 12.2% WER (2024) for one speaker.
delta_from_canon: Applies the pretrain-then-calibrate recipe to 27 participants with calibration budgets in minutes combined with a training-pool-size sweep from 1 to 26 participants, extending the known gain from more training speakers, in one leave-one-subject-out protocol; the headline is measured on sentences whose repetitions occur in other participants' pretraining.
position_in_field: Cross-speaker personalization study for sEMG text decoding: standard on training (M03), where the recipe dates from 2008, and behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12), where the headline uses a closed sentence set.
practical_value: Gives a planning figure for how many minutes of labeled sEMG a new user needs when the sentence inventory is fixed and shared with other users; it gives no such figure for open content.
axes_moved: Larger leave-one-subject-out cohort (27) with a pool-size curve (74.4% to 21.7% CER from 1 to 26 participants) and a calibration sweep (1 to 13 minutes) on one closed corpus.
axes_unresolved: Calibration budget on unseen sentences; matched update counts and repeated seeds; saturation of the pool-size curve beyond 26 participants; electrode re-donning and sessions; clinical users.
axes_regressed: Removing the five evaluation sentences from all training raises CER from 21.7% to 78.6% and WER from 31.9% to 99.9%; Subvocal trials were recorded but not decoded.
technical_limits: Closed 50-sentence corpus with test-sentence repetitions in other participants' pretraining; checkpoint from a different montage; random initialization failed in 5 of 27 folds under the fixed schedule; the subject-specific adapter gave no detectable gain.
evaluation_limits: One fixed 45/5 sentence split for all participants, selection criterion not in the article; one fixed seed each for calibration-trial shuffling and pool sampling, values not given and no repeated-seed runs; fixed epoch count so calibration budgets differ in update counts; unadjusted paired tests; final-epoch reporting without a validation set; CER/WER normalization not stated.
deployment_limits: Offline analysis of healthy adults; no latency, communication rate, closed-loop use, electrode re-donning or session-shift test.
scope_limits: Based on arXiv 2609.21288 v1 (text, tables and figures); supplementary material and the announced data and code release were not available.
task: Closed 50-sentence corpus sEMG-to-text decoding with leave-one-subject-out personalization. Not open-vocabulary conversational SSI.
input_modality: Lower-face/neck surface EMG (8 channels). Aloud and Mimed used; Subvocal excluded from decoding analyses. Not around-ear AESSI, textile SilentWear, camera VTP, EPG, or ultrasound.
sensor_hardware: Standardized 8-channel lower-face/neck sEMG montage (same nominal placements as prior work [5]); raw 2222.22 Hz → 1000 Hz → filtered → 689 Hz model input. Released single-subject checkpoint used a different 8-channel montage.
output_type: Character sequences decoded to text via CTC beam search + external KenLM (not refined on the 50-sentence inventory). Not waveform synthesis.
vocabulary_type: Closed sentence inventory; character-sequence decoding within that inventory. Not open vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: 50 closed sentences (TIMIT-based); fixed 45/5 calibration/evaluation split shared across subjects.
metrics: Table 1 (n=27, Aloud+Mimed macro): Pretrain+FT (MLP) 21.7% CER / 31.9% WER; Pretrain+FT (no MLP) 22.5/33.3; random-init Pretrain+FT 44.9/58.8; Pretrain zero-shot 49.3/63.1; Checkpoint+FT (MLP) 68.0/97.2. Table 2 calib: 1 min 25.4/36.6; 3 min 20.5/31.7 (vs full p=0.27/0.88); full ≈13 min 21.7/31.9. Scaling: 1 subject 74.4% CER → 26 subjects 21.7%. Table 3 unseen sentences 78.6% CER / 99.9% WER. Aloud vs Mimed CER 15.4% vs 27.9%. Author-reported; not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Leave-one-subject-out over 27 participants: pretraining on the other 26 (from a released single-subject checkpoint or random initialization), then fine-tuning on the held-out participant; controls are zero-shot transfer, direct checkpoint fine-tuning, with and without a subject-specific adapter, calibration budgets of 1, 3, 5, 10 and about 13 minutes, pool sizes of 1 to 26, and an unseen-sentence test with the evaluation sentences removed from all training.

evidence.statement: Primary setting is a closed 50-sentence TIMIT-based corpus with leave-one-subject-out personalization; not open-vocabulary conversational SSI.
27 speech-typical participants each contributed less than 0.5 h of data (21.3 min on average) across Aloud and Mimed; Subvocal trials were recorded but unused in decoding analyses.
Surface EMG used a standardized eight-channel lower-face and neck montage shared by all 27 participants; the released single-subject checkpoint used a different eight-channel montage.
Authors claim multi-subject pretraining plus target fine-tuning enables short-calibration personalization for closed-corpus sEMG speech decoding.
Pretrain + fine-tune (MLP) achieved macro-averaged 21.7% CER and 31.9% WER across 27 held-out subjects (Aloud+Mimed).
Pretrain zero-shot (no MLP) reached 49.3% CER / 63.1% WER; Checkpoint + fine-tune (MLP) reached 68.0% CER / 97.2% WER.
Three minutes of target-subject calibration reached 20.5% CER / 31.7% WER versus full ≈13-min pool 21.7% / 31.9% (paired Wilcoxon p=0.27 and p=0.88); not an equivalence test.
Macro-averaged CER declined from 74.4% with one pretraining participant to 21.7% with 26.
Unseen-sentence stress test: excluding the five evaluation sentences from all sEMG model-training data yielded 78.6% CER and 99.9% WER on the identical 269 held-out trials.
Subject-specific MLP adapter provided no detectable benefit (pooled CER change −0.8 points, 95% CI [−2.9,+1.2], p=0.44).
Authors state the main result should not be interpreted as open-vocabulary speech decoding; analyses are offline on healthy adults, without longitudinal or electrode-shift tests.
Novelty is the joint LOSO quantification of pretraining-cohort size and short calibration budgets with an explicit unseen-sentence collapse boundary, not a new sEMG sensor or decoder family.
Decoding architecture follows Gaddy and Klein convolution–transformer mapping silent sEMG to characters with CTC; checkpoint trained on ≈18.7 h from one subject.
De-identified dataset and code are planned for public release upon publication at huggingface.co/datasets/whisperle/multisubject-semg-text-v1; raw audio will not be released.

en.summary: Standard training recipe (M03) at larger scale: pretrain on 26, calibrate 3 min. The closed corpus carries the result: unseen sentences give 99.9% WER (M12, behind).
en.sensor: 8-channel lower-face/neck surface EMG
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: 21.7% CER / 31.9% WER, pretrain + fine-tune, closed 50 sentences; 78.6% CER on unseen sentences
en.limitations: Evaluation sentences can appear in other subjects' pretraining; performance collapses on unseen sentences; offline only, healthy adults, no latency or electrode re-donning tests.

title: NasoVoce: A Nose-Mounted Low-Audibility Speech Interface for Always-Available Speech Interaction
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
expert_take_short: Nose-pad mic plus vibration sensor (M05) and dual-input fusion (M06) are standard; noise is added to the mic only, so the robustness claim is untested in real noise (M12, behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@rekimoto2026nasovoce] changes the sensor site (M05) and the fusion model (M06); both are standard, since conducted sensors paired with an air microphone were in use by 2004, and their fusion for recognition and for whispered enhancement in noise predates it [@graciarena2004combination; @jou2004softwhisper; @tajiri2015nam]. The nose site is new to the ledger but untested against any other site. Every quantitative test adds noise to the microphone channel only, so the evaluation (M12) is behind the field, where 44 of 123 studies name noise physically present against 15 with digital noise and the closest works expose the conducted sensor to noise [@fukumoto2025whisphone].
expert_true_value: Puts a MEMS microphone and a vibration sensor together at the nose pad of glasses and fuses them with a dual-input enhancer trained against a frozen recognizer; noise robustness is shown only with noise added digitally to the microphone channel, while the vibration channel stays clean.
canon_before: Talker-worn conducted sensors paired with an air microphone were in use by 2004: combined standard and throat microphones for noise-robust large-vocabulary recognition, and throat-microphone recognition of soft whisper; air- and body-conductive microphones were fused to enhance non-audible murmur in noise in 2015, a 2018 glasses design already put a vibration sensor in the nose pad, and deep air/bone fusion beat single-sensor enhancement by 2020 and 2022.
delta_from_canon: Adds the air microphone at the same nose pad as the vibration sensor, trains a dual-input enhancer on 104 hours from 45 participants with a distillation loss from a frozen recognizer, and targets whispered as well as normal speech; no other sensor site and no single-input enhancer are compared.
position_in_field: Wearable conducted-plus-air speech capture: standard on the sensor pair (M05) and on two-channel fusion (M06); behind the field on the noise protocol (M12), where 44 of 123 studies name noise physically present against 15 with digital noise, and the closest works expose the conducted sensor to noise.
practical_value: Shows that a nose-pad pair fits a glasses form factor and gives a perceptual gain over a noisy microphone in simulation; it gives no recognition figure for whispered speech in real noise.
axes_moved: Sensor site moved to the nose pad with the microphone co-located; whispered input included; MUSHRA with 50 raters (68.7 enhanced vs 37.6 noisy microphone at 0 dB).
axes_unresolved: Recognition in physically present noise; comparison with throat, ear or philtrum placement; fusion gain against a single-input enhancer; streaming use; day-to-day nasal variability.
