technical_limits: Fusion model not streaming; whispered enhancement degrades considerably under noise; under the strongest noise the vibration channel alone can beat the fused output; no single-input enhancer control.
evaluation_limits: All quantitative tests add DEMAND noise to the microphone channel only while the vibration channel stays clean; WER reported only as curves without point values, dispersion or tests; 1,000 evaluation items not reconciled with 800 described test utterances; dB labels switch between SNR and noise level; field recordings qualitative.
deployment_limits: Fully streaming continuous operation, smartphone integration, adaptive sensor gating based on SNR, and calibration for physiological factors such as nasal patency remain future work.
scope_limits: Targets low-audibility whispered speech, not fully silent speech without any acoustic leakage; assumes hand-covering mouth for privacy.
task: speech-enhancement; speech-recognition for whispered and low-audibility speech to support always-available AI voice interaction
input_modality: acoustic; vibration; multimodal
sensor_hardware: MEMS microphone (Syntiant SPH0141LM4H-1) and MEMS vibration sensor (Syntiant V2S200D) integrated in smart glasses nose pads providing synchronized PDM output.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary speech
vocabulary_size: Open vocabulary via a downstream off-the-shelf recognizer
metrics: Recognition accuracy expressed in word error rate (WER) and character error rate (CER) under varying noise conditions; PESQ and STOI perceptual audio quality; MUSHRA subjective audio quality scores.
evaluation_mode: Offline: WER and CER from an off-the-shelf recognizer on enhanced, microphone-only and vibration-only audio from four test speakers under digitally added noise; PESQ and STOI against clean references; MUSHRA with 50 raters; qualitative recordings in four real environments.

evidence.statement: NasoVoce is a smart-glasses nose-pad interface integrating a MEMS microphone and vibration sensor to capture low-audibility whispered speech robustly under environmental noise.

The new element is co-locating the air microphone with the vibration sensor at the nose pad; nose-pad vibration capture on glasses (2018), conducted-plus-air fusion for recognition (2004) and fusion for whispered-murmur enhancement in noise (2015) predate it.
WER and CER of an off-the-shelf recognizer on 1,000 evaluation items under noise added digitally to the microphone channel only; PESQ and STOI; MUSHRA ratings with 50 participants.

Limitations include not yet achieving fully streaming speech processing integration, fusion performance degradation under extreme noise favoring vibration-only input, and the need for calibration to physiological variability such as nasal patency.

en.summary: Nose-pad mic plus vibration sensor (M05) and dual-input fusion (M06) are standard; noise is added to the mic only, so the robustness claim is untested in real noise (M12, behind).
en.sensor: Nose-pad MEMS microphone and vibration sensor in smart glasses
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: ASR evaluation uses synthetic noise; in-the-wild testing only qualitative; fusion not fully streaming; whispered vibration signals remain weak.

title: Physiological Noise Augmentation Improves Non-Invasive Brain-to-Speech
expert_take_short: Artifact-remix augmentation repeats 2024 reference-signal mixing, gains 3.3 points (not 4.7) only with 10-trial averaging, barely beats white noise, and does not directly test the claimed invariance.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training-set augmentation (M03), standard against the field: re-injecting recorded artifact signals from other trials was done for EEG speech decoding in 2024 and is not cited; ICA-based projection is the refinement. Its gain needs ten averaged imaginings per decision (M04), behind single-trial practice; at single trial neither model gains beyond seed error, as the authors concede. At 10 trials EEGNet rises from 73.0% to 76.3%, not the stated 4.7 points and 77.6%, generic white noise reaches 0.747 against 0.763, and baselines are tuned and placed differently. The claimed invariance to tracked artifacts is not directly tested.
expert_true_value: An ICA-based variant of artifact-signal augmentation for MEG imagined-digit decoding; its gain is small (3.3 points with 10-trial averaging, none at single trial) and the invariance it targets is not directly tested.
canon_before: Neural speech decoders used generic input-level augmentations (masking or channel dropout, additive noise, shifts); EEG speech decoding had already mixed recorded EOG or EMG from other trials into training data and shown that artifact-only input then decodes near chance (Sato et al. 2024); imagined-speech EEG/MEG decoding is usually reported at single trial.
delta_from_canon: Selects EOG/ECG-correlated ICA components, removes them, and re-adds rescaled artifact projections from donor trials during training; gives a Jacobian-regularization reading under stated assumptions.
position_in_field: Standard on training-set augmentation (M03; reference-artifact mixing is prior); behind on the use-time action (M04), since the gain needs ten averaged imaginings per decision; evaluation (M12) not reported well enough: headline 4.7 points against 3.3 in the tables, unnamed split, no significance test.
practical_value: Low: one subject, ten imagined digits, offline laboratory MEG, EOG/ECG references required, and ten repetitions per decision for any gain.
axes_moved: training augmentation drawn from the recording's own artifact components
axes_unresolved: direct invariance test (decoding from artifact components alone); repetitions needed for a fixed accuracy; matched tuning and ordering of baseline augmentations; held-out split, seeds and significance; more subjects and vocabularies
technical_limits: Requires EOG/ECG reference channels; correlation thresholds unstated; no benefit at single trial; the edge over white noise at 10 trials is 0.016 with standard errors near 0.011.
evaluation_limits: Headline +4.7 points and 77.6% do not match Tables 1-2 (73.0% to 76.3%); baselines tuned at single trial but compared at 10 trials and applied after averaging while PNA is applied before; split behind the tables unnamed; Table 2 seed count missing; no significance test.
deployment_limits: Offline laboratory MEG; ten imaginings averaged per decision; reference channels needed at recording.
scope_limits: One subject imagining ten digits in MegNIST; no other subject, vocabulary or modality tested.
input_modality: magnetic
sensor_hardware: magnetoencephalography (MEG) with electrooculography (EOG) and electrocardiography (ECG) reference sensors
vocabulary_type: digits
metrics: Ten-class imagined-digit accuracy (mean and standard error over seeds); EEGNet 10-trial 0.730 raw-only, 0.763 Raw+PNA, 0.747 Raw+white noise.
evaluation_mode: Single 10:1:1 train:validation:test split of one subject's trials; single-trial and 10-trial-averaged evaluation; offline.

evidence.statement: The authors propose PNA, which removes EOG/ECG-correlated ICA components and re-adds rescaled artifact projections from donor trials as label-preserving training samples, and interpret it as anisotropic Jacobian regularization under multi-trial averaging (Sec. 1, 3).

Mixing recorded artifact signals from other trials into neural training data predates the paper (Sato et al. 2024, EOG/EMG into EEG, with a direct artifact-only decoding test); PNA's new element is the ICA-based selection and scaling, and it reports no invariance test.

With 10-trial averaging, Raw+PNA raises EEGNet accuracy from 0.730 to 0.763 and MLP from 0.542 to 0.574 (Table 1); the abstract's +4.7 points and the contributions' 77.6% appear in no table; at single trial EEGNet is 0.332 with PNA against 0.337 raw.
The authors concede reliance on EOG/ECG reference channels and a single-subject, constrained imagined-digit task, and call for multi-subject and broader-vocabulary tests (Sec. 5).

en.summary: Artifact-remix augmentation repeats 2024 reference-signal mixing, gains 3.3 points (not 4.7) only with 10-trial averaging, barely beats white noise, and does not directly test the claimed invariance.
en.sensor: MEG with EOG and ECG reference sensors
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.session: One subject; session assignment not stated
en.key_result: EEGNet accuracy 73.0% to 76.3% with PNA and 10-trial averaging, 10 classes
en.limitations: Single-subject imagined digits; EOG/ECG references required; gain only with 10-trial averaging; headline 4.7 points not in the tables (3.3); no invariance or significance test.

title: Relating the Neural Representations of Vocalized, Mimed, and Imagined Speech
expert_take_short: Cross-mode transfer and rank scoring are standard tests; one participant, unstated alignment to vocalized targets and mismatched nulls leave the hierarchy and linear-better claims unsupported.
expert_take_long: The paper changes two components, both standard: it applies each condition-trained sEEG decoder to the other speech modes (M04), the field's usual transfer test (23 of 33 studies, confirmed, Appendix), and adds sentence-rank scoring to correlation (M12), which an overt-to-covert reconstruction study already ran against a 10,000-shuffle null in seven patients. The hierarchy claim rests on one participant and two repetitions of 100 sentences (Sec. 2.1), and the authors defer its direct test (Sec. 4). The strongest confound is timing: silent trials are scored against vocalized-audio targets (Sec. 2.1) with no stated alignment, where earlier work used dynamic time warping. "Linear better preserves sentence structure" is a slope (Fig. 4), not a level: of six pairs with both AUCs stated, the nonlinear model is higher in three, lower in two, tied in one (Secs. 3.3, 3.4; inference).
expert_true_value: Shows that cross-mode acoustic similarity and sentence-specific information can diverge, making evaluation choice central to representation claims.
canon_before: Prior work decodes each speaking mode or compares activation patterns. Ridge decoding and convolutional/recurrent spectrogram models are established approaches; high acoustic correlation alone does not establish linguistic identity preservation.
delta_from_canon: Uses condition-specific linear mappings as probes of cross-mode transfer and supplements correlation with top-k envelope-matching analysis, alongside a nonlinear baseline.
position_in_field: Single-participant invasive speech-mode transfer study, focused on neural/acoustic representation relationships rather than operational text entry.
practical_value: A compact linear baseline and an evaluation lesson for cross-mode neural decoding; insufficient evidence for a deployable speech restoration system.
axes_moved: Separates envelope reconstruction similarity from sentence-level discriminability and evaluates all nine train/test mode combinations.
axes_unresolved: Sentence-disjoint split integrity, repeated-trial grouping, target alignment in silent modes, rank-area scaling, statistical independence, cross-user transfer and direct tests of the proposed neural decomposition.
axes_regressed: Some transfers preserve envelope correlation without positive sentence-discrimination area; linear mimed-to-imagined rank area is -0.01. Nonlinear versus linear superiority varies by train/test pair.
technical_limits: The linear target is an NSL auditory representation whereas the nonlinear target is mel-spectrograms. Linear nulls shuffle trial pairings and nonlinear nulls circularly shift targets. The planning/articulation/feedback decomposition is assumed, and no direct subspace or sensory-feedback experiment is performed.
evaluation_limits: Train/test proportions, lag support, regularization grid and model selection boundaries are insufficiently reported. Sentence repetitions may require grouping across modes; this is not explicitly documented. Linear and nonlinear models use different target representations and different null constructions. Pairwise condition summaries are not independent participants.
deployment_limits: Retrospective, externally cued single-participant analysis with acoustic targets from vocalized speech; no online communication, listener intelligibility, word-error or latency evaluation.
scope_limits: The analyzed dataset is one Mandarin-speaking participant with repeated prompted sentences. Primary VocalMind acquisition was an epilepsy-monitoring participant with intact language, not a clinical speech-restoration trial.
input_modality: Intracranial stereotactic EEG during vocalized, mimed and imagined speech.
sensor_hardware: 110 retained sEEG contacts in the analyzed release. Primary VocalMind describes nine right-hemisphere depth shafts and 140 initial contacts, recorded at 1 kHz, with 30 abnormal contacts removed; these details describe the source dataset, not new acquisition. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-04741-2 .
vocabulary_type: fixed prompted sentence set; acoustic reconstruction rather than unrestricted text output
vocabulary_size: 100 prompted sentences, repeated twice per mode; lexical vocabulary size not reported.
metrics: Figure 3 rank area above chance, rows training V/M/I and columns testing V/M/I: linear [0.32,0.05,0.07; 0.11,0.13,-0.01; 0.11,0.08,0.07]; nonlinear [0.59,0.07,0.01; 0.14,0.06,0.04; 0.10,0.04,0.07]. This is top-k rank-curve area, not ROC AUC, classification accuracy or WER. Exact normalization is unclear. Reconstruction correlations are reported above their nulls (all p much less than 0.001); no numerical correlation table or listener result is supplied.
evaluation_mode: Offline within- and cross-mode reconstruction correlations, shuffled/shifted null comparisons, sentence-envelope top-k matching and area above the chance rank curve.

evidence.statement: The study uses one VocalMind participant, 100 Mandarin sentences repeated twice in each of three modes and signals from 110 electrodes, with vocalized audio as stimulus targets.
Condition-specific time-lagged ridge mappings are evaluated across all three modes, and sentence-envelope top-k ranking supplements reconstruction correlation.

Training/test division and a regularization grid search are mentioned without exact split sizes, lag values, repetition grouping or complete alignment procedure. Reviewer assessment: independence and reproducibility cannot be established from this description.

Figure 3 reports linear rank areas [0.32,0.05,0.07; 0.11,0.13,-0.01; 0.11,0.08,0.07] for V/M/I training and V/M/I testing. Mimed-to-imagined area is -0.01 despite the general above-null correlation result.

Figure 3 reports nonlinear vocalized-to-vocalized area 0.59 versus linear 0.32; mimed-to-mimed is 0.06 versus linear 0.13. Reviewer assessment: model ordering depends on condition and does not support universal linear superiority.

The linear decoder uses NSL time-frequency targets and trial-shuffled nulls, whereas the nonlinear decoder uses mel-spectrogram targets and circularly shifted nulls. Reviewer assessment: the comparison changes more than model linearity.

Equation 3 defines a sum of top-k performance minus k/N, while Figure 3 reports rank-area values without sufficient normalization and candidate-count detail. Reviewer assessment: this quantity must not be interpreted as ROC AUC or recognition accuracy.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 2.4 Equation 3; Figure 3; PDF pp. 2 and 4

evidence.statement: The planning, articulation and sensory decomposition in Equation 4 is assumed. Direct subspace alignment tests and a listening condition are explicitly proposed as future work.

Figure 4 compares relationships across nine condition pairs and reports a Steiger-test p value for differing correlation/rank relationships. Reviewer assessment: this is not a controlled overall decoder-superiority or cross-participant test.
The paper reports offline reconstructions and rank/correlation analyses, with no WER, listener intelligibility, online latency or prospective communication test.

en.summary: Cross-mode transfer and rank scoring are standard tests; one participant, unstated alignment to vocalized targets and mismatched nulls leave the hierarchy and linear-better claims unsupported.
en.sensor: Stereotactic intracranial EEG (public VocalMind dataset), 110 electrodes, one participant
en.task: Cross-mode spectrogram reconstruction from vocalized, mimed and imagined Mandarin speech with linear (ridge) and CNN-RNN decoders
en.vocabulary: 100 prompted sentences, two repetitions per mode; acoustic output, no lexicon or language model
en.speaker: One participant (speaker-dependent)
en.key_result: Rank AUC above chance: linear 0.32 and nonlinear 0.59 for vocalized-trained on vocalized; linear mimed-to-imagined -0.01; all envelope correlations above shuffled or shifted nulls
en.limitations: One participant; split, seeds, shuffle counts and alignment of silent trials to vocalized targets not reported; linear and nonlinear models differ in target representation and null

title: Silent Speech Interfaces in the Era of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Taxonomy and Systematic Review
expert_take_short: A broad and useful SSI taxonomy, but missing review-selection detail and concrete citation errors make its benchmark tables unsuitable for unverified rankings or deployment claims.
expert_take_long: This review is useful for orienting readers across neural, muscular, articulatory, imaging and active-sensing approaches to silent speech. Its separation of recognition, direct synthesis and language-model integration helps explain where linguistic priors enter a pipeline and why sensor information, user calibration and computational cost remain important. Its quantitative synthesis needs substantially more caution. Although the title calls it systematic, the paper does not provide a reproducible study-selection and quality-assessment procedure; a Web of Science publication-count figure is not a documented search-and-screening protocol for the review itself. Tables combine small-command accuracy, open-vocabulary error rates, acoustic distortion, auditory-perception decoding and even wrist typing, without the split and calibration details needed for fair comparisons. There are also concrete attribution errors: Table IV assigns a 125,000-word intracortical ALS result with 2.5% WER to reference 132, which the bibliography identifies as Silentspeller, an electropalatography text-entry paper. Table II places references 83 and 88 under ultrasound, although their listed titles concern electro-optical stomatography. These are not merely stylistic issues; they break the path from a claimed result to its evidence. The repeated 15% WER usability threshold and 50 ms latency requirement should therefore be treated as contextual claims, not general acceptance standards demonstrated by this survey. The paper can guide literature discovery and research questions, but its numerical tables should not be imported into a leaderboard or used to infer clinical readiness without checking the original studies.
expert_true_value: A cross-modal reading map that brings language-model priors and generative synthesis into the broader SSI landscape, with numerical claims requiring primary-source verification.
canon_before: Earlier SSI reviews organize biosignal sensors and recognition/synthesis pipelines. This review adds emphasis on modern generative models, representation alignment and wearable form factors.
delta_from_canon: Connects sensing positions along the speech-production chain with representation learning, direct synthesis and LLM-based correction or embedding alignment.
position_in_field: Broad SSI synthesis spanning restorative communication, consumer interaction, sensing and generative decoding.
practical_value: Useful for identifying sensor families, terminology and candidate references; quantitative or clinical decisions should return to source-level evidence.
axes_moved: Breadth of conceptual organization across sensing, recognition, synthesis and language-model integration.
axes_unresolved: Reproducible literature coverage, source-accurate quantitative extraction, matched cross-modal comparisons, and validation of broad usability and deployment conclusions.
axes_regressed: No controlled system regression; citation and table inconsistencies reduce the reliability of the proposed benchmark synthesis.
technical_limits: Reference mismatches, mixed metric scales, duplicate rows and underspecified cohort/split conditions limit the tables. Statements about inherent noise immunity, recovered intent and universal latency requirements exceed what a heterogeneous narrative review can establish.
evaluation_limits: No explicit reproducible search query/date, screening counts, eligibility rules, extraction procedure or study-quality assessment is reported. Tables mix recognition, reconstruction, perception, typing and articulator-analysis tasks with incompatible metrics and sparse split details. Citation mismatches and duplicated entries require correction.
deployment_limits: Wearable, clinical and noisy-environment examples are taken from different cited studies; no integrated system or deployment experiment is performed by this review.
scope_limits: Narrative synthesis of heterogeneous SSI and adjacent resources. Its tables include listening EEG and wrist typing, which do not directly establish silent speech-production decoding.
input_modality: Survey of neural, EMG, magnetic, ultrasound, optical, acoustic and RF sensing, including adjacent speech resources.
sensor_hardware: No new hardware; surveys EEG/ECoG, sEMG, EMA/PMA, ultrasound, MRI, cameras/depth, earables, contact sensors and radar.
body_site: brain; face; jaw; lip; oral-cavity; throat; tongue
output_type: Literature taxonomy, benchmark/dataset tables and research roadmap
vocabulary_type: Mixed closed-set, open-vocabulary, reconstruction and adjacent tasks
vocabulary_size: Varies across cited tasks from small command sets to large word inventories; no unified evaluated vocabulary.
metrics: No new system performance measurement. Tables II-IV reproduce accuracy, WER, CER, PER, MCD, MOS and other values from heterogeneous studies. Some rates appear as proportions and others as percentages. The review repeatedly proposes 15% WER and 50 ms latency thresholds, but supplies no common user study establishing them as universal criteria.
evaluation_mode: Narrative taxonomy and tabulation of published results; no matched benchmark, meta-analysis or new user evaluation.

evidence.statement: The review organizes SSI sensing along neural, neuromuscular and articulatory stages, then relates recognition, synthesis and language-model methods to these modalities.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections II-III; Tables I-IV; PDF pp. 3-10

evidence.statement: Figure 1 describes Web of Science keyword publication counts for 2011-2025. No explicit study-screening flow, inclusion/exclusion protocol or quality-assessment procedure accompanies the review.
evidence.section_or_location: Figure 1; Introduction and review structure; PDF pp. 1-3 and 10-14

evidence.statement: Table IV attributes an intracortical ALS result with 125,000-word vocabulary and 2.5% WER to reference 132; the bibliography identifies reference 132 as Silentspeller, an electropalatography text-entry paper.
evidence.section_or_location: Table IV and Reference 132; PDF pp. 9 and 18

evidence.statement: Table II classifies references 83 and 88 as UTI, while their bibliography titles explicitly concern electro-optical stomatography. This is a modality-to-reference mismatch.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II and References 83/88; PDF pp. 6 and 16-17

evidence.statement: Tables II-IV combine command accuracy, word/character/phoneme errors, distortion, top-10 perception accuracy and other measures. Evaluation splits and calibration conditions are not systematically tabulated, preventing fair cross-system ranking.

Table V includes wrist EMG typing, passive audiobook EEG and auditory-evoked EEG alongside speech-production datasets. Reviewer assessment: these are adjacent resources, not interchangeable silent speech-decoding evidence.
evidence.section_or_location: Section IV-B and Table V; PDF pp. 11-12

evidence.statement: The text repeatedly describes 15% WER as a usability threshold and 50 ms as an end-to-end latency requirement, without a common user evaluation establishing universal applicability across the surveyed tasks.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-D and IV-A; Section VI-B; PDF pp. 10-11 and 14

evidence.statement: The language-model discussion distinguishes post-processing, candidate rescoring and direct biosignal-to-embedding alignment, and acknowledges latency costs and over-correction that can diverge from user intent.

The roadmap identifies user/session variation, missing parallel targets, continual learning, multimodal alignment and privacy as unresolved directions; these are proposed research priorities rather than tested solutions.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections IV-C and VI; PDF pp. 11 and 13-14

en.summary: Taxonomy and review of silent speech interfaces in the LLM era across neural, EMG, magnetic, ultrasound, optical, acoustic and RF sensing, with benchmark and dataset tables.
en.sensor: Review: multiple SSI sensing modalities
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: No reproducible review selection procedure; citation errors and mixed metric scales make its tables unsuitable for rankings or deployment claims.

title: SilentWear: an Ultra-Low Power Wearable System for EMG-based Silent Speech Recognition
expert_take_short: Neckband EMG with on-body inference at 20.5 mW (M13) but no on-device accuracy; repositioning recovery by labeled fine-tuning is standard (M03); sensor reused from 2025.
expert_take_long: The paper [@spacone2026silentwear] changes deployment (M13), running a 15,489-parameter CNN on the neckband, and training (M03), fine-tuning on new-session batches. The sensor (M05) is the authors' 2025 neckband [@meier2025neckband] [concurrent], with its hardware reused (§III-A). M13 is the strongest part: 20.5 mW including inference is below every read wearable that streams raw data [@meier2025neckband; @wu2024necklace; @tang2024throat], but the quantized on-device model has no accuracy figure (§IV-E), so the deployed path is unvalidated. M03 is standard: supervised recovery after electrode repositioning dates from 2005 [@maierhein2005session], and no label-free baseline is run. The headline 77.5% silent accuracy tests days already in training; an unseen day gives 59.3% (Table II).
expert_true_value: Makes the cost of day-to-day sensor repositioning visible while providing a compact embedded baseline and a concrete supervised recalibration strategy.
canon_before: Electrode repositioning between sessions was already tested in sEMG speech recognition in 2005 (97.3% within session, 76.2% after repositioning, 87.1% with normalization and adaptation, ten digits). Dry worn-object EMG for speech existed as a dry-electrode necklace with a wet reference (2024), textile headphones (2025) and the authors' own 2025 fully dry neckband, all decoding off the body.
delta_from_canon: Keeps the authors' 2025 neckband hardware and adds a four-subject multi-day dataset, a 15,489-parameter CNN, supervised fine-tuning on new-session batches and on-device inference on GAP9 at a measured 20.5 mW total system power.
position_in_field: Personalized EMG command recognition: standard on recalibration (M03), sensing (M05) and evaluation splits (M12); on deployment (M13) it reports the lowest system power among read wearables and the only on-body inference, but not the accuracy of the quantized on-device model.
practical_value: Strong candidate baseline for research on low-power personalized command interfaces; hardware and day-transfer evidence identify practical development priorities.
axes_moved: On-body inference with measured latency (2.47 ms), energy (63.9 microjoules per inference) and total system power (20.5 mW); a four-subject multi-day vocalized and silent dataset with repositioning; a CNN that beats the paper's own Random Forest by 10.6 points across sessions (silent).
axes_unresolved: Closed-loop communication accuracy, accidental activations in daily activity, cross-user generalization, quantized-versus-floating accuracy, causal preprocessing parity, long-duration comfort and measured battery endurance.
axes_regressed: Silent balanced accuracy drops from 77.5% in pooled-day batch evaluation to 59.3% on a held-out day. An 800 ms window improves calculated throughput and compute cost at some accuracy loss.
technical_limits: Offline preprocessing uses a zero-phase 20 Hz high-pass filter plus 50 Hz notch; causal deployment equivalence is not established. Trigger timing imperfectly aligns articulation. Quantization changes recognition accuracy by an unreported amount. Whole-window ITR omits actual cue/rest/correction overhead.
evaluation_limits: Four subjects and eight commands plus rest. Global evaluation mixes every recording day into train and test through different batches; only leave-one-session-out isolates a new day. All models remain subject- and mode-specific. Rest is downsampled to class balance, unlike typical idle-heavy use. Online closed-loop validation is explicitly future work.
deployment_limits: Personalized fixed-command models, cued seated data and sensor-fit sensitivity. No closed-loop user study, walking/activity false-trigger study, patient cohort or measured all-day endurance. Recalibration is trained offline rather than demonstrated on-device.
scope_limits: Four seated participants, eight prompted English commands plus rest, three days and separate models for vocalized/silent conditions. No unseen words, sentences, patient communication or naturalistic continuous use.
input_modality: 14-channel differential surface EMG from a fully dry textile neckband.
sensor_hardware: 27 dry SoftPulse electrodes in a textile neckband form 14 differential channels: 10 overlapping central channels and four lateral channels; four shorted electrodes provide ground. BioGAP-Ultra uses two ADS1298 AFEs, GAP9/NE16 and nRF5340 BLE, in 26 x 65 x 13 mm electronics with a 150 mAh Li-Po battery.
vocabulary_type: closed-set isolated commands
vocabulary_size: Eight fixed commands plus one rest class, nine output classes total.
metrics: Table II, 1.4 s windows: SpeechNet balanced accuracy 84.8 +/- 4.6% vocalized and 77.5 +/- 6.6% silent for pooled-day held-out batches; 71.1 +/- 8.3% and 59.3 +/- 2.2% for held-out days. Random Forest silent results are 62.9% and 48.7%, respectively. Table III, 800 ms windows: 2.47 ms / 63.9 microjoules at 240 MHz, or 1.60 ms / 97.1 microjoules at 370 MHz. System power 20.5 mW with 100 ms stride; estimated battery life 27.1 h. Author-reported measurements, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Subject-specific balanced accuracy using pooled-day held-out batches, leave-one-session-out testing and sequential next-batch fine-tuning; window-length ablation and analytical ITR; embedded latency/energy benchmarking.

evidence.statement: Four subjects each provide three multiday sessions with neckband repositioning, containing eight prompted commands in vocalized and silent modes. Classification includes a ninth rest class, which is downsampled for balance.
SpeechNet uses temporal then spatial CNN blocks with 15,489 parameters; the dry neckband hardware extends prior conference work. GAP9 deployment uses 8-bit post-training quantization.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-A/E/G; Table I; PDF pp. 3-5

evidence.statement: Silent balanced accuracy is 77.5 +/- 6.6% for pooled-day held-out batches and 59.3 +/- 2.2% for held-out sessions, an 18.2 percentage-point gap. Corresponding Random Forest values are 62.9% and 48.7%.
The Global protocol trains and tests on separate batches from all three days. The Inter-Session protocol holds one day out. Models are explicitly subject-specific and condition-specific.

The text reports that one 1.4-second-window adaptation round improves silent accuracy from about 58% to 72%, with roughly 20 repetitions per word and about 10 minutes of acquisition. The protocol evaluates the following unseen batch.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-D and IV-D; Figures 7/8; PDF pp. 4 and 7-8

evidence.statement: For an 800 ms input, GAP9 achieves 2.47 ms and 63.9 microjoules per inference at 240 MHz/0.65 V, or 1.60 ms and 97.1 microjoules at 370 MHz/0.8 V.
evidence.section_or_location: Table III; Section IV-E; PDF pp. 7-8

evidence.statement: A 100 ms sliding-window stride gives reported total power 20.5 mW: 15.3 mW acquisition, 4.55 mW data handling/result streaming and 0.639 mW compute. Battery life of 27.1 h with 150 mAh is explicitly estimated.

Online validation under real-time closed-loop user interaction and adaptive recalibration is explicitly left for future work. Reviewer assessment: embedded latency does not establish operational communication accuracy or usability.

ITR uses class accuracy and input-window duration; reported silent peak is 69.2 bit/min at 800 ms. Reviewer assessment: this analytical rate omits the cued protocol, rest intervals and error correction and is not measured user throughput.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-B/F and IV-C; PDF pp. 3-6

evidence.statement: Offline preprocessing uses a zero-phase Butterworth high-pass filter; acquisition labels follow visual triggers with acknowledged reaction-time mismatch. Reviewer assessment: causal online filter/segmentation parity and post-quantization accuracy need explicit verification.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-C/G and V; PDF pp. 4-5 and 9-10

evidence.statement: Figures 7/8 use five tested batches with the first batch preceding adaptation, leaving four sequential updates in the specified protocol; the text nevertheless describes five fine-tuning rounds and Figure 8 repeats a vocalized caption. Reviewer assessment: update counts and condition labeling need correction.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections III-D and IV-D; Figures 7/8; PDF pp. 4 and 7-8

en.summary: Neckband EMG with on-body inference at 20.5 mW (M13) but no on-device accuracy; repositioning recovery by labeled fine-tuning is standard (M03); sensor reused from 2025.
en.sensor: Dry textile neckband, 14-channel differential surface EMG
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 59.3% silent balanced accuracy on held-out days (77.5% pooled-day), 9 classes; 2.47 ms inference
en.limitations: Only four subjects and subject-specific models; large drop on new days; no closed-loop user study, walking or false-trigger evaluation.

title: SLD-L2S: Hierarchical Subspace Latent Diffusion for High-Fidelity Lip to Speech Synthesis
expert_take_short: Codec-latent flow decoder (M06) is standard: quality lead rests on predictors that rate output above ground truth; WER trails V2SFlow; speaker similarity uses reference audio.
expert_take_long: SLD-L2S [@liang2026sldl2s] changes the decoder (M06) to flow matching on continuous neural-codec latents, a target found in 1 of 165 video-to-speech studies but never isolated from the rest of the system, so the component is standard. Its quality lead rests on reference-free predictors that score output above the recordings, at the same 10 steps as the cited but uncompared Faces-to-Voices [@kim2025faces]; WER trails V2SFlow [@choi2024v2sflow], and the speaker-similarity ranking mixes systems with and without a reference-audio embedding.
expert_true_value: Shows that continuous neural-codec latents can serve as the flow-matching target for lip-to-speech and gives the highest listener naturalness in its own comparison; the contribution of the latent target itself is not isolated from the rest of the system.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech systems already use AV-HuBERT, diffusion/flow models and neural codecs or speech units. Lip movements underdetermine phonetic detail, prosody and speaker voice; generative priors can improve naturalness without guaranteeing intended words.
delta_from_canon: Generates continuous X-Codec-hubert latents from visual features and a reference speaker embedding using subspace convolutional flow modeling, instead of directly predicting mel features or discrete residual tokens.
position_in_field: Video-to-speech decoder design (M06): flow matching on continuous X-Codec latents, standard against the field; codec-based video-to-speech before it generated discrete tokens. Evaluated offline on normal speech videos with an audio-derived speaker reference.
practical_value: A high-naturalness synthesis baseline; uses where the words must be right should weigh its WER, which trails V2SFlow and LipVoicer, and its need for reference audio.
axes_moved: Higher reference-free quality scores on two benchmarks and higher listener naturalness on LRS3; 10 function evaluations, the same step count the cited Faces-to-Voices already used; parameter-matched backbone and loss ablations on single runs.
axes_unresolved: Actual inference time/energy, reference-speaker utterance selection, silent-articulation/patient transfer, statistical reliability of listener differences, and disentangled contributions of subspace structure versus codec/pretraining.
axes_regressed: WER is worse than V2SFlow and LipVoicer on both datasets, and speaker similarity is below V2SFlow. Some loss removals improve quality predictors and WER while reducing embedding similarity.
technical_limits: Visual ambiguity persists despite perceptual priors. Full generator has 57.7M parameters in the DiCB comparison, excluding unspecified complete-system cost. Speaker identity requires GE2E reference audio. Data-prediction loss weights by 1/(1-t)^2; numerical endpoint handling is not specified. Semantic, quality and word metrics respond differently to loss choices.
evaluation_limits: Small subjective evaluation: 15 listeners and 30 synthesized samples, with randomization/blinding and uncertainty definitions not fully described. Baselines have heterogeneous reference-speaker and frontend dependencies. No repeated-seed uncertainty or latency benchmark. Table 3 duplicates a loss-removal label, leaving the final ablation ambiguous.
deployment_limits: Large pretrained visual encoder and iterative generator, with speaker identity obtained from reference audio. No measured latency, mobile power, streaming interaction or patient evaluation.
scope_limits: Offline English speech-video benchmarks and a small listening study. No actual silent articulation, patient communication, walking or longitudinal user evaluation.
input_modality: Mouth-region video for content plus a reference audio-derived speaker embedding for voice identity.
sensor_hardware: Existing RGB video processed into 88 x 88 grayscale mouth crops using facial landmarks; no acquisition hardware or new recording system reported.
vocabulary_type: continuous speech-video corpus synthesis
vocabulary_size: No fixed command vocabulary; exact evaluated lexical size is not reported.
metrics: Table 1: LRS3 UTMOS 4.2096, SCOREQ 4.6075, D-BERT 0.8284, WER 30.22%, SECS 0.804; LRS2 WER 39.54%. V2SFlow WER is 27.55%/34.17%, and LipVoicer 20.62%/24.92%. Table 2 listener naturalness/intelligibility/similarity: proposed 4.17/3.65/3.77, V2SFlow 3.88/3.69/3.90. Proposed uses 10 function evaluations versus V2SFlow 30. No measured inference time or independent reproduction.
evaluation_mode: Offline LRS3 synthesis and LRS2 transfer; learned quality metrics, recognizer-derived WER, speech/speaker embedding similarities, five-point listener ratings and architecture/loss ablations.

evidence.statement: The model combines AV-HuBERT visual features, parallel subspace decomposition, a convolutional flow backbone and continuous neural-codec latent generation with semantic and SLM auxiliary losses.

Task training uses LRS3 official splits; LRS2 is a transfer test. Speaker identity is supplied by a 256-dimensional GE2E embedding from a reference utterance. Reviewer assessment: the evaluated identity input is not purely visual.
evidence.section_or_location: Experimental Setup and Implementation Details; PDF pp. 5-6

evidence.statement: Table 1 reports WER 30.22%/39.54% on LRS3/LRS2, versus V2SFlow 27.55%/34.17% and LipVoicer 20.62%/24.92%. Quality gains therefore coexist with worse lexical error rates.
Fifteen listeners assess 30 synthesized samples. Table 2 gives proposed naturalness 4.17, intelligibility 3.65 and similarity 3.77, versus V2SFlow 3.88, 3.69 and 3.90 respectively.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2 and Evaluation Metrics; PDF p. 6

evidence.statement: Table 1 quality predictors score the proposed synthesis above ground-truth recordings on both datasets, while human naturalness remains below ground truth. Reviewer assessment: reference-free quality scores are not measures of exact reconstruction fidelity.
The DiCB versus DiT ablation approximately matches parameters at 57.7M versus 57.8M. Replacing DiCB reduces SECS from 0.804 to 0.618, with smaller changes in WER and quality metrics.

Removing SLM loss increases UTMOS from 4.2096 to 4.2885 and SCOREQ from 4.6075 to 4.6958, and lowers WER from 30.22% to 29.99%, while reducing D-BERT and SECS. Reviewer assessment: the loss has metric-specific trade-offs, not uniformly better intelligibility.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3; Auxiliary Losses discussion; PDF pp. 6-7

evidence.statement: Table 3 labels two different rows w/o Lsem, while the prose also discusses removing both losses. Reviewer assessment: the final ablation label must be clarified rather than silently reinterpreted.

Ten function evaluations are compared with thirty for V2SFlow, but no complete inference-time or energy measurement is reported. Reviewer assessment: fewer steps do not establish a faster end-to-end deployed system.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1; Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods; PDF pp. 5-7

evidence.statement: The experiments use ordinary LRS3/LRS2 speech videos; no new silent-articulation or speech-impaired participant study is presented.

en.summary: Codec-latent flow decoder (M06) is standard: quality lead rests on predictors that rate output above ground truth; WER trails V2SFlow; speaker similarity uses reference audio.
en.sensor: Existing RGB video (mouth crops)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: LRS3 WER 30.22%, UTMOS 4.21; listener naturalness 4.17 vs 3.88 (V2SFlow)
en.limitations: Needs reference audio for speaker identity; LRS3 WER trails V2SFlow, LipVoicer and Intelligible in its own table; small listener study; training compute reported but no inference runtime.

title: Soft Active EMG Interface for Machine Learning-Enabled Silent Speech Recognition
review_confidence: High for the reported full-text study; medium for field-positioning and deployment judgments
expert_take_short: Hand-pressed fingertip EMG (M05) is standard: privacy and noise benefits argued, not tested; 97.2% on 30 words rests on a random within-participant split with no session hold-out (M12, behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@kurotaki2026softemg] changes one component, the sensor (M05): dry electrodes on four fingertips (one channel each) of a hand-worn soft package, pressed to the perioral skin only during input. Earlier neck- and ear-worn dry electrodes [@wu2024necklace; @tang2025headphones] also avoid facial adhesives, and the claimed privacy and noise benefits are argued, not measured, so M05 is standard. The evaluation (M12) is behind the best comparable work: the 97.2% headline comes from a random class-stratified split within each participant, while worn sEMG systems tested on a held-out session lose 14 to 23 points on 8-word tasks [@meier2025neckband; @spacone2026silentwear]. The authors concede that hand pressing adds placement variability (§ Discussion), so the missing session-disjoint test is the strongest confound. Deployment (M13) is standard: PC decoding with no latency, power or command success figure.
expert_true_value: A hand-worn soft EMG interface whose dry electrodes on four fingertips (one channel each) touch the perioral skin only during input, classifying 30 silently articulated words per participant and driving a drone with four commands; the accuracy rests on a random within-participant split, and the privacy and noise benefits are argued rather than tested.
canon_before: Avoiding facial adhesive electrodes was already pursued with worn objects: a dry-electrode EMG necklace (2024), textile EMG electrodes in headphones (2025) and a fully dry EMG neckband (2025). Worn sEMG word studies that hold out a recording session report large drops from shuffled cross-validation (87% to 64% vocalized, 68% to 54% silent for the 2025 neckband).
delta_from_canon: Moves the electrodes to the fingertips of a hand-worn soft package (liquid-metal interconnects, active amplifier, wrist reference) so that sensing starts only when the user presses them to the face; the decoder (per-channel MFCC into a DNN) and the closed-vocabulary task follow the usual EMG word-classification lineage.
position_in_field: Standard on the sensor (M05): a different answer to facial attachment than neck- and ear-worn dry electrodes, with its privacy and noise benefits not measured. Behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12): a random class-stratified split within each participant, while a dry EMG neckband (2025) and 44 of 143 wearable-sensor word studies (pattern match) hold out a session; random or k-fold splits remain common (58 of 143), so the yardstick is not typical practice. Standard on deployment (M13): PC decoding with no latency, power or command success figure.
practical_value: Suggests a way to give users physical control over when silent-speech sensing starts; usable evidence needs a session-disjoint test with the device re-pressed between sessions, an attached-electrode baseline at the same sites, and command-level success and false-trigger rates.
axes_moved: User control of sensing onset through hand-pressed fingertip electrodes; stretchable liquid-metal wiring on the hand.
axes_unresolved: Accuracy across sessions and re-pressing, unseen participants, unintended activation, noise robustness, command latency and success, vocabulary beyond 30 words, continuous speech.
axes_regressed: Not hands-free: input requires pressing four fingertip electrodes to the perioral skin, which the authors concede adds variability from electrode placement and hand movement.
technical_limits: Manual contact pressure and placement can vary; only four channels fit the hand design; recognition depends on a PC; no latency, power, false-activation, repeat-session, or long-term durability evaluation of the complete worn system is reported.
evaluation_limits: Three participants and 30 words; random class-stratified split within each participant with no session grouping stated; the stated test set (N = 300) does not match 12 samples per class over 30 classes (360), and for S02 and S03 (900 raw trials, 1,800 in Supplementary Table 3) the order of split and augmentation is unstated; the pooled model mixes the same participants; no chance level, seeds or reruns; no quiet-versus-noisy comparison.
deployment_limits: Recognition ran on a PC connected to an Arduino, with commands sent to a Tello drone over Wi-Fi. End-to-end latency, battery operation, mobile execution, command success counts, environmental conditions, and sustained use were not quantified.
scope_limits: Thirty-word silent articulation by three participants (examples are English; the full language scope is not explicitly stated), with four-command drone control. No clinical users, unseen participants, unseen words, continuous speech, multilingual testing, or extended real-world use are reported.
task: closed-vocabulary silent-speech word and command recognition
input_modality: Four-channel surface EMG from the buccinator, orbicularis oris, depressor labii inferioris, and mentalis using fingertip dry electrodes
sensor_hardware: Ecoflex-encapsulated hand-worn interface with transparent FPC solder-coated fingertip dry electrodes, liquid-metal interconnects, an active EMG amplification circuit, a wrist reference electrode, and Arduino digitization at 1 kHz
output_type: 30 word-class labels; four labels mapped to drone commands
vocabulary_type: closed word-level command vocabulary; examples are English, but the full language scope is not explicitly stated
vocabulary_size: 30 words; four-command subset for drone control
metrics: Mean participant-dependent test accuracy 97.2 ± 1.3% (S01 97.5%, S02 98.3%, S03 95.8%); combined model test accuracy 92.1% and macro F1 0.921, with five-fold CV score 0.836; Conformer accuracy 91.1%; contact-pressure SNR 31.0–35.5 dB; liquid-metal interconnect ΔR/R0 stayed within ±0.5% across 10–50% strain tests.
evaluation_mode: Participant-dependent stratified train/test evaluation with five-fold cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning; a combined three-participant model; DNN-versus-Conformer comparison; electrical durability and contact-pressure SNR measurements; and a qualitative real-time drone-control proof of concept.

evidence.statement: The authors present a hand-worn soft active EMG interface that acquires perioral signals only during intentional fingertip contact, classifies 30 silently articulated words, and controls a drone with four recognized commands.
evidence.section_or_location: Abstract; Results, Design for Intent-Driven SSR; Application to Human-Computer Interaction

evidence.statement: Participant-dependent DNN models reach a mean held-out accuracy of 97.2 +/- 1.3% (97.5%, 98.3%, 95.8%); the pooled three-participant model reaches 92.1% and a five-fold CV score of 0.836; the mean five-fold CV score of the individual models is 0.916.
evidence.section_or_location: Results, Implementation of Machine Learning-Integrated Silent Speech Interface; Discussion; Supplementary Table 3

evidence.statement: Evaluation uses a class-stratified 80/20 sample split and five-fold CV within each participant; no session-disjoint or participant-held-out test is reported, and the S02/S03 sample counts do not reconcile across Results, Methods and Supplementary Table 3.
evidence.section_or_location: Results; Methods, Software for silent speech classification; Supplementary Table 3

evidence.statement: The privacy (no third-party triggering) and noise-robustness claims are design arguments without a trigger test, noise level or quiet-versus-noisy comparison; the authors name placement variability, vocabulary expansion and sentence-level recognition as future work.
evidence.section_or_location: Results, Design for Intent-Driven SSR; Discussion

evidence.statement: A PC ran the trained classifier in real time, received four-channel EMG through a microcontroller, and sent Start, Move, Turn and Stop to a drone over Wi-Fi; no attempt count, success rate, false-trigger rate or latency is reported.
evidence.section_or_location: Results, Application to Human-Computer Interaction; Methods, Drone operation application

en.summary: Hand-pressed fingertip EMG (M05) is standard: privacy and noise benefits argued, not tested; 97.2% on 30 words rests on a random within-participant split with no session hold-out (M12, behind).
en.sensor: Hand-worn fingertip dry electrodes, 4-channel facial surface EMG
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 97.2% mean within-participant accuracy on 30 silently articulated words, 3 participants, random class-stratified split; pooled three-participant model 92.1%
en.limitations: Random within-participant split with no session or participant hold-out; sample counts for two participants do not reconcile; privacy and noise claims untested; decoding on a PC with no latency, power or command success figure.

title: SoniSpeech: A Large-Scale Open-Vocabulary Tri-Modal Dataset for Wearable Silent Speech Interfaces
expert_take_short: Open-vocabulary acoustic sensing on glasses (M05) and a one-speaker paired corpus (M11) are standard; voiced-data gains follow 2020 EMG work; one-speaker, one-run tests lag the field (M12).
expert_take_long: The paper [@zhang2026sonispeech] moves eyewear acoustic sensing (M05) from command sets to open-vocabulary sentences and releases a one-speaker paired voiced and silent corpus (M11). Both are standard: open vocabulary is new for acoustic sensing (closest earlier system: 54 sentences [@luo2020acoustic]), but one speaker and one run cannot support an ahead verdict, and the 9,000 silent utterances are 1.2 times SSR7000 [@kimura2022ssr7000]. Its two findings, poor voiced-to-silent transfer (M04) and lower silent WER when voiced data are added (M03), follow the direction silent EMG showed in 2020 [@gaddy2020digital]. The evaluation (M12) is behind: one speaker, held-out sessions and one run, where earlier acoustic-sensing work held users out [@zhu2007ultrasonic; @luo2020acoustic; @zhou2025m2silent]. The 26.3% silent WER is a floor for this corpus, not evidence beyond this speaker.
expert_true_value: Releases paired voiced and silent sentence recordings of acoustic-sensing echoes, audio and frontal video from one glasses-worn device and one speaker, with a text split that keeps 242 test word types out of training; it gives acoustic sensing an open-vocabulary benchmark, with 9,000 silent utterances, about 1.2 times SSR7000.
canon_before: Acoustic sensing for speech had been tested on command sets or small sentence sets (54 sentences on a smartphone in 2020) and usually on held-out users; one-speaker open-vocabulary silent corpora already existed for EMG (3.6 hours of parallel silent speech, 9,828 word types, 2020) and ultrasound tongue imaging (7,484 silent utterances, 2022), and the EMG work had already shown the direction of both the poor transfer of voiced-only models to silent speech and the benefit of adding voiced data.
delta_from_canon: Moves eyewear FMCW echo sensing from command sets to open-vocabulary sentences (5,356 word types) and pairs it with audio and video; the silent part (9,000 utterances, about 13.5 hours by inference) is about 1.2 times SSR7000 and larger than the parallel silent EMG data, and the voiced/silent findings follow the direction silent EMG showed in 2020.
position_in_field: Acoustic-sensing eyewear dataset: standard on the sensor (M05), where the open-vocabulary step rests on one speaker and one run, on the corpus (M11) and on pooled voiced and silent training (M03); behind the acoustic-sensing field on evaluation (M12), where earlier work tests on held-out users and this paper tests one speaker on held-out sessions with one run per condition.
practical_value: Provides a concrete training benchmark and paired modalities for domain adaptation and fusion, with clear known limitations.
axes_moved: Vocabulary scale for acoustic sensing on glasses (open-vocabulary sentences, 5,356 word types); paired voiced and silent echoes with synchronized audio and video.
axes_unresolved: Multi-user transfer, noisy/mobile conditions, re-donning and placement variation, spontaneous articulation, and clinical use.
axes_regressed: Evaluation is narrower than earlier acoustic-sensing work: one speaker, one quiet room, session-held-out tests and one run per condition, against held-out-user tests in earlier systems.
technical_limits: Large voiced/silent mismatch, recorded microphone failures, and fixed-user/fixed-environment training; the echo-only baseline does not evaluate trimodal fusion.
evaluation_limits: Single author, one quiet setting, re-recorded disfluencies and errors, no reported multi-seed uncertainty. Baselines use the first 140 sessions per mode, not every recorded training session. Tokenizer training is described as using the transcript corpus without explicitly stating train-only scope.
deployment_limits: Custom frame, microcontroller/audio board and laptop capture; no measured recognition latency, power consumption, mobile inference or real-world communication study.
scope_limits: One author, read and corrected English sentence prompts, controlled quiet environment, baseline uses acoustic echoes only despite trimodal recording.
input_modality: Ultrasound acoustic echoes for baseline recognition; synchronized audible audio and frontal video also recorded.
sensor_hardware: Two speakers and two ultrasound microphones on an eyeglass frame; FMCW bands 18-28 and 29-39 kHz at 5 ms period, 100 kHz audio sampling, four differential-echo channels at 200 Hz and 80 range bins; laptop camera at 1080p/30 fps.
vocabulary_type: open-vocabulary conversational English sentence prompts
vocabulary_size: 5,356 word types overall; 1,000 subword output units.
metrics: Table 3 silent-test WER: voiced-only training 78.4%, silent-only 33.7%, mixed 26.3%. Voiced-test WER: 16.9%, 55.7%, 15.8%, respectively. Table 2: 5,356 total word types, 5,114 train and 1,684 test types, 242 test OOV types; 39/39 ARPABET phonemes. Session duration 34.1 h versus valid utterance duration 26.7 h. Author-reported results, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Within-speaker evaluation on held-out sentence/session sets; three training-mode combinations and training-data scaling; greedy CTC WER without an external language model.

evidence.statement: All data come from one non-native but fluent English-speaking author in a controlled quiet environment, with parallel voiced and strictly silent modes. Errors and disfluencies were re-recorded.
The dataset has 18,000 utterances and 34.1 hours of session-level recordings but 26.7 hours of valid utterance recordings; these durations should not be conflated.
Silent-test WER is 78.4% after voiced-only training, 33.7% after silent-only training, and 26.3% after mixed voiced/silent training.
The released sentence corpus has 8,000 training and 1,000 test texts per mode, 5,356 unique word types overall and 242 test word types absent from the training texts. No OOV-specific WER is reported.
Microphone channel 1 has high noise in the last 20 silent and last 11 voiced training sessions. The baseline configurations use the first 140 sessions of each mode.
The corpus synchronizes ultrasound echoes, audible audio and frontal video; its baseline uses four-channel differential echoes with ResNet-34 and CTC, greedy decoding and no external language model.

The discussion cites earlier EchoSpeech walking, noise and multi-user results, whereas SoniSpeech itself uses one speaker and one quiet environment. Reviewer assessment: those robustness claims cannot be transferred to this open-vocabulary benchmark.

en.summary: Open-vocabulary acoustic sensing on glasses (M05) and a one-speaker paired corpus (M11) are standard; voiced-data gains follow 2020 EMG work; one-speaker, one-run tests lag the field (M12).
en.sensor: Eyeglass-frame ultrasound speakers/microphones (FMCW echoes), audio, video
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.session: 360 sessions (180 per mode); 20 held-out test sessions per mode
en.key_result: 26.3% silent WER with mixed voiced/silent training (78.4% voiced-only training)
en.limitations: Single author in one quiet setting; population and everyday-environment generalization untested; baseline uses echoes only, not trimodal fusion; no latency or power measurements.

title: Speaking Without Sound: Multi-speaker Silent Speech Voicing with Facial Inputs Only
venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
expert_take_short: Face voices (M08) extend 2020 TTS and 2023 lip-to-speech designs to EMG; the pitch-flattening gain (M02) is within seed noise; silent WER 38.91% has no external baseline.
expert_take_long: The paper [@lee2025speaking] changes two components: the voice comes from a face image instead of reference audio (M08), and the EMG encoder's ContentVec target from pitch-flattened speech (M02). M08 is standard: face-image voice control dates to 2020 in text-to-speech (cited, §II-B) and 2023 in lip-to-speech [@sheng2023zeroshot; @choi2023diffv2s]; only the transfer to EMG is new. M02 is standard: flattening lowers silent WER from 40.12% to 38.91% but raises voiced CER from 9.96% to 13.28% (Table I), with no repeated training runs on one EMG speaker. The evaluation (M12) is behind: only the paper's own two variants are compared, while earlier work on the same split and ASR reports a published model, at 30.0% WER in the recorded speaker's voice [@ren2024diffets]. The cost of face-chosen voices is never separated from vocoder and content-estimator error. Audio-free multi-speaker voicing holds, and the face predicts global pitch beyond gender (Table III); timbre beyond gender and effective pitch disentanglement remain unsupported.
expert_true_value: Shows how to remove audible reference requirements at inference and tests a simple pitch-target intervention that benefits silent more than voiced EMG.
canon_before: Prior EMG synthesizers can separate content and target voice but commonly require target audio. Face-based voice conversion supplies statistical voice cues; it cannot uniquely determine a persons original voice from facial appearance.
delta_from_canon: Replaces source audio with an EMG-predicted ContentVec representation and target audio with face-conditioned identity/global pitch; pitch-flattens training speech to reduce target prosody mismatch.
position_in_field: Contact-EMG content decoding with image-conditioned voice synthesis; one source EMG participant and many synthesized target identities.
practical_value: A reference-audio-free option for selecting a plausible synthetic voice; current error rates and limited user validation prevent assuming communication readiness.
axes_moved: Enables face-conditioned target voices without target reference audio at inference; flattening improves reported silent WER/CER and pitch deviations over the same framework without flattening.
axes_unresolved: New EMG users, actual voice recovery versus plausible face-conditioned output, independence of repeated target assignments, exact evaluation sample counts, optimizer/checkpoint reproducibility and complete latency.
axes_regressed: Flattening worsens voiced WER from 16.98% to 17.48% and voiced CER from 9.96% to 13.28%. Subjective consistency gains are not significant, and silent WER remains 38.91%.
technical_limits: Broad claims that silent EMG contains no pitch information are not directly tested. Praat PSOLA flattening does not prove complete representation disentanglement. DTW aligns silent inputs to a separate voiced target, and local-pitch evaluation uses nearest interpolation. Generated identity is statistically conditioned, not uniquely recoverable from a face.
evaluation_limits: One EMG participant. Repeating target-face assignments ten times does not provide ten independently trained models or forty times as many independent source utterances. Main baseline is the same framework without flattening, not matched contemporary systems. Listener sample sizes and confidence intervals are omitted; paired t-test unit and dependence handling are unclear.
deployment_limits: Requires contact EMG plus a facial image; inference is audio-free but training uses speech data. No portable implementation, streaming timing, longitudinal calibration or intended-user communication trial.
scope_limits: One-participant EMG benchmark, LRS3 target images and offline ratings; no multi-user EMG or clinical validation.
input_modality: Silent or voiced surface EMG for content plus a target facial image for speaker identity and global pitch. Audio is needed for training targets and evaluation references.
sensor_hardware: Existing Gaddy surface-EMG recordings from facial/neck electrodes plus 112 x 112 center-cropped target face images from LRS3. No new sensing hardware.
vocabulary_type: corpus utterance synthesis with variable target voices
vocabulary_size: Exact test lexicon not reported.
metrics: Table I silent WER/CER 38.91%/24.28% with flattening versus 40.12%/26.14% without; voiced 17.48%/13.28% versus 16.98%/9.96%. Table II silent objective similarity 0.5657 versus 0.5626, same-gender random 0.5521; subjective consistency 3.29 versus 3.24 without significant difference. Table III silent local pitch deviation 17.93 versus 18.74, global pitch errors 24.80/30.83 Hz versus 28.91/36.45 Hz for male/female target groups. Author-reported, not independently reproduced.
evaluation_mode: Offline voiced/silent EMG synthesis into sampled target-face voices, Whisper medium.en WER/CER, same-gender-controlled speaker similarity, face/voice consistency ratings and pitch deviations.

evidence.statement: Inference combines EMG-derived content with face-derived identity and global pitch; speech-based modules supply training targets, and pitch flattening precedes ContentVec extraction.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III and Figure 1; PDF pp. 1-3

evidence.statement: The EMG dataset contains about twenty hours from a single speaker, while 50 male and 50 female LRS3 speakers provide target faces. Reviewer assessment: target-voice diversity is not multi-user EMG validation.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections IV-A and V; PDF pp. 3-4

evidence.statement: Table I silent WER/CER improve from 40.12%/26.14% to 38.91%/24.28%, but voiced WER/CER worsen from 16.98%/9.96% to 17.48%/13.28%.
Table II silent objective similarity is 0.5657 with flattening versus 0.5626 without; the same-gender random-speaker reference is 0.5521.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II and Section IV-C2; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Silent subjective face/voice consistency is 3.29 versus 3.24; the paper reports no significant subjective difference in either voiced or silent tests.
evidence.section_or_location: Table II and Section IV-C2; PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Table III silent local pitch deviation is 17.93 versus 18.74, while global errors are 24.80/30.83 Hz versus 28.91/36.45 Hz for male/female targets.

Local-pitch evaluation uses the source speakers face and the matching voiced rendition; nearest interpolation aligns silent-output and reference lengths. Reviewer assessment: this is not direct measurement of an unobserved silent acoustic target or all target voices.
evidence.section_or_location: Section IV-B3 and continuation; PDF pp. 3-4

evidence.statement: Two targets from each gender group are sampled per source utterance across ten repetitions, yielding forty times as many synthesized assignments. Reviewer assessment: these are repeated source utterances, not forty times as much independent EMG evidence.

Pitch flattening is performed with Praat autocorrelation and PSOLA. Reviewer assessment: downstream ablation improvements do not by themselves demonstrate complete pitch disentanglement in the learned content embedding.
evidence.section_or_location: Section III-A4 and results; PDF pp. 2-4

evidence.statement: The discussion explicitly recognizes one-speaker EMG data and treats multi-speaker EMG evaluation and stronger vocoding as future work.

en.summary: Face voices (M08) extend 2020 TTS and 2023 lip-to-speech designs to EMG; the pitch-flattening gain (M02) is within seed noise; silent WER 38.91% has no external baseline.
en.sensor: Existing facial/neck surface EMG plus target face image
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Silent WER 38.91% with pitch flattening vs 40.12% without
en.limitations: Only one EMG participant; multi-user decoding and faithful personal-voice recovery not shown; main baseline is the same framework without flattening.

title: Toward Robust, Reproducible, and Widely Accessible Intracranial Language Brain-Computer Interfaces: A Comprehensive Review of Neural Mechanisms, Hardware, Algorithms, Evaluation, Clinical Pathways and Future Directions
expert_take_short: A useful systems-level agenda for speech neuroprostheses, but its composite benchmark is unvalidated and several source attributions and mechanism claims need correction before reuse.
expert_take_long: The strongest contribution of this review is its insistence that speech neuroprostheses be judged as complete communication systems: electrode coverage, calibration burden, user control, latency, voice identity and longitudinal reliability belong alongside decoding accuracy. Its critical synthesis tables and explicit discussion of mixed chronic-stability evidence are useful starting points for planning studies. The proposed numerical benchmark should be treated more cautiously. Direction normalization and weighted averaging make a formula reproducible, but do not establish that heterogeneous tasks or languages measure equivalent user benefit. The default text-rate component saturates at 30 words per minute, for example, so faster systems become indistinguishable on that component; no prospective utility validation or sensitivity analysis is reported. Source attribution also needs correction. Section 4.2 credits a 78-word-per-minute result to Chartier with reference 8, although reference 8 is the Silva review and the paper itself attributes that result to Metzger in Table 1. The discussion further extends SPARC, an audio-to-articulation and speech-synthesis framework, into claims about neural intent and ownership without a corresponding BCI control experiment. Similarly, contextual sequence decoding and saliency are not themselves proof of a causal cortical mechanism. These limitations do not erase the value of the proposed design questions, but they make the review better suited as a structured agenda and checklist than as an authoritative benchmark, primary-result database or validated clinical selection guide.
expert_true_value: Organizes the questions a credible longitudinal communication study should answer, especially calibration, user agency and measurement boundaries.
canon_before: Speech neuroprosthesis reviews already discuss neural features, decoding and clinical translation. Individual studies report incompatible WER/PER, acoustic correlations, listening scores and latency boundaries, limiting direct comparisons.
delta_from_canon: Connects mechanism, recording choice, experiment design, decoder, evaluation and deployment; proposes utility scores and scenario-specific minimum-system profiles as organizing tools.
position_in_field: Broad intracranial language-BCI synthesis connecting neural mechanisms to experimental and deployment design, adjacent to non-invasive articulatory SSI.
practical_value: A useful checklist for research design and reporting after source verification; unsuitable for automatic import of benchmark values or clinical readiness scores.
axes_moved: Makes calibration, user agency, longitudinal stability, heterogeneous hardware and task-specific evaluation explicit parts of the design problem.
axes_unresolved: Validation of score weights/ranges, cross-language perceptual calibration, prospective user utility, source-attribution accuracy and evidence for the proposed modality-specific deployment profiles.
axes_regressed: No measured regression in a new system. Compression into a single normalized score can hide meaningful metric differences and trade-offs.
technical_limits: Composite scores depend on author-selected clipping ranges and weights; correlated metrics and perceptual proxies may double-count evidence. CTC path factorization does not explicitly model output-label dependencies, and saliency or recurrent-model gains do not independently validate cortical causality.
evaluation_limits: Narrative rather than reproducibly screened systematic coverage. The composite benchmark is not applied to a shared multilingual cohort, validated against user outcomes or subjected to reported weight/range sensitivity analysis. Underlying studies vary in participant population, speaking mode, output task and measurement boundary.
deployment_limits: The review itself supplies no prospective deployment validation. Its hardware tables mix acute clinical recording experience with investigational chronic communication systems; supplier examples are expressly illustrative rather than verified procurement or approval guidance.
scope_limits: Narrative literature review, not a new clinical trial, exhaustive evidence synthesis or validated consensus standard. Primary intracranial studies coexist with acoustic modeling and non-invasive perception examples.
input_modality: Primarily intracortical MEA, cortical-surface ECoG and depth SEEG; non-invasive and acoustic studies are included as supporting context.
sensor_hardware: Reviews penetrating microelectrode arrays, macro/high-density ECoG and SEEG depth electrodes, with qualitative coverage, resolution, stability and deployment trade-offs. No original acquisition system.
output_type: literature synthesis and proposed evaluation framework
vocabulary_type: Heterogeneous reviewed tasks, not one recognition vocabulary
vocabulary_size: Not applicable to this review; cited vocabularies range from fixed commands to large lexical sets.
metrics: No original decoder score or measured benchmark result. Table 5 proposes discrete-task weights: WER 0.35, PER 0.20, onset latency 0.15, communication rate 0.10 and perceptual score 0.20. Its rate range is 0-30 wpm and latency range 0-3 s. Other templates cover synthesis, prosody and conversation. All reported accuracy, correlation, speed and stability examples belong to cited studies and are not directly comparable pooled results.
evaluation_mode: Narrative literature synthesis, qualitative decision matrices and proposed direction-normalized weighted benchmark templates; no new experiment or pooled effect estimate.

evidence.statement: The review organizes five coupled questions across neural representations, recording, datasets, decoding and deployment, and proposes a unified evaluation framework rather than reporting a new decoder experiment.
Table 2 separates consensus, unresolved disputes, sources of discrepancy and proposed resolving experiments across four neural-mechanism themes.

The deployment utility in Equations 1-2 combines normalized accuracy/responsiveness with infection, power, packaging, care and home-use burdens. No empirical validation of this composite against user outcomes is reported.

Equations 3-5 and Table 5 specify clipped normalized metrics, task weights and language/task aggregation. The proposed text-rate component saturates at 30 wpm; reviewer assessment: higher rates receive the same component score, and sensitivity and user-utility validation are needed.

Section 4.2 attributes 78 wpm to Chartier et al. with reference 8, but reference 8 is the Silva et al. review. Table 1 instead attributes median 78 wpm to Metzger et al. reference 50. Reviewer assessment: the attribution is internally inconsistent.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1; Section 4.2; References 8/50; PDF pp. 4, 19, 32 and 34

evidence.statement: The paper describes SPARC as an acoustic-to-articulatory framework, yet later interprets its features as controlled by neural intent in a shared-control argument. Reviewer assessment: audio representation disentanglement does not establish BCI user-intent control or ownership.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 4.2 and 6.4; Reference 53; PDF pp. 18-19, 28 and 34

evidence.statement: The discussion describes CTC as implicitly modeling label dependencies and as an acoustic-linguistic dual path. Reviewer assessment: a contextual encoder and CTC path summation are not an explicit output-label language model or simultaneous acoustic reconstruction.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 2.4 and 4.4; Reference 108; PDF pp. 10, 20 and 37

evidence.statement: The reliability-first home-use profile recommends ECoG or SEEG, while the hardware matrix explicitly states that chronic unattended SEEG home-use evidence is limited. Reviewer assessment: the profile remains a design heuristic rather than demonstrated modality superiority.
Longitudinal sections contrast selected multimonth speech-control successes with continuing retraining, connectors and setup burden; broad unattended no-recalibration use is not established.

Table 1 combines text decoding, acoustic reconstruction, speech perception, voice conversion and clinical control, with different metrics and populations. Reviewer assessment: these examples should not be pooled into a single performance comparison.

The full review presents narrative coverage and 143 bibliography entries without a reproducible search/screening or evidence-quality audit protocol. Reviewer assessment: comprehensive scope is not proof of exhaustive systematic coverage.

en.summary: Review of intracranial language BCIs covering neural mechanisms, hardware, algorithms, evaluation and clinical pathways, proposing a composite weighted benchmark.
en.sensor: Review: intracortical arrays, ECoG, SEEG
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Composite benchmark is unvalidated with author-chosen weights; narrative rather than systematic; some source attributions and mechanism claims need correction.

title: Transfer Learning from ImageNet for MEG-Based Decoding of Imagined Speech
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
expert_take_short: ImageNet transfer on MEG scalograms (M03) and the learned sensor projection (M06) are standard; the ablation is new; rest and reading-order confounds limit the binary tasks (M12).
expert_take_long: The paper [@jhilal2026imagenet] fine-tunes ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 and ViT-Tiny on MEG scalograms mixed by a learned three-map sensor projection (M03, M06). M03 is standard: ImageNet-pretrained CNNs on MEG Morlet scalograms of imagined phrases were used earlier [@dash2020meg], and a frozen ImageNet ResNet50 on imagined-speech EEG [@panachakel2021tl]; the new evidence is an ablation over 21 participants with leave-one-subject-out testing. M06 is standard: the learned projection is compared only with PCA-3, not with the earlier sensor mosaic [@dash2020meg]. M12 is standard, with permutation tests against chance, but the binary tasks contrast imagery with rest and with silent reading that always precedes it, and no articulatory EMG is recorded, unlike [@orpella2022imagery].
expert_true_value: A controlled ablation, over 21 participants with leave-one-subject-out testing, of what ImageNet initialization adds to MEG scalogram decoding of imagined speech (5.7-8.9 points of balanced accuracy); the transfer design itself follows earlier MEG work.
canon_before: Before this paper, ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet, ResNet-101 and Inception-ResNet-v2 had been applied to Morlet scalograms of MEG during imagined phrases, reaching 93.24% for five phrases within subject with a 14x14 sensor mosaic (2020), and a frozen ImageNet ResNet50 had been applied to imagined-speech EEG (2021). MEG imagery-versus-reading and imagined-syllable decoding had been reported with articulatory EMG control (2022).
delta_from_canon: Replaces the fixed sensor mosaic with a learned three-map sensor projection, adds ViT-Tiny and partial fine-tuning, tests held-out participants, and ablates pretraining, projection and fine-tuning depth.
position_in_field: Standard on training (M03): ImageNet transfer on MEG scalograms is prior work; the ablation is new. Standard on representation (M06): the learned projection is not compared with the earlier mosaic. Standard on evaluation (M12): permutation nulls against chance, with rest and reading-order confounds in the binary tasks and no EMG.
practical_value: Useful evidence that ImageNet initialization helps MEG scalogram classifiers on a 21-participant imagined-speech set; the binary task results do not by themselves show decoding of speech content.
axes_moved: held-out-participant testing and pretraining ablation for ImageNet transfer on MEG imagined speech
