title: Articulatory Feature Prediction from Surface EMG during Speech Production
expert_take_short: Articulatory route works on vocalized EMG but trails the mel baseline on WER; it exists for ECoG since 2019, and the electrode subset is never tested against equal-size alternatives.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the EMG-to-speech intermediate target to audio-inverted articulatory features (M06) and proposes an electrode subset from feature associations (M05); both are standard. Intelligibility trails the mel-spectrogram baseline (WER 15.5% vs 12.6% for the paper's re-scored baseline), and the SpeechBERTScore gain comes with a different synthesizer (HiFi-GAN for the baseline, an articulatory synthesizer with an external speaker embedding for the proposed route), so the representation is not isolated. The average correlation of 0.9 for EMA and loudness is against pseudo-labels inverted from the same audio. The subset is not compared with searched or random subsets of equal size and ranked 5th of 70 in a later exhaustive test. Silent EMG, seeds and the interval construction are absent.
expert_true_value: Shows that an articulatory-feature intermediate can carry vocalized EMG to intelligible speech on the Gaddy corpus, and gives per-electrode associations with articulator features; it does not show a gain over the mel-spectrogram route or anything about silent speech.
canon_before: Surface-EMG speech synthesis mostly predicted spectral acoustic features (mel spectrogram, MFCC) or self-supervised speech units and vocoded them. A two-stage route through articulatory kinematics inferred from audio existed for ECoG (Anumanchipalli et al. 2019). Electrode subsets were chosen by search over trained models or by a priori information measures.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the spectral target of the Gaddy conv + Transformer encoder with 12-dimensional EMA, pitch and loudness inverted from the paired audio, and synthesizes speech with an articulatory synthesizer; proposes a four-electrode subset from electrode-to-feature associations.
position_in_field: Standard on the intermediate representation (M06): the articulatory route predates it for ECoG and it trails the mel baseline on WER. Standard on electrode subset selection (M05): no equal-size comparison, and a later exhaustive test ranks the subset 5th of 70.
practical_value: An interpretable intermediate and a reasoned starting point for reduced EMG arrays; the intelligibility cost of four electrodes (WER 22.9% against 15.5%) and the lack of silent-speech results limit direct use in a silent speech interface.
axes_moved: SpeechBERTScore 84.4 against 77.9 for the Gaddy baseline, with a different synthesizer; articulator-wise correlation analysis per electrode.
axes_unresolved: Gain over a direct acoustic target with the same encoder and synthesizer; agreement with measured articulation; silent EMG; other speakers; seeds and interval construction; online use and latency.
axes_regressed: PER 36.0% against 33.9% and WER 15.5% against 12.6% for the baseline; WER rises to 22.9%, 31.6% and 46.9% with four, three and two electrodes.
technical_limits: Targets and references are inverted from the same audio, so the average correlation of 0.9 for EMA and loudness measures agreement with the inversion model, not with articulation. Synthesis needs an external speaker embedding. The baseline uses HiFi-GAN, so representation and vocoder are confounded.
evaluation_limits: One male speaker, vocalized EMG, 99 test utterances. 95% intervals of unstated construction, no seeds or reruns. The partition used for electrode selection and for Fig. 4 and Tables 2-3 is not stated; the repository test list has 100 keys against 99 in the paper.
deployment_limits: Offline only; no latency, online, re-wearing, silent-speech or patient evaluation.
scope_limits: Vocalized open-vocabulary English sentences from one speaker of the Gaddy EMG corpus; articulatory features estimated from audio by an inversion model.
task: Predict 12-dimensional pseudo-EMA, pitch and loudness from vocalized-speech surface EMG and synthesize speech from them; compare electrode subsets.
input_modality: Surface EMG from eight face and neck electrodes during vocalized speech; paired audio is used only to derive training targets and references.
sensor_hardware: Eight surface-EMG electrodes at 1000 Hz (resampled to 689 Hz after 60 Hz notch, 2 Hz high-pass and de-spiking); 16 kHz built-in laptop microphone for the paired audio.
body_site: Face, jaw and neck (cheek, chin, under the jaw, near the larynx), per Table 1 and Fig. 1.
output_type: Intermediate: 12-dimensional EMA (three tongue, two lip, one jaw point), pitch, loudness and auxiliary phonemes; final output: synthesized speech waveform.
vocabulary_type: Open vocabulary, vocalized continuous sentences.
vocabulary_size: Not stated; 7,565 utterances is not a vocabulary size.
metrics: Correlation about 0.9 (EMA, loudness) and about 0.6 (pitch) against pseudo-ground truth. Table 2: proposed PER 36.0 +/- 2.7%, WER 15.5 +/- 3.5%, SBS 84.4 +/- 0.7; Gaddy baseline 33.9 +/- 3.1%, 12.6 +/- 2.2%, 77.9 +/- 0.8; resynthesis 32.9%, 10.6%, 86.1; ground truth 30.1%, 8.6%, 100.
evaluation_mode: Offline within-speaker evaluation: Pearson correlation with audio-inverted features, PER with a fine-tuned Wav2Vec2-XLSR phoneme recognizer, WER with Whisper-large-v3, SpeechBERTScore against the recording; electrode removal and subset ablations.

evidence.statement: The authors claim the first method that decodes speech waveforms from surface EMG via articulatory features; among the confirmed articulatory-intermediate studies, none before it uses surface EMG, while ECoG studies used the route earlier.
The encoder has three ResNet blocks and a six-layer Transformer with hidden size 768; linear heads predict EMA, pitch, loudness and auxiliary phonemes.
EMA, pitch and loudness use L2 losses and phonemes frame-wise cross-entropy, weighted 0.5, 1.0 and 0.5 for pitch, loudness and phonemes.
The corpus is 7,565 vocalized utterances (15.6 h) from one male American English speaker, with 200 validation and 99 test utterances; only vocalized open-vocabulary speech is used.
Eight face, jaw and neck electrodes are recorded at 1000 Hz and resampled to 689 Hz after preprocessing; audio is 16 kHz from a built-in microphone; electrode sites are in Table 1.

Articulatory targets are inverted from the paired audio, not measured EMA: 12 dimensions from three tongue, two lip and one jaw point, plus pitch and loudness, resampled from 50 Hz to 86.16 Hz; pitch is normalized by subtracting 130 and dividing by 70.
Training uses AdamW, batch 32, learning rate 0.0005, weight decay 10^-7, and is evaluated at epoch 80 on one A40 GPU; no inference time is measured.
Pearson correlation with the audio-inverted pseudo-ground truth is about 0.9 for EMA and loudness and about 0.6 for pitch; this is agreement with the inversion model, not measured articulation.
Electrode-removal and single-electrode conditions are compared with all eight electrodes by correlation drop; these are associations, not causal tests.
Electrode 4 alone, nearest the larynx, gives loudness correlation 0.73 and pitch 0.32, the highest among single electrodes.
PER uses a fine-tuned Wav2Vec2-XLSR phoneme recognizer and WER Whisper-large-v3 against forced-alignment transcripts; SpeechBERTScore compares with the recording and is not a listener test.

Proposed: PER 36.0 +/- 2.7%, WER 15.5 +/- 3.5%, SBS 84.4 +/- 0.7; Gaddy baseline: 33.9 +/- 3.1%, 12.6 +/- 2.2%, 77.9 +/- 0.8. Error rates favour the baseline, similarity the proposed route, which uses a different synthesizer.
Ground truth scores PER 30.1 +/- 5.3%, WER 8.6 +/- 3.7%, SBS 100; resynthesis from audio-inverted features scores 32.9 +/- 4.7%, 10.6 +/- 3.7%, 86.1 +/- 0.9. Neither uses EMG.
Electrodes 2, 3, 4, 6 give correlations 0.882 (EMA), 0.904 (loudness), 0.538 (pitch), PER 39.7%, WER 22.9%, SBS 83.2.
Three electrodes (2, 4, 6) give WER 31.6% and two electrodes (2, 4) WER 46.9%; correlations fall less steeply than intelligibility.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 3, Set of 3 and Set of 2 rows

evidence.statement: The authors choose four electrodes from feature associations and note agreement with an earlier well-performing subset, but report no comparison with searched or random subsets of equal size; a later exhaustive study ranks this subset 5th of 70.
The authors state that articulatory features are estimated from speech rather than measured and that the model is limited to one speaker.
The model does not generate the speaker embedding the synthesizer needs; an external model supplies it.
Evaluation is automatic, single-speaker and vocalized; silent articulation, patients, re-wearing, latency and listener tests are not reported.
Tables 2 and 3 give 95% intervals without their construction, and no seeds or reruns; the partition used for electrode selection is not stated.

en.summary: Articulatory route works on vocalized EMG but trails the mel baseline on WER; it exists for ECoG since 2019, and the electrode subset is never tested against equal-size alternatives.
en.sensor: 8-electrode surface EMG on face, jaw and neck (1000 Hz); paired 16 kHz laptop-microphone audio
en.task: Articulatory feature prediction (12-dim pseudo-EMA, pitch, loudness) from vocalized-speech EMG and speech synthesis from the predicted features
en.vocabulary: Open vocabulary, vocalized continuous English sentences (size not stated)
en.speaker: One male American English speaker; speaker-dependent
en.session: Gaddy corpus split: 200 validation and 99 test utterances
en.key_result: WER 15.5% and SpeechBERTScore 84.4 against 12.6% and 77.9 for the Gaddy mel-spectrogram baseline; four electrodes give 22.9% WER
en.limitations: Vocalized EMG of one speaker only; articulatory targets and references are inverted from the paired audio, not measured; baseline uses a different vocoder; electrode subset not compared with equal-size alternatives; no seeds, interval construction or latency.

title: CAT-Net: A Cross-Attention Tone Network for Cross-Subject EEG-EMG Fusion Tone Decoding
venue: arXiv preprint (first page carries an AAAI 2026 copyright line)
expert_take_short: Cross-attention EEG-EMG fusion is new among EEG-EMG decoders but rests on a five-fold ablation with no seed count; no EEG-only result, and the subject adversary adds 0.41 points.
expert_take_long: The paper changes EEG-EMG fusion (M06), EEG channel selection (M05) and adversarial subject removal (M03); all three are standard. Bidirectional cross-attention is absent from the 30 ledger studies recording both EEG and EMG, but the ablation behind it is a five-fold average with no stated seed count in which every ablated network falls about 10 points, below a DeepConvNet fed concatenated EEG and EMG (86.56% against 88.08%). The 20-channel subset loses 0.37 points against the full EEG set while EMG stays in every configuration, and no EEG-only or EMG-only model is reported. The subject discriminator adds 0.41 points of leave-one-subject-out accuracy, with no seed count stated. The leave-one-subject-out mean of 85.10% over ten subjects (53.33% to 95.00%) uses no test-subject data despite its Calibration heading, but the five-fold split unit, channel-selection data, early-stopping data and seeds are not stated.
expert_true_value: A controlled tone-level testbed for fusing EEG and EMG with cross-attention and for subject-adversarial training under leave-one-subject-out; it does not show that EEG adds to EMG, because no single-modality model is reported.
canon_before: EEG and EMG were recorded together in speech studies mostly to treat EMG as an EEG artifact; decoders that fused them concatenated features or fused late or at the decision level, and one prior compared fusion forms against EEG-only and sEMG-only models. Gradient-reversal speaker or subject classifiers were the usual identity-removal design.
delta_from_canon: Fuses EEG and EMG with bidirectional cross-attention, ranks EEG channels by trained channel-attention weights to keep 20 of 64, and adds a gradient-reversal subject discriminator, for four Mandarin tones in audible and silent articulation.
position_in_field: Standard on fusion (M06), channel selection (M05) and adversarial subject removal (M03): cross-attention is absent from the ledger EEG-EMG studies, but its ablation is a five-fold average with no stated seed count in which every ablated network falls below a DeepConvNet given concatenated EEG and EMG.
practical_value: A reference result for tone classification from EEG plus EMG across ten subjects; the benefit for communication, latency and daily wear is not measured.
axes_moved: Leave-one-subject-out silent tone accuracy of 85.10% (four classes, ten subjects) against 80.54% for the best listed baseline; five-fold 88.08% against 86.56% for DeepConvNet on concatenated inputs.
axes_unresolved: Contribution of EEG versus EMG; channel ranking inside each training fold; character-disjoint test; seeds and confidence intervals; other sessions, sites and speech-impaired users; online use and latency.
axes_regressed: Silent accuracy drops from 88.08% (five-fold) to 85.10% (leave-one-subject-out) and audible from 87.83% to 83.27%; per-subject silent accuracy spans 53.33% to 95.00%, and CAT-Net is not best on every subject (Table 4, Table C2).
technical_limits: No EEG-only or EMG-only model, so the role of EEG is not shown; the ablation replacing cross-attention does not state what fusion replaces it; channel weights come from a trained model with unstated data scope; SHAP attribution describes the classifier, not neural or muscular causes.
evaluation_limits: Ten healthy participants in one collection; five-fold split unit, early-stopping data, seeds and repeated runs are not stated; each character is shown four times and character-disjoint testing is not reported; no confidence intervals or statistical tests; the headline 88.08% is called accuracy in the text and average precision in Table 3.
deployment_limits: Prompted characters articulated audibly or silently in the laboratory with a 64-channel EEG cap and five facial and neck EMG sites; no online use, latency or patient data.
scope_limits: Four-class Mandarin tone classification from prompted characters; not character, word or sentence recognition and not speech synthesis.
task: Four-class Mandarin tone classification from prompted characters in audible and silent articulation, with leave-one-subject-out testing.
input_modality: Synchronous scalp EEG and surface EMG; the silent condition involves articulation without voicing and is not imagined speech.
sensor_hardware: 64-channel NeuSen W wireless EEG with 20 channels used in the main experiments, and five surface EMG sites, recorded at 1000 Hz and downsampled to 500 Hz.
body_site: Scalp; left and right buccinator, left and right cervical trapezius, and mentalis for EMG.
output_type: One of four Mandarin tone classes; no text or audio output.
vocabulary_type: Closed set of four tone labels; the prompted characters are cues, not output classes.
vocabulary_size: 4 output classes; 30 characters per tone (120 characters), each shown four times per articulation mode.
metrics: Silent five-fold: 88.08% (kappa 0.8415) against DeepConvNet 86.56% (Table 3). Silent leave-one-subject-out: 85.10% against GAT 80.54% (Table 4). Audible: 87.83% five-fold, 83.27% leave-one-subject-out (Tables C2, C3). Without subject discriminator 84.69% (Table 5); without cross-attention 77.63% precision (Table 6). All values are the authors' own.
evaluation_mode: Offline four-class classification for audible and silent articulation: five-fold cross-validation (unit not stated), leave-one-subject-out over ten subjects, channel-count comparison, ablations and SHAP attribution.

evidence.statement: Ten healthy native Mandarin speakers aged 24-35 performed audible and silent articulation; 30 characters per tone were each shown four times, and the output is one of four tones. This is not recognition of 120 characters or of free sentences.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.3–5, Signal Inputs; Experiment Setup / Data Collection; Figure 2

evidence.statement: The abstract reports 4,800 EEG and 4,800 EMG trials, while Data Collection describes 480 trials completed in both conditions; trial totals per condition and after exclusion are not reconciled.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.1,4–5, Abstract; Data Collection; Figure 2

evidence.statement: A 64-channel NeuSen W EEG system and five surface EMG sites were recorded together at 1000 Hz and downsampled to 500 Hz; the main analyses use 20 selected EEG channels and five EMG channels.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.4–5, Data Collection; Preprocessing; Channel Selection; p.9 Table A1 / Figures B1–B2

evidence.statement: CAT-Net combines per-signal spatial-temporal encoders, bidirectional cross-attention, a four-tone classifier and a gradient-reversal subject discriminator; it integrates existing components rather than a new sensing principle.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.3–4, Figure 1; Methods; Algorithm 1; Cross-Modal Attention Fusion

evidence.statement: Table 1 averages are 86.92% with 5 EEG channels, 87.02% with 10, 88.08% with 20 and 88.45% with the full set; 20 channels is not shown to be a minimum, and the five EMG channels are present in every configuration.
Silent five-fold Table 3 gives CAT-Net 88.08% average and kappa 0.8415, DeepConvNet 86.56%; the table labels the value average precision while the text calls it accuracy.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.6, Table 3 caption and K-Fold Cross Validation

evidence.statement: Leave-one-subject-out holds out one subject and trains on nine; baselines that do not use EMG receive concatenated EEG and EMG, so the comparison is not EEG alone against fusion.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.6, Baseline Comparisons / K-Fold Cross Validation; Cross-Subject Calibration

evidence.statement: Silent leave-one-subject-out gives CAT-Net 85.10% mean, GAT 80.54%, DeepConvNet 80.48%; CAT-Net scores 53.33% on S1 and 95.00% on S7, and on S9 it is below DeepConvNet (Table 4).
Without the subject discriminator the silent leave-one-subject-out mean is 84.69%, with it 85.10%, a 0.41-point difference; S1 rises from 48.96% to 53.33% while some subjects fall (Table 5).
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.7, Table 5; Generalization Across Subjects

evidence.statement: In five-fold Table 6, full CAT-Net reaches 88.08% precision, without cross-attention 77.63% and without BiLSTM 78.42%; removing one fusion direction gives 76.60% and 76.46%. None of these is an EEG-only or EMG-only model.

Audible Table C3 gives 87.83% average and kappa 0.8377; Table C2 leave-one-subject-out mean is 83.27%. On S10 GAT scores higher than CAT-Net, so the appendix statement of best accuracy on all ten subjects does not match the table.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.11–12, Tables C2–C3; Cross Subject Results

evidence.statement: The five-fold split unit, whether repetitions of a character are separated, and whether channel selection stays within each training fold are not stated; no confidence intervals or test procedures are given for the main results.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.5–7, Channel Selection; Baseline Comparisons; Tables 1–6; p.9 Table A1

evidence.statement: Preprocessing uses epochs of -2 to 2 s at 500 Hz while Signal Inputs states T=500 without describing the conversion; the centroid loss of Eq. 4 is absent from Algorithm 1 and Table A1.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.3–5, Signal Inputs; Algorithm 1; Equation 4; Preprocessing; p.9 Table A1

evidence.statement: Table 2 gives CAT-Net macro F1 88.08 and recall 88.06, while Table 6 gives recall 88.08 and F1 88.06; Tone 3 with 20 channels is 87.29 in Table 1 and 87.27 in Table 3. Reported values are kept as printed.
SHAP analysis reports larger EMG contributions in most conditions and a larger EEG contribution for silent Tone 2; this explains the classifier and does not establish brain or muscle causation.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.12, Appendix D; Figure D1

evidence.statement: The study evaluates offline four-tone classification of prompted characters by healthy speakers; patient communication, free-sentence decoding, real-time latency and daily wear are not tested, and broader datasets and deployment are left to future work.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.4–7, Experiment Setup; Figure 2; Baseline Comparisons; Conclusion

en.summary: Cross-attention EEG-EMG fusion is new among EEG-EMG decoders but rests on a five-fold ablation with no seed count; no EEG-only result, and the subject adversary adds 0.41 points.
en.sensor: 64-channel NeuSen W EEG plus 5-site face/neck sEMG
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: 85.10% leave-one-subject-out (silent, 4 classes); 88.08% 5-fold
en.limitations: No EEG-only or EMG-only model; cross-attention ablation is a five-fold average with no seed count, below a concatenation baseline; channel-selection data, early-stopping data, fold unit and seeds not stated.

title: Confidence-Based Self-Training for EMG-to-Speech: Leveraging Synthetic EMG for Robust Modeling
expert_take_short: Synthetic EMG with confidence filtering (M03, standard) gives a small real-EMG gain, 23.30% to 21.87% WER on one speaker; large gains appear only on synthetic test EMG.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training data (M03): EMG generated from LibriSpeech audio by a speech-to-EMG generator, filtered by phoneme loss and mixed 1:1 by utterance count with real voiced EMG. The design is standard: a speech-driven generator is the usual approach among 13 ledger studies on synthetic training signals, and lip reading scaled it earlier. The real-EMG gain is small, 23.30% to 21.87% WER on one voiced speaker, from single values without spread, against a baseline value reported by earlier work and not stated as re-run. The large gains, 37.63% to 8.75%, are on synthetic EMG from the same generator and show agreement with it, not robustness. Speaker independence, silent EMG and clinical use are not tested.
expert_true_value: Varies not only the amount of synthetic EMG but also its selection and the real-to-synthetic share, and retrains the transducer from scratch to check the effect on real EMG; it separates high scores on synthetic EMG from the gain on real EMG.
canon_before: Builds on existing EMG-to-speech transduction models and speech-to-EMG generators; paired EMG-speech recording is costly and corpora with different recording setups cannot simply be merged.
delta_from_canon: No new sensor or vocoder: an existing EMG generator turns external speech into pseudo-labelled EMG examples, a teacher phoneme loss selects them, and they are mixed with real data.
position_in_field: Data augmentation for speech reconstruction from vocalized EMG; related to silent speech interfaces but distinct from evaluations on silent articulation or with speech-impaired users.
practical_value: A candidate way to add training content without new EMG recording; there are no results for multiple real EMG users, silent speech or patients, so it does not translate into communication-device performance.
axes_moved: system_design; problem_reframing; data selection and real-synthetic mixing studied, with automatic and human evaluation reported separately for real voiced EMG and synthetic EMG.
axes_unresolved: Condition mapping of Fig. 2, preprocessing implementation, test independence across all components, real EMG from several people, transfer to silent speech, statistical uncertainty, real-time and clinical use.
axes_regressed: The phoneme-loss <0.5 filter shrinks the preliminary data from about 5.4 h to about 0.5 h; remaining phoneme or speaker bias is not measured. Gains are not monotonic in the synthetic share; 1:1 is best among the tested ratios (Fig. 3).
technical_limits: Selecting synthetic examples a teacher model prefers does not guarantee physiologically valid EMG; generator session embeddings and synthetic-speech voices do not correspond to real users. The clip range before the inverse tanh in Sec. III-C is printed as [-1+10^-10, -1-10^-10], with bounds reversed and the upper bound outside the domain.
evaluation_limits: Real EMG from one speaker. Because the continued-training base model saw all real voiced data, the authors move pure real-data evaluation to the from-scratch condition. Test exclusion across models, generator and teacher, split IDs, repetitions and confidence intervals are not given. Fig. 2 and the text disagree, and Table V does not reproduce the stated relative gain. Human transcription: one evaluator, 20 samples; MOS: ten raters.
deployment_limits: Silent articulation, speech-impaired users, spontaneous speech, other days or electrode re-placement, movement, long-term use, and on-device latency or power are not evaluated.
scope_limits: Fixed arXiv 2506.11862 v2 (8 pages) read in full, with figures, tables and preprocessing checked; the authors' public repository was inspected for evaluation conditions but not executed or reproduced.
task: Speech reconstruction from EMG recorded while speaking aloud; compares synthetic-EMG selection criteria, real-synthetic mixing ratio, data amount, and continued versus from-scratch training. Not a silent-speech reconstruction experiment.
input_modality: Surface EMG during vocalized speech plus synthetic EMG generated from speech; LibriSpeech audio, transcripts and phoneme alignments are used for generation and selection. Silent EMG is excluded from the real data.
sensor_hardware: Existing 8-electrode EMG data and matching synthetic signals; no new hardware. Generated signals are linearly interpolated, inverse-tanh transformed and scaled by 100; sampling rates before and after interpolation are not stated.
body_site: Existing surface recordings of speech-related muscles; individual placements of the 8 electrodes are not specified in the paper.
output_type: MFCCs predicted from EMG, converted to waveform by a frozen HiFi-GAN vocoder; DeepSpeech transcripts are an evaluation path for word error rate.
vocabulary_type: Continuous English read sentences; not closed-set word classification, and unseen words are not evaluated separately.
vocabulary_size: Vocabulary size not stated; 7,065 and 3,514 are utterance counts, not vocabulary sizes. ARPAbet phoneme labels.
metrics: Table IV: real single-speaker ASR WER 23.30% as reported by the prior voiced baseline (not stated as re-run) and 21.87% for mixed from-scratch training; on synthetic Libri-EMG 54.21% baseline, 15.90% continued training, 37.63% voiced baseline, 8.75% mixed from scratch. Table III: at 1:1 with 1,300/2,600/6,500 utterances, WER 23.85/21.88/18.03%. Table V human WER 27.35% to 23.58% (real); Table VI MOS 3.00 to 3.25 (real).
evaluation_mode: Offline comparison of phoneme accuracy, phoneme confusion and ASR WER of synthesized speech; mixing-ratio validation 200 real utterances and test 99 real plus 99 synthetic; from-scratch results split into real single-speaker and synthetic multi-speaker tests; human transcription and 5-point quality ratings.

evidence.statement: The task is vocalized EMG-to-speech; Sec. III-A explicitly excludes the silent part of the real corpus, so results do not generalize to silent SSIs.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.1,4; I Introduction; III-A Baseline Model and Dataset

evidence.statement: Soft Speech Units from speech feed a pretrained EMG generator with session embeddings; session indices are assigned randomly and uniformly to match the base model.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2; II-A Generation of Time-aligned EMG Features

evidence.statement: Generated EMG paired with real speech is not a measured ground-truth pair; speech-derived features or phonemes serve as pseudo-labels, and selection uses the cross-entropy between teacher phoneme predictions and true phonemes.

Fig. 1 and Sec. III-A describe a transducer with 3 convolutional blocks and 6 transformer layers predicting MFCCs; HiFi-GAN audio is transcribed by DeepSpeech for WER; the phoneme classifier and vocoder are frozen.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–4; Fig.1; III-A; III-B Automatic Evaluation Matrics

evidence.statement: The authors note that the continued-training base model saw all real voiced data and is unsuitable for pure real-data evaluation, so they add from-scratch training; test exclusion across all components is not shown.
Table II: real EMG from one male speaker, 7,065 utterances, about 15.2 h; Libri-EMG is EMG generated from speech of 1,532 voices, 3,514 utterances, about 8.3 h, not real EMG from 1,532 people.
Preliminary synthetic sets from dev-clean: unfiltered about 5.4 h, phoneme loss <0.8 about 5.0 h, <0.5 about 0.5 h; strict filtering greatly reduces data.
In Fig. 2 (x: training data, y: test data) the cell trained on PL<0.5 and tested on Raw reads 37.28%, while Sec. IV-A gives 29.36% for this condition; the figure-text mismatch is left unresolved.

evidence.statement: At 1:1 with 1,300/2,600/6,500 utterances, WER 23.85/21.88/18.03%, phoneme confusion 29.80/28.57/25.45%, phoneme accuracy 74.19/75.34/77.59%; these are mixed-test values, separate from the real single-speaker Table IV.
Table IV real single-speaker: prior voiced baseline 23.30% WER versus 21.87% for 1:1 mixed from-scratch training, a 1.43-point difference; not a silent-speech value.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.5–6; IV-C.1; Table IV first row

evidence.statement: Table IV synthetic Libri-EMG test: baseline 54.21%, continued training 15.90%, voiced baseline 37.63%, mixed from scratch 8.75%; not results on real unseen speakers.
evidence.section_or_location: p.6; Table IV second row; IV-C.2

evidence.statement: One evaluator blind to the references transcribed 20 random samples; Table V WER 27.35% to 23.58% (real) and 27.04% to 13.57% (synthetic).
evidence.section_or_location: p.6; IV-D.1 Speech Intelligibility; Table V

evidence.statement: The stated 15.1% relative real-data reduction does not match Table V (27.35% to 23.58%); the table values are kept and the stated rate is not adopted.

evidence.statement: Ten raters on a 5-point scale; Table VI mean ratings 3.00 to 3.25 (real) and 3.45 to 4.15 (synthetic); no sample counts, confidence intervals or tests, so significance cannot be established.

evidence.statement: The clip range before the inverse tanh in Sec. III-C is printed as [-1+10^-10, -1-10^-10], reversed and outside the real domain of the inverse tanh, so it is not a reproducible specification.

evidence.statement: The paper covers one real EMG speaker and multi-speaker synthetic data without split IDs, test independence across generator and teacher, repetitions or intervals; synthetic gains do not show generalization to unseen real users.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–6; II-E; III; IV-A–D; Tables II–VI

evidence.statement: The evaluation focuses on selection threshold, mixing ratio, amount, and continued versus from-scratch training for pseudo-EMG pairs from an existing generator; not a new sensor or a practical silent-speech device.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2–6; contributions; II-A–E; IV-A–D; V Conclusions

evidence.statement: Offline vocalized-EMG training and speech evaluation; silent articulation, patients, walking, spontaneous speech, real-time latency and power are not reported.

title: Conformer-based Ultrasound-to-Speech Conversion
review_confidence: High for the fixed-v1 full text, visually checked Figures 1-4 and Tables 1-2; limited for causal explanations, unreported operating conditions and deployment claims.
expert_take_short: Behind on M06: the Conformer reads beam lines of one frame, missing the multi-frame context mappers have used since 2020, with no objective gain; a small naturalness gain, no intelligibility test.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M06 (a Conformer, alone or with bi-LSTM, replacing a single-frame 2D-CNN) and is behind the field there: the Conformer is new to ultrasound-to-speech but both variants model beam lines within a frame rather than time, are compared only with the single-frame baseline, and do not improve MSE or MCD on the paper's own four speakers; as context only, a later re-implementation on one TaL1 speaker, a different setup, fails while multi-frame 3D-CNN and Transformer mappers lead. Evaluation (M12) is the usual MCD protocol, often paired with MUSHRA with a small naturalness gain for the bi-LSTM variant and no intelligibility measure; the abstract understates significant objective degradations, the parameter claim is wrong for the preferred model, and real-time potential is asserted without latency.
expert_true_value: Shows that a listener-preferred ultrasound-to-mel model can have no better, and sometimes worse, spectral scores; its Conformer works within single frames and does not test the multi-frame context that 3D-CNN mappers had used since 2020.
canon_before: Ultrasound-to-speech mapping by frame-wise regression to vocoder or mel features with a fully connected DNN (37 of 51 studies) or a CNN (31) (pattern match), with multi-frame 3D-CNN or ConvLSTM mappers in 8 prior studies; on another single-speaker corpus a 2020 3D CNN lowered test MSE from 0.366 to 0.315 against a 2D CNN. The paper's comparator is the open single-frame 2D-CNN ultrasound-to-mel implementation of Csapo et al.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the single-frame 2D-CNN with a Conformer block over the 64 beam lines of one frame, alone or with two bi-LSTM layers (same frame-level input); first Conformer in ultrasound-to-speech among 51 pattern-matched studies, but no inter-frame context and no multi-frame baseline.
position_in_field: Behind on M06 against multi-frame mappers (3D CNN since 2020; on its own evidence it does not beat the single-frame baseline; as context, a later 3D CNN plus Transformer reaches 15.93% ASR WER on one TaL1 speaker where a re-implemented Conformer-U2S fails); standard MCD evaluation with MUSHRA, without intelligibility.
practical_value: Offers two candidate predictors with different training-cost, model-size and perceptual tradeoffs. The reported low absolute naturalness and unmeasured intelligibility limit claims about usable speech communication.
axes_moved: Perceived naturalness for Conformer with bi-LSTM (32 vs 28); training-time reduction for both variants; parameter reduction for Conformer Base only.
axes_unresolved: Speech intelligibility, truly silent articulation, unseen speakers and words, repeated-session robustness, inference latency, energy consumption, and clinical communication.
axes_regressed: Conformer Base has significantly worse MSE for speaker 03mn and worse MCD for 01fi, 03mn and 04me. The bi-LSTM variant has worse MCD for 04me and more parameters than the CNN baseline.
technical_limits: Frame-level modeling treats the 64 ultrasound beam lines as sequence positions; this is not evidence of long-range inter-frame temporal learning. Spectral errors and listening judgments diverge. The Figure 4 silent-interval explanation is based on one selected utterance and remains hypothetical. Bi-LSTM is larger than the CNN despite the conclusion's contrary generalization.
evaluation_limits: Four speakers with ten test utterances each; listening uses five randomly selected utterances per speaker and 27 non-native English listeners. No repeated-training uncertainty, intelligibility transcription, formal equivalence test or held-out-speaker experiment is reported. Subjective-test statistical handling and multiplicity correction are insufficiently specified for independent validation from the paper alone.
deployment_limits: Offline speaker-specific corpus experiments using ultrasound equipment and a TITAN Xp server. No end-to-end online interaction, mobile inference, energy measurement, walking test or patient evaluation is reported.
scope_limits: Four known speakers, paired corpus recordings and held-out read sentences. No separately documented truly silent test condition, patient cohort, unseen-user evaluation, unknown-word analysis, spontaneous dialogue or environmental robustness experiment.
input_modality: ultrasound tongue imaging; paired audio supplies acoustic supervision and evaluation references, not a reported inference input
sensor_hardware: Articulate Instruments Micro ultrasound system, 81.5 fps; scanline frames resized by bicubic interpolation from 64x842 to 64x128 and normalized to [-1,1]. Training server includes an NVIDIA TITAN Xp with 12 GB VRAM and 32 GB host RAM.
output_type: speech-audio synthesized from predicted 80-dimensional mel spectrograms
vocabulary_type: Continuous speech-audio reconstruction from read-sentence recordings, not a word-classification benchmark; open-vocabulary generalization is not established.
vocabulary_size: Unknown; no lexicon size is reported. Ten test sentences per speaker are not ten word classes.
metrics: Figure 3 rounded average naturalness: natural 96, lower anchor 4, CNN 28, Base 28, bi-LSTM 32 (0-100 scale). Reported p-values: bi-LSTM vs CNN 0.037, Base vs CNN 0.698, bi-LSTM vs Base 0.015. Table 1 MSE for speakers 01fi/02fe/03mn/04me: CNN 0.464/0.623/0.395/0.484; Base 0.511/0.618/0.462/0.524; bi-LSTM 0.482/0.581/0.378/0.449. Base's 03mn worsening has p=0.026; no bi-LSTM MSE difference is significant. Table 2 MCD in dB: CNN 3.221/3.009/3.641/3.172; Base 3.517/3.121/4.133/3.465; bi-LSTM 3.253/3.037/3.704/3.258. Base worsens significantly for 01fi/03mn/04me (each p=0.001); bi-LSTM worsens for 04me (p=0.002). Parameters CNN/Base/bi-LSTM: 4.09M/2.66M/5.35M; proposed-model training times approximately 30%/80% of CNN per speaker, not inference times.
evaluation_mode: Speaker-dependent held-out-sentence regression and speech synthesis: sentence-level MSE and MCD, plus a MUSHRA-style 0-100 naturalness listening test with natural references and a noise-added lower anchor.

evidence.statement: The authors propose Base and bi-LSTM Conformer predictors for ultrasound-to-mel mapping and claim perceptual and training-time advantages over a 2D-CNN baseline, rather than a new sensor.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Abstract and Introduction; p.2 Figure 1; pp.2-3 Sections 3.2-3.5

evidence.statement: The dataset comprises four selected TaL80 speakers, two female and two male, with 204/141/193/190 recordings. Ten shared read sentences per speaker are test data; the remaining recordings are split 9:1 for train/development. Models are speaker-specific.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 2 Dataset and Section 3.2 Baseline; p.3 Section 4.1

evidence.statement: Micro ultrasound scanlines at 81.5 fps are synchronized with audio, resized from 64x842 to 64x128 and normalized to [-1,1]. The synthesis path predicts 80 mel dimensions and uses pretrained HiFi-GAN VCTK_V1.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 2 and Figure 1; p.3 Section 3.5

evidence.statement: The Base network uses linear layers around a Conformer block, with the bi-LSTM variant adding two recurrent layers. Section 3.3 explicitly treats beam lines as sequence steps while retaining frame-level learning, so long-range temporal speech learning is not established by this description.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Figure 2 and Section 3.3; p.3 Sections 3.3-3.4

evidence.statement: Training is limited to 20 epochs, batch size 128 and development-MSE early stopping with patience 3. Base uses encoder dimension 256, 32 heads, kernel 31 and feedforward expansion 3, with AdamW and cosine-decay restarts.

Sections 3.2-3.4 report CNN/Base/bi-LSTM parameter counts of 4.09M/2.66M/5.35M and Base/bi-LSTM training times of approximately 30%/80% of baseline per speaker. These are training-time comparisons, not inference measurements.

Table 1 lists MSE for 01fi/02fe/03mn/04me: CNN 0.464/0.623/0.395/0.484; Base 0.511/0.618/0.462/0.524; bi-LSTM 0.482/0.581/0.378/0.449. Base is significantly worse for 03mn (p=0.026); none of the proposed-model MSE improvements is significant.

Table 2 MCD in dB for 01fi/02fe/03mn/04me is CNN 3.221/3.009/3.641/3.172; Base 3.517/3.121/4.133/3.465; bi-LSTM 3.253/3.037/3.704/3.258. Lower is better. Base significantly worsens three speakers (each p=0.001); bi-LSTM significantly worsens 04me (p=0.002).

The naturalness test uses five randomly selected utterances per speaker, 20 total, rated by 27 non-native English listeners (14 female, 13 male, ages 20-55). Order is randomized and the scale is 0-100; the lower anchor is original speech with white noise at a stated 0.0005 level.

Visually checked Figure 3 labels rounded average naturalness as natural 96, anchor 4, CNN 28, Base 28 and bi-LSTM 32. The 03mn panel instead gives CNN 33, Base 31 and bi-LSTM 32, so the bi-LSTM advantage is not universal across speakers. Error bars are described as 95% confidence intervals.

The reported pooled listening comparisons give p=0.037 for bi-LSTM versus CNN, p=0.698 for Base versus CNN and p=0.015 for bi-LSTM versus Base. These are naturalness comparisons, not word-recognition or intelligibility results.

Section 5 says both proposed models have fewer parameters, contradicting the 5.35M bi-LSTM versus 4.09M CNN counts in Sections 3.2 and 3.4. Only Base's 2.66M count supports a reduction; do not propagate the conclusion's generalization.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Section 5, second paragraph; p.2 Section 3.2; p.3 Sections 3.3-3.4

evidence.statement: Figure 4 compares one 01fi test utterance (014_xaud). The authors suggest inaccurate silent intervals may explain disagreement between objective and subjective results, but explicitly leave this for future analysis. The figure is not a controlled causal test.

The paper evaluates synchronized ultrasound/audio corpus recordings and held-out read sentences, without a separately described truly silent articulation test, unseen-speaker experiment, lexical-overlap analysis or intelligibility transcription. Held-out sentences alone do not establish those capabilities.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 2; p.3 Sections 4.1-4.3; p.4 Section 4.4

evidence.statement: Section 5 suggests potential for real-time use based on computational advantages, but the reported measurements concern training duration. No inference latency, mobile energy, walking test or online communication outcome is presented.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 3.1; p.3 Sections 3.3-3.4; p.4 Section 5

evidence.statement: A nonsignificant p-value for Base versus CNN is not a formal equivalence test. The small four-speaker/20-listening-utterance evaluation and lack of reported repeated-training uncertainty constrain generalization; subjective comparison units and multiple-comparison correction require clarification.

The authors point to https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15544868 for full code and synthesized samples. This review records the source's availability statement, not an independent audit of artifact completeness or successful reproduction.

en.summary: Behind on M06: the Conformer reads beam lines of one frame, missing the multi-frame context mappers have used since 2020, with no objective gain; a small naturalness gain, no intelligibility test.
en.sensor: Ultrasound tongue imaging (TaL80, Micro system, 81.5 fps)
en.task: Ultrasound-to-speech synthesis: ultrasound frames to 80-band mel spectrogram, waveform by a pre-trained HiFi-GAN
en.vocabulary: Read TaL sentences; shared sentences 005-014 held out
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent, four TaL80 speakers (two female, two male)
en.session: Single session per speaker; train/development split 9:1 per speaker
en.key_result: Against a single-frame 2D-CNN, neither Conformer variant improves MSE or MCD (Conformer Base has higher MCD for all four speakers, significantly for three); MUSHRA naturalness 32 for Conformer with bi-LSTM against 28 for the baseline (p = 0.037), natural speech 96.
en.limitations: No multi-frame (3D-CNN) baseline; no intelligibility measure; no seeds or repeated runs; significance tests and corrections unstated; seen speakers and audible speech only; no inference latency despite the real-time claim.

title: Distinct Theta Synchrony across Speech Modes: Perceived, Spoken, Whispered, and Imagined
expert_take_short: 健康な10人の脳波で、聞く・有声発話・ささやき・想像発話の同期分布を比較する基礎研究。認識精度は測らず、有意差や予測性能を裏付ける詳細も不足している。
expert_take_long: この論文は、頭の中の言葉を読み取る装置を実証したものではなく、聞く・声に出す・ささやく・頭の中で発話するという4つの状態で脳波の同期がどう変わるかを調べる基礎的な比較研究である。健康な10人を128チャネルで計測し、主に4–8 Hzのシータ帯域の同期を図示する。著者は、有声発話では前頭・中心・側頭へ広い結合が見られ、ささやきはその中間、知覚では側頭・後方の結合が目立つと解釈する。Table Iにはシータ帯域の前頭同士が972接続・平均重み−0.103、前頭と中心が311接続・−0.073と報告される。ただし接続の選択基準、使った指標、差を引く向き、集計の分母が明確でなく、この負値をそのまま同期強度や統計的な効果量と解釈してはいけない。声を出さない入力を目指すSSIにとっては、有声発話の特徴を想像発話へそのまま移してよいかを考える材料になる。一方、単語や文章の認識正解率、本人以外への転用、実時間動作は一切評価されていない。結論の有意差や予測可能性に対応する検定結果・予測実験も見当たらない。さらに、想像発話の主要な部位について要約と本文の説明にずれがあり、PLIの印刷された式と0から1という説明にも不整合がある。10人での記述的な観察として読み、信頼できる発話認識や脳内の因果関係を示したものとは扱わないのが妥当である。
expert_true_value: 声を出す条件と想像する条件の電極間同期を同じ枠組みで見比べ、発話状態ごとに入力特徴の妥当性を検証すべきだと考えるための探索的資料。結合の図示と実際の言語解読の成功を区別して読める点に価値がある。
canon_before: 本文は、個別の発話状態を対象とする先行研究と、PLV・PLI・コヒーレンスによる既存の結合解析を背景にする。本レビューでは引用文献の優先性や主張を独立検証していない。
delta_from_canon: 知覚から実際の発音、想像までの4条件について、主としてシータ帯域の群平均の電極間同期を横並びに示す。未知語認識や認識精度を前進させた実証ではない。
position_in_field: 非侵襲の神経信号を用いるSSIに関連する基礎的な状態比較研究。発話内容の認識器、音声再構成、臨床用インターフェースの性能研究とは区別する。
practical_value: 将来の発話状態別の特徴選択や比較実験を設計するための仮説を与える。シータ特徴を使えば認識が改善すると判断するには、別途、認識器を使った評価が必要。
axes_moved: 異なる発話条件を同じ計測枠組みで比較する記述的な分析。群平均の同期図と周波数帯別の領域対集計を示した。
axes_unresolved: 統計的有意差、個人差、同期差の再現性、頭皮電極からの脳内発生源の特定、発話内容の認識への寄与、オンライン利用、患者への一般化。
axes_regressed: 認識器の比較を行っていないため、従来法からの性能低下・改善は判定できない。
technical_limits: PLIの式2は位相差の符号の平均として印刷され、式1と異なり外側の絶対値が見当たらず、0–1という本文の範囲説明と整合しない。実装が印刷式どおりかは不明。PLVとコヒーレンスの図は示すがPLIの個別の結果は明確でない。眼球由来の不良チャネル除外は述べる一方、発音時の筋活動・運動・聴覚刺激の影響を切り分ける比較や脳内発生源推定は示されず、頭皮電極間の同期から直接に神経因果を結論できない。
evaluation_limits: 健康な10人の群平均中心で、個人別分布や不確かさを示さない。結論は有意差を述べるが、検定名、実験単位、p値、補正方法を確認できない。図の辺を選ぶ閾値、領域集計の分母、Table Iの指標・差の向きも不明。
deployment_limits: 頭部の128チャネル計測を用いる事後解析。実時間の意思伝達、利用者が自由に開始する入力、装着負担、移動中、患者、長期間の運用は評価しない。
scope_limits: 固定コンテキストのarXiv v1全4ページと参考文献を確認し、PDFの2–4ページで図1・2、式1–3、Table Iを目視照合した。結合行列や生脳波は入手しておらず、数値・統計・実験の独立再現と引用文献の検証は行っていない。
task: 4つの発話関連状態の電極間機能的結合を比較する探索的解析。語や文章の認識、状態の自動分類を評価する課題ではない。
input_modality: 非侵襲の頭皮脳波（EEG）。音声知覚、有声発話、ささやき、想像発話の条件を比較する。
sensor_hardware: 国際10–5法の128チャネル能動Ag/AgCl電極帽、FCz参照・FPz接地、1000 Hz収録。Brain Vision/RecorderとMATLAB 2023aを記載。MNE-PythonとBBCI toolboxで0.5–125 Hz帯域通過、60/120 Hzノッチ、品質不良チャネル除外、重複しない1.5秒区間へ分割する。
body_site: 頭皮上の脳波電極。前頭・中心・側頭・頭頂・後頭などの電極群を比較し、脳内の発生源そのものを直接測定するものではない。
output_type: 研究上の出力は電極間の結合行列、円形の同期図、領域対別の集計表。認識した語・文章・合成音声・操作命令を出力するシステムではない。
vocabulary_type: 不明。刺激の具体的な語・言語と開集合／閉集合の認識条件は示されない。
vocabulary_size: 不明。20クラスという記載はあるが内容が特定されず、認識語彙数へ置き換えない。
metrics: Table Iのシータ帯域：前頭↔前頭972接続／Mean Weight −0.103、前頭↔頭頂344／−0.059、前頭↔中心311／−0.073、中心↔頭頂298／−0.044、中心↔中心290／−0.060。著者が有声・想像条件に関して報告する集計値で、指標・閾値・差の向き・分母は不明。δ・α・β・γ帯域も掲載。分類正解率、単語誤り率、情報伝達速度、実測遅延、検定のp値や信頼区間は報告されない。
evaluation_mode: 事後の脳波結合解析。4条件の群平均シータPLV図とコヒーレンス図、有声発話・想像発話に関する5帯域の領域対別ConnectionsとMean Weightを提示。学習・評価分割を伴う認識実験ではない。

evidence.statement: 著者は知覚・有声発話・ささやき・想像発話の4条件のシータ同期を比較し、発話状態に適応する脳波インターフェースの基礎を目指す。認識性能を示す論文ではない。
evidence.section_or_location: pp.1–2, Abstract and I Introduction; pp.3–4, III–IV

evidence.statement: 参加者は健康な10人、男性6人・女性4人、平均23.7歳・標準偏差3.23。128チャネル能動Ag/AgCl電極帽を10–5法で装着し、FCz参照・FPz接地、1000 Hzで収録する。
0.5–125 Hz帯域通過、60 Hzと120 Hzのノッチ、品質不良チャネルの除外を記載。重複しない1.5秒区間へ分割し、1200試行、20クラス各60試行とする。
20クラスの具体的な刺激・言語・4発話条件との関係と、1200試行が参加者ごとか全体かは本文から特定できない。20クラスを20語の認識実績とは扱えない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, II-A/B; pp.1–4, experimental description and results

evidence.statement: STFTでδ1–4、θ4–8、α8–12、β12–30、γ30–45 Hzのパワーを抽出し、結合指標にはPLV・PLI・コヒーレンスを挙げる。PLVに用いる位相はHilbert変換から得る。
図1は4条件の群平均シータPLV、図2は同帯域のコヒーレンスの円形結合図である。認識器の評価分割や正解率、語・文章の復元結果は示さない。
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2–3, Figures 1–2 and III Results and Discussion; pp.3–4, IV

evidence.statement: 本文は、知覚では側頭・後方、有声発話では前頭・中心・側頭の広い結合、ささやきでは有声発話より弱い前頭・中心結合と解釈する。これは著者による群平均図の記述であり、認識成績ではない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, III Results and Discussion, Figures 1–2

evidence.statement: Table Iのシータ帯域は、前頭↔前頭972接続・平均重み−0.103、前頭↔頭頂344・−0.059、前頭↔中心311・−0.073、中心↔頭頂298・−0.044、中心↔中心290・−0.060と報告する。
Table Iは有声発話と想像発話についての集計だが、Mean Weightに用いた結合指標、差の向き、辺の選択閾値と集計の分母が明記されない。γ帯域には前頭↔頭頂と頭頂↔前頭が同じ54・−0.023で両方掲載され、重複を含むかも不明。負の重みを生の0–1同期値や確定した効果量として解釈しない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, II-C and III final paragraph; p.4, Table I

evidence.statement: 結論は統計的に有意なシータ差と状態間変動の予測を述べるが、検定名・p値・補正手順・不確かさと予測モデル・精度は提示されない。序論の個人差解析についても個人別の結果を確認できない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, I continuation; pp.3–4, III–IV and Table I

evidence.statement: 要約は想像発話の同期を主に前頭・補足運動領域と説明する一方、結果本文は前頭前部・運動関連で低下し後方・側頭に残ると述べる。本文には知覚との比較で前頭の増加もあり、指標と比較対象を揃えた説明がないまま部位の結論を統一できない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.1, Abstract; p.3, III Results and Discussion

evidence.statement: PDFの式2はPLIを位相差の符号の平均として印刷し、式1と異なり外側の絶対値を示さない。そのままでは負の値を取り得るため、本文の0–1という範囲説明と整合しない。印刷の問題か実装の問題かは不明。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, equation 1; p.3, equation 2 and following paragraph; PDF visual check

evidence.statement: 眼球由来の不良チャネルを除外すると記載するが、発音時の筋活動や運動、聴覚刺激による寄与を分離した比較と脳内発生源推定は示さない。信号混入があったと断定はしないが、頭皮の同期だけから脳内の因果的な相互作用を確定できない。
4発話条件を同一の計測枠組みで比較する探索的な価値はあるが、声を出さない語・文章の解読、患者での意思伝達、未学習参加者や別日の性能、実時間利用はこの研究では検証していない。1.5秒は解析区間であり応答遅延ではない。
