title: EEG-to-Voice Decoding of Spoken and Imagined speech Using Non-Invasive EEG
expert_take_short: Drops DTW from an EEG-to-Mel generator (M06, standard) but tests only the ten trained classes (M12, behind); one frozen ASR both trains and scores it, and EEG output beats recorded-speech WER.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the decoder (M06): it regresses Mel spectrograms from trial-locked EEG without the DTW alignment and discriminator of its closest prior, NeuroTalk, and otherwise inherits NeuroTalk's spoken-audio targets, HuBERT-CTC loss, HiFi-GAN vocoder and spoken-to-imagined transfer. Regression is a common objective among EEG and MEG decoders, so M06 is standard, and no ablation tests the DTW removal; timing is fixed by the protocol instead. The evaluation (M12) is behind: voice reconstruction from imagined speech is shown only for the ten trained classes under a random split, while sentence-disjoint tests are the usual approach and NeuroTalk held out a word. The same frozen HuBERT recognizer gives the CTC training loss and scores the output, which, with reproduction of trained class templates, fits the 2-s result that EEG output scores better on WER (not CER) than that recognizer on the recorded speech. LLM correction (M07) is standard and gives small pooled gains.
expert_true_value: An integrated, auditable example of local-context EEG-to-acoustic regression evaluated in overt and imagined conditions, showing why acoustic similarity, recognized text and language-model post-processing must be assessed separately.
canon_before: Prior EEG imagined-speech work includes restricted-vocabulary recognition and reconstruction using overt-speech acoustic targets. Removing DTW from a Generator does not eliminate supervised timing assumptions, paired spoken targets, or the need to test novel linguistic content.
delta_from_canon: Uses a subject-specific EEG embedding, encoder, local-context adapter and Mel decoder without explicit attention alignment or generated-speech feedback, followed by frozen HiFi-GAN and HuBERT components. Spoken-pretrained weights initialize a separate imagined-speech Generator; optional Llama correction and personalized xTTS resynthesis follow decoding.
position_in_field: Non-invasive neural SSI reconstruction study with learned acoustic targets and downstream pretrained speech modules, not a demonstrated general-purpose or clinical communication interface.
practical_value: Provides a concrete pipeline and separate acoustic/text evaluations for studying constrained imagined-speech reconstruction. Clinical utility and natural conversational performance remain untested.
axes_moved: Evaluates trial-level EEG-to-audio-to-text reconstruction under both overt and imagined production, with separate acoustic and text metrics, two utterance-duration conditions, and an explicit before/after correction analysis.
axes_unresolved: Unseen words or sentences, new users, held-out sessions or cue blocks, imagined-speech-specific neural information versus cue or artifact effects, exact spoken-target pairing and preprocessing split isolation, reproducible model configuration, listener intelligibility and real-time assistive use.
axes_regressed: The 4-s condition has worse acoustic similarity than the 2-s condition, while its participants, stimulus composition and loss emphasis also differ. Acquisition uses a wet 130-channel cap in a shielded room, with long subject-specific training and offline whole-trial inference rather than practical streaming communication.
technical_limits: Imagined trials lack contemporaneous acoustic ground truth and are supervised with overt recordings of the same content. Generator architecture and frozen ASR checkpoint details are incomplete. The source describes session-wise and trial-wise normalization, fixed loss weights and later adjustment of L1 weight, and normalized versus directly estimated Mel scales; these descriptions require implementation clarification. ICA is described but does not itself establish that decoding is independent of residual muscle activity or auditory-cue effects. MCD uses DTW despite the Generator's no-DTW framing.
evaluation_limits: Random subject-specific 2:1:1 splits include every class in training, validation and test. Grouping of the four same-cue repetitions, session isolation and preprocessing fit boundaries are not specified. The 2-s participant count conflicts between Methods and Results. Duration conditions differ in cohort, vocabulary and training loss emphasis, so their differences cannot be attributed to duration alone. No shuffled-EEG, class-template or component-ablation baseline, clinical cohort or blinded listener test is reported. Pooled correction tables do not provide imagined-only gains or a transparent reconciliation with the separate-mode tables.
deployment_limits: Wet electrodes require KCl preparation and stable scalp contact; subjects sit with minimal movement in a shielded laboratory. Processing and inference are offline and consume the entire EEG sequence. Reported training takes about 48 h per subject for 2-s tasks or 84 h for 4-s tasks on one RTX 4090. No latency, power, walking, patient communication or everyday-use evaluation is reported.
scope_limits: Twenty-page arXiv v1 full text; no independent execution of author experiments or external verification of data/code availability. Results concern cued 2-s word/sentence and 4-s sentence tasks, not spontaneous thought or unrestricted communication.
task: Offline reconstruction of cued overt and imagined speech as audio and text.
input_modality: Non-invasive scalp EEG during overt speech and instructed subvocal imagination without overt muscle movement. Spoken audio supplies training/evaluation targets, not an inference input to the EEG Generator.
sensor_hardware: EGI wet-type 130-channel high-density EEG, geodesic scalp montage, Cz reference, 250 Hz sampling, KCl wetting and nominal pre-recording impedance below 50 kΩ; spoken audio recorded at 44.1 kHz and processed at 22.05 kHz.
output_type: Reconstructed speech audio and ASR text; optional corrected text and personalized TTS resynthesis.
vocabulary_type: Closed, repeatedly cued stimulus classes; English words and sentences are listed, with participants described as native Korean speakers.
vocabulary_size: Ten classes per evaluated condition: five words plus five sentences at 2 s; ten sentences at 4 s after excluding ten word-only classes from the 20 collected classes. Number of unique lexical word types is not reported.
metrics: Before correction/TTS, Table 1 imagined 2-s results (mean ± s.d.) are CER 0.2710 ± 0.0459, WER 0.4748 ± 0.0947, PCC 0.7484 ± 0.0522, RMSE 1.7163 ± 0.2308 and MCD 7.5284 ± 0.3200 dB. Table 2 imagined 4-s results are CER 0.2474 ± 0.0361, WER 0.4346 ± 0.0525, PCC 0.5834 ± 0.0584, RMSE 2.2331 ± 0.2605 and MCD 9.5125 ± 0.6660 dB. Spoken WER is 0.4466 ± 0.1064 at 2 s and 0.4893 ± 0.0948 at 4 s. Pooled spoken/imagined correction results: 2-s CER 0.2618→0.2487 and WER 0.4586→0.4451; 4-s CER 0.2763→0.2723 and WER 0.4870→0.4658. Word-position associations have p<0.01 in all conditions but R²≤0.02. These are reported values, not independently reproduced or reconciled pooled statistics.
evaluation_mode: Offline subject-dependent training with random class-balanced train/validation/test allocation of 2:1:1 and no unseen classes. Tables 1 and 2 use 100 samples per subject and report CER, WER, PCC, RMSE and MCD before optional correction/TTS. Table 3 uses sentence-clustered regression for word-position effects; Tables 4 and 5 pool both speech modes to compare ASR output before and after language correction with ASR on recorded voice.

evidence.statement: Methods enroll 23 healthy Korean-native adults (20 male, three female), with 11 in the 2-s condition and 12 in the 4-s condition. Results instead describe ten subjects for 2-s evaluation, without explaining the difference. Acquisition is seated in a shielded room with wet EGI 130-channel scalp EEG at 250 Hz and a Cz reference.
evidence.section_or_location: Method: Participants and EEG Recording, PDF p. 3; 2-s/4-s speech condition, p. 6; Result before Table 1, p. 14

evidence.statement: Each auditory cue is followed by a fixation/task pair repeated four times; participants overtly produce or imagine the cued content without overt vocalization. The 2-s condition has 400 trials per task over ten word/sentence classes; 4-s acquisition has 800 trials per task over 20 classes, but ten word-only classes are excluded from training and inference, leaving ten sentence classes. Split grouping of the same-cue repetitions is unspecified.
evidence.section_or_location: Experimental paradigm and Figure 1, PDF pp. 5–6; Dataset, p. 7; Result between Tables 1 and 2, p. 14

evidence.statement: The dataset is randomly split 2:1:1 into training, validation and test with subject-specific training and all classes in every split, explicitly avoiding unseen classes. Imagined-speech acoustic targets are recordings of the same sentences from overt speech, not contemporaneous imagined audio. This is not an unseen-content or unseen-user evaluation.

The Generator consists of EEG embedding, encoder, local-context adapter and Mel decoder, without explicit attention alignment or output feedback. Frozen HiFi-GAN and HuBERT convert generated Mel representations to audio and text. Separate subject/mode Generators use spoken-to-imagined initialization and L1 plus CTC training; the paper reports no isolated component ablation.
evidence.section_or_location: EEG-to-Voice pipeline and Figure 2, PDF pp. 7–8; Training Loss Term and Figure 3, pp. 8–10; Result, pp. 13–19

evidence.statement: No DTW inside the Generator is not equivalent to an alignment-free workflow: task annotations and CPU timestamps are explicitly used to verify synchronized EEG/audio segments, while MCD evaluation aligns reference and reconstructed mel-cepstral sequences with DTW after voice-activity filtering.
evidence.section_or_location: Signal Segmentation, PDF p. 4; EEG-to-Voice pipeline, p. 7; Evaluation Metrics: MCD, p. 12

evidence.statement: Table 1 reports imagined 2-s mean ± s.d.: CER 0.2710 ± 0.0459, WER 0.4748 ± 0.0947, RMSE 1.7163 ± 0.2308, MCD 7.5284 ± 0.3200 and PCC 0.7484 ± 0.0522. Spoken CER is 0.2519 ± 0.0539 and WER 0.4466 ± 0.1064. Evaluation uses 100 samples per subject, mixing words and sentences, before optional correction and TTS.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1 and surrounding Results, PDF p. 14; Language Model setting and TTS evaluation exclusions, pp. 11–12

evidence.statement: Table 2 reports imagined 4-s mean ± s.d.: CER 0.2474 ± 0.0361, WER 0.4346 ± 0.0525, RMSE 2.2331 ± 0.2605, MCD 9.5125 ± 0.6660 and PCC 0.5834 ± 0.0584. Spoken CER is 0.2929 ± 0.0668 and WER 0.4893 ± 0.0948. Twelve subjects are evaluated with 100 sentence samples per subject. Compared with 2-s tasks, cohorts, stimulus composition and loss emphasis differ, so the acoustic decrease is not a controlled duration-only effect.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2 and surrounding Results, PDF pp. 14–16; experimental condition cohorts, p. 6

evidence.statement: Table 4 pools spoken and imagined outputs: at 2 s, CER changes from 0.2618 ± 0.0480 to 0.2487 ± 0.0504 and WER from 0.4586 ± 0.0968 to 0.4451 ± 0.0972 after correction. Table 5 pooled 4-s CER changes from 0.2763 ± 0.0658 to 0.2723 ± 0.0665 and WER from 0.4870 ± 0.0699 to 0.4658 ± 0.0788. These are not imagined-only correction results; the source does not transparently reconcile the pooled values with Tables 1 and 2.
evidence.section_or_location: Figure 7 caption and Tables 4–5 with captions, PDF pp. 18–19; separate-mode Tables 1–2, p. 14

evidence.statement: Sentence-clustered word-position regression reports positive coefficients with p<0.01 in all conditions, but the source states R²≤0.02 and non-monotonic binned patterns. The imagined coefficients are 0.136 (SE 0.018, p<0.001) at 2 s and 0.051 (SE 0.015, p<0.01) at 4 s. Position explains only a small fraction of the decoding-error variation.
evidence.section_or_location: Figure 6, Table 3 and Word position effects on character error rate, PDF pp. 16–17

evidence.statement: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct generates five correction candidates, filters allowed characters, word-count changes and article preservation, and scores similarity to the original ASR text plus perplexity. The original text is retained as a candidate; these constraints are a design intent, not an independent test that every correction preserves meaning. Personalized xTTS-v2 resynthesis is auxiliary and excluded from primary quantitative evaluation.
evidence.section_or_location: Language Model setting, PDF pp. 10–11; TTS Model Few-shot Fine-tuning, pp. 11–12

evidence.statement: The paper explicitly states that all generation is offline, without real-time constraints, using the entire EEG sequence. Training takes approximately 48 h per subject at 2 s or 84 h at 4 s on one RTX 4090, for about 1500 epochs. No real-time, power, walking, clinical communication or listener-intelligibility result is reported.
evidence.section_or_location: EEG-to-Voice pipeline, PDF pp. 7–8; Generator Training, p. 10; Participants/EEG Recording, p. 3; complete Results, pp. 13–19

evidence.statement: Implementation details need clarification: normalization is described both per session and per trial; loss weights are described as fixed but L1 weight is later reduced when training is unstable; normalized Mel outputs and direct target-scale estimation are both described. Exact layer configuration, ASR checkpoint, loss coefficients, split isolation for preprocessing, cue-block/session holdout and imagined/overt trial pairing are not sufficiently specified for reproduction.
evidence.section_or_location: Neural signal processing, PDF pp. 3–4; Dataset, pp. 6–7; Pretrained Components, p. 8; Coefficient Tuning and Generator Training, pp. 9–10; Results, p. 14

evidence.statement: ICA artifact removal is reported, but no shuffled-EEG, class-template, cue-specific or residual-muscle control is evaluated in Results. With repeated known classes and random within-subject splitting, the study does not establish decoding of arbitrary imagined sentences or performance on a new session, user or clinical population. This is a limitation of validation scope, not a claim that leakage or artifact dependence was demonstrated.
evidence.section_or_location: Neural signal processing, PDF p. 4; Experimental paradigm and Dataset, pp. 5–7; complete Results, pp. 13–19

evidence.statement: The authors claim direct open-loop EEG-to-Voice reconstruction without DTW or explicit temporal alignment, comparable linguistic accuracy for spoken and imagined conditions, and minimal correction without semantic distortion. Their reported quantitative experiments are offline subject-specific tests of known cued stimuli and correction metrics pooled across speech modes.
evidence.section_or_location: Abstract, PDF p. 1; Introduction, p. 2; Dataset and pipeline, pp. 7–8; Figure 7 and Tables 4–5, pp. 18–19

en.summary: Drops DTW from an EEG-to-Mel generator (M06, standard) but tests only the ten trained classes (M12, behind); one frozen ASR both trains and scores it, and EEG output beats recorded-speech WER.
en.sensor: EGI 130-channel wet high-density scalp EEG
en.task: Speech synthesis and text from EEG
en.vocabulary: 10 closed classes per condition (words and sentences)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Imagined WER 47.48% at 2 s, 43.46% at 4 s, closed classes, before correction
en.limitations: Random splits include every class in training and test, imagined trials use overt audio as targets, and no unseen content, real-time use or clinical test is shown.

title: emg2speech: Synthesizing speech from electromyography using self-supervised speech models
expert_take_short: Ports a 2023 ECoG recipe (text-to-speech HuBERT units, CTC) to EMG; phoneme guidance (M02) and covariance input (M06) are standard. Table 6 mixes listener and decoder scoring, so it ranks no route.
expert_take_long: The paper [@gowda2025emg2speech] ports to surface EMG the ECoG synthesis pipeline it says it adopts [@metzger2023]: HuBERT units from text-to-speech audio, learned with CTC (§5.3) and voiced by a pretrained Tacotron "vocoder" (§2). Its own changes, an auxiliary phoneme CTC head with a consistency loss (M02) and a covariance input from the same group's earlier work (M06) [@gowda2025], are standard; auxiliary phoneme losses for EMG voicing date from 2021 [@gaddy2021improved]. The strongest confound is the paper's Table 6: its text route reports 51.17% WER (decoder output) against 61.02% for direct synthesis (listener transcripts, 460 sentences, Appendix D.3), but the scoring differs and the text decoder was trained "on all 460 sentences" (Appendix D.4), so the table ranks neither route, and the "more fluid, natural interaction" claimed for direct synthesis is untested. Listener WERs of 62.55% (healthy, vocalized) and 50.82% (one ALS participant, silent) stay far above 11.89% to 12.2% for silent EMG on the Gaddy benchmark [@lee2026gets; @benster2024crossmodal], with other corpora and scoring.
expert_true_value: A public pair of surface-EMG speech corpora (about 9 hours vocalized from one healthy participant, about 1 hour silent from one participant with ALS) with sentence-disjoint splits, and a measured, seed-averaged effect of auxiliary phoneme guidance on HuBERT-unit decoding; listener WERs (62.55% and 50.82%) set a baseline for synthesis without the user's own audio.
canon_before: Training speech decoders on HuBERT units derived from text-to-speech or reference-speaker audio, learned with CTC and voiced by a pretrained Tacotron unit vocoder, was established for ECoG in 2023 (Metzger et al.); synthetic targets from cued text were used for an ALS participant's intracortical voice synthesis in 2024 (Wairagkar et al.). Auxiliary phoneme losses for EMG voicing date from 2021 (Gaddy and Klein), and covariance-type EMG input from the same group's 2025 EMG-to-text work.
delta_from_canon: Applies the text-to-speech HuBERT-unit recipe to 31-channel surface EMG, replaces frame-aligned phoneme labels with an auxiliary phoneme CTC head plus a unit-phoneme consistency loss, and demonstrates it on one healthy (vocalized) and one ALS (silent) participant.
position_in_field: Surface-EMG speech synthesis without the user's audio: standard on training-only supervision (M02) and intermediate representation (M06), standard on evaluation (M12) with sentence-disjoint tests; its Table 6 comparison of a text route (51.17% WER, decoder output) with direct synthesis (61.02%, listener transcripts) mixes scoring methods and does not rank the routes.
practical_value: Shows that intelligible-in-part speech can be synthesized from EMG for a person who cannot produce audio, without recorded target speech; at 50.82% listener WER on an about 300-word corpus it is not yet a communication channel.
axes_moved: Phoneme-guided training lowers unit error rate from 56.08% to 51.81% (healthy) and from 52.29% to 46.98% (ALS), five seeds; covariance input beats EMG spectrogram input (56.08% against 62.71% UER); listener transcription of all 460 test sentences.
axes_unresolved: Whether HuBERT units beat a spectral target for EMG; the cost of a text-to-speech target against the user's own audio; silent articulation at large vocabulary; more than one participant per condition; sessions, days and electrode re-placement; real-time use.
axes_regressed: Table 6 puts direct synthesis behind the paper's own phoneme-to-word text route, 61.02% against 51.17% WER (42.79% against 38.19% PER), but the first is listener-scored and the second decoder-scored, with the text decoder trained on 'all 460 sentences'; output voice and timing follow the text-to-speech system, not the user.
technical_limits: Targets are units of a single text-to-speech voice, so prosody and timing of the user are not modelled; no spectral-target baseline; the phoneme-guided gain is shown on unit error rate only; the EMG2TEXT comparison is trained on 'all 460 sentences' with no stated held-out split.
evaluation_limits: One participant per corpus; recording sessions and session separation not stated; Tables 1 to 4 average five seeds with the meaning of the plus-minus value not stated; the seed or checkpoint behind the listener audio is not named; the mean opinion score (3.79) covers 35 sentences; ALS and healthy WERs come from vocabularies of about 300 and over 6,800 words.
deployment_limits: Offline laboratory recording with 31 gel electrodes and mouse-marked sentence boundaries; no latency, closed-loop, day-to-day or long-term test; the authors leave distribution shifts and sustained performance to future work.
scope_limits: Based on arXiv 2510.23969 v2 (text, Tables 1 to 6, Appendices A to D) and the public code for unstated conditions.
task: Synthesize speech audio from orofacial and neck surface EMG for cued, unseen English sentences; the healthy participant vocalized and the ALS participant articulated silently. A separate experiment clusters 13 orofacial gestures from 12 healthy participants.
input_modality: Face, jaw, lip and neck surface EMG; training targets are HuBERT units from TTS audio of the transcripts, and the participant's recorded audio is used only for a linearity probe.
sensor_hardware: Monopolar surface electrodes at 31 sites recorded at 5,000 Hz with reference subtraction, 80 to 1,000 Hz band-pass filtering and per-channel z-normalization; the gesture study uses 22 electrodes.
body_site: Skin over the neck, chin, jaw, cheeks and lips; the device measures muscle activity, not brain activity or inner speech.
output_type: Speech audio rendered by a pretrained Tacotron vocoder from 100 HuBERT-BASE layer-6 units; an appendix reports a separate phoneme-to-word text route with lexicon and 4-gram language model.
vocabulary_type: Open set of cued English sentences, with test sentences absent from training and validation.
vocabulary_size: About 6,800 words (healthy corpus) and about 300 words (ALS corpus); 100 output units and 40 phonemes; the appendix text route uses a LibriSpeech-100 lexicon of about 35,000 words.
metrics: Unit error rate (healthy): EMG spectrogram 62.71%, diagonal power 62.16%, covariance 56.08%, with phoneme guidance 51.81% (Tables 1, 3); ALS: 59.18%, 54.27%, 52.29%, 46.98% (Table 4); five-seed means. Listener WER (three raters): 62.55% healthy, 50.82% ALS (Table 5). Pooled 460 sentences: 61.02% WER and 42.79% PER for direct synthesis, 51.17% and 38.19% for the text route (Table 6). Mean opinion score 3.79 on 35 sentences (App. D.3).
evaluation_mode: Offline, per-participant, sentence-disjoint test: unit and phoneme edit-distance error rates, transcription of all 400 + 60 synthesized test sentences by three listeners, and a 35-sentence mean opinion score.

evidence.statement: One healthy participant (about 6,800 words, 9,660 sentences, split 8,500/760/400) and one ALS participant (about 300 words, 600 sentences, split 500/40/60); test sentences are absent from training and validation. The healthy participant vocalized; the ALS participant articulated silently.
A separate gesture study has 12 healthy participants, 13 movements, 10 repetitions each, 22 electrodes at 5,000 Hz and 1.5-second trials; it does not evaluate speech synthesis.
k-medoids gesture clustering reaches 61.41% with diagonal power and 73.7% with full covariance, against 7.69% chance; these are gesture-cluster accuracies, not speech recognition rates.

A linear map from self-supervised speech features to EMG power reaches test correlation r = 0.85; EMG spectrogram features reach about 0.57 and audio spectrogram to EMG power 0.61. The correlation does not establish the inverse EMG-to-speech mapping.

Synthesis targets are 100 HuBERT-BASE layer-6 units from TTS audio of the cued text, not the participant's recordings, learned with CTC without frame alignment; the authors adopt this high-level pipeline from Metzger et al. (2023) and Littlejohn et al. (2025).
Healthy-corpus unit error rate: EMG spectrogram 62.71±0.50%, diagonal power 62.16±0.50%, covariance 56.08±0.91%; phoneme error rate 44.40±2.28%, 44.40±1.51%, 32.78±0.66%; five-seed means.
Phoneme guidance lowers the healthy-corpus unit error rate from 56.08±0.91% to 51.81±0.62% (reported p < 10^-6); no listener test compares the two objectives.

ALS unit error rate: EMG spectrogram 59.18±2.81%, diagonal power 54.27±0.56%, covariance 52.29±0.91%, covariance with phoneme guidance 46.98±1.11%; five-seed means; unit error rate is not word error rate.

Three listeners transcribed all test audio (400 healthy, 60 ALS sentences): mean WER 62.55±2.40% healthy and 50.82±1.59% ALS; individual raters 65.09/59.32/63.23% and 52.69/50.97/48.81%. The two corpora differ in vocabulary size.
Mean opinion score 3.79 of 5 from 35 sentences (25 healthy, 10 ALS); it measures plausibility, not word accuracy, as the authors note.

Listeners could write any English words and were not told the ALS corpus vocabulary; sentence-disjoint tests do not show recovery of words absent from training, and word-overlap statistics are not given.

Over 460 sentences, direct synthesis gives 61.02% WER and 42.79% PER; the text route (phoneme decoder, LibriSpeech-100 lexicon, 4-gram language model, beam width 50) gives 51.17% and 38.19%, with its phoneme model trained on 'all 460 sentences'.

31 signal electrodes plus reference and ground, 5,000 Hz, gel; reference subtraction, 80 to 1,000 Hz third-order Butterworth band-pass and per-channel z-normalization of each sentence; seated recording with mouse-marked sentence start and end.

Features every 20 ms with a 25-ms window and a causal model with about 1-second receptive field, but no measured output latency or online use; per-sentence normalization means causality of the network alone does not establish real-time operation.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4: §4.3; p.12: Appendix A; pp.17–18: Appendix D.5

evidence.statement: Phoneme guidance uses two CTC losses and a consistency loss weighted 0.8/0.1/0.1, with a unit-to-phoneme table from a bidirectional GRU; that GRU's 0% PER maps TTS units to phonemes and says nothing about EMG decoding accuracy.

Channel-shift MLP (384 dimensions), four causal TDS blocks, 512-dimensional bottleneck, unit (101) and phoneme (41) heads; AdamW, learning rate 3e-4, weight decay 1e-4, 50 epochs with 5-epoch warm-up and cosine decay, temporal jitter.

The authors state that the clinical demonstration uses about one hour from one ALS participant and does not characterize day-to-day shifts (electrode placement, skin impedance, fatigue, disease progression) or sustained performance; multi-person EMG pretraining is left to future work.
The appendix lists WERs of other EMG and invasive studies but states they cannot be compared one-to-one because data, targets, alignment assumptions and evaluation differ.

en.summary: Ports a 2023 ECoG recipe (text-to-speech HuBERT units, CTC) to EMG; phoneme guidance (M02) and covariance input (M06) are standard. Table 6 mixes listener and decoder scoring, so it ranks no route.
en.sensor: actiCHamp Plus wired gel surface EMG (31 channels)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Human-transcribed WER 50.82% (ALS, silent), 62.55% (healthy), unseen sentences
en.limitations: One subject per synthesis condition, high WER, wired gel electrodes, and no cross-day, re-wearing or everyday-use evaluation.

title: From Silent Signals to Natural Language: A Dual-Stage Transformer-LLM Approach
expert_take_short: GPT-2 correction of one ASR transcript is neither first nor near the field: LLM correction of silent-EMG hypotheses already reached 12.2% WER on this benchmark; here 30% on ~100 utterances, one run.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the recognizer of EMG-synthesized speech (M06, standard) and adds GPT-2 correction of its single transcript (M07, behind). The claim to be the first LLM correction stage for silent speech does not hold: an earlier study passed beam lists and model ensembles from silent EMG on the same benchmark to an LLM and reached 12.2% test WER, against 30% here. The recognizer gain, 36% to 32.5%, swaps the scoring ASR on the same synthesized audio rather than improving the silent-speech system, and later work shows the scorer alone moves WER from 21.32% to 11.89%. Results come from one run on about 100 test utterances whose split is not identified, with no seeds, uncertainty or selection data for the 0.7 threshold.
expert_true_value: Separates the recognition and text-correction stages after EMG-to-speech synthesis; it does not show that a 1-best GPT-2 rewrite beats earlier LLM correction of silent-EMG hypotheses, and the recognizer gain is a change of scorer.
canon_before: Gaddy's Digital Voicing pipeline synthesizes speech from silent EMG and scores it with an ASR (DeepSpeech, later Whisper). Language models already worked on decoder hypotheses: GPT-2 beam rescoring in lip reading, 5-gram plus LLM rescoring in intracortical decoding, and LLM selection over beams and model ensembles from silent EMG on the same benchmark (12.2% test WER).
delta_from_canon: Keeps the Gaddy EMG-to-mel transducer and vocoder, replaces the DeepSpeech scorer with a trained six-layer Transformer ASR, and adds GPT-2 rewriting of the single ASR transcript with a 0.7 confidence threshold.
position_in_field: Standard on the recognizer (M06): the gain swaps the scoring ASR on the same synthesized audio. Behind on the use-time language model (M07): earlier work passed several hypotheses to an LLM on the same benchmark and reached 12.2% WER, against 30% here. Evaluation details (M12) are not reported.
practical_value: A simple post-processing stage for transcripts of EMG-synthesized speech; it gives no evidence that corrections preserve the intended meaning or help a user.
axes_moved: Reported WER on about 100 utterances falls from 36% to 32.5% with the Transformer ASR and to 30% with GPT-2; mean time per utterance falls from 1.42 s to 0.78 s.
axes_unresolved: Separation of scorer change from system change; N-best versus one-transcript LLM input; test split, speakers, seeds and intervals; meaning preservation; listener intelligibility; timing endpoints and on-device use.
axes_regressed: Adding GPT-2 raises mean time per utterance from 0.73 s to 0.78 s; the final 30% does not beat the 28.8% test WER of Gaddy's 2022 direct EMG-to-text decoder on this benchmark.
technical_limits: GPT-2 checkpoint, prompt and confidence definition are unstated, and the 0.7 threshold and edit filters have no stated selection data; the LLM sees one transcript, not beam lists; training data and objective of the Transformer ASR are unstated; sEMG is given as 1000 Hz (Sec. 2.2) but processing as 16 kHz (Sec. 3); Fig. 2 and Sec. 2.3 disagree on a convolutional front end.
evaluation_limits: About 100 test utterances, one run, no seeds, intervals or significance tests; test split, speakers and sessions not identified; no selection data for checkpoints or the 0.7 threshold; WER normalization unstated; no listener test of the synthesized speech; the baseline may be quoted rather than re-run.
deployment_limits: Offline GPU timing (RTX 6000A) without defined endpoints; no streaming, on-device or user study.
scope_limits: Silent EMG from the existing Gaddy corpus, read English sentences, offline text output only.
task: Text from speech synthesized out of silent facial EMG: Transformer ASR on the synthesized audio, then GPT-2 rewriting of the transcript.
input_modality: Silent-articulation surface EMG; the recognizer's direct input is audio synthesized from it; vocalized EMG and audio are used in training.
sensor_hardware: 8-channel surface EMG of the existing Gaddy corpus, given as 1000 Hz; no new hardware.
body_site: Facial and neck skin surface; electrode positions follow the corpus and are not given in the paper.
output_type: Corrected text transcript; synthesized speech is an intermediate and is not evaluated directly.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary read sentences; closed or open test conditions not stated.
vocabulary_size: Not reported.
metrics: WER 36% (DeepSpeech), 32.5% (Transformer ASR), 30% (plus GPT-2); mean time per utterance 1.42 s, 0.73 s, 0.78 s; about 100 test utterances, one run.
evaluation_mode: Offline comparison of three recognizer and correction conditions on about 100 test utterances of the Gaddy corpus.

evidence.statement: The changed stages are the recognizer of the synthesized audio and a GPT-2 correction of its transcript; the EMG-to-speech synthesis is inherited from the Gaddy pipeline.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Sec.2.1; p.3 Fig.2 and caption

evidence.statement: The corpus is described as multi-speaker silent and vocalized speech with 8-channel sEMG at 1000 Hz; the speakers and data version used for testing are not given.
EMG features use 31 ms frames, 11.6 ms stride, five time-domain descriptors and 16-point STFT magnitudes, 112 dimensions per frame.
The EMG-to-mel transducer is a six-layer Transformer (8 heads, dimension 768, feed-forward 3072, dropout 0.2) with DTW/CCA audio target transfer and a HiFi-GAN vocoder.
The transcription Transformer has six encoder and six decoder layers, 8 heads, dimension 512, feed-forward 2048, dropout 0.1 and beam width 500.

title: IR-UWB Radar-Based Contactless Silent Speech Recognition with Attention-Enhanced Temporal Convolutional Networks
expert_take_short: 唇の近くに置いた非接触レーダーで、1人の英単語50語を平均91.1%の正解率で分類し、従来方式の74.0%を上回った。別の人、未知語、自由な姿勢や日常会話での性能は未実証。
expert_take_long: この研究の価値は、新しいセンサの発明ではなく、非接触レーダーの反射信号から単語の特徴を直接学習できることを、同じ人の未学習セッションで比較した点にある。唇の正面5〜10cmに置いたIR-UWBレーダーを使い、30歳の男性1人が英単語50語を20回ずつ発音した計1000標本を収録する。各発音前には基準信号との相関による位置合わせがある。軽い前処理後の信号を時間方向の畳み込みと注意機構で処理し、既知50語のいずれかに分類する。20セッションを順にテストへ回した平均正解率は91.1%で、手設計特徴とDNN–HMMの74.0%を17.1ポイント上回る。提案方式の各回の正解率は84〜98%、著者報告の標準偏差は3.3%で、従来方式の10.3%より小さい。ただし全回で勝つわけではなく、第7回は92%対94%で従来方式が上回る。表の20値から平均と標本標準偏差の丸め値は確認できるが、有意差検定や注意機構を外す比較はなく、改善を注意機構だけの効果とは断定できない。これは20人の実験でも、未知の単語を読める結果でもない。声を入力しない方式として有望だが、無声収録を音響で確認した手順、別日への安定性、距離や姿勢の変化、患者での性能は不明。約100フレーム毎秒の信号取得も認識の実時間性を意味せず、全区間を集約する分類器の実測遅延は報告されない。現時点では、位置を合わせた1人の限定語彙認識を改善した研究として評価すべきで、日常会話や一般利用者での実用性能に広げてはいけない。
expert_true_value: レーダー信号の手設計特徴から学習可能な特徴へ移る際の、限定条件下の比較資料。セッションを分離した成績と、非接触でも位置合わせが必要という実用上の条件を併せて読む価値がある。
canon_before: 本文が引用する従来のIR-UWB方式は手設計特徴を用い、単語や母音・子音・句の認識を扱ってきた。本論文は既存装置と収録画面を引き継ぎ、唇の正面のレーダー1台を使用する。
delta_from_canon: レーダーの時間・距離方向の信号に軽い前処理を施し、手設計特徴とDNN–HMMの組から、特徴抽出と50クラス分類を同時に学習する構成へ移す。同じ人の未学習セッションでの比較であり、未知語や話者非依存への拡張ではない。
position_in_field: 唇付近の電波反射を使う非接触の無声発話インターフェース。固定語分類に対する学習方式の改善であり、開放語彙や汎用会話システムではない。
practical_value: 身体にセンサを貼らずに限定語を入力する方式の候補。位置合わせを伴う単一利用者の研究室評価なので、実際の意思伝達の使いやすさや臨床的価値は不明。
axes_moved: この1人・固定50語のセッション分離評価で、平均分類正解率とセッション間の安定性を改善。手設計特徴への依存を減らす学習方式を示す。
axes_unresolved: 未学習の利用者・単語、自由会話、距離や姿勢の変化、別日での再現性、注意機構の個別寄与、実時間処理、患者での有効性。
axes_regressed: 測定に基づく退行は不明。計算量、推論遅延、消費電力、学習データ量と精度の関係は従来方式と比較されない。
technical_limits: 前処理なしの生信号ではなく、静的反射と平均値の除去、距離ビン1〜100の選択を含む。可変長系列のバッチ化やマスクの詳細は不明。自己注意・SEの除去比較がなく、個別の改善寄与は識別できない。
evaluation_limits: 参加者1人の20分割であり20人評価ではない。別日の収録かは不明。注意やSEを外す比較、複数乱数設定の再学習、信頼区間・有意差検定、語ごとの混同行列は示されない。従来方式の具体的な再学習・調整条件も本論文では十分に説明されない。
deployment_limits: 卓上装置で唇とアンテナの距離は5〜10cm。各発音前に基準信号との相関で位置を合わせる。自由な頭部運動、歩行、遮蔽物、異なる環境、患者、連続会話での試験はない。
scope_limits: arXiv v1全5ページの本文・式1〜8・参考文献を確認し、図1〜3と表IをPDF表示で照合。表の平均・標準偏差のみ再計算。引用先の実験を本論文の実績として補わず、コード・原データによる独立再現は行っていない。書誌情報は固定コンテキストを保持。
input_modality: radar
sensor_hardware: Novelda NVA-R661を唇正面に1台使用。元装置は正面と頬下の2台だが、本実験は正面のみ。距離5〜10cm、MATLAB収録画面、各発音前の基準位置との信号相関による位置合わせ。1フレーム256距離ビン、約100フレーム毎秒。
output_type: 既知の英単語50クラスのラベル。自由文の文字列生成や音声合成ではない。
vocabulary_type: 固定された英単語50語の閉じた集合。各単語を20セッションで反復する。
metrics: 表I: 20回の平均単語分類正解率は提案91.1%、手設計特徴＋DNN–HMM74.0%（差17.1ポイント）。提案の範囲84〜98%、比較方式56〜94%。第7回は提案92%対比較94%。本文のセッション間標準偏差は3.3%対10.3%で、表の20値の標本標準偏差を小数第1位に丸めた値と一致する。検定法・p値・信頼区間は未報告。文章の単語誤り率ではない。
evaluation_mode: 20セッションのうち1つをテストに回す評価を20回実施。残る19のうち16を学習、3を検証に使用し、検証セッションは固定乱数種で各回選択。同一利用者・既知50語の単語標本分類正解率を算出。

evidence.statement: 著者は、軽い前処理後のIR-UWB信号に時間畳み込み・自己注意・SEを組み合わせ、手設計特徴方式より高い50語分類正解率を得たと主張する。

evidence.statement: 先行研究由来の2台構成のうち、本実験はNovelda NVA-R661の唇正面1台のみを使用。唇から5〜10cmで、各発音前に基準信号との相関を使って位置を合わせる。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 II.A Data Collection, paragraphs 1–3; Fig.1

evidence.statement: 参加者は30歳の韓国語母語男性1人で、英語教育20年以上、既知の発話・聴覚障害なし。英単語50語を20セッションで反復し、計1000標本を得る。

title: Landmark Guided Visual Feature Extractor for Visual Speech Recognition with Limited Resource
venue: Proceedings of the 4th International Workshop on Multimodal Human Understanding for the Web and Social Media (MUWS '25)
review_confidence: Medium to high: arXiv v1 read in full with Tables 1-5 and the released evaluation code; reported values are certain, the word-boundary condition, perturbation sizes and run-to-run variation are not stated in the paper.
expert_take_short: Lip-landmark graph plus pixel fusion is a standard design (2020 precedent); the 0.90-point low-data gain comes from one unseeded run, and LRW 91.69% stays below 95.0%.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the visual processing (M06) by fusing a graph stream over 20 lip landmarks with a pixel ResNet-18 and DC-TCN word classifier; the design is standard, since a 2020 model fused a graph over 20 lip key points with an image branch on LRW. The central claim, better accuracy with one third of the training data, rests on a 0.90-point LRW-ID gain from a single run with no seeds, so its reliability is unknown. Corrupting the landmarks costs 0.20 points under perturbations of unstated size, and no test drops the landmark stream, so robustness cannot be told apart from low reliance on that stream. On LRW the reported 91.69% stays below the best earlier result trained on LRW clips alone (93.2%, 95.0% with word boundaries), and the released test script defaults to word-boundary input that the paper never states. Evaluation (M12) is not reported to the needed standard: no seeds, perturbation magnitudes or boundary condition.
expert_true_value: Shows that a lip-landmark graph stream reused from the existing face-alignment step can be fused with a pixel lip-reading model at modest cost; the accuracy gain is small and comes from one unseeded run.
canon_before: Pixel lip reading with a 3D-convolution and ResNet-18 front-end and a DC-TCN back-end trained with the Ma et al. recipe (mixup, time masking, word-boundary indicators). Landmark streams were already fused with pixels: a graph network over 20 lip key points with an image branch on LRW (Liu et al. 2020) and a visual-landmark transformer for unseen speakers (LipFormer, 2023).
delta_from_canon: Adds a landmark stream with three graphs (coordinates, distances, feature similarity) and staged fusion into the pixel features, trained without mixup, and evaluates on LRW-ID with full and one-third training data.
position_in_field: Standard on the visual processing (M06): the graph-plus-pixel landmark design has a 2020 precedent (0.96-point LRW gain from a weaker 83.29% baseline, so the two gains do not rank the designs). Evaluation (M12) is not reported to the needed standard: one run, word-boundary input only in the code, no perturbation sizes. On LRW the 91.69% stays below the 93.2% / 95.0% (word boundary) of earlier work trained on LRW clips alone.
practical_value: A candidate add-on for fixed-vocabulary lip reading where landmarks are already computed; the gain does not justify the 18.9% larger model without seeds and a matched-recipe comparison.
axes_moved: LRW-ID one-third training: Acc 85.75% to 86.65% and mAcc 83.41% to 84.25%; full training: 91.15% to 91.48% and 89.44% to 89.61%; LRW 91.69% against a 91.00% DC-TCN row without mixup; one run each.
axes_unresolved: Effect of each graph type alone; seeds and variance; word-boundary condition of Tables 3-4; perturbation magnitudes; silent articulation, sentences, other languages, landmark-detection failures and on-device latency.
axes_regressed: Parameters 52.55M to 62.48M and FLOPs 10.69G to 11.09G; the distance graph alone leaves low-resource accuracy at 85.74% against 85.75%; the 91.69% on LRW is below the 92.1% of the borrowed DC-TCN recipe with mixup.
technical_limits: Depends on a pretrained face-alignment network for 20 lip points; graph matrix products add parameters and compute, which the authors concede may hinder edge deployment; the fixed order of graph additions does not isolate each graph's effect.
evaluation_limits: One run per condition, no seeds, intervals or significance tests; the 20 held-out LRW-ID speakers form both validation and test sets, as the authors state following earlier LRW-ID settings; the released test script defaults to word-boundary input that the paper never mentions; Table 5 perturbation sizes are not given and no test drops the landmark stream.
deployment_limits: Offline word classification on recorded broadcast video; no latency, power or device test, no segmentation of continuous speech.
scope_limits: English 500-word LRW and LRW-ID broadcast video of voiced speech; no silent articulation, sentences, unseen words, other languages or patients.
task: Isolated-word visual speech recognition: one of 500 English words per clip from lip video plus a derived lip-landmark graph stream.
input_modality: Video: RGB mouth crops and 20 lip landmarks extracted from the same frames by a pretrained face-alignment network; no additional sensor.
sensor_hardware: Existing LRW broadcast video, camera not specified; training and testing on an RTX 2080 Ti (11 GB).
output_type: Word label (500-class classification); no speech synthesis or sentence output.
vocabulary_type: closed-set isolated-word classification
vocabulary_size: 500 English word classes
metrics: LRW-ID Acc/mAcc, one-third training: 86.65%/84.25% vs DC-TCN 85.75%/83.41%; full training: 91.48%/89.61% vs 91.15%/89.44%. LRW Acc 91.69% vs DC-TCN without mixup 91.00%. 62.48M parameters and 11.09G FLOPs vs 52.55M and 10.69G. Noise plus landmark perturbation: 85.80%/83.33% (one-third), 90.75%/88.75% (full).
evaluation_mode: Offline closed-set 500-word classification on LRW-ID (full and one-third training, 20 held-out speakers) and LRW; fusion and graph ablations; Gaussian image noise and landmark offsets of unstated size. Acc is sample accuracy, mAcc the mean of per-speaker accuracies.

evidence.statement: Twenty lip landmarks form coordinate, distance and feature-similarity graphs whose features are fused with frame features; landmark streams fused with pixels already exist (Liu et al. 2020, LipFormer 2023), so the novelty is the three-graph split, not the input.

The model combines a 3D convolution and shared ResNet-18 frame features with temporal and graph convolutions and a bidirectional GRU on the landmark stream, a DC-TCN back-end and an MLP word classifier.
LRW has more than 1,000 speakers and 500 words, 29-frame clips (1.16 s), and 488,766 / 25,000 / 25,000 training, validation and test clips; it is voiced broadcast speech, not silent articulation.

LRW-ID holds out 20 speakers with at least 900 videos each; the rest train the models, and the low-resource arm samples one third per training identity. Following earlier LRW-ID settings, the authors use the same 20 speakers for validation and test, as the released manifests confirm.

Text reports 96 x 96 crops, flips and time masking without mixup, 512-dimensional features, AdamW and label smoothing 0.1, an RTX 2080 Ti, and 4 / 9 training days; the released code takes the usual 88 x 88 crop and defaults to word-boundary input at test.
evidence.section_or_location: p.6, Section 4.2; pp.2–3, pretrained face detector/align network

evidence.statement: Acc is accuracy over all samples and mAcc the mean of per-speaker accuracies; neither is a class-balanced score or a word error rate.
Table 3 on LRW-ID: one-third training 86.65% / 84.25% (Acc / mAcc) against DC-TCN 85.75% / 83.41%; full training 91.48% / 89.61% against 91.15% / 89.44%; one run each.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, Table 3 Performance comparisons on LRW-ID dataset

evidence.statement: Table 2 low-resource Acc: baseline 85.75%, plus distance graph 85.74%, plus coordinate graph 86.28%, all three 86.65%; full training 91.15%, 91.38%, 91.40%, 91.48%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, Table 2 Ablation study on LRW-ID Result

evidence.statement: The full model has 62.48M parameters and 11.09G FLOPs against 52.55M and 10.69G, as the authors report; their no-extra-cost statement concerns landmark extraction only, and they concede graph computation may hinder edge deployment.

Table 1 fusion variants range from 85.45% (weighted sum of three graphs) to 86.65% (selected fusion) in low-resource Acc; they are different models from one run each, so they give no estimate of run-to-run variation.
evidence.section_or_location: p.6, Table 1 and Section 4.3 Lip Dynamics Fusion

evidence.statement: Table 4 on LRW: 91.69% against DC-TCN 91.00% marked without mixup; that row matches the with-word-boundary, no-mixup ablation of Ma et al., whose full recipe reaches 92.1%, and earlier work trained on LRW clips alone with audio-token targets reports 93.2% (95.0% with word boundaries).

title: Lightweight Diffusion-based Framework for Online Imagined Speech Decoding in Aphasia
expert_take_short: Diffusion EEG decoder (M06) standard: Diff-E lineage, no ablation, not smaller. Online use (M13) standard: one patient, 20 trials. M12: Table I overall row disagrees with class rows.
expert_take_long: The paper [@ko2025lightweight] changes the decoder (M06) and runs it online with one person with aphasia (M13). M06 is standard: the design belongs to the Diff-E lineage, which already classified without reverse sampling [@kim2023diffe; @kim2024ensemble; @park2025viseme], and at 14.11 M parameters the network is larger than Diff-E, not lighter (§II-D.3). M13 is standard: online decoding departs from the offline default (112 of 167 imagined-speech EEG studies, pattern match, Appendix), but an earlier online study tested 20 participants over two sessions [@wu2024adaptive] against one participant and 20 trials here. The main problem is M12: the All row of Table I (65% top-1, 70% top-2) does not follow from its class rows. Without baseline or ablation (§III), what diffusion adds is untested. What holds is a working clinical pipeline: about 30 minutes of calibration, about 20 seconds of fitting (§III-A).
expert_true_value: Joins a patient's own EEG collection, a subject-specific fit of about 20 seconds and confidence-scaled audiovisual feedback into one real-time prototype run with a person with chronic anomic aphasia in a clinical therapy room; this is separate from how reliable the reported accuracy is.
canon_before: Before this paper, diffusion-based imagined-speech EEG decoding (the Diff-E lineage, 2023-2025) trained a DDPM with a conditional autoencoder and classified with the encoder and classifier only, about 0.7 M parameters in Diff-E, with ablations in two of the three studies showing lower accuracy without the DDPM; online imagined-speech EEG with feedback had been run with 20 healthy participants over two sessions (2024). Most imagined-speech EEG studies analyse recorded trials offline.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the conditional autoencoder with a class- and timestep-conditioned three-level U-Net (14.11 M parameters, larger than Diff-E) and runs it online in one 20-trial session with one participant with aphasia; omitting reverse sampling at inference is inherited from the lineage, and no ablation or baseline tests what diffusion adds.
position_in_field: Imagined-speech EEG, closed four-class set, one patient: standard on the decoder (M06, Diff-E lineage) and on online operation (M13, offline is the default but online work with 20 participants precedes it); evaluation (M12) not reported, because the overall row of Table I does not follow from the per-class rows and per-class trial counts are not given.
practical_value: A reference design for connecting a patient's own few-word calibration, fitting and feedback in one session. Before use, the accuracy needs per-class trial counts, a chance reference, repeated sessions on different days and a measure of communication success.
axes_moved: Online four-class imagined-speech decoding with confidence-scaled audiovisual feedback in one person with chronic anomic aphasia, after about 30 minutes of calibration and about 20 seconds of fitting.
axes_unresolved: Consistency of the overall and per-class values in Table I; per-class online trial counts; train/validation split; how the class condition is supplied at online inference; transfer across days and people; end-to-end latency; benefit over a non-diffusion decoder; effect on everyday communication.
axes_regressed: No like-for-like comparison is reported, so a loss against earlier methods cannot be measured; per-class top-1 values vary widely (Toilet 20%, resting state 40% in Table I), and the network (14.11 M parameters) is larger than the Diff-E decoder it descends from.
technical_limits: The abstract credits group normalization while the Fig. 2 diagrams show batch normalization; the encoder is class-conditioned in training, and how the condition is given for unlabelled online input is not described; differences between training and inference structure, losses and splits are under-specified; no control separates ocular, muscle or cue-evoked components from imagined-speech activity.
evaluation_limits: One participant, 20 online trials. No per-class trial counts, train/validation split sizes, seeds or repeated runs, confidence intervals, statistical test, chance reference, baseline decoder or ablation. The overall row of Table I (65% top-1, 70% top-2) does not follow from the per-class rows, and the confusion matrices said to be computed are not shown.
deployment_limits: A 64-electrode cap and an NVIDIA Titan XP in a research setting; operation on a portable device, wearing burden, battery life, continuous self-paced input, use outside the clinic and long-term use are not evaluated. About 30 minutes of the user's own data collection precede the 20-second fit.
scope_limits: Based on arXiv v3 (4 pages), including Fig. 1, Fig. 2 and Table I, compared with the Diff-E lineage and an earlier online imagined-syllable study. The authors' code and data were not used to reproduce results.
task: Four-way classification of imagined speech of three cued Korean words (glossed Clock, Toilet, Water) and a resting state; not decoding of spontaneous free text.
input_modality: Non-invasive scalp EEG. Text and audio are used for cues and feedback, not as recognition input.
sensor_hardware: 64 scalp electrodes (actiCAP slim) placed by the international 10-20 system, 500 Hz, recorded via BrainVision Lab Streaming Layer and preprocessed in MNE; fifth-order Butterworth band-pass stated as 0-120 Hz, 60 Hz notch, baseline subtraction over the 0.2 s before imagery onset, common average reference. How a 0 Hz lower edge was implemented is not stated.
output_type: Four-class probabilities for three Korean word labels and rest, shown as feedback whose visual clarity and sound intensity scale with prediction confidence; no free text or synthesized speech.
vocabulary_type: Closed Korean set, glossed in the paper as Clock, Toilet and Water, described as chosen for the participant's daily needs.
vocabulary_size: Three words plus rest, four classes.
metrics: Author-reported values (Table I, Sec. III-B): overall 65% top-1 and 70% top-2; Clock 60%/80%, Toilet 20%/80%, Water 80%/100%, resting state 40%/60%. Per-class top-2 gains (20, 60, 20 and 20 points) imply an overall gain of at least 20 points under any split of the 20 trials, against 5 reported; every per-class percentage needs a class size that is a multiple of 5, so the classes hold five trials each and the per-class rows give 50%/80%. Secs. II-D and III-A report 14.11 M parameters, about 2 ms inference per 2-second window on a Titan XP and about 20 seconds of fitting.
evaluation_mode: Subject-specific model trained on the participant's 400 offline trials, then 20 real-time trials with visual and auditory feedback of the prediction; top-1 and top-2 accuracy over four classes (three cued Korean words and rest).

evidence.statement: One participant: a 54-year-old woman with chronic anomic aphasia and mixed dysarthria after a left-hemisphere stroke; the ethics approval number (KUIRB-2023-0429-01) is given.
Acquisition: four classes (Korean words glossed Clock, Toilet, Water, and rest), 100 trials each, 400 in random order; 2 s text and audio cue, then 2 s imagined speech; a rest break every 20 trials.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, II-A1 Data Acquisition Phase; Fig.1a

evidence.statement: Online phase: 20 trials, about 5 minutes, after about 30 minutes of data collection and about 20 seconds of fitting; per-class online trial counts are not given.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, II-A2; pp.3-4, III-A and III-B

evidence.statement: 64-electrode actiCAP slim at 500 Hz, preprocessed in MNE: fifth-order Butterworth 0-120 Hz band-pass, 60 Hz notch, baseline over the 0.2 s before imagery onset, common average reference.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2-3, II-C Data Acquisition and Preprocessing

evidence.statement: Diffusion-based representation learning with a three-level 1D U-Net conditioned on timestep and class; online, reverse sampling is omitted and one forward pass runs at a fixed noise level of 0.5.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, II-D1 Model Architecture and II-D3 Real-Time Decoding; Fig.2

evidence.statement: Adam, learning rate 0.001; training stops when training accuracy exceeds 75% or validation accuracy exceeds 40%; split method and validation size are not given.
14.11 M parameters, about 2 ms inference per 2-second EEG window on an NVIDIA Titan XP, about 20 seconds of fitting; none of these is the end-to-end time including collection, cue and feedback.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, II-D3 and III-A; p.2, II-A2

evidence.statement: Table I (top-1/top-2): Clock 60%/80%, Toilet 20%/80%, Water 80%/100%, resting state 40%/60%, all 65%/70%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, Table I; pp.3-4, III-B Performance in Real-Time Session Evaluation

evidence.statement: Reviewer's consistency check of Table I: per-class top-2 gains are 20, 60, 20 and 20 points, so any split of the 20 trials gives an overall gain of at least 20 points, against 5 reported. Every per-class percentage needs a class size that is a multiple of 5, so the classes hold five trials each and the rows give 50%/80%; the paper does not state the per-class counts.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, Table I (arithmetic consistency check); p.2, II-A2 (20 online trials)

evidence.statement: 3 s of feedback whose visual clarity and audio intensity scale with prediction confidence; audiovisual feedback on a class decision, not speech synthesis.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2, II-A2 and Fig.1b; p.3, II-D3

evidence.statement: Online cue (2 s), imagery (2 s) and feedback (3 s) are stated, but the waiting time during classification is about 2 s in II-A2 and 1 s in Fig.1b, so the full timing is not uniquely defined.
The abstract credits group normalization, while the Fig. 2 classifier diagrams show batch normalization; the text describes class conditioning but not how the unknown label is handled online.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1, Abstract; p.3, Fig.2 and II-D1

evidence.statement: Results give only the proposed model's per-class values: no comparison model and no ablation of diffusion or of the efficiency changes; confusion matrices are said to be computed but are not shown. Neither the lightweight claim nor a benefit of diffusion is established.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, II-D2, Table I and III; p.4, III-B

evidence.statement: The authors name limited generalizability from one participant, dependence on subject-specific calibration and the four-class task, and propose more participants, adaptation and a larger command set.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4, III-C Limitations and Future Directions

evidence.statement: Value as a prototype linking own-data collection, short fitting and real-time feedback in one person with aphasia; improved everyday communication, therapeutic effect, and validity across days, people or untrained words are not shown.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.1-4, I, II-A/B/D, III-A/B/C and IV

evidence.statement: No comparison separates ocular or muscle activity or responses to the text and audio cues; contamination is not asserted, but classification from imagined-speech activity alone is not established.

en.summary: Diffusion EEG decoder (M06) standard: Diff-E lineage, no ablation, not smaller. Online use (M13) standard: one patient, 20 trials. M12: Table I overall row disagrees with class rows.
en.sensor: 64-electrode actiCAP slim scalp EEG
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.session: One offline calibration session, then one online session
en.key_result: Author-reported 65% top-1 and 70% top-2 accuracy over 4 classes in 20 online trials (one participant); the per-class rows of Table I are inconsistent with this overall row; their percentages force five trials per class and give 50% / 80%.
