title: LipDiffuser: Lip-to-Speech Generation with Conditional Diffusion Models
expert_take_short: Diffusion decoder with per-frame MP-FiLM (M06) and audio-only pretraining (M02) are standard; quality and speaker-similarity leads rest on enhanced targets and a clean-reference enrollment.
expert_take_long: LipDiffuser [@richter2025lipdiffuser] changes the decoder (M06), conditioning a magnitude-preserving diffusion denoiser on video frame by frame, and the training targets (M02), with audio-only pretraining and enhanced LRS3 audio; neither change is ablated, and audio-only pretraining was already tested, with mixed effect, by Kefalas et al. [@kefalas2023audio], so both are standard. Its quality lead rests on predictors that place it level with the clean recordings (DNSMOS above, NISQA below), and its speaker-similarity lead on an enrollment taken from the clean reference, an advantage that V2SFlow [@choi2024v2sflow] shows changes speaker similarity but not WER; on WER it does not beat LipVoicer or IL2S (SSL).
expert_true_value: A diffusion lip-to-speech system whose quality and speaker-similarity scores can be read against speech-enhancement baselines in one table; the contribution of its per-frame MP-FiLM conditioning, audio-only pretraining and enhanced targets is not isolated.
canon_before: Video-to-speech decoders were mostly adversarially trained; diffusion decoders such as DiffV2S conditioned on concatenated visual features and a speaker embedding; Lip2Speech and IL2S added an enrollment speaker embedding; Kefalas et al. (2023) had already pretrained video-to-speech decoders on audio only, with ablations.
delta_from_canon: Conditions an MP-ADM diffusion denoiser frame by frame on interpolated video features through magnitude-preserving FiLM, pretrains on 960 hours of enhanced LibriSpeech, and trains on LRS3 audio enhanced by a Schroedinger-bridge model. A conditioning and training change, not a new sensor.
position_in_field: Standard on the decoder (M06) and the training targets (M02): neither change is ablated, and audio-only pretraining has an earlier ablated precedent. Evaluation (M12) follows the usual listener-test and ASR protocol, but speaker similarity is measured against an enrollment taken from the clean reference.
practical_value: A lip-to-speech option when clean enrollment audio of the speaker exists and the audio track is unusable; for content accuracy it is not better than LipVoicer or IL2S (SSL) in its own table.
axes_moved: Higher DNSMOS, NISQA and speaker similarity than the lip-to-speech baselines on 1,321 LRS3-CHiME3 files; DNSMOS 3.64 against 3.56 for the clean reference (inside either standard deviation) and NISQA 4.57 against 4.65, so quality reaches the clean recordings rather than exceeding them; 15-listener ratings point the same way.
axes_unresolved: Enrollment from a different utterance; speaker similarity from an encoder not used for conditioning; unseen-speaker split; cross-dataset results; ablations of MP-FiLM, audio-only pretraining and target enhancement; seeds; inference time.
axes_regressed: WER 0.38 against 0.36 for LipVoicer and IL2S (SSL); phoneme similarity 0.64 against 0.67 and lip-sync scores below IL2S (SSL) (Table 1); requires enrollment audio, unlike DiffV2S and LipVoicer.
technical_limits: Lip movements map to several phonemes, so natural-sounding output does not ensure correct content; the system depends on enrollment audio; the effects of MP-FiLM, audio-only pretraining and enhanced targets are not separated.
evaluation_limits: Table 1 gives means and standard deviations only, with no intervals or tests; the listening test gives no sample count or test and rates against an unspecified reference; enrollment derives from the clean reference; training-test speaker overlap, seeds and checkpoint selection are not stated.
deployment_limits: Needs clean enrollment audio and a visible mouth; tested offline on recorded TED talks with overt speech; no silent articulation, speech-impaired users, camera variation or runtime figures.
scope_limits: Offline lip-to-speech on LRS3 and LRS3-CHiME3 (overt speech with the audio replaced or noised); claims of cross-dataset generalization and enrollment robustness have no reported result.
input_modality: Mouth-region video plus enrollment audio of the target speaker; in Table 1 the enrollment derives from the clean reference. Noisy input audio is not used, but inference is not audio-free; training uses paired audio.
sensor_hardware: No new sensor: existing video cropped to 88x88 grayscale mouth regions at 25 fps, encoded by BRAVEn into 1,024-dimensional features; 16 kHz audio; 256-dimensional Wespeaker embedding; training on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary English continuous speech reconstructed as audio.
vocabulary_size: Not stated; 1,321 is the number of test files and 960 hours the LibriSpeech pretraining audio, neither a vocabulary size.
metrics: Table 1, LRS3-CHiME3 at -10 dB, 1,321 files, mean and standard deviation: LipDiffuser DNSMOS 3.64, NISQA 4.57, LPS 0.64, WER 0.38, SpkSim 0.63, LSE-C 6.84, LSE-D 7.78; LipVoicer WER 0.36; IL2S (SSL) WER 0.36, LPS 0.67; AV-Gen WER 0.56; SGMSE+ 0.75; clean reference DNSMOS 3.56, WER 0.09. 15 listeners rated quality and speaker similarity on 0-100.
evaluation_mode: Offline synthesis and speech-enhancement comparison on LRS3-CHiME3: reference-free quality predictors, phoneme similarity, QuartzNet WER, speaker cosine similarity to the enrollment, SyncNet lip-sync scores, and a 15-participant listening test.

evidence.statement: The authors propose an MP-ADM diffusion model conditioned on lip video and a speaker embedding, with MP-FiLM video fusion, and claim gains in quality and speaker similarity.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Abstract and Introduction; pp.2–3 Sections 3.1–3.4

evidence.statement: MP-FiLM (Eq. 5) is a magnitude-preserving mixture applied per frame after interpolating video features to the acoustic frame rate; beta and gamma use a kernel-5 convolution and a pointwise convolution, and gamma is clamped to 0-1. No ablation compares it with other fusion.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 3.3, Equations 4–5; p.3 Section 3.3 continuation; p.4 Results

evidence.statement: Synthesis uses lip video and enrollment audio of the target speaker; the Table 1 caption states that the enrollment derives from the clean reference. Not using noisy input audio is not audio-free inference.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Section 3.4; p.4 Table 1 caption and Input column

evidence.statement: Video is an 88x88 grayscale mouth crop at 25 fps encoded by BRAVEn into 1,024 dimensions; audio is 16 kHz with 80 mel bins, FFT 1024 and hop 256 (62.5 Hz); the Wespeaker embedding has 256 dimensions.
Generation runs 32 steps of a second-order deterministic sampler to a mel-spectrogram, converted to waveform by HiFi-GAN; no inference time or streaming latency is reported.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Sections 3.4 and 4.2; pp.3–4 Experimental setup and Results

evidence.statement: Training: 32M samples, batch 256, peak learning rate 0.005, Adam beta1 0.9 and beta2 0.99, about 205M parameters, typically 60 GPU-hours on NVIDIA H100.
Audio-only pretraining on 960 hours of LibriSpeech precedes training on LRS3; both audio sets are enhanced with a pretrained Schroedinger-bridge model trained on EARS-WHAM and VB-DMD.
LRS3 is overt TED-talk speech; LRS3-CHiME3 mixes CHiME3 noise at six SNRs (5, 0, -5, -10, -15, -20 dB) and is tested on 1,321 files. No silent articulation or clinical participants are tested.

Table 1 at -10 dB reports LipDiffuser DNSMOS 3.64, NISQA 4.57 and SpkSim 0.63 (means), above the lip-to-speech baselines; DNSMOS is above the clean reference (3.56) by less than either standard deviation, NISQA below it (4.65).
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1 caption, LipDiffuser row; p.3 Section 4.3

evidence.statement: Table 1 WER: LipDiffuser 0.38 (SD 0.35), LipVoicer 0.36, IL2S (SSL) 0.36, AV-Gen 0.56, SGMSE+ 0.75, clean reference 0.09; the authors call the best three comparable, and Table 1 gives standard deviations of 0.33-0.35 with no interval or test.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1 WER column and caption

evidence.statement: LPS: LipDiffuser 0.64 against IL2S (SSL) 0.67; lip sync LSE-C 6.84 and LSE-D 7.78 against IL2S (SSL) 8.03 and 6.54, so LipDiffuser is not best on every metric.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1 LPS, LSE-C and LSE-D columns; pp.3–4 Section 4.3

evidence.statement: WER uses NeMo QuartzNet15x5Base-En, LPS a w2v LV-60K phoneme predictor; SpkSim is the cosine between embeddings of the enrollment and the output; lip sync uses SyncNet scores.
The listening test had 15 participants rating randomly selected -10 dB LRS3-CHiME3 samples for quality and speaker similarity against a reference on 0-100; no sample count, interval or test is given.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Figure 1 and caption; p.4 Section 4.3 continuation and Section 5

evidence.statement: Fig. 2: LipDiffuser WER is constant over input SNR because it does not use input audio; the authors place its advantage over enhancement below -5 dB. Figure values are not restated.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Figure 2 and Section 5 second paragraph

evidence.statement: LipDiffuser, Lip2Speech and IL2S receive the enrollment, DiffV2S and LipVoicer only video; speaker-similarity differences therefore mix generator quality with access to the speaker reference.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1 caption and Input column; p.3 Sections 3.4 and 4.2

evidence.statement: The introduction claims cross-dataset generalization and the conclusion robustness to enrollment scenarios, but the results cover only LRS3-CHiME3: Table 1 and the listening test at -10 dB and WER over input SNR (Figs. 1-2).
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Introduction final paragraph; pp.3–4 Sections 4–6, Figures 1–2 and Table 1

evidence.statement: No experiment removes MP-FiLM, audio-only pretraining or target enhancement; the authors state that audio-only pretraining is required but give no number.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 2.1 final paragraph and Section 3.3; p.3 Section 4.1; p.4 Section 5

evidence.statement: The study evaluates offline synthesis from recorded overt speech; silent articulation, unseen-speaker splits, speech-impaired users, mobile use and real-time conversation are not reported.
Audio-visual examples are linked; code and pretrained checkpoints are promised upon acceptance.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Introduction final paragraph and footnote 1

en.summary: Diffusion decoder with per-frame MP-FiLM (M06) and audio-only pretraining (M02) are standard; quality and speaker-similarity leads rest on enhanced targets and a clean-reference enrollment.
en.sensor: Existing video (88x88 grayscale mouth crop); no new sensor
en.vocabulary: Open vocabulary English continuous speech (size not stated)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: WER 38%, NISQA 4.57, speaker similarity 0.63 on LRS3-CHiME3 at -10 dB (1321 test files)
en.limitations: Requires clean enrollment audio, which Table 1 takes from the clean reference; quality gains follow training on enhanced targets; no ablation of MP-FiLM or audio-only pretraining; cross-dataset claim without results.

title: LTA-L2S: Lexical Tone-Aware Lip-to-Speech Synthesis for Mandarin with Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning
expert_take_short: Mandarin lip-to-speech whose gain over Intelligible matches its English-initialization ablation; the tone components move CER little with no repeats reported, and pitch removal leaves TER at 40.9%.
expert_take_long: The paper's three changes (English-pretrained AV-HuBERT encoder, ASR-fine-tuned unit targets, flow-matching F0 and postnet) are standard against the field. Its lowest CER and TER on CN-CVS unseen speakers hold against its five baselines, but the ablations tie the gain to the cross-lingual initialization; no repeats are reported for the tone-specific parts, and the unit target lowers TER while removing the pitch predictor leaves it unchanged. The closest prior design, V2SFlow, is not compared, the only other CN-CVS video-to-speech study in the wiki population is not cited, and the FunASR re-transcribed test labels come without a real-audio error floor (M11, behind).
expert_true_value: Shows on CN-CVS that an English-pretrained AV-HuBERT encoder carries most of the Mandarin lip-to-speech gain (random initialization returns CER to the level of the Intelligible baseline); no repeats are reported for the tone-specific components, and removing the pitch predictor leaves TER unchanged.
canon_before: Video-to-speech before it already used pretrained visual front ends, self-supervised speech-unit targets (Intelligible, HuBERT units), a pitch predictor inferring F0 (VCVTS) and a content, pitch and speaker decomposition with a rectified-flow decoder (V2SFlow). English-to-Mandarin transfer of self-supervised visual encoders was shown for recognition (Zinonos et al., 2023). FA-GAN had reported CN-CVS lip-to-speech on single-speaker data.
delta_from_canon: Initializes AV-HuBERT Base from 1,759 hours of English and fine-tunes on CN-CVS; targets 2,000 k-means units from layer 9 of an ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 chosen for tone classification; generates continuous F0 by rectified flow matching and refines a coarse mel with a flow-matching postnet.
position_in_field: Mandarin video-to-speech (CN-CVS, unseen-speaker split). Changes M02, M03 and M06, all standard against the field; evaluation reference (M11) behind the best comparable work because the test labels are FunASR transcripts with no real-audio error reported.
practical_value: A Mandarin lip-to-speech baseline on CN-CVS unseen speakers (CER 61.2%, TER 40.9%); the evidence favours cross-lingual initialization of the visual encoder, not the tone-specific components. Not evidence for silent articulation, clinical users or real-time use.
axes_moved: Lower CER and TER than five re-run baselines on CN-CVS unseen speakers; random-initialization ablation 74.6% CER; HuBERT-unit ablation 64.4% CER; listener MOS above all baselines.
axes_unresolved: Whether the tone components matter beyond run-to-run variation (no seeds); tone accuracy of the generated F0 itself; agreement of the FunASR test labels with the CN-CVS labels; source of the speaker embedding at test; split counts; comparison with V2SFlow and FA-GAN under one protocol.
axes_regressed: In Table 3 the variant without the postnet has the best CER (61.0%) and TER (40.7%); removing the pitch predictor leaves TER unchanged at 40.9%. LTBS has higher STOI-Net and DNSMOS in Table 1.
technical_limits: Relies on a pretrained English AV-HuBERT encoder, an ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 unit target, a speaker-verification embedding and a HiFi-GAN vocoder; the audio source of the speaker embedding at test is not stated, so voice identity from lip video alone is not established.
evaluation_limits: CER and TER come from FunASR transcripts converted by g2pM, scored against test labels also re-transcribed by FunASR; no real-audio CER, no FunASR model or settings, no repeats or seeds reported, and MOS plus-minus values undefined (15 listeners, 30 samples per model).
deployment_limits: Offline synthesis from recorded CN-CVS speech video; no silently articulated data, users with voice disorders, on-device or real-time evaluation, and no inference runtime.
scope_limits: Based on arXiv v1 (text, Fig. 1, Tables 1-4, references) and the wiki ledger tallies; comparisons with V2SFlow, FA-GAN, Intelligible, SVTS, VCA-GAN, the multi-task model and cross-lingual recognition rest on those papers' reported values.
task: Lip-to-speech synthesis for Mandarin: speech audio generated from lip video, scored for character and tone error, quality and speaker similarity.
input_modality: Lip video (96x96 grayscale mouth crops); a speaker-verification embedding is an additional condition; paired audio is used in training.
sensor_hardware: Existing CN-CVS audio-visual recordings; 68 dlib landmarks for alignment; camera model and distance not stated.
vocabulary_type: Mandarin continuous speech from CN-CVS; open vocabulary in the corpus sense.
vocabulary_size: Not stated; 2,000 is the number of speech-unit clusters, not words.
metrics: Table 1: LTA-L2S STOI-Net 0.907, DNSMOS 3.200, CER 61.2%, TER 40.9%, SECS 0.828; Intelligible CER 74.9%, TER 50.3%; LTBS STOI-Net 0.909, DNSMOS 3.291, CER 87.3%, TER 56.4%. Table 2 MOS: naturalness 3.95, intelligibility 3.88, similarity 3.89; ground truth 4.48 and 4.54.
evaluation_mode: Offline comparison on the CN-CVS unseen-speaker split with non-Mandarin sentences removed; objective STOI-Net, DNSMOS, CER, TER (FunASR plus g2pM) and SECS (Resemblyzer); 15 native listeners rating 30 samples per model on a 5-point scale; no repeats reported for the ablations.

evidence.statement: The authors propose cross-lingual transfer from English, F0 generation conditioned on tone-bearing speech units, and two-stage refinement of the acoustic features for Mandarin lip-to-speech.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Abstract, Introduction, Section 2; p.2 Figure 1

evidence.statement: The visual encoder is AV-HuBERT Base initialized from weights pretrained on 1,759 hours of English and fine-tuned on Mandarin in the first stage.
Speech units are 2,000 k-means clusters of layer-9 features of an ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0, predicted by four Conformer blocks with cross-entropy and label smoothing 0.1; 2,000 is not a word count.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section 2.2 and Eq.1; p.3 Section 3.2

evidence.statement: F0 and voiced/unvoiced labels are extracted with YAAPT; F0 is generated from visual features, speech units and a speaker embedding from a pretrained speaker-verification model whose reference audio is not specified.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2–3 Section 2.3, Figure 1, Eqs.2–3 and footnote 2

evidence.statement: Stage-one loss weights are 0.1 for units and 1.0 for voicing, F0 and mel; stage two freezes stage one and trains only the flow-matching postnet; a HiFi-GAN vocoder pretrained on CN-CVS produces the waveform.

CN-CVS speech subset: 273.4 hours from 2,529 speakers; the original unseen-speaker split is used, non-Mandarin sentences are excluded and test labels are re-transcribed with FunASR; split sizes are not given.

Lip crops are 96x96 grayscale after 68-landmark alignment; audio is 16 kHz with 80 mel bands, 40 ms window and 10 ms hop; training is 100 epochs per stage on two GPUs; F0 and postnet use 24 function evaluations; no runtime is reported.
CER and TER are computed from FunASR transcripts post-processed by g2pM, so TER depends on machine transcription rather than direct judgment of the tone in the waveform.
Table 1: LTA-L2S CER 61.2% and TER 40.9%, below Intelligible (74.9%, 50.3%); STOI-Net 0.907 and DNSMOS 3.200 below LTBS (0.909, 3.291); SECS 0.828, the highest listed.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1 and Section 4.1; PDF table visually checked

evidence.statement: Fifteen native Mandarin listeners rated 30 samples per model on a 5-point scale: LTA-L2S naturalness 3.95, intelligibility 3.88, similarity 3.89; ground truth 4.48 and 4.54; the plus-minus values are not defined.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Section 3.4; p.4 Table 2 and Section 4.2; PDF table visually checked

evidence.statement: Without the postnet DNSMOS falls from 3.200 to 2.942 while CER improves from 61.2% to 61.0% and TER from 40.9% to 40.7%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 3, w/o postnet row, Section 4.3; PDF table visually checked

evidence.statement: Replacing flow-matching F0 by L1 regression gives CER 63.2% and TER 42.0%; removing the pitch predictor gives CER 61.5% and TER 40.9%, the same TER as the full model.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 3 and Section 4.3; PDF table visually checked

evidence.statement: Without speech-unit supervision CER is 69.2% and TER 46.2%; with random visual-encoder initialization CER is 74.6% and TER 49.1%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Tables 3–4 and Section 4.3; PDF tables visually checked

evidence.statement: Replacing the units by layer-9 HuBERT units (2,000 clusters) gives CER 64.4% and TER 42.8%, while DNSMOS 3.206 and SECS 0.831 are slightly higher than the proposed system's.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 4, HuBERT Unit row, Section 4.3; PDF table visually checked

evidence.statement: Improvements are called significant without a statistical test, run count or definition of the MOS plus-minus; Sec. 4.3 says CER and PER where Table 4 reports CER and TER.

Evaluation is offline synthesis on CN-CVS speech video; no silently articulated data, users with voice disorders, mobile, on-device or real-time evaluation; other Chinese dialects and accents are left to future work.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.1–4 Sections 1–5, especially Section 3.1 and Section 5 Conclusion

en.summary: Mandarin lip-to-speech whose gain over Intelligible matches its English-initialization ablation; the tone components move CER little with no repeats reported, and pitch removal leaves TER at 40.9%.
en.sensor: Existing video (CN-CVS), 96x96 mouth crops
en.vocabulary: Mandarin continuous speech; size not stated
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: CER 61.2%, TER 40.9% on CN-CVS unseen-speaker split
en.limitations: Gain tied to English initialization; no repeats reported for the tone components; FunASR re-transcribed test labels without a real-audio floor; speaker-embedding source unstated; offline, voiced speech only.

title: MultiDiffNet: A Multi-Objective Diffusion Framework for Generalizable Brain Decoding
venue: arXiv preprint; preliminary version at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: Foundation Models
expert_take_short: Diff-E-style decoder (M06) whose own ablation does not show diffusion helping; 1.01-point imagined-speech gain over EEGNet on two held-out subjects, normalized on scored trials (M03).
expert_take_long: MultiDiffNet [@zhang2025multidiffnet] changes the decoder (M06) and the evaluation protocol (M12); both are standard. The decoder continues the Diff-E design of a diffusion model trained with an autoencoder and a latent classifier [@kim2023diffe], but the paper's own ablation does not support the claim that diffusion drives generalization: the configuration without the diffusion model scores 13.76% on unseen imagined-speech subjects against 11.62% for the full model (Tables 13 and 17), the reverse of the within-subject drops reported for this design family [@kim2023diffe; @kim2024ensemble]. The base model gains 1.01 points over EEGNet on two held-out imagined-speech subjects (1.51 with Mixup), and unseen-subject normalization takes label-free statistics from trials that are then scored (M03, not reported in the paper).

en.summary: Diff-E-style decoder (M06) whose own ablation does not show diffusion helping; 1.01-point imagined-speech gain over EEGNet on two held-out subjects, normalized on scored trials (M03).
en.sensor: Existing 62-channel scalp EEG datasets
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Unseen-subject accuracy 11.62% vs EEGNet 10.61% (12.12% with Mixup), 11-class imagined speech
en.limitations: Near-chance accuracy, two held-out imagined-speech subjects, own ablation does not show diffusion helping, and unseen-subject normalization uses scored trials.

title: NaturalL2S: End-to-End High-quality Multispeaker Lip-to-Speech Synthesis with Differential Digital Signal Processing
expert_take_short: DDSP prior and jointly trained vocoder (M06) are standard: joint waveform training predates it; quality leads its baselines, but LRS3 WER 30.4% trails the uncompared LipVoicer (21.4%).
expert_take_long: NaturalL2S [@liang2025naturall2s] changes the waveform generator (M06), a DDSP harmonic-and-noise prior feeding a conditional HiFi-GAN trained jointly behind a frozen AV-HuBERT, and drops use-time speaker input (M07). Both are standard: joint end-to-end waveform generation for many speakers predates it, on word-level LRW and 33-speaker GRID [@mira2021endtoend; @um2021facetron], so the "first attempt" claim (§I) fails as worded, and reference-free use follows DiffV2S [@choi2023diffv2s]. The quality lead over the four compared systems (Tables I–III) recurs in a [later] same-group test [@liang2026sldl2s]. Content does not: LRS3 WER is 30.4%, behind Lip2Speech Unit (27.7%, Table II), as the authors concede (§V-B), and behind the cited but uncompared LipVoicer (21.4% under its own ASR) [@yemini2024lipvoicer]. The joint-training ablation also removes DDSP and changes the vocoder corpus, and removing DDSP alone lowers DNS-MOS only from 2.95 to 2.89 (Table IV), so the source of the gain is not isolated.
expert_true_value: Brings a DDSP harmonic-and-noise prior into lip-to-speech and shows, against four compared systems, higher predicted and rated quality with no speaker input at use time; it also shows that this quality does not bring lower word error.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech systems combine pretrained visual features (often AV-HuBERT), speech units or mel-spectrograms and a pretrained or separately trained neural vocoder. End-to-end waveform GANs from video already existed for GRID and LRW speakers. DiffV2S derives the speaker embedding from video; Lip2Speech Unit and others add a reference-audio speaker embedding. DDSP itself comes from speech and singing synthesis.
delta_from_canon: Instead of feeding a predicted mel-spectrogram to the vocoder, content embeddings and F0 drive a DDSP coarse harmonic-and-noise waveform that a conditional HiFi-GAN refines; the mel prediction only corrects F0. AV-HuBERT stays frozen; the generators and the vocoder are trained jointly.
position_in_field: Standard on the waveform generator (M06) and on use-time speaker information (M07): joint end-to-end waveform generation for many speakers and reference-free synthesis both predate it. Evaluation (M12) is standard in protocol but omits LipVoicer, the strongest prior on word error. Overt-speech video with the audio removed, not silent articulation.
practical_value: A research option for producing pleasant-sounding speech from mouth video when no reference recording of the speaker exists; applications that need correct words still need a lower-WER system.
axes_moved: Among the systems the paper compares on LRS2 and LRS3, the highest STOI-Net, DNS-MOS, audio-visual synchronization and F0 correlation; in the 15-listener test the highest mean quality, naturalness, intelligibility and voice-similarity scores; no reference speaker input at use time.
axes_unresolved: Silent articulation, speech-impaired users, speaker overlap with training and AV-HuBERT pre-training, unseen words, other languages, lighting, pose and occlusion, streaming latency, device power and memory, and which component causes the quality gain.
axes_regressed: WER is 36.5% on LRS2 and 30.4% on LRS3, worse than Lip2Speech Unit (33.5%, 27.7%) and the uncompared LipVoicer (17.8%, 21.4%); automatic voice similarity 0.63/0.63 is below the reference-embedding Lip2Speech Unit (0.72/0.76). Some ablated variants score better on single metrics.
technical_limits: Lip movements do not determine phonemes or prosody uniquely, so natural-sounding output can carry wrong words. DDSP receives ground-truth F0 in training and predicted F0 at inference. Joint training sits behind a frozen pretrained encoder. The text states F0 at 50 Hz while the equations predict F0 at four times the video rate.
evaluation_limits: DiffV2S and the LRS2 Lip2Speech Unit are scored on author-supplied samples, so not all systems are rerun on the full test sets with one codebase; clip counts and the MOS assignment are not stated; MOS pools LRS2 and LRS3; the ± in Table III is a standard deviation; no confidence intervals or significance tests. The ablation removing joint training also removes DDSP and trains the vocoder on another corpus.
deployment_limits: Assumes face alignment, an 88x88 mouth crop and a large pretrained visual model; no on-device conversation, recording control, latency, power or memory measurements.
scope_limits: Read: arXiv:2502.12002 v1, all 13 pages, Figs. 1-4 and Tables I-IV. The journal template header (2021) on the PDF is not treated as a venue or acceptance date. External materials and independent reproduction were not examined.
input_modality: Grayscale mouth video at inference, with no reference audio or speaker embedding. Training uses the paired audio, its acoustic features and speech units; the visual model is pretrained on audio-visual data and fine-tuned for lip reading.
sensor_hardware: No new sensor. 25 fps video and 16 kHz audio; dlib face alignment and an 88x88 grayscale mouth crop; AV-HuBERT Large (ResNet-18 plus 24 Transformer layers) as visual front end; training on one NVIDIA A100.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary English continuous speech reconstructed as audio; not word classification, and correct output of arbitrary vocabulary is not guaranteed.
vocabulary_size: Number of distinct words not stated; the 200 clusters are speech-unit targets, not a vocabulary.
metrics: Table I (LRS2): STOI-Net 0.92, DNS-MOS 2.95, WER 36.5%, LSE-C 8.74, LSE-D 5.84, F0 PCC 0.61, voice similarity 0.63. Table II (LRS3): 0.94, 3.23, 30.4%, 8.08, 6.46, 0.65, 0.63. Lip2Speech Unit WER 33.5%/27.7%, voice similarity with a reference embedding 0.72/0.76. Table III 5-point MOS (mean ± SD): quality 4.40±0.26, naturalness 4.34±0.30, intelligibility 4.39±0.32, voice similarity 3.98±0.33; 15 listeners, 50 samples from each test split. Table IV (LRS2): without DDSP DNS-MOS 2.89 and WER 37.0%; without unit supervision WER 38.8%; without joint training DNS-MOS 2.39 and WER 36.3%. Lower is better for WER and LSE-D. Authors' values, not an independent reproduction.
evaluation_mode: Offline comparison on the original LRS2 and LRS3 splits: predicted quality, ASR word error, audio-visual synchronization, normalized F0 correlation, speaker-embedding similarity and a 15-listener 5-point test; four ablations on LRS2 and qualitative figures.

evidence.statement: The authors name three contributions for multi-speaker lip-to-speech: joint training of the vocoder, a DDSP acoustic prior, and generation without a reference speaker embedding. The 'first' claim is the authors' positioning; earlier end-to-end waveform generators for GRID and LRW speakers exist.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.1–2, Abstract; I Introduction, contribution list 1–3

evidence.statement: In Fig. 1 the inference input is video; content features and F0 generate a DDSP signal and a conditional HiFi-GAN produces the waveform. No reference audio is input, but training uses acoustic features and speech units of the paired audio.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–7, III Model Architecture; Fig.1; IV.B–D

evidence.statement: AV-HuBERT is a frozen visual feature extractor; the generators and the vocoder are trained jointly. The mel prediction corrects F0 and is not the direct vocoder input, which takes content features and the DDSP waveform.
DDSP sums harmonic and aperiodic noise signals with amplitudes from F0 and content features; the setup uses 32 harmonics and FFT size 1024.

LRS2 is described as 144,300 BBC clips of about 200 hours and LRS3 as about 150,000 TED/TEDx clips from over 5,000 speakers and about 439 hours, used with their original training, validation and test splits. These are existing overt audio-visual recordings, not a new test with silent-speaking patients.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, IV.A Datasets; p.10, V.B Subjective Evaluation Results

evidence.statement: Input is 25 Hz video and 16 kHz audio, with dlib face alignment and an 88x88 grayscale mouth crop. Audio supervision uses 80-band mel, 200-cluster HuBERT units and RAPT F0.
DDSP uses ground-truth F0 in training and predicted F0 at inference; the model is not trained from the mouth alone, and the F0 condition differs between training and inference.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, IV.D Training, ground-truth versus predicted F0

evidence.statement: Training runs 500k steps per dataset on one A100 with batch size 48 and mixed precision, on slices of 5,920 waveform samples and 37 feature frames. These are training conditions, not inference latency.

STOI-Net and DNS-MOS are automatic predictors, WER comes from a recognizer, F0 correlation from normalized contours and voice similarity from Resemblyzer. None of these is a human word-identification score.

Because DiffV2S code is not public and the Lip2Speech Unit LRS2 inference code is missing, the comparison uses synthesized samples supplied by those authors. The number of matched evaluation items is not given.
evidence.section_or_location: p.8, V Results, baseline implementation paragraph

evidence.statement: Table I: on LRS2 NaturalL2S scores STOI-Net 0.92, DNS-MOS 2.95, WER 36.5%, LSE-C 8.74, LSE-D 5.84, F0 correlation 0.61 and voice similarity 0.63; Lip2Speech Unit has WER 33.5% and voice similarity 0.72 with a reference speaker embedding.
evidence.section_or_location: p.8, Table I, Proposed and Lip2Speech Unit rows, reference-embedding footnote

evidence.statement: Table II: on LRS3 NaturalL2S scores STOI-Net 0.94, DNS-MOS 3.23, WER 30.4%, LSE-C 8.08, LSE-D 6.46, F0 correlation 0.65 and voice similarity 0.63; Lip2Speech Unit has WER 27.7% and voice similarity 0.76 with a reference speaker embedding.
evidence.section_or_location: p.8, Table II, Proposed and Lip2Speech Unit rows, reference-embedding footnote

evidence.statement: Voice similarity of NaturalL2S and DiffV2S is 0.63 against 0.58 on LRS2 and 0.63 against 0.63 on LRS3. The text on p. 9 states the reverse (better on LRS3, equal on LRS2); the table values are used.
evidence.section_or_location: p.8, Tables I–II, Voice Similarity; p.9, V.A, voice similarity comparison

evidence.statement: The listener test uses 15 participants and 50 samples from each of the LRS2 and LRS3 test splits, rating quality, naturalness, intelligibility and voice similarity from 1 to 5. Table III gives means and standard deviations, not recognition accuracy or confidence intervals.
evidence.section_or_location: p.10, V.B; Table III title and caption

evidence.statement: Table III reports NaturalL2S quality 4.40±0.26, naturalness 4.34±0.30, intelligibility 4.39±0.32 and voice similarity 3.98±0.33. These exceed the compared systems but stay below the recordings (quality 4.88, naturalness 4.94, intelligibility 4.93).
evidence.section_or_location: p.10, Table III, Proposed and Ground Truth rows

evidence.statement: In Table IV (LRS2), removing DDSP changes DNS-MOS from 2.95 to 2.89 and WER from 36.5% to 37.0%, with voice similarity unchanged at 0.63; removing speech-unit supervision gives WER 38.8%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.11, Table IV, Full NaturalL2S, wo-DDSP and wo-unit rows

evidence.statement: The condition without joint training removes the F0 predictor and DDSP, changes the content features to mel prediction, and cascades a vanilla HiFi-GAN trained on LRS3. It therefore does not measure the effect of joint training alone.
evidence.section_or_location: p.10, V.C.1 NaturalL2S-wo-e2e; p.11, Table IV

evidence.statement: Table IV shows WER 36.3% without joint training against 36.5% for the full model, and LSE-C 8.76 and LSE-D 5.79 without the mel predictor and F0 correction against 8.74 and 5.84 for the full model. Not every component improves every metric.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.10–11, V.C.1 and V.C.4; Table IV

evidence.statement: Preprocessing states F0 at 50 Hz, while Eqs. (5)-(7) predict F0 over length M, four times the video length, with mel at 100 Hz. The AdamW coefficients print beta1 twice; the implementation is not inferred.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, III, M=4T; p.5, III.B equations (5)–(7); p.7, IV.B and IV.D

evidence.statement: Figs. 3 and 4 show spectrograms, normalized F0 and harmonic and noise components as qualitative examples, not complete reconstruction of every utterance. The caption of Fig. 4(e) attributes the noise to the harmonic synthesizer, while Fig. 2 and Sec. III-C describe a separate noise synthesizer.
evidence.section_or_location: p.9, Fig.3; p.11, Fig.4; pp.5–6, III.C and Fig.2

evidence.statement: The conclusion names dependence on large pretrained models and lightweight implementation as future work. The experiments include no mobile inference speed or power, streaming conversation, walking, or silent input by speech-impaired users.

Use of the original splits is stated, but speaker disjointness, overlap with pre-training and unseen-word evaluation are not. The reconstruction of overt-speech video is not extended to unseen users or true silent speech.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, IV.A Datasets and IV.C.1 Video Encoder; pp.8–11, V Results

en.summary: DDSP prior and jointly trained vocoder (M06) are standard: joint waveform training predates it; quality leads its baselines, but LRS3 WER 30.4% trails the uncompared LipVoicer (21.4%).
en.sensor: Existing video (88x88 grayscale mouth crop); no new sensor
en.vocabulary: Open vocabulary English continuous speech (size not stated)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: WER 30.4% on LRS3 and 36.5% on LRS2, against 27.7%/33.5% for Lip2Speech Unit in the paper's tables and 21.4%/17.8% for LipVoicer in its own paper; highest predicted and rated quality among the compared systems.
en.limitations: Joint waveform training and reference-free use predate it; the joint-training ablation also removes DDSP and changes the vocoder corpus; run count and seeds not stated; LipVoicer omitted; baselines scored on supplied samples; speaker overlap not stated.

title: NeuroTTT: Bridging Pretrain–Downstream Task Misalignment in EEG Foundation Models via Test-Time Training
expert_take_short: SSL fine-tuning losses (M02) and test-time updates (M03) are standard: SSL-TTT never beats Tent; 0.59 balanced accuracy trails the 82.6% competition winner if scored on its test set.
expert_take_long: NeuroTTT [@wang2025neurottt] adds domain-specific self-supervised losses to EEG foundation-model fine-tuning (M02) and unlabeled test-time updates (M03). Both are standard. The M02 design is rare in the ledger, but Stage I alone is shown only in a CBraMod figure (Fig. 3) and imagined-speech runs with it train 150 epochs against 100 for supervised runs (Sec. 4.1). The proposed one-step self-supervised test-time training does not beat off-the-shelf Tent on balanced accuracy in any of six backbone-task pairs (Tables 1-3), and five of the six gaps are within the reported spread. The state-of-the-art claim rests on internal baselines: if its test trials are the competition's released set, its best balanced accuracy, 0.5898, is 23.6 points below the 82.6% winner [@jeong2022bcicomp] (inference). Cross-subject gains rest on two and four test subjects with no seeds or significance tests, and test-time cost is not reported (M13).
expert_true_value: Shows how to test task-specific auxiliary losses and test-time adaptation on public EEG checkpoints across three tasks; its own tables show that off-the-shelf Tent matches or beats the proposed self-supervised test-time training.
canon_before: Supervised fine-tuning of public EEG checkpoints (CBraMod, LaBraM) with linear or MLP heads, LoRA, and source-free adaptation (SHOT). On BCIC2020-III imagined speech, the 2020 competition winner reached 82.6% on the released test trials (2022).
delta_from_canon: Adds stopped-band and task-specific self-supervised losses to supervised fine-tuning (M02) and unlabeled test-time updates, one self-supervised gradient step per sample or Tent (M03). It does not change the sensors, the vocabulary or the output.
position_in_field: Standard on both changed components: an added self-supervised fine-tuning loss is rare among neural foundation-model studies, but its effect is not separated in the tables; the self-supervised test-time step never beats Tent on balanced accuracy. On imagined speech its best balanced accuracy (0.5898) is below the 2020 competition winner (82.6%) on the same corpus.
practical_value: A starting point for adapting EEG checkpoints to closed-set tasks without test labels; deployment needs per-sample backpropagation whose latency and memory are not reported.
axes_moved: within-subject 5-class imagined-speech balanced accuracy for CBraMod above the paper's own fine-tuning baselines
axes_unresolved: separate effect of Stage I; seeds and significance; external baselines on BCIC2020-III; cross-subject imagined speech (at chance); test-time cost
axes_regressed: imagined-speech training with self-supervised losses runs 150 epochs against 100 for supervised-only runs; per-sample gradient updates at inference
technical_limits: Hand-designed self-supervised tasks; full-parameter test-time updates may be unstable on noisy trials and Tent may under-correct large shifts (authors, Appendix C). Public code differs from the paper in stress band bins, test-time optimizer and steps, and Tent's normalization layers.
evaluation_limits: No seed count, no definition of the plus-minus term and no significance tests; cross-subject gains rest on two (motor imagery) and four (stress) test subjects; Stage I alone is shown only in Fig. 3 for CBraMod; no external result is tabulated.
deployment_limits: Offline classification of existing datasets; imagined speech needs labeled data from the same user; no latency, memory or power for test-time adaptation.
scope_limits: Closed-set classification on three public EEG benchmarks (five imagined phrases, binary stress, four-class motor imagery); no continuous speech or text output.
task: Closed-set EEG classification: five imagined phrases (BCIC2020-III), binary mental stress, four-class motor imagery
input_modality: Scalp EEG
sensor_hardware: Existing datasets: 64 channels at 256 Hz (imagined speech), 20 at 500 Hz (stress), 22 at 250 Hz (motor imagery); resampled to 200 Hz, 1-second segments
vocabulary_type: Closed set of short phrases
vocabulary_size: 5 phrases (hello, help me, stop, thank you, yes)
metrics: Balanced accuracy, Cohen's kappa and weighted F1 (multi-class); balanced accuracy, AUC-PR and AUROC (stress). BCIC2020-III CBraMod: 0.4733 (MLP head), 0.5887 (Stage I + SSL test-time training), 0.5898 (Stage I + Tent).
evaluation_mode: Offline; imagined speech within subject on the competition split; stress (subjects 33-36) and motor imagery (subjects 8-9) on held-out test subjects

en.summary: SSL fine-tuning losses (M02) and test-time updates (M03) are standard: SSL-TTT never beats Tent; 0.59 balanced accuracy trails the 82.6% competition winner if scored on its test set.
en.sensor: 64-channel scalp EEG (existing dataset)
en.vocabulary: 5 phrases (hello, help me, stop, thank you, yes)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Balanced accuracy 0.5898 (CBraMod, Stage I + Tent), within-subject, 5 classes, BCIC2020-III; the 2020 competition winner reached 82.6% on the same corpus
en.limitations: Stage I and test-time effects not separated in tables; self-supervised test-time training never beats Tent; no seeds, significance tests, external baselines or test-time cost.

title: Non-invasive electromyographic speech neuroprosthesis: a geometric perspective
expert_take_short: Silent-EMG-to-text without vocalized pairing and SPD inputs are both standard: subvocal-only label training predates it, and 73.53% WER from one person is tested only against a near-chance baseline.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training-only supervision (M02: phoneme transcriptions of silent EMG, no vocalized recordings) and the input representation (M06: SPD covariance matrices into a GRU with CTC); both are standard. Subvocal-only phoneme models for 2,200-word continuous phrases were trained without vocalized pairing by 2018, at 8.9% mean WER over four phrase sets under a grammar, so the priority claim rests on its qualifiers (general English corpora, modern methods); the paper cites that work only as a 200-word grammar system. The SPD gain (PER 89.25% to 48.47%, WER 100% to 73.53%) is measured against a spectrogram baseline close to the 97.5% chance PER, in one participant with no repeated runs reported. The paper does not evaluate on the public silent-EMG benchmark, where text decoding with vocalized pairing reaches 12.2% WER, so the cost of dropping vocalized supervision is unmeasured.
expert_true_value: A large single-speaker silent-EMG corpus recorded without any vocalized speech, and a covariance (SPD) input that decodes it to phonemes far above chance; it does not show that dropping vocalized supervision is competitive with paired training.
canon_before: Open-vocabulary silent-EMG decoders mostly train with targets transferred from parallel vocalized recordings by DTW (Gaddy and Klein 2020; Benster et al. 2024, 12.2% WER). Subvocal-only phoneme HMMs trained on transcripts alone already reached 8.9% mean WER over four phrase sets from a 2,200-word vocabulary under a grammar (Meltzner et al. 2018). The same group's concurrent work introduced SPD embeddings of orofacial EMG for classification.
delta_from_canon: Trains a GRU with CTC on regularized channel-covariance matrices from silent EMG and phoneme transcriptions only, with no vocalized recording, and decodes words with a LibriSpeech-100 4-gram LM.
position_in_field: Standard on training-only supervision (M02) and on the input representation (M06): label-only training on silent articulation predates it, and the SPD gain is shown against a near-chance spectrogram baseline in one participant. The text-only route is not tested on the public silent-EMG benchmark.
practical_value: A training route for users who cannot vocalize, plus a released corpus; at 73.53% WER the open-vocabulary output is not yet usable for communication, and the 14% WER closed-set result does not transfer to it.
axes_moved: PER 89.25% to 48.47% and WER 100% to 73.53% on 1,970 held-out sentences when SPD inputs replace spectrogram inputs to the same GRU; EMG2QWERTY test CER 15.38% to 14.03% (no LM) and 9.55% to 7.95% (6-gram LM) with other training changes.
axes_unresolved: Cost of dropping vocalized supervision on a shared benchmark; comparison with time-domain features and learned encoders; more speakers and seeds; cross-session and electrode re-application stability; streaming latency; clinical users.
axes_regressed: No regression is reported against the paper's own baseline; one of eight EMG2QWERTY users does not improve (Fig. 5).
technical_limits: The eigenbasis is fitted once from one person's data (in the released code, training plus validation sentences); word decoding depends on the lexicon and 4-gram LM; the bidirectional GRU and per-sentence normalization need the whole sentence.
evaluation_limits: One participant; corpus-order sentence split with session separation not stated; no seeds or repeated runs reported; a single near-chance baseline; the EMG2QWERTY comparison also changes epochs (250 vs 150) and weight decay, and omits the baseline's SpecAugment; the p<0.015 test is unspecified; the NATO appendix reuses the group's 2024 four-subject split.
deployment_limits: 31 gel electrodes with a laboratory amplifier and mouse-click segmentation; no latency, cross-day or electrode-shift evaluation, which the authors defer (Sec. 7).
scope_limits: Offline sentence decoding from instructed silent articulation by one healthy participant; appendix closed-vocabulary, NATO-code and wrist-typing tasks are separate evidence.
task: Silent-articulation surface EMG to phoneme sequences and English words; appendix 67-word date sentences, NATO-code spelling, and wrist-EMG typing (EMG2QWERTY).
input_modality: surface electromyography (sEMG)
sensor_hardware: 31 monopolar surface sites on face, jaw, cheek, lips, chin and neck with an earlobe reference; active gel electrodes and an actiCHamp Plus amplifier at 5,000 Hz; 22 sites in the NATO-code task.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary English sentences decoded via phonemes, lexicon and 4-gram LM; appendix closed sets of 67 words or 26 NATO code words.
vocabulary_size: Over 6,500 unique words in about 11,000 sentences; LM and lexicon from LibriSpeech-100 transcripts; appendix 67 words or 26 code words.
metrics: Main: PER 48.47%, WER 73.53% (spectrogram baseline 89.25% / 100%; chance PER 97.5%). 67-word task: PER 13%, WER 14%. NATO codes: CER 55.7 / 55.0 / 70.4 / 56.4% (chance 96%). EMG2QWERTY test CER 14.03% (no LM) and 7.95% (6-gram LM).
evaluation_mode: offline; subject-dependent; held-out sentences; separate closed-vocabulary and typing benchmarks

evidence.statement: The main contribution is about 8 hours of silent EMG with over 6,500 words from one healthy participant, and EMG-to-phoneme and word decoding without time-aligned audio.
Channel covariance matrices are regularized to SPD form (eta = 0.1) and approximately diagonalized with a shared basis from a Frechet mean of training matrices, then fed to a sequence model.
CTC removes the need for exact EMG-phoneme alignment; the model predicts 40 phoneme probabilities per step and a language model maps phonemes to words.
The shared basis is subject-specific; differences between people are interpreted as basis changes, but no cross-person performance is tested.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.4–5, §3.3 Geometric perspective aligns well with biology

evidence.statement: The main corpus has about 11,000 sentences and 6,500 words of silent EMG only, with no vocalized EMG or audio; word decoding uses LibriSpeech-100 transcripts for the lexicon and LM.
Main recordings use 31 monopolar sites with separate reference and ground, active electrodes and gel at 5,000 Hz; 80-1,000 Hz band-pass and per-sentence, per-channel normalization.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.5, §4.1 Experimental details; p.6, Figure 2

evidence.statement: The seated participant silently articulates and marks each sentence's start and end with mouse clicks; continuous recognition without manual segmentation is not evaluated.
Split 8,000 / 1,000 / 1,970 sentences with test sentences absent elsewhere; 50 ms windows, 20 ms step, 31x31 matrices, 3-layer GRU, 100 epochs, lowest validation loss; no unseen-word-only score.
Word decoding uses an HLG WFST with a lexicon and KenLM 4-gram, beam width 50; no recorded audio is needed, but transcripts, lexicon and LM are.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.6, §5 Results, WFST decoding paragraph

evidence.statement: Table 1: proposed PER 48.47% and WER 73.53%; spectrogram baseline PER 89.25% and WER 100% (lower is better).
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.7, Table 1; p.6, §5 metric definitions; p.12, Figure 6 and Appendix B

evidence.statement: The main comparison matches time resolution and 31x31 input shape and feeds both representations to the same GRU; the spectrogram model collapses to few phoneme sequences.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.6, §5 spectrogram comparison; p.7, footnote 2

evidence.statement: Figs. 3-4 show PER falling with model size and training sentences within the tested ranges; they do not establish performance beyond those ranges.
EMG2QWERTY is wrist-EMG typing, not silent articulation; eight personalized models are trained from scratch, without the 100-user pretraining setup or unseen-user tests.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.7–8, §5.1 Comparison with prior work

evidence.statement: Besides the input change, the EMG2QWERTY run omits SpecAugment, trains 250 rather than 150 epochs and adds weight decay, so the feature effect is not isolated.
EMG2QWERTY mean test CER: 15.38 to 14.03% without LM and 9.55 to 7.95% with a 6-gram LM; Table 2 states p<0.015 without naming the test; Fig. 5 shows improvement for all users except USER 6.
The bidirectional GRU needs the full sentence and does not support streaming; one healthy participant, and no cross-day stability, electrode-shift or fatigue evaluation (Sec. 7).
Follow-up ALS and causal-model work mentioned in Sec. 7 is separate and is not evidence from this paper's experiments.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.9, §7 Limitations, follow-up study references

evidence.statement: Appendix A cautions against one-to-one WER comparison with earlier studies because recording, supervision, alignment, task and evaluation differ.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.11, Appendix A Detailed literature review

evidence.statement: Appendix B shows PER and WER distributions over 1,970 test sentences (means 48.47% and 73.53%); the 97.5% chance PER is a uniform-guess calculation over 40 phonemes, not a decoded random control.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.12, Appendix B, Figure 6 and chance-level formula

evidence.statement: The small-vocabulary task has 500 sentences from one participant built from 67 words (weekdays, months, dates, years), split 370 / 30 / 100, recorded at 31 sites and 5,000 Hz.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.13, Appendix C.1 DATA SMALL-VOCAB

evidence.statement: The small-vocabulary model is a 1-layer GRU trained 100 epochs with closest-word matching to the 67-word set; Table 3 gives 13% PER and 14% WER, not open-vocabulary performance.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.13, Appendix C.1 Results, Table 3 and Figure 8

evidence.statement: The NATO-code task uses four participants, 22 sites at 5,000 Hz and 26 code words, split 416 / 104 / 1,968 articulations as in the group's 2024 paper; no held-out-person test.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF pp.13–14, Appendix C.2 DATA NATO-WORDS

evidence.statement: NATO-code CER for subjects 1-4 is 55.7%, 55.0%, 70.4% and 56.4% (chance 96%); Fig. 9 shows per-subject PER against model size, separate from Table 4.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.14, Table 4, Figure 9, Appendix C.2

evidence.statement: Table 5 lists the three best and three worst decoded sentences as qualitative examples, not average communication quality.
IRB approval, written consent and consent to share de-identified data are reported; the authors disclose inventorship of related university-owned intellectual property.
evidence.section_or_location: PDF p.9, §8 Ethical considerations and Conflict of interest

en.summary: Silent-EMG-to-text without vocalized pairing and SPD inputs are both standard: subvocal-only label training predates it, and 73.53% WER from one person is tested only against a near-chance baseline.
en.sensor: 31 monopolar surface EMG sites on face, jaw, chin, lips and neck; active gel electrodes, actiCHamp Plus amplifier, 5,000 Hz
en.task: Silent-articulation sentence decoding to phonemes and English words without vocalized recordings; appendix closed-vocabulary date sentences, NATO-code spelling, and wrist-EMG typing (EMG2QWERTY)
en.vocabulary: Over 6,500 unique words in about 11,000 sentences; 4-gram LM and lexicon from LibriSpeech-100 transcripts; appendix 67-word and 26-code tasks
en.speaker: One healthy participant for the main corpus; four for NATO codes; eight EMG2QWERTY users with personalized models
en.session: Sentence-disjoint split 8,000 / 1,000 / 1,970 by corpus order; session separation not stated
