title: Poster: Recognizing Hidden-in-the-Ear Private Key for Reliable Silent Speech Interface Using Multi-Task Learning
venue: Companion of the 2025 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp Companion '25)
review_confidence: High for the source-grounded assessment and its explicitly marked uncertainties; confidence in deployment and security claims is limited by the preliminary experiment and internal inconsistencies.
expert_take_short: Sensing, shared model and joint word-plus-identity output are each standard; whisper adds nothing over the 91.4% ultrasonic-only baseline, and impostors are training participants (M12 behind).
expert_take_long: HEar-ID [@dong2025hearid] changes the sensing (in-ear ultrasound plus whisper, M05), the model (shared encoder with contrastive, triplet and CTC heads, M06), enrollment (M03) and the output (word plus accept or deny, M08). Each is standard: audio-plus-ultrasound fusion [@zhu2007multimodal], headphone echo sensing [@zhang2023hpspeech], verification from murmured speech [@okamoto2007nam] and content-plus-identity output [@chetty2008avfusion] predate it; what is new is the combination on one earbud. The whisper stream shows no gain: on the 8 of 11 users without degraded ultrasonic sensing, Top-1 is 90.25% against 91.4% for the authors' ultrasonic-only ReHEarSSE pipeline [@dong2024rehearsse], and 67.3% over all users (§4.1.2). Authentication is tested only against the other participants, whose data also train the model (§4.1.1), so M12 is behind; replay, the attack that motivates the paper (§1), is never tried.
expert_true_value: A preliminary demonstration that paired whisper and ultrasonic ear-canal signals can support a shared spelling/authentication pipeline, exposing that content-recognition success and identity-verification success can fail differently across users.
canon_before: The paper builds on ear-canal ultrasonic spelling recognition, particularly ReHEarSSE, and on earable biometric authentication. Its motivating gap is that decoding what was articulated does not by itself establish who articulated it.
delta_from_canon: Pairs whisper mel-spectrogram features with autoregressive features of ultrasonic ear-canal motion, aligns them contrastively, and shares learned representations between a user-verification head and a letter-sequence spelling head.
position_in_field: An exploratory earable SSI poster linking content decoding and biometric verification, with stronger value as a joint-model design and failure analysis than as evidence of deployable authentication security.
practical_value: A research direction for verifying the identity behind low-audibility ear-based text entry. Practical value remains conditional on reliable sensing across users, explicit threat-model testing, reduced calibration burden, and a usable implementation.
axes_moved: Makes identity verification an explicit companion task to ear-based spelling recognition, using cross-modal alignment and a shared encoder rather than treating SSI solely as content decoding.
axes_unresolved: Truly voiceless use, unseen words, unseen impostor identities, replay or signal-injection resistance, long-term and continuous verification, robustness to earbud replacement and placement, calibrated security operating points, and real-time end-to-end use.
axes_regressed: The added whisper stream does not establish aggregate recognition superiority: reported Top-1 is 67.3% across all 11 participants and 90.25% only for eight participants without degraded ultrasonic sensing, compared with a reported 91.4% ReHEarSSE baseline. Three users have below-10% recognition and two have near-zero genuine-user acceptance.
technical_limits: Earbud placement and articulation are proposed causes of severe participant failures, not experimentally isolated explanations. Dependence on whisper features leaves strictly voiceless operation unvalidated. No component ablation establishes which loss or stream causes any gain. Authentication is a learned similarity decision, not a cryptographic key construction; inconsistent margin values and incomplete calibration details hinder reproduction.
evaluation_limits: Small, predominantly male cohort; repeated closed 50-word lexicon; one held-out re-wearing session, not held-out identities. Authentication and contrastive components use all participants' identities in training and testing, while the SSI head uses only the genuine user's data. No replay/injection attack experiments, unseen-impostor protocol, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or isolated loss/component ablations are reported. EER is named but no numerical value is supplied. Figure 3(b) and prose disagree on S5 TPR, and the authentication margin has inconsistent specifications.
deployment_limits: The experimental Edifier W380NB earbuds were modified: the in-ear microphone was removed from the earbud circuitry and wired directly to a Google Pixel 3a via a 3.5 mm jack for raw audio. The poster reports no end-to-end latency, power use, standalone earbud inference, walking test, or deployed communication study; per-user training uses other participants' data.
scope_limits: Eleven users, a repeated 50-word English lexicon, whispered letter spelling, and held-out re-wearing sessions. No unseen-word test, unrestricted dictation, fully voiceless validation, unseen-impostor test, replay/injection challenge, or clinical communication evaluation.
input_modality: Low-frequency whisper audio plus 17.5–23 kHz ultrasonic reflections of ear-canal dynamic motion. The authors explicitly equate silent speech with whispering because participants produced subtle voice.
sensor_hardware: Edifier W380NB active noise-canceling earbuds with the in-ear microphone detached from its circuitry and directly wired through a 3.5 mm jack to a Google Pixel 3a. Transmitted OFDM cycles contain 2046 samples at 48 kHz; ultrasonic band 17.5–23 kHz.
output_type: Spelled word text derived from 26 letter classes plus a CTC blank; separate binary user accept/reject decision.
vocabulary_type: Closed evaluation lexicon selected from frequent Oxford English Dictionary words; users spell letter names with subtle voice rather than freely dictating sentences.
vocabulary_size: 50 tested words; spelling output alphabet is 26 letters plus a CTC blank.
metrics: Section 4.1.2 reports mean Top-1 word accuracy 67.3% across all 11 users; 90.25% only for eight without degraded ultrasonic sensing, alongside a 91.4% ReHEarSSE baseline. S5/S9/S10 recognition is below 10%. Reported mean authentication TPR is 81.76% and FPR 3.2%; S9/S10 have near-zero TPR. S5 TPR is inconsistent: 99.9% in prose versus 98.00% in Figure 3(b), with 3.4% FPR in both. EER is listed as a metric but no result is reported; the aggregate values above are reported, not independently reconciled.
evaluation_mode: For each of 11 participants in turn, train a genuine-user-specific system and use the other ten as impostors. Hold out one randomly selected re-wearing session per participant. Evaluate Top-1/2/3 word accuracy against an implemented ReHEarSSE baseline and report per-user and average TPR/FPR for authentication, with 50 genuine and 500 impostor attempts per user model. Threshold selection uses Youden's J; the threshold-calibration data split is not clearly specified.

evidence.statement: HEar-ID proposes joint spelling and user verification from whisper audio and ultrasonic ear-canal reflections, with contrastive alignment and two task heads. The private-key wording describes the learned mapping rather than a specified cryptographic key-generation protocol.
evidence.section_or_location: Abstract and Section 1, PDF pp. 1–2; Section 3.2 and Figure 2, PDF pp. 2–3

evidence.statement: The authors explicitly treat silent speech as whispering because participants still make subtle voice; the data-collection description also states that all participants spelled words with subtle voice. Fully voiceless operation is therefore not validated by this experiment.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 1, PDF p. 2; Section 4, PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: The system uses 2046-sample OFDM cycles at 48 kHz, a 17.5–23 kHz ultrasonic band, 426 ms windows with 85 ms stride, 200-lag autoregressive ultrasonic features, and low-pass-filtered, downsampled whisper mel-spectrograms.

The shared representation feeds an authentication branch with angular-triplet loss and a CTC spelling branch over 26 letters plus blank. Contrastive, authentication and CTC loss weights are 0.1, 0.5 and 0.3. The paper does not provide isolated component or loss ablations.
evidence.section_or_location: Sections 3.2–3.4 and Figure 2, PDF pp. 2–4; Section 4, PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: The study has 11 users (ten reused ReHEarSSE participants and one recruit), nine male and two female, mean age 22. Each spelled four rounds of the same 50-word lexicon selected from 1000 frequent Oxford English Dictionary words.

For each genuine-user model, one re-wearing session per participant is randomly selected for testing and the other sessions train the model. Authentication and CLWUM use all participant identities; the SSI head uses genuine-user data only. Each model receives 50 genuine and 500 other-participant impostor attempts at test time; this is session holdout, not unseen-impostor evaluation.

Reported Top-1 word accuracy is 67.3% across all 11 users and 90.25% only for eight users without degraded ultrasonic sensing; the stated ReHEarSSE baseline is 91.4%. S5, S9 and S10 are below 10%. The eight-user figure must not replace the all-user result or be described as outperforming the baseline.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 4.1.2, Silent-speech recognition, and Figure 3(a), PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Section 4.1.2 reports mean authentication TPR 81.76% and FPR 3.2%, with near-zero TPR for S9 and S10. The prose gives S5 TPR as 99.9%, but visually inspected Figure 3(b) labels S5 TPR 98.00%; both give S5 FPR 3.4%. These inconsistent S5 values are not reconciled by the paper. EER is named but no numerical EER is reported.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 4.1.2, Authentication, and Figure 3(b), PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Although described as commodity earbuds, the experimental Edifier W380NB setup removes the in-ear microphone from the earbud circuitry and wires it directly to a Google Pixel 3a through a 3.5 mm jack for unprocessed audio. The paper does not demonstrate unmodified standalone wireless-earbud inference.

Section 3.3.1 describes the authentication margin m as 11.45 and later as 30 degrees. It states threshold calibration by Youden's J but does not clearly specify a separate calibration-data split; these details need clarification for faithful reproduction.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 3.3.1, User Authentication, PDF p. 3; Section 3.4, PDF p. 4

evidence.statement: Replay and injection attacks motivate the introduction, but the experiment evaluates other cohort participants' attempts rather than replay or injection attacks. The poster reports neither an explicit evaluated attack protocol for those threats nor numerical real-time, power, walking, unseen-word or long-term continuous-verification results; expanding lexicons and refining continuous verification are future work.
evidence.section_or_location: Section 1, PDF p. 1; Sections 4–5 and Figure 3, PDF p. 4

en.summary: Sensing, shared model and joint word-plus-identity output are each standard; whisper adds nothing over the 91.4% ultrasonic-only baseline, and impostors are training participants (M12 behind).
en.sensor: Modified ANC earbud in-ear microphone (whisper + ultrasound)
en.task: Spelling-based text entry and user authentication
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 67.3% Top-1 word accuracy across 11 users; authentication TPR 81.76%, FPR 3.2%
en.limitations: Depends on whisper, three users fail badly, hardware is modified, and no replay/injection attacks or unseen-impostor tests are evaluated.

title: Pretraining Large Brain Language Model for Active BCI: Silent Speech
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '25)
review_confidence: medium: target read in full (arXiv v2, all sections, Tables 1-8); comparators Du-IN and the 2026 EEG foundation-model benchmark read in full.
expert_take_short: In-domain EEG pretraining adds 4.3 points on 24 mouthed words (35.3% to 39.6%), one session, no seeds; Du-IN showed this earlier. Muscle artefact and new users remain untested.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training (M03) and the decoder (M06); both are standard against the field. Pretraining on about 105 h of the same 12 participants' unlabeled EEG raises 24-word accuracy from 35.3% to 39.6%, a relative gain similar to the one Du-IN reported earlier for 61-word sEEG with six seeds, here from one test session per participant without seeds or tests. The headline 7.3-point margin over TCNet also contains an architecture gain from a far larger model. Mouthed articulation leaves facial muscle activity uncontrolled, the semantic mean is misprinted as 42.8% in §5.1 against 47.0% in Table 2, and transfer to new users or datasets, which the 'large brain language model' label implies, is not tested.
expert_true_value: Shows that pretraining on unlabeled EEG of the same participants, with masked and future-prediction objectives, adds about 4 points to per-participant 24-word classification; it does not show a general brain language model or transfer to new users.
canon_before: Self-supervised (masked) pretraining is the usual approach (31 slot-filled studies in the topic table); Du-IN (2024) had shown in-domain masked pretraining for speech decoding with a from-scratch control and six seeds; the generic EEG model LaBraM scored below from-scratch models on speech tasks in Du-IN and in this paper.
delta_from_canon: Adds autoregressive future-prediction (waveform, amplitude, phase) to masked pretraining and applies it to mouthed-word scalp EEG; the gain over its own from-scratch model is 4.3 word points (12.2% relative), a relative gain similar to the earlier sEEG result on a different task and chance level.
position_in_field: Standard in training (M03) and decoder (M06); evaluation (M12) not reported to field standard (no seeds, chance level or test).
practical_value: A recipe for using unlabeled sessions of the same user to improve per-user EEG word classification; accuracy (39.6% on 24 words) and the offline setting are far from a communication device.
axes_moved: Per-participant cross-session accuracy with in-domain self-supervised pretraining.
axes_unresolved: Unseen participants, other datasets, imagined (non-mouthed) speech, EMG contamination, online use, open vocabulary, dataset release.
axes_regressed: Model is 22.61M parameters against baselines of 8.54K-5.80M; four of 12 participants lose accuracy with pretraining.
technical_limits: 122-channel research cap; 22.61M-parameter model; forecasts diverge beyond about 120 ms (Sec. 5.3); priority claim for future prediction applies at most to scalp EEG (Brant forecasts sEEG).
evaluation_limits: One held-out test session per participant; no seeds, intervals, chance level or significance test; held-out session identities and model-selection rule not stated; semantic mean inconsistent (42.8% vs 47.0%).
deployment_limits: Seated, cued laboratory task with a dense wet EEG cap; no online or real-time evaluation; hardware savings from forecasting proposed but not tested.
scope_limits: 12 healthy native English speakers, 24 words and 6 semantic groups, mouthed silent articulation, per-participant models.
input_modality: Non-invasive scalp EEG during mouthed (silently articulated) words; not imagined speech.
sensor_hardware: 128-channel Neuroscan cap and amplifier at 1000 Hz; 122 EEG channels; 1-75 Hz band-pass, 50 Hz notch, common average reference, ICA artifact removal at 90% confidence; 250 Hz for training.
output_type: Class label: one of 24 words or 6 semantic groups; auxiliary EEG forecasts.
vocabulary_type: Closed set.
vocabulary_size: 24 words; 6 semantic groups.
metrics: Table 1 (24 words, mean of 12 participants): LBLM with MSTP+ASTP 39.6%, MSTP only 36.9%, from scratch 35.3%, TCNet 32.3%, EEGNet 30.5%, LaBraM 20.6%; per participant 11.7-73.8%. Table 2 (6 groups): 47.0%, 44.8%, 42.2%, TCNet 41.6%. Table 6 forecast (46 of 250 samples): MSE/MAE 0.27/0.32 vs PatchTST 0.84/0.62, TimesFM 1.40/0.76.
evaluation_mode: Offline, per-participant, cross-session accuracy on one held-out test session; EEG forecasting MSE/MAE.

evidence.statement: 12 healthy right-handed native English speakers attempted silent articulation without emitting sounds.
About 105 h of unlabeled EEG from the study recordings are used for pretraining; two of 16 sessions per participant are held out for validation and test.
24-word accuracy: 39.6% with MSTP+ASTP, 36.9% MSTP only, 35.3% from scratch, TCNet 32.3%.
6-group accuracy: 47.0% with MSTP+ASTP, 42.2% from scratch, TCNet 41.6%.
Sec. 5.1 prints a semantic mean of 42.8%, against 47.0% in the Abstract and Table 2.
No seeds, intervals, chance level or statistical test are reported for the classification results.
Six reference electrodes record muscle and environment noise; ICA removes muscle components at 90% confidence; no analysis uses the muscle channels as a control.
Forecasts follow the true signal only for about 120 ms, then diverge (authors).
Du-IN (2024) raised 61-word sEEG accuracy from 56.29% to 62.70% with in-domain masked pretraining, six seeds.
A 2026 benchmark found no consistent advantage of EEG foundation models over compact CNNs on speech EEG and chance-level cross-subject decoding.

en.summary: In-domain EEG pretraining adds 4.3 points on 24 mouthed words (35.3% to 39.6%), one session, no seeds; Du-IN showed this earlier. Muscle artefact and new users remain untested.
en.sensor: 128-channel Neuroscan scalp EEG cap, 122 EEG channels, 1000 Hz (downsampled to 250 Hz)
en.task: Closed-set classification of silently articulated (mouthed) words from scalp EEG
en.vocabulary: 24 fixed English words; also 6 semantic groups
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent (per-participant fine-tuning; no unseen participant)
en.session: Cross-session: one held-out validation and one held-out test session per participant
en.key_result: 24-word accuracy 39.6% with pretraining vs 35.3% for the same model from scratch and 32.3% for TCNet (Table 1); 6-group accuracy 47.0% vs 42.2% (Table 2); one test session per participant, no seed count reported.
en.limitations: Pretraining and testing use the same 12 participants; no unseen-user or second-dataset test; no seeds, chance level or statistical test; mouthed articulation; the six muscle-noise reference electrodes are not used as an EMG control; semantic mean misprinted as 42.8% in Sec. 5.1 (Table 2 per-participant values average to 47.0%); dataset not yet released.

title: Reconstructing Unseen Sentences from Speech-related Biosignals for Open-vocabulary Neural Communication
expert_take_short: EEG+EMG fusion (M05) and overt-audio DTW targets (M02) are standard; the unseen-sentence claim lacks a cohort WER (M12), and no EMG-only arm or EMG regression is reported.
expert_take_long: The paper [@kim2025reconstructing] changes two components: it adds 10 face and neck EMG channels to 128-channel EEG (M05), and it trains whispered and imagined inputs on the overt recording of the same sentence through phoneme-weighted DTW (M02). Both are standard: EEG and sEMG fusion for silent-speech synthesis, with single-modality ablations, appeared in 2023 [@li2023hybrid] and is not among the paper's 53 references, and the training recipe is the EMG voicing recipe [@gaddy2021improved] that NeuroTalk had moved to imagined EEG [@lee2023towards]. The sentence-disjoint test (M12) follows field practice, but the evaluation is behind the best comparable work: the open-vocabulary claim rests on phoneme accuracy and DTW-aligned MFCC distances, with no cohort word or character error rate. The strongest confound is muscle: overt EEG is kept at 0.5–200 Hz with no regression of the simultaneously recorded EMG [@sato2024delineating], and there is no EMG-only arm, so what EEG adds to EMG is not measured.
expert_true_value: A concrete held-out-sentence and modality-comparison protocol that separates phoneme prediction from acoustic reconstruction; its value is experimental evidence about biosignal reconstruction, not ready-to-use silent conversation.
canon_before: The paper situates itself against non-invasive EEG studies dominated by predefined word/sentence categories, while acknowledging earlier unseen-word reconstruction and held-out-sentence EEG-to-text work.
delta_from_canon: Extends the reconstruction question to disjoint sentence texts with phoneme/acoustic prediction and compares available biosignal modalities, rather than demonstrating unrestricted thought decoding or a new general-purpose language interface.
position_in_field: Non-invasive, speaker-dependent biosignal-to-speech reconstruction with held-out sentence texts; a relevant SSI research step with much narrower validation than unrestricted neural conversation.
practical_value: Offers a protocol for comparing acoustic and phoneme objectives and the added value of EMG where muscle activity is available. Benefit for routine assistive communication remains unknown.
axes_moved: Subject-specific held-out sentence reconstruction beyond repeated sentence classes; explicit EEG versus EEG+EMG comparison for overt and whispered speech; exploratory attempted-overt evaluation in one person with ataxic dysarthria.
axes_unresolved: Unseen users and sessions; truly novel lexical words; spontaneous imagined communication; neural specificity versus muscle/cue contamination; whole-test intelligibility; online latency and usability; wider clinical benefit.
axes_regressed: Adding ten face/neck EMG channels increases sensing burden relative to EEG alone. Whispered EEG+EMG has MCD 4.73 versus 4.71 for EEG alone and the same rounded RMSE 0.58, so not every reconstruction metric improves.
technical_limits: Whispered/imagined training targets use corresponding overt audio, not contemporaneous silent acoustic ground truth. Filtering and common-average referencing alone do not establish neural specificity or exclusion of muscle artifacts; fixed overt→whispered→imagined order may carry echoic traces, acknowledged by authors. The input/feature/checkpoint details and phoneme scoring require clarification. Source localization is descriptive, not causal evidence for a speech mechanism.
evaluation_limits: Main aggregate metrics are 15 subject means over 30 test sentences. The text reports paired Wilcoxon p<0.0001 for specified modality improvements, but confidence intervals, exact p values, multiple-comparison handling and error-bar definition are not specified in the main text. CER is shown only for two examples from one subject, not an overall test rate. Fig. 7 and Table V concern a representative subject; supplementary material is referenced but absent from the reviewed 11-page PDF.
deployment_limits: High-density cap plus optional face/neck electrodes, individual training and trial segmentation. Button-controlled cued acquisition; no autonomous start/stop, mobile use, walking, longitudinal deployment or measured end-to-end latency reported.
scope_limits: Reviewed all 11 pages of arXiv v1, including main-text figures/tables and references; key pipeline, aggregate and frequency tables visually checked. Referenced supplementary tables/figures are not contained in this PDF and were not verified. No independent experimental reproduction or verification of external code/data availability.
task: Reconstruct cued, held-out English sentences from overt/whispered/imagined biosignals, with primary aggregate comparison in overt and whispered conditions.
input_modality: High-density scalp EEG, alone or channel-concatenated with face/neck surface EMG; overt audio and sentence text supply training targets, not inference inputs.
sensor_hardware: Brain Vision/Recorder at 1000 Hz; Standard 128-channel actiCAP with FCz reference; ten EMG channels on face/neck; synchronized 44100-Hz microphone. Network input is described as 127 EEG plus ten EMG channels; the channel-count reconciliation is not explicit in the main text.
body_site: Scalp for EEG; face and neck for EMG.
output_type: Predicted acoustic features and 40-class phoneme sequences; HiFi-GAN synthesized audio followed by DeepSpeech text for evaluation.
vocabulary_type: Cued English sentences with nonoverlapping training/test sentence texts; open sentence-sequence output within a fixed phoneme inventory, not verified unrestricted lexical generalization.
vocabulary_size: 39 phoneme classes plus silence; 474 English sentence stimuli for healthy participants and 155 attempted-overt patient stimuli. Number of distinct lexical words is unknown.
metrics: Healthy-participant mean phoneme accuracy: overt EEG 36.83%, EEG+EMG 48.58%; whispered EEG 30.54%, EEG+EMG 40.97%. In that order, RMSE 0.50/0.46 and 0.58/0.58; MCD 4.18/3.81 and 4.71/4.73; F1 0.34/0.47 and 0.16/0.24. Authors use an 11% most-frequent-silence baseline. Table II selected-example CER: overt 0.18 and 0.36, whispered 0.50 and 0.40, all EEG+EMG. Table V representative-subject imagined delta/high-gamma phoneme accuracy: both 31.35%, with RMSE 0.65/0.71 and MCD 5.33/5.72. Single-patient attempted-overt EEG/EEG+EMG phoneme accuracy: 42.85%/45.63%.
evaluation_mode: Offline, personalized held-out sentence reconstruction with EEG-only and EEG+EMG comparisons; exploratory single-patient attempted-overt reconstruction and representative-subject frequency/source analyses.

evidence.statement: Fifteen healthy adults perform 474 English sentences in fixed overt, whispered and imagined order; 444 training and 30 test sentences do not overlap. Only the final repeated attempt is retained.
Acquisition uses a 128-channel actiCAP, ten face/neck EMG channels at 1000 Hz and synchronized 44100-Hz audio; the network description later specifies 127 EEG input channels.

The decoder is personalized per subject. Corresponding overt recordings supply whispered/imagined acoustic targets, while inference explicitly receives neither recorded audio nor target sentence text.

Three ConvBlocks and a Bi-GRU predict acoustic features and phonemes; HiFi-GAN generates audio and DeepSpeech produces text. Silent-mode training combines phoneme-informed DTW with CTC rather than demonstrating a new sensor or deployment platform.
Across 15 participants, overt phoneme accuracy increases from EEG 36.83% to EEG+EMG 48.58%, and whispered accuracy from 30.54% to 40.97%. These are phoneme metrics, not sentence accuracy.
Overt EEG/combined RMSE is 0.50/0.46, MCD 4.18/3.81 and F1 0.34/0.47. Whispered values are RMSE 0.58/0.58, MCD 4.71/4.73 and F1 0.16/0.24; combined sensing does not improve every whispered metric.

Each subject contributes an average over 30 test sentences; authors report paired Wilcoxon p<0.0001 for all overt metrics and whispered phoneme accuracy/F1. The 11% baseline is the most frequent silence class, not a shuffled temporal null model.
CER 0.18/0.36 for overt and 0.50/0.40 for whispered speech are two EEG+EMG examples from one representative subject, not overall test-set character error rates or human-listener intelligibility.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, Table II; p.7, IV.A continuation

evidence.statement: One 66-year-old man with ataxic dysarthria provides 155 attempted-overt sentences split 145/10. EEG/combined phoneme accuracy is 42.85%/45.63%; this is not a patient imagined-speech test or evidence of broad clinical benefit.
evidence.section_or_location: p.7, IV.B Sentence Reconstruction in a Speech-impaired Patient

evidence.statement: Table V is explicitly from a representative subject: imagined delta and high-gamma EEG both reach 31.35% phoneme accuracy. Delta/high-gamma RMSE is 0.65/0.71 and MCD 5.33/5.72; these are not 15-person aggregate imagined-speech scores.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.8–9, IV.E; p.9, Table V caption and rows

evidence.statement: Fig.7 relates sentence length and phoneme accuracy in a representative subject (PCC −0.459 overt, −0.623 whispered). These correlations do not establish causation; W-score panel labels/caption and text require implementation reconciliation.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.7–8, IV.D; p.8, Fig.7 and Table IV

evidence.statement: sLORETA maps at 1, 1.25 and 1.5 seconds describe estimated activity from a representative subject. They do not establish that reconstructed content is causally driven by the highlighted cortical areas.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, III.F; pp.8–9, IV.E and Fig.8

evidence.statement: Authors acknowledge that the fixed overt-to-whispered-to-imagined order may introduce echoic traces. Main preprocessing describes filters and common-average referencing, not a control proving independence from residual muscle activity.

Disjoint sentence texts support unseen-sentence evaluation, but the main text does not report lexical word overlap, cross-user/session tests, whole-test CER or online latency; broad unrestricted neural communication remains unverified.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2–4, II.A and III.A–D; pp.9–10, V.A and V.E

evidence.statement: Training uses AdamW, learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-5, cosine scheduling, at most 200 epochs, early stopping, GRU dropout 0.1 and length-2048 batching. Validation allocation is not specified in the main training description.

The conclusion links reconstructed audio and a toy dataset from one subject. Supplementary figures/tables referenced throughout are absent from this 11-page PDF; completeness of external data/code and those supplements was not verified in this review.
evidence.section_or_location: p.10, VI Conclusion; pp.2,5,7–8 supplementary references

en.summary: EEG+EMG fusion (M05) and overt-audio DTW targets (M02) are standard; the unseen-sentence claim lacks a cohort WER (M12), and no EMG-only arm or EMG regression is reported.
en.sensor: 128-channel actiCAP EEG plus 10 face/neck EMG channels
en.vocabulary: 474 cued English sentences; 39 phonemes plus silence
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Overt phoneme accuracy 48.58% EEG+EMG, 36.83% EEG, held-out sentences, baseline 11%
en.limitations: Strongest evidence is overt/whispered, imagined results are from a representative subject, CER only for examples, and silent targets use overt audio.

title: RESOUND: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Videos via Acoustic-Semantic Decomposed Modeling
expert_take_short: Decoder split (M06) and lip-reader text plus audio prompt (M07) are standard; WER gain comes from the lip reader, LRS3 WER level with LipVoicer, prosody leads confounded by the prompt.
expert_take_long: RESOUND [@pham2025resound] changes the decoder (M06), splitting it into excitation and formant paths, and the use-time inputs (M07), adding lip-reader text and a 0.5 s audio prompt. Both are standard: vid2voc predicted F0, aperiodicity and spectral envelope from silent video for a source-filter vocoder [@michelsanti2020vocoder], and Let There Be Sound used pitch and energy predictors [@kim2024let], so the claim to be "the first study to incorporate source-filter theory into L2S synthesis" (§1; Appendix, M06) holds only as a label. The WER gain comes from the lip reader: without L2T and SRA, LRS3 WER rises from 20.06 to 27.49, level with Intelligible L2S at 27.69 (Tables 1, 3). With it, RESOUND is level with the best on LRS3 (20.06 against 21.04 for LipVoicer in its table, 21.4% in LipVoicer's paper [@yemini2024lipvoicer]) and trails LipVoicer on LRS2 (28.55 against 17.04). The prosody and similarity leads (MAEF0 49.52 against 81.63, SECS 0.777 against 0.591 for LipVoicer) pit a system prompted with audio (§3.3) against LipVoicer, given none. The SOTA claim (§5) has no reported repeated runs.
expert_true_value: Shows that, in a speech-unit lip-to-speech lineage, adding text from an external lip reader brings LRS3 WER to the level of LipVoicer while keeping fast feed-forward synthesis; the source-filter decoder split itself is not isolated by its ablations.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech systems combine pretrained visual features (often AV-HuBERT), speech units or mel-spectrograms and a vocoder. Source-filter synthesis from silent video dates to Vid2Speech (2017); pitch predictors (VCVTS) and pitch and energy predictors (Let There Be Sound) already exist; LipVoicer conditions on lip-reader text; reference-audio speaker embeddings are the usual use-time speaker input.
delta_from_canon: Splits the decoder into an excitation generator fed by prompt-conditioned pitch and energy predictors and a formant generator fed by visual features and phonemes from Auto-AVSR text (fused by Semantic Reference Attention), summed into a coarse mel; mel and speech units drive a multi-input vocoder.
position_in_field: Standard on the decoder (M06) and on use-time inputs (M07): source-filter synthesis, pitch and energy predictors, lip-reader text and reference-audio conditioning all predate it. Evaluation (M12) is standard in protocol; baseline provenance, speaker split and repeated runs are not stated. Overt-speech video with the audio removed, not silent articulation.
practical_value: A fast feed-forward option for re-voicing silent video when a short recording of the speaker is available; its intelligibility depends on an external lip reader, and its prosody advantage depends on that audio prompt.
axes_moved: Among the systems in its tables, on LRS3: highest UTMOS, SECS, ESTOI and lowest MAEF0 and MCD; WER 20.06 against 21.04 for LipVoicer; highest LRS3 listener MOS for naturalness, intelligibility and similarity. On LRS2 better on all listed metrics except WER.
axes_unresolved: Prompts from a different utterance or no prompt; speaker overlap with training and AV-HuBERT pre-training; whether baseline rows were rerun; timing scope and hardware of RTF; repeated runs; silent articulation; other languages and accents; an ablation of the excitation/formant split alone.
axes_regressed: LRS2 WER 28.55 against 17.04 for LipVoicer; RTF 0.063 is slower than Intelligible L2S (0.041); without the lip-reader text, LRS3 WER (27.49) equals Intelligible L2S (27.69).
technical_limits: Lip-reader errors pass into the phoneme path. The excitation and formant representations are learned latents, not measured glottal or vocal-tract signals. The acoustic-branch ablation removes the prosody encoder and the excitation generator together, and the L2T ablation removes L2T and SRA together. The LRS2 WER gap is attributed to noise without a test.
evaluation_limits: No seeds, repeated runs or significance tests for objective metrics. The 30-listener MOS reports 95% confidence intervals, but rater details, assignment and interval method are not given. The test-time prompt source, baseline provenance and input conditions, RTF hardware and timing scope, and speaker overlap are not stated. LSE metrics are omitted.
deployment_limits: Needs mouth video, a reference audio prompt, a pretrained lip reader, G2P, AV-HuBERT and a vocoder. No mobile device, walking, occlusion, continuous conversation or speech-impaired users were tested; RTF alone does not give end-to-end latency.
scope_limits: Read: arXiv:2505.22024 v1 (Secs. 1-5, Fig. 1, Tables 1-3) and the public repository configs. Limited to English LRS2/LRS3 offline reconstruction and LRS3 listener and ablation tests. No independent reproduction.
input_modality: Mouth video plus a 0.5 s audio prompt for timbre, pitch and energy (taken from ground-truth audio in the implementation), and text predicted by a lip reader. Training uses paired audio, mel, speech units, F0 and energy. Not a video-only system.
sensor_hardware: Existing LRS2/LRS3 video; MediaPipe mouth crop 96x96 with random 88x88 crops; audio resampled to 16 kHz. No new camera or contact sensor.
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary English continuous speech reconstructed as audio; not word classification, and correct output of arbitrary vocabulary is not shown.
vocabulary_size: LRS3 is described as having over 50,000 words; the test vocabulary and out-of-training words are not stated.
metrics: Table 1 LRS3: UTMOS 3.002, SECS 0.777, WER 20.06, MAERMSE 0.025, MAEF0 49.52, ESTOI 0.423, MCD-DTW-SL 8.71, RTF 0.063. LRS2: 2.382, 0.730, 28.55, 0.025, 51.79, 0.420, 10.56. LipVoicer WER 21.04 (LRS3) and 17.04 (LRS2), RTF 14.117. Table 2 LRS3 MOS: naturalness 3.86±0.13, intelligibility 3.86±0.15, similarity 3.57±0.14. Table 3 LRS3: without L2T and SRA WER 27.49; without the acoustic branch UTMOS 2.176, MAEF0 69.219. Authors' values.
evaluation_mode: Offline comparison on LRS2 and LRS3: predicted naturalness (UTMOS), speaker-embedding similarity, ASR word error, pitch and energy errors, ESTOI, MCD, real-time factor; LRS3 listener MOS and component ablations.

evidence.statement: The authors separate prosody and content into two paths and use mel-spectrograms and discrete speech units for waveform generation. The claim to be the first source-filter L2S study is the authors' positioning; Vid2Speech (2017) already used an LPC source-filter synthesizer from video.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Abstract and Introduction; pp.2–3 Sections 2.1–2.3; Figure 1

evidence.statement: At inference the model receives an audio prompt besides the mouth video, used by the timbre and prompt encoders. The implementation extracts a random 0.5 s segment of ground-truth audio; results with a prompt from a different utterance are not reported.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Figure 1 and Section 2.1; p.3 Section 3.3, audio prompt paragraph

evidence.statement: AV-HuBERT gives visual features; a lip reader (Auto-AVSR) and grapheme-to-phoneme conversion give phoneme features, fused with the visual features by Semantic Reference Attention and a Conformer.

Excitation and formant representations from two generators are summed into a coarse mel; speech units are predicted separately and passed with the mel to a multi-input vocoder. These are learned representations, not measured vocal-fold or vocal-tract signals.

LRS2 is described as over 220 hours of English BBC video with pretraining, training and test sets; LRS3 as 438 hours of TED/TEDx video with over 50,000 words, training on 131,000 and testing on around 1,300 utterances. These are existing overt recordings, not new silent-articulation data.

A 96x96 mouth crop with random 88x88 crops, flipping, erasing and temporal masking; audio at 16 kHz with HuBERT-BASE 200-cluster speech units. AV-HuBERT, pretrained on LRS3, is frozen for LRS3 and fine-tuned for LRS2.

Training: 80 epochs, 40k steps per dataset, initial learning rate 0.001; loss weights 100 (mel), 0.1 (pitch), 0.1 (energy), 0.01 (units), label smoothing 0.1; an 8-layer Conformer and three FFT blocks per branch generator (hidden 512, 8 heads).

Naturalness is a UTMOS prediction, speaker similarity uses Resemblyzer, WER uses Auto-AVSR; pitch and energy errors, ESTOI, MCD-DTW-SL and real-time factor are also reported. Automatic metrics and listener ratings are separate evaluations.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Section 3.2 Evaluation Metrics; p.4 Table 2

evidence.statement: Table 1, LRS3: RESOUND UTMOS 3.002, SECS 0.777, WER 20.06, MAERMSE 0.025, MAEF0 49.52, ESTOI 0.423, MCD-DTW-SL 8.71; LipVoicer WER 21.04. Ground truth UTMOS 3.519.
Table 1, LRS2: RESOUND UTMOS 2.382, SECS 0.730, WER 28.55, MAERMSE 0.025, MAEF0 51.79, ESTOI 0.420, MCD-DTW-SL 10.56; LipVoicer WER 17.04, so RESOUND is not best on every dataset and metric.

RTF: RESOUND 0.063, LipVoicer 14.117, Intelligible L2S 0.041. RESOUND is faster than LipVoicer but not the fastest in the table; hardware and the timed pipeline are not stated, so end-to-end latency cannot be derived.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1, Efficiency column; Section 4.1 speed paragraph; p.3 Sections 3.2–3.3

evidence.statement: LRS3 listener test: 30 participants rate 20 samples per method on a 5-point scale in 0.5 steps, with 95% confidence intervals. This is a rating, not a word-recognition score; assignment and interval method are not described.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Section 4.1 MOS paragraph and Table 2

evidence.statement: LRS3 MOS for RESOUND: naturalness 3.86±0.13, intelligibility 3.86±0.15, similarity 3.57±0.14; ground truth 4.80±0.05, 4.76±0.07, 4.92±0.04. Above the compared systems, below the recordings.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 2; Section 4.1 specifies 95% confidence intervals

evidence.statement: Removing L2T and SRA together raises LRS3 WER from 20.06 to 27.49 and lowers UTMOS from 3.002 to 2.840. The two modules are removed together, so their separate effects are not isolated.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 3, w/o L2T & SRA row; Section 4.2

evidence.statement: Without the acoustic branch: UTMOS 2.176, WER 21.93, SECS 0.713, MAEF0 69.219, ESTOI 0.385. Without the energy predictor: UTMOS 2.698, WER 20.22, SECS 0.744, MAEF0 51.22, ESTOI 0.400.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 3 and Section 4.2, acoustic branch and energy predictor paragraphs

evidence.statement: The authors attribute the LRS2 WER gap to LRS2 noise and LipVoicer being a denoising diffusion model; no noise-controlled experiment is reported, so the cause is not established.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Section 4.1, LRS2 discrepancy paragraph; Tables 1 and 3

evidence.statement: Limited to two English datasets and offline synthesis: no silent articulation, speech-impaired users, mobile or walking use, or vocabulary-split tests. Speaker split details and independent-prompt conditions are not stated. Other languages and accents are left to future work.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–4 Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–4.2; p.4 Section 5 Conclusion

evidence.statement: The Vocoder row of Table 1 feeds ground-truth mel and speech units to the vocoder; it is a reference, not a video-input system. Its LRS3 SECS is 0.89 against 0.777 for RESOUND.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table 1, Vocoder dagger rows and footnote

evidence.statement: The main contribution combines existing lip reading, speech units and source-filter-inspired synthesis into content and prosody paths with joint outputs; the components themselves predate it.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Introduction and cited prior approaches; pp.2–3 Sections 2.1–2.4

evidence.statement: The paper points to a demo page and code; the repository configs fix seeds (1337 encoder, 1234 vocoder), but repeated-run variance of the objective metrics is not reported.
evidence.section_or_location: p.1 Introduction final paragraph and footnote 1; p.3 Section 3.3; p.4 Tables 1–3

en.summary: Decoder split (M06) and lip-reader text plus audio prompt (M07) are standard; WER gain comes from the lip reader, LRS3 WER level with LipVoicer, prosody leads confounded by the prompt.
en.sensor: Existing video (LRS2/LRS3) plus reference audio
en.vocabulary: English continuous speech; LRS3 over 50,000 words
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: LRS3 WER 20.06 against 21.04 for LipVoicer in the paper's table and 21.4% in LipVoicer's own paper; LRS2 WER 28.55 against 17.04; without lip-reader text LRS3 WER is 27.49.
en.limitations: Source-filter synthesis, pitch and energy predictors and lip-reader text predate it; the prompt is a ground-truth audio segment with test-time source not stated; ablations remove modules in pairs; no seeds or repeated runs; baseline provenance and RTF hardware not stated.

title: Silent Speech Sentence Recognition with Six-Axis Accelerometers using Conformer and CTC Algorithm
expert_take_short: CTC decoder (M06), concatenated training sentences (M03) and six IMUs (M05) are standard: CTC silent-phrase decoding predates it; 97.17% is a word ratio on 4 people, split unstated.
expert_take_long: The paper [@xie2025sixaxis] changes the decoder (M06, Conformer with CTC), the training data (M03, concatenated words plus noise) and the sensing (M05, six six-axis IMUs); all three are standard. Continuous silent recognition (8.9% WER, 2,200 words) [@meltzner2018semg] and CTC decoding of silent phrases [@chen2023hdsemg; @benster2024mona] predate it, and the cited Luo et al. already trained CTC for silent sentences [@luo2020acoustic], so the §1 novelty claim fails (Appendix). Liu et al. trained IMU decoders on concatenated sentences and tested on spoken ones [@liu2024lipimu]; this paper does not say whether its length curve (Fig. 3a) scores recorded or concatenated sequences. The headline 97.17% is a word ratio on 4 participants with a 70:15:15 split of unstated unit; repetition leakage across it is not excluded (M12).
expert_true_value: A small wearable-IMU example of reading known word sequences with CTC instead of classifying whole sentences, with one laryngectomized participant, a blind cross-subject condition and few-shot recovery; its most useful finding is that single gyroscope axes outperformed single accelerometer axes.
canon_before: Silent word classification from facial accelerometers (four sensors, 40 words), CTC decoding of silently articulated phrases from HD-sEMG, CTC compared with attention for silent sentences from acoustic sensing, and IMU sentence decoders trained on concatenated word recordings all existed before this paper.
delta_from_canon: Six six-axis IMUs (acceleration and angular velocity) on the face feed a convolution plus local self-attention network trained with CTC and cross-entropy; training sentences are made by concatenating word recordings and adding noise; channel-count and single-axis ablations are reported. No new learning principle.
position_in_field: Standard on the decoder (M06), the training data (M03) and the sensing (M05): CTC decoding of silent phrases and concatenated training sentences predate it. Small offline prototype of a wearable silent-articulation interface with a closed vocabulary; not inner-speech decoding, open-vocabulary conversation or speech synthesis.
practical_value: A reference for short known phrases and for reducing the number of facial sensors, and a reason to keep gyroscope channels; one laryngectomized participant does not establish benefit for patients or daily use.
axes_moved: system_design; problem_reframing; known word sequences from facial motion with CTC, per-participant adaptation, and sensor-count and axis comparisons.
axes_unresolved: Unseen words, natural continuous speech, how the long test sequences were built, split unit and run count, few-shot sample count, the 36 versus 30 input mismatch, agreement between figures and text, other days and re-attachment, device latency, long-term wear, and a wider patient group.
axes_regressed: Accuracy drops for some participants in the blind cross-subject condition; a single sensor gives 90.22-93.19%. No same-condition comparison with earlier methods, so gains or losses against them are unknown.
technical_limits: Preprocessing yields 36 features while the first convolution takes 30 inputs. The CTC vocabulary and Chinese segmentation, how classification and sequence outputs are used, start and end detection in continuous input, and causal filtering are not stated.
evaluation_limits: Four participants, two recorded English sentences and a closed vocabulary. The unit of the 70:15:15 split, day and session separation, per-person test counts, few-shot sample counts and the origin of the length-wise sequences are not stated; insertion and deletion handling and run counts are not given, and the comparison with 94.65 +/- 2.54% from another paper is not a same-condition rerun.
deployment_limits: Accuracy falls for unseen users and, in Fig. 3(b), at least one participant appears below 90% after few-shot calibration. Real-time operation, power, long wear, walking, re-attachment, other days, a wider patient group and free conversation are untested.
scope_limits: Read: arXiv:2502.17829 v3, all five pages, Figs. 1-4 and Table 1. External data and code, training runs, independent reproduction and clinical benefit were not examined.
task: Recognition of known words and word sequences from facial motion during silent articulation; besides whole-sentence classification, CTC outputs word sequences without word-boundary time labels. Not speech synthesis.
input_modality: Three-axis acceleration and three-axis angular velocity from six wearable IMUs, measuring mechanical motion of silent articulation; not brain decoding.
sensor_hardware: Six MEMS six-axis IMUs (three-axis accelerometer plus three-axis gyroscope) at six facial sites, sampled at 50 Hz. Sensor model, link and power consumption are not stated.
body_site: Skin of the face and neck; Fig. 1 shows six sites around the mouth, jaw, cheek and throat. Exact positions and re-attachment tolerance are not stated.
output_type: Word or sentence class output and a CTC word sequence (text). CTC learns sequences without a fixed frame-to-word alignment.
vocabulary_type: Closed set: combinations of the recorded vocabulary; not open vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: Recorded items: 16 English words, 2 English sentences and 8 Chinese phrases. The CTC output vocabulary, Chinese word segmentation and the class set are not stated.
metrics: Sec. 3.1 defines accuracy as correctly recognized words over total words in a sentence or dataset: overall 97.17%, words 97.24%, sentences 97.16%; not exact-sentence accuracy, and insertion and deletion handling are not stated. Fig. 3(a) reports above 90% over lengths 1-19 with unit and sequence construction unstated. Single sensor 90.22-93.19%, two or three sensors above 95%. Single gyroscope axis 92.39-93.39%, single accelerometer axis 87.62-92.42%. Two axes 95.37% against 95.57% with six axes in the text.
evaluation_mode: Offline: word and sentence conditions on the standard split for four participants, accuracy by length, per-participant standard, blind and few-shot conditions, and sensor-count and axis comparisons; error bars shown, but run counts, split membership and few-shot sample counts are not stated.

evidence.statement: Six sensors record three-axis acceleration and three-axis gyroscope data at 50 Hz.
Participants are one laryngectomized person and three undergraduates; this is not a test of general benefit for a patient population.

The task covers 16 English words, 2 English sentences and 8 Chinese phrases; the English sentences are 'Drink water' and 'Hello, please wait'. No independent test of out-of-vocabulary words is described.

Words are recorded 100 times with 80 points and sentences and phrases 30 times with 180 points; at 50 Hz this is 1.6 s and 3.6 s of input, not inference latency. Whether repetitions are per person or in total is not stated.

Data are split 70:15:15 into training, validation and test sets, and the training set is augmented tenfold by word concatenation and Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of one-third of the original values.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 §2.1.2, final paragraph spanning the two columns

evidence.statement: Preprocessing uses a 3-point moving average, a 4th-order Butterworth high-pass filter at 2 Hz and z-score normalization, and flattens samples to 36 x window length.

Three convolutional blocks and three local self-attention blocks feed linear classification and CTC outputs. CTC sums over possible alignments of input and target sequence; no new CTC principle is proposed.
Against the 36 input features of Sec. 2.2, Fig. 2 and Sec. 2.3.1 give 30 inputs to the first convolution; what was removed is not stated and the review does not guess a correction.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 §2.2 and Fig.2 first Conv Block 30×128×3×1×1; p.3 §2.3.1

evidence.statement: Training minimizes the sum of CTC and cross-entropy losses with learning rate 0.001, decay 0.00001, batch 32 and 50 epochs; the optimizer is printed as 'Adams'.
Accuracy is correctly recognized words over total words in a sentence or dataset: 97.17% overall, 97.24% for words and 97.16% for sentences; not exact-sentence match.
The comparison value 94.65 +/- 2.54% is reported by prior study [9]; no rerun on shared data or same-condition comparison is shown, and insertion and deletion handling is not stated.

Fig. 3(a) plots lengths 1-19 and the text reports above 90%; the unit, how long sequences were built and their relation to the two recorded English sentences are unclear, so it is not a result on natural free speech.
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 §2.1.2 and Table 1; p.3 Fig.3(a), caption and §3.2

evidence.statement: The standard condition averages above 95%, while blind tests on unseen people vary widely by person; in Fig. 3(b) the blind bars of the patient and Student 3 are well below their standard bars.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–4 §3.3; p.3 Fig.3(b), green Blind and red Normal bars

evidence.statement: The text says few-shot samples improve accuracy to above 90%, but in Fig. 3(b) Student 3's few-shot bar appears below 90%; not every participant reads above 90%, and the number of added samples is not stated.
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 §3.3 final paragraph; p.3 Fig.3(b), Student 3 blue bar

evidence.statement: Mean single-sensor accuracy is 90.22-93.19% and two or three sensors keep above 95%; this is a candidate for simplifying the device, not a measure of long-term comfort.

title: Subject-Independent Imagined Speech Detection via Cross-Subject Generalization and Calibration
expert_take_short: Cyclic training and 10% target calibration (M03) are standard; uncalibrated detection is near chance (MCC 0.044–0.123), and labels are timed from overt speech.
expert_take_long: The paper [@ko2025subject] changes only the training regime (M03) of an inherited EEG speech-versus-idle detector: a subject-cyclic schedule and fine-tuning on 5–15% of the held-out subject's samples. Both are standard. The cyclic schedule has no counterpart among 141 EEG imagined-speech studies, but only two settings are compared, with no pooled baseline and seeds not reported; target-subject calibration after source-subject training predates it [@panachakel2021transfer]. Without calibration the detector barely separates the classes (MCC 0.044 and 0.123, Table I), so subject independence holds only with the target's labelled data; overlapping windows without a stated trial-level split leave the calibrated gains open to leakage (inference), and every label is a surrogate timed from overt speech [@soroush2022nested].
expert_true_value: Separates, on one detector and dataset, EEG imagined-speech detection with no target-subject data from detection after a small target-subject calibration, and shows that the uncalibrated detector is close to chance by MCC.
canon_before: Imagined-speech EEG decoders are usually trained per subject; held-out-subject tests run leave-one-subject-out and often fall to chance. Fine-tuning a model trained on source subjects with target-subject data was described by 2021. EEG speech/non-speech state detection dates from 2020. The authors' MRF-EEGNet detector was evaluated within subject.
delta_from_canon: Trains the inherited MRF-EEGNet in subject cycles (N epochs per subject, R shuffled cycles) instead of one pooled stream, and fine-tunes it for two epochs on 5, 10 or 15% of the held-out subject's samples; the detector, labels and data are unchanged.
position_in_field: Standard on the changed training regime (M03): the cyclic schedule has no counterpart in the ledger but its effect is unsupported, and target-subject calibration predates it. Evaluation (M12) is a standard six-subject LOSO; labels (M11) are surrogates timed from overt speech; calibration cost and use-time behaviour (M13) are not reported.
practical_value: A reference point for how much a small target-subject calibration recovers in binary EEG speech-state detection; not evidence of a calibration-free or online system.
axes_moved: Calibrated LOSO with 10% of target samples: accuracy 0.781, MCC 0.382, AUC 0.801 against 0.817, 0.561 and 0.860 subject-dependent.
axes_unresolved: Effect of cyclic versus pooled training; whether the detector tracks imagery or cue-locked responses; trial-level separation of calibration and test windows; class balance and chance level; calibration time; continuous-use false activations and latency; patients.
axes_regressed: Changing the cyclic schedule from N=5, R=6 to N=3, R=10 lowers strict-LOSO accuracy from 0.694 to 0.670 while MCC and AUC rise; calibration needs labelled target-subject data.
technical_limits: MRF-EEGNet architecture and preprocessing inherited unchanged; labels aligned by an overt-speech-based method whose imagined-speech intervals are surrogates; no analysis of what the detector responds to.
evaluation_limits: Six subjects; no seeds, repetition count or definition of the plus-minus values; no validation or selection data; no chance level or class balance; 500-ms windows with 50-ms shift and no stated trial-level split between calibration and test; one MCC spread printed as 0.791; Fig. 2 caption labels both curves N=5, R=6.
deployment_limits: Offline window classification only; no calibration time, decision latency, false activation rate, online or patient test.
scope_limits: Binary imagined-speech versus idle detection from scalp EEG of six subjects from the authors' earlier dataset; no word or text decoding.
task: Binary EEG classification of imagined-speech versus idle state in 500-ms windows; not word recognition.
input_modality: Scalp EEG; label timing derived from overt speech.
sensor_hardware: EEG from the authors' earlier dataset; device, channel count and sampling rate not stated in this paper; 5th-order 0.5-125 Hz band-pass, 60 and 120 Hz notch, common average reference.
vocabulary_type: No vocabulary; speech-state detection
vocabulary_size: 2 classes (speech state, idle); not 2 words
evaluation_mode: Offline; six subjects; subject-dependent, strict leave-one-subject-out and subject-calibrated leave-one-subject-out with 5, 10 or 15% of the target subject's samples.

title: Toward Practical BCI: A Real-time Wireless Imagined Speech EEG Decoding System
review_confidence: Target read in full (arXiv v1, Table I, Figs. 1-2); comparators read at the cited passages; venue confirmed via Crossref.
expert_take_short: Not ahead on any component: consumer headsets and imagined-speech user identification predate it; no online accuracy, latency or split, so the real-time practical claim is unsupported.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M05, M03, M13 and M06 but is ahead on none. Consumer headsets for imagined speech, user identification from imagined-speech EEG and the group's identification-plus-intention framework predate it. M03 and M13 are not reported: no identification accuracy, calibration result, latency or online accuracy. Table I (62.00% wired, 46.67% wireless, three participants) has no stated split, and the wired-wireless drop confounds device, channel count, EOG input and recordings. The claim of bridging laboratory and real-world use does not hold.
expert_true_value: A working pipeline that chains resting-EEG user identification, per-user fine-tuning on ten trials per class, LSL streaming and on-screen display of four imagined commands, on a wired BrainAmp and a 12-channel Emotiv EPOC X. It reports 62.00% (wired) and 46.67% (wireless) four-class accuracy in three participants, but no identification accuracy, calibration result, latency or online accuracy, and no train/test split; consumer headsets for imagined speech and imagined-speech user identification predate it.
canon_before: Imagined-speech EEG on consumer headsets predates 2018: a 14-channel Emotiv EPOC imagined-word dataset, whose protocol dates to 2013, was reused for subject identification in 2018. Subject identification from imagined-speech EEG reached 0.92 (Emotiv, 2018) and 99.44% with sessions held out (2025). The same group's 2024 framework combined user identification (0.995, trials permuted across sessions) with four-class speech-imagery classification (0.47, ShallowConvNet). Online imagined-syllable control reached 55.7% against 50% chance in 20 participants (2024).
delta_from_canon: Adds a real-time application (LSL streaming, 2-s sliding window, immediate display), a 12-channel consumer wireless headset and a temporal-then-spatial transformer to the group's identification-plus-intention framework. None of these changes is isolated: no online accuracy or latency, no identification accuracy, no calibration curve, no model baseline, and the wired-wireless comparison confounds device, channel count, EOG input and recordings.
position_in_field: Imagined-speech EEG command classification (four classes, three participants) with a consumer headset and user identification; standard on M05 and M06, not reported on M03 and M13, ahead on none.
practical_value: A system outline to test, not evidence of practical use: the wireless 46.67% is not labelled online or offline, has no stated split, and no latency or false-activation data are given.
axes_moved: Real-time application integrating user identification, per-user fine-tuning and streaming; consumer wireless headset added to a wired setup.
axes_unresolved: Online accuracy and latency, false activations at rest, identification accuracy on a new session, calibration-size effect, model baseline, device effect with EOG removed, outside-laboratory protocol.
axes_regressed: None measured; the wireless accuracy is 15.33 points (24.7% relative) below the wired accuracy, but the comparison is confounded.
technical_limits: EOG channels enter the decoder with only a 60 Hz notch on the wired data; EPOC X sampling rate and preprocessing not stated, and only 12 of its 14 electrodes listed; the display is gated on a rest state the four-class decoder does not have; pretraining data and protocol not described.
evaluation_limits: Three participants; no train/test split, seeds or definition of the +/- values; no statistical test against the 25% chance level; no identification accuracy; ten-trial calibration not linked to Table I; no comparison with another model or system.
deployment_limits: No online accuracy, latency, decision rate or false-activation data; the outside-laboratory claim gives no setting, movement or headset-fit protocol; no patient testing.
scope_limits: Three healthy Korean participants, four cued imagined commands (help me, tell me, bored, tired), 2-s trials, per-user models.

title: Towards Unified Neural Decoding with Brain Functional Network Modeling
review_confidence: Target read in full (arXiv v1 text, captions of Fig. 1-4 and S1-S5, Tables S1-S5); comparators read in the passages holding the cited values. Absolute accuracies exist only as figure bars and were not read from the PDF.
expert_take_short: Pooled sEEG training (M03) and region-token input with imputation (M06) are standard: both predate it (Du-IN, Chen 2024); no absolute accuracy is given and the baselines are weak checkpoints.
expert_take_long: MIBRAIN [@wu2025mibrain] changes training (M03), pooling an 11-person sEEG cohort behind participant-specific encoders after masked-reconstruction pretraining, and the decoder input (M06), region tokens with learned prototypes for unrecorded regions. Both are standard: region-level masked pretraining for Mandarin sEEG speech [@zheng2024duin] and layout-agnostic pooled intracranial decoders tested on held-out participants [@chen2024subjectagnostic] predate it. The generalization claim is not supported as stated: no absolute accuracy or chance value is given, multi-subject gains are named for two participants without units, the online test participants' data are in the training pool, and unseen participants are decoded by voting through other participants' encoders. Brant and BrainBERT, the only baselines, were already known to fall far below region-level task pretraining on sEEG word decoding [@zheng2024duin].
expert_true_value: A study design for pooling intracranial recordings with different electrode placements into one sEEG phoneme classifier, with both within-participant and held-out-participant tests; not a demonstrated general decoder.
canon_before: Most intracranial speech decoders are trained per participant. Pooled decoders with subject-specific or layout-agnostic input layers (Chen et al. 2024) and region-level masked pretraining on Mandarin sEEG speech (Du-IN 2024, 62.70% top-1 on 61 words) predate the paper; general checkpoints such as Brant and BrainBERT were already known to score near chance on sEEG word decoding.
delta_from_canon: Pools 11 participants behind subject-specific encoders after masked-reconstruction pretraining on the task cohort (M03) and maps channels to anatomical region tokens with learned prototypes for unrecorded regions (M06).
position_in_field: Standard on both changed components (M03, M06): both designs predate it. The generalization claim is not supported as stated: no absolute accuracy or chance value is given, gains are named for two participants without units, online test participants are in the training pool, and unseen participants are decoded by voting through other participants' encoders.
practical_value: A starting point for using other patients' sEEG when a new patient's recordings are scarce; clinical value for people with speech impairment is untested.
axes_moved: Accuracy of pooled over single-participant models for two named participants (units not stated); above-chance decoding on held-out participants.
axes_unresolved: Absolute accuracy and chance level; comparison with region-level per-subject pretraining (Du-IN); session-held-out testing; seeds; latency; patients with speech impairment.
axes_regressed: Adding fewer than three participants lowered accuracy; unseen participants require majority voting across existing encoders.
technical_limits: Participant-specific encoders remain, so unseen-participant inference needs ensemble voting; imputed regions are validated only by feature correlation and above-chance decoding.
evaluation_limits: Main offline test holds out seven samples per class per participant from the same recordings; online test with two participants whose data are in the training pool; no seeds, no absolute accuracies or chance values in the text; channel selection precedes the split.
deployment_limits: Bedside clinical sEEG in epilepsy patients, server-side GPU decoding, cued 2-second articulation windows; no latency reported.
scope_limits: 23-class Mandarin syllable-initial classification (21 initials plus finals i and u), audible and mouthed articulation, 11 epilepsy patients with intact language.
input_modality: Stereo-EEG (sEEG) depth electrodes; audio used only for onset annotation and contamination checks.
sensor_hardware: Clinical sEEG amplifiers (Neurofax EEG-1200 at 2000 Hz, Natus Quantum at 2048 Hz), resampled to 512 Hz; 8-13 electrodes and 30-88 selected channels per participant.
vocabulary_type: Closed set of syllable-initial classes.
vocabulary_size: 23 classes; 407 characters as reading material.
metrics: Classification accuracy; absolute values only in figures. Multi- over single-subject gains for participants 10 and 11: 8.08% and 6.83% (audible), 5.10% and 4.97% (silent) offline; 3.62%, 2.90%, 7.97% and 4.35% online after practice (units not stated).
evaluation_mode: Offline within-participant hold-out (11 audible, 5 silent participants), leave-one-subject-out, and online cued decoding with 2 participants.

title: Transfer Learning for Covert Speech Classification Using EEG Hilbert Envelope and Temporal Fine Structure
review_confidence: Target read in full (arXiv v1, Tables I-IV, Fig. 3 values approximate); comparators read in their sources; the dataset paper (Rekrut et al. 2022) used from its published abstract and the target's Table IV.
expert_take_short: Overt-to-covert EEG transfer (M04) is not new, even on this dataset; the overt-only control is missing, the from-scratch baseline is unmatched, and 79.82% is tied to no fine-tuning fraction.
expert_take_long: The paper [@duraisamy2025transfer] changes the use-time action (M04, with M01 and M03): a BiLSTM trained on a person's overt-speech EEG is frozen and its output layer re-trained on 15-30% of that person's covert trials; Table II gives 79.82% on five commands against 66.94% from scratch, but not which fraction yields it. Its claim that no one had transferred an overt classifier to imagined speech is wrong: Lee et al. did so in EEG with five words [@lee2023spoken], and the paper's own dataset study did so on these recordings, 61.78% against 71.48% for silent training [@rekrut2022improving]. M04 is not reported: the overt-only condition both studies report is missing, so pretraining is not separated from covert fine-tuning. The 12.88-point gain (inference) is also confounded with an unstated from-scratch data amount and a within-person split. The features and BiLSTM (M06) are standard and never ablated.
expert_true_value: Shows that, within one person, an overt-pretrained BiLSTM whose output layer is re-trained on covert trials (15-30% in four runs; the fraction behind the mean is not stated) reaches 79.82% on five commands, against 66.94% from scratch. The transfer itself is not new (Lee et al., EEG, 2022; the dataset study, 61.78% overt-only on the same recordings) and is not isolated: there is no overt-only condition, no frozen random-network control and no matched covert data amount for the from-scratch baseline.
canon_before: Lee et al. (2022) applied a spoken-EEG classifier to imagined EEG (5 words, 7 participants): 26.8% against 30.5% for imagined-only training. On the target's own dataset, Rekrut et al. (2022) applied an overt-trained classifier to silent speech: 61.78% against 71.48% for silent training. Overt-to-silent transfer is reported as a degradation in 13 prior studies across EEG, ECoG, EMG, ultrasound and video.
delta_from_canon: Replaces zero-shot overt-to-covert transfer with overt pretraining plus output-layer fine-tuning on covert data, using Hilbert envelope and temporal fine structure features and a BiLSTM. The overt-only condition the field and the dataset study report is dropped, so the contribution of overt pretraining is not separated from covert fine-tuning.
position_in_field: Subject-specific scalp-EEG covert command classification (five commands) with overt pretraining; M04 not reported, as the overt-only condition is omitted; standard features and model on M06.
practical_value: A calibration recipe to test, not yet a reduction of covert training: covert data are still needed (about 48% at 15% and 81% at 30% in Fig. 3), the same features fall to 18.41% on a held-out subject in later work on the same data, and session-held-out tests elsewhere find spoken-to-imagined EEG transfer near chance (25.4% and 29.2% against 25%, 6.7% against 6.25%).
axes_moved: Overt pretraining with covert fine-tuning for EEG command classification; covert data fractions of 15-30% compared.
axes_unresolved: Overt-only transfer, frozen random-network control, matched covert data for from-scratch training, session-held-out testing, seeds, which fraction yields 79.82%, feature ablation, unseen users, online use.
axes_regressed: Drops the overt-only condition that earlier transfer studies, including the dataset study, report.
technical_limits: Overt EEG may carry speech muscle activity in the 0.5-80 Hz band and the ICA rule is not given; no ENV-only, TFS-only or raw-EEG model; Table I lists a 256 x 5 output layer after a bidirectional 256-unit layer.
evaluation_limits: 79.82% not tied to a fine-tuning fraction; covert test is 20% of covert data with no session boundary stated; from-scratch data amount not stated; printed means (79.82%, 86.44%) differ from row means (79.07%, 86.07%); text says 20 points where the tables give 12.88 (19.50 is overt minus from-scratch); contradictory significance statement; no seeds or chance level; Table IV compares tasks with 5-12 classes and ECoG.
deployment_limits: Offline laboratory analysis with a 64-channel cap; no online control, cross-day or re-capping test.
scope_limits: 15 healthy participants, five cued commands, 2-s trials, subject-specific models.
input_modality: Scalp EEG during overt speech (pretraining) and covert repetition (fine-tuning and test)
sensor_hardware: Brain Products LiveAmp 64, 64 channels, 500 Hz
vocabulary_type: Closed command set
vocabulary_size: 5 (LEFT, RIGHT, UP, PICK, PUSH)
metrics: Subject-specific five-class accuracy: overt BiLSTM 86.44% (5-fold); covert after transfer 79.82% (fraction not stated; covert rows 58.33-90.81%); covert from scratch 66.94 +- 4.65% (Table III); gap 12.88 points, 19.2% relative (reviewer's calculation); Fig. 3 about 48% at 15% and 81% at 30% covert data (approximate).
evaluation_mode: Offline, subject-specific; overt 5-fold cross-validation, covert 20% held-out trials; no session-held-out or cross-subject test

evidence.statement: Transferred covert BiLSTM 79.82% against 66.94% from scratch; overt BiLSTM 86.44%.

The paper claims no prior direct overt-to-imagined transfer, but Lee et al. (2022) transferred a spoken-EEG classifier to imagined EEG, and the dataset study (Rekrut et al. 2022) reported 61.78% overt-only transfer on the same recordings.
No overt-only condition, no random-network control and no stated from-scratch data amount; 79.82% not tied to a fine-tuning fraction.

title: VSpeechLM: A Visual Speech Language Model for Visual Text-to-Speech Task
expert_take_short: Lip-timed phonemes into a codec LM (M06) are standard; Chem WER edges EmoDubber 12.5% vs 12.8%, no SyncNet scores, and the stated sync gains do not follow from Table 1.
expert_take_long: VSpeechLM [@wang2025vspeechlm] changes one component, synthesis (M06): a per-frame phoneme aligner feeds a pretrained codec language model instead of a duration-based, diffusion or flow decoder. Both halves are standard: lip-set phoneme durations without a duration predictor appear in Hegde et al. [@hegde2023towards] (§3.2.2), and the authors cite an earlier speech-LLM dubbing system, DubWise, with global duration control only (§1). The content gain over the strongest baseline is small, 12.5% against 12.8% WER on Chem (Table 1); the baseline value is the non-ground-truth-reference row of the [concurrent] DiFlowDubber, which reports 11.12% against 12.81% in the same setting [@nguyen2026diflowdubber]. The synchronization claim is the weakest: it rests on a length-weighted spectral distance (§4.1), and its headline reductions do not follow from Table 1. The evaluation (M12) omits the SyncNet scores that DiFlowDubber's tables give for six earlier dubbing systems, four of them this paper's baselines.
expert_true_value: Shows that lip-derived per-frame phoneme timing can drive a pretrained codec language model for dubbing; the visual aligner lowers Chem WER from 15.02% (no video) to 12.48% in the paper's own ablation.
canon_before: Visual TTS and video dubbing derive phoneme timing from the lips or from attention to the video and decode with duration-based mel synthesis, diffusion or flow matching (Hegde et al. 2023 set durations from video-text attention without a duration predictor). EmoDubber reported Chem WER 12.8% in the paper's Table 1.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the decoder with an autoregressive EnCodec language model initialised from ESPnet and feeds it a phoneme sequence expanded per lip frame by argmax classification (M06). Sensors, task inputs and output are unchanged.
position_in_field: Standard on the changed component: lip-set durations predate it and the authors cite an earlier speech-LLM dubbing system. Chem WER edges EmoDubber (12.5% vs 12.8%); the concurrent DiFlowDubber reports a larger relative gain over the same baseline row (11.12% vs 12.81%, non-ground-truth reference). It reports no SyncNet lip-sync score, unlike its own dubbing baselines as scored in DiFlowDubber.
practical_value: A design option for dubbing when the script and a reference voice are available; it does not read content from the lips.
axes_moved: Chem and GRID WER slightly below the compared dubbing baselines in the paper's Table 1; visual timing better than no video or a video prefix (Table 2)
axes_unresolved: lip sync by SyncNet scores; reference utterance at test; seeds; common ASR scoring of baselines; decoder pretraining corpus and LRS2 overlap; phoneme order errors from per-frame argmax
axes_regressed: UTMOS below EmoDubber and capped by codec resynthesis (3.77 vs 4.19 ground truth on Chem); without the video the Chem UTMOS is higher (3.81 vs 3.73)
technical_limits: Per-frame argmax alignment with no monotonic constraint; strong dependence on decoder pretraining (Chem WER 151% without it); codec quality limits naturalness (authors). Partially invisible lips and low-quality video are left to future work (authors).
