title: Wireless Silent Speech Interface Using Multi-Channel Textile EMG Sensors Integrated into Headphones
expert_take_short: Headphone-integrated textile EMG (M05) is standard, after a dry-electrode necklace; 96% on ten words is one random sample split over four people, speaker separation not stated.
expert_take_long: The paper [@tang2025] changes the sensor (M05): four dry textile EMG electrodes in a headphone earmuff. This is standard: moving dry electrodes from the face into a worn object follows a dry-electrode necklace [@wu2024necklace], and no condition compares the earmuff with conventional electrodes on the same words. The decoder (M06), a 1D SE-ResNet, is standard; its claimed adaptation to contact quality rests on one example (Fig. 5). The 96% on ten words comes from one random 80/20 sample split pooled over four people, without seeds, repeated runs or stated speaker separation (Sec. III.A), and rests on about 200 test samples (inference from Fig. 4). "Real-time" and "low-power" are not measured.
expert_true_value: Offers a way of wearing EMG electrodes other than patches on the face, and compares filtering and multiple recording sites as supports for small-vocabulary recognition. Its value is as a prototype that combines ease of wearing with contact stability, more than the classification score itself.
canon_before: Silent word recognition from surface EMG, dry towel electrodes, residual networks and feature-channel weighting all exist in earlier work. Electrodes stuck to the face or neck are a burden to wear, and with dry electrodes changes in contact pressure disturb the signal.
delta_from_canon: Builds the group's existing towel electrodes into ordinary headphones and combines wireless four-channel recording with a 1D SE-ResNet. The main change is the wearing form of the sensing part and the integration of processing for contact variation, not a new EMG sensing principle.
position_in_field: A prototype wearable surface-EMG silent speech interface for conveying command words without voice. It is neither decoding of inner speech from brain signals nor reconstruction of open conversation.
practical_value: A design reference for small command-word input using headphones. Whether performance holds for unseen users, after re-wearing, on other days, while walking, for patients or in long-term use is not shown.
axes_moved: system_design; problem_reframing; wireless EMG recording integrated into the earmuff; 96% reported for fixed ten-word classification using filtering and four channels.
axes_unresolved: Generalization to unseen people, other days and re-wearing; mapping between physical electrodes and internal weights; a controlled test of the SE block alone; larger vocabularies; false activations; long-term wear; measurement on a mobile device; low-power operation; clinical use.
axes_regressed: The authors concede that contact pressure varies more than with facial adhesive electrodes. Removing the filter lowers accuracy from 96% to 76.5%, and a single channel also lowers it markedly. The performance difference from conventional electrode placement under the same conditions is not given.
technical_limits: Pressure changes, slippage and air gaps between fibres and skin in dry contact can disturb the signal. How the internal features weighted by the SE block map to physical electrodes is not explained. The start condition of the 3-s windows and the handling of non-speech periods during continuous input are not described.
evaluation_limits: Four people, fixed ten words, random sample-level split. The counting unit of the 100 repetitions, per-person breakdown, session structure, validation set, number of repetitions, error-bar definition and statistical significance are not given. Matching of conditions across the other classifiers in Fig. 6 is not fully described.
deployment_limits: Signals are sent wirelessly to an external computer; end-to-end latency, power and battery life of the device are not given. Long-term wear, walking, re-wearing, unseen users, patients and free conversation are not tested. The authors state that silver-paste attachment in the prototype is a challenge for mass production.
scope_limits: Fixed arXiv 2504.13921 v1 read in full (9 pages), with Figs. 1-7, Table I and Algorithm 1 checked in the PDF. Availability of external data or code was not surveyed; no code was run, and no independent reproduction or clinical validation was done.
task: Classification of ten English device-control words from EMG recorded while the mouth moves without voice; not open sentence recognition or speech synthesis.
input_modality: Four-channel surface EMG from dry textile electrodes built into headphone earmuffs; the input is muscle activity accompanying silent articulation.
sensor_hardware: Graphene/PEDOT:PSS-coated towel textile electrodes, four SeeedStudio EMG readout boards, ESP32-S3, LiPo battery; recorded at 1 kHz and sent over Wi-Fi to an external PC or smartphone. Fig. 1 also shows reference and ground besides the four recording sites.
body_site: Skin around the ear where the earmuff touches. Fig. 1 shows the layout, but the anatomical position and spacing of each electrode are not detailed. Not a brain-reading method.
output_type: Classification label among ten command words; no text or speech waveform is generated.
vocabulary_type: closed-set: predefined English command words.
vocabulary_size: 10 words: Open, Close, Start, Stop, Yes, No, Next, Back, Okay, Cancel.
metrics: Authors report 96% overall accuracy; 76.5% without the filter in the text, a 19.5-point difference. The text states a drop of about 40% with a single channel without saying whether relative or in points; no exact value is supplied. Fig. 6 compares 1D SE-ResNet, 1D ResNet, 1D VGG, SVM, RF, MLP and XGBoost without bar values or an error-bar definition. In Fig. 4, Open, Start and Cancel are 100%, Back 90%, the other six words 95%.
evaluation_mode: Accuracy on a random sample-level 80/20 split over four people and ten words. Compares several classifiers, with and without the filter, and four channels against the best single channel; shows a confusion matrix, example weights and feature-distribution plots. Not an independent test by person or by day.

evidence.statement: Four dry textile EMG electrodes are built into the earmuff, with four readout boards, an ESP32-S3 and a LiPo battery. Fig. 1 also shows reference and ground besides the four recording sites.
The electrodes are graphene/PEDOT:PSS-coated towel fabric from the authors' earlier electrode work. This is surface EMG recording, not direct decoding of inner speech or brain activity.
EMG is sampled at 1 kHz and sent over Wi-Fi to an external PC or mobile device; running recognition on the ESP32-S3 is not described.
Each 3-s window for a command word has 3000 points per channel, and a fourth-order Butterworth 20-450 Hz band-pass filter is applied to each channel.
The 1D SE-ResNet computes weights from time-averaged features inside the residual structure and multiplies them onto feature channels; the final output is class probabilities over ten words.

Training augmentation in the text: time shift up to +/-100 ms, Gaussian noise at 30 dB SNR, scaling 0.9-1.1, offset +/-0.1 mV. Algorithm 1 gives a noise standard deviation of 0.02; how the two descriptions relate is not stated.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.4–5, II.B.2 augmentation bullets and Algorithm 1 Step 2 (PDF image)

evidence.statement: Four participants. The text says each word was repeated 100 times among the four, but whether this is a total or per person is unclear. 80% of the balanced data go to training and 20% to test, split randomly by sample.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, III.A Collected Silent Speech Dataset

evidence.statement: Table I lists the ten words Open, Close, Start, Stop, Yes, No, Next, Back, Okay, Cancel; unseen words are not tested separately.
The authors report 96% overall accuracy for four-channel silent command-word classification, on a random sample split of a fixed ten-word set.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, III.B Model Performance; p.6 Fig.6 caption

evidence.statement: Fig. 4 diagonal values: Open, Start and Cancel 100%, Back 90%, the other six words 95%; Back misclassified as Cancel is shown at 10%.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, Fig.4 confusion matrix (PDF image); p.6 III.B discussion

evidence.statement: Without the filter, 1D SE-ResNet accuracy is 76.5% in the text against 96% for the standard setting; the 19.5-point gap is the simple difference of these two values. Fig. 6 bars carry no exact values.

The single-channel condition uses the best channel, and the text states that 1D SE-ResNet accuracy drops by about 40%; relative versus point difference and the exact single-channel value are not stated.

Fig. 6 compares 1D SE-ResNet, 1D ResNet, 1D VGG, SVM, RF, MLP and XGBoost under standard, no-filter and single-channel settings; error-bar definition, number of repetitions and statistical tests are not given.

In the Fig. 5 example, channels 1 and 2 with stable contact receive larger weights than unstable channels 3 and 4; the authors take this as evidence of adaptive selection. The size of any test aggregated by contact condition is not stated.

The equations and Algorithm 1 apply SE to internal feature channels after convolution, but how these map to per-electrode weights for the four physical electrodes in Fig. 5 is not fully explained. Causal detection of contact state cannot be concluded from example weights alone.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.4–6, II.B.2 equations, Algorithm 1, Fig.5 and III.C

evidence.statement: Fig. 7 compares t-SNE plots of raw input and learned features; it shows feature clustering, not an independent evaluation on unseen people or other days.

The authors assume about 10^7 operations per inference and a CPU throughput of 10 GFLOPs/ms and state microsecond-level latency; no measurement device or measured result is given, and this does not cover response time including the 3-s input, transmission and preprocessing.
evidence.section_or_location: p.3, II.A.2 last paragraph and II.B.1; p.5 II.B.2 realtime claim

evidence.statement: The authors themselves describe instability with dry electrodes from contact-pressure changes, small shifts and air gaps between fibres and skin; no quantitative test while walking or during long wear is shown.

The authors list as open problems the mass-production scalability of silver-paste attachment, the small vocabulary and participant pool, and improving on-device processing; performance at scale, for unseen users or for patients is not validated.

Battery operation, low power and comfort are claimed, but power consumption, battery life, weight and comfort are not quantified in the paper; non-speech detection and false-activation rate during continuous input are also not given.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.3–5, II.A.2 and II.B; pp.7–8 IV. Discussion and V. Conclusion

evidence.statement: In this review's assessment, the main contribution is a wearable design that combines existing textile EMG electrodes, wireless readout and an SE residual classifier into headphones, not a new sensing principle or general learning principle.
evidence.section_or_location: pp.2–4, Introduction, II.A and II.B.2; pp.8–9 references 22–25

evidence.statement: Speaker-held-out tests, other-day or re-wearing tests, recording-session breakdown, validation split, optimizer, learning rate and number of training iterations are not stated. Speaker-independent performance cannot be inferred from 96% on a sample split over four people.
evidence.section_or_location: p.5, Algorithm 1 and III.A; pp.6–8 Results and Discussion

en.summary: Headphone-integrated textile EMG (M05) is standard, after a dry-electrode necklace; 96% on ten words is one random sample split over four people, speaker separation not stated.
en.sensor: 4-channel dry textile EMG electrodes in headphone earcups
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 96% accuracy, 10 words, 4 participants, random sample-level 80/20 split (76.5% without filtering)
en.limitations: Only 4 participants with a sample-level random split; unseen users, other days, re-wearing, walking, latency and power consumption are untested.

title: Advancing NAM-to-Speech Conversion with Novel Methods and the MultiNAM Dataset
review_confidence: 固定arXiv v2の全5ページ、図1、表I・IIを確認した範囲では高い。試験分割、配布物の完全性、実験の独立再現、実用性能は未確認。
expert_take_short: 耳の後ろの微弱な振動を音声に変えるため、学習用音声の作り方を比較した研究。Diff-NAMの最終単語誤り率は2人で32.39%・38.94%と比較した映像利用法より低いが、両話者のNAMと文字を使うMFA-TTSの26.38%・32.61%には及ばない。価値は7.96時間の同時収録と教師音声設計にあり、患者向けの無音会話機器を実証したわけではない。
expert_take_long: 本論文は、非可聴つぶやき（NAM）の皮膚振動から音声を作る際、同時に録れない通常音声の代わりに何を学習目標にするかを扱う。市販の無線聴診器を耳の後ろに当て、健康な31歳の男女各1人からNAM・ささやき・顔映像・文章を計7.96時間集めた。小声のささやきで指定文を読む条件であり、口を動かさない内言や完全な無音会話ではない。提案Diff-NAMは映像と合成NAM特徴を条件にした拡散生成で教師音声を作り、別の系列変換器が実測NAMから最終音声を出す。ここを分ける必要があり、表IIの17.24%・21.73%は教師音声の単語誤り率で、最終出力では32.39%・38.94%となる。正解文字を使うLipvoicer教師による最終出力54.11%・59.66%より低い一方、両話者のNAMと文字を用いたMFA-TTSは26.38%・32.61%でさらに低い。したがって映像系との比較の改善であって、全条件で最高ではない。また教師音声作成に正解文字を使い、合成NAM生成器も実測NAMで学習するため、文字もNAM収録も不要な音声復元とはいえない。本文では学習と試験の分割や評価文数が明確でなく、対象の全映像・文字による特徴モデル追加学習と試験例の関係も未確認である。自動認識器の誤り率を人の聞き取り率に読み替えることはできず、部品別の効果、未知人物、患者、遅延、装着負担も未検証。SSI（声を出さずに伝えるための入力技術）研究としての意義は、教師音声を用意する選択肢と同時収録の基盤を示した点にある。
expert_true_value: 最終変換器の改良だけでなく、合成する教師音声の条件と質を切り分けて議論できる点。データ量があるMFA-TTSと映像系Diff-NAMの結果を並べ、利用可能な情報に応じた選択を促す。
canon_before: NAMでは通常の発声音声を同時に得られないため、別録り音声の時間変形、ささやきからのHuBERT-HiFi合成、NAMと文字の音素時間対応を用いるStethoSpeech系MFA-TTSが教師作成に使われてきた。映像からの合成にはCross-AttentionやLipvoicerがある。
delta_from_canon: 2人・7.96時間の4種類同時収録と、教師合成に使う情報を変えた比較を追加する。Diff-NAMは映像・合成NAMの条件付き拡散を取り入れるが、両話者を使うMFA-TTSを超える全面的な性能更新ではない。
position_in_field: 非可聴つぶやきの音声化における教師データ不足を扱う、データセットと学習目標設計の研究。無音入力の完成製品ではなく、学習用の音声をどう用意するかを検討する資料として重要。
practical_value: ささやきの収録が使えないときに、NAM・文字・映像のどの組合せを教師作成に利用できるかを比較する出発点となる。市販聴診器の収録例も参考になるが、そのまま患者向けの利用性能を示すものではない。
axes_moved: 教師音声作成の選択肢; ささやきなしの学習目標; NAMと映像の同時収録基盤; 映像系教師を使う最終変換の誤り率
axes_unresolved: 未知人物・未知語への一般化; データ分割の独立性; 人の聞き取り; 各構成の独立効果; 患者利用; 手放し固定; 実時間・携帯利用
axes_regressed: Diff-NAMの最終WERは両話者のNAMと文字を使うMFA-TTSより高い。処理量や収録負担の増減は測定されていない。
technical_limits: 正解文字を使う教師合成と、未知の発話内容をNAMから推定する最終課題を混同できない。Diff-NAMは学習時の合成NAM作成に実測NAMを必要とし、表IIでもLip・NAM・textを条件とする。映像だけ・NAM収録不要の系とはいえない。
evaluation_limits: 学習・検証・試験の分割割合、評価文数、文章重複の排除方法が本文では不明。AV-HuBERTを利用可能な全映像・文字で追加学習すると書かれ、試験例を隔離したか確認できない。誤り率の信頼区間、検定、反復学習、人の聞き取り評価は報告されない。
deployment_limits: 発話障害のある利用者、未知人物、別日・再装着、歩行や雑音条件の比較、装着負担、総遅延、消費電力は未評価。オフィス収録だけで雑音耐性や実用性は保証できない。
scope_limits: 健康な2人が小声のささやきで指定文を読む収録と、別の女性1人の既存データによる比較。完全な無音の口の動き、内言、自由会話や患者への適用の検証ではない。
task: NAMから音声への再構成; 同時の通常発声音声を得られない条件での時間整合した教師音声作成; MultiNAMデータセットの構築
input_modality: 耳の後ろの皮膚で拾う非可聴つぶやき（NAM）の振動。教師音声の合成には条件別にささやき音声、口元映像、正解テキストを用い、Diff-NAMは口元映像とNAM特徴、正解テキストを利用する。最終段のNAMから音声への変換と教師音声作成を分けて評価する。
sensor_hardware: 市販のBluetooth接続デジタル聴診器を耳の後ろに当て、MacBook Proで顔映像と口元のささやきを記録。映像1920×1080・25 fps、NAMとささやき48 kHz。
body_site: 耳の後ろの皮膚; 口唇・顔
vocabulary_type: LJSpeech由来の文章を読む課題。固定命令の分類ではないが、教師音声作成に正解テキストを利用し、未知語だけを分離した検証はない。
vocabulary_size: 語彙の固有語数は不明。MultiNAMはS1の2354発話とS2の969文を収録し、これは語彙数や独立した試験例数ではない。
metrics: Whisper音声認識器による単語誤り率（WER）と文字誤り率（CER）。表IIのDiff-NAM: 教師合成音声のWERはS1/S2で17.24/21.73%、最終NAM変換音声は32.39/38.94%、そのCERは19.47/24.91%。Lipvoicerの正解文字条件の最終WERは54.11/59.66%、両者のNAMと文字を用いるMFA-TTSは26.38/32.61%、本人別MFA-TTSは56.65/69.45%。表Iのささやきから作るMFA-TTS教師音声は5.84/11.23%であり、最終NAM変換の成績ではない。
evaluation_mode: 保存済み収録に対する話者別の自動音声認識誤り率比較。表Iはささやき由来の教師合成音声、表IIはささやきを使わない教師合成音声と、それを使って学習した最終変換音声を分けて報告。人の聞き取り試験や実時間対話試験ではない。

evidence.statement: NAM振動・ささやき・顔映像・文字を同時収録し、市販Bluetooth聴診器を耳の後ろの皮膚に当てる。MacBook Proで1920×1080・25 fpsの映像と口元の音声、NAMとささやきを48 kHzで記録した。
参加者は既知の聴覚・発話障害がない31歳の男性S1・女性S2で、LJSpeechの異なる文章を小声のささやきで読む。S1は2354発話・5.66時間、S2は969文・2.30時間、合計7.96時間。
補助のCSTR NAM TIMIT Plusは女性1人の421文・40分・16 kHzのスタジオ収録で、NAM・ささやき・文字を含む。新規の患者試験ではない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section II Datasets, CSTR paragraph

evidence.statement: 評価はWhisper認識器による誤り率。生のささやきのWERはCSTRで1.07%、MultiNAMのS1/S2で5.54/12.97%、生NAMはそれぞれ66.99%、200.50/192.77%と報告される。これらは人の聞き取り試験の結果ではない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.2 Section II Datasets, final paragraph

evidence.statement: 処理は時間整合した教師音声の合成とNAMから音声への系列変換学習の二段階。ささやきからのHuBERT-HiFiと、NAMまたはささやきに正解文字を対応させMFAで音素長を求めFastSpeech2に与えるMFA-TTSを比較する。
映像系教師生成は通常の正解音声が対象データにないためLRS3で学習する。口元を88×88の灰色画像にし、対象の利用可能な全映像・文字対でAV-HuBERTをCTC損失により追加学習して特徴を抽出すると記述する。
Diff-NAMは映像と合成NAMで拡散モデルを条件付ける。LRS3の音声から合成NAMを得るためのHiFiGANは対象の実測NAMで学習するため、NAM収録を一切使わない方式ではない。
Diff-NAMは口元とNAM特徴を結合した1536次元の条件を用い、本人の画像特徴による条件付けを避ける。推論時の教師音声生成は読唇予測文字ではなく利用可能な正解文字を使う。
最終変換では6層の非自己回帰TransformerがNAM特徴から教師音声特徴を予測し、平均二乗誤差と文字予測のCTC損失を用いる。HiFiGANで予測特徴を音声化する。
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Section III-D Seq2Seq learning network and speech decoder

evidence.statement: ささやき由来の教師音声のWERは、HuBERT-HiFi/MFA-TTSがCSTRで23.77/41.07%、S1で100.14/5.84%、S2で84.53/11.23%。表Iは最終NAM変換出力ではない。
evidence.section_or_location: p.3 Table I; pp.3–4 Section IV-A

evidence.statement: Diff-NAMの教師合成音声はS1/S2のWERが17.24/21.73%、CERが11.31/13.97%。最終NAM変換音声はWER32.39/38.94%、CER19.47/24.91%。
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table II, Diff-NAM row; Section IV-B NAM-to-speech conversion

evidence.statement: 両話者のNAMと文字を使うMFA-TTSの教師WERはS1/S2で12.37/19.64%、最終WERは26.38/32.61%。本人別MFA-TTSでは教師WER23.81/33.62%、最終WER56.65/69.45%。
evidence.section_or_location: p.4 Table II, MFA-TTS all-speaker/per-speaker rows

title: Adaptation of Tongue Ultrasound-Based Silent Speech Interfaces Using Spatial Transformer Networks
expert_take_short: STN-only adaptation (M03) closes 75-76% of the retraining gap, not the 88% the abstract states; untested against lower-layer adaptation; dev-set MSE only (M12 behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@toth2023adaptation] changes speaker and session adaptation (M03) by retraining only a learned affine transform of the input image (a spatial transformer, STN) placed before the usual CNN regressor (M06). The design is new for articulatory-to-speech adaptation (Appendix), but M03 is standard: the obvious baseline, the same group's lower-layer adaptation [@gosztolya2020applying], is never run. M06 is standard: in matched conditions the STN moves development MSE by at most 0.021 (session 5: 0.504 without, 0.483 with; Table 1; inference). M12 is behind: one regression error on an unnamed split, without the held-out passage and listening test of the prior study. The abstract overstates: it credits "adapting just the STN module" with 88%, which in Table 2 is the average of the "STN + out" column and a share of the no-adaptation-to-full-retraining gap, not an MSE reduction; the STN alone closes 75–76%.
expert_true_value: A new adaptation handle for ultrasound-to-speech mapping: retraining only a learned input affine (STN, about 10% of weights) closes 75-76% of the gap between no adaptation and full retraining, 88-92% with the output layer. Its advantage over the group's earlier lower-layer adaptation is not tested.
canon_before: Ultrasound-to-speech models were known to fail after probe remounting; the same group had already shown that adapting the lower layers of the network with about 10 sentences gives roughly the same correlation as training from scratch on 20 sentences of the session (Gosztolya et al. 2020). Lip reading had frozen-backbone, input-side speaker adaptation (user-dependent padding, 2022).
delta_from_canon: Replaces weight adaptation with a per-frame learned image affine in front of the regressor, and measures adaptation as the share of the no-adaptation-to-full-retraining MSE gap closed (75-76% STN only, 88% speakers and 92% sessions with the output layer).
position_in_field: Standard on adaptation (new design, but not compared with lower-layer adaptation and with the adaptation data per run not stated) and on architecture; behind the field and its own prior on evaluation (development-set MSE only).
practical_value: Suggests a small, interpretable module to retrain after remounting, but adaptation time, data needed and speech quality after adaptation are not measured, so the practical gain over existing lower-layer adaptation is open.
axes_moved: speaker and session adaptation via a learned input affine transform
axes_unresolved: comparison with lower-layer adaptation; amount of adaptation data; held-out test and intelligibility of synthesized speech; silent articulation; more than one base speaker
technical_limits: A single affine per frame with a 2D localizer, also in the 3D model; a mean transform per target closes only 35% (speakers) and 26% (sessions) of the gap on average, 11-42% per target, so the per-frame localizer must be retrained for each new speaker or session.
evaluation_limits: Mel-spectrogram MSE only, on a development set (Table 1) or an unnamed partition (Tables 2-3); random 85:10:5 split with unstated unit; no seeds, variance, listening or intelligibility tests; three target speakers and four short sessions of one speaker, all adapted from one base speaker.
deployment_limits: Requires supervised paired ultrasound and audio for every adaptation; recordings are voiced read speech; adaptation time and data needed are not reported.
scope_limits: Offline ultrasound-to-mel-spectrogram regression on Hungarian read speech under laboratory conditions.
input_modality: ultrasound-based silent speech interface
sensor_hardware: Articulate Instruments Ltd. Micro ultrasound system with probe-fixing headset
metrics: Mel-spectrogram MSE and relative gap closure (no adaptation = 0%, full retraining = 100%): 2D STN only 76% (speakers) and 75% (sessions), STN plus output layer 88% and 92%; 3D STN 80% and STN plus output 87% (speakers only); mean transform 35% and 26% on average (11-42% per target).
evaluation_mode: Offline cross-speaker (three targets) and cross-session (four sessions of one speaker) adaptation from a speaker-048 base model; development or unnamed split; single runs.

evidence.statement: The abstract credits adapting just the STN module with an 88% average MSE reduction relative to retraining the whole network.
Table 2 gives 76% (speakers) and 75% (sessions) gap closure for STN only and 88% and 92% for STN plus output layer; the percentages are relative closure of the no-adaptation-to-full-retraining gap.
Four Hungarian speakers with 209 read sentences each; four extra remounted sessions of speaker 048 averaging 3.5 minutes against about 15 minutes for the main session; random 85:10:5 split.
Table 1 reports development-set MSE and Tables 2-3 name no partition; no seeds, variance or speech-level evaluation are reported, and smaller adaptation sets are left to future work.

en.summary: STN-only adaptation (M03) closes 75-76% of the retraining gap, not the 88% the abstract states; untested against lower-layer adaptation; dev-set MSE only (M12 behind).
en.sensor: Micro ultrasound tongue probe with fixing headset
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: STN-only adaptation closes 75-76% of the gap between no adaptation and full retraining (2D CNN, MSE); adding the output layer closes 88% (three speakers) and 92% (four sessions of one speaker); development or unnamed split, single runs
en.limitations: No comparison with lower-layer adaptation at matched size; adaptation data per run not stated, only implied by the 85:10:5 split; mel-spectrogram MSE only, no held-out test, listening or intelligibility score; random split with unstated unit; no seeds or variance; voiced read speech only; session data much shorter than the base session.

title: AKVSR: Audio Knowledge Empowered Visual Speech Recognition by Compressing Audio Knowledge of a Pretrained Model
expert_take_short: The quantized audio memory (M02) is a standard memory-recall design; its gains repeat over a no-memory baseline, but the LRS3 state-of-the-art claim and the edge over distillation do not hold.
expert_take_long: The paper [@yeo2024akvsr] changes training-only supervision (M02): HuBERT features are quantized into a 200-slot memory recalled from video, so lip-reader training needs no audio. Recalling an audio memory from video is the same group's earlier design [@kim2021multimodality; @kim2022distinguishing], so the verdict is standard. Its gain over the no-memory AV-HuBERT baseline repeats across LRS3, LRS2, two model sizes and a second backbone. Its edge over distillation is 2.0 points from one LRS3 run, and the memory carries transcripts of 656 h, 22 times the labels of the 30 h comparators (inference). The abstract's unqualified LRS3 state-of-the-art claim fails against a cited work: SynthVSR Large reaches 18.2% without a language model [@liu2023synthvsr] [concurrent], 5.4 points below the paper's 23.6% (inference), though with more training data and an unstated language-model condition.
expert_true_value: Shows that a quantized, pre-trained audio memory recalled from video lowers WER over the no-memory AV-HuBERT baseline across LRS3, LRS2, two model sizes and a second backbone. Memory recall itself is the same group's earlier design, and the 2.0-point edge over distillation is one run with a memory trained on 656 h of transcripts, so the advantage of quantization over distillation is not established.
canon_before: Existing VSR methods have started to incorporate audio knowledge through distillation or multimodal memory to complement insufficient visual signals, but often retain speaker and noise factors or require audio inputs during inference.
delta_from_canon: Replaces raw audio features in an audio memory recalled from video (prior memory-recall designs from the same group) with k-means units of HuBERT features whose memory is trained beforehand by ASR, removing audio from lip-reader training. The usual route, knowledge distillation, is beaten by 2.0 points in one LRS3 run; the abstract's unqualified LRS3 state-of-the-art claim does not hold against the cited SynthVSR Large row, which trains on more data.
position_in_field: Audio-memory lip reading on LRS2 and LRS3 that extends the same group's memory-recall line with a quantized, pre-trained memory; consistent gains over a no-memory baseline, a small single-run edge over distillation, and no LRS3 state of the art.
practical_value: Lip-reader training no longer needs audio once the memory is built, at about 5M extra parameters, but building the memory needs paired audio-text (656 h in the paper). The LRS3 result (23.6%) trails SynthVSR Large (18.2% without a language model, on more labelled, pseudo-labelled and synthetic data) and later pseudo-labelling (23.7% at 30 h vs 29.1%).
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: real-time deployment; preprocessing cost of memory construction; broader interface relevance beyond sentence-level VSR
technical_limits: Offline compact audio memory construction required before training VSR; increases preprocessing cost and complexity; no real-time or streaming validation; no latency reported.
evaluation_limits: Evaluations are benchmark WER measures on LRS2 and LRS3 datasets using only video inputs at inference; no live or real-time demonstrations; performance gains demonstrated via multiple ablation studies but no external data or environment tests.
deployment_limits: Requires offline compact audio memory construction stage prior to VSR training; no evidence for real-time or embedded deployment; limited to sentence-level benchmarks without live camera or latency studies.
scope_limits: Sentence-level visual speech recognition on public datasets LRS2 and LRS3; no live or streaming experiments; no multi-environment or multi-speaker live deployment tested.
input_modality: video (silent lip movement)
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: sentence-level open vocabulary
metrics: LRS3 WER (single runs): no-memory AV-HuBERT BASE 30 h baseline 46.1% vs AKVSR 41.6%; LARGE 29.1% (30 h; AV-HuBERT and RAVEn 32.5%), 27.6% (433 h), 23.6% (433 h plus 1,326 h pseudo-labelled; RAVEn 24.4%). LRS2 LARGE 28.7% (28 h) and 24.1% (223 h). Distillation on the same student 43.6% vs 41.6%. Memory built from 656 h of paired audio-text (Table IX: 44.7% / 43.3% / 41.5% for 223 / 433 / 656 h).
evaluation_mode: Quantitative WER comparison on LRS2 and LRS3 visual speech recognition benchmarks, including multiple ablation experiments over choice of pretrained audio model (CPC, wav2vec2.0, HuBERT), memory cluster size, embedding dimension, ABM cross-attention layers, and training dataset sources.

evidence.statement: We propose an Audio Knowledge empowered Visual Speech Recognition framework (AKVSR) which (1) utilizes rich audio knowledge encoded by a large-scale pretrained audio model, (2) saves the linguistic information by discarding non-linguistic information through quantization in compact audio memory, and (3) includes Audio Bridging Module which finds best-matched audio features from compact audio memory for training without audio inputs once the memory is composed.

The proposed method stores refined linguistic audio knowledge in a compact discrete memory obtained by vector quantization from a pretrained audio model (HuBERT) and injects matched memory information into visual features via cross-attention in the Audio Bridging Module (ABM), obviating the need for audio inputs during training or inference.

Table I shows the baseline visual speech recognition WER on LRS3 is 46.1%, while AKVSR with HuBERT-based compact audio memory reduces it to 41.6% (BASE Transformer), with further improvements in LARGE models (29.1%, 27.6%, 23.6%) surpassing the AV-HuBERT rows listed without language models (the proposed rows do not state language-model use).

Table II on LRS2 confirms the proposed method improves WER over AV-HuBERT across Transformer BASE and LARGE models in low-resource (28h) and high-resource (223h) settings, e.g. from 32.2% to 28.7% WER in LARGE with 28h labeled data and from 25.5% to 24.1% in 223h data.

Experiments are performed on the sentence-level LRS2 and LRS3 datasets, including low-resource and high-resource labeled data splits, as well as pseudo-annotated VoxCeleb2 additions to extend training data.
The method is evaluated strictly on benchmark datasets with WER as metric; there is no real-time or live camera study, and no latency analysis presented.

The proposed method requires an offline stage to build the compact audio memory before training the VSR model, which adds preprocessing time and complexity, making real-time deployment currently unavailable.

The evaluation is limited to sentence-level visual speech recognition benchmarks LRS2 and LRS3; there is no demonstration of generalization to real-world conditions, streaming, multi-speaker, or noisy environments.

The key novelty is explicitly removing speaker and noise characteristics from the pretrained audio model's features via vector quantization and storing linguistic content in discrete clusters, then retrieving matched audio memory contents via cross-attention ABM injecting purely video-conditioned audio knowledge during VSR training and inference.

en.summary: The quantized audio memory (M02) is a standard memory-recall design; its gains repeat over a no-memory baseline, but the LRS3 state-of-the-art claim and the edge over distillation do not hold.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: LRS3 WER 41.6% vs 46.1% no-memory baseline (BASE, 30 h) and 43.6% for distillation; LARGE 23.6% with 1,326 h pseudo-labels, behind SynthVSR Large at 18.2% without a language model on 3,068 h plus 3,652 h synthetic
en.limitations: Memory trained on 656 h of paired audio-text, so low-resource rows are not label-matched, and its data effect mixes size with in-domain LRS3 audio; single runs without seeds; language-model use of the proposed rows not stated; table-text inconsistencies (Tables VI, VIII, IX); offline benchmark only, no latency.

title: Audio-visual video-to-speech synthesis with synthesized input audio
expert_take_short: A second synthesis pass on first-pass speech (M06) and modality dropout (M03) are standard; gains are small and inconsistent, earlier systems keep lower WER, and no equal-training control exists.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the decoder (M06), adding a second synthesis pass that takes the first pass's speech as input with the video, and training (M03), with modality dropout. Both are standard: autoregressive decoders already feed their own synthesized frames back at inference, so the paper's claim that no earlier method used audio inputs at inference holds only for a separate audio encoder, and modality dropout is common in audio-visual recognition. The gains are small and inconsistent: on GRID unseen speakers the pre-trained base reaches 17.63% WER and its best second pass 17.70%, and earlier systems keep lower WER on three of the four WER splits, leading everywhere except GRID four speakers (3.67% against 4.07%). The strongest confound is extra training: the second pass adds an encoder and retrains the shared modules, with no equal-training control. There is no listener test and no repeated run, so the claim that synthesized audio helps is not supported.
expert_true_value: Demonstrates a novel two-stage audiovisual speech synthesis pipeline that leverages synthesized audio as an intermediate representation, trained with modality dropout, achieving improved objective metrics and enabling robust audiovisual speech reconstruction from silent videos.
canon_before: Most video-to-speech synthesis systems used either video only or included audio during training but discarded audio input at inference, treating missing audio as unavailable rather than as an explicit intermediate representation.
delta_from_canon: Introduces a two-stage pipeline leveraging synthesized audio from a first-stage V2A model as explicit input to a second-stage AV2A model, trained with modality dropout to robustly combine video and audio modalities for speech reconstruction.
position_in_field: A strong contribution to video-to-speech synthesis literature centered on staged audiovisual reconstruction incorporating synthesized audio.
practical_value: Provides a benchmarked, replicable approach to combining synthesized audio with silent video for improved speech synthesis; relevant for researchers of audiovisual speech synthesis and multimodal enhancement.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: impact of different training variants across datasets; live deployment suitability; correlation with real-time constraints; dependence on synthesized audio quality
technical_limits: Effectiveness depends on the quality of synthesized audio from the first-stage V2A model; WER improvements are inconsistent across datasets and model variants; no demonstrated results for in-the-wild noisy conditions or real-time inference.
evaluation_limits: Objective metrics (PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, WER) on benchmark datasets; lack of in-the-wild, noisy environment, or real-time latency evaluations; WER unavailable for TCD-TIMIT due to lack of suitable pre-trained ASR models.
deployment_limits: Benchmark evaluations only; relies on pretrained base models; no real-time or latency evaluation; no in-the-wild or noisy environment testing; dependency on quality of synthesized audio inputs.
scope_limits: Applies to video-to-audio reconstruction tasks in benchmark datasets with limited speaker diversity and controlled conditions; does not address noisy or real-time conditions.
input_modality: Silent video plus synthesized audio
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: Sentence-level benchmark vocabularies
metrics: GRID (4 speakers, seen): PESQ 1.95, STOI 0.698, ESTOI 0.532, WER 3.67%; GRID (33 speakers, seen): PESQ 2.10, STOI 0.723, ESTOI 0.553, WER 2.65%; TCD-TIMIT (3 lipspeakers, seen): PESQ 1.44, STOI 0.566, ESTOI 0.411; LRW unseen: WER down to 24.96% in best raw waveform models; metrics reported include PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, WER.
evaluation_mode: Multi-dataset quantitative benchmark comparison with multiple training variants and modalities in raw waveform and mel-spectrogram domains, including seen and unseen speaker splits.

evidence.statement: In this work we investigate video-to-speech synthesis models that include audio and video inputs during both training and inference. We do so in both the raw waveform and mel spectrogram domains.

We propose a video-to-speech synthesis approach that employs audio and video inputs during both training and inference by transforming the V2A model into a corresponding AV2A model, using the V2A model to synthesize the input audio, and training under modality dropout.

We construct the audio-visual-to-audio Generator by appending an audio encoder to the video-to-audio Generator, which receives the synthesized audio as input and concatenates audio and video features with a speaker embedding before feeding to temporal and decoding modules.
Experiments evaluate the models on GRID in seen speaker splits with 4 and 33 speakers, on unseen GRID with 33 speakers, on TCD-TIMIT lipspeakers, and on LRW in an unseen speaker setting.

On GRID 4-speaker seen split, the best AV2A-WaveGAN model with audio pretraining and modality dropout using ground truth audio achieved PESQ 1.95, STOI 0.698, ESTOI 0.532, and WER 3.67 percent, outperforming base V2A-WaveGAN and other baselines.

On GRID 33-speaker seen split, AV2A-WaveGAN with audio pretraining and modality dropout (GT audio) achieved PESQ 2.10, STOI 0.723, ESTOI 0.553, and WER 2.65, surpassing the base V2A-WaveGAN and several prior methods.
For TCD-TIMIT with 3 lipspeakers (seen), AV2A-WaveGAN with audio pretraining and modality dropout (GT audio) reached PESQ 1.44, STOI 0.566, ESTOI 0.411.
The paper relies on objective metrics and WER across benchmark corpora, and WER is unavailable for TCD-TIMIT as no accurate pre-trained ASR model could be found.

en.summary: A second synthesis pass on first-pass speech (M06) and modality dropout (M03) are standard; gains are small and inconsistent, earlier systems keep lower WER, and no equal-training control exists.
en.sensor: Camera (mouth video); synthesized audio from a first-stage model as a second input
en.vocabulary: GRID fixed 51-word vocabulary; TCD-TIMIT and LRW larger vocabularies
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Best WER 3.67% on GRID 4 seen speakers; 17.69% on GRID unseen speakers against 16.05% for an earlier end-to-end system; 14.24% on LRW against 12.90% for SVTS
en.limitations: No equal-training control for the second pass; training-set synthesized audio comes from a base model fitted to the same set; no listener test; single runs without seeds.

title: High-Quality Automatic Voice Over with Accurate Alignment: Supervision through Self-Supervised Discrete Speech Units
expert_take_short: This video-conditioned AVO system innovatively supervises alignment by predicting discrete speech units rather than reconstructing acoustic features, leading to better lip-sync and speech quality on a single-speaker dataset; however, it is not an SSI interface paper.
expert_take_long: This paper presents DSU-AVO, an automatic voice over system that innovatively supervises the multimodal alignment learning through discrete speech unit prediction derived from self-supervised HuBERT models and clustering. By replacing acoustic feature reconstruction with classification of discrete units at the context level, the approach provides more direct learning signals that yield improved lip-sync accuracy and speech naturalness. The system integrates a pretrained unit vocoder for synthesis conditioned on predicted units, effectively alleviating the mismatch typical in prior acoustic decoding. Experimental evaluation on the single-speaker Chem dataset demonstrates significant gains over baselines in synchronization metrics (LSE-C 6.81 vs. 6.11 for Neural Dubber), duration deviation (FD 3.23 vs. 9.39), intelligibility (WER 24.7% vs. 75.8%), and subjective quality (MOS 3.98 vs. 2.43). Despite these strong contributions, the work is limited to single-speaker settings without multi-speaker or in-the-wild testing and depends on pretrained components, limiting immediate deployment scope. Furthermore, it does not constitute a silent speech interface per se but advances alignment supervision in video-conditioned speech synthesis.
expert_true_value: The key advance is reframing alignment supervision from acoustic regression to discrete speech unit prediction using self-supervised speech representations, delivering more direct and effective training for lip-synchronized speech generation in automatic voice over.
canon_before: Prior AVO systems used acoustic feature (mel-spectrogram) reconstruction as a learning objective, which provides indirect supervision for alignment and suffers from mismatch between context and acoustic features.
delta_from_canon: Replaces acoustic feature regression with discrete speech unit prediction derived via HuBERT and k-means clustering for direct alignment supervision, and uses Unit HiFi-GAN vocoder for synthesis conditioned on predicted units, reducing mismatch and improving synchronization and naturalness.
position_in_field: Advances automatic voice over and video-conditioned TTS; adjacent but not focused on silent speech interfaces.
practical_value: Improves synchronization accuracy and speech naturalness for scripted dubbing applications, useful in media production and related domains.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Multi-speaker generalization; expressive prosody; strict SSI relevance
technical_limits: Single-speaker Chem dataset only; reliant on pretrained unit tokenizer and vocoder; no tests on multi-speaker, unseen words, or moving conditions; contextual mismatch remains an open issue outside studied domain.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation limited to single-speaker Chem dataset; WER from ASR pretrained on Librispeech only and not adapted; no unseen words or walking tests reported.
deployment_limits: Requires input of video frames and text scripts; depends on pretrained unit tokenizer and vocoder; only validated on single-speaker Chem dataset; no multi-speaker or in-the-wild testing yet.
scope_limits: Specific to automatic voice over with text and video inputs; not a generic silent speech interface solution.
input_modality: text + video (lip image frames)
sensor_hardware: camera
metrics: Lip Sync Error Confidence (LSE-C) 6.81, Lip Sync Error Distance (LSE-D) 7.56, Frame Disturbance (FD) 3.23, Word Error Rate (WER) 24.7%, Mean Opinion Score (MOS) 3.98 ± 0.08, Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) best 84.0% / worst 1.3%
evaluation_mode: Objective metrics (LSE-C, LSE-D, FD, WER) and subjective listening tests (MOS, BWS)

evidence.statement: We propose a novel AVO method leveraging the learning objective of self-supervised discrete speech unit prediction, which not only provides more direct supervision for the alignment learning, but also alleviates the mismatch between the text-video context and acoustic features.

We propose to guide the context modeling and alignment learning of AVO more directly by imposing discrete speech unit prediction as supervision at the context representation level, replacing mel-spectrogram reconstruction supervision, thus enabling more accurate lip-speech synchronization.
evidence.section_or_location: We propose to guide the context modeling

evidence.statement: We utilize Chem dataset, a single-speaker audio-visual English speech dataset, with official transcripts from YouTube, using 6088 training samples, 200 validation, and 200 test samples for evaluation of our AVO systems.

DSU-AVO achieves Lip Sync Error - Confidence (LSE-C) of 6.81, Lip Sync Error - Distance (LSE-D) of 7.56, Frame Disturbance (FD) of 3.23, Word Error Rate (WER) of 24.7%, Mean Opinion Score (MOS) of 3.98 ± 0.08, and Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) for lip-speech synchronization best 84.0% and worst 1.3%.

The method is trained and tested only on the single-speaker Chem dataset; it relies on paired video, text, and audio data and pretrained unit tokenizer and vocoder; generalization to multi-speaker, unseen words, and walking conditions is not reported.

DSU-AVO requires text and video frame inputs, pretrained SSL-based discrete unit tokenizer and vocoder models, and has only demonstrated results on single-speaker data, limiting immediate deployment in multi-speaker or diverse dubbing scenarios.

en.summary: An automatic voice-over system that supervises alignment by predicting self-supervised discrete speech units from text and lip video, improving lip-sync and speech quality on a single-speaker dataset. Not an SSI paper.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video) plus text script
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: WER 24.7%, LSE-C 6.81, LSE-D 7.56, MOS 3.98 on single-speaker Chem dataset
en.limitations: Validated only on one single-speaker dataset; requires text scripts and pretrained unit tokenizer and vocoder; no multi-speaker or in-the-wild testing.

title: Improving the Gap in Visual Speech Recognition Between Normal and Silent Speech Based on Metric Learning
review_confidence: Medium to high: arXiv v2 read in full with Table 1 and the Fig. 3 description; reported values are certain, but Table 1 reports no run count or spread, the split that selected the loss weights is not stated and speaker disjointness of the split is not stated.
expert_take_short: Joint normal-silent training does most of the gap closing; the viseme KL terms add 0.93 WER points with no run count reported, so the metric-learning gain is not established.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training (M03): a lip-video model is trained on normal and silent recordings together, with KL terms pulling the viseme posteriors of the two modes toward each other. The verdict is standard: overt recordings already enter silent-speech training as paired-audio supervision (31 of 138 slot-filled studies), as in EMG, and the paper does not show that its loss beats those routes. Most of the reported gap closing comes from adding silent training data: the normal-to-silent WER gap falls from 10.97 to 2.70 points with cross-entropy on both modes and only to 1.77 points with the full loss. The headline gain, silent WER from 12.91% to 9.97%, is reported without a run count or spread, after a loss-weight search that does not say which split selected the weights. A later EMG study of the same idea, on a different task, reports a seed-to-seed WER standard deviation of about 1 point and used 10 seeds to show a 1.61-point gain; by that analogy the gain is not established, and run variance (M12) is not reported.
expert_true_value: Shows on a 10-phrase lip-video benchmark that training on normal and silent recordings together nearly removes the normal-to-silent gap; the added viseme KL terms give a further gain, with no run count reported, whose reliability is unknown.
canon_before: Silent visual speech recognition degrades when trained on normal speech (8.5-point phrase accuracy drop on the same corpus, Petridis et al. 2018). Other signals tie overt and silent recordings in training by time-aligned target transfer (EMG, Gaddy and Klein 2020) or domain-adversarial joint training (ultrasound, Zheng et al. 2023).
delta_from_canon: Adds symmetric and count-weighted KL divergence between the viseme posteriors of paired normal and silent utterances, plus within-mode KL terms, to a two-stage viseme-then-word model with a frozen pretrained front-end.
position_in_field: Standard on training (M03): the earliest of 5 studies whose full text names a divergence, metric or contrastive loss between modes (pattern match), but the gain over a two-mode cross-entropy baseline (silent WER 12.91% to 9.97%) is reported without a run count or spread; a 2026 EMG alignment loss on a different task needed 10 seeds to show a 1.61-point gain. Standard on the normal-to-silent degradation (M04). Run variance (M12) not reported.
practical_value: Supports collecting some silent recordings for silent lip reading and training on both modes; the KL terms are cheap to add but their benefit is not established beyond Table 1, which reports no run count.
axes_moved: Silent WER 22.55% (normal-only) to 12.91% (both modes, cross-entropy) to 9.97% (full loss); silent VER 12.49% to 7.48% to 6.66%; normal-to-silent WER gap 10.97 to 2.70 to 1.77 points; on A V Digits phrases, run count not reported.
axes_unresolved: Seed variance of Table 1; which split selected the loss weights; comparison with target transfer or domain-adversarial training on the same data; open vocabulary; WER under reduced silent data.
technical_limits: Two-stage model with a frozen front-end pretrained on normal speech; viseme labels from a text dictionary; the word model is trained only on normal-speech viseme predictions and decodes a 10-phrase closed set.
evaluation_limits: No run count or spread for Table 1, after a loss-weight search that does not say which split selected the weights; rows differ by tenths of a VER point and metrics disagree across rows; Fig. 3 uses 1,000 normal utterances instead of 2,560, five subset runs and VER only; the fine-tuning comparator has no number; no significance test or chance level.
deployment_limits: Offline recognition of pre-segmented phrases from frontal lab video; no latency, device or online test.
scope_limits: Ten English phrases from the A V Digits and OuluVS2 corpora; silent speech mouthed by typical speakers in the lab; no open vocabulary, continuous speech or patients.
task: Visual speech recognition of 10 fixed phrases in normal and silent (mouthed) speech, via a viseme sequence and a viseme-to-word model.
input_modality: Video: grayscale 112 x 112 lip crops located with Dlib from frontal recordings.
sensor_hardware: Existing corpus video (A V Digits frontal camera, OuluVS2); no new sensor.
output_type: Word sequence from a 10-phrase vocabulary, with a 13-class viseme sequence as intermediate output.
vocabulary_type: fixed phrase
vocabulary_size: 10 phrases
metrics: Silent VER / WER: normal-only 12.49% / 22.55%; two-mode cross-entropy 7.48% / 12.91%; full loss 6.66% / 9.97%. Normal VER / WER for the full loss 5.03% / 8.20%.
evaluation_mode: Offline test on 550 A V Digits phrase utterances from 11 speakers per mode; 13 loss combinations, run count not reported; data-reduction study with five subset runs per size (VER).

evidence.statement: The authors present viseme-level metric learning (KL divergence between normal and silent viseme posteriors) to reduce the normal-to-silent gap in lip reading.

The cross-mode KL term on viseme posteriors is the earliest divergence-type loss between modes among 5 pattern-match studies; other signals already tie overt and silent recordings by target transfer or domain-adversarial training.
Best silent results are 6.66% VER and 9.97% WER with all loss terms, against 7.48% and 12.91% for the two-mode cross-entropy baseline; no run count or spread is reported.
Evaluation uses A V Digits phrases (20/8/11 speakers; 550 test utterances per mode) with 1,560 OuluVS2 normal utterances added to training.
Scope is 10 fixed phrases from lab video; the authors leave unknown vocabulary and larger normal-speech data to future work.

In the data-reduction study (normal data fixed at 1,000 utterances, five subset runs per size), the proposed model at 400 silent utterances matches the baseline at 800 in VER; no WER or test is given.

en.summary: Joint normal-silent training does most of the gap closing; the viseme KL terms add 0.93 WER points with no run count reported, so the metric-learning gain is not established.
en.sensor: Single frontal camera; Dlib lip crops
en.task: Closed-set phrase recognition from silent and normal lip video
en.speaker: Held-out speakers (20/8/11 split; disjointness not stated)
en.key_result: Silent WER 9.97% vs 12.91% two-mode baseline and 22.55% normal-only; run count not reported
en.limitations: No run count or spread for Table 1; selection split not stated; 10 fixed phrases; no comparison with other overt-silent training methods.

title: Intelligible Lip-to-Speech Synthesis with Speech Units
expert_take_short: Unit target (M02) and unit-conditioned vocoder (M06) are standard; units cut LRS3 WER 21.8 points, AV-HuBERT 20.4 more, the vocoder 0.3; unit gain untested on AV-HuBERT, single runs.
expert_take_long: The paper [@choi2023intelligible] changes the training target (M02, 200 HuBERT units predicted beside the mel-spectrogram) and the vocoder (M06, conditioned on units and a speaker embedding); both are standard. The units carry the content gain (LRS3 ASR WER 72.5% to 50.7%, one run), the vocoder and mel augmentation move WER by 0.3 and 0.2 points (Table 3), and the headline 29.8% comes from swapping in a pretrained AV-HuBERT encoder, a step of 20.4 points (41% relative) against 21.8 points (30%) for the units, with the unit gain never measured on that encoder. The [concurrent] ReVISE also predicts HuBERT units from an AV-HuBERT-initialised encoder, at 33.9% [@hsu2023revise]; the [later] V2SFlow is 1.3 points lower with the same ASR model, and its listeners rate the target 2.46 of 5 for naturalness, while the paper's own 4.40 comes from its non-AV-HuBERT variant on 20 clips [@choi2024v2sflow]. The input includes a speaker embedding from a speech segment of unstated origin, and no result is repeated over seeds.
expert_true_value: Shows that predicting 200 HuBERT units beside the mel target cuts LRS3 ASR WER from 72.5% to 50.7% without text labels (one run, ResNet-18 encoder). The design is standard in the field, the multi-input vocoder and mel augmentation change WER by 0.3 and 0.2 points, and the headline 29.8% depends on swapping in a pretrained AV-HuBERT encoder.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech models typically either use blurry acoustic targets alone for supervision or require paired text labels as stronger content guidance.
delta_from_canon: Adds discrete HuBERT units as a second training target beside the mel-spectrogram and as a vocoder input. The unit target carries the content gain; the vocoder and mel augmentation change WER by under 1% relative. The concurrent ReVISE also predicts units from an AV-HuBERT-initialised encoder.
position_in_field: Core video-to-speech / silent-speech reconstruction work utilizing self-supervised speech units for content modeling.
practical_value: A cheap recipe when text labels are unavailable: the unit target cut LRS3 WER by about 30% relative in one run. The multi-input vocoder is optional (0.3 points), and test-time use needs a speech segment of the speaker for the embedding.
axes_moved: content_supervision; vocoder_design; reconstruction_intelligibility
axes_unresolved: live_inference; occlusion_robustness; unconstrained_capture
technical_limits: Limited by dependence on benchmark video quality, vocoder stack complexity, and residual challenge in matching natural speech quality; no tested robustness to pose, occlusion, or spontaneous environment variability.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation is limited to test sets from LRS2 and LRS3 datasets, with no cross-dataset or live deployment exploration; human evaluation is limited to 15 participants rating MOS on 20 samples.
deployment_limits: No latency analysis, on-device implementation, or in-the-wild robustness to camera position/lighting/occlusion is demonstrated, limiting immediate real-world deployment.
scope_limits: Focuses strictly on lip-to-speech synthesis (speech reconstruction) without addressing text entry, command recognition, or speech enhancement. Evaluation confined to standard benchmarks LRS2 and LRS3.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: Lip video with visual front-end optionally replaced by AV-HuBERT models pretrained on LRS3 and VoxCeleb2
metrics: LRS3 ASR WER 29.8% with the AV-HuBERT encoder and 50.2% with ResNet-18, against 65.8% for Multi-Task (single runs); LRS2 35.7% and 44.8%; on LRS3 speech units take WER from 72.5% to 50.7%, the vocoder and augmentation add 0.3 and 0.2 points (Table 3); STOI, ESTOI, PESQ; MOS naturalness 4.40 from 15 raters on 20 LRS3 clips of the non-AV-HuBERT variant.
evaluation_mode: Quantitative evaluation on standard benchmarks (LRS2, LRS3) using STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, WER metrics and a small-scale human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) study.

evidence.statement: We propose a novel Lip-to-Speech synthesis (L2S) framework that uses quantized self-supervised speech representations, named speech units, as an additional prediction target alongside mel-spectrogram, allowing strong content supervision without text labels, and introduce a multi-input vocoder conditioned on mel-spectrogram and speech units to generate clear waveforms even from noisy mel-spectrograms.

Units as a second training target beside mel and as a vocoder input; both are standard against the field (M02, M06). The unit target carries the gain (LRS3 WER 72.5% to 50.7%, one run); the vocoder and mel augmentation change WER by 0.3 and 0.2 points (Table 3).

On LRS3 the proposed method with AV-HuBERT reaches STOI 0.578, ESTOI 0.393, PESQ 1.31 and WER 29.8%, against 65.8% WER for Multi-Task; on LRS2 STOI 0.585, ESTOI 0.412, PESQ 1.34 and WER 35.7% (Tables 1 and 2). Single runs; the 29.8% depends on the AV-HuBERT encoder.

Evaluation is performed on LRS2 and LRS3 large-scale sentence-level lip-to-speech datasets with thousands of speakers in natural and wild environments; human MOS evaluation involved 15 participants rating naturalness, intelligibility, and clearness on 20 test samples from LRS3.

The approach depends on quality of benchmark video datasets (LRS2 and LRS3) and the vocoder stack complexity; the synthesized speech audio quality remains far from natural speech and no evaluation on real-world deployment scenarios, occlusion robustness, or user mobility has been conducted.

No latency analysis, on-device deployment, or robustness under uncontrolled camera settings has been demonstrated; thus, deployment readiness for real-world applications remains limited despite benchmark performance gains.

en.summary: Unit target (M02) and unit-conditioned vocoder (M06) are standard; units cut LRS3 WER 21.8 points, AV-HuBERT 20.4 more, the vocoder 0.3; unit gain untested on AV-HuBERT, single runs.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video; optional AV-HuBERT encoder); speaker embedding from a speech segment
en.speaker: Speaker-independent on LRS3 (unseen-speaker split); LRS2 overlap unknown
en.key_result: LRS3 ASR WER 29.8% with the AV-HuBERT encoder (50.2% with ResNet-18); speech units cut WER from 72.5% to 50.7% (21.8 points) and AV-HuBERT a further 20.4 points; single runs
en.limitations: Single runs, no seeds; speaker embedding from an unspecified speech segment; unit gain untested with the AV-HuBERT encoder; the 20-clip MOS (4.40) is of the non-AV-HuBERT variant and V2SFlow's listeners (2.46, variant unstated) do not confirm it.

title: IR-UWB Radar-Based Contactless Silent Speech Recognition of Vowels, Consonants, Words, and Phrases
expert_take_short: FERASEC is a standard engineered radar front end with a large gain over 2016 features; phoneme novelty holds only for consonant syllables, and evaluation is within-speaker.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the radar feature front end (M06), which is standard for the field and well supported against the authors' 2016 baseline, but its case against learned front ends rests on raw frames fed to a DNN-HMM and is contradicted, on one participant and 50 words, by the first author's later network on the same testbed. The first-phoneme claim holds only as contactless classification of consonant syllables, since silent vowel classification with contactless IR-UWB radar predates it. Evaluation (M12) is within-speaker leave-one-out without seeds or spread, with words and phrases from 4 speakers; placement results confound position with antenna and distance, and device integration is not measured.
expert_true_value: A radar-specific engineered front end (FERASEC) that lifts contactless IR-UWB classification of silent vowel and consonant syllables well above the 2016 features over 20 participants; consonant-syllable classification is new, vowel classification is not.
canon_before: Contactless IR-UWB radar had classified five silently read vowels for one speaker and ten words per speaker (2016); contact radar had recognised 25 phonemes (2018); a radar had classified five spoken vowels (2022). No contactless radar study had classified consonants.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the two 2016 CLEAN features with six envelope and derivative features and adds contactless classification of 11 consonant syllables, with within-speaker leave-one-out tests.
position_in_field: Contactless radar silent speech: closed-set syllable, word and phrase classification with engineered features, the usual radar design.
practical_value: Shows within-speaker closed-set feasibility in the laboratory; phone or watch use is asserted, not measured, and the single-radar position aid was tested on one participant.
axes_moved: engineered_radar_features; contactless_consonant_syllables
axes_unresolved: speaker_independent_testing; learned_front_end; open_vocabulary; device_integration
technical_limits: Performance affected by articulator alignment; signal blockage by teeth can obscure tongue motion with upper radar; FERASEC depends on effective clutter mitigation and engineered transforms.
evaluation_limits: Within-speaker leave-one-out over 20 repetitions; no seeds, spread or chance level; words and phrases from 4 speakers; lip versus chin confounded with antenna and distance.
deployment_limits: Needs robust user-position handling, mitigating signal blockage (e.g. teeth), and hardware integration to small devices for daily use.
scope_limits: Closed-set prompted isolated and short phrase recognition; no open vocabulary, spontaneous speech, or broader speaker variability tested.
input_modality: radar
sensor_hardware: Upper and lower IR-UWB radar sensors; upper uses patch antennas facing lips, lower uses sinuous antennas below chin.
vocabulary_type: 8 vowels, 11 consonants, 25 words, and 12 phrases
vocabulary_size: 56 speech items across four task sets
metrics: Classification accuracy evaluated via leave-one-out cross-validation across 20 reps per phoneme/word/phrase; vowels achieved 86.47%, consonants 81.59%, words 88.95%, phrases 96.88% with FERASEC + DNN-HMM upper radar.
evaluation_mode: Leave-one-out cross-validation across repeated prompted articulation; separate experiments per speech unit type and radar position.

evidence.statement: This study represents the first demonstration of phoneme-level SSR using contactless radar and proposes a novel speech feature extraction algorithm specifically designed for IR-UWB radar-based SSR.

Twenty participants silently produced 8 CVC and 11 VCV syllables; only the 4 native American-English speakers also produced the 25 words and 12 phrases; each item was repeated 20 times, with two IR-UWB radars facing the lips and below the chin.

Introduces FERASEC, a novel radar-specific speech feature extraction algorithm reducing dimensionality of IR-UWB radar frames into envelope features capturing articulator movement, essential for phoneme-level SSR accuracy.

FERASEC utilizes concatenation of raw and clutter-reduced radar frames, envelope detection, downsampling, DC removal, plus first and second derivatives, creating six-dimensional feature set for classification.
Evaluation is within-speaker leave-one-out cross-validation over 20 repetitions: 20 participants for vowel and consonant syllables, 4 for words and phrases.
FERASEC combined with DNN-HMM and upper radar antenna placement yields recognition accuracies of 86.47% vowels, 81.59% consonants, 88.95% words, and 96.88% phrases.
Raw or clutter-reduced frame sets fed to a DNN-HMM stay below 50% on vowels and consonants; no other learned front end was tested.
evidence.section_or_location: 1 Necessity of Developing a Feature Extraction Algorithm for IR

evidence.statement: Although current proof-of-concept uses a hardware testbed, IR-UWB radar modules based on CMOS transceiver chips and antenna integration feasibility imply potential embedding of contactless SSR into smartphones or wearables.
A supporting aiding algorithm checks that the user's lips are properly aligned and within radar detection range before silent speech capture, improving usability for consumer device integration.

en.summary: FERASEC is a standard engineered radar front end with a large gain over 2016 features; phoneme novelty holds only for consonant syllables, and evaluation is within-speaker.
en.sensor: Two IR-UWB radars facing lips and below chin
en.speaker: Within-speaker; 20 participants for syllables, 4 for words and phrases
en.key_result: 86.47% vowels, 81.59% consonants, 88.95% words, 96.88% phrases (leave-one-out CV, upper radar)
en.limitations: Controlled lab study with prompted closed-set items and limited speaker diversity; sensitive to user alignment and tooth blockage; no open vocabulary or conversational speech tested.

title: Knowledge Distilled Ensemble Model for sEMG-based Silent Speech Interface
venue: arXiv preprint (submitted to the IEEE Region 8 Student Paper Contest 2023)
expert_take_short: Ensemble-to-student distillation (M02, M06, M13) is standard: same-modality distillation predates it; 85.9% is one unseeded split of unstated unit, and 7x smaller is against six models.
expert_take_long: KDE-SSI [@lai2023kdessi] changes three components: ensemble soft targets (M02), a single distilled decoder (M06), and reported time and size (M13). All three are standard: same-modality distillation of word classifiers was published for lip reading three years earlier [@ma2021towards]; only the ensemble teacher is new, on one split. "7.0× smaller, 20.8× faster" compares the student with six models (N = 6, Table II) on a GPU (Fig. 5): N explains the size ratio, not the speed ratio. The comparison that matters, student against one ResNet1D (85.9% vs 81.2%, Table II), is one split with no seed or repeats reported and an unstated grouping unit (§IV.E), and the student's architecture is not given. So 85.9% is not comparable with the later subject-independent 85.8% on the same words [@hong2026cvos], and deployment (§V.B) is unmeasured.
expert_true_value: Brings ensemble-to-student knowledge distillation to a three-channel facial sEMG classifier of the 26 NATO code words and reports the student at 85.9% against 81.2% for one ResNet1D, on one unseeded split.
canon_before: Surface-EMG word classifiers are trained on hard labels; knowledge distillation in speech decoding mostly uses audio or ASR teachers, and same-modality distillation into lighter word classifiers (with and without distillation reported) was published for lip reading in 2020.
delta_from_canon: A soft-voting ensemble of ResNet1D models trained on the same sEMG data supplies soft targets (KL plus cross-entropy, alpha 0.5, T 5 or 10) for a single student; size and per-sample time are reported against the ensemble on a GPU.
position_in_field: Standard on training supervision (M02), decoder (M06) and operating constraints (M13); test split not reported (M12). The 85.9% cannot be compared with the later subject-independent 85.8% on the same 26 words.
practical_value: Shows that one distilled network can approach a six-model ensemble on this dataset; it does not show use on a wearable processor or by unseen speakers.
axes_moved: Accuracy of a single deployed network on the 26-class NATO set (85.9% vs 81.2% for ResNet1D, one split); GPU time and size against the ensemble.
axes_unresolved: Split unit and speaker or session independence; seeds; student-without-teacher control; student architecture; on-device latency and energy; female or older speakers; end-to-end spelling.
technical_limits: Three facial channels on LAO, DAO and ZM, which the authors concede are insufficient for some words; seven classes below F1 0.80; student architecture not stated; two-stage training.
evaluation_limits: Pooled 4:1:1 split of 3,900 samples from five male speakers aged 22 to 24 with the grouping unit not stated; no seeds or spread; backbone chosen on test results; averaging of precision, recall and F1 not stated; no chance level.
deployment_limits: Time and size measured against the ensemble on a Tesla P100; no phone or microcontroller measurement, power or price; spelling, confirmation and correction not evaluated.
scope_limits: Isolated 26-class classification of prompted, paced silent mouthing; not continuous speech or open vocabulary.
input_modality: emg
sensor_hardware: BITalino MuscleBIT bundle with prefixed electrode distances and adhesive Ag/AgCl electrodes on 3 facial muscles (levator anguli oris, depressor anguli oris, zygomaticus major).
vocabulary_type: NATO phonetic alphabet
vocabulary_size: 26 classes
metrics: Table II: KDE-SSI precision 87.4%, recall 85.7%, F1 0.855, accuracy 85.9%; VE-ResNet (N = 6) 86.0%; ResNet1D 81.2%. Table III: N = 4 teacher 88.0%, students 83.2% (T = 5) and 84.5% (T = 10). Fig. 5: 2.50 ms vs 0.12 ms per sample and 147.9 MB vs 21.1 MB (ensemble vs student, GPU).
evaluation_mode: Offline 4:1:1 train, validation and test split of pooled samples (unit not stated); single ResNet1D and three other backbones, VE-ResNet with N = 4, 6, 8, 10 and KDE-SSI at T = 5 and 10.

evidence.statement: The main contribution of our work is threefold: 1) construct a 26 words NATO phonetic alphabet dataset (3900 data samples in total) from the facial sEMG signals of 5 male subjects; 2) achieve 81.2% test accuracy for the single model on the created dataset; 3) implement a Knowledge Distilled Ensemble Model for Silent Speech Interface (KDE-SSI), a lightweight convolutional network that extracts knowledge from a pre-trained voting ensemble ResNet model (VE-ResNet) while maintaining performance, achieving 85.9% accuracy.

The dataset consists of 3900 samples, collected from 5 male subjects aged 22 to 24; each subject repeated the 26 NATO phonetic alphabet words 30 times, resulting in 150 samples per class, recorded via BITalino MuscleBIT bundle on 3 facial muscles: levator anguli oris, depressor anguli oris, and zygomaticus major.

KDE-SSI achieves 85.9% accuracy with 87.4% precision, 85.7% recall and 0.855 F1-score on the 26-class NATO phonetic alphabet classification; VE-ResNet teacher ensemble reaches 86.0% accuracy; inference time and model size of KDE-SSI are 0.12 ms and 21.1 MB versus 2.50 ms and 147.9 MB for VE-ResNet.

The evaluation is limited to 5 young male subjects; only with the split unit not stated training and testing are conducted; no cross-subject or cross-session robustness analysis; the system requires adhesive electrodes placed on three facial muscles; does not address speaker independence or broader demographics.

The proposed method reduces model size by a factor of 7 and speeds inference by about 20x compared to the teacher ensemble, enabling portable, practical deployment with COTS hardware and low latency, while preserving accuracy.

en.summary: Ensemble-to-student distillation (M02, M06, M13) is standard: same-modality distillation predates it; 85.9% is one unseeded split of unstated unit, and 7x smaller is against six models.
en.sensor: 3-channel facial sEMG (BITalino, adhesive Ag/AgCl electrodes)
en.speaker: Five male speakers pooled; split unit not stated
en.key_result: 85.9% on 26 NATO words (one 4:1:1 split, unit not stated) vs 81.2% for one ResNet1D; 21.1 MB and 0.12 ms per sample on a GPU vs 147.9 MB and 2.50 ms for the six-model ensemble.
en.limitations: Same-modality distillation predates it; no student-without-teacher control; no seeds; split unit not stated; five male speakers; no on-device measurement.

title: Large-scale unsupervised audio pre-training for video-to-speech synthesis
expert_take_short: Audio-only decoder pre-training (M03) is standard after TTS decoder transfer; it lowers WER in 7 of 16 pairs, earlier systems keep lower WER, and no equal-training control or listener test exists.
expert_take_long: The paper changes training (M03): it pre-trains the speech decoder on 3,572 hours of audio alone and transfers it to video-to-speech models. The design is standard: transferring a decoder trained without the input signal is used at least since 2021, and the paper's departure is dropping the transcripts a text-to-speech decoder needs. The transfer does not reliably help: it lowers WER against the same model trained from scratch in 7 of 16 model and split pairs and raises it in 9. Earlier systems keep lower WER on all four splits. The strongest confound is unequal training, since only pre-trained variants inherit a fully trained audio model, and every row is a single run with no listener test, so the claim that audio pre-training improves video-to-speech is not supported.
expert_true_value: A large-scale test of whether a speech decoder pre-trained on audio alone helps video-to-speech synthesis. Its value is mainly as evidence on that question: the transfer lowers WER in only 7 of 16 model and split pairs, and without an equal-training control the gains it does show cannot be attributed to the audio data.
canon_before: Video-to-speech systems largely rely on paired audio-visual data, limiting the use of large audio-only corpora.
delta_from_canon: Moves decoder learning into an audio-only pretraining stage and transfers it back into video-to-speech.
position_in_field: A video-to-speech training study that applies decoder transfer, used since TTS-decoder transfer in 2021, with audio-only pre-training at larger scale. Its systems trail earlier video-to-speech systems on WER on all four WER splits.
practical_value: Shows how to pre-train a video-to-speech decoder on audio-only corpora, but does not show that this reliably improves the synthesized speech. Useful as a baseline and as a design to retest against scratch models given equal training.
axes_moved: decoder_pretraining; audio_only_transfer
axes_unresolved: consistent_wer_gains; live_capture; deployment_latency
technical_limits: Pretraining does not reliably improve WER uniformly; benchmark audio quality remains modest; model complexity and latency implications not analyzed.
evaluation_limits: Benchmark evaluation on standard datasets with objective metrics only; no human perceptual tests or deployment contexts evaluated.
deployment_limits: No latency or real-world capture robustness study is given. No evidence of real-time deployment or joint visual robustness under diverse conditions.
scope_limits: Focus on video-to-speech waveform and mel spectrogram reconstruction only; no text-entry or command recognition addressed.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: Video input plus large-scale audio-only corpora used in pretraining; video from mouth region extraction; pretrained face/speaker embeddings for identity
metrics: PESQ, STOI, ESTOI and ASR WER on GRID (four seen speakers, 33 seen, 33 unseen), TCD-TIMIT (three lipspeakers, seen; no WER) and LRW. The paper's own models span PESQ 1.30-2.07, STOI 0.478-0.720, ESTOI 0.274-0.539 and WER 2.66%-41.00% (Tables IV-VIII); earlier systems in the same tables keep lower WER on every WER split. Single runs, no listener test.
evaluation_mode: Seen and unseen speaker evaluation on GRID, TCD-TIMIT, and LRW datasets, with quantitative metrics (PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, WER)

evidence.statement: In this paper we propose to train encoder-decoder models on more than 3,500 hours of audio data at 24kHz, and then use the pre-trained decoders to initialize the audio decoders for the video-to-speech synthesis task.

We pre-train the audio-to-audio models on a combination of speech corpora in an unsupervised manner and use these pre-trained models to initialize and fine-tune the corresponding video-to-audio models.

We propose a modification to the batch normalization module which enables cross-modal parameter fine-tuning by keeping track of separate running statistics for the audio and video modalities. We apply this to the batch normalization layers of the decoder.
We conduct experiments on popular audio-visual datasets on seen (GRID, TCD-TIMIT) and unseen (GRID, LRW) speakers.

On GRID unseen, V2A-MelSpec-S-SP with the fine-tuned pre-trained decoder reaches PESQ 1.43, STOI 0.598, ESTOI 0.335 and WER 17.90%; on LRW, V2A-MelSpec-M-SP trained from scratch reaches 1.48, 0.649, 0.484 and 14.96%, better than its pre-trained variant on all four metrics, so pre-training does not reliably help quality or WER.
No latency or real-world capture robustness study is given, so deployment readiness is limited.
Pretraining does not uniformly improve WER and benchmark audio quality is still modest.
All evidence is benchmark-based with no live interface or user-facing deployment.

en.summary: Audio-only decoder pre-training (M03) is standard after TTS decoder transfer; it lowers WER in 7 of 16 pairs, earlier systems keep lower WER, and no equal-training control or listener test exists.
en.sensor: Camera (mouth-region video)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Paper's models: PESQ 1.30-2.07, STOI 0.478-0.720, WER 2.66%-41.00% across GRID, TCD-TIMIT and LRW; audio pre-training lowers WER in 7 of 16 model and split pairs; earlier systems keep lower WER on all four WER splits.
en.limitations: WER improvements not consistent; objective benchmark metrics only, with no human listening tests, latency or real-world robustness evaluation.

title: Let There Be Sound: Reconstructing High Quality Speech from Silent Videos
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24)
expert_take_short: HuBERT-unit, pitch and energy targets (M02) and flow post-net (M06) are standard, after ReVISE and VCVTS; GRID WER 17.07% vs 17.62%; seen-speaker tests only (M12 behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@kim2024let] changes the training targets (M02: 200 HuBERT units, pitch and energy from the paired audio) and the decoder (M06: variance predictors and a flow post-net); both are standard, the units follow ReVISE [@hsu2023revise] and the unit-plus-pitch design VCVTS [@wang2022vcvts], neither cited, and the ablations do not single out the units. The "large margin" holds for MOS and for Lip2Wav WER (34.71% against 48.73% for VCA-GAN), but GRID WER is 17.07% against 17.62% under a scorer at 12.20% on real speech (Table 1). Its test sets draw on the training speakers (Sec. Datasets), behind earlier unseen-speaker GRID tests including its own comparator [@kim2021vcagan]. On LRS3, which the paper did not use, two [later] re-runs by the authors' group give 79.7% and 84.08% WER under different scorers, against 28.5% and 30.45% for their successors [@choi2024v2sflow; @kim2025faces].
expert_true_value: A clean lip-to-speech recipe that combines HuBERT unit, pitch and energy targets with a flow post-net; HuBERT-unit prediction from video follows ReVISE (2022) and the unit-plus-pitch decomposition VCVTS (2022), and its gains are shown on seen speakers in single runs.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech quality was limited by homophenes, over-smoothed outputs, and weak prosodic control.
delta_from_canon: Moves text-to-speech variance modelling (unit, pitch and energy predictors, flow post-net) into lip-to-speech; HuBERT-unit targets appeared in ReVISE, a unit-plus-pitch decomposition in VCVTS and a flow-based generator in GlowLTS, so the change is standard rather than new.
position_in_field: Standard design (M02, M06) with a behind evaluation (M12: seen speakers only); overtaken by flow-matching and token-based successors from the same group.
practical_value: Useful as an ablated reference for variance-adaptor lip-to-speech on GRID and two-speaker Lip2Wav; later LRS3 re-runs on unseen speakers (79.7% and 84.08% WER under two different scorers, a dataset the paper did not use) show it does not transfer to open-speaker video.
axes_moved: lip2wav_intelligibility; prosody_modeling
axes_unresolved: unseen-speaker generalization; seed variance; scorer-independent intelligibility; real-time inference
technical_limits: Multi-stage pipeline; no latency or streaming evaluation; complex architecture not end-to-end; needs neural vocoder at inference.
