evaluation_limits: GRID and Lip2Wav test sets drawn from the training speakers; Lip2Wav two speakers trained jointly; single runs; Whisper scorer at 12.20% WER on real GRID speech; baselines retrained by the authors on the same settings, SVTS reproduced on MT's code.
deployment_limits: No real-time or on-device deployment targets; system is a multi-stage research pipeline without simplified inference or low-latency optimization.
scope_limits: Lip-to-speech reconstruction from silent video only; no multi-modal or audio-assisted input considered.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: phonetic
vocabulary_size: GRID: 51; Lip2Wav: large vocabulary
metrics: GRID: WER 17.07% / CER 9.17% vs VCA-GAN 17.62% / 9.55%, real speech 12.20%, vocoded 12.44%; MOS 4.46 / 4.63 vs VCA-GAN 3.46 / 4.10; MOS gap to vocoded 0.28 naturalness, 0.16 intelligibility (0.13 in the paper's prose). Lip2Wav (2 speakers): WER 34.71% vs 48.73%, vocoded 6.05%. Later LRS3 re-runs: 79.7% (V2SFlow, its ASR scorer) and 84.08% (Faces-to-Voices, Whisper Medium).
evaluation_mode: MOS for naturalness and intelligibility, WER/CER via ASR transcription comparison, pitch-energy statistical analysis, and ablations.

evidence.statement: We propose a novel lip-to-speech system that alleviates the one-to-many mapping problem by incorporating self-supervised speech representations to disambiguate homophenes, modeling acoustic variance for speech variation, and employing a flow-based post-net to refine synthesized speech details.

Our method combines self-supervised linguistic targets from intermediate HuBERT layers, explicit variance predictors for pitch and energy, and a flow-based post-net to enhance speech reconstruction quality, addressing one-to-many ambiguity more explicitly than previous work.

On the GRID dataset, our model achieves a MOS gap from vocoded speech of only 0.28 in naturalness and 0.13 in intelligibility; WER and CER are 17.07% and 9.17% respectively, outperforming previous lip-to-speech methods.

We evaluate on the constrained GRID dataset and larger Lip2Wav Chemistry and Chess multi-speaker subsets; evaluation includes MOS naturalness/intelligibility, WER/CER via ASR, and pitch-energy statistics.
The system is a multi-stage research pipeline without real-time or on-device deployment claims; end-to-end simplification and inference latency remain for future work.
Evaluations are limited to GRID and Lip2Wav datasets which do not cover open-world or real-time deployment, with manual transcription used in Lip2Wav due to lack of text labels.

Each component independently contributes to quality: linguistic predictor clarifies homophenes improving intelligibility and errors; pitch and energy variance predictors improve prosodic modeling; flow post-net improves naturalness and detail.

Using the 12th layer of HuBERT-large with 200 K-means clusters for quantized linguistic representation yields the best intelligibility (lowest phoneme error rate) and contributes strongly to pronunciation accuracy in the model.

en.summary: HuBERT-unit, pitch and energy targets (M02) and flow post-net (M06) are standard, after ReVISE and VCVTS; GRID WER 17.07% vs 17.62%; seen-speaker tests only (M12 behind).
en.sensor: Camera (lip video)
en.speaker: Seen speakers only (GRID 33, Lip2Wav 2)
en.key_result: GRID WER 17.07% vs 17.62% for VCA-GAN (scorer 12.20% on real speech) but MOS 4.46 vs 3.46 naturalness and 4.63 vs 4.10 intelligibility; two-speaker Lip2Wav WER 34.71% vs 48.73%; later LRS3 re-runs (a dataset the paper did not use, different scorers): 79.7% and 84.08% WER on unseen speakers
en.limitations: Test sets drawn from the training speakers (GRID 80/10/10 over all 33 speakers, Lip2Wav 2 speakers split 80/10/10); single runs; baselines retrained by the authors (SVTS reproduced); unit targets follow ReVISE (2022) and unit-plus-pitch decomposition follows VCVTS (2022), neither cited; speaker identity from a table of training speakers.

title: LipLearner: Customizable Silent Speech Interactions on Mobile Devices
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23)
expert_take_short: All three changed components are standard: on-device few-shot head untested against prototypes or fine-tuning; voiced enrollment loses 5.6 points; visual KWS predates it uncited.
expert_take_long: LipLearner [@su2023liplearner] changes command registration (M03), enrollment from a voiced utterance (M01) and activation by visual keyword spotting (M06); all three are standard. Its frozen-encoder linear head is the only one among 30 few-shot vocabulary studies (pattern match, Appendix), but the one-shot 25-command F1 of 0.8947 over 1,000 random draws (§5.3) faces no prototype or fine-tuning head (§5.2–5.4). The voiced-to-silent loss (87.29% against 81.67%, §8.2.2) is the known overt-to-silent degradation, and KWS activation is new only for lipreading interfaces, as the paper says (§6.1): visual-only spotting predates it uncited [@momeni2020seeing; @stafylakis2018zeroshot]. The superiority claim rests on an in-house counterpart trained from scratch (0.9895 against 0.7147 F1, §5.4).
expert_true_value: The key advance is enabling end-to-end on-device silent speech interaction with few-shot customizable command registration via Voice2Lip, practical keyword spotting, and incremental learning, rather than just offline lipreading accuracy. This system design and evaluation close a major gap towards real mobile SSI deployment.
canon_before: Mobile lipreading interfaces were typically fixed-vocabulary or relied on costly per-user data collection and retraining from scratch, limiting personalization and deployment on commodity devices.
delta_from_canon: LipLearner replaces training-from-scratch approaches with a few-shot mobile workflow incorporating Voice2Lip for easy command enrollment, a keyword spotting system robust to misactivation, and on-device incremental fine-tuning enabling practical customization.
position_in_field: One of the clearest mobile SSI papers tying model design directly to practical enrollment and real-time use on commodity devices.
practical_value: High for enabling privacy-preserving, hands-free silent speech command input on smartphones that users can adapt with minimal effort.
axes_moved: few_shot_customization; mobile_ssi; keyword_spotting; on_device_learning
axes_unresolved: open_vocabulary_interaction; lower_effort_active_learning
technical_limits: Fails on very similar commands causing confusion; requires visible lip movements; incremental learning demands user participation.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation on 25-command classification, and 30-command live study, both limited scale and vocabulary; testing mainly on frontal lip videos under defined lighting/posture/gesture manipulations; unknown performance on open vocabulary or completely unseen environments beyond tested conditions.
deployment_limits: User burden remains due to active learning and need for correction when similar commands cause confusion; reliance on visible lips limits use in occluded conditions; current vocabulary and study scale modest relative to open natural language; threshold tuning for keyword spotting remains user-dependent.
scope_limits: Mobile silent command interaction on smartphone, not general open-vocabulary speech recognition.
input_modality: video (front camera lip region)
sensor_hardware: smartphone front camera
vocabulary_type: command vocabulary; multilingual user-defined
vocabulary_size: customizable user-defined with tested 25 to 30 commands
metrics: One-shot 25-command F1 0.8947; mobile app 30-command one-shot accuracy 81.7%, five-shot 98.8%; keyword spotting average EER 6.75%; on-device latency about 422 ms.
evaluation_mode: few-shot with cross-condition robustness, keyword spotting evaluated by EER, one-shot F1, user study involving real-time silent speech command issuance and incremental learning

evidence.statement: The paper proposes customizable mobile silent-speech interaction with few-shot lipreading, Voice2Lip registration, visual keyword spotting, and on-device incremental learning.

For 25-command classification, F1-score of 0.8947 was achieved with one shot; app study reports 30-command one-shot accuracy 81.7% and five-shot 98.8%; keyword spotting average EER 6.75%; on-device latency about 422 ms.
LipLearner runs on a commodity smartphone in real-time with latency about 422 ms, all processing on-device supporting hands-free silent speech interaction without network connection.

Evaluation conducted with LRW public dataset for contrastive pretraining plus an in-the-wild dataset collected with 11 participants in 7 conditions for a total of 9625 clips; a 16-participant live user study tested real-time activation, command registration, and recognition, including multilingual and user-defined commands.
Technical limits include reliance on visible lips, confusion between very similar commands, and cognitive and physical user burden in active learning.

en.summary: All three changed components are standard: on-device few-shot head untested against prototypes or fine-tuning; voiced enrollment loses 5.6 points; visual KWS predates it uncited.
en.sensor: Smartphone front camera (lip video)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 98.8% five-shot (81.7% one-shot) accuracy, 30 commands, mobile app; ~422 ms on-device latency
en.limitations: Modest vocabulary and study scale; confuses similar commands, requires visible lips, and incremental learning adds user burden.

title: LipVoicer: Generating Speech from Silent Videos Guided by Lip Reading
venue: The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024)
expert_take_short: Lip-reader text conditioning (M07) is new but standard: words come from the lip reader (19.1% reading WER becomes 21.4%; 86.2% unguided), and no cascade control is run.
expert_take_long: LipVoicer [@yemini2024lipvoicer] changes three components: lip-reader text steers synthesis at use time (M07), a CTC recognizer trained on noised mel-spectrograms carries all text supervision (M02), and a video-conditioned diffusion model generates the mel-spectrogram (M06). The authors' claim (Sec. 1) to be the first to condition a video-to-speech synthesizer on lip-reader text holds against 165 ledger studies (Appendix), with [@hegde2023towards] [concurrent]. M07 is still standard: lip-to-text plus TTS already used such text [@hegde2022arbitrary], and no gain over it is shown. The words come from the lip reader, not the synthesizer: on LRS3 output WER is 21.4% against the lip reader's 19.1%, 5.4% with ground-truth text, and 86.2% without guidance, worse than the Lip2Speech baseline at 57.4% (Tables 4, 6, 7). No baseline received that text, so "state-of-the-art results" (Sec. 1) pit a 2023 lip reader against text-free synthesizers. M02, M06 and M12 are standard; the main tables score words with an ASR from the same work as the lip reader.
expert_true_value: Shows that feeding text from a lip reader into video-to-speech at inference, through ASR classifier guidance of a diffusion mel generator, cuts word error on LRS2 and LRS3 far below text-free synthesizers; the gain follows the lip reader's own accuracy.
canon_before: Prior lip-to-speech systems map silent lip video directly to audio or audio features, often producing ambiguous or unintelligible speech on in-the-wild datasets with diverse speakers and open vocabulary.
delta_from_canon: LipVoicer incorporates inferred text from a lip-reading network at inference time as guidance for diffusion-based speech generation, reducing ambiguity and improving intelligibility and synchronization.
position_in_field: Standard on use-time text (M07): it is the first video-to-speech synthesizer in the wiki conditioned on lip-reader text, as the authors claim, but lip-to-text plus TTS already used such text and no gain over that cascade is shown; later AUTO-AVSR re-scores still rank it lowest in LRS3 WER. The diffusion decoder (M06) and the noise-conditioned CTC recognizer (M02, after Guided-TTS) are standard. Intelligibility and naturalness remain below ground truth in the paper's own listener ratings.
practical_value: A reference design for adding lip-reading text to video-to-speech; its word accuracy is bounded by the lip reader and depends strongly on the guiding ASR, and it is offline with hundreds of diffusion steps.
axes_moved: text_guidance; intelligibility; in_the_wild_video_to_speech
axes_unresolved: real-time deployment; misuse mitigation; dependence on lip-reader quality
axes_regressed: Intrusive STOI on LRS3 is the lowest of the compared systems (0.38 against 0.50 for Lip2Speech, Table 10); without ASR guidance MelGen reaches 86.2% WER, worse than the Lip2Speech baseline (57.4%).
technical_limits: Depends on quality and performance of large pretrained lip-reader and ASR models plus heavy diffusion model; generation is offline with hundreds of inference steps limiting real-time use; quality degrades with less accurate lip-readers; risk of adversarial misuse via text injection.
evaluation_limits: No baseline receives the lip reader's text and no lip-to-text plus TTS control is run; the main-table evaluation ASR and the lip reader are both Ma et al. (2023); listener intelligibility is a 1-5 rating, not transcription; the meaning of the ± values, seeds and speaker overlap are not stated; guidance weights were tuned by listening tests on unstated data.
deployment_limits: Heavy model stack including lip-reader, ASR, and diffusion; no focus on low-latency or on-device deployment; recognized risk of misuse from malicious text injection.
scope_limits: Lip-to-speech from silent lip video only; does not handle audio/video noisy inputs or multimodal fusion beyond lip video and inferred text guidance.
input_modality: silent lip video
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: open
vocabulary_size: open vocabulary including hundreds of speakers' utterances as in LRS2/LRS3 datasets
metrics: LRS3 (Table 4): WER 21.4%, STOI-Net 0.92, DNSMOS 3.11, LSE-C 6.239, LSE-D 8.266; Lip2Speech 57.4%, SVTS 82.4%, VCA-GAN 90.6%. LRS2 (Table 3): WER 17.8% against 51.4% for Lip2Speech. Lip-reader WER 19.1% (LRS3) and 14.6% (LRS2); with ground-truth text 5.4%; without ASR guidance 86.2%; with an early-stopped guiding ASR 76.3% (Tables 6, 7, 11). MOS on LRS3 intelligibility 3.44 against 4.38 for ground truth (Table 2), 16 annotators per sample, 50 samples.
evaluation_mode: Human mean opinion scores (MOS) on intelligibility, naturalness, quality, synchronization; objective metrics including WER, DNSMOS, STOI-Net, SyncNet metrics on LRS2 and LRS3 test sets.

evidence.statement: The paper proposes LipVoicer, which first predicts text from lip video and then uses that text to guide diffusion-based speech generation.
LipVoicer combines lip-reading, diffusion generation, classifier-free guidance, and ASR classifier guidance in one inference loop, a novel system design in lip-to-speech.

LipVoicer is evaluated on LRS2 and LRS3, in-the-wild audiovisual datasets with hundreds of speakers and open vocabulary; evaluation includes human MOS and objective WER, DNSMOS, STOI-Net, and synchronization with SyncNet metrics.

On LRS3 ablation, removing ASR guidance increases WER from 21.4% to 86.2%, showing that text guidance is essential for intelligibility; LipVoicer outperforms baselines Lip2Speech, VCA-GAN, SVTS in human and objective evaluations.

The stack depends on a lip-reader, an ASR model, and a relatively heavy diffusion model; inference is not real-time and deployment on mobile or low-latency platforms is not claimed or targeted; misuse risk from injected text at inference is acknowledged.

LipVoicer requires a heavy model stack for inference and does not claim real-time or on-device deployment readiness; social misuse risks from incorrect or malicious text guidance are noted but not addressed here.
LipVoicer achieved human mean opinion scores near ground truth on LRS2 and LRS3 on intelligibility (3.44-3.53 vs 4.33-4.38), naturalness, quality, and synchronization, outperforming recent baselines.

LipVoicer uses pretrained lip-reader Ma et al. (2023) with WER 14.6% on LRS2 and 19.1% on LRS3 to generate text at inference time; uses a modified ASR Burchi & Timofte (2023) fine-tuned on noised data for classifier guidance.

en.summary: Lip-reader text conditioning (M07) is new but standard: words come from the lip reader (19.1% reading WER becomes 21.4%; 86.2% unguided), and no cascade control is run.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: LRS3 WER 21.4% (lip reader 19.1%; ground-truth text 5.4%; no ASR guidance 86.2%); LRS2 17.8%.
en.limitations: Words come from the lip reader; output WER is very sensitive to the guiding ASR (Table 11); no cascade control; evaluation ASR from the same work as the lip reader; no seeds; speaker overlap not stated; offline diffusion with hundreds of steps.

title: RobustL2S: Speaker-Specific Lip-to-Speech Synthesis exploiting Self-Supervised Representations
expert_take_short: SSL-feature target (M02) and Seq2Seq-to-unit-vocoder decoder (M06) are standard after ReVISE; GRID-4S WER 11.21% is set against baselines scored with other ASRs.
expert_take_long: RobustL2S [@sahipjohn2023robustl2s] changes the training target (M02), regressing continuous HuBERT features, and the decoder (M06), a Seq2Seq stage before a unit HiFi-GAN. Both are standard because the vocoder input is still HuBERT units: RobustL2S quantizes its predictions back to 100 units (§IV.B.4), and ReVISE already linked an AV-HuBERT-initialized predictor to such units and a unit HiFi-GAN [@hsu2023revise]. Features beat units on one Lip2Wav speaker, against a unit variant that also changes the input and scores below the model without Seq2Seq (STOI 0.18 against 0.50, Table I). The state-of-the-art claim rests on unrerun comparator values and an unnamed ASR: GRID-4S WER 11.21% against VCA-GAN's listed 12.25%, while the cited, uncompared GAN of Mira et al. reports 7.03% and 4.07% when Kefalas et al. score it [@mira2021endtoend; @kefalas2023large].
expert_true_value: Shows that regressing continuous HuBERT features from fine-tuned AV-HuBERT features, then re-quantizing them for a unit vocoder, gives speaker-specific lip-to-speech with high STOI on GRID-4S, TCD-TIMIT-3S and Lip2Wav; the pipeline follows ReVISE and the features-over-units evidence is one speaker.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech systems predicted mel-spectrograms or waveforms from lip video and vocoded them; ReVISE (2022) already connected an AV-HuBERT-initialized predictor to HuBERT-derived units and a unit HiFi-GAN, and VCVTS transferred discrete units to lips.
delta_from_canon: A non-autoregressive transformer maps fine-tuned AV-HuBERT features to continuous HuBERT features with an L1 loss; at inference the predicted features are k-means clustered into 100 units for a per-dataset unit HiFi-GAN.
position_in_field: Standard on the training target (M02) and decoder (M06) after ReVISE; WER comparisons set an unnamed ASR against comparator values not stated as rerun, and ESTOI trails VCA-GAN on GRID-4S and the visual-voice-memory model on two Lip2Wav speakers.
practical_value: A speaker-specific research baseline for SSL-based lip-to-speech on GRID, TCD-TIMIT and Lip2Wav; its WER cannot be placed against other systems until scored with a named ASR.
axes_moved: ssl_representation_learning; intelligibility; multi_dataset_benchmarking
axes_unresolved: Prosody, multilingual transfer, and broader speaker generalization remain unresolved.
axes_regressed: ESTOI on GRID-4S (0.571 against 0.609 for VCA-GAN) and on two Lip2Wav speakers against the visual-voice-memory model.
technical_limits: Limited prosody modeling due to speech SSL embeddings; speaker-independence and generalization remain unaddressed.
evaluation_limits: Evaluations are dataset-constrained with no real-world latency or deployment testing; transcripts missing for Lip2Wav requiring whisper for finetuning; limited testing on unseen words and speaker independence.
deployment_limits: No real-time or on-device deployment demonstrated; evaluation limited to speaker-dependent or seen-speaker scenarios.
scope_limits: Focuses on lip-to-speech synthesis from silent lip video in speaker-specific or seen-speaker conditions with no claimed generalization to unseen speaker or real-time applications.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: constrained (GRID-4S) and unconstrained (Lip2Wav, TCD-TIMIT-3S)
vocabulary_size: Lip2Wav speakers > 5000 words; GRID-4S limited to 51 words, TCD-TIMIT-3S includes 375 sentences per speaker.
metrics: STOI, ESTOI, WER, and Mean Opinion Score (MOS) evaluated on Lip2Wav, GRID-4S, and TCD-TIMIT-3S datasets; e.g., on TCD-TIMIT-3S STOI 0.596, ESTOI 0.452, WER 29.03; on Lip2Wav improvements in STOI/ESTOI up to 0.627/0.419
evaluation_mode: Objective (STOI, ESTOI, WER) and subjective (MOS) evaluations on standard benchmarks GRID-4S, TCD-TIMIT-3S, and Lip2Wav datasets, under speaker-dependent and constrained settings.

evidence.statement: We propose RobustL2S, a modularized framework for Lip-to-Speech synthesis that first maps self-supervised visual features to disentangled speech content representations, then converts these to waveforms with a vocoder.

RobustL2S explicitly separates the lip encoder extracting AV-HuBERT SSL representations, the non-autoregressive seq2seq mapping to speech HuBERT SSL representations, and the vocoder for waveform synthesis, moving away from direct mel-spectrogram regression.
On TCD-TIMIT-3S, RobustL2S achieves STOI 0.596, ESTOI 0.452, and WER 29.03; Lip2Wav speaker-dependent results improve STOI and ESTOI up to 0.627 and 0.419 respectively on Deep Learning speaker.
RobustL2S is evaluated on speaker-dependent settings on unconstrained Lip2Wav and constrained GRID-4S and TCD-TIMIT-3S datasets; no claim for real-time or speaker-independent evaluation is made.
The paper notes prosody remains limited due to speech SSL embeddings and strongest results remain speaker-specific; deployment is not addressed for real-time or mobile.

en.summary: SSL-feature target (M02) and Seq2Seq-to-unit-vocoder decoder (M06) are standard after ReVISE; GRID-4S WER 11.21% is set against baselines scored with other ASRs.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video)
en.vocabulary: GRID 51 words; TCD-TIMIT 375 sentences per speaker; Lip2Wav over 5000 words
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: STOI 0.596, ESTOI 0.452, WER 29.03 on TCD-TIMIT-3S
en.limitations: Speaker-dependent or seen-speaker evaluation only; limited prosody modeling; no real-time or on-device deployment.

title: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Tongue and Lip Articulation By Pseudo Target Generation and Domain Adversarial Training
expert_take_short: DTW pseudo targets (M02) follow prior EMG target transfer; the mode discriminator (M03) is untested by its ablation; silent MCD/STOI use self-made references and 18 speakers are dropped.
expert_take_long: The paper [@zheng2023pseudo] changes the silent training target (M02) and adds joint silent-vocalized training with a speaking-mode discriminator (M03); both are standard. DTW transfer of vocalized targets to silent articulation was established for silent EMG [@janke2017emg], with realignment by the partially trained model [@gaddy2020digital]; neither is cited. The read priors aim domain-adversarial training at speakers or sessions [@wand2017lipreading; @wand2018session], so the speaking-mode label is new, but its single-run ablation drops the vocalized loss with the discriminator. Silent MCD and STOI are scored against the method's own vocoded pseudo targets, and 18 of 81 speakers were dropped from the silent test by the same DTW cost (Sec. 4.2). The silent WER gain (59.960% to 43.114%, Table 1) is relatively smaller than the vocalized gain (28% against 36%); the absolute silent-vocalized gap narrows by 7.3 points, but the ratio widens from 2.2 to 2.5 (inference).
expert_true_value: Brings DTW target transfer from paired vocalized recordings, known from silent EMG, to ultrasound tongue and lip video on TaL, with alignment in encoder space, DTW-cost sample selection and a speaking-mode discriminator; the discriminator's own effect is not isolated.
canon_before: Silent EMG-to-speech trained on targets transferred from the paired vocalized take by DTW (Janke and Diener 2017; Gaddy and Klein 2020, with periodic realignment by the partially trained model and pooled vocalized data). On TaL, recognizers trained on modal speech were adapted to silent speech with fMLLR and unsupervised adaptation (Ribeiro et al. 2021); TaLNet reconstructed speech from vocalized articulation only.
delta_from_canon: Aligns TaLNet encoder outputs of silent and vocalized takes by DTW to make silent pseudo targets (M02), keeps only low-cost samples, regenerates targets in three rounds, and trains jointly on both modes with a gradient-reversal speaking-mode discriminator (M03).
position_in_field: Standard on both changed components: the pseudo-target recipe and its realignment predate it in EMG and are uncited; the speaking-mode domain label is new against the read priors (speakers, sessions), but its ablation also drops the vocalized loss. Silent WER 43.114% against 59.960% for TaLNet on retained speakers.
practical_value: A training recipe for silent ultrasound-plus-lip speech reconstruction when paired silent and vocalized takes exist; silent output remains far less intelligible than vocalized output (43.114% against 17.309% WER).
axes_moved: silent-mode WER and MOS over TaLNet on TaL (retained speakers); vocalized-mode WER over TaLNet
axes_unresolved: effect of the discriminator alone; encoder-space against feature-space alignment; generalization to unseen speakers; the 18 excluded speakers; run-to-run variance
technical_limits: Needs paired silent and vocalized recordings of the same prompts; DTW-cost thresholds set heuristically; speakers whose alignments all fail get no silent supervision.
evaluation_limits: Silent MCD and STOI use vocoded pseudo targets as reference; 18 of 81 speakers excluded from the silent test by the method's DTW cost; utterance-level split with shared speakers; single runs without seeds; unspecified commercial ASR configuration.
deployment_limits: Offline corpus study; no latency, runtime or hardware figures; ultrasound and lip cameras required.
scope_limits: Speech reconstruction from ultrasound tongue images and lip video on the TaL corpus in silent and vocalized modes.
input_modality: ultrasound tongue imaging; optical lip video
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound tongue imaging system; optical lip video camera
metrics: Silent (Table 1): MCD 3.935 dB, STOI 0.517, WER 43.114%, MOS 3.330 against TaLNet 4.423, 0.432, 59.960%, 2.990. Vocalized: WER 17.309% against 26.890%. Silent MCD/STOI are against vocoded pseudo targets.
evaluation_mode: Offline; objective MCD, STOI and iFLYTEK ASR WER plus 5-point MOS (21 raters per mode); ablations without iterative training and without domain-adversarial training.

evidence.statement: The paper proposes pseudo target generation using DTW alignment between vocalized and silent articulations, domain adversarial training to learn robust domain-invariant articulatory representations, and iterative training strategy to improve speech reconstruction from silent tongue and lip articulation.

The paper combines dynamic time warping-based pseudo target generation, domain adversarial training, and iterative retraining tailored for silent articulatory-to-acoustic conversion from multimodal tongue ultrasound and lip video input, addressing domain mismatch and lack of paired acoustic targets for silent speech reconstruction.
In silent mode the paper reports MCD 3.935 dB, STOI 0.517, WER 43.114%, and MOS 3.330, improving on TaLNet by about 15 WER points and 0.34 MOS; in vocalized mode WER reduces from 26.890% to 17.309%.

The evaluation is performed on the TaL corpus containing synchronized audio, ultrasound tongue images, and lip videos in vocalized and silent speaking modes from 81 native English speakers, with 1212 paired utterances, in a speaker-independent setting.

Silent-mode speech reconstruction performance remains worse than vocalized mode, and some speakers with unreliable silent articulations are excluded; specialized ultrasound and optical lip video hardware constrain deployment.

en.summary: DTW pseudo targets (M02) follow prior EMG target transfer; the mode discriminator (M03) is untested by its ablation; silent MCD/STOI use self-made references and 18 speakers are dropped.
en.sensor: Ultrasound tongue imaging plus optical lip camera
en.speaker: 81 TaL speakers; utterance-level split, so test speakers also appear in training; 18 speakers dropped from the silent test
en.key_result: Silent mode on retained speakers: WER 43.114% vs 59.960% for TaLNet (iFLYTEK ASR), MOS 3.330 vs 2.990; vocalized WER 17.309% vs 26.890%
en.limitations: Silent MCD/STOI scored against the method's own vocoded pseudo targets; 18 of 81 speakers excluded by the method's DTW cost; the w/o DAT ablation also removes vocalized training; single runs, no seeds; prior DTW target transfer in EMG uncited.

title: Ultrasensitive Textile Strain Sensors Redefine Wearable Silent Speech Interfaces with High Machine Learning Efficiency
expert_take_short: Standard sensor (M05) and decoder (M06): one throat strain channel, small CNN. 95.25% on 20 words, with split grouping and production mode unstated, does not show silent, session-independent decoding.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the sensor (M05), a single graphene-textile strain channel in a throat choker, and the decoder (M06), a compact 1D CNN with recorded-noise augmentation; both are standard, since the same group had already decoded words from a single graphene strain gauge on the throat and CNNs are common closed-vocabulary classifiers. The claim that sensor sensitivity is what lets one channel and a small network reach 95.25% is untested: no lower-sensitivity sensor, channel or augmentation ablation is run on the same words. The evaluation (M12) leaves the split grouping unstated, pools three participants and reports no chance level or repeated runs, so the accuracies do not show session- or speaker-independent decoding. The paper never states whether the words were mouthed or voiced (M04).
expert_true_value: One graphene-textile strain channel in a throat choker plus a small 1D CNN classify 5 to 20 isolated words at 93-96%; sensor sensitivity is not shown to cause the accuracy, and split grouping and production mode are unstated.
canon_before: The same group had already classified 15 words at 54.6% from a single graphene strain gauge on the throat (one subject, one sitting); facial strain-gauge arrays reached 87.53% on 100 words with eight channels, with accuracy rising with channel count.
delta_from_canon: Changes the sensor fabrication (graphene on textile with ordered cracks, gauge factor 317 within 5% strain) and uses a compact 1D CNN with recorded-noise augmentation; the channel count and placement are unchanged from the group's earlier throat sensor.
position_in_field: Standard on sensor (M05) and decoder (M06); split grouping not reported (M12, where speaker-disjoint tests are the most common pattern); production mode not reported (M04).
practical_value: A comfortable throat sensor for closed-set word input; evidence for silent, session-independent use is still missing.
axes_moved: sensor fabrication: textile graphene with ordered cracks; decoder size: 0.09 GFLOPs per inference
axes_unresolved: mouthed versus voiced production; session- and speaker-disjoint tests; chance level and repeated runs; sensor, channel and augmentation ablations; on-device latency and power
technical_limits: Single strain channel; 3-s fixed word windows; no ablation separating sensor sensitivity, augmentation and network design.
evaluation_limits: Per-word 80/20 split of 100 samples with session grouping unstated; three participants pooled; no chance level, seeds or repeated runs; few-shot test sets undescribed; efficiency compared across papers with different vocabularies and protocols.
deployment_limits: Offline; potentiostat readout; no on-device latency or power; production mode (mouthed or voiced) not stated.
scope_limits: Closed sets of 5 to 20 isolated English words from three participants plus one transfer participant.
input_modality: throat skin strain (single channel)
sensor_hardware: Graphene-coated textile strain sensor with ordered microcracks integrated into a throat choker worn around the neck.
vocabulary_type: Closed-set isolated words
vocabulary_size: 20 frequent words; 10 confusable words; 5 long words at three reading speeds
metrics: Accuracy 95.25% (20 words), 93% (10 confusable words), 96% (5 long words); few-shot 80% with 15-20 and 90% with 30 samples per class; 0.09 GFLOPs per inference.
evaluation_mode: Offline word classification on a per-word 80/20 split; few-shot fine-tuning to one new user (5 words) and ten new words.

evidence.statement: The authors report a graphene-textile strain sensor in a throat choker that withstands over 10,000 stretch-release cycles at 1.5% strain (Sec. II, Fig. 2i).

The authors report a gauge factor of 317 within 5% strain and a 420% gain over textile strain sensors for motion and health monitoring (Fig. 1c, References 33-47); the link from this sensitivity to word accuracy is not tested.
Three closed word sets from three participants, 100 samples per word split 80/20 with session grouping unstated; few-shot transfer to one new user (5 words) and ten new words (Sec. II).
Accuracy is 95.25% on 20 words, 93% on 10 confusable words and 96% on 5 long words; few-shot transfer reaches 80% with 15-20 and 90% with 30 samples per class (Sec. II, Fig. 4-5).
Three participants, closed sets of 5 to 20 isolated words, no chance level or repeated runs, and no statement of whether words were mouthed or voiced.
The authors frame the system as real-time and energy-efficient; only FLOPs per inference are reported, with no on-device latency or power (Supplementary Table 1).

en.summary: Standard sensor (M05) and decoder (M06): one throat strain channel, small CNN. 95.25% on 20 words, with split grouping and production mode unstated, does not show silent, session-independent decoding.
en.sensor: One graphene-on-textile strain sensor with ordered microcracks in a throat choker; potentiostat readout at 1 V, 500 Hz
en.task: Isolated word classification from 3-s single-channel strain windows with a 1D residual CNN
en.vocabulary: 20 frequent English words; 10 confusable words; 5 long words at three reading speeds
en.speaker: Three participants pooled; one further participant for few-shot transfer
en.session: Not stated; 100 samples per word split 80/20 without stated session grouping
en.mode: Offline; production mode (mouthed or voiced) not stated
en.key_result: 95.25% on 20 words, 93% on 10 confusable words, 96% on 5 long words; 80% with 15-20 and 90% with 30 fine-tuning samples per class on a new user or new words.
en.limitations: Split grouping, chance level and repeated runs not reported; production mode not stated; no sensor, channel or augmentation ablation; no on-device latency or power.

title: WESPER: Zero-shot and Realtime Whisper to Normal Voice Conversion for Whisper-based Speech Interactions
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23)
expert_take_short: WESPER trains a whisper-to-normal converter with no paired data (M02, ahead); its unit route (M06) is untested against baselines, and its ASR gain trails a recognizer fine-tuned on labelled whisper.
expert_take_long: WESPER [@rekimoto2023wesper] changes two components: training without paired recordings (M02), which is ahead, and conversion through self-supervised units (M06), which is standard because it is never compared with a spectral or paired baseline. Later work also trains on synthetic whisper without real pairs [@ritter2026floww2n]. The speech-recognition claim is the weakest: conversion lowers cloud-ASR WER from 44.70% to 26.68% on an unstated wTIMIT subset that pretraining also used, while its own Table 2 gives 13.75% without conversion for a HuBERT recognizer fine-tuned on labelled wTIMIT speech. "Zero-shot" covers the input speaker only, since each target voice needs 26 hours of decoder training time, and "realtime" is an utterance-level processing ratio without latency (M13). The disorder results rest on five and four speakers, one sentence each, rated for quality rather than intelligibility.
expert_true_value: The practical contribution is a low-friction whispered-speech conversion stack that can run in real time without per-user paired corpora.
canon_before: Whisper-to-normal conversion typically required paired whisper-normal corpora or speaker-dependent training, making discreet speech interfaces hard to deploy.
delta_from_canon: WESPER removes the paired-data requirement by learning common speech units from unpaired whisper and normal speech.
position_in_field: A strong adjacent paper on discreet speech interaction, but it sits next to SSI rather than inside fully silent speech.
practical_value: Useful for privacy-preserving whispered interaction and accessibility, especially when a standard microphone is preferred over special sensors.
axes_moved: discreet_speech; real_time_conversion; speaker_independent_conversion
axes_unresolved: Full-silence interaction and broader real-world robustness remain unresolved.
technical_limits: The method still depends on whispered speech rather than truly silent articulation.
evaluation_limits: The core evidence is on whispered conversion datasets and listening studies, not on silent-speech benchmarks.
deployment_limits: Although real time is shown, the paper does not establish a full silent interface or broad public-use robustness.
scope_limits: Whisper-to-normal conversion only; this is not fully silent speech.
input_modality: whispered speech from an ordinary microphone
sensor_hardware: ordinary microphone
metrics: On wTIMIT whispers, Google ASR reports WER 44.70 and CER 28.38, while WESPER-converted whispers improve to WER 26.68 and CER 12.70; the HuBERT-base setup pretrained on Librispeech+wTIMIT reaches WER 13.75 and CER 5.47.
evaluation_mode: MOS, MUSHRA, and speech-recognition evaluation on whispered and converted speech

evidence.statement: The abstract says WESPER is a zero-shot real-time whisper-to-normal conversion mechanism built from a speech-to-unit encoder and a unit-to-speech decoder.
The introduction states that the encoder and decoder operate in a non-autoregressive manner so the entire system works in real time and does not need per-user training.

Table 2 shows Google ASR on whispered wTIMIT at WER 44.70/CER 28.38, while WESPER-converted whispers improve to WER 26.68/CER 12.70; the HuBERT-base setup pretrained on Librispeech+wTIMIT reaches WER 13.75/CER 5.47.

The introduction explicitly motivates the work with whispered speech, not fully silent articulation, because ordinary microphones can capture whispers whereas silent speech systems often need special sensors.

en.summary: WESPER trains a whisper-to-normal converter with no paired data (M02, ahead); its unit route (M06) is untested against baselines, and its ASR gain trails a recognizer fine-tuned on labelled whisper.
en.sensor: Ordinary microphone (whispered speech)
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: WER 44.70 to 26.68 (CER 28.38 to 12.70) on wTIMIT whispers, Google ASR
en.limitations: Relies on whispered rather than truly silent speech and is evaluated on whisper datasets, not silent-speech benchmarks or broad public use.

title: Zero-Shot Personalized Lip-to-Speech Synthesis with Face Image Based Voice Control
expert_take_short: Face-image voice control (M07) and VAE/cross-modal training (M03) are standard: Facetron did face-derived zero-shot voice on GRID in 2021; face EER 36.72 vs 26.57 with reference audio; no WER.
expert_take_long: The paper [@sheng2023zeroshot] changes two components: a face embedding instead of reference audio sets the voice at use time (M07), and training separates content from identity with a VAE prior and teaches the face encoder from a speech speaker encoder (M03). Both are standard. Facetron already predicted speaker features from face images with an encoder trained by cosine similarity to a pre-trained prosody embedding, tested on held-out GRID speakers [@um2021facetron]; it is not cited, so the "first attempt" claim (Abstract) fails. The face route trails the audio route it replaces: unseen-speaker EER 36.72 against 26.57 (Table 1), 38% higher (inference). The ablations do support both training pieces. No ASR word error is reported, though Table 2's baselines have published word error on that split [@kefalas2023large], and Table 2 scores the reference-speech model, not the zero-shot one.
expert_true_value: Shows on 13 unseen GRID speakers that a face embedding trained against a speech speaker encoder, plus a VAE prior on the video content code, gives listeners a face-voice match close to the reference-speech variant (MOS-FVM 3.133 vs 3.172), while automatic speaker similarity stays well behind (EER 36.72 vs 26.57).
canon_before: Multi-speaker lip-to-speech usually takes the voice from a reference-audio speaker embedding (VCVTS and others). Facetron (2021) already predicted speaker features from face images with an encoder trained by cosine similarity to a pre-trained speech embedding and tested held-out GRID speakers. Identity removal from GRID video encoders used adversarial losses (Wand and Schmidhuber 2017; Oneata et al. 2021).
delta_from_canon: A speaker-verification encoder, not a prosody encoder, teaches the face encoder, with added gender-contrastive and face-classification losses; a VAE KL prior replaces the adversary for content/identity separation; the evaluation adds EER and a face-voice match MOS on 13 unseen speakers.
position_in_field: Standard on use-time speaker information (M07) and on training (M03): face-derived zero-shot voice and identity removal on GRID video both predate it. Griffin-Lim waveform generation (M06) trails the field's neural vocoders. Evaluation (M12) omits ASR word error, which the baselines it lists report on the same split.
practical_value: A research demonstration that a face photo can set the gender and part of the voice of lip-to-speech output when no recording of the speaker exists; intelligibility of the zero-shot output is not measured.
axes_moved: Identity-level evaluation (EER, face-voice match MOS) of face-controlled voice on 13 unseen GRID speakers; ablations showing the VAE prior and cross-modal losses lower unseen-speaker EER.
axes_unresolved: Word error of the zero-shot output, open vocabulary and in-the-wild video, comparison with Facetron and with gradient reversal, run-to-run variance, overlap of GRID speakers with the identity-encoder pretraining data.
axes_regressed: Seen-speaker naturalness drops with the VAE (MOS-SN 3.049 vs 3.246); face control trails reference speech on EER (36.72 vs 26.57).
technical_limits: Face identity carries mostly gender and only part of the voice; Griffin-Lim caps quality (ground truth through Griffin-Lim PESQ 3.293); speaker-independence of the content code shown only by t-SNE.
evaluation_limits: GRID only (six-word grammar); no ASR WER; Table 2 compares only the reference-speech variant on a separate 15/8/10 split with values taken from earlier papers; runs and seeds not stated; EER backend, trials and objective-test counts not stated; MOS from 20 sentences and 20 listeners.
deployment_limits: Offline research system; needs a frontal first frame and a lip crop; no runtime, model size or robustness tests.
scope_limits: Read: arXiv:2305.14359 v1, all sections, Tables 1-2, Figs. 1-2. Overt GRID speech video with the audio removed, not silent articulation.
input_modality: video (lip-centered frames) plus face image
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: sentence-level utterances constrained by GRID grammar
vocabulary_size: Constrained GRID grammar with 6-word utterances
metrics: STOI, ESTOI, PESQ for intelligibility and quality; Equal Error Rate (EER) for speaker similarity; Mean Opinion Score for Speech Naturalness (MOS-SN); Mean Opinion Score for Face-Voice Matching (MOS-FVM) for identity consistency
evaluation_mode: Objective intelligibility and quality metrics (STOI, ESTOI, PESQ), speaker similarity (EER), and subjective mean opinion scores (MOS-SN for naturalness, MOS-FVM for face-voice matching) on Mechanical Turk ratings.

evidence.statement: In this paper, we propose a zero-shot personalized Lip2Speech synthesis method, in which face images control speaker identities.

We present a method of associated voice-face representation learning that transfers knowledge from a speech identity encoder to a face identity encoder, enabling face images to control voice characteristics in Lip2Speech synthesis without requiring reference speech.

Experiments were conducted on the GRID dataset consisting of 33 speakers with constrained vocabulary utterances. Training used 20 speakers (10 female + 10 male), with 13 speakers held out for unseen testing.

Evaluation uses objective metrics STOI, ESTOI, PESQ for intelligibility and naturalness assessment; EER for speaker similarity; and subjective MOS-SN for naturalness and MOS-FVM for face-voice matching to assess identity matching.

The method is limited to the GRID dataset constrained vocabulary setting; synthesis speech quality is below ground truth and seen-speaker upper bound, and is not tested on open vocabulary or in-the-wild video conditions.
Zero-shot personalized Lip2Speech can be achieved from face images without enrollment speech at inference, enabling new assistive applications where speech is unavailable as reference.

The system uses a VAE structure to disentangle speaker identity and linguistic content in video, enabling control of voice characteristics through concatenation of face-based speaker embeddings and latent content codes for decoding speech.

Face identity encoder is trained by multi-losses (cosine similarity, gender contrastive, cross-entropy) to produce face embeddings aligned with speech identity embeddings for voice control at inference stage.
Evaluation is conducted with seen and unseen speakers from GRID; subjective tests with MOS-SN and MOS-FVM on Amazon Mechanical Turk with 20 listeners over 20 randomly selected sentences.

Table 1 (unseen speakers): reference-speech control gives EER 26.57 and face control 36.72, with MOS-FVM 3.172 and 3.133 and ESTOI 0.407 and 0.389; face control trails on automatic speaker similarity while listeners rate the face-voice match close.
Proposed-VAE variant sometimes produces incorrect speaker gender voice, indicating challenges in disentangling speaker identity in the latent space effectively.
MOS-FVM rates how well the synthesized voice matches the face on a 1-5 scale (20 listeners, 20 sentences); Facetron had tested only gender recognition for unseen speakers.

en.summary: Face-image voice control (M07) and VAE/cross-modal training (M03) are standard: Facetron did face-derived zero-shot voice on GRID in 2021; face EER 36.72 vs 26.57 with reference audio; no WER.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video plus face image)
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: Unseen GRID speakers (13): face-image control EER 36.72 vs 26.57 with reference speech, MOS-FVM 3.133 vs 3.172; ESTOI 0.389; no ASR word error reported.
en.limitations: Face-derived zero-shot voice predates it (Facetron 2021); no WER; Table 2 scores the reference-speech variant; Griffin-Lim waveform; GRID only, no seeds; overlap of GRID with pretraining identities not stated.

title: FastLTS: Non-Autoregressive End-to-End Unconstrained Lip-to-Speech Synthesis
venue: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '22)
expert_take_short: Parallel decoder, learned-feature GAN generator and transformer front end (M06) are standard; 9.14x mel speedup is real, but evaluation (M12) drops the STOI/ESTOI its Lip2Wav baseline reported.
expert_take_long: FastLTS [@wang2022fastlts] changes the decoding path (M06): a parallel acoustic decoder, a GAN generator on learned features, and a transformer front end. All three are standard: direct waveform generation predates it [@mira2021endtoend], and so does a transformer visual front end for lip reading [@prajwal2021vtp]. The non-autoregressive effect is the 9.14× mel-level speedup; the 19.76× waveform figure the abstract headlines mostly reflects replacing Griffin-Lim, as §5.5 itself notes, and no parallel mel-plus-vocoder system is timed. Evaluation (M12) is standard but narrower than its baseline's protocol: it drops the STOI/ESTOI/PESQ that Lip2Wav reported on the same three speakers [@prajwal2020learning].
expert_true_value: The full text supports a real systems gain: FastLTS keeps competitive perceptual quality while pushing waveform inference to 19.76x the autoregressive baseline at 3-second input length.
canon_before: Unconstrained lip-to-speech systems typically predicted mel-spectrograms first and then relied on slow autoregressive or heavy flow-based waveform generation.
delta_from_canon: FastLTS removes the intermediate spectrogram bottleneck from the main inference path and uses a fully parallelized decoder plus GAN vocoder.
position_in_field: Strong unconstrained lip-to-speech systems paper centered on latency reduction rather than a new sensing modality.
practical_value: Useful when lip-to-speech quality matters but the older autoregressive waveform stack is too slow for interactive use.
axes_moved: system design; model efficiency; evaluation
axes_unresolved: live deployment; robustness to unconstrained capture artifacts; broader speaker coverage
technical_limits: Evidence is still limited to benchmark corpora with offline generation windows and three evaluated speakers per dataset slice.
evaluation_limits: The main quality evidence is subjective MOS plus GRID PESQ; there is no in-the-wild user study or end-to-end conversational latency test.
deployment_limits: The paper supports lower-latency generation, but not a live camera-to-audio interactive deployment.
scope_limits: Unconstrained lip-to-speech synthesis from face video only.
input_modality: silent talking-face video
vocabulary_type: large-vocabulary unconstrained speech
vocabulary_size: Lip2Wav: 5000+ words; GRID: 51 words
metrics: MOS quality/intelligibility/naturalness; PESQ; waveform acceleration ratio; parameter count
evaluation_mode: subjective MOS on Lip2Wav and GRID, PESQ on GRID, plus mel and waveform inference-speed comparison

evidence.statement: The abstract presents FastLTS as an end-to-end non-autoregressive lip-to-speech model that directly generates waveform audio from unconstrained talking-face video with low latency.
Section 5.1 states that experiments use the Lip2Wav corpus with 5 speakers but evaluate on 3 speakers, and also test adaptation on 3 speakers from the constrained GRID dataset.
On GRID, FastLTS reports MOS 3.59 for quality, 3.68 for intelligibility, and 3.73 for naturalness, versus 3.27, 3.47, and 3.54 for Lip2Wav.
Section 5.5 reports that waveform synthesis reaches a 19.76x acceleration ratio at 3-second input length.

en.summary: Parallel decoder, learned-feature GAN generator and transformer front end (M06) are standard; 9.14x mel speedup is real, but evaluation (M12) drops the STOI/ESTOI its Lip2Wav baseline reported.
en.sensor: Silent talking-face video
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent: 3 Lip2Wav speakers, 3 unnamed GRID speakers
en.key_result: MOS above Lip2Wav on most Lip2Wav rows; GRID PESQ 1.939; 9.14x mel-level speedup over Lip2Wav at 3 s
en.limitations: Benchmark corpora only with three speakers per dataset slice; no in-the-wild user study or live camera-to-audio latency test.

title: Improved Processing of Ultrasound Tongue Videos by Combining ConvLSTM and 3D Convolutional Networks
expert_take_short: ConvLSTM top layer (M06) is standard: new to ultrasound-to-speech, but a 2.1% MSE edge over BiLSTM, one speaker, one run; later work dropped it. No MCD or listener test (M12 behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@shandiz2022improved] changes one component (M06): a unidirectional ConvLSTM replaces the top layers of its group's 3D-CNN ultrasound front end, and test MSE on 80 standardized mel targets falls from 0.293 (3D-CNN) and 0.282 (3D-CNN + BiLSTM) to 0.276, 5.8% and 2.1% relative (inference). M06 is standard: the layer is new to ultrasound-to-speech mapping (9 ConvLSTM pattern matches among 148 ultrasound studies, none an earlier speech-output study; Appendix), but the edge over the BiLSTM is one run on one speaker, with dropout raised from 0.3 to 0.35 and pooling changed alongside (Table 1). Later work dropped it [@toth2023adaptation; @sonkar2026tongue2speech]. Evaluation (M12) is behind the best comparable work, not the field's typical practice: MSE and mean R² only, although the group's listener-tested studies of this speaker and of the same WaveGlow synthesis stage [@csapo2017dnn; @grosz2018f0; @csapo2020waveglow] predate it. "Smaller and faster" (Abstract) is unmeasured.
expert_true_value: A ConvLSTM layer, new to ultrasound-to-speech mapping in the ledger tallies: one unidirectional ConvLSTM on top of a 3D-CNN front end lowers test MSE of 80 standardized mel targets from 0.293 (3D-CNN) and 0.282 (3D-CNN + BiLSTM) to 0.276 for one speaker, single runs; later work did not adopt it.
canon_before: Ultrasound-to-speech mapping was mostly frame-wise DNN or CNN regression; the same group had introduced a (2+1)D 3D-CNN over a 25-frame window (2020), and CNN+LSTM models existed. ConvLSTM had been used on ultrasound only for image prediction (tongue motion; lip-to-ultrasound reconstruction), not for speech output.
delta_from_canon: Replaces the top Conv3D and dense layers of the 3D-CNN with one unidirectional ConvLSTM that fuses the 5 time steps of the front end; dropout and pooling change at the same time, and no parameter count is reported.
position_in_field: Standard on the processing component (M06): a new layer type for this task, but a 2.1% relative MSE edge over a BiLSTM top layer from one speaker and one run; the group's 2023 work returned to the plain 3D-CNN and the 2026 state of the art (Tongue2Speech, 3D front end plus Transformer, 15.93% WER on TaL1) tests no ConvLSTM. Behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12): MSE and R2 only, while the group's earlier mel-plus-WaveGlow study ran a MUSHRA test.
practical_value: Shows that a single ConvLSTM can replace a BiLSTM as the temporal fusion layer of a 3D-CNN ultrasound front end without loss on one speaker; it gives no evidence on intelligibility, model size or speed.
axes_moved: temporal fusion layer on top of a 3D-convolution ultrasound front end (ConvLSTM)
axes_unresolved: matched comparison of fusion layers at equal dropout and pooling; repetition over seeds, sessions and speakers; intelligibility of the WaveGlow output; parameter count and training time; silent articulation
technical_limits: The ConvLSTM fuses only 5 time steps; the hybrid also changes dropout (0.35 vs 0.3) and pooling; Sec. 2 claims fewer parameters while Sec. 5 says ConvLSTM has many more trainable parameters than Conv3D; window look-ahead not stated.
evaluation_limits: MSE and mean R2 of standardized mel targets on 87 test sentences of one speaker; single runs without seeds or variance; no MCD, listening test or ASR on the WaveGlow output; no 2D-CNN+LSTM row despite the introduction.
deployment_limits: Voiced read speech only; no silent articulation, latency, causal variant, training-time or parameter measurement.
scope_limits: Offline, speaker-dependent regression of mel-spectrograms from ultrasound tongue video of one Hungarian speaker.
task: Speech reconstruction from ultrasound tongue video sequences
input_modality: Ultrasound tongue video sequences (82 fps) synchronized with audio (11,025 Hz)
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound tongue imaging probe (Micro system by Articulate Instruments) with stabilizing headset; Audio-Technica ATR 3350 microphone
output_type: Speech audio spectra reconstructed via mel-spectrogram regression followed by WaveGlow vocoder synthesis
metrics: MSE and mean R2 of 80 standardized mel targets: test MSE 0.293 (3D-CNN), 0.282 (3D-CNN + BiLSTM), 0.276 (3D-CNN + ConvLSTM); mean R2 0.710, 0.721, 0.73. Table 3 layer orders: test MSE 0.27 to 0.35.
evaluation_mode: Offline, one speaker, fixed 310/41/87 sentence split; single runs; selection partition not stated.

evidence.statement: The abstract states that the 3D-CNN + ConvLSTM hybrid is slightly faster, smaller and more accurate than the earlier 3D-CNN model.
Table 2: test MSE 0.293 (3D-CNN), 0.282 (3D-CNN + BiLSTM), 0.276 (3D-CNN + ConvLSTM); mean R2 0.710, 0.721, 0.73.
One Hungarian female speaker reading aloud, 438 sentences split 310/41/87; no seeds, run counts or variance reported.
The ConvLSTM layer has many more trainable parameters than Conv3D, so its filter size was reduced; the bidirectional variant was dropped for its parameter cost; many configurations remain untested.

en.summary: ConvLSTM top layer (M06) is standard: new to ultrasound-to-speech, but a 2.1% MSE edge over BiLSTM, one speaker, one run; later work dropped it. No MCD or listener test (M12 behind).
en.sensor: Micro ultrasound tongue probe with headset, plus microphone
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: MSE ~0.276, mean R2 ~0.73 on mel-spectrogram regression
en.limitations: Single-speaker dataset with no perceptual intelligibility testing, cross-speaker evaluation, or real-time tests.

title: Lip-to-Speech Synthesis for Arbitrary Speakers in the Wild
venue: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '22)
expert_take_short: VAE-GAN lip-to-speech with a reference-audio voice: a standard design whose gains are in distribution and sync metrics; no WER is reported, behind its own lineage on evaluation.
expert_take_long: The paper [@hegde2022lip] changes the training target (M02, frozen ASR-encoder content), the decoder (M06, VAE latent with adversarial critic) and voice control (M08, reference-audio embedding); each is standard. Its in-the-wild claim rests on distribution and sync metrics and a listener test on 15 LRS2 samples (Sec. 4.3), without the word error rate its own lineage reported [@prajwal2020learning] (M12, behind on protocol). On LRS2 it beats the authors' sequence-to-sequence baseline on FDSD and sync (LSE-C 2.507 against 1.991) but not on PESQ and STOI (Table 3); content is unmeasured. In the same group's [later], harder test (10 LRS3 sentences of 10 s or longer), its intelligibility is rated 1.07 of 5 against 3.49 for their successor [@hegde2023towards]. SED is not shown to be independent of the voice loss's identity network (Sec. 3.2.7, 4.1.2), and the test-time voice reference is not stated (Sec. 3.2.4). The claim to be the first to handle ambiguity explicitly (Sec. 1) omits an earlier variational-autoencoder model sharing an author [@yadav2021speech] (Appendix).
expert_true_value: A speaker-general VAE-GAN lip-to-speech system; its gains are in distribution and sync metrics, while PESQ and STOI fall below a plain L1 sequence-to-sequence baseline and content is unmeasured (no word error rate).
canon_before: Most lip-to-speech systems were either single-speaker, constrained-lab models or needed much more per-speaker data to work at all.
delta_from_canon: This paper pushes the task toward arbitrary identities in the wild and argues that distributional modeling plus speaker conditioning is necessary.
position_in_field: Strong speaker-general lip-to-speech paper focused on unconstrained identity and vocabulary conditions.
practical_value: Useful when collecting tens of hours per target speaker is unrealistic and the system must generalize across identities.
axes_moved: speaker generalization; problem framing; evaluation
axes_unresolved: robustness to head pose; language modeling; live deployment
technical_limits: The model still struggles with severe head movement, non-frontal heads, and language-level ambiguity that lip motion alone cannot resolve.
evaluation_limits: The unconstrained evidence is benchmark-based and the human study uses 15 LRS2 samples rated by 20 participants, not a deployment scenario.
deployment_limits: No live product path, robustness-to-camera-noise study, or interactive latency measurement is reported.
scope_limits: Arbitrary-speaker lip-to-speech synthesis from silent video, with the voice set by a reference-audio embedding.
input_modality: silent lip video
vocabulary_type: open vocabulary in the wild
vocabulary_size: LRW: 500 words; LRS2: 59k vocabulary
metrics: PESQ; STOI; SED; FDSD; KDSD; LSE-C; LSE-D; human ratings; fine-tuning data-efficiency curves
evaluation_mode: constrained GRID/TCD-TIMIT benchmarks, unconstrained LRW/LRS2 comparison, human evaluation, and low-data fine-tuning study

evidence.statement: The abstract says the model generates speech from silent lip videos for arbitrary speakers in the wild and is not restricted to a fixed number of speakers.
Section 3.3.1 says unconstrained evaluation is built on LRW and the full LRS2 train plus pre-train data, with LRS2 covering thousands of speakers and about 59k vocabulary.
Table 3 reports the proposed model at 1.273 FDSD, 0.2 KDSD, 2.507 LSE-C, and 8.155 LSE-D on LRS2, outperforming the compared lip-to-speech baselines there.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3: All models are pre-trained on LRW dataset and then trained on LRS2.

evidence.statement: The limitations section says the model still struggles with drastic head movement, non-frontal heads, and outputs that do not form the right words or phrases.

en.summary: VAE-GAN lip-to-speech with a reference-audio voice: a standard design whose gains are in distribution and sync metrics; no WER is reported, behind its own lineage on evaluation.
en.sensor: Silent lip/face video plus a one-second reference-audio clip for the voice
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: LRS2 FDSD 1.273 (lip-to-text plus TTS 0.984) and LSE-C 2.507; PESQ/STOI 0.60/0.34, below the sequence-to-sequence baseline (0.97/0.43); no WER reported
en.limitations: No word error rate on the output; listener test on 15 LRS2 samples; voice reference source at test not stated; SED not shown to be independent of the voice-loss identity network; single runs; struggles with non-frontal faces and produces wrong words.

title: Movement Detection of Tongue and Related Body Parts Using IR-UWB Radar
expert_take_short: Chin-aimed radar and an envelope + GMM-HMM front end are standard; the binary rest-vs-touch task shows some closed-mouth movement, not tongue-specific sensing.
expert_take_long: The paper changes radar placement (M05, chin instead of mouth) and the front end (M06, RMS envelope into GMM-HMMs); both are standard. The chin placement is rare but untested against a mouth-facing radar, and the authors' later two-radar study found the chin-facing radar worse, with it placed farther away. The envelope beats CLEAN for all four participants, but feature and classifier change together. A binary rest-versus-palate-touch task with co-moving throat muscles shows detection of closed-mouth movement, not tongue-specific sensing; evaluation (M12) is within-participant leave-one-out on 40 trials for 4 participants, one an author.
expert_true_value: A chin-aimed contactless IR-UWB radar separates closed-mouth rest from a tongue-tip palate touch at 90-100% per participant (4 participants, within-participant leave-one-out); the signal is not shown to be tongue-specific.
canon_before: Contactless IR-UWB radar aimed at the lips and jaw had classified silent vowels and words with CLEAN features and MD-DTW (2016); radar speech studies pointed the radar at the face or mouth.
delta_from_canon: Aims the radar at the chin and replaces CLEAN + MD-DTW with an RMS-envelope feature into class-wise GMM-HMMs, on a binary rest versus palate-touch task.
position_in_field: Early contactless radar feasibility study on closed-mouth oral movement; placement and front end are standard for radar speech sensing, and the later two-radar study by the same group found the chin-facing radar worse than the lip-facing one.
practical_value: Shows that a chin-facing radar picks up closed-mouth movement in the laboratory; it does not show tongue-specific sensing or speech recognition.
axes_moved: chin-facing radar placement; envelope front end
axes_unresolved: tongue specificity; speech units; feature versus classifier attribution; speaker-independent testing
technical_limits: Only two states, four participants, manual trial boundaries, and a stationary lab setup are tested.
evaluation_limits: No continuous speech, no unseen-user split, and no vocabulary-level recognition are reported.
deployment_limits: The hardware is promising but far from a complete radar SSI system.
scope_limits: Binary tongue-motion detection only.
input_modality: IR-UWB radar pointed at the chin
sensor_hardware: IR-UWB radar module with LNA evaluation board, sinuous antennas, and dielectric lens
vocabulary_type: binary tongue-state classification
vocabulary_size: 2 classes
metrics: classification accuracy by participant
evaluation_mode: leave-one-out cross-validation against CLEAN+MD-DTW baselines on two tongue-motion states

evidence.statement: The abstract states that the study classifies motionless and moving states of an invisible tongue using an IR-UWB radar pointed toward the participant's chin.
Section A says the experiment uses four participants, two tongue-motion states, and twenty repetitions of each state per participant.
Section B explains that the proposed method turns radar frame sets into envelope features and classifies them with a five-state left-to-right GMM-HMM.
evidence.section_or_location: B. Feature Extraction and Classifier Selection

evidence.statement: Table I reports participant-wise classification accuracy of 100, 90, 90, and 90 percent for the proposed feature extraction plus GMM-HMM pipeline.

en.summary: Chin-aimed radar and an envelope + GMM-HMM front end are standard; the binary rest-vs-touch task shows some closed-mouth movement, not tongue-specific sensing.
en.sensor: IR-UWB radar with sinuous antennas and dielectric lens
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: >=90% accuracy per participant, 2 tongue states, 4 participants
en.limitations: Only two states, four participants, manual trial boundaries, stationary lab setup; no continuous speech, unseen-user, or vocabulary-level tests.

title: Multi-modality Associative Bridging through Memory: Speech Sound Recollected from Face Video
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
expert_take_short: Audio memory recall (M02) is ahead as a design, but the LRW state-of-the-art claim misses a prior 87.9% model, the edge over distillation is one run, and GRID gains are small.
expert_take_long: The paper [@kim2021multimodality] stores audio features in a memory during training and recalls them from video at test (M02), feeding them ahead of the backend (M06). The recall design is ahead: no earlier study among 54 on audio-to-video knowledge transfer records it (pattern match), and its gain over a no-memory baseline repeats on LRW and LRW-1000; its edge over distillation is one LRW run of 0.91 points. The LRW state-of-the-art claim fails: 85.41% is 2.5 points below an uncited earlier single model at 87.9% [@ma2021towards]; on public LRW-1000, 50.82% leads earlier models without word-boundary input by 2.8 points but not the 55.7% reached with boundaries [@feng2020learn]. Every headline number is the best memory size of an ablation, from one run. On GRID the objective lead over Lip2Wav is 0.007 STOI with no no-memory score in the main text, and the opinion-score jump comes from swapping in WaveNet.
expert_true_value: The full text supports that the memory bridge is doing real work on benchmarks: gains are modest on LRW but large on LRW-1000 and enough to edge prior methods on GRID reconstruction.
canon_before: Audio-visual fusion and common-representation methods usually needed both modalities at inference or failed when one modality was missing.
delta_from_canon: This paper claims that memory can preserve cross-modal associations so a visual-only downstream model can still borrow audio structure.
position_in_field: Interesting cross-modal architectural paper adjacent to lip reading and lip-to-speech reconstruction.
practical_value: Useful when paired audio-video data exists at training time and the goal is to improve visual-only inference with recalled audio structure.
axes_moved: cross-modal system design; benchmark quality
axes_unresolved: speaker-independent reconstruction; in-the-wild deployment; online use
technical_limits: The speech-reconstruction claim remains on speaker-dependent GRID, and the best subjective scores require an added WaveNet vocoder.
evaluation_limits: No live deployment, no uncontrolled capture conditions, and no speaker-independent reconstruction result are shown.
deployment_limits: The method needs paired audio-video supervision and benchmark-like preprocessing.
scope_limits: Benchmark lip reading and speech reconstruction from face video.
input_modality: silent face video with recalled audio memory during training
vocabulary_type: word-level lip reading plus fixed-phrase speech reconstruction
vocabulary_size: LRW/LRW-1000 word vocabularies and GRID phrase set
metrics: word accuracy; STOI; ESTOI; PESQ; human naturalness and intelligibility ratings
evaluation_mode: word-level lip-reading benchmarks on LRW/LRW-1000 plus speaker-dependent GRID speech reconstruction with objective and human evaluation

evidence.statement: The abstract says the paper introduces an audio-visual multimodal bridging framework that can exploit both modalities even when only unimodal input is available at inference.
Table 1 reports the proposed method at 85.4 word accuracy on LRW and 50.82 on LRW-1000, ahead of the listed prior methods on both datasets.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1. Lip reading word accuracy comparison with visual modal inputs on LRW and LRW-1000 dataset.

evidence.statement: Section 4.2.1 says the speech-reconstruction experiments use speaker-dependent GRID with subjects 1, 2, 4, and 29 following prior work.
Table 2 reports speaker-dependent GRID reconstruction scores of 0.738 STOI, 0.579 ESTOI, and 1.984 PESQ for the proposed method.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2. Performance of speech reconstruction comparison with visual modal inputs in a speaker-dependent setting on GRID.

en.summary: Audio memory recall (M02) is ahead as a design, but the LRW state-of-the-art claim misses a prior 87.9% model, the edge over distillation is one run, and GRID gains are small.
en.sensor: Silent face video
en.task: Lip reading and speech synthesis from video
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: LRW 85.41% (+1.27 over baseline, +0.91 over distillation), below a prior 87.9% single model; LRW-1000 50.82% (+5.89), 2.8 above the best prior model without word boundaries; GRID seen speakers STOI 0.738 vs 0.731 (Lip2Wav), no WER
en.limitations: Best memory size of an ablation, one run, with no stated validation rule; edge over distillation is one LRW run; LRW state-of-the-art claim misses a prior 87.9% model and the LRW-1000 lead holds only without word boundaries; no GRID no-memory score in the main text; GRID objective scores use Griffin-Lim and the MOS gain comes from WaveNet; no WER; offline only.

title: Sequence-to-Sequence Voice Reconstruction for Silent Speech in a Tonal Language
expert_take_short: Duration-regulated seq2seq with toneme loss voices silent Mandarin EMG; gains rest on the auxiliary loss, not the architecture, and prompt grouping in the utterance split is unreported.
expert_take_long: The paper changes two components of silent-EMG voicing: the timing map from EMG frames to audio frames (M06), now a duration predictor with a length regulator, and training-only supervision (M02), extended from phonemes to Mandarin tonemes [@li2022ssrnet]. Both are standard against the field: the duration-regulated model is rare but fails without the auxiliary loss, and auxiliary phonetic losses predate it [@toth2018multitask]. The headline result, 21.99% objective CER and a gain stated as 24.63% over the baseline (§IV-B.1), is confounded because the baseline [@gaddy2020digital] has no auxiliary loss. Tone itself changes CER by +6.51 in a single run (§IV-C.3), and no CER change in the paper says whether it is absolute or relative. The largest unaddressed risk is the split: five silent repetitions per prompt are divided 8:1:1 by utterance with no stated prompt grouping, so test sentences can occur in training. The results show in-speaker Mandarin voicing on read prompts, not tone-preserving silent speech in general.
expert_true_value: Shows that a duration-regulated sequence-to-sequence EMG-to-speech model trained with an auxiliary toneme loss can produce intelligible Mandarin for speakers seen in training, with test sentences that can also occur in training; the model depends on the auxiliary loss, and the tone-specific change is +6.51 CER in one run.
canon_before: Prior sEMG silent speech reconstruction approaches mostly treated decoding as frame-level tasks in non-tonal languages, without explicit duration alignment or handling tonal features critical in Mandarin Chinese silent speech synthesis.
delta_from_canon: Replaces frame-synchronous regression on DTW-transferred targets with a duration predictor and length regulator, and extends auxiliary phonetic supervision to tonemes. The predicted-audio alignment cost is inherited from Gaddy and Klein 2020, and the length regulator is never ablated.
position_in_field: Standard on the changed components: the duration-regulated design is rare among EMG synthesis studies (3 of 76, pattern match) but unproven, and auxiliary phonetic losses predate it; the authors' 2023 follow-up reaches 10.52% CER from sEMG with the same design.
practical_value: A reference design and corpus for Mandarin silent-EMG voicing; not yet evidence for unseen sentences, unseen speakers or real-time use.
axes_moved: system_design;evaluation
axes_unresolved: Cross-speaker transfer, real-time latency, walking/mobile robustness
technical_limits: Speaker-dependent training, limited to controlled read sentences, no cross-speaker generalization, no evaluation of real-time latency or robustness to noise or motion, few electrodes with limited articulatory coverage, limited vocabulary
evaluation_limits: Six speakers, per-speaker models, utterance-level 8:1:1 split with five silent repetitions per prompt (prompt grouping not stated); single runs, no significance test; MASR checkpoint and normalization unstated; listener sample allocation unstated.
deployment_limits: Speaker-dependent models trained on six specific Mandarin speakers; requires five facial sEMG electrodes with fixed placement; no reported real-time inference or latency analysis; lacks cross-speaker or cross-environment robustness evaluation; no assessment in walking or mobile conditions.
scope_limits: Limited to silent speech reconstruction from facial sEMG in Mandarin Chinese with fixed electrode setup; no evaluation in other languages, body sites, or conversational scenarios.
input_modality: Five-channel facial surface electromyography (sEMG) recorded at 2000 Hz with Ag/AgCl electrodes placed near mouth and neck muscles
sensor_hardware: Five facial surface Ag/AgCl electrodes positioned near nose, mouth corners, and chin with a sampling frequency of 2000 Hz; differential electrode for channel 1 and single electrodes for others
vocabulary_type: Mandarin read sentences
vocabulary_size: 2260 words / 1373 characters from AISHELL-3 corpus read sentences
metrics: Objective ASR (MASR) CER 21.99% ± 4.99 across six speakers, stated as 24.63% better than the Gaddy-Klein 2020 baseline (absolute or relative not stated); ground-truth audio scores 11.30% under the same scorer; listener CER 6.41% (baseline 39.76%) from 10 listeners; MCD/STOI given only in Fig. 9; ablation ΔCER(%) from single runs, absolute or relative not stated (toneme loss +132.75, toneless phonemes +6.51, vocal-EMG reconstruction +9.38).
evaluation_mode: Quantitative: ASR character error rate (CER), Mel-Cepstral Distortion (MCD), Short-Term Objective Intelligibility (STOI). Qualitative: Human listener transcription CER and naturalness ratings per speaker.

evidence.statement: We propose SSRNet, the first Seq2Seq-based method for silent speech reconstruction in Mandarin Chinese, extracting duration alignment between silent sEMG and vocal audio, with joint toneme classification and vocal sEMG reconstruction losses, and use a state-of-the-art vocoder to generate audio waveform.

Five channels of facial sEMG are recorded using wet Ag/AgCl electrodes positioned around the face and neck, sampled at 2000 Hz. Electrodes are placed 1cm from nose, mouth corners, and chin, with one channel differential.
Dataset includes six native Mandarin speakers reading phonetically balanced AISHELL-3 sentences, totaling about 5.79 hours of silent speech, split 8:1:1 for training, validation, testing per speaker.

SSRNet introduces a duration extractor using DTW to obtain alignment between silent sEMG and audio, duration predictor to predict length alignment, and length regulator to resample features, enabling Seq2Seq mel-spectrogram prediction with tonal-aware multitask learning.

On six speakers, SSRNet achieves average ASR character error rate (CER) of 21.99% (SD 4.99%), outperforming baseline with CER 46.62% objectively. Subjective human transcription CER is 6.41% average (best 1.19%) across six speakers, with naturalness ratings improved.

The system uses speaker-dependent training, limited to six Mandarin speakers with no cross-speaker or cross-environment generalization tested, no latency or real-time inference evaluation, and no mobile or walking scenario testing.

The approach requires wearing five specific facial sEMG electrodes; no real-time operation, cross-speaker transfer, or mobile scenario tested, limiting deployment readiness currently to controlled lab environments.
Output audio waveforms are generated by a pre-trained Parallel WaveGAN vocoder conditioned on predicted mel-spectrograms.

Training loss includes mean absolute error between predicted and target mel-spectrograms, mean squared error for predicted duration against ground truth from DTW alignment, cross-entropy toneme classification loss, and a vocal sEMG reconstruction loss, jointly optimized.

Evaluation metrics include objective ASR CER via Mandarin ASR system, Mel-Cepstral Distortion (MCD), Short-Term Objective Intelligibility (STOI), as well as subjective human listener transcriptions and naturalness ratings over reconstructed voices from six speakers.

en.summary: Duration-regulated seq2seq with toneme loss voices silent Mandarin EMG; gains rest on the auxiliary loss, not the architecture, and prompt grouping in the utterance split is unreported.
en.sensor: Five facial wet Ag/AgCl sEMG channels, 2000 Hz
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent (six speakers, one model each)
en.key_result: 21.99% objective ASR CER (MASR, mean of six speakers), stated as 24.63% better than the Gaddy-Klein 2020 baseline (absolute or relative not stated); 6.41% listener CER; single runs, utterance-level split with five repetitions per prompt and no stated prompt grouping
