en.limitations: Gain confounded by an auxiliary toneme loss the baseline lacks; length regulator never ablated and the model fails without the toneme loss; tone changes CER by +6.51 in one run; units of Table VI changes unstated; prompt grouping in the split not reported; no seeds, significance test or latency; MASR checkpoint unstated.

title: SilentSpeller: Towards mobile, hands-free, silent speech text entry using electropalatography
expert_take_short: SilentSpeller is a strong, rigorously tested SSI system that reframes silent speech as silent spelling, enabling large vocabulary, live text entry, and walking robustness with in-mouth electropalatography sensors.
expert_take_long: SilentSpeller offers a carefully validated alternative to classic silent speech interfaces by changing the recognition task from continuous silent speech to discrete silent spelling. This reframing produces a more structured signal that, together with electropalatography sensors and a user-dependent HMM recognizer, supports a large vocabulary of 1164 words with high offline accuracy. The system uniquely supports live interactive text entry at speeds around 37 wpm with 87% accuracy, including robust performance while walking, demonstrating tolerance to motion artifacts. Limitations include the requirement for custom dental impressions, obtrusive mouth hardware, strong user dependence for training, and struggles with user independence and social acceptability. Overall, the work advances SSI toward viable mobile, hands-free text entry applications in privacy-sensitive or hands-busy scenarios, providing extensive empirical evidence backing claims.
expert_true_value: The paper's main contribution is the novel problem reframing from silent speech to silent spelling using an electropalatography retainer, which yields practical live text entry over large vocabularies including unseen words, with empirical validation of robustness to walking and comparison to mainstream mobile text input.
canon_before: Most silent speech interfaces were limited to small vocabularies (~100 words), stationary use, and offline, non-interactive experiments, with little evidence for practical live text entry.
delta_from_canon: The key change is reframing the task from silent speech recognition to silent spelling recognition, allowing a larger vocabulary (1164 offline words), robust unseen-word generalization, tolerance to walking motion, and live hands-free text entry at reasonable speeds (~37 wpm average).
position_in_field: One of the clearest practical SSI task-reframing papers to date; less natural than silent speech but more usable for mobile text entry.
practical_value: High for privacy-sensitive communication and hands-busy users; useful where speech is socially inappropriate and users can manage oral hardware.
axes_moved: large_vocabulary; unseen_word_generalization; walking_robustness; live_text_entry; hands_free_texting
axes_unresolved: user_independence; comfort; social_acceptability; broader_symbol_input
technical_limits: Recognition confusions occur mainly for letters with similar palatograms, especially EE-sound letters (B/P, D/T/Z). Strong user-dependence; user-independent recognition remains poor.
evaluation_limits: Offline experiments rely on data from only two main participants for tuning; live text entry and walking tests include seven users but under constrained phrase tasks; vocabulary is limited to English letters and space without punctuation or capitalization.
deployment_limits: The system requires a custom-fitted in-mouth SmartPalate retainer with 124 electrodes connected by a wired (now partially wireless prototype) interface. The retainer remains obtrusive, and the user-dependent training required limits scalability and ease of deployment.
scope_limits: The system targets discreet text entry, explicitly trading away naturalness of silent speech for reliability; not a conversational silent speech system.
input_modality: electropalatography
sensor_hardware: SmartPalate custom dental retainer with 124 capacitive electrodes sampled at 100 Hz, connected wired or wireless to processing device.
vocabulary_type: Dictionary-based silent spelling with triletter HMM decoding, phrase composition, and bigram correction
vocabulary_size: 1164 isolated-word dictionary offline; live text entry with 321 unique words in phrase corpus
metrics: Offline HMM accuracy: ~97% character, 92% word; Unseen word offline test: 94.5% character, 85.5% word accuracy; Walking and seated phrase recognition: ~97.5% vs 96.5% character accuracy; Live text entry average 37 words per minute at 87% accuracy, best participant 53 wpm at 91%.
evaluation_mode: Offline isolated word recognition with 10-fold cross validation; reserve testing on 100 unseen words; seated vs walking phrase recognition; live interactive text entry with push-to-talk interface and edit gestures.

evidence.statement: We introduce silent spelling as an alternative for silent speech interaction (SSI). In silent spelling, the user spells words without voicing, which increases signal reliability and enables larger vocabularies (1164 words in this work) and on-the-go interaction.

Offline HMM recognition on 2328 isolated words (1164 unique) achieves an average of 97% character accuracy and 92% word accuracy; unseen word testing on 100 words removed from training achieves 94.5% character and 85.5% word accuracy; walking phrase recognition yields 97.5% character accuracy walking vs. 96.5% seated; live text entry across seven users averaged 37 words per minute at 87% accuracy, with a top participant reaching 53 wpm at 91% accuracy.
SilentSpeller employs a custom in-mouth SmartPalate retainer with 124 binary capacitive electrodes at 100 Hz, which senses tongue-palate contact patterns; a custom dental impression is required.

Evaluation includes offline isolated word recognition with ten-fold cross validation on two participants, unseen word tests with 100 randomly removed words, walking vs seated phrase recognition on two participants, and live interactive text entry experiments on seven participants using 321-word phrase vocabulary.

SilentSpeller is wearable, hands-free, mobile suitable and real-time capable; however, current hardware requires a wired connection to external hardware, making it obtrusive. Wireless prototypes using Bluetooth Low Energy dongles have been developed, but the device remains obtrusive and requires custom dental impressions, limiting deployment readiness.

The system's user-dependent training regime requires about 1-2 hours of data collection (2328 isolated words) per participant to reach optimal accuracy; user independent models tested so far yield poor accuracy (~55% character), limiting deployment readiness.

Although SilentSpeller shows little performance degradation during walking, the current in-mouth retainer and wired setup remain intrusive and socially conspicuous, which social acceptability remains unresolved and limits deployment.

SilentSpeller recognizes sequences of 26 English letters spelled silently using tongue-palate contact patterns, decoding via HMMs with triletter states, using PCA features reduced to 16 top eigen-palate components, sampled at 100 Hz.

en.summary: SilentSpeller enables silent spelling text entry with an in-mouth electropalatography retainer, reaching 37 wpm at 87% accuracy in live entry and comparable accuracy while walking.
en.sensor: SmartPalate retainer, 124 capacitive electrodes (EPG)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Live entry 37 wpm at 87% accuracy (best 53 wpm, 91%); 92% word accuracy offline
en.limitations: Strongly user-dependent; requires an obtrusive custom-fitted in-mouth retainer; offline tuning used only two main participants.

title: SVTS: Scalable Video-to-Speech Synthesis
expert_take_short: Conformer mel predictor plus pretrained vocoder (M06) and data scaling (M03) are standard; GRID/LRW gains hold, but later tests put SVTS at 78-82% WER on LRS3.
expert_take_long: SVTS [@mira2022svts] changes the synthesis path (M06), a conformer mel predictor before a frozen LibriTTS Parallel WaveGAN, and the training scale (M03), up to 1,556 hours of LRS3 plus VoxCeleb2. Both are standard: a neural vocoder on predicted features is the most common design (49 of 165 studies, pattern match, Appendix), the [concurrent] VCVTS uses the same vocoder [@wang2022vcvts], and the [concurrent] LipSound2 had pre-trained on about 2400 hours of VoxCeleb2 [@qu2022lipsound2]. The GRID-seen and LRW gains hold when the same group re-scores them in a [later] table (2.37% and 12.90% WER) [@kefalas2023large]. The LRS3 claim does not: the paper gives no LRS3 WER, as the authors note, and a [later] test of the authors' own LRS3 files finds 82.4% WER and intelligibility MOS 2.17 [@yemini2024lipvoicer], with 78.0% in a second [later] test [@choi2024v2sflow]. Crediting the gains to scalability is unsupported: model size, data and an audio speaker embedding change together.
expert_true_value: A simple, reproducible video-to-speech baseline: a conformer mel predictor with two losses and an off-the-shelf pretrained vocoder that beats its own GAN predecessor on GRID seen speakers and LRW, later reproduced as a comparison row by the same lab.
canon_before: Video-to-speech systems predicted spectrogram or vocoder features from mouth video and turned them into waveforms with Griffin-Lim, parametric vocoders, neural vocoders or end-to-end waveform GANs, mostly on GRID and LRW. Concurrent work already used a LibriTTS Parallel WaveGAN (VCVTS) and VoxCeleb2 pre-training (LipSound2).
delta_from_canon: Drops adversarial waveform training for a ResNet-18 plus conformer mel predictor with L1 and spectral-convergence losses, a frozen pretrained vocoder and an audio speaker embedding; enlarges model and data together, up to LRS3 plus VoxCeleb2 (1,556 hours).
position_in_field: Standard on all components: synthesis path (M06), training scale (M03), use-time speaker embedding (M07), WER reference (M11) and evaluation (M12, no listener test and no LRS3 WER). Later tests on the authors' own LRS3 files find 82.4% WER and intelligibility MOS 2.17 (LipVoicer), and 78.0% WER on the SVTS split (V2SFlow).
practical_value: A baseline and a shared LRS3 unseen-speaker split for later video-to-speech work; not usable as intelligible open-vocabulary speech on LRS3.
axes_moved: GRID seen-speaker WER (2.36%) and LRW WER (13.40%) against the paper's baselines; simpler training with an off-the-shelf vocoder.
axes_unresolved: Intelligibility on LRS3, effect of data versus model size, effect of the audio speaker embedding (LRW uses the test clip's own audio), run-to-run variance.
axes_regressed: GRID unseen-speaker WER 17.85% against 16.12% for the authors' earlier GAN.
technical_limits: Needs a reference audio clip of the speaker at use time; model size grows with the dataset; vocoder pretrained on LibriTTS and not adapted.
evaluation_limits: No LRS3 WER, no listener test, no seeds or repeated runs; LRW speaker embedding from the evaluated clip's audio; perceptual claims rest on the authors' listening.
deployment_limits: Requires reasonably cropped, aligned lip video and substantial, curated audiovisual training data; no unconstrained deployment validation yet.
scope_limits: Limited to lip-video to speech reconstruction, does not address cross-modal or other silent speech modalities.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: word- and sentence-level audiovisual speech
vocabulary_size: GRID (51 words), LRW (500 words), LRS3 (>50,000 words), LRS3+VoxCeleb2 (~1,500+ hours data)
metrics: PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, and WER evaluated on generated speech with pretrained ASR models; GRID and LRW WER reported, but no WER for LRS3 due to ASR unreliability; vocoder speed measured in clips/second; loss function ablations measured by same metrics.
evaluation_mode: Quantitative benchmark evaluations and ablation studies including vocoder and loss comparisons.

evidence.statement: We introduce a scalable video-to-speech framework consisting of two components: a video-to-spectrogram predictor and a pre-trained neural vocoder, which converts the mel-frequency spectrograms into waveform audio, achieving state-of-the-art results on GRID and LRW, and intelligible results on LRS3.

Our model uses a simpler, scalable predictor/vocoder split, with a ResNet18+conformer video-to-spectrogram predictor trained on scaled training data, combined with a pretrained Parallel WaveGAN vocoder; this enables efficient and scalable training unlike more complex architectures or bespoke loss engineering of prior work.

We evaluate on the small GRID dataset (27 hours), medium-scale LRW (around 150 hours), the challenging large-scale LRS3 corpus (312 hours), and a combined LRS3+VoxCeleb2 corpus exceeding 1,500 hours, with seen and unseen speaker splits where applicable.

Quantitative evaluation metrics include PESQ, STOI, ESTOI for speech quality and intelligibility assessment, as well as WER measured using pretrained ASR models on generated audio for GRID and LRW; WER on LRS3 was not reported due to ASR unreliability on generated samples.

In the GRID seen-speaker vocoder ablation, Parallel WaveGAN beats Multiband and Style MelGAN on all four metrics; Griffin-Lim has slightly higher PESQ (2.00 against 1.97) and WER 2.41% against 2.36%; Parallel WaveGAN processes 54.7 clips/s on an RTX 2080 Ti.

SVTS achieves on GRID seen speakers PESQ 1.97, STOI 0.705, ESTOI 0.523, and WER 2.36%; on GRID unseen speakers PESQ 1.40, STOI 0.588, ESTOI 0.318, and WER 17.85%; on LRW unseen speakers PESQ 1.49, STOI 0.649, ESTOI 0.483, and WER 13.4%. LRS3 tasks yield intelligible results without reported WER.

The approach depends on large, curated audiovisual datasets and trained models do not yet achieve high fidelity or robustness on unconstrained unseen data, with ASR evaluation unreliable on LRS3 generated speech and no user studies reported.

Deployment requires cropped and aligned lip video input and substantial training data; real-time usage is plausible given vocoder speed but not explicitly validated; end-user deployment requires further robustness and validation.

en.summary: Conformer mel predictor plus pretrained vocoder (M06) and data scaling (M03) are standard; GRID/LRW gains hold, but later tests put SVTS at 78-82% WER on LRS3.
en.sensor: Camera (lip video)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: WER 2.36% on GRID seen speakers and 13.40% on LRW; no LRS3 WER reported (later tests measure 82.4% and 78.0% on LRS3).
en.limitations: No listener test or LRS3 WER; single runs; model size and data scaled together; LRW speaker embedding from the test clip's audio.

title: Towards Neural Decoding of Imagined Speech based on Spoken Speech
expert_take_short: Spoken-to-imagined EEG transfer (M04) is the standard overt-to-covert design; 26.8% vs 30.5% on 5 classes, no chance level, and "comparable" rests on a non-significant omnibus test.
expert_take_long: The paper [@lee2022towards] changes the use-time action (M04, with M01 and M03): a CSP+SVM model trained on spoken-speech EEG classifies the same participants' imagined speech. The design is standard: 25 confirmed studies apply an overt-trained decoder to silent or covert speech, 9 of them prior, Martin et al. for covert speech in ECoG [@martin2014] (Appendix), and Rekrut et al. ran it in scalp EEG [concurrent], outside the table [@rekrut2022improving]. The transfer stays below the imagined-speech baseline, 26.8% against 30.5% on five classes and lower in 5 of 7 subjects (Table I), and 10 spoken trials per class average 1.2 points above all trials (28.0%, untested, inference). "Comparable performance" (§III.A) rests on a non-significant omnibus Kruskal–Wallis test over seven subjects, without equivalence test or chance level (M12). The claim that imagined speech is closer to spoken speech than visual imagery is unsupported: full-trial transfer reaches 26.8% on imagined speech and 26.3% on visual imagery (Tables I–II).
expert_true_value: A small, honest negative-leaning datapoint for scalp EEG: a CSP+SVM model trained on spoken-speech EEG and applied unchanged to imagined speech scores 26.8% against 30.5% for imagined-speech training on five classes in seven subjects, with no chance reference.
canon_before: Applying a decoder trained on overt speech to silent or covert speech without retraining was already the usual cross-mode test (ultrasound, video, EMG, ECoG); Martin et al. (2014) did it for covert speech in ECoG against a resting-state null. Imagined-speech EEG studies mostly trained on imagined data and often gave no chance level.
delta_from_canon: Moves overt-to-covert transfer to scalp EEG with a classic CSP+SVM pipeline, adds a 10-trials-per-class spoken model and a visual-imagery comparison; no fine-tuning.
position_in_field: Standard on the use-time action (M04): the transfer design predates it in other signals, and a concurrent EEG study (Rekrut et al. 2022) reports a stronger transfer above chance. Evaluation (M12) follows the field's majority practice of no chance reference, which here leaves the main claim untested.
practical_value: A pointer that spoken-speech EEG alone does not yet replace imagined-speech calibration; no communication system is evaluated.
axes_moved: Spoken-to-imagined transfer evaluated in scalp EEG on the same participants and words, including a 10-trials-per-class spoken model.
axes_unresolved: Whether transfer exceeds chance; held-out-session and held-out-subject transfer; fine-tuning with imagined data; larger vocabularies; online use.
axes_regressed: Transfer is below the imagined-speech baseline (26.8% vs 30.5%, lower in 5 of 7 subjects); transfer to imagined speech (26.8%) and to visual imagery (26.3%) are nearly equal, so the speech-specificity inference is not supported.
technical_limits: Five classes, seven subjects, CSP+SVM with unreported preprocessing and classifier settings; whether the SVM or only the CSP filters were trained on spoken speech is unclear.
evaluation_limits: Baseline is a random 90/10 split inside imagined data while transfer crosses paradigms; session arrangement, trial counts and the five words are not stated; one omnibus Kruskal-Wallis test over three conditions (chi-square 4.64, p = 0.0983) is read as 'comparable'; no pairwise, equivalence or chance test.
deployment_limits: Offline only; no online decoding, latency or user study; the conclusion's speech-synthesis claim is not evaluated.
scope_limits: Read: arXiv:2212.02047 v2, all sections, Tables I-II and figure captions.
input_modality: eeg
sensor_hardware: 64-channel EEG cap with active electrodes placed according to international 10-10 system, referenced at FCz.
vocabulary_type: closed-class word set
vocabulary_size: 5 classes
metrics: Five-class accuracy, mean of 7 subjects: imagined-speech 10-fold CV 30.5% (SD 4.9), spoken full-trial transfer 26.8% (SD 2.0), spoken 10-trial transfer 28.0% (SD 3.9); visual imagery CV 31.8% (SD 4.1), transfer 26.3% (SD 2.4), 10-trial 25.6% (SD 3.1). Kruskal-Wallis: imagined chi-square 4.64, p = 0.0983; visual imagery chi-square 7.64, p = 0.022. No chance level stated.
evaluation_mode: Offline within-subject evaluation: random 90/10 10-fold CV on imagined (or visual-imagery) data as baseline; spoken-trained model tested on imagined or visual-imagery trials; Kruskal-Wallis with bootstrap post-hoc.

evidence.statement: In this paper, we performed a preliminary analysis to find out whether if it would be possible to utilize spoken speech electroencephalography data to decode imagined speech, by simply applying the pre-trained model trained with spoken speech brain signals to decode imagined speech.

The classification performance of imagined speech data solely used to train and validation was 30.5 ± 4.9 %, the transferred performance of spoken speech based classifier to imagined speech data was 26.8 ± 2.0 %.
For visual imagery, solely trained performance was 31.8 ± 4.1 % and transferred performance of 26.3 ± 2.4 % with statistically significant difference p = 0.022.
The dataset involved 7 subjects and 5-class words/phrases recorded with a 64-channel EEG system.
The model used was classical CSP+SVM on 64-channel EEG with only five classes and seven subjects, without online or cross-subject evaluation.
No online BCI, assistive-user study, latency analysis, or practical silent communication demonstration was performed.

en.summary: Spoken-to-imagined EEG transfer (M04) is the standard overt-to-covert design; 26.8% vs 30.5% on 5 classes, no chance level, and "comparable" rests on a non-significant omnibus test.
en.sensor: 64-channel active-electrode EEG cap (10-10 system)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 26.8% (spoken-trained, tested on imagined speech) vs 30.5% (imagined-trained 10-fold CV), 5 classes, 7 subjects; omnibus p = 0.0983; no chance level.
en.limitations: Standard transfer design; transfer below baseline in 5 of 7 subjects; omnibus non-significance read as comparable; no chance level, trial counts or session arrangement; full-trial transfer is nearly equal for imagined speech and visual imagery.

title: VCVTS: Multi-Speaker Video-to-Speech Synthesis via Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer from Voice Conversion
expert_take_short: VCVTS's unit targets, speech-trained decoder and F0 predictor (M02, M03, M06) came early but are untested by ablation: standard. No WER, unlike its baselines: evaluation (M12) behind.
expert_take_long: VCVTS [@wang2022vcvts] changes three components: lips predict the codebook indices of a voice-conversion content encoder (M02), that system is trained on speech alone and reused as the synthesizer (M03), and its decoder adds an F0 predictor (M06). Unit targets reach video-to-speech here earlier than in any other ledger study (Appendix), F0 decoding from video follows vid2voc [@michelsanti2020vocoder], decoder transfer follows TaLNet [@zhang2021talnet]; unit targets became common from 2023 and the other two recur ([later]: [@choi2023intelligible; @kefalas2023large; @kim2025faces]). Each is standard: Table 1 compares whole systems, with no ablation (§3). Evaluation (M12) is behind on protocol: intelligibility is claimed without any word error rate, although both baselines [@prajwal2020learning; @oneata2021speaker] and the best comparable earlier study [@mira2021endtoend] score output with ASR. With Griffin-Lim on both sides, the GRID listener-test lead over Lip2Wav lies inside the 95% intervals (Table 1). Speaker control (M07) is the usual reference-audio embedding.
expert_true_value: Combines discrete speech-unit targets predicted from lips (earliest in video-to-speech in the ledger), a voice-conversion decoder trained on speech alone and reused, and a separate F0 predictor. None is ablated, and the paper reports no word error rate.
canon_before: Multi-speaker video-to-speech mapped lip video directly to spectra with a speaker embedding (Lip2Wav multi-speaker variant, speaker-disentanglement XTS) and scored content by ASR WER; TaLNet (2021) had already transferred a speech-trained decoder into tongue-and-lip-to-speech.
delta_from_canon: Lips predict the 200 codebook indices of a VQCPC voice-conversion content encoder (M02); the voice-conversion decoder, trained on speech only, synthesizes from them with a Resemblyzer reference embedding and a predicted F0 (M03, M06, M07).
position_in_field: Standard on the three changed components: unit targets come earlier than in any other video-to-speech study in the ledger tables, F0 decoding follows vid2voc (2020) and decoder transfer follows TaLNet (2021), and none is ablated; behind on evaluation protocol, because it drops the ASR WER that its own baselines and Mira et al. (2021) report, including the 34.2% LRW WER of the Lip2Wav row it reproduces.
practical_value: A modular route to multi-speaker video-to-speech that later unit-based systems follow; the paper alone does not show which part brings the gain.
axes_moved: STOI, ESTOI and PESQ over Lip2Wav and XTS on GRID seen and unseen speakers and LRW (whole-system comparison)
axes_unresolved: intelligibility by ASR WER; effect of each transferred component; speaker similarity for unseen GRID speakers; LRW speaker disjointness
axes_regressed: evaluation protocol: no WER, although both baselines report it
technical_limits: MOS-SS for unseen GRID speakers falls from 4.38 to 2.66 (Griffin-Lim); F0-RMSE depends on the vocoder (43.16 Griffin-Lim, 52.14 Parallel WaveGAN, GRID seen).
evaluation_limits: No WER, no ablation, no Lip2Ind accuracy, no run count; GL-versus-GL MOS intervals overlap Lip2Wav on GRID; reference utterances and objective test counts not given; LRW speaker disjointness assumed.
deployment_limits: Offline benchmark synthesis; needs a reference utterance of the target voice; no code, runtime or model size.
scope_limits: Overt-speech lip video, GRID (33 speakers, 52 words) and word-level LRW (more than 500 words).
input_modality: silent lip video plus reference speech for speaker control
vocabulary_type: constrained and open-vocabulary video-to-speech
vocabulary_size: GRID: 52 words; LRW: 500+ words
metrics: PESQ; STOI; ESTOI; MCD; F0-RMSE; MOS speech naturalness; MOS speaker similarity
evaluation_mode: objective and subjective VTS comparison on GRID and LRW for seen and unseen speakers

evidence.statement: The abstract presents VCVTS as a multi-speaker video-to-speech system built on cross-modal knowledge transfer from voice conversion.
Section 2.3 says the proposed system concatenates a Lip2Ind network with the speaker encoder, pitch predictor, and decoder of a voice-conversion system to form multi-speaker VTS.
Section 3 says experiments use GRID with seen and unseen speaker partitions and LRW with default splits for unconstrained evaluation.
Table 1 reports VCVTS on unseen GRID speakers at 1.417 PESQ, 0.582 STOI, 0.330 ESTOI, 3.25 MOS speech naturalness, and 2.66 MOS speaker similarity with Griffin-Lim.
