en.summary: VCVTS's unit targets, speech-trained decoder and F0 predictor (M02, M03, M06) came early but are untested by ablation: standard. No WER, unlike its baselines: evaluation (M12) behind.
en.sensor: Silent lip video plus reference speech
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: GRID unseen speakers (Griffin-Lim): STOI 0.582 vs 0.419 for Lip2Wav; no WER
en.limitations: Large seen/unseen speaker gap and vocoder-dependent quality; offline benchmarks only, requires reference speech, not validated interactively.

title: VisageSynTalk: Unseen Speaker Video-to-Speech Synthesis via Speech-Visage Feature Selection
expert_take_short: The paper is really about disentangling identity, and that is why the unseen-speaker results hold up.
expert_take_long: The paper presents a novel disentanglement-based approach for video-to-speech synthesis that separates speech content and speaker identity from silent talking-face video using multi-head speech-visage feature selection masks, and synthesizes speech conditioned on these disentangled features. Evaluated on three datasets (GRID, TCD-TIMIT, LRW), the method achieves state-of-the-art objective metrics (STOI, ESTOI, PESQ) on unseen speakers with multi-speaker independent splits, as well as highest subjective MOS scores for naturalness, intelligibility, and voice matching. Ablations confirm the importance of the disentanglement and the multi-head mask design. Speaker verification analysis via EER demonstrates effective separation of identity and content features. Limitations include reliance on aligned, controlled videos, lack of real-time or in-the-wild evaluation, and relatively modest speech quality compared to natural voices. Nonetheless, the work meaningfully advances unseen-speaker video-to-speech robustness via representation learning rather than larger datasets or enrollment procedures.
expert_true_value: The paper matters because the content-style split is operational, not decorative: it beats prior video-to-speech systems on unseen-speaker GRID and TCD-TIMIT and scales to LRW with a principled feature selection and visage-style conditioned synthesizer architecture.
canon_before: Lip-to-speech systems improved waveform quality, but most treated face video as a single entangled signal and were weak on unseen speakers.
delta_from_canon: Makes identity disentanglement explicit through speech-visage feature selection and a visage-style conditioned synthesizer.
position_in_field: Strong video-to-speech synthesis paper focused on unseen-speaker generalization rather than core SSI hardware.
practical_value: Useful when face-video synthesis must generalize beyond training identities without a speaker-specific enrollment pipeline.
axes_moved: system design; evaluation; speaker generalization
axes_unresolved: in-the-wild robustness; real-time inference; noisy capture conditions
technical_limits: Even best scores fall short of natural speech; requires clean, aligned talking-face videos; no demonstrated robustness to occlusion or pose variation.
evaluation_limits: Offline benchmark evaluations only; MOS study limited to 20 GRID samples rated by 16 participants; no in-the-wild tests.
deployment_limits: No evaluation under camera noise, varying head poses, or real-time inference; limited to aligned, controlled talking-face video.
scope_limits: Talking-face speech synthesis for unseen speakers with benchmark datasets; no broader SSI application beyond video-to-speech synthesis is addressed.
input_modality: video
metrics: STOI, ESTOI, PESQ; MOS naturalness, intelligibility, and voice matching; Equal Error Rate (EER) for speaker verification of disentangled features.
evaluation_mode: Multi-speaker independent and dependent benchmark evaluation plus MOS for naturalness, intelligibility, and voice matching; disentanglement validated via speaker verification EER.

evidence.statement: Disentangles speech content and visage style from silent talking-face video to synthesize speech for unseen speakers.
The model explicitly separates speech-content features from identity-style features before synthesis using multi-head speech-visage feature selection masks.

On unseen-speaker GRID, the proposed model reaches STOI 0.567, ESTOI 0.308, and PESQ 1.373, improving on End-to-end GAN and VV-Memory. On unseen-speaker TCD-TIMIT it reaches 0.478, 0.217, and 1.410. MOS naturalness 2.96, intelligibility 3.35, voice matching 3.34 on GRID dataset with 20 samples rated by 16 participants.

Evaluated on GRID corpus, TCD-TIMIT volunteer, and LRW datasets with multi-speaker independent and dependent settings; unseen speaker splits are employed; LRW contains 17,580 clustered speaker identities.

Best achievable speech quality remains far from natural speech; method depends on high quality talking-face video aligned and cropped; no in-the-wild or real-time study; MOS ratings based on only 20 GRID samples rated by 16 participants.
No evaluation or discussion of deployment under realistic capture conditions such as camera noise, head pose drift, or occlusion; no latency or live interactive system reported.

en.summary: VisageSynTalk disentangles speech content and visage (identity) features for video-to-speech synthesis, yielding robust results for unseen speakers on benchmarks.
en.sensor: Talking-face video
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Offline benchmarks only with a small MOS study (20 GRID samples, 16 raters); needs clean aligned video, no robustness to pose or occlusion.

title: VisualTTS: TTS with Accurate Lip-Speech Synchronization for Automatic Voice Over
expert_take_short: VisualTTS effectively improves lip-speech synchronization in scripted voice over by conditioning TTS on lip video, but does not tackle silent speech decoding or unscripted scenarios.
expert_take_long: VisualTTS presents an audio-visual multi-speaker neural TTS system conditioned on both text and lip video inputs to synthesize speech synchronizing accurately with lip motions. Key innovations include textual-visual attention that aligns textual embeddings with visual lip embeddings extracted by a pretrained lip-reading model, and a visual fusion strategy that incorporates temporal visual features into the acoustic decoder. Experiments on the constrained GRID dataset show significant improvements in lip-speech synchronization metrics (LSE-C, LSE-D, frame disturbance) compared to Tacotron baselines, including one with textual-visual attention but without fusion. Subjective listening tests show no improvement in speech naturalness, indicating VisualTTS primarily enhances audiovisual synchrony. Limitations include reliance on scripted video-text input pairs, fixed vocabulary and speaker identities, and no demonstration of real-time synthesis or generalization. The work constitutes a meaningful contribution for dubbing and automated voice over applications but does not address silent speech recognition or free speaking SSI tasks, positioning it adjacent to but not core within silent speech interfaces.
expert_true_value: Demonstrates that integrating lip-video visual embeddings via novel textual-visual attention and visual fusion within TTS measurably improves audiovisual synchronization, advancing automatic voice over technology.
canon_before: Traditional TTS systems synthesize speech from text input without considering lip video or lip-speech temporal synchronization, often generating natural but temporally unsynchronized speech.
delta_from_canon: Unlike canonical single-modal TTS, VisualTTS integrates lip motion visual embeddings at alignment and acoustic decoding stages to optimize speech output timing to synchronize with video lip motion.
position_in_field: A specialized audiovisual synchronization-enhanced TTS related but not core to silent speech interfaces; does not decode speech from silent video without text input.
practical_value: Valuable for automatic voice over and dubbing applications with available scripted silent videos; improves perceived audiovisual synchrony without compromising naturalness.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: The system requires both text script and lip video as input; it does not address decoding from video-only silent speech or speaker adaptation to unseen speakers.
technical_limits: Requires paired text scripts aligned with video; training and evaluation restricted to fixed grammar GRID corpus; visual encoder weights fixed during TTS training; no speaker-independent or vocabulary adaptation shown.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation restricted to the scripted GRID dataset; no tests on spontaneous speech, large-vocabulary, unseen speakers, or real-time synthesis; subjective voice quality comparable to baselines with no improvement.
deployment_limits: Requires pre-recorded silent lip video and matching text script; limited to scripted GRID dataset utterances; unknown real-time capability; fixed speaker set and vocabulary; no adaptation to unseen speakers or spontaneous speech.
scope_limits: Limited to GRID dataset scripted utterances with paired silent video and text; no demonstration on spontaneous or unconstrained speech or unseen speakers.
task: automatic voice over with lip-speech synchronization
input_modality: Text script plus silent lip video from a mono camera capturing lip region.
sensor_hardware: Mono video camera capturing lip region from video frames.
vocabulary_type: Executing fixed grammar scripted sentences from predefined GRID dataset.
vocabulary_size: 33,000 utterances from GRID corpus spanning 33 speakers with fixed sentence grammar.
metrics: LSE-C (higher better): 5.87; LSE-D (lower better): 8.45; Frame Disturbance (lower better): 5.92; MOS: 4.17±0.06 on GRID test set averaged across 33 speakers, comparing favorably in lip-speech synchronization to baselines.
evaluation_mode: Objective lip-speech synchronization metrics (LSE-C, LSE-D, Frame Disturbance) and subjective listening tests including MOS and preference tests on synthetic speech paired with test videos.

evidence.statement: The paper formulates the automatic voice over (AVO) task and proposes VisualTTS, a visual-conditioned TTS model with textual-visual attention and visual fusion strategies for accurate lip-speech synchronization.

VisualTTS adopts two novel mechanisms: 1) textual-visual attention (TVA) aligning textual and visual embeddings for alignment, and 2) visual fusion strategy during acoustic decoding to incorporate visual embeddings into mel-spectrogram generation, improving lip-speech synchronization.
Experiments conducted on the GRID dataset with 33 speakers, 900 training and 100 test utterances each, use 24kHz audio and 25Hz video with lip region cropping.

Lip-speech synchronization is evaluated with LSE-C (higher better), LSE-D (lower better), and Frame Disturbance (FD, lower better). VisualTTS achieves LSE-C 5.87, LSE-D 8.45, FD 5.92, outperforming baselines Tacotron and Tacotron with TVA.
Subjective listening tests with 12 listeners show VisualTTS has comparable mean opinion score (MOS) 4.17±0.06 to baselines, indicating similar speech naturalness.

Limitations include requirement of paired text script and silent video, evaluation only on scripted GRID dataset with fixed grammar and vocabulary, no demonstration on real-time synthesis, or generalization to unseen speakers or spontaneous speech.

VisualTTS requires a pre-recorded silent video and matching text script for synthesis, limiting deployment to scripted applications like automatic dubbing; real-time capability and mobile suitability are not reported.

en.summary: VisualTTS conditions TTS on silent lip video to improve lip-speech synchronization for automatic voice-over, evaluated on the scripted GRID corpus.
en.sensor: Mono video camera (lip region) plus text script
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: LSE-C 5.87, LSE-D 8.45, MOS 4.17 on GRID test set
en.limitations: Restricted to scripted GRID data with paired text; no unseen speakers, spontaneous speech, or real-time tests; does not decode silent speech.

title: 3D Convolutional Neural Networks for Ultrasound-Based Silent Speech Interfaces
venue: Artificial Intelligence and Soft Computing (ICAISC 2020), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12415
expert_take_short: (2+1)D front end (M06) is standard: established in lip reading, ported to ultrasound; a 6.3% MSE edge over CNN+LSTM, one speaker, one run; MSE-only evaluation (M12 behind).
expert_take_long: The paper [@toth2020threed] changes the image front end (M06): a (2+1)D convolution over five ultrasound frames sampled with stride 6, a 25-frame span that the authors put at about 300 ms. The authors credit video action recognition and earlier 3D CNNs (Sec. 1–2). M06 is standard, not ahead: spatiotemporal convolution was established in lip reading by 2017 [@assael2016lipnet; @stafylakis2017combining], and a [concurrent] ultrasound-to-formant network split part of its 3D convolution into parallel 2D spatial and 1D temporal branches [@saha2020ultra2speech]. The headline win over CNN+LSTM is small and unrepeated: test MSE 0.336 to 0.315, 6.3% relative (inference), one speaker, one run, against a baseline the authors retrained with changed input and output sizes. The original CNN+LSTM took 32-frame chunks (Sec. 5), so context width confounds only the gains over the one-frame FCN and 2D CNN (Sec. 4). Evaluation (M12) is behind the best comparable work: MSE and R² of 13 vocoder parameters only, while the group's own earlier studies of the same speaker ran MUSHRA listening tests [@csapo2017dnn; @grosz2018f0].
expert_true_value: An early ultrasound-to-speech use of the spatiotemporal convolution front end established in lip reading by 2017 (the authors credit video action recognition): a (2+1)D CNN over a 25-frame span lowers test MSE of vocoder parameters from 0.366 (2D CNN) to 0.315 for one speaker; the 6.3% edge over a retrained CNN+LSTM is a single run.
canon_before: Ultrasound-to-speech mapping was mostly frame-wise DNN or CNN regression; the same group had fed five neighbouring frames with feature selection (2017) with almost no gain, and an author-retrained CNN+LSTM existed. 3D (spatiotemporal) convolution front ends were established in lip reading by 2017 (LipNet, 2016; Stafylakis and Tzimiropoulos, 2017).
delta_from_canon: Replaces single-frame or stacked-frame input with a factorized (2+1)D convolution over five frames sampled with stride 6 (about 300 ms); a [concurrent] ultrasound-to-formant network (Ultra2Speech, 2020-06) split part of its 3D convolution into parallel 2D spatial and 1D temporal branches.
position_in_field: Standard on the front end (M06): a design established in lip reading, ported to ultrasound, early but not alone; behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12): MSE and R2 only, while the group's own earlier studies of the same speaker ran MUSHRA listening tests.
practical_value: Supports using a compact 3D convolution front end for ultrasound-to-speech models, a choice later systems kept (Tongue2Speech, 2026, adds a Transformer); the evidence is one speaker, offline, without speech-level evaluation.
axes_moved: temporal context in the ultrasound image front end (factorized 3D convolution with strided frame sampling)
axes_unresolved: matched-context comparison with 2D CNN and CNN+LSTM; repetition over seeds and speakers; intelligibility of synthesized speech; silent articulation; look-ahead and real-time use
technical_limits: 13 vocoder parameters without F0; the 3D model sees 25 frames while the FCN and 2D CNN see one, so those gains are confounded with context width (the original CNN+LSTM took 32-frame chunks); window centring and look-ahead not stated.
evaluation_limits: MSE and mean R2 only on an 87-sentence test set of one speaker; single runs without seeds or variance; CNN+LSTM retrained with changed input and output sizes; no MUSHRA, MCD, listener transcription or ASR on synthesized speech; '14% absolute' R2 gain is +0.085 absolute.
deployment_limits: Voiced read speech only; no silent articulation, latency, causal variant or training-time measurement.
scope_limits: Offline, speaker-dependent regression of vocoder parameters from ultrasound tongue video of one Hungarian speaker.
input_modality: ultrasound
sensor_hardware: Micro ultrasound system by Articulate Instruments Ltd. with 2-4 MHz 64-element convex transducer at 82 fps
metrics: MSE and mean R2 of 13 standardized vocoder parameters (12 MGC-LSP plus gain): test MSE 0.400 FCN, 0.366 2D CNN, 0.336 CNN+LSTM, 0.315 3D CNN (s=6); mean R2 0.598, 0.633, 0.661, 0.683.
evaluation_mode: Offline, one speaker, fixed 310/41/87 sentence split; stride chosen on the development set; single runs.

evidence.statement: The abstract states that the 3D network outperforms the CNN+LSTM model and presents 3D CNNs as a feasible alternative for SSI.
One Hungarian female speaker, 438 sentences split 310/41/87; no seeds, run counts or variance reported.
The authors concede that superiority over CNN+LSTM would need more thorough comparison and that objective scores do not perfectly track perceived quality; no listening test is run.

en.summary: (2+1)D front end (M06) is standard: established in lip reading, ported to ultrasound; a 6.3% MSE edge over CNN+LSTM, one speaker, one run; MSE-only evaluation (M12 behind).
en.sensor: Micro ultrasound system, 64-element convex transducer, 82 fps
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Test MSE of 13 standardized vocoder parameters: 3D (2+1)D CNN 0.315 vs retrained CNN+LSTM 0.336, 2D CNN 0.366, FCN 0.400; mean R2 0.683 vs 0.661, 0.633, 0.598; one speaker, single runs
en.limitations: One Hungarian speaker reading aloud; MSE and R2 of vocoder parameters only, no F0, no listening, intelligibility or ASR test; no seeds or variance; context width not matched across models; CNN+LSTM retrained with changed sizes; no silent articulation or latency.

title: Advances and Challenges in Deep Lip Reading
expert_take_short: Good survey, not a model result.
expert_take_long: The paper is strongest as field organization. The introduction explicitly says the survey focuses on dataset obstacles, evaluation metrics, and impediments across the VSR pipeline. Section 3.1.2 reviews why in-the-wild datasets matter because controlled corpora do not transfer cleanly to real-world conditions. Section 3.4 then summarizes the metric families, including word accuracy, sentence accuracy, error-rate metrics, and BLEU. That makes it useful background for SSI-adjacent visual speech work, but it cannot be cited as evidence that any specific lip-reading or lip-to-speech system works.
expert_true_value: The full text supports using this paper as orientation, not as system evidence: it is a structured review of where lip reading was succeeding and where data and evaluation were still bottlenecks.
canon_before: The lip-reading literature was growing quickly, but its datasets, task variants, and evaluation practices were still fragmented.
delta_from_canon: This paper organizes the field into datasets, pipeline modules, data challenges, and evaluation metrics rather than proposing another model.
position_in_field: Background survey for visual speech recognition and SSI-adjacent lip-reading context.
practical_value: Useful for mapping datasets, metrics, and open problems before choosing a technical direction.
axes_moved: field synthesis; evaluation framing
axes_unresolved: survey coverage is bounded by the literature up to 2021
technical_limits: Survey article; it does not contribute a new model or experimental benchmark of its own.
evaluation_limits: All claims are literature synthesis rather than original experiments.
deployment_limits: No deployment path is evaluated because this is a review paper.
scope_limits: Deep lip-reading survey only.
input_modality: video
metrics: surveyed metrics include word accuracy, sentence accuracy rate, error-rate family metrics, and BLEU
evaluation_mode: literature survey over datasets, pipeline modules, challenges, and evaluation criteria in deep lip reading

evidence.statement: The abstract frames the paper as a comprehensive survey of deep-learning-based visual speech recognition focused on data challenges, task complications, and corresponding solutions.
The introduction says the survey specifically reviews major datasets, metrics, sub-modules of the VSR pipeline, and open problems rather than proposing a new model.
Section 3.1.2 explains why in-the-wild datasets are necessary, noting that controlled datasets do not transfer cleanly to real-world conditions.
evidence.section_or_location: 3.1.2   Lip Reading Datasets in the Wild

evidence.statement: Section 3.4 reviews the field's evaluation metrics, including word accuracy, sentence accuracy, error-rate metrics, and BLEU.

en.summary: Survey of deep lip reading covering datasets, pipeline modules, challenges and evaluation metrics; contributes no new model or experiments.
en.sensor: Video (lip/face)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Literature synthesis only, with no original experiments or deployment evaluation.

title: An Improved Model for Voicing Silent Speech
venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 2: Short Papers)
expert_take_short: Conv-plus-Transformer EMG encoder (M06) is reused by the 2026 state of the art; the phoneme loss (M02) follows 2018 ultrasound work. Single runs; ablations explain 16.3 of 25.8 points.
expert_take_long: The paper [@gaddy2021improved] changes two components of the 2020 EMG voicing system [@gaddy2020digital]: a learned convolution-plus-Transformer encoder over minimally filtered EMG (M06) and an auxiliary phoneme loss (M02). M06 departs from the feature-plus-recurrent designs of its time but is standard, not ahead, as every comparison is a single run; it lasted: the 2026 state of the art [later] initializes its encoder from it [@lee2026gets]. M02 is standard: phone-state multi-task training for synthesis was already shown on ultrasound [@toth2018multitask] (credited in §1), though here it gives the largest ablation effect (51.7% against 42.2%, Table 1). Crediting the drop from 68.0% to 42.2% to the three changes outruns the evidence: if their effects add, the ablations account for 16.3 of the 25.8 points (inference), and a modified alignment and a new batching regularizer are never ablated (§2.3). A later Whisper rerun scores 25.74% [@lee2026gets]: recognizer and run move the score more than any ablation (inference).
expert_true_value: Provides a strong step forward in speaker-dependent facial EMG silent speech reconstruction, demonstrating the value of learned features, Transformer architectures, and auxiliary phoneme prediction loss to substantially lower WER and improve intelligibility over prior work.
canon_before: Prior work used hand-crafted facial EMG features with recurrent LSTM-based models achieving 68.0% WER in open-vocabulary silent speech voicing.
delta_from_canon: Replaces hand-designed features with learned convolutional features, swaps LSTM with Transformer layers, and adds auxiliary phoneme prediction loss during training.
position_in_field: Strong speaker-dependent facial EMG silent speech reconstruction paper demonstrating large intelligibility improvements in open-vocabulary synthesis.
practical_value: Serves as a strong open-vocabulary facial EMG voicing baseline and demonstrates the efficacy of learned EMG feature extraction and auxiliary phoneme supervision; useful for single-speaker experimental research but not yet practical deployment.
axes_moved: Model quality and open-vocabulary intelligibility improved significantly; also adds detailed phoneme-level error analysis.
axes_unresolved: Speaker independence and session robustness remain unaddressed; wearable practicality and long-term use not evaluated.
technical_limits: Model trained on single speaker without addressing speaker independence or robustness across sessions; no wearable or real-world mobility evaluation; phoneme distinctions like voicing remain challenging.
evaluation_limits: Human evaluation on only 40 silent speech samples with two raters; no session-independent or cross-speaker evaluation; automatic WER metric validated but still limited.
deployment_limits: Single-speaker lab data only; no tests on wearable electrodes, mobility, or long-term recalibration; no cross-session or cross-speaker evaluation.
scope_limits: Single speaker, facial EMG signals, open-vocabulary silent speech voicing only.
input_modality: emg
metrics: Primary metric is word error rate (WER) evaluated both automatically and by human transcription; ablations report WER values of 45.2%, 46.0%, and 51.7% when specific components are removed.
evaluation_mode: Automatic and human transcription evaluations using word error rate (WER) on open-vocabulary silent speech synthesis from facial EMG.

evidence.statement: Improves silent-speech voicing by replacing hand-designed EMG features with learned convolutional features, using a Transformer, and adding a phoneme auxiliary loss.
Our model improves WER absolute by 25.8% from prior 68.0% to 42.2% as measured by automatic transcription, with human transcription averaging 32.3% WER on held-out samples.

The gain comes from replacing hand-crafted EMG features by convolutional feature extraction, employing a Transformer encoder on top, and adding an auxiliary phoneme prediction loss to improve learning.

All data is from a single English speaker with 19 hours of facial EMG recordings in silent and vocalized speech; evaluation includes open-vocabulary automatic WER and human transcription on 40 samples by two raters; no cross-speaker or multi-session tests reported.
The system is limited to a single speaker, no session or speaker independence evaluation, and lacks tests for wearable robustness, mobility, or long-term recalibration.

en.summary: Conv-plus-Transformer EMG encoder (M06) is reused by the 2026 state of the art; the phoneme loss (M02) follows 2018 ultrasound work. Single runs; ablations explain 16.3 of 25.8 points.
en.sensor: Facial surface EMG electrodes
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 42.2% automatic WER (DeepSpeech) from 68.0%, single runs; 32.3% mean human WER from two listeners on 40 samples; a later rerun of the model scores 25.74% under Whisper; one speaker, open vocabulary
en.limitations: One speaker; no seeds or reruns; ablations account for 16.3 of the 25.8-point gain only if effects add, while alignment and batching changes are not ablated; DeepSpeech version and scorer unstated; test split inherited from 2020 with no held-out session; last-epoch checkpoint; human check of 40 samples by two listeners 7.6 points apart.

title: Convolutional Neural Network-Based Age Estimation Using B-Mode Ultrasound Tongue Image
expert_take_short: Age output from tongue ultrasound (M08) is new but unproven: the random frame split shares children between training and validation (M12), so speaker identity can explain the gain.
expert_take_long: The paper changes one component, the output (M08): a speaker's age regressed by a CNN from single B-mode tongue frames [@xu2021age]. The output is new (none of the 99 paralinguistic studies in the Appendix matches an age-estimation pattern), but the verdict is standard because the evidence does not show that age is decoded. The 80/20 split is random over frames with no grouping by child (§4.1), so frames of the same children almost certainly fall on both sides (inference), and a network that recognises the child returns that child's age; a 0.25 s ultrasound segment identifies 50 speakers with 3.16% error in [concurrent] work [@shandiz2021neural]. Evaluation (M12) is standard but weaker than the best comparable work, which tests held-out children on the same UXTD corpus and finds them well below seen children [@ribeiro2019speaker]. The abstract's "MAE" values are validation MSE in the body (§4.4), and the speech-therapy use is untested. The claim that tongue images carry age information beyond speaker identity (§4.4) is unsupported.
expert_true_value: Poses speaker-age regression from single child tongue-ultrasound frames; with frames of the same children in training and validation, the gain over a mean-age predictor does not separate age from speaker identity.
canon_before: Ultrasound tongue imaging is used for articulatory analysis, speech therapy, recognition and articulatory-to-acoustic mapping; paralinguistic decoding from production signals targets emotion or speaker identity, and child-ultrasound classifiers on the same corpus are tested on held-out speakers.
delta_from_canon: Treats each child's age as a regression target for a 2D CNN on one ultrasound frame, evaluated on a random 80/20 frame split pooled across children.
position_in_field: Output (M08) new by pattern count but standard by verdict; evaluation (M12) standard but weaker than the held-out-speaker testing already used on the same UltraSuite corpora; decoder (M06) standard.
practical_value: Useful if a speech-therapy workflow wants age-sensitive ultrasound analysis, but not useful as a communication interface result.
axes_moved: Output target (speaker age).
axes_unresolved: Age information beyond speaker identity, held-out children, error in years, within-child change across sessions, adult speakers.
technical_limits: Small child-only datasets, low-SNR ultrasound, and no evidence beyond two UltraSuite cohorts limit the result.
evaluation_limits: Random frame-level 80/20 split with no stated grouping by child, session or utterance; no test set; augmentation chosen and headline value reported on the same validation data; no seeds; MAE in the abstract versus MSE in the body; age unit not stated.
deployment_limits: No interface, runtime, or user-facing system is built.
scope_limits: Exploratory age estimation from tongue ultrasound rather than silent speech.
task: age estimation from ultrasound tongue images
input_modality: ultrasound tongue image
metrics: Validation MSE 2.03 on UXTD with random rotation; validation MSE 4.87 on UPX; mean-age baselines 3.64 and 5.35
evaluation_mode: validation MSE comparison on UXTD and UPX child cohorts against mean-age baselines

evidence.statement: The paper explores whether speaker age can be inferred from ultrasound tongue imaging using a deep convolutional neural network.
For typically developing children, the minimum validation MSE is about 2.03, compared with a mean-age baseline of 3.64.
evidence.section_or_location: 4.4. Experiments Results for Typically Developing Children

evidence.statement: The authors state the ultrasound dataset is much smaller than speech-based age datasets and that performance needs validation on larger data.

en.summary: Age output from tongue ultrasound (M08) is new but unproven: the random frame split shares children between training and validation (M12), so speaker identity can explain the gain.
en.sensor: B-mode ultrasound tongue images
en.speaker: 58 UXTD and 20 UPX children; grouping of children across the split not stated
en.key_result: Validation MSE 2.03 on UXTD (baseline 3.64); 4.87 on UPX (baseline 5.35)
en.limitations: Children not held out (random frame split), so speaker identity can explain the result; validation data also used for selection; MAE/MSE label conflict; no test set or seeds; therapy use not tested.

title: EMA2S: An End-to-End Multimodal Articulatory-to-Speech System
venue: 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS)
expert_take_short: Speech-latent target (M02) has a 2017 precedent and small, mixed single-run gains; spectrogram-loss-only end-to-end loses to WORLD (M06); a preference test replaces listener transcription (M12).
expert_take_long: EMA2S [@chen2021ema2s] changes two components: a training-only spectral encoder whose embedding the EMA encoder must match (M02), and an end-to-end mapping voiced by a pretrained Parallel WaveGAN instead of WORLD (M06). Both are standard. The speech-latent target already existed in lip-to-speech [@akbari2018lip2audspec], and its increment over the mel-loss variant is 2.2% in MCD and 3.2% in CCR from single training runs (Table I, inference). With spectrogram loss only, the end-to-end system loses to the WORLD baseline on all four metrics; adding either the mel loss or the deep feature loss lifts PESQ, STOI and CCR past the baseline, and only the mel loss also lowers MCD below it (Table I). The evaluation (M12) is behind: the baseline paper scored listener transcription [@taguchi2018articulatory], while EMA2S reports a two-way preference test and an unnamed ASR on a same-speaker split.
expert_true_value: Provides a more natural and intelligible articulatory-to-speech synthesis baseline by effectively leveraging a neural vocoder and multimodal joint loss, improving reconstruction quality beyond prior parametric vocoder pipelines.
canon_before: EMA-to-speech systems typically relied on parametric vocoders with a single acoustic loss, limiting naturalness and intelligibility.
delta_from_canon: Replaces traditional parametric vocoders with an end-to-end neural vocoder architecture (Parallel WaveGAN) and incorporates a combined loss over spectrogram, mel-spectrogram, and deep features for improved articulatory-to-speech mapping.
position_in_field: EMA-based articulatory-to-speech synthesis with the integration of modern neural vocoding and multimodal loss training, showing incremental but well-documented gains.
practical_value: Serves as a significant improved lab baseline for EMA articulatory-to-speech synthesis; useful for research on data-efficient, multimodal articulatory representations but limited for immediate practical use due to hardware requirements.
axes_moved: System design; reconstruction quality improved via neural vocoder and joint multimodal loss training.
axes_unresolved: Hardware practicality; cross-speaker robustness; naturalness ceiling remain unresolved.
technical_limits: Small dataset size (three speakers, 354 utterances each), dependence on intrusive EMA sensors, and lack of large-scale or diverse speaker evaluation.
evaluation_limits: Evaluations are confined to a small dataset with only three speakers; the subjective A/B listening test involved only 10 participants with 15 questions total, and no cross-speaker generalization testing was reported.
deployment_limits: The system requires laboratory-grade EMA hardware, which is intrusive and limits portability. Even the reduced four-sensor configuration still depends on EMA instrumentation and controlled environment recording conditions.
scope_limits: Focused on laboratory EMA articulatory-to-speech synthesis with neural vocoder reconstruction; not addressing wearable or silent speech device deployment.
input_modality: magnetic (EMA)
sensor_hardware: Electromagnetic midsagittal articulography (EMA) with nine sensors including lips, jaw, and multiple tongue positions.
metrics: Mel-cepstral distortion, PESQ, short-time objective intelligibility, character correct rate by ASR, and subjective A/B listening preference percentages.
evaluation_mode: Objective evaluation metrics (mel-cepstral distortion, PESQ, STOI, character correct rate with pre-trained ASR) combined with subjective A/B listening preference test and ablation with fewer sensors.

evidence.statement: We present EMA2S, an end-to-end multimodal articulatory-to-speech system that directly converts articulatory movements to speech signals using a neural-network-based vocoder combined with multimodal joint-training of spectrogram, mel-spectrogram, and deep features.

EMA2S uses a combined multimodal loss consisting of spectrogram loss, mel-spectrogram loss, and deep feature loss, leveraging the idea of multimodal learning by calculating dissimilarity between articulatory and spectral embeddings during training.
The system replaces traditional parametric vocoders with a Parallel WaveGAN-based neural vocoder, allowing an end-to-end trainable articulatory-to-speech waveform synthesis pipeline.

Objective evaluation metrics used include mel-cepstral distortion (MCD), perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ), short-time objective intelligibility (STOI), and character correct rate (CCR) from a pre-trained automatic speech recognition (ASR) system.

Experiments performed on the NTT EMA corpus with three speakers, each contributing 354 utterances, split into 304 training and 50 testing utterances per speaker, with sensors placed on upper lip, lower lip, upper jaw, lower jaw, tongue tip, tongue blade, tongue dorsum, tongue rear, and velum.
The EMA2S system achieves superior objective scores compared to the baseline: MCD 7.176 vs 7.815, PESQ 1.350 vs 1.279, STOI 0.716 vs 0.696, and CCR 0.868 vs 0.818, as shown in Table I of the paper.
The subjective A/B listening test with 10 participants and 15 questions in total shows that EMA2S speech output was preferred 83% over the baseline's 17%.
The dataset is limited to three speakers and 354 utterances each, recorded in laboratory conditions with EMA sensors, which are intrusive and impractical for general deployment.
Even with only four less invasive EMA sensors, the system still outperforms the baseline, but still depends on EMA hardware and controlled conditions, limiting portability and real-world deployment.

en.summary: Speech-latent target (M02) has a 2017 precedent and small, mixed single-run gains; spectrogram-loss-only end-to-end loses to WORLD (M06); a preference test replaces listener transcription (M12).
en.sensor: EMA with nine sensors (lips, jaw, tongue)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Small dataset (three speakers, 354 utterances each), small listening test, no cross-speaker testing, and intrusive lab-grade EMA hardware.

title: Improving Neural Silent Speech Interface Models by Adversarial Training
expert_take_short: Standard on the adversarial loss (M02): it predates the paper in video-to-speech and its gains are small, with no variance reported; behind on evaluation (M12): no listening test.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the training-only supervision (M02): a Patch-GAN discriminator adds an adversarial loss, weighted 0.25 against 0.75 MSE, to an ultrasound-to-mel 3D CNN. M02 is standard: the authors claim a first only for ultrasound, and a critic loss added to a regression loss for speech from a silent signal already existed in video-to-speech. The effect is not established: no repeated runs or variance are reported, and test STOI rises 0.24% relative in Hungarian and 1.8% in English (inference). The GAN model also has lower test MSE than the MSE-only model, which is unexplained: a weak baseline, a regularizing effect of the adversarial term, or the change from 1 to 5 output frames would each produce it (inference). Evaluation (M12) is behind on the group's own earlier practice: its 2020 study ran a MUSHRA test with 22 listeners, four earlier ultrasound-to-speech studies of the group ran MUSHRA (pattern match), and this one runs none, so improved quality rests on objective metrics only.
expert_true_value: Shows that an adversarial loss can be added to an ultrasound-to-mel network without harm; does not show that it improves what listeners hear, because gains are small, reported without variance and measured only by objective metrics.
canon_before: Ultrasound-to-speech mapping networks were trained with a regression loss (MSE) on vocoder or mel targets; a critic loss added to a regression loss had been used for video-to-waveform synthesis in 2019. The authors' group evaluated earlier ultrasound-to-speech systems with MUSHRA listening tests.
delta_from_canon: Adds a Patch-GAN discriminator (hinge loss) to the MSE training of the group's 3D CNN ultrasound-to-mel generator, weighted 0.25 against 0.75, and predicts 5 mel frames per input block.
position_in_field: Standard on the training-only supervision (M02): adversarial training of the mapping predates it in video-to-speech, though not in ultrasound; behind the best comparable work on evaluation (M12): no listening or intelligibility test.
practical_value: A drop-in loss term for ultrasound-to-spectrogram networks; its value for intelligibility or naturalness remains untested.
axes_moved: training objective of ultrasound-to-mel mapping (regression plus adversarial loss)
axes_unresolved: effect on listener-rated quality and intelligibility; run-to-run variance; a baseline with the same output window; held-out sessions and speakers
technical_limits: Discriminator judges mel patches only; WaveGlow renders the waveform; the generator output window changed from 1 to 5 frames for the GAN runs; loss weights chosen on an unstated set.
evaluation_limits: No repeated runs or variance reported; objective metrics only (MSE, R2, STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, PMSQE, MCD, SDR, SI-SDR), with SDR and SI-SDR meaningless for vocoded speech; 87 Hungarian and 24 English test utterances from the training speakers; no listening, intelligibility or significance test.
deployment_limits: Offline study on vocalized speech; no silent articulation, real-time or multi-speaker test.
scope_limits: One Hungarian female speaker and the single TaL1 English speaker, read sentences, ultrasound only.
input_modality: ultrasound
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound probe (Micro system by Articulate Instruments Ltd.) positioned under the chin for tongue imaging in midsagittal plane.
metrics: Test STOI 0.7050 to 0.7067 (Hungarian) and 0.612 to 0.623 (English); PESQ 1.282 to 1.311 and 1.464 to 1.503; MCD 4.627 to 4.558 and 3.38 to 3.229 dB; test MSE 0.326 to 0.29 and 0.317 to 0.293.
evaluation_mode: Objective metrics on held-out utterances of the same speaker, MSE-only versus MSE plus adversarial loss, no variance reported; no listening test.

evidence.statement: The paper applies GAN-style adversarial training to ultrasound-based articulatory-to-acoustic mapping and compares it against pure MSE training for silent speech interface models.

We extend the conventional MSE training loss with an adversarial loss component provided by a Patch-GAN discriminator network to improve perceptual speech quality in articulatory-to-acoustic mapping from ultrasound data.
evidence.section_or_location: 3 Generative Adversarial Networks for Articulatory-to-Acoustic Mapping

evidence.statement: Across MSE, R2, STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, SI-SDR, SDR, PMSQE and MCD the adversarial model scores better on both corpora, by 0.2-5.2% relative on the perceptual metrics, with no repeated runs or variance reported (Tables 2-3).

Experiments used two single-speaker corpora: a Hungarian female speaker with 438 sentences and the TAL1 English subset with 1015 train, 50 dev, and 24 test utterances, focusing on speaker-dependent ultrasound-to-speech reconstruction.
No listening or intelligibility test was run; the authors cite the effort of a MUSHRA test, although their group ran one with 22 listeners in 2020.
The training framework operates offline on lab-recorded single-speaker ultrasound data with no real-time demonstration or multi-speaker generalization.

en.summary: Standard on the adversarial loss (M02): it predates the paper in video-to-speech and its gains are small, with no variance reported; behind on evaluation (M12): no listening test.
en.sensor: Midsagittal ultrasound tongue imaging, Articulate Instruments Micro, 82 fps, resized to 64x128
en.task: Ultrasound-to-mel-spectrogram mapping with a 3D CNN, WaveGlow synthesis; MSE-only versus MSE plus Patch-GAN adversarial loss
en.vocabulary: Read sentences (Hungarian; English TaL1), vocalized; vocabulary not stated
en.speaker: One speaker per corpus (Hungarian female; TaL1 English); train and test from the same speaker
en.session: Not stated; split procedure not given (counts only), no held-out session reported
en.key_result: Test STOI 0.7050 to 0.7067 (Hungarian) and 0.612 to 0.623 (English); MCD 4.627 to 4.558 and 3.38 to 3.229 dB; no variance reported, no listening test.
en.limitations: No repeated runs or variance reported; MSE-only baseline also loses on MSE; output window changed for the GAN runs; loss weights selected on an unstated set; objective metrics only, including SDR and SI-SDR on vocoded speech; one speaker per corpus.

title: Neural Speaker Embeddings for Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Interfaces
expert_take_short: Standard on embedding conditioning (2.4% relative MSE gain on seen speakers); behind on speaker recognition, which never separates speaker from recording session.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M06 (an x-vector extractor trained on ultrasound) and M03 (that x-vector as auxiliary input to a multi-speaker spectral estimator). M03 is standard: signal-derived speaker vectors predate it, and its gain is 2.3% (development) and 2.4% (test) relative MSE (inference), with no repeated runs, on speakers seen in SSI training, as the authors state. M06 is behind on test protocol, against the best comparable work: the 0.70% held-out-speaker error pools segments from one recording session per speaker (inference), so speaker and probe placement are not separated. Nothing shows a benefit for new users.
expert_true_value: Shows that an x-vector trained on ultrasound separates TaL80 recordings well, but not that it separates speakers from sessions, and its use as decoder input gains 2.3-2.4% relative MSE on seen speakers.
canon_before: Speaker recognition from non-acoustic speech signals (NAM, lip motion, EMG) and speaker vectors estimated from the visual articulatory signal for lip reading predate the paper; TaL conditioned ultrasound-to-speech on acoustic x-vectors.
delta_from_canon: Brings the x-vector to ultrasound tongue video and uses it as auxiliary input to a multi-speaker ultrasound-to-spectrum estimator, so no audio is needed for speaker conditioning.
position_in_field: Standard on embedding conditioning (M03); behind on speaker recognition (M06), whose test does not separate speaker from recording session.
practical_value: A starting point for audio-free speaker conditioning in ultrasound SSI; no evidence yet of benefit for new users.
axes_moved: speaker representation from the articulatory signal
axes_unresolved: session-held-out speaker recognition; SSI tests on held-out speakers; repeated runs; speaker-similarity and intelligibility scores
technical_limits: x-vector injected after the convolutional layers; average pooling only; conditioning gain 2.3-2.4% relative MSE.
evaluation_limits: 1-NN leave-one-out over pooled segments from about one recording session per speaker (inferred); embedding layer chosen on the same pool; x-vector test blocks never scored; SSI trained and tested on the same 31 speakers; single runs, no chance levels.
deployment_limits: Offline corpus study; no cross-session or live test.
scope_limits: Vocalized TaL80 read speech; ultrasound only.
input_modality: ultrasound
sensor_hardware: Articulate Instruments’ Micro ultrasound system capturing 64x842 pixel mid-sagittal tongue images at 82 fps, resized to 64x128 for processing.
metrics: Speaker error 1.96-3.16% on the 50-speaker development set; 0.70% 1-NN leave-one-out on 31 held-out speakers; multi-speaker test MSE 0.669 without and 0.653 with x-vector (single-speaker 0.265).
evaluation_mode: Speaker identification error (development set; 1-NN leave-one-out on pooled held-out-speaker segments) and spectral MSE on seen speakers.

evidence.statement: We adjusted the x-vector framework popular in speech processing to operate with ultrasound tongue videos, producing speaker embedding vectors which we tested in multi-speaker ultrasound-to-speech conversion.
Speaker recognition error rates on development set for the 50-speaker training subset decreased to 1.96% with 164-frame (2 sec) segments (Table 1).
Speaker recognition error for the 31 held-out speakers is 0.70% with 1-NN leave-one-out over pooled development and test segments, with the FC#2 linear embedding chosen on the same pool (Table 2).

The mean squared error (MSE) for the ultrasound-to-spectrum spectral estimation task in the single-speaker setup is about 0.265 on the test set; in a multi-speaker setup without x-vector conditioning it rises to 0.669; adding x-vector conditioning marginally improves MSE to 0.653 (Table 3).

The multi-speaker synthesis experiment trains and tests on the same 31 speakers; speaker recognition pools segments from about one recording session per speaker (inferred), so speaker and session are not separated.
The authors inject the x-vector after the convolutional layers and say this fusion may be suboptimal and needs further study (Sec. 5.3).
No probe-shift, session-variation, or live SSI deployment study is provided, and results remain offline and lab-bound, limiting deployment readiness.

en.summary: Standard on embedding conditioning (2.4% relative MSE gain on seen speakers); behind on speaker recognition, which never separates speaker from recording session.
en.sensor: Midsagittal ultrasound tongue imaging, Articulate Instruments Micro, 82 fps (TaL80 corpus)
en.task: Speaker recognition from ultrasound (x-vector) and multi-speaker ultrasound-to-mel-spectrum estimation conditioned on it
en.speaker: x-vector trained on 50 speakers, scored on 31 held-out speakers; SSI trained and tested on the same 31 speakers
en.session: About one TaL80 recording session per speaker (inferred from corpus totals); speaker and session not separated
en.key_result: 0.70% 1-NN speaker error on 31 held-out speakers (pooled segments); x-vector input lowers multi-speaker test MSE from 0.669 to 0.653, 2.4% relative, one reported run.
en.limitations: Speaker recognition not tested across sessions; SSI tested only on seen speakers; single runs without seeds or chance levels; no listening, MCD or intelligibility score for multi-speaker systems.

title: Silent Speech and Emotion Recognition from Vocal Tract Shape Dynamics in Real-Time MRI
expert_take_short: LipNet decoder on rtMRI (M06) and new sentence-text output (M08) are standard; one unseen-speaker split without repeats; a shared 460-sentence list likely puts training sentences in the test.
expert_take_long: The paper moves the LipNet decoder onto USC-TIMIT real-time MRI (M06) and makes sentence text the output of a vocal-tract MRI decoder (M08). The decoder is standard, the field's most common articulator-video design. The text output is new among 88 vocal-tract MRI studies and goes past HMM sequence recognition of continuous rtMRI speech (Katsamanis et al., 2011), but it stays standard because one split without repeats does not meet the ahead rule. The evaluation (M12) is standard: an unseen-speaker test, stronger than the one-speaker prior, but no repeats. The strongest confound is the closed sentence list: every USC-TIMIT speaker reads the same 460 sentences, so the 40.6% PER most likely measures speaker transfer, not open sentence recognition (inference). The title overreaches: the speech is audible, and no emotion is recognized.
expert_true_value: Shows that a LipNet-style decoder trained with CTC can output sentence text from midsagittal real-time MRI of two held-out speakers; the test most likely reuses the training sentences, so open-sentence recognition from rtMRI is not yet shown.
canon_before: Vocal-tract MRI work mostly produced descriptive analyses, contours or articulation-class labels; HMM recognition of articulation-class sequences in continuous rtMRI speech (2011) and rtMRI VCV classification (2018) preceded it. Sentence-level lip reading used 3D convolution, recurrent layers and CTC (LipNet).
delta_from_canon: Applies the LipNet design (three spatiotemporal convolutions, two Bi-GRUs, CTC, character language model in beam search) to USC-TIMIT rtMRI and outputs character text; adds a neutral-referenced vocal-tract deviation analysis of emotional speech for two words.
position_in_field: Standard on the decoder (M06), the output (M08, new among vocal-tract MRI studies but shown on one split) and the evaluation (M12, unseen speakers but no repeats). Audible speech in the scanner, not silent articulation; no emotion classifier.
practical_value: A laboratory benchmark of what full vocal-tract imaging can encode for text decoding; no use as an input device.
axes_moved: Text output from vocal-tract MRI with speaker-held-out testing.
axes_unresolved: Sentence-disjoint testing, repeated runs, the language model's training text, PER definition for character outputs, silent articulation, emotion classification.
technical_limits: 75-frame (about 3 s) input windows truncate longer sentences; the language model is described both as a 5-gram and as an LSTM network; the MRI scanner is immobile.
evaluation_limits: One split with two held-out speakers, no seeds, repeats or intervals; test speakers most likely read the same 460 sentences as training speakers; hyperparameters tuned without a named validation partition; comparison against converted accuracies of different tasks on another corpus.
deployment_limits: No latency, device or user study; the authors concede the technology for everyday use does not yet exist.
scope_limits: Offline rtMRI recognition on USC-TIMIT and an emotion-geometry analysis on USC-EMO-MRI.
input_modality: real-time MRI video
sensor_hardware: real-time MRI scanner
vocabulary_type: sentence transcription
metrics: Test PER/CER/WER 44.1/41.7/45.4% without and 40.6/39.4/42.1% with the language model (two held-out speakers, 920 videos); NEDM averages per region, boundary, word, gender and emotion (Table 3).
evaluation_mode: Offline; speaker-held-out test (8 training, 2 test speakers) on USC-TIMIT; descriptive emotion-geometry averages without statistical tests.

evidence.statement: The framework translates variable-length rtMRI vocal-tract shape sequences into text using an end-to-end deep neural network.
The phrases-with-LM model reports 40.6 PER, 39.4 CER, and 42.1 WER on USC-TIMIT unseen data.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2: Performance of the three examined speech recognition models exploiting vocal tract dynamics on unseen data.

evidence.statement: The discussion frames the approach as potentially useful but explicitly notes that the enabling technology for day-to-day use does not yet exist.

en.summary: LipNet decoder on rtMRI (M06) and new sentence-text output (M08) are standard; one unseen-speaker split without repeats; a shared 460-sentence list likely puts training sentences in the test.
en.sensor: Real-time MRI scanner (full vocal tract)
en.speaker: 8 training, 2 held-out test speakers
en.key_result: PER 40.6%, CER 39.4%, WER 42.1% with the language model on two held-out USC-TIMIT speakers (one split).
en.limitations: One split without repeats; shared 460-sentence list likely overlaps train and test; audible, not silent, speech; no emotion classifier; language model and PER definition inconsistent.

title: Silent versus modal multi-speaker speech recognition from ultrasound and video
expert_take_short: Standard on both changed components: modal-to-silent loss and fMLLR were known; later work narrows the absolute gap but not the fMLLR ratio, and adaptation gains rest on single runs.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M04 (modal training, silent test) and M03 (fMLLR and unsupervised adaptation); both are standard. Its lasting value is the size of the mode gap on a large corpus; its adaptation claim (small silent gains alongside modal losses) and its multi-speaker framing outrun single-run, seen-speaker evidence.
expert_true_value: The size of the modal-to-silent gap on a large ultrasound corpus: with fMLLR, silent WER 30 points (about 76%) above modal; a later system on the same corpus narrows the absolute gap to about 20 points but not the fMLLR ratio.
canon_before: Modal-to-silent degradation in ultrasound recognition was known from small isolated-word studies (2010); fMLLR/SAT was the usual adaptation for articulatory recognizers.
delta_from_canon: Measures the same degradation for continuous speech across 82 speakers with prompt-matched test sets; adds unsupervised test-set adaptation with small, single-run silent gains that raise modal WER.
position_in_field: Standard on both changed components (M04 modal-to-silent transfer, M03 adaptation); the reference measurement of the mode gap on TaL.
practical_value: Useful as a TaL baseline for the modal-to-silent gap; not evidence for new users, since test speakers are in the training set.
axes_moved: scale of the modal-to-silent measurement
axes_unresolved: speaker-held-out evaluation; training on silent speech; repeated runs and significance; LM test-prompt overlap
technical_limits: Silent WER stays near 70% with fMLLR on TaL80; adaptation adds at most 3.36 points.
evaluation_limits: Test speakers seen in training; single runs without seeds or tests; adaptation scored on its own adaptation data; LM prompt superset not stated to exclude test prompts.
deployment_limits: Offline corpus study; no deployment claim.
scope_limits: Read prompts in the TaL corpus; modal-only training.
task: speech recognition from ultrasound and lip video
input_modality: ultrasound tongue imaging and lip video
sensor_hardware: ultrasound probe and camera
vocabulary_type: open-vocabulary ASR
metrics: TaL80 multi-speaker WER with fMLLR: silent 70.21, modal 39.79 (raw silent 77.79); unsupervised adaptation lowers silent WER by 0.37 to 3.36 points and raises TaL80 modal WER by 1.58 to 2.42; TaL1 speaker-dependent silent 38.42 vs modal 29.59 with fMLLR.
evaluation_mode: WER on prompt-matched modal, silent and whispered test sets (TaL80: 1,374 utterances each; TaL1: 106), test speakers seen in training; syllable-rate and tongue-space analysis.

evidence.statement: The TaL corpus contains six sessions from one professional speaker in TaL1 and single-session recordings from 81 additional native English speakers in TaL80.
On TaL80 multi-speaker evaluation with fMLLR, silent WER is 70.21 and modal 39.79; unsupervised adaptation lowers silent WER to 69.84.

en.sensor: Ultrasound tongue imaging and lip video (TaL corpus)
en.task: Sentence recognition from articulatory images: modal-trained, tested on modal, silent and whispered speech

title: Speaker disentanglement in video-to-speech conversion
expert_take_short: Speaker-conditioned video-to-speech with adversarial identity removal: both standard (gradient reversal on GRID lips dates from 2017); EER uses the training embedding network; one run.
expert_take_long: The paper [@oneata2021speaker] changes the speaker input and its training (M03: an identity vector or frozen audio speaker embedding, plus an entropy or gradient-reversal speaker classifier stripping identity from the lip encoder) and the voice choice at inference (M08); both are standard. Its gradient-reversal variant is the device Wand and Schmidhuber put on a GRID lipreader in 2017 [@wand2017improving], absent from the paper's references, and Lip2Wav fed a speaker embedding to a lip-to-speech model a year earlier [@prajwal2020learning], which the paper calls "concurrent work" (Section II). The Abstract's "first" claim (voice control and unseen identities) therefore rests on adding identity removal, the feature the authors use to set Lip2Wav apart. The strongest confound: speaker control (EER) is scored with the embedding network that also feeds the SE models (Section IV.B). Seven of Table II's 18 speaker-conditioned rows (3-20) exceed baseline B's 41.9% unseen-speaker WER (inference), so "All these variants maintain or improve the content intelligibility" (Section V) is wrong.
expert_true_value: Provides an explicit mechanism to separate speaker identity from visual speech content enabling flexible multi-speaker voice control in video-to-speech conversion, overcoming limitations of previous single-speaker or entangled models.
canon_before: Prior video-to-speech methods assumed a single speaker or implicitly entangled speaker identity with content in visual features without explicit speaker control.
delta_from_canon: Reconceptualizes multi-speaker video-to-speech as a controllable speaker disentanglement task with explicit auxiliary speaker inputs and adversarial disentanglement losses.
position_in_field: A key reference in multi-speaker controllable video-to-speech synthesis demonstrating explicit speaker disentanglement mechanisms.
practical_value: Enables personalized and multi-speaker lip-to-speech synthesis with explicit voice control, promising for assistive technologies requiring speaker adaptation.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Trade-offs remain between intelligibility and speaker control on unseen speakers, with improved disentanglement often decreasing intelligibility.
technical_limits: Fixed vocabulary; trade-off between intelligibility and speaker control, especially on unseen speakers; no demonstration of open-vocabulary or spontaneous speech generalization.
evaluation_limits: Evaluated only on closed-vocabulary GRID corpus; intelligibility and speaker control evaluated primarily on synthetic unseen speaker setups without spontaneous or open-vocabulary speech tests.
deployment_limits: Limited to GRID dataset’s fixed vocabulary and read speech; performance degrades on unseen speakers; requires speaker identity or embedding at inference, limiting zero-shot naturalness and real-world open-vocabulary scenarios.
scope_limits: Only closed-vocabulary GRID dataset with read speech; unseen speaker testing relies on synthetic pairing, no real-world open-vocabulary evaluation.
input_modality: video (silent lip region) plus explicit speaker identity or speaker embedding
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: GRID fixed sentence grammar
vocabulary_size: 52 words
metrics: On unseen speaker identity control, best results include WER around 38.9% with EER about 11.9% using gradient reversal model; speaker-independent linear model achieves WER 42.7% and EER 7.3%.
evaluation_mode: Objective metrics including WER, EER, STOI, PESQ, MCD; additional listening tests for intelligibility and speaker similarity; speaker embeddings for similarity evaluation.

evidence.statement: We introduce a new video-to-speech architecture and extend it to multi-speaker scenario by augmenting the network with an additional speaker-related input feeding either a discrete identity or a speaker embedding, enabling control of the target voice and synthesis for unseen identities.
The model uses adversarial losses that dispel the identity from the video embeddings to better disentangle linguistic content and speaker identity.

They augment a visual processing front-end (3D conv, ResNet, LSTM) and Tacotron2 decoder with a speaker embedding component injected into the decoder and a speaker classifier applied on visual features to remove speaker information and disentangle content and identity.
Experiments are conducted on the GRID corpus dataset with 34,000 samples from 34 speakers and a 52-word fixed vocabulary with fixed sentence grammar.
On unseen speaker control, the best speaker identity normalized rev-grad model achieves WER 38.9% and EER 11.9%; a speaker independent linear rev-grad model obtains WER 42.7% and EER 7.3%.
For speaker-dependent evaluation on 4 speakers, models achieve WER as low as 17.8% (speaker-dependent baseline) and STOI around 0.468, PESQ around 1.85, and MCD around 32 decibels.
The methods are limited to the GRID closed vocabulary and read speech with evaluation on synthetic unseen speaker setups; no results on open vocabulary or spontaneous speech are provided.
There is an observed trade-off between content intelligibility and speaker control, especially for unseen speakers, with improvements in disentanglement sometimes degrading intelligibility.

en.summary: Speaker-conditioned video-to-speech with adversarial identity removal: both standard (gradient reversal on GRID lips dates from 2017); EER uses the training embedding network; one run.
en.sensor: Camera (silent lip video) plus speaker embedding
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: About 38.9% WER, 11.9% EER (gradient reversal), unseen speaker identity control, GRID
en.limitations: Closed-vocabulary read GRID speech only; intelligibility-control trade-off worsens on unseen speakers and speaker identity or embedding is required at inference.

title: Speech Synthesis from Text and Ultrasound Tongue Image-based Articulatory Input
expert_take_short: Helpful side information, not standalone SSI.
expert_take_long: The paper earns its improvement claim. For every speaker in Table 1, the combined text-plus-ultrasound system beats text-only MCD by a small but consistent margin, which is exactly what you want from side information in a limited-data setup. But the same full text also states the system is not suitable for direct SSI because the best pipeline needs both text and articulatory input, and probe misalignment remains a serious failure mode.
expert_true_value: The full text supports a narrower claim than the title suggests: the best system is not a standalone SSI but a text-to-speech system helped by ultrasound side information under limited data.
canon_before: Articulatory-to-speech work usually used ultrasound alone, while DNN-TTS usually used text alone.
delta_from_canon: Combines conventional text-side linguistic features with ultrasound-derived articulatory features inside one DNN-TTS pipeline.
position_in_field: Adjacent articulatory-synthesis paper relevant to SSI but not itself a complete silent-speech interface.
practical_value: Useful when limited-data TTS can exploit synchronized articulatory recordings to improve spectral prediction.
axes_moved: system design; limited-data synthesis analysis
axes_unresolved: speaker independence; direct SSI without text; probe-robust capture
technical_limits: Speaker-dependent training, limited data, and sensitivity to probe misalignment constrain the result.
evaluation_limits: All evidence is speaker-dependent offline synthesis metrics without listening tests.
deployment_limits: The best system still requires text input and a probe-mounted headset.
scope_limits: Articulatory-augmented TTS, not pure silent-speech reconstruction.

For every reported speaker in Table 1, the combined text-plus-ultrasound system has lower test MCD than text-only, for example 5.442 versus 5.652 for 03mn and 5.236 versus 5.447 for 06fe.

title: Sub-word Level Lip Reading With Visual Attention
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
expert_take_short: Attention pooling of the lip map (M06) was ahead in 2021 but not the route to later SOTA; WordPiece output (M08) was preceded by BPE in 2020; the SOTA table mixes data budgets.
expert_take_long: The paper [@prajwal2022] changes the visual front-end (M06) and the output unit (M08) of sentence-level lip reading. Attention pooling over a 24x24 feature map was ahead in October 2021: earlier lip-reading uses of spatial attention fused streams or sat inside a ResNet that still averaged (Appendix), and the gain holds on LRS2 WER (37.2 to 30.9%) and on speech-detection mAP (80.2 to 88.2). It did not become the route to the state of the art: the lowest [later] LRS3 WER, 12.8%, uses a linear-projection front-end on 100,000 hours, and the best public-data systems keep ResNet-18 trunks and gain from data and semi-supervision; within its own generation VTP beat the ResNet plus Conformer baseline. WordPiece output is not new, since byte-pair outputs were used for LRS2 a year earlier, so the claim of first use is wrong, though the 41.0 to 37.2% ablation is a clean gain. The state-of-the-art claim rests on systems trained on 389 to 31,000 hours, with no seeds or repeated runs and unstated WER normalisation.
expert_true_value: This is a strong visual speech recognition paper with real benchmark gains, but it is camera-only lip reading rather than an articulatory SSI modality.
canon_before: Lip-reading systems often used character-level decoding and average pooling over face features, leaving performance and data efficiency on the table.
delta_from_canon: Introduces visual transformer pooling and WordPiece decoding, then reuses the encoder for visual speech detection.
position_in_field: Top-tier lip-reading paper adjacent to SSI.
practical_value: Useful when the problem is silent-video speech recognition and data-efficient visual speech detection, especially without audio.
axes_moved: model quality; data efficiency; transfer to VSD
axes_unresolved: in-the-wild silent dictation; occlusion robustness; privacy-sensitive deployment
technical_limits: The system still depends on face video quality and benchmark-style training corpora.
evaluation_limits: All results are offline benchmarks; no live silent dictation study is reported.
deployment_limits: No discussion of on-device latency, privacy, or in-the-wild robustness beyond benchmarks.
scope_limits: Camera-only visual speech recognition and detection.

evaluation_mode: LRS2 and LRS3 WER benchmarks with ablations, plus AVA ActiveSpeaker visual speech detection transfer

evidence.statement: The paper proposes attention-based pooling, sub-word units, and a visual speech detection model to improve lip reading from silent videos.
The best public-data model reports 28.9 WER on LRS2 and 40.6 on LRS3, while the larger-data version reaches 22.6 and 30.7.

title: Voice Activity Detection for Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Interfaces using Convolutional Neural Networks
expert_take_short: Preprocessing paper, narrow but legitimate.
expert_take_long: The paper does not solve ultrasound SSI, but it does close a real preprocessing gap. The classifier reaches 85.2% test accuracy with 0.859 ROC AUC on the ultrasound speech/silence task, and the downstream experiment shows that keeping long silence can worsen MCD. The scope remains narrow because everything is single-speaker TaL1 and the gains are incremental rather than transformative.
expert_true_value: The result is modest but real: ultrasound-based speech-versus-silence detection works reasonably well on one speaker, and silence trimming slightly helps downstream SSI reconstruction.
canon_before: Ultrasound SSI systems usually assumed speech frames or used speech-side VAD labels without testing ultrasound-only VAD itself.
delta_from_canon: Adds an explicit ultrasound VAD stage and checks how silence removal affects articulatory-to-acoustic synthesis metrics.
position_in_field: Core ultrasound SSI preprocessing paper.
practical_value: Useful if an ultrasound SSI pipeline needs a simple front-end to drop silence before synthesis.

axes_unresolved: cross-speaker robustness; real-time deployment; broader corpora

evaluation_limits: No cross-speaker validation or live interactive test is provided.
deployment_limits: Practical robustness to probe shift, silence styles, and new users is unknown.

evaluation_mode: single-speaker TaL1 classification accuracy/AUC plus SSI reconstruction with and without silence removal

title: A comparison of oscillatory characteristics in covert speech and speech perception
expert_take_short: Strong covert-speech EEG analysis, not an SSI system.
expert_take_long: The full text supports a narrow but meaningful claim: this paper maps how covert speech and speech perception differ in EEG oscillatory structure, with covert speech favoring higher-frequency activity and perception showing stronger delta/theta involvement. The most useful result for SSI-adjacent BCI work is the reported relationship between perception theta and covert-speech gamma, which motivates passive-training ideas for future covert-speech decoders. But the study remains a small-participant analysis paper with no interface, no decoding benchmark, and a lexicon limited to short words.
expert_true_value: Useful foundational EEG evidence for covert-speech BCI modeling, but not itself an SSI system or decoder.
canon_before: Covert-speech BCI studies often borrowed intuition from speech perception without directly characterizing how their oscillatory roles differ.
delta_from_canon: Adds a direct EEG comparison showing covert speech favors higher-frequency activity while speech perception shows stronger delta/theta structure and cross-task theta-gamma coupling.
position_in_field: Foundational covert-speech neuroscience paper adjacent to SSI rather than a deployable interface study.
practical_value: Helps future covert-speech BCI work decide which oscillatory bands may transfer from speech perception signals.
axes_moved: evaluation; problem_reframing
axes_unresolved: Larger lexicon; stronger decoding link; real BCI transfer
technical_limits: Eight-participant EEG study with a small lexicon; no real SSI decoder, no user study, and no deployment experiment.
evaluation_limits: Participant variability is visible in the classification table, and the limited lexicon may make some cross-task rhythmic similarities partly task-driven.
deployment_limits: Would need a full covert-speech BCI stack and richer lexical coverage before any interface use.
scope_limits: Oscillatory analysis of covert speech versus speech perception only.

sensor_hardware: EEG cap
vocabulary_type: 1-2 syllable spoken words
vocabulary_size: small fixed lexicon

evaluation_mode: 10-fold cross-validated classification with Wilcoxon frequency-band statistics and PAC analysis

evidence.statement: The study directly compares covert speech and speech perception with EEG and argues that covert speech favors higher-frequency activity while perception shows stronger lower-frequency structure.

The classification table reports per-participant 10-fold SVM precision, recall, and F1 scores, and the text states that speech perception engages significantly more delta and theta while covert speech shows more low-gamma involvement.

title: An Overview of Deep-Learning-Based Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement and Separation
expert_take_short: Strong AV speech survey, not an SSI system paper.
expert_take_long: The full text is strong as a survey: it synthesizes how AV speech enhancement and separation systems are built, where visual input helps most, what fusion choices dominate, and why evaluation remains hard to compare across papers. Its practical value is field-mapping rather than new algorithmic evidence. For SSI work, it is adjacent because it touches silent-video speech reconstruction and multimodal speech processing, but it does not introduce a new silent-speech interface or benchmark.
expert_true_value: Good map of AV speech enhancement/separation design choices and evaluation gaps, but not a primary SSI contribution.
canon_before: AV speech enhancement and separation knowledge was dispersed across modality choices, fusion strategies, datasets, and evaluation practices.
delta_from_canon: Organizes the area into acoustic features, visual features, deep learning methods, fusion techniques, training targets, datasets, and evaluation gaps.
position_in_field: Survey paper adjacent to SSI via audio-visual speech processing rather than silent-speech interaction itself.
practical_value: Useful orientation document for choosing AV speech enhancement/separation components and understanding current evaluation weaknesses.
axes_moved: evaluation; problem_reframing
axes_unresolved: Standardized AV evaluation; low-resource deployment; robust fusion under real-world conditions
technical_limits: No new benchmark, no unified re-evaluation, and no direct empirical comparison across systems.
evaluation_limits: The paper explicitly states that lack of standardized AV evaluation makes broad performance ranking hard to interpret.
deployment_limits: Not a deployable system; conclusions remain dependent on the underlying papers it surveys.
scope_limits: Survey of AV speech enhancement and separation, plus adjacent silent-video and non-speech AV source separation work.
input_modality: audio + video
sensor_hardware: microphone + camera
metrics: Survey identifies PESQ, STOI/ESTOI, SDR/SI-SDR, and WER as common metrics, while noting the lack of standardized audio-visual evaluation procedures
evaluation_mode: literature review

evidence.statement: The paper presents an overview of deep-learning-based audio-visual speech enhancement and separation systems, including features, fusion methods, training targets, datasets, and evaluation methods.

The conclusion states that visual information benefits both enhancement and separation, and that AV systems can outperform audio-only systems especially at low SNR or when source permutation is an issue.
The paper explicitly says that fair comparison is hard because of application-specific constraints and the lack of standardized audio-visual evaluation procedures.

en.summary: Survey of deep-learning audio-visual speech enhancement and separation, mapping design choices and noting the lack of standardized audio-visual evaluation.
en.sensor: Microphone and camera (review)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Not a primary SSI contribution; no new benchmark or unified re-evaluation, and lack of standardized evaluation limits performance comparisons.

title: Continuous Silent Speech Recognition using EEG
expert_take_short: Standard on silent reading (M04) and CTC decoding (M06); 83% WER on 30 sentences repeated in training, with an undisclosed 4-gram LM and no chance baseline, does not show EEG decoding.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the use-time action (M04, silent reading of displayed sentences) and applies continuous CTC decoding to it (M06); both are standard, since the authors' earlier papers had already applied CTC to EEG recorded during overt speech and listening, and silent reading falls within the reading and imagined-speech actions the field already uses. The feasibility claim does not hold as stated: 83.34% WER is measured on repeats of 30 training sentences, with a 4-gram LM of unreported corpus (M07, not reported) and no chance or shuffled-label baseline. The repeat protocol itself is lenient: on it, the concurrent decoder of Makin et al. reaches about 3% WER for its example participant, though from intracranial ECoG during overt speech. The paper does not show EEG decoding of unseen silently read sentences.
expert_true_value: Applies the authors' CTC-on-EEG recognizer to silent reading of 30 displayed sentences; the 83% WER on sentences repeated in training, with an undisclosed 4-gram LM and no chance baseline, does not show EEG decoding.
canon_before: The authors' earlier papers, among them ICASSP 2019, had already decoded EEG recorded during overt speech and listening with CTC and other end-to-end models; EEG imagined-speech work classified small closed sets of words or syllables.
delta_from_canon: Moves the same CTC-plus-n-gram pipeline from overt speech and listening to silent reading of displayed sentences.
position_in_field: Standard on use-time action (M04) and continuous CTC decoding (M06); LM corpus not reported (M07); repeat-sentence test, usual before 2020 but no longer open decoding (M12).
practical_value: A negative baseline at best: no evidence yet that silent-reading EEG carries decodable sentence content beyond LM and trial-length cues.
axes_moved: use-time action: silent reading instead of overt speech or listening
axes_unresolved: sentence-disjoint test; chance and shuffled-label baselines; LM-free decoding; reading vs inner-speech separation; repeated runs
technical_limits: Handcrafted features reduced to 20 KPCA components; small character CTC model; external 4-gram LM of unreported corpus; trial length reaches the decoder.
evaluation_limits: Random 80/20 split over 360 recordings of 30 sentences, so test sentences repeat training sentences (inferred); no chance or shuffled baseline; single runs; one held-out subject; WER averaging not stated.
deployment_limits: Offline laboratory study; 92.55% WER on a held-out subject; full wet EEG cap.
