scope_limits: Four male participants; first 30 USC-TIMIT sentences read silently from a screen.
task: Continuous silent speech recognition from EEG.
input_modality: 31-channel scalp EEG recorded while subjects silently read sentences mentally.
sensor_hardware: 32-electrode (31 EEG + ground) wet EEG cap with sensors placed according to standard 10-20 montage.
vocabulary_type: First 30 USC-TIMIT sentences, read silently from a screen.
vocabulary_size: 30 unique sentences; test subsets of 5 to 30 unique sentences (12 to 72 recordings), all repeated in training (inferred).
metrics: WER 74.86% to 84.08% across test subsets (83.34% on all 30 sentences); lobe subsets 84.22-86.73%; held-out subject 92.55%.
evaluation_mode: Offline WER on a random 20% of recordings, character CTC with beam search and external 4-gram LM; one train-on-three, test-on-fourth run.

evidence.statement: The paper demonstrates the feasibility of using EEG signals for continuous silent speech recognition while subjects silently read English sentences without vocalizing.

The authors' earlier papers had already applied CTC to EEG recorded during overt speech and listening (Sec. 1); the change here is the silent-reading task, with sentences displayed on screen (Sec. 3).

EEG was recorded from four male subjects using a 32-electrode (31 channels plus ground) wet EEG cap placed according to standard 10-20 system at 1000 Hz sampling frequency while subjects silently read 30 USC-TIMIT English sentences.
evidence.section_or_location: 3. Design of Experiments for building the ing rate,moving window average,kurtosis and power spectral

evidence.statement: The EEG features extracted per channel are root mean square, zero crossing rate, moving window average, kurtosis, and power spectral entropy, totalling 155 features over 31 channels, which are reduced to 20 dimensions using Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) with polynomial kernel of degree 3.

The automatic speech recognition (ASR) model is based on Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) with an encoder of two GRU layers (128 and 64 units) followed by a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with 32 filters and a decoder with softmax output for character-level transcription.

Test WER ranges from 74.86% to 84.08% over subsets of 5 to 30 unique sentences, 83.34% on 72 recordings covering all 30 (Table 1); lobe subsets give 84.22-86.73% and a held-out subject 92.55% (Sec. 6).
Test sentences repeat training sentences under the random split (inferred from Sec. 2-3 and Table 1); the 4-gram LM corpus, chance level and repeated runs are not reported.
The approach is not presently suitable for deployment given high WER, requirement of full 31-channel EEG cap, and lack of real-time decoding results.

en.summary: Standard on silent reading (M04) and CTC decoding (M06); 83% WER on 30 sentences repeated in training, with an undisclosed 4-gram LM and no chance baseline, does not show EEG decoding.
en.sensor: 31-channel wet scalp EEG (32-electrode cap incl. ground, 10-20 placement), 1000 Hz; five statistical features per channel at 100 Hz, KPCA to 20 dimensions
en.task: Continuous character-level CTC recognition of silently read sentences from EEG, with beam search and an external 4-gram language model
en.vocabulary: First 30 USC-TIMIT sentences; test subsets of 5 to 30 unique sentences, all repeated in training
en.speaker: Four male participants (three non-native English speakers); one train-on-three, test-on-fourth run
en.session: Three repetitions of the 30 sentences per participant; session boundaries not stated
en.key_result: 83.34% WER on 72 test recordings covering all 30 sentences (74.86% to 84.08% across subsets); 92.55% WER on a held-out subject.
en.limitations: Test sentences repeat training sentences; language-model corpus and weight not reported; no chance or shuffled-label baseline; single runs without seeds; sentence displayed on screen, so reading and inner speech are not separated.

title: Digital Voicing of Silent Speech
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
expert_take_short: Silent-EMG target transfer (M02) extends a 2016 DTW recipe; the open corpus scored by WER (M12) became the shared test bed. Headline 94% gain is closed-vocabulary, 20 clips, one evaluator.
expert_take_long: The paper [@gaddy2020digital] changes two components: silent EMG learns audio targets transferred from a vocalized repetition (M02), and silent-EMG voicing gets an open 18.6-hour corpus scored by word error rate (M12). M02 is standard: Janke's 2016 dissertation already trained EMG-to-speech on silent EMG with DTW-transferred acoustic targets from audible recordings of the same sentences (§6.3.1) [@janke2016emg], so the claim to be first to train on silent EMG fails (Appendix, M02). M12 is standard: ASR scoring of EMG-to-speech output predates it [@janke2016emg], and its 68.0% WER fell to 42.2% a year later on the same split and recognizer [@gaddy2021improved] and to 11.89% with Whisper by 2026 [@lee2026gets]. The headline 94% reduction is a 67-word task with 20 clips per system and one evaluator (§4.1); open-vocabulary human WER falls 21% relative (95.1% to 74.8%; inference). CCA and the electrode ranking are single runs with no reported seed spread, and all 100 released test utterances come from one book.
expert_true_value: Strong EMG SSI paper showing that silent EMG can produce intelligible speech if training explicitly handles the mismatch between silent and vocalized articulations.
canon_before: Prior EMG-to-speech work largely trained on vocalized EMG and transferred poorly to silent EMG because aligned speech targets were missing.
delta_from_canon: Introduces target transfer, CCA alignment, and predicted-audio refinement so silent EMG can train a speech generator directly.
position_in_field: Core EMG silent-speech reconstruction paper with clear methodological relevance to SSI.
practical_value: Important evidence that alignment strategy, not just model size, is the bottleneck in silent-EMG-to-speech generation.
axes_moved: system_design; problem_reframing; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Cross-speaker transfer; lighter sensors; better open-vocabulary intelligibility
technical_limits: Speaker-dependent setup with substantial data collection and still-high WER in open-vocabulary conditions.
evaluation_limits: Open-vocabulary outputs remain far from production quality, and all results come from the authors' data collection setup.
deployment_limits: Requires facial EMG instrumentation and a speaker-specific training pipeline.
scope_limits: Silent EMG to speech reconstruction only.
input_modality: surface emg
sensor_hardware: facial EMG electrodes
vocabulary_type: closed vocabulary dates/times plus open vocabulary book text
vocabulary_size: 9828 words in open-vocabulary condition
metrics: Closed-vocabulary human WER reaches 3.6% with a 94% relative error reduction from the strongest baseline; open-vocabulary human WER drops from 95.1% to 74.8%; automatic open-vocabulary WER drops from 91.2% to 68.0%
evaluation_mode: human transcription WER, automatic ASR WER, and ablations on data size and electrode subsets

evidence.statement: The paper studies digital voicing of silent speech from facial EMG and proposes target transfer from vocalized recordings so silent EMG can train a speech generator.

Section 3.2 explains that audio target transfer aligns silent and vocalized EMG so silent EMG can receive speech targets, which is the core step that differentiates the method from direct transfer baselines.
The closed-vocabulary human evaluation reports 3.6% WER for the full model, described as a 94% relative error reduction from the strongest baseline.

en.summary: Silent-EMG target transfer (M02) extends a 2016 DTW recipe; the open corpus scored by WER (M12) became the shared test bed. Headline 94% gain is closed-vocabulary, 20 clips, one evaluator.
en.sensor: Facial and throat surface EMG electrodes
en.vocabulary: Closed dates/times set; open vocabulary of 9828 words
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 3.6% human WER closed vocabulary; 74.8% human WER open vocabulary
en.limitations: Speaker-dependent with substantial data collection; open-vocabulary WER remains high and all results come from the authors' own data setup.

title: End-to-End Silent Speech Recognition with Acoustic Sensing
expert_take_short: Standard on sensing and decoding: phone-sonar phase features and an attention decoder work on 54 mouthed sentences of 29 words; the cross-user claim rests on tuning data that include the test users.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M05 (carrier phase on 8 near-ultrasonic tones instead of Doppler) and M06 (attention decoder chosen over CTC). Both are standard: the phase gain comes from one unrepeated ablation in which raw phase is worse than Doppler, and attention over CTC repeats a 2018 lip-reading result while hybrid CTC/attention goes untested. The headline speaker- and environment-independent 8.4% WER is weakened by hyperparameters tuned on a random split that includes the held-out users, and every test stays within 54 sentences built from 29 words.
expert_true_value: Shows that phase features from a phone's own speaker and microphone separate a closed set of 54 mouthed sentences (29 words); recognition beyond that set and a clean user-independent test are not shown.
canon_before: Acoustic lip sensing used Doppler shift from a continuous-wave carrier (16 of 28 acoustic-sensing studies, pattern match); attention had beaten CTC on a shared lip-reading front end in 2018, and hybrid CTC/attention was already in use.
delta_from_canon: Replaces Doppler with carrier phase, delta and double-delta on 8 near-ultrasonic tones, and an attention decoder over CTC; the phase gain rests on one unrepeated ablation in which raw phase is worse than Doppler.
position_in_field: Standard on sensing (M05) and decoding (M06); phase tracking came from acoustic gesture sensing, later acoustic work moved to FMCW echo profiles and open-vocabulary recognition (2026), and lip reading moved to joint CTC/attention.
practical_value: A usable proof that commodity phone sonar carries lip information for a fixed command set; latency, power and distance tolerance are not reported.
axes_moved: sensing representation for speech (phase instead of Doppler) on commodity hardware
axes_unresolved: user-disjoint tuning and testing; word-disjoint or open vocabulary; matched phase vs Doppler vs FMCW ablation; hybrid CTC/attention; on-device latency and power
technical_limits: Closed vocabulary of 54 sentences from 29 words; one phone model; lip-to-phone distance left to the user.
evaluation_limits: Hyperparameters tuned on a random split that includes the held-out users; fold composition not given; one run per test, no seeds; unseen sentences recombine training words.
deployment_limits: No latency, compute or power figures for the claimed deployment on existing smart devices.
scope_limits: Silent Standard Chinese command sentences from lip movements only.
input_modality: acoustic
sensor_hardware: smartphone speaker and microphone
vocabulary_type: 54 fixed sentences (29 words) with a leave-one-sentence-out split
vocabulary_size: 54 sentences, 29 words
metrics: WER is 2.6% in domain-dependent testing, 8.4% average in domain-independent testing, and 8.1% in unseen-sentence testing; the worst unseen-sentence WER shown in the Top-10 list is 18.2%
evaluation_mode: Random 70/10/20 split, leave-one-domain-out (user and position), leave-one-sentence-out, CTC comparison; WER, one run each

evidence.statement: The paper proposes a non-invasive silent speech recognition method using inaudible acoustic signals generated by smart devices for lip-reading.
The conclusion reports WERs of 2.6% for domain-dependent testing, 8.4% for domain-independent testing, and 8.1% for unseen-sentence testing.
Section 4.3 states that the unseen-sentence evaluation is leave-one-sentence-out over 54 sentences built from 29 words, with an average WER of 8.1% and a worst Top-10 WER of 18.2%.

en.summary: Standard on sensing and decoding: phone-sonar phase features and an attention decoder work on 54 mouthed sentences of 29 words; the cross-user claim rests on tuning data that include the test users.
en.sensor: Smartphone speaker and microphone, 8 near-ultrasonic carriers (17–23 kHz), I/Q phase features
en.task: Silent sentence recognition from lip movements (active acoustic sensing)
en.vocabulary: 54 fixed Standard Chinese sentences built from 29 words
en.speaker: 10 volunteers; random split, leave-one-domain-out (user and position) and leave-one-sentence-out tests
en.session: 5 sessions per volunteer on different days; split across sessions not stated
en.key_result: WER 2.6% (random split), 8.4% (leave-one-domain-out), 8.1% (leave-one-sentence-out); attention beats CTC by 0.7 to 2.1 points.
en.limitations: Closed 29-word vocabulary; hyperparameters tuned on a random split that includes held-out users; one run per test, no seeds; phase gain shown in one ablation; no latency or power figures.

title: Silent Speech Interfaces for Speech Restoration: A Review
expert_take_short: Core SSI survey with concrete deployment constraints.
expert_take_long: The full text is strongest where it stops being a catalog and starts naming bottlenecks. The latency discussion is unusually concrete, arguing that 50 ms is ideal and 100 ms may still be acceptable, which sharply favors direct synthesis over slower ASR-TTS cascades. The later challenge section also makes clear that SSI progress is held back less by model fashion than by tiny patient datasets, weak public data availability, and difficult real-world sensor placement.
expert_true_value: A strong field survey that is most useful for identifying what blocks SSI deployment: latency, scarce patient data, and modality-specific tradeoffs.
canon_before: SSI literature was fragmented across modalities and clinical populations.
delta_from_canon: This review consolidates the sensing landscape and makes latency, patient data scarcity, and deployment practicality explicit cross-cutting bottlenecks.
position_in_field: Core SSI background review for speech-restoration framing.
practical_value: Useful as a top-level map of SSI modalities and system bottlenecks.
axes_moved: field_mapping; latency_requirements; modality_tradeoffs
axes_unresolved: patient-scale data, robust public datasets, and clinically viable deployment remain unresolved.
technical_limits: It is a review and therefore inherits the uneven quality and comparability of the literature it summarizes.
evaluation_limits: The paper synthesizes prior results rather than running a unified benchmark.
deployment_limits: It identifies many deployment obstacles but does not itself resolve them.
scope_limits: Speech-restoration SSI review, not a new system.
input_modality: non-acoustic biosignals and articulator sensing
sensor_hardware: multimodal biosignal sensors
body_site: brain; face; lip; oral-cavity; throat; tongue
metrics: The review cites an ideal SSI latency of about 50 ms, acceptable latency up to 100 ms, and disruptive delayed-feedback effects by 200 ms.
evaluation_mode: comparative review of sensing modalities, restoration scenarios, latency requirements, and dataset constraints

evidence.statement: The abstract frames the paper as a review of SSI research for speech restoration using non-acoustic biosignals and articulator sensing.
The latency discussion states that 50 ms is ideal for SSI, values up to 100 ms may still be acceptable, and larger delays disrupt communication.
The challenges section says SSI studies mostly rely on small datasets recorded by different groups and that public datasets remain a major bottleneck.
evidence.section_or_location: V. C URRENT CHALLENGES AND FUTURE RESEARCH

evidence.statement: The review explicitly covers brain activity sensors, muscle activity sensors, and articulator tracking as alternative SSI sensing routes.

en.summary: Review of SSI modalities for speech restoration, focusing on deployment bottlenecks such as latency, scarce patient data and modality trade-offs; cites ideal latency of about 50 ms, acceptable up to 100 ms.
en.sensor: Multimodal biosignal and articulator sensors (review)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: A review that synthesizes uneven prior results without a unified benchmark and does not itself resolve deployment obstacles.

title: Speech Prediction in Silent Videos using Variational Autoencoders
expert_take_short: Strong video-to-speech paper that models ambiguity explicitly.
expert_take_long: The full text supports the central claim: the paper is trying to solve multimodality, not merely squeeze a few points from a deterministic baseline. Table 1 shows the result is nuanced rather than absolute domination, with better ESTOI and PESQ than prior spectrogram-based systems but not the top STOI overall. The real contribution is Section 4.3, where diverse outputs from the same silent clip justify the variational framing.
expert_true_value: A meaningful step for video-to-speech because it attacks one-to-many ambiguity directly, though the gains are concentrated in quality metrics rather than a clean sweep of all measures.
canon_before: Prior silent-video speech systems mostly assumed a deterministic mapping from lip movements to audio.
delta_from_canon: This paper uses a variational formulation to model uncertainty and generate multiple plausible audio realizations for the same video.
position_in_field: Core video-based speech reconstruction work within SSI-adjacent silent-video research.
practical_value: Useful when the target is plausible speech synthesis from silent video rather than text decoding.
axes_moved: multimodality_modeling; video_to_speech; diversity
axes_unresolved: speaker generalization, higher-fidelity vocoding, and deployment remain unresolved.
technical_limits: Waveform recovery still depends on Griffin-Lim and the benchmark remains constrained to GRID.
evaluation_limits: No open-world or speaker-independent deployment evaluation is provided in the extracted text.
deployment_limits: No real-time or in-the-wild deployment story is established.
scope_limits: Silent-video speech reconstruction only.
input_modality: silent lip video
sensor_hardware: camera
metrics: On GRID the proposed model reports STOI 0.724, ESTOI 0.540, and PESQ 1.932; it trails Lip2Wav on STOI by 0.007 but leads on ESTOI and PESQ.
evaluation_mode: GRID benchmark with STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, qualitative comparison, and diversity sampling

evidence.statement: The abstract says the paper presents a stochastic model for generating speech from silent video instead of assuming a deterministic one-to-one mapping.
Table 1 reports the proposed model at STOI 0.724, ESTOI 0.540, and PESQ 1.932 on GRID.
Section 4.3 argues that varying the latent variable z produces multiple plausible speech waveforms for the same input video, supporting the multimodality claim.
The model reconstructs time-domain audio via Griffin-Lim from mel spectrograms, which keeps the pipeline in the spectrogram-reconstruction regime rather than end-to-end waveform vocoding.

en.summary: Variational autoencoder model for speech synthesis from silent lip video that models one-to-many ambiguity; on GRID reports STOI 0.724, ESTOI 0.540 and PESQ 1.932, leading Lip2Wav on ESTOI and PESQ.
en.sensor: Camera (silent lip video)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: STOI 0.724, ESTOI 0.540, PESQ 1.932 on GRID
en.limitations: Limited to the GRID benchmark with Griffin-Lim waveform recovery; no speaker-independent, open-world or real-time evaluation.

title: Ultra2Speech -- A Deep Learning Framework for Formant Frequency Estimation and Tracking from Ultrasound Tongue Images
expert_take_short: Strong ultrasound SSI paper with unusually clear quantitative gains.
expert_take_long: The full text shows this is more than a formant-regression curiosity. U2F cleanly beats the Conv-BiLSTM and plain 3D CNN baselines, and the joint f1-f2 result at 99.96 mean R2 is far above the recurrent baseline. The interesting systems insight is that hybrid spatial-temporal blocks plus channel shuffling are not cosmetic: the ablations show each piece contributes, and the conclusion frames the model as a path toward less manual tongue-contour extraction in SSI pipelines.
expert_true_value: A strong SSI paper because it turns ultrasound tongue video into a high-quality articulatory-to-acoustic mapping problem with convincing quantitative gains.
canon_before: Ultrasound SSI work often depended on handcrafted tongue features or weaker sequence models.
delta_from_canon: U2F uses hybrid 2D spatial and 1D temporal convolutions with shuffling to learn end-to-end formant tracking from raw ultrasound clips.
position_in_field: Core ultrasound-based SSI work for speech restoration.
practical_value: Useful as a full-text-backed reference for ultrasound-to-acoustic mapping and articulatory feature learning.
axes_moved: ultrasound_ssi; articulatory_to_acoustic_mapping; tongue_tracking
axes_unresolved: broader speech coverage and real-time patient deployment remain unresolved.
technical_limits: The reported system focuses on formant tracking and synthesized vowel trajectories rather than full open-vocabulary speech reconstruction.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation is on the collected ultrasound dataset and does not establish cross-speaker clinical deployment.
deployment_limits: The work motivates SSI use but does not present a real-time deployed device.
scope_limits: Ultrasound tongue-image to formant / synthesized speech pipeline.
input_modality: ultrasound tongue image sequences
sensor_hardware: ultrasound probe
metrics: The best U2F configuration reaches mean R2 99.96 on joint f1-f2 prediction, versus 90.01 for the Conv-BiLSTM baseline on the same joint task.
evaluation_mode: train-dev-test split on ultrasound videos with MAE and mean R2 plus baseline and ablation comparisons

evidence.statement: The abstract says U2F maps ultrasound tongue images to formant trajectories and then synthesizes continuous vowel trajectories with a Klatt synthesizer.
Table 1 reports the best U2F configuration at mean R2 99.96 on joint f1-f2 prediction, outperforming the recurrent and standard 3D CNN baselines.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1. Performance comparison with baseline methods

evidence.statement: The discussion lists the hybrid spatial-temporal feature extraction and channel shuffling as the central architectural contribution.
The paper evaluates end-to-end mapping to formant frequencies and vowel trajectories, not a full open-vocabulary speech restoration benchmark.

en.summary: Estimates and tracks formant frequencies from ultrasound tongue image sequences for speech synthesis; best U2F configuration reaches mean R2 99.96 on joint f1-f2 prediction versus 90.01 for a Conv-BiLSTM baseline.
en.sensor: Ultrasound probe (tongue images)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Mean R2 99.96 on joint f1-f2 prediction vs 90.01 baseline
en.limitations: Focuses on formant tracking and vowel trajectories rather than full speech reconstruction; single collected dataset, no cross-speaker or real-time device evaluation.

title: Vocoder-Based Speech Synthesis from Silent Videos
expert_take_short: WORLD features (M06) beat the 2019 GAN on seen GRID speakers; on unseen ones PESQ ties and ESTOI is higher. The CTC text loss (M02) adds under 0.015 ESTOI; the WER is the text head's.
expert_take_long: The paper [@michelsanti2020vocoder] changes two components: a CTC character head trained jointly with the acoustic decoders (M02) and WORLD vocoder features as the acoustic route (M06); both are standard. The text loss follows the multi-task idea of a 2018 ultrasound system [@toth2018multitask] (HMM states there, CTC characters here) and moves ESTOI by 0.007 to 0.013 in one run per configuration, too little to credit. The WORLD route beats the 2019 GAN on seen GRID speakers (ESTOI 0.455 against 0.329), and a later scoring of the released samples keeps that order [@kefalas2023large]; on unseen speakers PESQ ties and ESTOI is higher (0.227 against 0.198). The reported WER comes from the CTC head of a PESQ-selected model, not from the synthesized speech. Today the same speech scores 9.29% ASR WER on seen speakers against 4.07% for the best raw-waveform system, and 38.15% against 16.05% on unseen ones [@kefalas2023large].
expert_true_value: Demonstrates that full vocoder parameter prediction from video plus auxiliary speech recognition creates a practical baseline with better quality and intelligibility than prior partial feature or direct waveform methods.
canon_before: Prior video-to-speech systems predicted partial acoustic features or directly generated waveforms causing artifacts, with vocoder fundamental frequency and aperiodic parameters often synthesized or omitted.
delta_from_canon: Estimates all vocoder features (SP, F0, AP) directly from raw video frames with optional VSR auxiliary task improving reconstruction; uses deep video encoder and GRU-based recursive module with dedicated decoders for each vocoder parameter.
position_in_field: Provides a well-designed full vocoder parameter lip-to-speech baseline illustrating limits of speaker-independent generalization on GRID with multi-task VSR training.
practical_value: Useful as an interpretable baseline for controlled speaker-dependent video-to-speech applications, highlighting benefits of predicting full vocoder parameters.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Speaker-independent generalization remains weak with large performance drops compared to speaker-dependent conditions.
technical_limits: Restricted to closed vocabulary GRID, speaker-dependent models perform well but speaker-independent results degrade sharply, limiting real-world application.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation performed only on GRID corpus with fixed sentence grammar under controlled speaker-dependent and independent splits; no tested generalization to open vocabulary, noisy, or varied environments.
deployment_limits: Limited to closed-vocabulary GRID sentences, requires frontal silent video input; speaker-independent performance is significantly worse, limiting generalization to unseen speakers and real-world environments.
scope_limits: Silent frontal video on GRID corpus with speaker-dependent and independent protocols; closed English vocabulary fixed sentence grammar; not tested for noisy or in-the-wild conditions.
input_modality: video (silent frontal face or mouth region)
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: closed-vocabulary English sentences
vocabulary_size: GRID dataset vocabulary with fixed sentence structure of 6 words
metrics: Speaker-dependent vid2voc with VSR achieves PESQ 1.90, ESTOI 0.455, WER 15.1%; speaker-independent version drops to PESQ 1.23, ESTOI 0.227, WER 51.6%.
evaluation_mode: Objective speech quality (PESQ), intelligibility (ESTOI), and word error rate (WER) from auxiliary VSR system measured under speaker-dependent and speaker-independent settings.

evidence.statement: We present a way to synthesise speech from the silent video of a talker using deep learning that learns a mapping from raw video frames to acoustic features and reconstructs speech with a vocoder synthesis algorithm, trained also to predict text in a multi-task fashion for simultaneous speech reconstruction and recognition in real time.

Our method differs from prior work by predicting all vocoder features (spectral envelope, fundamental frequency, and aperiodic parameters) directly from raw video frames rather than only spectral envelope or estimating waveforms directly, enabling focus on speech intelligibility and quality and outperforming prior GAN-based approaches.

Experiments are conducted on the GRID corpus consisting of audio and video from 34 speakers uttering 1000 six-word closed vocabulary sentences, with evaluations in speaker-dependent and speaker-independent settings using distinct training, validation, and test partitions per setting.

The system is evaluated using PESQ for speech quality, ESTOI for intelligibility, and WER from the auxiliary VSR decoder's CTC-based transcription in speaker-dependent and speaker-independent conditions, with higher PESQ/ESTOI and lower WER indicating better results.

In speaker-dependent experiments, the mouth-input system with VSR achieves PESQ 1.90, ESTOI 0.455, and WER 15.1%, outperforming prior GAN-based and bottleneck feature methods; speaker-independent results degrade to PESQ 1.23, ESTOI 0.227, and WER 51.6%.

Performance drops substantially in the speaker-independent scenario, showing weaker generalization to unseen speakers with a large spread in scores due to differing facial characteristics and speech traits.

The approach requires silent frontal face or mouth region video input, relies on the controlled closed-vocabulary GRID dataset, and shows limited ability to generalize to unseen speakers, constraining its applicability in real-world settings.

The system uses a deep network mapping silent video frames concatenated in temporal context through 3-D convolutions, followed by a GRU-based recursive module and separate decoders for spectral envelope, aperiodic parameters, voiced/unvoiced state, fundamental frequency, and auxiliary VSR output decoded with CTC loss to jointly learn speech reconstruction and recognition.

The system reconstructs speech waveforms from predicted WORLD vocoder parameters using the STRAIGHT vocoder synthesis algorithm and obtains text transcriptions from the auxiliary VSR decoder by best path CTC decoding.

Previous methods predicted incomplete spectral features or direct waveforms causing artifacts; this work instead estimates spectral envelope, F0, and aperiodic parameters, enabling better speech intelligibility and quality.

en.summary: WORLD features (M06) beat the 2019 GAN on seen GRID speakers; on unseen ones PESQ ties and ESTOI is higher. The CTC text loss (M02) adds under 0.015 ESTOI; the WER is the text head's.
en.sensor: Camera (silent frontal face/mouth video)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Seen GRID speakers: PESQ 1.90, ESTOI 0.455 against 0.329 for the 2019 GAN; unseen speakers: ESTOI 0.227 against 0.198 with PESQ tied (1.23 against 1.24). WER 15.1% (seen) and 51.6% (unseen) is from the CTC text head, not ASR on the speech.
en.limitations: GRID only, one run per configuration with the checkpoint chosen by PESQ; text loss adds under 0.015 ESTOI; no ASR on the synthesized speech, no chance level, and the real-time claim has no latency figure.

title: A Novel Task-Oriented Text Corpus in Silent Speech Recognition and its Natural Language Generation Construction Method
expert_take_short: Useful EEG-SSR corpus framing paper, but evidence is lighter than a full benchmark paper.
expert_take_long: The full text supports the paper as a corpus-construction argument, not as a mature SSR system result. Its strongest move is to reject open-domain language coverage and instead build a life-support-oriented corpus with controlled seed templates and neural diversification. The weakness is equally clear: the extracted paper states that the hybrid approach beats pure methods, but it does not surface the quantitative table needed to judge the margin, so the review should stay scoped to dataset design.
expert_true_value: Its value is dataset framing rather than decoder performance: it is trying to make EEG SSR data collection tractable by shrinking the language problem.
canon_before: EEG-based SSR lacked a consensus text corpus, making large paired EEG-text collection prohibitively expensive.
delta_from_canon: The paper narrows the target domain to life-support conversations and uses hybrid NLG to grow a structured SSR corpus from a controlled seed set.
position_in_field: SSI-adjacent corpus paper for EEG-based SSR.
practical_value: Useful if the goal is bootstrapping domain-specific EEG-text data collection, not demonstrating end-to-end SSR decoding.
axes_moved: dataset_design; domain_restriction; eeg_ssr_bootstrapping
axes_unresolved: actual decoder gains and transfer beyond the task-oriented domain remain unresolved.
technical_limits: The paper does not itself solve EEG decoding and relies on a narrow task-oriented domain.
evaluation_limits: Quantitative evidence is weak in the extracted full text, so comparative strength cannot be audited tightly.
deployment_limits: No deployed SSR system is shown.
scope_limits: Corpus construction for EEG-based SSR only.
input_modality: EEG-oriented SSR text corpus design
sensor_hardware: EEG headset
metrics: The full text claims the hybrid method outperforms pure template-based and pure neural NLG approaches in SSR experiments, but the extracted paper text does not expose a numeric benchmark table.
evaluation_mode: methodological corpus construction with qualitative and comparative SSR experiment claims

evidence.statement: The abstract says the paper constructs a task-oriented text corpus for SSR and proposes a hybrid construction method based on natural language generation.
Section 3.2 defines the hybrid workflow: build a small high-quality seed corpus and then expand it with a neural generation model.
Section 4 says the hybrid model outperforms pure template-based and pure neural NLG methods in SSR experiments, but the extracted text does not expose numeric margins.
Section 2 explains that EEG-based SSR lacks ready-made EEG-text pair datasets and that broad open-domain collection is prohibitively expensive, which is why the paper narrows to task-oriented scenes.

en.summary: Proposes a task-oriented text corpus and a hybrid natural language generation method for building EEG silent speech recognition datasets; claims gains over template and neural NLG but gives no numeric benchmark.
en.sensor: EEG headset
en.task: Corpus construction for EEG silent speech recognition
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Does not solve EEG decoding, relies on a narrow domain, and quantitative evidence is too weak to audit the comparative claims.

title: Autoencoder-Based Articulatory-to-Acoustic Mapping for Ultrasound Silent Speech Interfaces
expert_take_short: Standard on the encoder: autoencoder features predate it and it is never compared with PCA or DCT; behind on F0, which is copied from the recording, so the listening test is not of a silent system.
expert_take_long: The paper changes the ultrasound encoder (M06): a one-layer autoencoder bottleneck, stacked over up to 17 frames, replaces raw pixels as input to a spectral DNN. M06 is standard: autoencoder features of tongue images predate it, and its only baseline is raw pixels, not the PCA or DCT coefficients that are the field's usual input and that beat dense autoencoder features in word recognition on the Silent Speech Challenge; no such comparison exists for synthesis. The 25-29% NMSE reduction sets multi-frame autoencoder inputs against a pixel baseline that gained almost nothing from context; at one frame each the gain is 13.5-19.7% relative (inference). M08 is behind the best comparable work: 12 prior studies predict F0 from the articulatory signal, while F0 here is copied from the recording, so the listening test scores a system no silent user could run.
expert_true_value: Shows that a compact learned input lets a spectral DNN use more ultrasound context than raw pixels, but not that a one-layer autoencoder beats the PCA or DCT features the field already used.
canon_before: Ultrasound SSI front ends compressed tongue (and lip) images with PCA EigenTongues or 2D-DCT; deep autoencoder features had been used for singing synthesis (2016) and Silent Speech Challenge recognition (2017), where dense autoencoders trailed DCT in word error rate. The authors' own ultrasound-to-speech line fed raw pixels.
delta_from_canon: Puts a one-layer autoencoder bottleneck (64-512 units) in front of the group's raw-pixel spectral DNN and stacks it over up to 17 frames.
position_in_field: Standard on the encoder (M06): autoencoder features predate it and it is compared only with raw pixels; behind the best comparable work on F0 (M08), which is copied from the recording while 12 prior studies predict it.
practical_value: A cheap way to give a spectral DNN more ultrasound context; the choice between autoencoder and PCA/DCT input remains open.
axes_moved: input compression and temporal context for ultrasound-to-spectrum mapping
axes_unresolved: comparison with PCA/DCT and convolutional autoencoder features for synthesis rather than recognition; F0 prediction in the listening test; held-out sessions and speakers; intelligibility
technical_limits: Shallow dense autoencoder with no further hidden layers; bottleneck activation and autoencoder training data not stated; F0 copied from the parallel recording.
evaluation_limits: Only a raw-pixel baseline (1 or 5 frames) against autoencoder inputs up to 17 frames; best configuration named on development and test scores together; no seeds or significance test; MUSHRA naturalness only, 14 listeners and 10 sentences; one speaker, sessions not stated.
deployment_limits: Offline study; no silent articulation and no F0 from the articulatory signal.
scope_limits: One Hungarian female speaker, vocalized read sentences, ultrasound only.
input_modality: ultrasound video
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound imaging system with a 2-4 MHz convex array transducer producing mid-sagittal tongue images at 82 fps.
metrics: Test NMSE 0.534 (pixels, 1 frame), 0.462-0.429 (autoencoder, 1 frame), 0.377 (N=256, 13 frames); Pearson r 0.680 to 0.787; MUSHRA 16.58 (pixels) to 40.98 (autoencoder) against 75.16 vocoded.
evaluation_mode: Spectral NMSE and Pearson correlation on held-out sentences of the same speaker; MUSHRA naturalness with original F0.

evidence.statement: In this study we train an autoencoder neural network on the ultrasound images; the estimation of the spectral speech parameters is done by a second DNN, using the activations of the bottleneck layer of the autoencoder as features.
Against raw resized pixels only, autoencoder features lowered test NMSE (0.534 to 0.377 at best) and raised MUSHRA naturalness, with the original F0 used in synthesis; no PCA or DCT baseline was run.
The method was evaluated only on ultrasound recordings from one Hungarian female speaker reading 438 sentences; no cross-speaker or cross-session generalization was tested.
No real-time or live deployment and no silent articulation were tested; synthesis used the F0 of the parallel recording.

en.summary: Standard on the encoder: autoencoder features predate it and it is never compared with PCA or DCT; behind on F0, which is copied from the recording, so the listening test is not of a silent system.
en.sensor: Midsagittal ultrasound tongue imaging, Articulate Instruments Micro, 82 fps, resized to 64x128
en.task: Ultrasound-to-spectrum estimation (25 MGC-LSP plus gain) for direct synthesis, with autoencoder bottleneck features as input
en.vocabulary: Read Hungarian sentences (vocalized); vocabulary not stated
en.speaker: One female speaker; train, development and test from the same speaker
en.session: Not stated; session-disjoint splits not reported
en.key_result: Test NMSE 0.534 (pixels, 1 frame) to 0.377 (autoencoder N=256, 13 frames); MUSHRA naturalness 16.58 to 40.98 against 75.16 for vocoded speech, with original F0.
en.limitations: Only a raw-pixel baseline, no PCA or DCT; F0 copied from the recording; configuration named on development and test scores together; one speaker; no seeds, significance test or intelligibility test.

title: Brain2Char: a deep architecture for decoding text from brain recordings
expert_take_short: Character CTC decoding from ECoG; all changes are standard. The 7.0-10.6% WER relies on repeated sentences, as the authors concede, and unseen sentences average 80% WER.
expert_take_long: Brain2Char [@sun2020] changed the output unit (M08, characters), the decoder (M06, CTC with a 4-gram LM) and the training-only targets (M02, MFCC and articulatory regression); all three are standard. The auxiliary MFCC loss appeared in [concurrent] work from the same lab [@makin2020], and characters were never tested against phonemes or words on the same data. The headline 7.0–10.6% WER does not support the claimed new state of the art: the test partition is unstated, the best results rely on repeated sentences (Sec. 4), and the language model is trained on the task corpus (Sec. 2.4). On sentence-disjoint tests the decoder averages 80% WER, against 25.5% for [later] ECoG decoding with a 1,024-word constrained vocabulary [@metzger2023].
expert_true_value: Provides the first demonstration of sentence-level brain-to-character decoding with modern neural sequence models and independent evaluation on multiple subjects, going beyond toy imagined-word classification models toward realistic speech recognition from brain signals.
canon_before: Prior brain-to-text decoding from ECoG data had not achieved continuous sentence-level character decoding with competitive WER on vocabulary sizes above approximately 50 words, often limited to phoneme or word classification.
delta_from_canon: Introduces a modular architecture combining 3D multi-scale inception convolutional encoder, bidirectional LSTM layers, dilated CNN decoder layers with CTC loss and language model beam search, plus latent feature regularization using speech acoustics, articulatory kinematics, and session embeddings.
position_in_field: Strong benchmark in sentence-level ECoG-based brain text decoding with larger vocabularies and physiological regularization.
practical_value: Potentially useful for clinical communication BCIs once invasiveness and calibration challenges are addressed.
axes_moved: evaluation; system_design
axes_unresolved: cross-subject transfer; larger vocabulary decoding
technical_limits: Limited dataset size; invasive sensor modality; session to session neural variability; vocabulary limited to 1200-1900 words; no cross-subject transfer; silent speech decoding at higher error rates.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation restricted to 4 participants with invasive ECoG, limited sentence sets, and no cross-subject testing or long-term deployment; silent speech tested only on two participants with about 20 sentences each; no walking or mobile scenarios assessed.
deployment_limits: Invasive ECoG recording modality requiring clinical implantation; calibration needed per subject and per session; vocabulary sizes remain limited for realistic free text use; no real-world deployment tested.
scope_limits: Sentence-level decoding from invasive ECoG collected during speech tasks in 4 participants; no non-invasive or cross-subject generalization assessed.
input_modality: electrocorticography (ECoG) invasive brain recordings
sensor_hardware: 16x16 and 16x8 electrode ECoG grids implanted on ventral sensorimotor cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, superior temporal gyrus
vocabulary_type: sentence-level English
metrics: Word Error Rate (WER): 10.6%, 8.5%, and 7.0% for three participants on vocabularies from 1200 to 1900 words; Silent speech decoding WER: ~40% and 67% for two subjects on 20 sentences.
evaluation_mode: Experimental study with neural signals and synchronous audio-text; train/test splits with increasing data sizes; partial neural data tests; silent speech trials.

evidence.statement: Brain2Char achieves low word error rates (10.6%, 8.5%, and 7.0%) decoding character sequences directly from ECoG brain recordings with vocabularies of 1200 to 1900 words.

Brain2Char combines 3D inception layers for multi-band spatiotemporal ECoG feature extraction, bi-directional LSTM layers, dilated CNN layers with CTC loss, and language model beam search to decode text from brain signals.

Evaluation performed on ECoG recordings from 4 participants reading prompted sentences with vocabularies between 400 and 1900 words, recorded over several sessions; also tested silent mimed speech in 2 participants with acceptable error rates.
Reported word error rates of Brain2Char reach as low as 7.0% for one participant and 10-11% for others on vocabulary tasks of 1200-1900 words; silent speech decoding WER is around 40-67%.

Brain2Char is limited by reliance on invasive ECoG sensor hardware, session-specific calibration, and limited dataset per participant; generalization to other subjects or larger vocabularies remains unproven.
Although Brain2Char demonstrates hands-free, incremental, and real-time capable decoding, deployment for practical communication BCIs is limited by invasiveness and need for extensive calibration.

en.summary: Character CTC decoding from ECoG; all changes are standard. The 7.0-10.6% WER relies on repeated sentences, as the authors concede, and unseen sentences average 80% WER.
en.sensor: Implanted ECoG grids (16x16, 16x8) on speech cortex
en.task: Sentence-level text decoding from brain signals
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: WER 7.0-10.6% for three participants on repeated sentences (1200-1900 word vocabularies); unseen sentences average 80% WER
en.limitations: Invasive implant, per-subject calibration, four participants, best results rely on repeated sentences, no cross-subject transfer.

title: Denoising convolutional autoencoder based B-mode ultrasound tongue image feature extraction
expert_take_short: DCAE provides cleaner, more robust ultrasound tongue features leading to improved silent speech recognition, outperforming prior feature extraction strategies.
expert_take_long: This paper presents a feature representation study applying denoising convolutional autoencoders (DCAE) to ultrasound tongue image sequences in the context of silent speech interfaces. The authors evaluate DCAE against previous methods such as discrete cosine transform and conventional autoencoders using both reconstruction metrics (Mean Square Error and Complex Wavelet Structural Similarity) and speech recognition performance on the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge dataset. Results indicate DCAE provides improved robustness to noise and preserves spatial tongue structure better than both traditional and deep autoencoder approaches, leading to the lowest word error rates among evaluated methods. While the contribution is modest and focused on feature extraction rather than full SSI system architecture, it establishes a useful baseline for ultrasound SSI feature compression with evidence-backed performance gains. Limitations include evaluation on a single dataset with no cross-speaker generalization and reliance on ultrasound hardware, thus deployment readiness remains medium with scope for broader validation.
expert_true_value: A well-supported demonstration that denoising convolutional autoencoders improve feature representation quality for ultrasound tongue images in silent speech tasks, offering a stronger baseline for ultrasound SSI research.
canon_before: Ultrasound tongue feature extraction primarily used direct-image representations or hand-crafted basis decomposition methods such as PCA (EigenTongue) and DCT.
delta_from_canon: Introduces an unsupervised denoising convolutional autoencoder as a feature extractor compressing noisy ultrasound frames into latent representations for downstream recognition, replacing direct or handcrafted features.
position_in_field: Feature-extraction focused contribution advancing ultrasound-based silent speech interfaces.
practical_value: Provides a method yielding cleaner latent ultrasound features that can improve downstream speech recognition in ultrasound SSI pipelines.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Generalization to broader cross-subject scenarios beyond the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge dataset
technical_limits: Single-speaker data; speckle noise and motion artifacts inherent in ultrasound; unknown cross-subject generalization.
evaluation_limits: Evaluated only on a single speaker-specific dataset (2010 silent speech challenge); no multi-speaker or cross-corpus validation provided.
deployment_limits: Need for specialized ultrasound imaging hardware; robustness to varying ultrasound systems and head movements not fully validated for real-world deployment.
scope_limits: Limited to ultrasound tongue image feature extraction; no multimodal fusion or speech synthesis explored.
input_modality: ultrasound
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound imaging system with 4–8 MHz, 128-element microconvex probe
vocabulary_type: Not specified
vocabulary_size: Not specified
metrics: Mean Square Error (MSE), Complex Wavelet Structural Similarity Index (CW-SSIM), Word Error Rate (WER) of 6.17% (best with DCAE)
evaluation_mode: experimental study

evidence.statement: The denoising convolutional autoencoder (DCAE)-based method outperforms other feature extraction methods on reconstruction and silent speech recognition tasks.
DCAE achieves Word Error Rate (WER) of 6.17%, better than state-of-the-art 6.45% using DCT features on the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge corpus.
Ultrasound tongue images are high-dimensional, suffer from low signal-to-noise ratio and speckle noise, and can be affected by head movement causing rotation or displacement.
The dataset used is the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge dataset with mid-sagittal ultrasound tongue image sequences recorded at 60 fps using a 4-8 MHz, 128-element microconvex probe.
Evaluation is limited to a single-speaker dataset with no cross-speaker validation, raising questions about generalization.
Application of denoising convolutional autoencoder for feature extraction on ultrasound tongue images to reduce noise and preserve spatial structure better than prior AE and DCT methods.
The approach requires ultrasound imaging equipment and stabilization hardware, limiting deployment to systems where such hardware is available.
CAEs and DCAEs outperform traditional deep autoencoders and DCT in reconstruction metrics (MSE and CW-SSIM), indicating better preservation of spatial structure in ultrasound images.

en.summary: Uses a denoising convolutional autoencoder to extract ultrasound tongue image features, improving silent speech recognition over prior feature extraction methods on the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge data.
en.sensor: Ultrasound tongue imaging (4-8 MHz microconvex probe)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: WER 6.17% with DCAE features, single-speaker Silent Speech Challenge data
en.limitations: Single-speaker dataset only, no cross-corpus validation, and robustness to different ultrasound systems and head movement is not validated.

title: Lipper: Synthesizing Thy Speech using Multi-View Lipreading
expert_take_short: Strong multi-view lip-to-speech baseline with honest quality limits.
expert_take_long: The full text gives Lipper more credit than a quick skim would. The best three-view configuration at 0°, 45°, and 60° materially beats the single-view setups, and Table 11 shows why the authors can plausibly call it near real-time: 0.169 s versus roughly 0.94 to 1.95 s for the speechreading comparison. But the conclusion is equally important, because it openly admits robotic audio, controlled-camera assumptions, and weak speaker-independent behavior. This is a strong baseline, not a solved deployment story.
expert_true_value: A serious early multi-view video-to-speech system whose importance is the regression framing and practical latency analysis, though audio quality remains robotic and speaker independence is weak.
canon_before: Most lipreading systems classified phrases or words rather than synthesizing speech directly, and usually from a single view.
delta_from_canon: Lipper combines multiple camera views, regression-based speech reconstruction, OOV testing, and explicit delay analysis.
position_in_field: Core multi-view video speech-reconstruction work in SSI-adjacent silent video research.
practical_value: Useful as a baseline for multi-view lip-to-speech systems, especially when latency and OOV behavior matter.
axes_moved: multi_view_fusion; regression_framing; latency
axes_unresolved: speaker independence, naturalness, and in-the-wild robustness remain unresolved.
technical_limits: The generated audio is still robotic and lip-only sensing cannot recover prosody or full vocal tract information.
evaluation_limits: The work is confined to controlled OuluVS2 conditions and speaker-independent results remain weak.
deployment_limits: Real-world pose variation and broader speaker coverage are not solved.
scope_limits: Multi-view lip-video speech reconstruction only.
input_modality: multi-view lip video
sensor_hardware: camera
metrics: Best three-view setting 0°+45°+60° reaches PESQ 2.315, end-to-end delay stays at 0.169 s across phrases, and user-study accuracy is 80.25% audio-only / 81.25% audio-visual.
evaluation_mode: speaker-dependent and speaker-independent OuluVS2 PESQ benchmarks, OOV phrase tests, delay comparison, and user study

evidence.statement: The abstract says Lipper reconstructs speech from silent multi-view videos by treating lipreading as a regression task rather than classification.
Table 6 reports the best three-view combination at 0°+45°+60° with PESQ 2.315, higher than any single-view result in Table 4.
Table 11 shows Lipper at 0.169 seconds delay across phrases, substantially below the 0.94 to 1.95 second delays of the speechreading comparison.
The conclusion says the audio remains robotic, the system assumes controlled camera conditions, and speaker-independent performance is not good enough for deployment.

en.summary: Lipper reconstructs speech from multi-view lip video on OuluVS2 as a regression problem; the best three-view setting reaches PESQ 2.315 with 0.169 s end-to-end delay, though audio remains robotic.
en.sensor: Multi-view cameras (lip video)
en.task: Speech synthesis from multi-view lip video
en.vocabulary: OuluVS2 phrases, including OOV phrase tests
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: PESQ 2.315 (0 deg+45 deg+60 deg views), 0.169 s delay; user study 80.25% audio-only accuracy
en.limitations: Robotic audio, lips alone cannot recover prosody, controlled OuluVS2 conditions only, and weak speaker-independent results.

title: SottoVoce: An Ultrasound Imaging-Based Silent Speech Interaction Using Deep Neural Networks
expert_take_short: A solid proof of concept that reconstructs speech audio from ultrasound for controlling unmodified smart speakers, showcasing important system design insight despite prototype limitations in latency, hardware bulk, and speaker dependency.
expert_take_long: Kimura et al. present a well-engineered proof of concept for silent speech interaction using ultrasonic imaging and deep neural networks. Their primary contribution is a two-stage neural pipeline converting ultrasonic images captured below the jaw into Mel-spectrogram features and refining those into audio signals, which can then control unmodified commercial smart speakers like Amazon Alexa. This architectural decision to reconstruct audio, rather than directly classify commands, is a significant reframing within SSI research. The study provides modest yet concrete quantitative results: a 65% command recognition success rate with the two-network pipeline, 33.56% word error rate on Google STT, and demonstration of system use with limited command sets. They explicitly discuss limitations such as speaker dependence, system latency (~2.61 s), bulky hardware, and user adaptation requirements for silent speech without vocal fold vibration. These aspects clarify that while the prototype is not ready for real-world deployment or continuous real-time interaction, it is a strong conceptual and technical foundation for future research on SSI architectures that reuse existing voice ecosystems via speech regeneration.
expert_true_value: This paper's key value lies in reframing silent speech interaction as a speech regeneration and ecosystem reuse problem, deploying a two-stage DNN approach to produce audio from ultrasonic tongue and jaw imaging. It demonstrates practical integration with existing voice agents, highlighting a promising architectural direction distinct from direct command recognition methods.
canon_before: Most prior silent speech interfaces recognized commands directly or relied on visible cameras or other sensors, lacking integration with unchanged smart speaker ecosystems.
delta_from_canon: This work shifts SSI from direct command recognition to speech audio regeneration that can be fed to standard speech recognition engines and smart speakers without modification.
position_in_field: An early and influential demonstration of ultrasound-based speech regeneration SSI with system-level insights stronger than its present prototype performance.
practical_value: medium as a systems design contribution and research direction; low-to-medium as a direct deployable interface in reported form
axes_moved: ecosystem_integration; speech_regeneration; smart_speaker_control; user_adaptation_loop
axes_unresolved: real_time_interaction; open_vocabulary; speaker_independence; wearable_ultrasound
technical_limits: Speaker-dependent training; latency unsuitable for real-time use (2.61 s per utterance); differences in silent versus voiced articulation require user adaptation; bulky hardware; potential unknown safety issues with continuous ultrasound emission; small vocabulary size.
evaluation_limits: Only two participants were used for training and testing; the command vocabulary is small (four Alexa commands) in end-to-end testing, repeated five times each; and no speaker-independent or open vocabulary evaluations were performed.
deployment_limits: The device requires a bulky 3.5 MHz convex probe attached under the jaw and digitized display capture; continuous ultrasonic emission safety is not evaluated; the system is not wearable or miniaturized; and its latency (~2.61 s per command) is too slow for real-time use.
scope_limits: Prototype supports only a fixed small command vocabulary in speaker-dependent training; no demonstration of open vocabulary or continuous real-time interaction.
input_modality: ultrasound
sensor_hardware: 3.5 MHz convex ultrasound probe attached under the jaw, with ultrasound images captured to display monitor and digitized video stored
vocabulary_type: Command-level
vocabulary_size: Approximately 500 training spoken commands per collaborator; end-to-end evaluation on four specific Alexa commands repeated five times each
metrics: Network 1 alone achieved an average 42.5% smart speaker command recognition success; Network 1 plus Network 2 achieved 65.0%; ground-truth audio reached 90.0%. Google speech-to-text word error rates were 41.03% for Network 1 outputs and 33.56% for Network 2 outputs, versus 20.61% for ground truth audio.
evaluation_mode: Quantitative smart speaker success rates, word error rates with Google speech-to-text, and qualitative user adaptation observations.

evidence.statement: An ultrasound-only silent-voice system that regenerates audio and controls an unchanged smart speaker with deep neural networks.

Network 1 plus Network 2 reached 65.0% smart-speaker command success versus 42.5% for Network 1 alone and 90.0% ground-truth audio; Google speech-to-text WER for Network 2 was 33.56%; total processing time was 2.61 s for a roughly 3.68 s command clip.

Approximately 500 speech commands were collected from each of two collaborators using an ultrasound probe under the jaw with paired audio, speaker-dependent training only, and end-to-end testing used four Alexa commands repeated five times each.

The system is speaker dependent, slow (2.61 seconds per command), limited to four end-to-end commands, uses bulky 3.5 MHz probe hardware under the jaw, and users must adapt their silent articulation for best results.
Generated audio signals can control existing smart speakers like Amazon Echo and Echo Show without modification, demonstrated with four Alexa commands.

The paper's main novelty lies in system design to reconstruct speech audio from ultrasound images and use that to control unmodified smart speakers, rather than direct command recognition from ultrasound features.
The system is not real-time; with 3.68 s of input, neural networks processing consumes 2.36 s and total processing time is 2.61 s, unsuitable for real-time interaction.

en.summary: SottoVoce reconstructs speech audio from under-jaw ultrasound images with two DNNs to control unmodified smart speakers; command success rose from 42.5% to 65.0% with the second network, versus 90.0% for real audio.
en.sensor: 3.5 MHz convex ultrasound probe under the jaw
en.task: Speech synthesis from ultrasound for voice-assistant control
en.vocabulary: ~500 training commands; 4 Alexa commands in end-to-end test
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 65.0% smart speaker command success (4 commands x5, two networks) vs 90.0% ground-truth audio
en.limitations: Only two participants, speaker-dependent, tiny end-to-end command set, bulky non-wearable probe, 2.61 s latency, and unassessed ultrasound safety.

title: Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Interface Built on a Continuous Vocoder
review_confidence: Target read in full (arXiv v1, Table 1, Fig. 3 labels); eight comparators read in their sources.
expert_take_short: Continuous F0 targets from articulation were prior work; MVF carrying voicing instead of a flag is new but unproven: the F0 RMSE gain uses different reference contours and naturalness is not better.
expert_take_long: The paper [@csapo2019ultrasound] swaps one parametric vocoder for another (M06) and changes the excitation (M08) of ultrasound-to-speech synthesis: continuous F0 and maximum voiced frequency replace the voiced/unvoiced flag and F0. Interpolated F0 targets were already used from articulatory signals [@liu2016articulatory; @gonzalez2017evaluation; @taguchi2018articulatory], so M08 is standard; what is new is letting MVF, taken from the group's speech-synthesis vocoder, carry voicing in place of the binary flag, and nothing shows it helps. The headline 31 Hz against 65 Hz RMSE compares predictions with two different reference contours, and the listening test finds no significant difference. M12 is behind the best comparable work: 11 earlier studies tested listener intelligibility of speech synthesized from non-acoustic signals, among them EMA-driven synthesis with 30.1% listener WER [@taguchi2018articulatory]; this one rates naturalness only. The parametric vocoder (M06) matched the field in 2019 and was replaced by a neural vocoder in the same lineage within a year [@csapo2020waveglow].
expert_true_value: Shows that ultrasound-driven CNNs can predict continuous F0 and maximum voiced frequency for a continuous vocoder without a binary voicing decision. Interpolated F0 targets from articulation were already prior work (Liu et al. 2016, Gonzalez et al. 2017, Taguchi and Kaburagi 2018); the new step, MVF from the group's speech-synthesis vocoder carrying voicing in place of the flag, is not shown to help: the listening test finds no significant difference and the F0 RMSE comparison uses different reference contours.
canon_before: Articulation-to-speech systems predicted an explicit voiced/unvoiced decision plus F0 (31 pattern-match studies, 12 prior), several of them with interpolated continuous log F0 as the regression target (EMA, PMA; Taguchi and Kaburagi 2018: 10.49 Hz F0 RMSE, 10.32% v/uv error, one speaker), and used parametric vocoders (34 of 51 ultrasound-to-speech studies).
delta_from_canon: Drops the binary voicing flag and lets maximum voiced frequency carry voicing, while swapping one parametric vocoder for another (continuous vocoder in place of MGLSA); no condition isolates this change from the change of F0 reference contour.
position_in_field: Ultrasound-to-speech synthesis with speaker-specific CNNs and a continuous parametric vocoder; standard on M06 and M08, behind the best comparable work on M12 (no intelligibility test; EMA-driven synthesis had 30.1% listener WER in 2018). The same lineage replaced the continuous vocoder with WaveGlow a year later (significant listener preference, MCD 5.47 to 5.37 dB).
practical_value: Removes the separate V/UV classifier, but brings no measured quality gain: naturalness with all parameters predicted is about equal (19.91 baseline vs 18.59), spectral prediction limits quality more than excitation (43.45 with predicted excitation and original spectra, 18.59 with both predicted), and the field has moved to neural vocoders.
axes_moved: Excitation representation for articulation-to-speech (continuous F0 plus MVF, no voicing flag).
axes_unresolved: Like-for-like F0 error on voiced frames, a continuous-F0-plus-flag control, intelligibility, unseen speakers, repeated runs, latency.
technical_limits: Single-frame CNN input by choice; baseline and proposed F0 scored against different reference contours; false voicing in MVF predictions (authors); MVF RMSE 654-1177 Hz by speaker.
evaluation_limits: Nine test sentences per speaker; no stated significance test for the RMSE claim; no chance level or class balance for V/UV accuracy; MUSHRA naturalness only (23 listeners, 12 sentences), no significant pair; no intelligibility test; no seeds or repeated runs.
deployment_limits: Offline, speaker-dependent, vocalized reading; real-time synthesis asserted without latency or hardware figures.
scope_limits: Four Hungarian speakers, about 15 minutes of recordings in total, speaker-specific models, vocalized speech only.
input_modality: ultrasound tongue imaging
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound tongue imaging system capturing midsagittal tongue ultrasound cine at ~82 fps.
metrics: Table 1 averages over four speakers (9 test sentences each): V/UV accuracy 78.84% (baseline); F0 RMSE 65.34 Hz (baseline, discontinuous reference) vs ContF0 RMSE 30.56 Hz (interpolated reference, all frames); MVF RMSE 864.69 Hz. MUSHRA naturalness (Fig. 3): natural 86.49; analysis-synthesis 56.06 vs 55.03; predicted excitation with original spectra 40.87 vs 43.45 (not significant); all predicted 19.91 vs 18.59.
evaluation_mode: Offline, speaker-dependent; objective per-speaker test sets plus online MUSHRA naturalness test with 23 native Hungarian listeners; no intelligibility test.

evidence.statement: ContF0 RMSE 30.56 Hz vs baseline F0 RMSE 65.34 Hz, but against different reference contours (interpolated vs discontinuous); no test named for the stated significance.
MUSHRA: 43.45 vs 40.87 with predicted excitation and original spectra; no tested pair differs significantly.
Interpolated continuous F0 targets from articulatory signals were already used by Liu et al. (2016), Gonzalez et al. (2017) and Taguchi and Kaburagi (2018), all with a voicing flag.
No intelligibility test; 11 earlier studies tested listener intelligibility of speech synthesized from non-acoustic signals.

en.summary: Continuous F0 targets from articulation were prior work; MVF carrying voicing instead of a flag is new but unproven: the F0 RMSE gain uses different reference contours and naturalness is not better.
en.sensor: Midsagittal ultrasound tongue imaging (Micro system, 81.67 fps), one 64x128 frame per prediction
en.task: Ultrasound-to-speech synthesis with a continuous vocoder (continuous F0, maximum voiced frequency, MGC-LSP)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: ContF0 RMSE 30.56 Hz vs 65.34 Hz for discontinuous F0, measured against different reference contours; MUSHRA naturalness 43.45 vs 40.87 with predicted excitation and original spectra, not significant; four speakers, 9 test sentences each
en.limitations: Continuous F0 targets from articulation were prior work; RMSE comparison not like-for-like and untested; no significant naturalness gain; no intelligibility test, no flag-plus-continuous-F0 control, no seeds; speaker-dependent, vocalized speech only; real-time claim unmeasured.

title: Video-Driven Speech Reconstruction using Generative Adversarial Networks
expert_take_short: Direct-waveform GAN (M06) and speech-encoder perceptual loss (M02) are early but standard; the perceptual loss carries the words. Unseen-speaker WER 40.5% (successor 16%); no listener test.
expert_take_long: The paper [@vougioukas2019video] changes two components, both standard on its evidence: waveform samples straight from a Wasserstein GAN (M06) and a perceptual loss through a pretrained speech encoder (M02). The perceptual loss carries the words: without it WER is 83.3%, near the 81% of random GRID slot choices (inference, for an ASR emitting only GRID words). Waveform output is not shown to help: a WORLD-vocoder system beat it on ESTOI within a year [@michelsanti2020vocoder], and its successor's gain came with new critics and losses (M06). Its unseen-speaker test goes beyond its cited priors, but 40.5% WER is not shown intelligible without a chance level or listeners. Evaluation (M12) is behind: "natural sounding" rests on no listener test.
expert_true_value: A foundational lip-to-speech paper because it demonstrates intelligible direct audio generation from silent video, but the unseen-speaker degradation is substantial and the method is frontal-view only.
canon_before: Earlier video-to-speech pipelines often relied on intermediate speech features or text and were mostly speaker-dependent.
delta_from_canon: This model learns direct silent-video to raw-audio synthesis with GAN and perceptual losses and evaluates both seen and unseen speakers.
position_in_field: Core early video-driven speech reconstruction work.
practical_value: Useful as a historically important baseline for direct video-to-audio synthesis.
axes_moved: direct_audio_generation; lip_to_speech; synchrony
axes_unresolved: unseen-speaker fidelity, broader visual conditions, and natural voice quality remain unresolved.
technical_limits: Artifacts remain, unseen-speaker voice consistency is poor, and the model is restricted to frontal faces.
evaluation_limits: All reported experiments are on GRID, which constrains linguistic and visual diversity.
deployment_limits: In-the-wild pose variation and real-world deployment are future work.
scope_limits: Frontal silent-video speech reconstruction only.
input_modality: silent frontal face video
sensor_hardware: camera
metrics: In the speaker-dependent setup the model reports WER 26.6%, STOI 0.518, MCD 22.29, and AV confidence 4.4 with one-frame offset; unseen speakers drop to WER 40.5% and PESQ 1.24.
evaluation_mode: GRID speaker-dependent and speaker-independent evaluation using PESQ, WER, AV synchrony, STOI, and MCD plus ablations

evidence.statement: The abstract says the model directly synthesizes audio from silent video and evaluates both speaker-dependent and speaker-independent scenarios on GRID.
Table 2 reports speaker-dependent WER 26.6%, STOI 0.518, MCD 22.29, and AV confidence 4.4 with one-frame offset for the proposed model.
The ablation study says the adversarial loss is necessary for speech production and the perceptual loss is critical for preserving content.
The conclusion says unseen speakers still produce degraded voices and that the method operates solely on frontal faces, leaving in-the-wild video as future work.

en.summary: Direct-waveform GAN (M06) and speech-encoder perceptual loss (M02) are early but standard; the perceptual loss carries the words. Unseen-speaker WER 40.5% (successor 16%); no listener test.
en.sensor: Camera (silent frontal face video)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: Seen GRID speakers: ASR WER 26.6%, STOI 0.518 (Lip2AudSpec 32.5%, 0.446), PESQ 1.71 below Lip2AudSpec 1.82; without the perceptual loss WER 83.3%. Unseen speakers: WER 40.5%, STOI 0.445, PESQ 1.24.
en.limitations: GRID only, single runs, no listener test or chance level; a persistent hum lowers PESQ; unseen speakers get wrong-gender or morphing voices and 40% to 60% WER per speaker; the perceptual encoder's training speakers are unstated; frontal faces only.

title: Harnessing AI for Speech Reconstruction using Multi-view Silent Video Feed
venue: Proceedings of the 26th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '18)
expert_take_short: Multi-view input (M05) is new for video-to-speech but standard on its evidence: 2 speakers, gains overstated (11.4% in Table 1, 26% in text); PESQ only, no listener test (M12).
expert_take_long: The paper [@kumar2018harnessing] changes one component, the camera input (M05), feeding two OuluVS2 views to a video-to-speech regressor; no earlier video-to-speech ledger paper names multi-view input (Appendix). The design is new for speech output but standard on its evidence: two speakers, no repeats or split stated, best pairs only (Sec. 4.3, Sec. 6). Table 1 gives +11.4% and +12.2% PESQ for 0°+30° over 0° (inference), not the stated 26% and 27%. The 30° to 60° placement rule rests on two pairs; follow-up work by the same group finds 0°+45° best and 0°+60° below 0°+90° [@kumar2019lipper] [concurrent], and a 1.1% gain for 0°+30° on held-out data [@uttam2019hushhush] [later] (inference). The evaluation (M12) is behind: PESQ only, where the systems it builds on all ran listener tests.
expert_true_value: Introduces multi-camera synchronized video input to reconstruct intelligible and synchronized speech audio directly, overcoming pose limitations in prior lipreading works that generated text only.
canon_before: Prior lipreading and speech reconstruction works were mostly single-view and generated text transcripts rather than synchronized audio.
delta_from_canon: Introduces multi-view video input instead of single view and reconstructs synchronized speech audio directly rather than text, with consideration of camera placement to handle pose variability.
position_in_field: Early work demonstrating multi-view silent-video based audio speech reconstruction using deep learning.
practical_value: Offers practical improvements for applications needing synchronized speech audio from silent video, including assistive tech, security, and multimedia, but requires further robustness and deployment engineering.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: Generalization beyond controlled dataset (OuluVS2) unknown.
technical_limits: Requires controlled lighting, multiple camera views, speaker-dependent training; limited robustness to real-world variability.
evaluation_limits: Evaluation limited to controlled dataset (OuluVS2) with limited speakers and sessions; does not test unseen vocabulary or natural noisy environments.
deployment_limits: Requires multiple cameras placed optimally (30° to 60° apart), controlled lighting and speaker-dependent training; large-scale or real-world deployment constrained by hardware and environment challenges.
scope_limits: Focus restricted to multi-view silent-video speech reconstruction using deep learning on controlled datasets.
input_modality: multi-view silent video feed
sensor_hardware: Multiple cameras recording video from 5 different angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°).
vocabulary_type: Common English phrases and digits; no mention of open vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: Limited (phrases, digits, TIMIT sentences from OuluVS2 dataset).
metrics: Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) scores used for quantitative audio quality assessment comparing original and reconstructed audio signals.
evaluation_mode: Experimental study on OuluVS2 with quantitative metric PESQ.

evidence.statement: This paper presents the world's first multi-view speech reading and reconstruction system generating intelligible speech audio from silent video feeds.
The method uses a CNN-LSTM based model to learn mapping from silent multi-view video frames to speech audio represented with LPC features, enabling synchronized audio reconstruction.
Evaluations were conducted on the OuluVS2 dataset featuring 53 speakers recorded from 5 different angles; PESQ was used as metric to assess audio quality of reconstructed speech.
Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) scores showed that combining camera views around 30° to 60° yields up to ~26-27% improvement over single best view in reconstructed audio quality.
Optimal camera placement around 30° to 60°, and availability of multiple cameras, are essential for best speech reconstruction results; deployment requires multiple cameras and controlled conditions.
Dataset is controlled with multiple views and different speakers but limited vocabulary; generalization beyond OuluVS2, speaker-independency, and real-world robustness remain unaddressed.

en.summary: Multi-view input (M05) is new for video-to-speech but standard on its evidence: 2 speakers, gains overstated (11.4% in Table 1, 26% in text); PESQ only, no listener test (M12).
en.sensor: Two of five synchronized OuluVS2 camera views (0/30/45/60/90 deg)
en.task: Speech waveform reconstruction from multi-view silent video
en.vocabulary: OuluVS2 phrases, digit sequences and TIMIT sentences
en.speaker: Two reported speakers (1 and 10); training split not stated
en.key_result: PESQ 1.9683 / 1.9978 for 0+30 deg against 1.7674 / 1.7812 for 0 deg (Table 1)
en.limitations: Two speakers, no repeats or split stated, best pairs only, PESQ only with no listener test; every stated gain exceeds Table 1.

title: Visual-Only Recognition of Normal, Whispered and Silent Speech
venue: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
expert_take_short: Ahead on data: the first public three-mode lip-video corpus. Standard on transfer: the silent drop was known, and most of it is test-mode difficulty, not the training mode.
expert_take_long: The paper changes M11 (a public lip-video corpus with normal, whispered and silent speech) and M04 (a train-mode by test-mode grid). The corpus is ahead and was still the visual reference in 2023. The transfer finding is standard: the silent drop was known from ultrasound and visual-whisper work, and on a fixed silent test set training on silent speech gains only 2.5 to 3.2 points, so the authors' "significant performance drop" from vocalised-only training, given without a significance test, outruns the evidence.
expert_true_value: The first public lip-video corpus with normal, whispered and silent speech; its transfer grid shows that most of the normal-to-silent drop is test-mode difficulty, with silent training gaining only 2.5 to 3.2 points on a fixed silent test.
canon_before: Training on vocalised speech was known to degrade silent recognition from a 4-speaker ultrasound study (2010); EMG corpora already held three speaking modes (2014).
delta_from_canon: Adds a 53-speaker public lip-video corpus in three modes and a full train-mode by test-mode grid with 10 runs; does not separate the train-mode effect from test-mode difficulty.
position_in_field: Ahead on the corpus (M11), still the visual normal-and-silent reference in 2023; standard on the transfer finding (M04).
practical_value: Useful as a speaker-independent benchmark for silent lipreading; the small train-mode effect does not by itself justify collecting silent training data.
axes_moved: public three-mode visual data
axes_unresolved: train-mode vs test-mode separation; significance tests; open vocabulary; mixed-mode training at fixed data size
technical_limits: Closed 10-class tasks; matched silent accuracy 62.2% (digits) and 64.4% (phrases).
evaluation_limits: No chance level or significance test; seeds and stopping rule not stated; utterance boundaries still under correction at publication.
deployment_limits: Offline laboratory study; no deployment claim.
scope_limits: Visual-only, frontal view, digits and short phrases.
input_modality: visual speech video across normal, whispered, and silent modes
sensor_hardware: Three cameras capturing frontal, 45-degree, and profile views at 1280x780 and 30 fps
vocabulary_type: digits and short phrases
vocabulary_size: 10 digits and 10 fixed short phrases
