metrics: Normal-trained: digits 68.0% normal vs 59.7% silent test; phrases 69.7% vs 61.2%. Silent test: silent-trained 62.2% (digits) and 64.4% (phrases); whispered-trained 65.1% on silent phrases.
evaluation_mode: Speaker-independent splits (digits 30/10/13, phrases 20/8/11 speakers), 3 x 3 train-mode by test-mode grid, mean and SD over 10 runs.

evidence.statement: The database contains 53 participants for digits and 39 participants for phrases, recorded in normal, whispered, and silent speech with frontal, 45-degree, and profile cameras.

In the digits experiment, Table 1 reports matched-condition classification rates of 68.0% for normal, 70.5% for whispered, and 62.2% for silent speech, while normal-trained testing on silent drops to 59.7%.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 1. Mean classification rate (and standard deviation) for the digits experiment.

evidence.statement: In the phrases experiment, Table 2 reports matched-condition classification rates of 69.7% for normal, 70.8% for whispered, and 64.4% for silent speech, while normal-trained testing on silent drops to 61.2%.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2. Mean classification rate (and standard deviation) for the phrases experiment.

evidence.statement: The conclusion states that vocalised training data are not the best approach for silent recognition; on a fixed silent test set, silent training gains 2.5 (digits) and 3.2 (phrases) points over normal training, and whispered training does as well as silent training on silent tests.

en.summary: Ahead on data: the first public three-mode lip-video corpus. Standard on transfer: the silent drop was known, and most of it is test-mode difficulty, not the training mode.
en.sensor: Video cameras, frontal view used (45-degree and profile recorded)
en.task: Closed-set visual-only utterance classification across normal, whispered and silent speech
en.speaker: Speaker-independent (digits 30/10/13, phrases 20/8/11 train/validation/test speakers)
en.key_result: Normal-trained: 68.0 to 59.7% (digits) and 69.7 to 61.2% (phrases) from normal to silent test; on the silent test, silent training gains only 2.5 and 3.2 points over normal training, and whispered training is best for silent phrases (65.1%).
en.limitations: Closed 10-class tasks; train-mode and test-mode effects not separated; no significance tests or chance level; seeds and stopping rule not stated; utterance boundaries still under correction at publication.

title: Improved Speech Reconstruction from Silent Video
venue: 2017 IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops (ICCVW)
expert_take_short: Optical-flow tower (M05) and mel-to-linear post-net (M06) are standard: no flow gain in Table 5; trails Le Cornu on S3; no listener test (M12); Lip2Wav's re-run: 27.83% vs 14.08% WER.
expert_take_long: The paper [@ephrat2017improved] changes the visual input (M05: an optical-flow tower beside full-face pixels) and the decoder (M06: a mel-to-linear post-net, then Griffin-Lim); both are standard on its own evidence. Flow lowers STOI from 0.670 to 0.665 on GRID S3 in one reported split (Table 5); the full-model row adds 0.015, but it mixes two synthesis paths (M06). The gain over Vid2speech [@ephrat2017vid2speech] holds on objective scores (S4 STOI 0.584 to 0.700, Table 3), but on S3 Le Cornu and Milner [@lecornu2017generating] [concurrent] score higher ESTOI (0.437 against 0.398) and PESQ (2.055 against 1.974) in the same table. The evaluation (M12) drops the listener test both comparators ran; in Lip2Wav's [later] re-run of this method in its own setup it scores 27.83% WER on GRID and 53.52% on TCD-TIMIT, against 14.08% and 31.26% for Lip2Wav [@prajwal2020learning]. The "unconstrained dictionary" result rests on one of three TCD-TIMIT speakers (Table 4).
expert_true_value: Its lasting value is the move from LSP coefficients to mel and linear spectrograms with Griffin-Lim, which lifted objective scores over Vid2speech (GRID S4 STOI 0.584 to 0.700). Its own ablation does not support the optical-flow tower (STOI 0.670 pixels only, 0.665 with flow, GRID S3, one reported split), it trails Le Cornu and Milner on S3 ESTOI and PESQ, and it has no listener test; in Lip2Wav's re-run of the method under its own setup it scores 27.83% GRID WER against 14.08% for Lip2Wav.
canon_before: Video-to-speech speechreading methods mostly treated as visual-to-text classification with limited vocabularies; voxel-to-audio regression methods existed but yielded robotic or unintelligible speech due to limited network architectures and loss functions.
delta_from_canon: Against its predecessors (Vid2speech: full-face CNN to LSP with unvoiced excitation; Le Cornu and Milner: mouth AAM features to STRAIGHT), it predicts mel spectrograms, adds an optical-flow tower and a Tacotron-style mel-to-linear post-net, and inverts with Griffin-Lim. Only the spectrogram output is backed by its results; the flow tower shows no gain, and the post-net gain (0.015 STOI, one speaker, one split) comes from a full-model row that mixes two synthesis paths.
position_in_field: Early speaker-dependent video-to-speech baseline on GRID and TCD-TIMIT; superseded by sequence-to-sequence and vocoder-based systems (Lip2Wav 2020 halves its GRID WER in Lip2Wav's own re-run of the method).
practical_value: A speaker-dependent GRID and TCD-TIMIT baseline with spectrogram output and Griffin-Lim; useful as a historical reference point, not as a design to copy: the flow tower adds nothing in its ablation and the intelligibility claim is untested by listeners or ASR in the paper.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: speaker-independent reconstruction; real-time processing; in-the-wild capture; unconstrained vocabulary full intelligibility
technical_limits: Speaker-dependent modeling requiring per-speaker training; unconstrained vocabularies only partially intelligible; audio quality still limited; no demonstration of real-time or unseen speaker generalization.
evaluation_limits: Objective scores only, single random splits per corpus with no seeds, intervals or repeated runs; comparator scores in Table 3 without stated split or data parity; S3 'Ours' row mixes two synthesis modes; no listener or ASR test although both comparators ran listener tests; speaker-dependent, no unseen-speaker test; unseen-word share in TCD-TIMIT not given.
deployment_limits: Speaker-dependent model requiring per-speaker training on cropped, registered full-face video; no demonstrated use on unknown speakers or unconstrained real-world conditions; no real-time deployment shown.
scope_limits: Speaker-dependent speech reconstruction from full-face silent video; two benchmark datasets GRID and TCD-TIMIT Lipspeakers; no unseen speaker or real-world environment tested.
input_modality: silent full-face video frames plus dense optical flow derived from consecutive frames
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: mixed benchmark vocabulary
vocabulary_size: 51-word GRID grammar plus many unseen words in TCD-TIMIT testing
metrics: STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, ViSQOL only. GRID S3 best-of-two-synthesis row STOI 0.680, ESTOI 0.398, PESQ 1.974, ViSQOL 3.349; S4 Lin-synth STOI 0.700, ESTOI 0.462, PESQ 1.922; TCD-TIMIT Lipspeaker 3 Lin-synth STOI 0.630, ESTOI 0.447, PESQ 1.612 (Lipspeakers 1-2: 0.318, 0.357). No listener test or ASR WER in the paper; Lip2Wav (2020) re-ran the method under its own setup: 27.83% GRID WER and 53.52% TCD-TIMIT WER.
evaluation_mode: Objective speech quality and intelligibility metrics plus human intelligibility study and ablation experiments.

evidence.statement: We present an end-to-end model based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) for generating an intelligible and natural-sounding acoustic speech signal from silent video frames of a speaking person, trained and evaluated on GRID and TCD-TIMIT datasets with significant quality improvements over prior methods.

The proposed model includes a dual-tower Residual neural network (ResNet) encoder processing grayscale face images and optical flow separately, whose embeddings are concatenated and fed to a decoder and a post-processing CBHG network inspired by Tacotron to produce mel and linear spectrograms representing speech.

Experiments are performed on GRID dataset speakers S1-S4 using 80/20 train/test splits and on TCD-TIMIT lipspeakers 1-3, showing quantitative improvements on objective intelligibility metrics (STOI, ESTOI) and speech quality metrics (PESQ, ViSQOL).

On GRID test speaker S3 the model achieves STOI 0.68, ESTOI 0.398, PESQ 1.974, ViSQOL 3.349 when reconstructing speech; on TCD-TIMIT lipspeaker 3 it achieves STOI 0.63, ESTOI 0.447, PESQ 1.612, with many test words outside training.

The method is explicitly speaker-dependent requiring per-speaker training; the TCD-TIMIT dataset unconstrained vocabulary setting results in less intelligible reconstructed speech; no unseen speaker or real-time deployment evaluation was conducted.
The model requires individual per-speaker training on registered full-face video frames, limiting real-world deployment; speaker independence and in-the-wild robustness are not addressed.

The approach models speechreading as a direct regression from silent video frames to speech spectrogram features instead of a classification approach, allowing reconstruction of speech from unconstrained word dictionaries.

The method improves prior video-to-speech work by fusing raw pixels and optical flow features within a dual-stream CNN encoder, replacing VGG with ResNet, and employing a Tacotron-based post-processing network to enhance speech naturalness and smoothness.

Evaluation includes objective intelligibility and speech quality metrics, human intelligibility experiments (Mechanical Turk), and ablations of optical flow and postnet components, demonstrating pixels carry most information but flow and postnet improve results.
The system reconstructs multi-frame speech audio by jointly predicting mel-scale spectrograms over multiple consecutive video frames, improving smoothness over prior single-frame prediction methods.

en.summary: Optical-flow tower (M05) and mel-to-linear post-net (M06) are standard: no flow gain in Table 5; trails Le Cornu on S3; no listener test (M12); Lip2Wav's re-run: 27.83% vs 14.08% WER.
en.sensor: Camera (full-face video plus optical flow)
en.vocabulary: 51-word GRID grammar plus unseen words in TCD-TIMIT
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: GRID S4 STOI 0.700 vs 0.584 for Vid2speech, but behind Le Cornu and Milner on S3 ESTOI (0.398 vs 0.437) and PESQ; in Lip2Wav's re-run of the method, 27.83% GRID WER vs 14.08% for Lip2Wav
en.limitations: Speaker-dependent; objective metrics only, no listener or ASR test; single splits without seeds or intervals; optical-flow tower shows no gain in its ablation; post-net gain comes from a row mixing two synthesis paths; TCD-TIMIT result holds for one of three speakers.

title: Lip2AudSpec: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Lip Movements Video
venue: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
expert_take_short: Bottleneck target (M02) and auditory-spectrogram route (M06) are standard; gains rest on one speaker, a re-implemented baseline and a vocabulary-cued test on four seen GRID speakers.
expert_take_long: Lip2AudSpec [@akbari2018lip2audspec] changes the training target (M02, a noisy 32-unit autoencoder bottleneck) and the acoustic route (M06, an 8 kHz auditory spectrogram with iterative inversion); both are standard. The bottleneck gain is shown on one speaker in one run, and four of five bottleneck settings score lower PESQ than direct spectrogram regression (Tables 7-8). The pitch and naturalness gains are not credited to the representation, because the baseline is a re-implementation with an unreported protocol and no ablation swaps the representation. On the same four GRID speakers later work reaches STOI 0.731 against 0.446 for Lip2AudSpec [@kefalas2023large; @vougioukas2019video], and on unseen speakers it produced no intelligible speech [@vougioukas2019video].
expert_true_value: Demonstrates that leveraging a deep compressed auditory spectrogram representation as a reconstruction target materially improves intelligibility and pitch preservation in lip-to-speech systems over prior spectrogram or LPC-based methods on a well-known benchmark.
canon_before: Prior lip-to-speech systems like Vid2Speech reconstructed speech but suffered weak pitch and quality due to target representations missing excitation parameters.
delta_from_canon: Shifts from using classical LPC or spectrogram targets to auditory spectrogram compressed by a deep autoencoder for better speaker and pitch preservation; evaluates with human transcription and objective metrics.
position_in_field: Strong lip-to-speech reconstruction baseline focused on improved acoustic targets rather than solely on visual feature encoders.
practical_value: Useful as a reference lip-to-speech system that highlights the impact of appropriate speech representation on intelligibility and speaker characteristics preservation.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: open-vocabulary reconstruction, speaker independence beyond GRID, richer articulation features beyond lips
technical_limits: Lip-only video input misses tongue and throat information affecting some vowels and high-frequency speech; only evaluated on limited closed vocabulary and speaker set.
evaluation_limits: Evaluations are on the 4-speaker GRID corpus only; human intelligibility measured via Mechanical Turk limited to vocabulary and speakers in dataset.
deployment_limits: Trained and evaluated strictly on 4 GRID speakers with controlled vocabulary; lacks real-world recordings and speaker variability; lip-only input misses tongue/throat cues affecting vowel/high-frequency fidelity.
scope_limits: Closed vocabulary lip-to-speech reconstruction on GRID corpus videos of 4 speakers only.
input_modality: silent lip video
sensor_hardware: camera
vocabulary_type: closed vocabulary
vocabulary_size: 51 words
metrics: Average over four speakers: STMI 0.80 vs 0.52 baseline, PESQ 1.88 vs 1.76 baseline, Corr2D 0.88 vs 0.61 baseline; human word accuracy 55.8% vs 50.9%, correct gender 85.1% vs 43.2%.
evaluation_mode: Quantitative objective metrics (Corr2D, PESQ, STMI) plus human transcription and quality/naturalness/female/male recognition surveys on Mechanical Turk.

evidence.statement: Introduces a deep neural network that reconstructs intelligible speech from silent lip movement videos using auditory spectrogram targets and compares it to Vid2Speech.
The model first compresses auditory spectrograms through an autoencoder and then predicts those bottleneck features from silent lip video using CNN, LSTM, and fully connected layers.
Average STMI improved from 0.52 to 0.80, PESQ improved from 1.76 to 1.88, Corr2D improved from 0.61 to 0.88 compared to Vid2Speech across four GRID corpus speakers.
Human evaluation showed average word accuracy improved from 50.9% to 55.8%, and correct gender recognition improved from 43.2% to 85.1% over Vid2Speech.

Lip-only video input misses tongue and throat information, making it difficult to reconstruct high frequency details and different vowels accurately; limited to 4 speakers and closed vocabulary in GRID corpus.
The network is trained and tested on a small closed-vocabulary dataset of 4 GRID corpus speakers; lacking real-world generalization and speaker variability for direct practical deployment.

en.summary: Bottleneck target (M02) and auditory-spectrogram route (M06) are standard; gains rest on one speaker, a re-implemented baseline and a vocabulary-cued test on four seen GRID speakers.
en.sensor: Camera (silent lip video)
en.task: Speech synthesis from silent lip video
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Human word accuracy 55.8% vs 50.9% baseline; STMI 0.80 vs 0.52, four GRID speakers
en.limitations: Only four GRID speakers and closed vocabulary; lip-only input misses tongue and throat cues; no real-world recordings.

title: Seeing Through Noise: Visually Driven Speaker Separation and Enhancement
expert_take_short: Strong audiovisual speech separation and enhancement leveraging face video for speaker-dependent masking; not a silent speech interface paper.
expert_take_long: This paper presents a visually driven speech separation and enhancement system that uses speaker-dependent video-to-speech network predictions as spectrogram priors to build masking filters over mixed audio input. Experiments on synthetic two-speaker mixtures from GRID and TCD-TIMIT show the approach significantly outperforms audio-only baselines and raw video-to-speech outputs, with ratio masking achieving GRID SDR 5.62 and PESQ 2.6 (vs. audio-only 1.74/1.85), and TCD-TIMIT SDR 8.68 and PESQ 2.71 (vs. audio-only 2.91/2.16). Enhancement experiments similarly surpass raw predictions. An unknown-speaker transfer experiment on GRID demonstrates reduced but viable performance after limited fine-tuning (SDR 3.06, PESQ 2.42). The approach leverages visual information to overcome challenges in audio-only same-gender speaker separation but still requires known faces and training per speaker, limiting direct application in silent speech interfaces. Although effective for audiovisual separation and enhancement in controlled datasets, the method has medium-high deployment readiness gaps due to reliance on speaker-dependent models, lack of comprehensive real-world noisy testing, and limited zero-shot generalization.
expert_true_value: Demonstrates that visual speech predictions can effectively guide mask construction for separating or enhancing a known target speaker from noisy audio mixtures, notably improving on audio-only separation especially for same-gender mixtures.
canon_before: Audio-only speech separation methods struggled especially on same-gender mixtures, and prior video-to-speech methods generated speech directly without using them as separation priors.
delta_from_canon: Reframes vid2speech predictions as an intermediate prior for constructing masks for speech separation and enhancement, rather than as final speech output.
position_in_field: Strong 2017 audiovisual speech separation paper that effectively uses visual priors for masking, adjacent to but distinct from silent speech interface research.
practical_value: Useful in scenarios requiring isolation of a visible speaker's voice from mixtures or background noise using audiovisual data.
axes_moved: system_design; evaluation
axes_unresolved: real-world multi-speaker video; zero-shot unknown speakers; end-to-end training
technical_limits: Limited to speaker-dependent models; unknown-speaker separation requires fine-tuning with audiovisual samples; evaluated mostly on synthetic mixtures; real-world noisy environment performance not fully benchmarked.
evaluation_limits: Evaluations use synthetic benchmark mixtures (GRID and TCD-TIMIT) with known speakers; unknown speaker separation evaluated with 5-min fine-tuning; no large-scale real-world noisy environment benchmarks.
deployment_limits: Requires visible speaker face video and speaker-dependent model training; unknown speaker separation requires fine-tuning with audiovisual data.
scope_limits: Audiovisual speaker separation and enhancement tested on synthetic GRID and TCD-TIMIT two-speaker mixtures and limited unknown speaker transfer on GRID.
input_modality: audio plus face video
sensor_hardware: camera + microphone
metrics: Table 1 reports GRID ratio-mask separation SDR 5.62 and PESQ 2.6 vs. audio-only 1.74 and 1.85; TCD-TIMIT ratio-mask SDR 8.68 and PESQ 2.71 vs. audio-only 2.91 and 2.16. Table 3 shows unknown-speaker GRID fine-tuned separation SDR 3.06 and PESQ 2.42.
evaluation_mode: Speech separation and enhancement evaluated with SDR, SIR, SAR, PESQ metrics, plus unknown-speaker transfer test.

evidence.statement: Uses face video to separate or enhance a target speaker from noisy mixtures by applying video-to-speech neural network predictions as filters on the mixed audio. Compares results to audio-only baselines and raw vid2speech predictions.

The system predicts mel-scale speech spectrograms from the speaker's face video using a vid2speech neural network and uses these spectrograms as control signals to construct time-frequency masks (binary or ratio) to separate or enhance the target speaker from the audio mixture.

Table 1 reports GRID ratio-mask separation SDR 5.62 and PESQ 2.6 vs. audio-only 1.74 and 1.85; TCD-TIMIT ratio-mask SDR 8.68 and PESQ 2.71 vs. audio-only 2.91 and 2.16. Table 3 shows unknown-speaker GRID fine-tuned separation SDR 3.06 and PESQ 2.42.

Evaluations use synthetic benchmark mixtures (GRID and TCD-TIMIT) with known speakers; unknown speaker separation evaluated with 5-min fine-tuning; no large-scale real-world noisy environment benchmarks.
Requires visible speaker face video and speaker-dependent model training; unknown speaker separation requires fine-tuning with audiovisual data.
This is an audiovisual separation system, not a silent speech interface. Unknown speaker separation still requires fine-tuning and visible face video, limiting immediate deployment.

en.summary: Uses visual speech predictions from face video to build masks that separate or enhance a target speaker from audio mixtures, beating audio-only separation on GRID and TCD-TIMIT. Not an SSI paper.
en.sensor: Camera plus microphone (face video and audio)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: GRID separation SDR 5.62, PESQ 2.6 vs audio-only 1.74, 1.85
en.limitations: Not SSI; speaker-dependent models, unknown speakers need fine-tuning, and evaluation uses synthetic two-speaker mixtures.

title: Updating the Silent Speech Challenge benchmark with deep learning
expert_take_short: Kaldi DNN-HMM cuts SSC WER from 17.4% to 6.45% (M06, M12: standard), but with the same bigram its own GMM gives 12.71%, so the DNN halves WER; one speaker, single runs.
expert_take_long: The paper [@ji2018updating] changes the recognizer (M06), a Kaldi DNN-HMM plus deep-autoencoder (DAE) features, and resets the Silent Speech Challenge (SSC) reference number (M12). Both are standard: the same group had already run a DNN-HMM on the SSC (38% WER, §1.2), and a multimodal DAE on tongue and lip images predates it [@jaumardhakoun2016articulatory]. The drop from 17.4% to 6.45% WER holds, but with the same WSJ bigram the paper's own LDA+MLLT triphone GMM reaches 12.71% (Table 3), so against its best GMM the DNN halves the WER rather than cutting it by "almost a factor of 3" (inference). The number is tied to one speaker, 1023 test words, single runs and a closed 5,000-word bigram; an end-to-end model with a 65,000-word language model reached 20.5% on the same test [@kimura2020end]. The DAE's advantage at 5 dimensions rests on DCT systems that fail outright (98.24% to 100% WER), a collapse the paper leaves unexplained, so it does not show the DAE keeps information DCT loses.
expert_true_value: A benchmark-anchored SSI paper: on the same archive and decoding, the DNN-HMM brings SSC WER from 17.4% to 6.45%; against the paper's own triphone2b GMM-HMM with the same WSJ bigram (12.71%) it halves the WER.
canon_before: The Silent Speech Challenge was a fixed ultrasound-plus-lip benchmark whose published reference point was 17.4% WER with an HTK GMM-HMM system.
delta_from_canon: The paper reruns the benchmark with matched decoding in Kaldi; a DNN-HMM reaches 6.45% WER with the closed WSJ 5k bigram and 11.44% with a less task-specific 5k bigram.
position_in_field: Canonical benchmark update for ultrasound-plus-lip silent speech recognition.
practical_value: High for benchmarking and for understanding what part of the gain comes from model class versus feature or language-model choice.
axes_moved: benchmark reproducibility; evaluation; modeling baseline
axes_unresolved: speaker independence; larger corpora; live deployment
technical_limits: Everything remains single-speaker, controlled, and benchmark-bounded; there is no evidence of speaker independence or real-world robustness.
evaluation_limits: The archive is small and single-speaker, so large gains on this benchmark do not automatically transfer to broader SSI deployment.
deployment_limits: No live deployment, calibration burden analysis, or user-facing interface is reported.
scope_limits: Speaker-dependent ultrasound-plus-lip benchmark study.
input_modality: ultrasound tongue imaging and lip video
sensor_hardware: Ultrasound transducer placed under the chin plus a small lip video camera
vocabulary_type: continuous-speech benchmark vocabulary
vocabulary_size: WSJ0 5000-word lexicon; task-specific WSJ 5k bigram and less task-specific CSR 5k bigram
metrics: Table 2 reports 17.4% WER for the original HTK benchmark, 17.4% for a Kaldi GMM-HMM (stage and LM not named; equal to Table 3's triphone2b under the CSR LM), and 6.45% for the Kaldi DNN-HMM with 30-element DCT features. Table 3 shows DNN WER of 6.45% with the task-specific WSJ LM and 11.44% with the less task-specific CSR LM; the triphone2b GMM-HMM gives 12.71% with the WSJ LM.
evaluation_mode: Direct comparison to the original Silent Speech Challenge benchmark plus language-model and feature sweeps on the same single-speaker archive.

evidence.statement: The abstract says the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge benchmark is updated with deep-learning results and that a best word error rate of 6.4% is obtained compared with the published 17.4% value.
The Silent Speech Challenge benchmark is a single-speaker archive built from ultrasound and lip video recorded from one native English speaker with an independent test corpus.
Table 2 reports 17.4% WER for the original HTK benchmark, 17.4% for the Kaldi GMM-HMM reproduction, and 6.45% for the Kaldi DNN-HMM using 30-element DCT features.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2. Comparison with original HTK result of [52], using 30-element DCT features

evidence.statement: Table 3 shows that with 30-element DCT features the DNN system gets 11.44% WER under the WSJ language model and 6.45% under the task-specific CSR language model.
evidence.section_or_location: Table 3. Comparing results for the 2 different LM, for 30-element feature vectors of both types

en.summary: Kaldi DNN-HMM cuts SSC WER from 17.4% to 6.45% (M06, M12: standard), but with the same bigram its own GMM gives 12.71%, so the DNN halves WER; one speaker, single runs.
en.sensor: Under-chin ultrasound transducer plus lip camera
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 6.45% WER on the SSC test (Kaldi DNN-HMM, 30 DCT features, closed WSJ 5k bigram) vs the 17.4% benchmark; with the same bigram the paper's own triphone2b GMM-HMM gives 12.71%, and the less task-specific CSR 5k bigram gives 11.44%.
en.limitations: One speaker, 1023 test words, single runs without seeds or significance tests; only 5k-vocabulary WSJ0 bigram language models; the DAE advantage at 5 dimensions rests on DCT runs that fail (98-100% WER), a collapse the paper leaves unexplained.

title: Vid2speech: Speech Reconstruction from Silent Video
expert_take_short: Real lip-to-speech progress, still tightly benchmark-bounded.
expert_take_long: The full text backs a stronger claim than the abstract-only version. On the constrained GRID setup, reconstructed speech becomes much more intelligible than prior work: Table 2 shows 82.6% audio-only intelligibility on S4 and about 80% audio-visual intelligibility on S4 and S2, versus 40.0% and 51.9% in the cited baseline. The OOV experiment is also real rather than decorative: Table 3 reports 51.6% accuracy when two digits are held out of training, far above the 10% chance rate. The limits are equally clear: speaker dependence, LPC-like synthesis artifacts, and a fixed 51-word grammar keep this from being a practical open-world SSI.
expert_true_value: The paper is an early but real lip-to-speech milestone: within GRID, silent video can drive intelligible reconstructed speech and even partial OOV recovery.
canon_before: Most visual silent-speech work focused on recognition rather than direct speech reconstruction, and earlier reconstruction quality was substantially lower.
delta_from_canon: The paper models automatic speechreading as regression to acoustic features and shows materially improved human intelligibility, including a held-out-digit OOV test.
position_in_field: Important early visual speech-reconstruction paper in SSI-adjacent lip-to-speech research.
practical_value: High as a proof of concept for lip-to-speech generation, though still too constrained for open deployment.
axes_moved: problem framing; evaluation; speech reconstruction
axes_unresolved: speaker independence; naturalness; unconstrained vocabulary and capture
technical_limits: The system depends on speaker-specific training, a constrained GRID grammar, and an LPC-style resynthesis path that still sounds unnatural.
evaluation_limits: Evidence is limited to GRID and a relatively small listening study rather than an open-vocabulary or in-the-wild evaluation.
deployment_limits: No live camera-to-audio system or user-facing deployment is shown.
scope_limits: Constrained lip-to-speech reconstruction study.
input_modality: silent face video
sensor_hardware: 25 FPS, 720x576 video from the GRID audiovisual corpus
vocabulary_type: GRID sentence grammar
vocabulary_size: 51 words
metrics: Table 2 reports 82.6% audio-only intelligibility for S4 and 79.9% / 79.0% audio-visual intelligibility for S4 / S2, compared with 40.0% audio-only and 51.9% audio-visual in prior work [10]. Table 3 reports 51.6% OOV audio-visual intelligibility versus 10.0% chance and 93.4% when no digits are held out.
evaluation_mode: Human intelligibility studies on reconstructed audio-only, audio-visual, and out-of-vocabulary settings using MTurk listeners.

evidence.statement: The paper presents an end-to-end CNN-based model that generates an intelligible audio signal directly from silent video of a speaking person and shows promising results for out-of-vocabulary words.
The main reconstruction experiment uses the 1000 videos of speaker S4 from GRID, while the corpus as described here contains 51 words and fixed 3-second clips.
Table 2 reports 82.6% audio-only intelligibility for speaker S4 and 79.9% / 79.0% audio-visual intelligibility for speakers S4 / S2, versus 40.0% audio-only and 51.9% audio-visual in prior work [10].
evidence.section_or_location: Table 2. Our reconstructed speech is significantly more intelligible than the results of [10].

evidence.statement: Table 3 reports 51.6% OOV audio-visual intelligibility, compared with 93.4% when no digits are held out and 10.0% chance.

en.summary: Vid2speech reconstructs intelligible speech from silent face video on GRID with speaker-specific models and LPC-style resynthesis, reaching about 80% human intelligibility and partial out-of-vocabulary recovery.
en.sensor: Camera (GRID face video, 25 fps)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 82.6% audio-only intelligibility (S4) vs 40.0% prior work; OOV 51.6% vs 10% chance
en.limitations: Speaker-specific training, constrained GRID grammar, unnatural-sounding resynthesis, and a small listening study without open-vocabulary or live testing.

title: Contour-based 3d tongue motion visualization using ultrasound image sequences
expert_take_short: Useful tongue-modeling tool, not a recognizer.
expert_take_long: The full text supports a more careful reading than the seed version. The method is technically specific: contour extraction from ultrasound drives a finite-element tongue model through modal reduction and modal warping, and the runtime system searches a 1000-shape database using contour similarity. Section 5 reports about 1.2 seconds per frame association on desktop hardware, which is better than a purely offline toy demo but still not a proven real-time SSI. The authors are also explicit that quantitative evaluation is missing and that midsagittal-only information cannot capture out-of-plane tongue motion. So this is valuable adjacent modeling work, but not a speech-decoding paper.
expert_true_value: This is an SSI-adjacent articulatory visualization paper, not a speech recognizer, but it offers a concrete modeling pipeline for turning ultrasound contours into 3D tongue motion.
canon_before: Ultrasound tongue work often focused on contour tracking or 2D visualization rather than a contour-driven 3D deformation model.
delta_from_canon: The paper links ultrasound contour extraction to a 3D finite-element tongue model via modal reduction, modal warping, and contour-matching over a precomputed shape database.
position_in_field: Adjacent tongue-modeling and visualization work that can support SSI interpretation and articulation analysis.
practical_value: Moderate for articulatory analysis and future SSI tooling, limited as a direct communication interface.
axes_moved: articulatory modeling; visualization; problem framing
axes_unresolved: quantitative validation; out-of-plane motion; end-to-end interactive performance
technical_limits: The model uses only midsagittal information, relies on a simplified four-node driving scheme, and lacks a quantitative accuracy benchmark.
evaluation_limits: Validation is qualitative and runtime-oriented; no MRI- or EMA-backed quantitative benchmark is reported.
deployment_limits: This is not a communication interface and does not show user-facing SSI deployment.
scope_limits: SSI-adjacent visualization and modeling paper, not speech recognition.
input_modality: B-mode ultrasound tongue images
sensor_hardware: B-mode ultrasound imaging with contour extraction from the midsagittal tongue surface
metrics: The database contains 1000 sample 3D tongue shapes, and Section 5 reports about 1.2 seconds on average to build the association between the current ultrasound frame and the 3D tongue model on the reported desktop hardware. The paper explicitly says no effective quantitative evaluation method is yet available.
evaluation_mode: Qualitative visualization with runtime reporting and midsagittal overlay validation against ultrasound contours.

evidence.statement: The abstract describes a contour-based 3D tongue deformation visualization framework that uses B-mode ultrasound sequences, a generic finite-element tongue model, modal reduction, and modal warping.
The method builds a 1000-shape 3D tongue database and selects the tongue shape whose projected contour best matches the contour extracted from the current ultrasound frame.
Section 5 reports an average processing time of about 1.2 seconds to build the association between the current ultrasound frame and the 3D tongue model on the reported desktop platform.

The discussion says there is still no effective quantitative evaluation method, midsagittal-only motion is insufficient for full tongue accuracy, and future validation should use modalities such as MRI and EMA.

en.summary: Builds a contour-based pipeline that maps midsagittal ultrasound tongue contours to 3D tongue motion using a database of 1000 3D shapes; evaluation is qualitative, with about 1.2 s per frame association.
en.sensor: B-mode ultrasound tongue imaging
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported (about 1.2 s average to associate a frame with the 3D model)
en.limitations: Not a recognizer; uses only midsagittal information with a simplified driving scheme and has no quantitative accuracy benchmark.

title: AlterEgo: A Personalized Wearable Silent Speech Interface
venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '18), pp. 43-53
expert_take_short: Landmark wearable EMG SSI framed as a closed-loop assistant; headline accuracy rests on tiny task vocabularies.
expert_take_long: AlterEgo is one of the most visible SSI papers because it packages surface neuromuscular sensing, a personalized recognizer and bone-conduction audio feedback into a single head-worn loop for talking to a computer without audible speech or visible movement. The abstract reports a 92% median word accuracy in user studies, and the MIT press release describes a 10-subject arithmetic study with about 15 minutes of per-user customization and task vocabularies of about 20 words. That makes the result a closed-vocabulary, per-user command/word recognition claim rather than evidence for open-vocabulary silent dictation. The full PDF could not be accessed for this review, so electrode-level details, model architecture, split design and cross-session behavior are taken from secondary sources or left unverified.
expert_true_value: Its lasting value is the interaction framing: a discreet, bidirectional silent-speech loop (silent input, bone-conduction output) built around personalization, not a new recognition benchmark.
canon_before: EMG silent speech recognition was mostly laboratory work with taped electrode arrays and offline evaluation, rarely framed as an always-available personal interface with private audio feedback.
delta_from_canon: Integrates face/jaw neuromuscular sensing, a per-user recognizer and bone-conduction output into a wearable closed loop for querying computing services, and evaluates it with users on task-specific vocabularies.
position_in_field: Highly cited HCI landmark for wearable EMG silent speech; frequently used as the reference point for 'intelligence augmentation' framing of SSI.
practical_value: Useful as a design reference for discreet bidirectional SSI interaction; weak as a quantitative baseline because vocabularies are small and full protocol details are hard to compare.
axes_moved: interaction_design; wearable_form_factor; personalization
axes_unresolved: Open vocabulary; cross-session and re-wear robustness; speaker independence; truly 'internal' versus articulated speech
technical_limits: Recognition is personalized and reported on small task vocabularies (about 20 words per application according to MIT News); the abstract describes signals during 'internal' speech, but how much articulation is required is not verifiable from the sources seen.
evaluation_limits: Only the 92% median word accuracy is verifiable from the abstract; split design, session separation and per-task breakdown could not be checked in the full text.
deployment_limits: Requires a custom head-worn electrode headset in contact with the face and jaw and per-user customization.
scope_limits: Closed-vocabulary silent word/command recognition for human-computer interaction; not speech synthesis or open dictation.
input_modality: surface neuromuscular (EMG) signals from face and jaw
sensor_hardware: head-worn electrode headset with bone-conduction headphones
vocabulary_type: closed task-specific vocabulary
vocabulary_size: about 20 words per application (MIT News; not verified in full text)
metrics: 92% median word accuracy in user studies (abstract); about 92% average transcription accuracy in a 10-subject arithmetic study (MIT News)
evaluation_mode: user studies with per-user customization on task-specific vocabularies (details unverified)

evidence.statement: The abstract describes a wearable interface that captures neuromuscular signals from internal speech articulators, feeds reconstructed words to a computing system, and returns output via bone-conduction audio, enabling discreet bidirectional communication.
The abstract reports a 92% median word accuracy in user studies.

MIT News describes a 10-subject usability study in which each subject spent about 15 minutes customizing the arithmetic application and about 90 minutes using it, with about 92% average transcription accuracy and task vocabularies of about 20 words.

MIT News states that an electrode-placement study started with 16 facial sites and the prototype uses seven contact points on either side of the mouth and along the jaws, with personalization by retraining the last two network layers.
The full paper PDF could not be retrieved for this review, so architecture, split and cross-session details remain unverified.

en.summary: Wearable headset that recognizes silently articulated words from face and jaw neuromuscular signals and answers through bone-conduction audio; abstract reports 92% median word accuracy in user studies.
en.sensor: Head-worn surface EMG electrodes on face and jaw, with bone-conduction headphones
en.vocabulary: Small task vocabularies (about 20 words per application, per MIT News)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: 92% median word accuracy in user studies (abstract)
en.limitations: Small closed vocabularies and per-user customization; full protocol (splits, sessions, architecture) not verified because only the abstract and press coverage were available.

title: EchoSpeech: Continuous Silent Speech Recognition on Minimally-obtrusive Eyewear Powered by Acoustic Sensing
expert_take_short: Glasses-mounted inaudible FMCW sonar recognizes 31 silent commands (4.5% WER) and connected digits (6.1% WER) across remounts, with walking tests and a 73.3 mW smartphone demo, but needs per-user fine-tuning.
expert_take_long: EchoSpeech is one of the most cited wearable SSI papers of the period and a clean example of active acoustic sensing. Two speakers and two microphones on a glasses frame emit 18-21 kHz and 21.5-24.5 kHz FMCW sweeps; differential echo profiles from four speaker-microphone paths capture skin deformation during silent speech, and a ResNet-18 with CTC decodes discrete commands or connected 3-6-digit numbers. In 12 participants, with the device removed and re-donned between sessions, user-specific fine-tuning (about 30 min) gave 4.5% WER on 31 commands and 6.1% on connected digits; with 6-8 minutes WER rose to 9.5%/14.4%, and without fine-tuning to about 40%. Walking without mobile training data raised WER to 16.8%, reduced to 10.7-13.1% with added walking data; a second 12-person study in a noisier room reached 4.7% with mobile fine-tuning. Injected 64-76 dB(A) noise changed WER by only 2-3%. A low-power BLE variant runs at 73.3 mW with smartphone inference. Limits: small closed vocabulary, user-dependent calibration, sensitivity to glasses slippage, no activation detection, and an ear-canal SPL near recommended limits at full amplitude.
expert_true_value: Shows that minimally obtrusive eyewear with commodity speakers and microphones can support continuous silent command and digit recognition robust to remounting, noise and walking at smartphone-level power.
canon_before: Acoustic-sensing SSIs used phones held near the mouth or isolated-word recognition; wearable SSIs often relied on skin-contact EMG or cameras.
delta_from_canon: Glasses-frame FMCW sonar with multi-path echo profiles and CTC-based continuous recognition, evaluated with remounting, walking and noise, plus a low-power real-time demo.
position_in_field: Representative CHI wearable acoustic SSI; benchmark for later earable/headphone sonar SSIs (e.g., HPSpeech) in the acoustic section.
practical_value: Practical form factor and power budget for command-level silent input; strong template for evaluation under remounting and walking.
axes_moved: Wearable unobtrusiveness; continuous (connected-digit) recognition; remount, walking and noise robustness; power consumption.
axes_unresolved: Open-vocabulary sentences; calibration-free use; activation detection; long-term in-the-wild use; acoustic exposure safety.
axes_regressed: Accuracy degrades without user-specific fine-tuning (about 40% WER) and when glasses slip.
technical_limits: Performance degrades when glasses are pushed or slip, especially for smaller faces; single speaker-microphone path doubles WER (5.8% to 12.0%).
evaluation_limits: Small closed vocabularies (31 commands, digits); 12+12 participants, mostly non-native speakers; lab settings only; end-to-end latency not reported.
deployment_limits: Requires 6-30 min user-specific data for best accuracy; no activation detection; estimated ear-canal SPL 78.6 dB at 100% amplitude (62.2 dB at 20%).
scope_limits: Read the author-hosted CHI '23 PDF via automated extraction (about the last 6% of text, likely references, not read); figures not visually inspected. Full-text alternative to an abstract-based EchoSpeech record.
task: Silent recognition of discrete commands and continuous connected digits from facial skin deformation.
input_modality: Active acoustic sensing (inaudible FMCW echoes) from glasses-mounted speakers and microphones.
sensor_hardware: Two speakers (18-21 kHz, 21.5-24.5 kHz FMCW, 12 ms sweeps) and two microphones on the glasses frame, 50 kHz sampling, Teensy 4.1; low-power BLE variant with nRF52840.
body_site: Face (cheek/skin around mouth, sensed from glasses frame).
vocabulary_type: Closed vocabulary: 31 discrete commands and connected 3-6-digit numbers.
vocabulary_size: 31 commands; 10 digits.
metrics: Main study (12 participants, user fine-tuning ~30 min): command WER 4.5% (SD 3.5), connected digits 6.1% (SD 4.2). With 6-8 min: 9.5%/14.4%; no fine-tuning ~40%. Walking without mobile data 16.8%; with others' walking data 13.1%/13.2%; with follow-up data 10.7%. Follow-up study (12 new participants): 4.7% with 10 mobile sessions, 8.2% with 2. Noise 64-76 dB(A): +2-3% WER static. Power 73.3 mW.
evaluation_mode: User-dependent training with remounting between sessions, walking sessions, injected noise; real-time smartphone demos (CAD, music control, text input).

evidence.statement: Two speakers on the left frame edge emit 18-21 kHz and 21.5-24.5 kHz FMCW sweeps (12 ms) and two microphones on the right edge sample at 50 kHz; four speaker-microphone paths form differential echo profiles.
ResNet-18 with spatial pooling and CTC loss decodes both discrete commands and continuous connected digits from echo profiles; LSTM/GRU layers did not help.
Across 12 participants with remounting between sessions, WER was 4.5% (SD 3.5) for 31 commands and 6.1% (SD 4.2) for connected digits using about 30 min of user data.
With 6-8 minutes of fine-tuning data WER was 9.5% (commands) and 14.4% (digits); without fine-tuning about 40%.
Walking without mobile training data gave 16.8% WER; adding other users' walking data lowered commands to 13.1% and adding follow-up data to 10.7%.
A follow-up study with 12 new participants in a noisier room reached 4.7% WER (10 mobile sessions) and 8.2% (2 sessions) on commands.
Street (64 dB(A)) and restaurant (76 dB(A)) noise raised static WER by about 2% and 3%.
A low-power variant (one speaker, two microphones, BLE) consumes 73.3 mW with inference on a smartphone; demos used 1-6 min of training data.
Glasses slippage degrades accuracy, activation detection is not evaluated, native vs non-native comparison is underpowered, and estimated ear-canal SPL is 78.6 dB at full amplitude.

en.summary: Glasses-mounted inaudible FMCW sonar recognizes silent speech from facial skin echoes: 4.5% WER on 31 commands and 6.1% on connected digits in 12 users, with walking/noise tests and a 73.3 mW demo.
en.sensor: Glasses-mounted speakers and microphones (inaudible FMCW active acoustic sensing)
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: WER 4.5% commands, 6.1% digits; 16.8% walking without mobile data
en.limitations: Closed vocabulary; needs user fine-tuning (~40% WER without); sensitive to glasses slippage; no activation detection.

title: Silent speech interfaces
expert_take_short: The founding SSI review: defines the field and its seven sensing families, but its numbers are pre-deep-learning.
expert_take_long: This special-issue overview is the paper that named and scoped silent speech interfaces as speech processing without an intelligible acoustic signal. It organizes the field into seven technology families (EMA/magnetic sensing, ultrasound and optical imaging of tongue and lips, NAM microphones, glottal EM/vibration sensors, surface EMG, EEG and intracortical implants) and motivates them through three application drivers: speech-handicapped users such as laryngectomees, private phone use in quiet places, and noisy environments. Its six-criterion comparison table (works in silence, in noise, for laryngectomy, non-invasive, ready for market, low cost) remains a useful lens, and the challenge list (sensor positioning, speaker independence, Lombard/silent-speech effects, prosody, limited dictionaries) is still largely open. The cited performance numbers are early small-vocabulary results and should not be used as current baselines.
expert_true_value: Defines the SSI problem space and the evaluation criteria still used to compare modalities; essential historical framing rather than technical evidence.
canon_before: Work on non-acoustic speech sensing was scattered across speech production research, speech pathology, telecom privacy and BCI, without a shared name or comparison frame.
delta_from_canon: Unifies these lines under the SSI label, surveys seven demonstrator technologies, scores them on six practical criteria and lists common challenges and future directions.
position_in_field: Foundational reference for the SSI field; the standard citation for its definition and modality taxonomy.
practical_value: Useful for framing and for the modality comparison criteria; numeric results are historical only.
axes_moved: field_definition; modality_taxonomy; deployment_criteria
axes_unresolved: Speaker independence; sensor positioning robustness; silent-vs-vocalized mismatch; prosody; large vocabularies
technical_limits: Review article; reported results come from early systems with small vocabularies and heterogeneous protocols.
evaluation_limits: No unified benchmark; the comparison table uses author-assigned 1-5 scores rather than measured quantities.
deployment_limits: Concludes that no technology met all six criteria at the time; does not itself resolve deployment barriers.
scope_limits: Survey of SSI technologies up to about 2009.
input_modality: non-acoustic articulatory, muscular and neural signals (review)
sensor_hardware: review of EMA/magnetic, imaging, NAM, glottal EM/vibration, sEMG, EEG and intracortical sensors
metrics: Cites early results such as over 90% recognition for EMA on 9 words and 13 phonemes, 93% sEMG accuracy on English digits, about 70% sEMG accuracy on 100 words, and about 60% correct phonetic targets for ultrasound/optical recognition from a one-hour two-speaker database
evaluation_mode: narrative review with a six-criterion, 1-5 scored comparison of seven SSI technologies

evidence.statement: The abstract defines SSIs as systems enabling speech communication without an intelligible acoustic signal and presents demonstrators built on seven technology types.
Section III reviews EMA/magnetic sensing, ultrasound and optical imaging of tongue and lips, NAM microphones, glottal EM/vibration sensors, surface EMG, EEG and intracortical implants.
The sEMG section cites 93% accuracy on English digits, 92% on six control words, and around 70% on 100 words, with up to 90% speaker-dependent results.
Section IV.B scores each technology from 1 to 5 on working in silence, in noise, for laryngectomy, non-invasiveness, market readiness and cost.
Section IV.A lists common challenges: sensor positioning and robustness, speaker independence, Lombard and silent-speech effects, prosody and nasality, and limited dictionary size.

en.summary: Founding review that defines silent speech interfaces, surveys seven sensing technologies from EMA to intracortical implants, and scores them on six practical criteria; concludes no technology meets all of them.
en.sensor: Seven SSI technology families (review)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Pre-deep-learning review; cited results are small-vocabulary and heterogeneous, and the comparison scores are qualitative.

title: Biosignal-Based Spoken Communication: A Survey
venue: IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing 25(12), 2257-2271
expert_take_short: Key mid-period survey that widens SSI to all speech biosignals; reviewed here from the abstract only.
expert_take_long: Written by many of the field's core groups, this survey reframes silent speech as part of a broader area of biosignal-based spoken communication, covering signals from the articulators, the muscles that move them, the neural pathways and the brain. The abstract positions the goals as everyday communication devices, speech rehabilitation and a better understanding of speech production, and emphasizes the interdisciplinary nature of the work. Only the abstract and bibliographic metadata could be accessed for this review, so specific modality comparisons, numeric results and conclusions are not summarized here and should be checked against the full text.
expert_true_value: A bridge between the 2010 SSI definition and later neural speech-decoding work, placing articulatory, muscular and neural signals in one framework.
canon_before: SSI was framed mainly around articulatory and muscle sensing, while neural speech decoding developed largely in parallel in the BCI community.
delta_from_canon: Treats articulatory, muscular and neural speech biosignals as one research area with shared goals in communication, rehabilitation and speech science.
position_in_field: Widely cited survey linking SSI and speech BCI; companion to the TASLP special issue on biosignal-based speech processing.
practical_value: Useful entry point for readers moving between EMG/articulatory SSI and neural speech decoding.
axes_moved: field_mapping; scope_broadening
axes_unresolved: Not assessable from the abstract alone
technical_limits: Survey; contributes no new system.
evaluation_limits: Not verifiable from the abstract; any cross-study comparison inherits the heterogeneity of the underlying literature.
deployment_limits: Not addressed in the abstract.
scope_limits: Survey of speech biosignals up to 2017.
input_modality: articulatory, muscular and neural speech biosignals (review)
sensor_hardware: multimodal biosignal sensors (review)
evaluation_mode: literature survey (details not verified beyond the abstract)

evidence.statement: The abstract states that speech production yields biosignals from the articulators, the muscles that move them, the neural pathways and the brain, and that these can overcome limits of conventional speech processing.
The abstract frames the goals as biosignal-based devices for everyday communication and speech rehabilitation, and better understanding of speech production, across an interdisciplinary field.
Only the abstract and bibliographic metadata were accessible for this review; section-level claims and numbers were not verified.

en.summary: Survey that frames silent speech within biosignal-based spoken communication, spanning articulatory, muscular and neural signals for communication devices, rehabilitation and speech science.
en.sensor: Articulatory, muscular and neural biosignal sensors (review)
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: Not reported
en.limitations: Reviewed from the abstract only; a survey without a unified benchmark, so its detailed comparisons were not checked.

title: LipNet: End-to-End Sentence-level Lipreading
expert_take_short: Historic first end-to-end sentence-level lipreader, but only on the tiny, rigid GRID grammar.
expert_take_long: LipNet showed that spatiotemporal convolutions, bidirectional GRUs and CTC could be trained end to end to map lip video to character sequences, removing hand-crafted features and frame alignments. On GRID it reports 4.8% WER on the overlapped-speaker split and 11.4% on held-out speakers, with clear gains over its own LSTM and 2D-CNN baselines and over three hearing-impaired lipreaders (47.7% average WER). The weakness is the benchmark: GRID is a fixed six-slot grammar with a few dozen words, so the result says little about open-vocabulary lipreading, and the headline comparison to a prior word-level 86.4% accuracy is not like-for-like. For SSI, it is mainly the architectural template that later camera-based silent speech systems built on.
expert_true_value: Established the end-to-end sequence lipreading template (STCNN + RNN + CTC) that later visual SSI work inherited.
canon_before: Lipreading was mostly word classification or relied on hand-engineered visual features and separate sequence models.
delta_from_canon: Trains a single network end to end from video frames to character sequences with CTC, at sentence level.
position_in_field: Seminal deep lipreading paper; background for camera-based SSI rather than an SSI system itself.
practical_value: Architectural reference and GRID baseline; limited direct value for real silent-speech use.
axes_moved: end_to_end_modeling; sentence_level_decoding
axes_unresolved: Open vocabulary; in-the-wild video; truly silent articulation
technical_limits: Video-only model trained on GRID's restricted grammar; unseen-speaker WER (11.4%) is more than twice the overlapped-speaker WER (4.8%).
evaluation_limits: Single constrained dataset; human baseline is 3 people on 300 videos; the 86.4% prior comparison is word-level and speaker-dependent.
deployment_limits: Offline evaluation on recorded frontal video; no real-time or silent-speaker testing.
scope_limits: Lipreading of vocalized speech video on GRID; not silent speech specifically.
input_modality: video
sensor_hardware: camera (GRID frontal face video)
vocabulary_type: closed grammar (GRID command + color + preposition + letter + digit + adverb)
vocabulary_size: GRID grammar with 64,000 possible sentences
metrics: GRID WER 4.8% / CER 1.9% overlapped speakers (95.2% sentence-level accuracy); WER 11.4% / CER 6.4% unseen speakers; hearing-impaired lipreaders 47.7% WER
evaluation_mode: GRID overlapped-speaker and unseen-speaker splits; baselines and human lipreader comparison

evidence.statement: The paper presents LipNet as an end-to-end sentence-level lipreading model combining spatiotemporal convolutions, a recurrent network and CTC loss.
Table 2 reports LipNet WER 4.8% (CER 1.9%) on overlapped speakers and 11.4% (CER 6.4%) on unseen speakers, versus Baseline-NoLM 5.6%/13.6%.
The unseen-speaker split holds out speakers 1, 2, 20 and 22 (3,971 test videos); the overlapped split holds out 255 random sentences per speaker.
Three hearing-impaired lipreaders average 47.7% WER on unseen-speaker GRID videos (300 videos).
Evaluation is limited to GRID, whose grammar allows only 64,000 sentences; audio-visual integration and larger datasets are left to future work.

en.summary: End-to-end lipreader (spatiotemporal CNN, Bi-GRU, CTC) decoding GRID sentences from video; 4.8% WER on overlapped speakers and 11.4% on unseen speakers.
en.sensor: Camera (frontal face/lip video)
en.speaker: Both
en.key_result: 4.8% WER overlapped speakers, 11.4% WER unseen speakers on GRID
en.limitations: Only GRID's tiny fixed grammar with vocalized speech; no open vocabulary, in-the-wild, silent-articulation or real-time evaluation.

title: Lip Reading Sentences in the Wild
expert_take_short:
変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（口元映像と音声を別々の LSTM で符号化し、二つの注意で読む文字単位の系列変換 WLAS）、**M03 学習**（単語の例から始めて系列長を伸ばすカリキュラム）、**M11 評価用の正解**（BBC 放送から自動で作った文単位データ LRS、放送日で分割）の三つである。M12 の人間との比較には付随の指摘がある。
映像だけの最良は WAS+CL+SS+BS で WER 50.2%、専門の読唇者は 73.8%（表5、本文確認）。ただし読唇者の値は回答を断った例を除いたもので、含めると 87.6% になる（表5 脚注）。読唇者はテストから無作為に選んだ 200 本を読み、機械の 50.2% がその 200 本で測った値かは書かれていない。
学習手順の寄与は表5 で、何もしない WAS 76.5% からカリキュラムで 61.1%（−15.4 ポイント、相対 −20%）、予定サンプリングで 58.1%、ビーム探索で 50.2%（査読者の計算）。どれも 1 回の学習の値で、乱数種や繰り返しの記載はない。
音声に口元を足すと、きれいな音声で 17.7% → 13.9%（相対 −21%）、0 dB で 62.9% → 42.0%（相対 −33%）になる（表5、査読者の計算）。音声だけでは再学習した Kaldi の 16.8% のほうが LAS の 17.7% より低い。
LRS は放送日で分けているが、話者の重なりは書かれていない。著者は「数千人の話者がいるので話者に依存しない」と述べるだけである（§4）。arXiv v2 §1 は「データを公開する」と書いたが、固定版の CVF 版ではこの文が消えており、後続論文 [[2]](#ref-2)（後続）によれば権利の都合で公開されなかった。

変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（口元映像と音声を別々の LSTM で符号化し、二つの注意で読む文字単位の系列変換 WLAS）、**M03 学習**（単語の例から始めて系列長を伸ばすカリキュラム）、**M11 評価用の正解**（BBC 放送から自動で作った文単位データ LRS、放送日で分割）の三つである。M12 の人間との比較には付随の指摘がある。

学習手順の寄与は表5 で、何もしない WAS 76.5% からカリキュラムで 61.1%（−15.4 ポイント、相対 −20%）、予定サンプリングで 58.1%、ビーム探索で 50.2%（査読者の計算）。どれも 1 回の学習の値で、乱数種や繰り返しの記載はない。
音声に口元を足すと、きれいな音声で 17.7% → 13.9%（相対 −21%）、0 dB で 62.9% → 42.0%（相対 −33%）になる（表5、査読者の計算）。音声だけでは再学習した Kaldi の 16.8% のほうが LAS の 17.7% より低い。
LRS は放送日で分けているが、話者の重なりは書かれていない。著者は「数千人の話者がいるので話者に依存しない」と述べるだけである（§4）。arXiv v2 §1 は「データを公開する」と書いたが、固定版の CVF 版ではこの文が消えており、後続論文 [[2]](#ref-2)（後続）によれば権利の都合で公開されなかった。
expert_true_value:
文単位・開語彙・実環境の唇読みを、測れる課題にした点が大きい。LRS 自体は公開されなかったが、手順は LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED [[12]](#ref-12)（後続）に引き継がれ、以後の標準ベンチマークになった。
一方で、データは通常の発声を撮った放送映像で、無声発話の利用者にそのまま移せる根拠はない。復号は文全体を見てから行う一括方式で、著者自身が逐次型への拡張を今後の課題に挙げている（§6）。
canon_before:
**M06（注意つき系列変換）**：音声以外の信号から注意つきの符号器・復号器で記号列を出す研究は、wiki 内の検索では対象より前（2016-05 以前）にも同時期（〜2017-05）にも見つからなかった（付録A、この期間の候補はすべて読んだ。話題全体の再現率の目安は 0.33）。
同時期の LipNet [[4]](#ref-4)（同時期）は CTC で GRID の文を読み、著者も関連研究で触れている（§1.1）。系列変換そのものは音声認識の LAS（Chan ら）から採ったと著者が明記しており、wiki 外の技術の持ち込みである。
注意を使わない符号器・復号器は、後続の皮質電位からの文復号 [[5]](#ref-5)（後続）が使い、注意つきは後続の EEG [[6]](#ref-6)（後続）や音響センシングの無声発話 [[7]](#ref-7)（後続）に広がった。

**M03（長さのカリキュラム）**：系列長を伸ばす学習手順は、wiki 内の検索では対象より前に見つからなかった（再現率の目安 0.78、既知項目 5/5）。同時期の単語分類の研究には後段を段階的に足す学習があるが、系列長は変えない。

**M11（実環境の文単位データ）**：それまでの公開の唇読みデータは GRID（語彙 51、33,000 文）と単語単位の LRW（500 語）で、固定版の表3 はこの二つに MODALITY（語彙 182）を加えた三つと比べている（arXiv v2 の表3 は二つ）。同時期の Miao ら [[8]](#ref-8)（同時期）は先行研究の課題設定に従い、YouTube の作業解説動画 94 時間（訓練 90・テスト 4 時間）で音声映像認識を評価したが、映像は話者が映らないこともある場面特徴で、口元のデータではない（境界例として除外）。

**継いだ部品**：M01・M04（放送の通常発声）、M02（字幕の強制整列と市販音声認識での選別）、M05（口元の切り出しと 5 フレームの早期融合）は LRW [[3]](#ref-3) の手順を継ぐ。M07 は LAS 型の復号器に内在する言語モデルとビーム探索、M08 は文字列、M13 は単一 GPU での学習で、いずれも通例どおりである。
delta_from_canon:
**M06**：二重注意により、片方の入力がない場合や二つの入力の時刻がずれている場合でも同じモデルで読める、と著者は述べる（§2.3）。注意なしでは WER が 100% を超えたので結果は載せない、双方向の符号器は改善がなかった、とも書くが、どちらも数値は示されていない。
映像だけの 50.2% が従来手法より良いことは、同じデータでの別方式の比較がないので、方式の効果とデータ規模の効果を分けられない。外部データでの比較も、LRS で事前学習したモデルを 1 エポック微調整した値と、LRS を使わない従来値の比較である（§5.3–5.4）。後続の LSVSR [[9]](#ref-9)（後続）は同じデータで WAS 型の再実装（WER 76.8%）と自身の CTC 方式（40.9%）を並べており、データを揃えれば WLAS 型が最良とは限らないことを示す（同論文の表、本文確認）。
GRID の 3.0% は、各話者から 255 文をテストに取る無作為分割（話者が重なる条件）の値で、同時期の LipNet の 4.8% も同じ分割の値である（表8、本文確認）。
後続では、同じグループの Transformer 系列変換 [[10]](#ref-10)（後続）、[[2]](#ref-2)（後続）が WLAS の構成を置き換え、後者は LRS2-BBC での WAS の値を 70.4% として載せる（後続、同論文の表2 で本文確認、評価条件の記載なし）。

**M03**：カリキュラムだけで WER が 76.5% → 61.1% と最も大きく下がる（表5）。著者は「収束が数倍速く、過学習も大きく減る。おそらく自然なデータ増強として働くため」と述べるが、収束曲線や訓練誤差は示していない（§3.1）。
最も強い交絡は、学習の順序（短い→長い）の効果と、文の部分系列を学習例に足す増強の効果が分けられていないことである。著者自身が増強の可能性を挙げ、後続の Prajwal ら [[11]](#ref-11)（後続）は「改善はカリキュラムではなくデータ増強から来る」と主張して、部分系列の増強だけで置き換えた。
76.5% の基準は文全体で最初から学習したもので、§3.5 の停止規則（検証誤差が 5,000 反復改善しなければ停止）が基準モデルにも同じく適用されたかは書かれていない。後続ではこの手順を 17 本（本文確認 13、台帳のみ 4）が使い（付録A）、Deep AVSR [[2]](#ref-2)（後続）§5.2 はほぼ同じ文で「新しい戦略」と書いている。

**M11**：LRS は語彙 17,428 で、GRID・LRW より一桁以上大きい（表3）。テスト語彙の 6,882 語のうち 629 語（9.1%）は訓練・検証に現れない（査読者の計算）。また 6,641 語（96.5%）は音声のみの訓練データに現れる（表2 脚注、査読者の計算）。このデータは復号器も学ぶので、内在言語モデルはテストの語をほぼ見ている。
放送日で分けても、ニュースの司会者や常連の出演者は訓練とテストの両方に出うる。同時期の LRW [[3]](#ref-3)（同時期）自身が、BBC News の司会者などが繰り返し映ると書いている（§2）。後続の LRS3 論文 [[12]](#ref-12)（後続）は、同じ BBC 由来の LRS2-BBC について同じ人物が回をまたいで出やすいと書いている。
position_in_field: 文単位・開語彙・実環境の唇読みを測れる課題にした出発点。構成要素では M06（注意つき系列変換）、M03（長さのカリキュラム）、M11（LRS）を変え、いずれも wiki 内では先行例が見つからなかった。ただしカリキュラムの効果は 1 回の学習で部分系列による増強と分けられておらず、系列変換の効果はデータ規模と分けられていない（M06 の話題の再現率の目安は 0.33）。手順は LRS2-BBC・LRS3-TED と後続の Transformer 系列変換に引き継がれた。
practical_value:
文単位・開語彙・実環境の唇読みを、測れる課題にした点が大きい。LRS 自体は公開されなかったが、手順は LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED [[12]](#ref-12)（後続）に引き継がれ、以後の標準ベンチマークになった。
一方で、データは通常の発声を撮った放送映像で、無声発話の利用者にそのまま移せる根拠はない。復号は文全体を見てから行う一括方式で、著者自身が逐次型への拡張を今後の課題に挙げている（§6）。
axes_moved: 文単位・開語彙の唇読み、注意つき系列変換の導入、長さのカリキュラム、人間の読唇者との文単位の比較。
axes_unresolved: 話者の分離、繰り返しによるばらつき、人間との対等な比較、雑音種の幅、逐次復号。
axes_regressed: なし（ただしデータは公開されず、同じ数値を他者が再現できなかった）。
technical_limits: 注意に単調性の制約がなく、文全体を見てからの一括復号。方式の効果とデータ規模の効果が分けられていない。
evaluation_limits: 固定版の本文と表5 で CER の値が食い違う（16.2→13.3 と 10.4→7.9）。テスト話者の重なり未記載、1 回の学習、読唇者との比較は条件が異なり機械の評価対象（200 本か全テストか）が未記載、雑音テストの雑音種が未記載。
deployment_limits: オフライン評価のみ。学習は GPU 1 枚で約 10 日。LRS は非公開に終わった。
scope_limits: BBC 放送の通常の発声（英語）に限る。無声発話への適用は検証していない。
task: 文単位の唇読みと音声映像音声認識
input_modality: 口元映像と音声
sensor_hardware: 放送用カメラ映像 25 Hz（口元 120×120 濃淡）、13 次元 MFCC
vocabulary_type: 開語彙
metrics: WER（映像のみ 50.2%、専門読唇者 73.8%、音声映像 13.9%、LRS テスト）
evaluation_mode: オフライン、放送日で分けたテスト集合

evidence.statement: 映像のみの WAS+CL+SS+BS は LRS テストで WER 50.2%（CER 39.5%）。専門読唇者は 200 本で 73.8%（断った例を含めると 87.6%）。
カリキュラムで WER 76.5% → 61.1%、予定サンプリングで 58.1%、ビーム探索で 50.2%。いずれも 1 回の学習。
音声に口元を足すと clean 17.7% → 13.9%、0 dB 62.9% → 42.0%。音声のみでは Kaldi 16.8% が LAS 17.7% より低い。
LRS は放送日で分割され、話者の重なりは未記載。著者は数千人の話者がいるので話者に依存しないとだけ述べる。

en.summary: Introduces Watch, Listen, Attend and Spell and the BBC LRS dataset. Lips-only decoding reaches 50.2% WER on open-vocabulary broadcast sentences against 73.8% for a professional lipreader, but the lipreader worked on 200 clips under different viewing conditions with declined clips excluded (87.6% with them), and the machine score is not stated to be on the same clips. The word-to-sentence curriculum gives the largest single gain (76.5% to 61.1%), from one training run.
en.sensor: Camera (broadcast mouth crops, 120 px grey, 25 Hz), optional audio (13-dim MFCC)

title: Learning Audio-Visual Speech Representation by Masked Multimodal Cluster Prediction
expert_take_short: AV-HuBERT's masked audio-visual cluster pre-training (M03) was a large step past distillation, but its LRS3 gains lack repeated runs and later work beats it at matched budgets.
expert_take_long: The paper [@shi2022avhubert] changes two components: the pre-training objective (M03), masked prediction of audio-visual cluster labels refined over five iterations, and audio as training-only supervision (M02), with video alone at test. The M03 gain is large on the paper's own terms: its scratch baseline falls from 92.3% to 32.5% WER at 30 h of labels, and it is far below the 59.8% of cross-modal distillation [@afouras2020asr], although that margin also mixes 334 h against 1,759 h of unlabelled video. Both components remain standard by our rules, because the effect is shown on one test set with no repeated runs in Table 1. Later work now beats the design at the same budget: 23.7% against 32.5% with the same model size, unlabelled data and 30 h of labels [@haliassos2026usr2] [later]. The headline claim of beating the best prior system with 1/1000 of the labels overreaches: 32.5% against 33.6% [@makino2019rnnt] is a 1.1-point gap between different training regimes with no variance reported.
expert_true_value: Showed that self-supervised audio-visual pretraining cuts labeled-data needs for lipreading by orders of magnitude, providing a reusable visual speech backbone.
canon_before: State-of-the-art lipreading relied on very large transcribed video corpora, sometimes tens of thousands of hours of non-public data.
delta_from_canon: Masked multimodal cluster prediction with iterative target refinement and modality dropout learns visual speech features from unlabeled audio-visual video.
position_in_field: Core VSR representation-learning paper; widely used backbone for visual SSI and lip-to-speech research.
practical_value: High as a pretrained visual encoder; direct silent-speech performance is not evaluated.
axes_moved: self_supervised_learning; label_efficiency; visual_representation
axes_unresolved: Silent articulation; non-English and low-resource lipreading; short-utterance homophene ambiguity
technical_limits: Large models (103M/325M parameters) and heavy pretraining compute; short utterances remain hard because of homophenes.
evaluation_limits: English LRS3 only; adding non-English pretraining helps only when English data are scarce; no noisy AVSR results in this paper.
deployment_limits: Offline benchmark evaluation; no real-time or on-device testing.

evidence.statement: The abstract introduces AV-HuBERT, which masks multi-stream video input and predicts automatically discovered and iteratively refined multimodal hidden units.
With 30 h labeled LRS3 and 1,759 h unlabeled pretraining, the LARGE model reaches 32.5% lipreading WER, versus 33.6% for a prior system trained on 31,000 h of transcribed video.
With 433 h labeled data the LARGE model reaches 28.6% WER, and 26.9% with self-training.
Pretraining uses LRS3 (433 h) plus English VoxCeleb2 (1,326 h), 1,759 h total.
Appendix analysis attributes higher error on short utterances to homophenes, and the ethics statement notes speaker-distribution bias and surveillance risk.

title: Visual Speech Recognition for Multiple Languages in the Wild
expert_take_short: Joint distillation losses are a standard idea worth 1.5-2.0 LRS3 points, less than recipe and masking; LRS3 31.5% trails 16.9% from public data; 4 of 6 languages lack external baselines.
expert_take_long: The paper [@ma2022multilingual] adds one new component, M02: joint losses that predict pretrained audio and visual representations from video. This is a standard variant of cross-modal distillation already used by LiRA, ASR-is-all-you-need and Hearing Lips [@ma2021lira; @afouras2020asr; @zhao2020hearinglips]; the ten-run ablation shows it helps, by 2.0 points on LRS3 at 595 h and 1.5 points at 1,459 h (Tables 5, S26; inference). The headline LRS3 gain rests more on the recipe (M03): tuning and an improved language model give 5.8 points (Table S9) and time masking 2.7 (Table 5), against 2.0 for both new losses together (inference). On LRS3 (M12) the 31.5% WER follows the field's usual supervised design and is 14.6 points behind a [later] system trained on public data only [@liu2023synthvsr] (inference). The six-language state-of-the-art claim has published baselines only for English and Mandarin; the other four languages are compared only with a baseline the authors trained.
expert_true_value: Shows that auxiliary feature-prediction losses and augmentation let public-data lipreaders compete with systems trained on far larger private corpora, across several languages.
canon_before: Best English VSR results came from models trained on thousands to tens of thousands of hours of non-public data, and non-English VSR was weak.
delta_from_canon: Adds prediction-based auxiliary tasks, time masking and tuned training to a Conformer CTC/attention VSR model, and extends evaluation to Mandarin, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and French.
position_in_field: Major VSR reference for multilingual lipreading; background for camera-based SSI.
practical_value: Strong reusable recipe and pretrained models for multilingual visual speech front-ends.
axes_moved: multilingual_vsr; training_recipe; evaluation_rigor
axes_unresolved: Silent and Lombard speech; accent and demographic bias; lipreading robustness to pose, lighting and resolution
technical_limits: Gains shrink as training data grow; Mandarin and Spanish gains smaller than English, attributed to language mismatch in auxiliary models.
evaluation_limits: Benchmarks are vocalized in-the-wild videos; small non-English test sets make close comparisons uncertain; AVSpeech labels are machine-generated.
deployment_limits: Offline evaluation only; authors flag dual-use surveillance risk and call for regulation before commercialization.

evidence.statement: The paper presents a VSR model improved with prediction-based auxiliary tasks, time masking and hyperparameter optimization, arguing design choices matter as much as data size.
Trained on 1,459 h of public data, the model reaches 25.5% best WER on LRS2 (25.8±0.4 mean) and 31.5% on LRS3 (32.1±0.3 mean).
On CMLR Mandarin the model reaches 8.0% best CER, versus 22.0% for the prior method listed; on CMU-MOSEAS Spanish it reaches 43.9% best WER.
Ablations show that removing both auxiliary tasks and time masking raises WER from 29.5 to 35.0 on LRS2 and from 35.8 to 39.1 on LRS3.
The challenges section notes that silent speech and Lombard speech remain largely unexplored and that person-independence, pose and non-English accents are open problems.

title: Development of sEMG sensors and algorithms for silent speech recognition
expert_take_short: Important large-vocabulary sEMG silent speech result (8.9% WER, 2,200 words); reviewed from the abstract only.
expert_take_long: This paper reports one of the strongest pre-deep-learning sEMG silent speech recognition results: face- and neck-worn sensors with algorithms developed in stages, from isolated words to grammar-constrained word sequences to phoneme-based models that recognize previously untrained words. The abstract reports an 8.9% WER (91.1% recognition rate) on more than 1,200 phrases from a 2,200-word vocabulary and frames applications for laryngectomy, covert communication and private phone use. The full text could not be retrieved for this review, so sensor count and placement, number of participants, speaker dependence, grammar constraints and session design are unverified; the vocabulary size alone does not establish open-vocabulary performance if a task grammar constrains decoding.
expert_true_value: Evidence that wearable sEMG with phoneme-based modeling can scale silently mouthed recognition to a vocabulary in the low thousands, an important bar for later EMG SSI work.
canon_before: sEMG silent speech recognition was mostly limited to small isolated-word vocabularies with taped laboratory electrodes.
delta_from_canon: Purpose-built face and neck sEMG sensors plus staged recognition (isolated words, grammar-based sequences, phoneme models for untrained words) reach low WER on a 2,200-word vocabulary.
position_in_field: Key sEMG SSI reference for vocabulary scaling and clinical (laryngectomy) motivation.
practical_value: Benchmark-level reference for large-vocabulary EMG SSI; details needed to judge comparability were not verifiable here.
axes_moved: vocabulary_scale; sensor_design; phoneme_based_generalization
axes_unresolved: Speaker independence; grammar-free open vocabulary; cross-session robustness (all unverified)
technical_limits: Not verifiable from the abstract beyond reliance on custom face and neck sEMG sensors.
evaluation_limits: Only the 8.9% WER on 1,200+ phrases from a 2,200-word vocabulary is verifiable; grammar constraints, participants and splits were not checked.
deployment_limits: Requires face- and neck-worn sEMG sensors; real-time or field use not verifiable from the abstract.
scope_limits: Silent (mouthed) speech recognition to text from sEMG.

The abstract reports an 8.9% word error rate (91.1% recognition rate) on more than 1,200 phrases from a 2,200-word vocabulary.

title: Unvoiced: Designing an LLM-assisted Unvoiced User Interface using Earables
venue: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM Conference on Embedded Networked Sensor Systems (SenSys '24), pp. 784-798
expert_take_short: Earable jaw-motion SSI that leans on Whisper and GPT-4 to fill gaps; promising task completion, user-dependent.
expert_take_long: Unvoiced uses a twin-IMU earable (one IMU at the temporal bone, one at the temporomandibular joint as a noise reference) to capture jaw motion during unvoiced speech, generates word-level spectrograms with a BiLSTM-attention model and a six-term custom loss, transcribes them with Whisper, and lets GPT-4 plus a vowel-class SVM fill missing words. With 19 participants it reports task completion of 93.1-98.6% across four command tasks, WER of 0.07 on in-training phrases and 0.14 on 50 unseen words, and above 90% top-1 on isolated commands. Robustness to walking and 60 dB noise is tested. The models are personalized (training uses 20 audible samples per item per user), latency and power are not reported, and the LLM step means accuracy partly reflects language priors over a small task space rather than signal decoding alone.
expert_true_value: Shows how an LLM can be used as an explicit error-correction layer over a weak, low-bandwidth jaw-motion signal to make earable silent commands usable.
canon_before: Earable jaw-motion SSI (e.g., MuteIt) recognized small command sets with signal processing or classifiers and had no mechanism to recover missing or ambiguous words.
delta_from_canon: Maps IMU jaw motion to spectrograms recognized by Whisper and adds GPT-4 gap filling with phonetic (vowel-class) filtering, plus a twin-IMU noise reference.
position_in_field: Representative earable IMU SSI paper and an early example of LLM-assisted silent speech decoding.
practical_value: Practical template for earable silent commands; field use limited by personalization and unreported latency/power.
axes_moved: llm_assisted_decoding; earable_form_factor; motion_noise_cancellation
axes_unresolved: User-independent models; latency and power; commercial earable compatibility; broader vocabularies
technical_limits: Per-user models trained with audible samples; LLM correction can hallucinate plausible but wrong words; reliance on Whisper and GPT-4 adds compute and possibly cloud dependence.
evaluation_limits: 19 participants with small task phrase sets; some inconsistencies between reported numbers in text and figures (e.g., 25-day vs 4-week longitudinal study); latency and power not reported.
deployment_limits: Research prototype not tested on commercial earables; motion noise types limited; users with speech impairments not studied.
scope_limits: Unvoiced command and short-phrase recognition from jaw motion via earables.
input_modality: IMU jaw motion (accelerometer and gyroscope)
sensor_hardware: twin-IMU earable prototype (temporal bone and temporomandibular joint)
vocabulary_type: task phrases, isolated commands, digits and general phrases

metrics: Task completion 98.6%, 97.7%, 94.8%, 93.1% on four tasks; WER 0.07 in-training phrases, 0.11 out-of-training phrases, 0.14 unseen words; isolated-command top-1 above 90%; TCR 93% at 60 dB acoustic noise
evaluation_mode: 19-participant user study with per-user models, baselines (MuteIt, LIMU-BERT, BiDiLSTM), motion and acoustic noise, longitudinal and leave-one-user-out fine-tuning tests

evidence.statement: The paper presents an earable unvoiced user interface that converts jaw motion to word spectrograms, transcribes them with Whisper, and uses GPT-4 with phonetic filtering to fill missing words.
The prototype uses two IMUs, one at the temporal bone and one at the temporomandibular joint as a reference for adaptive noise cancellation; audio is used only in training.
Task completion rates are 98.6%, 97.7%, 94.8% and 93.1% for media control, home control, messaging and quick notes.
Table 2 reports WER 0.07 for in-training phrases, 0.11 for out-of-training phrases and 0.14 for 50 unseen words.
19 participants (11 female, 8 male) with five native languages; 8 took part in noisy sessions; per-user training uses 20 audible samples per phrase, command or digit.
The authors list personalized models, an early prototype not tested on commercial earables, limited noise types and a small, non-diverse population as limitations.
