title: A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis
expert_take_short: Large-vocabulary attempted-speech decoding in one participant holds; sensor, decoder and LM are now field standard, but the spiking attribution and cross-study ratios outrun the evidence.
expert_take_long: The paper changed three components: intracortical arrays in area 6v as the speech sensor (M05), a GRU phoneme decoder trained with CTC (M06), and an online 125,000-word language model (M07). All three are standard against today's ledger because the field adopted them, and a [later] system on the same design reached 2.5% WER on the same vocabulary. The main claim holds as a single-participant demonstration: 23.8% online WER at 62 words per minute on a large vocabulary was new for attempted speech. Crediting spiking resolution for the gain is overreach, since a [concurrent] ECoG system reached a similar error at a higher rate. The 2.7x and 3.4x margins are untested ratios across participants, sensors and tasks, and the online numbers carry no seeds or stated selection data.
expert_true_value: Establishes that intracortical recordings from a few square millimetres of ventral precentral cortex suffice for large-vocabulary, real-time attempted-speech decoding, and that silent mouthing yields nearly the same accuracy as vocalized attempts.
canon_before: Prior speech BCIs (e.g., ECoG-based word classification in anarthria) decoded tens of words at around 15 words per minute; large-vocabulary sentence decoding had been shown mostly offline or in able speakers.
delta_from_canon: Real-time phoneme-level RNN plus large n-gram language model decoding from intracortical arrays, extending vocabulary to 125,000 words and speed to 62 words per minute, with day-specific input layers to handle non-stationarity.
position_in_field: Reference point for invasive speech neuroprostheses; the brain-section anchor against which later intracortical (Card 2024) and ECoG (Metzger 2023) systems are compared.
practical_value: Demonstrates a viable architecture (phoneme RNN + LM) and quantifies how much LM quality and recalibration matter. Not yet a take-home device.
axes_moved: Vocabulary size (50 to 125,000 words) for real-time decoding; communication speed (62 wpm); silent (mouthed) versus vocalized attempted speech comparison; cortical localization (6v vs 44).
axes_unresolved: Multiple participants; independent home use; recalibration-free stability; people with more profound orofacial weakness; WER low enough for everyday use.
axes_regressed: Requires daily training data (260-480 sentences, about 41 min) and day-specific decoder layers; invasive percutaneous arrays.
technical_limits: Neural non-stationarity handled by day-specific input layers and rolling feature adaptation; without same-day training data WER was 30%. Area 44 arrays contributed little; performance relied on two small 6v arrays.
evaluation_limits: Single participant; real-time evaluation over 8 days (5 vocalized, 3 silent) with 80 (125k) and 50 (50-word) trials per day. Offline improvements (17.4%, 11.8%) are retrospective analyses, not real-time results.
deployment_limits: Percutaneous intracortical arrays, researcher-run sessions and daily recalibration; the authors state it is not yet a complete, clinically viable system.
scope_limits: Main article text read via an automated full-text extraction of the Nature open-access page (figures not visually inspected; Methods/Extended Data and Supplementary not exhaustively checked; data/code availability not verified). No independent reproduction.
task: Real-time decoding of attempted (vocalized or silently mouthed) sentences into text.
input_modality: Intracortical spiking activity (threshold crossings / spike-band features) from microelectrode arrays.
sensor_hardware: Four intracortical microelectrode arrays: two 3.2 x 3.2 mm arrays in area 6v (ventral premotor) and two in area 44 (Broca's area).
body_site: Brain (left ventral precentral cortex area 6v and area 44).
output_type: Text (phoneme probabilities decoded to words with an n-gram language model).
vocabulary_type: Closed 50-word set and large open-domain English vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: 50 words; 125,000 words.
metrics: Real-time WER: 50-word 9.1% vocalized / 11.2% silent; 125,000-word 23.8% vocalized / 24.7% silent; 62 words per minute. Offline: improved LM 17.4%, plus temporally closer test sentences 11.8%; adding dorsal to ventral 6v array lowered offline WER from 32% to 21%; no same-day training 30% WER. Naive Bayes 1 s area 6v classification: 92% (33 orofacial movements), 62% (39 phonemes), 94% (50 words); area 44 below 12%.
evaluation_mode: Real-time closed-loop evaluation on held-out sentences over 8 days, plus offline analyses of language model, array subsets and training data.

evidence.statement: Participant T12 has bulbar-onset ALS, retains limited orofacial movement and vocalization but cannot produce intelligible speech; four microelectrode arrays were placed, two in area 6v and two in area 44.
Real-time WER was 9.1% (vocalized) and 11.2% (silent) for a 50-word vocabulary, and 23.8% and 24.7% for a 125,000-word vocabulary.
Decoded attempted speech ran at 62 words per minute on average.
A five-layer GRU RNN outputs phoneme probabilities every 80 ms with day-specific input layers and rolling feature adaptation, followed by a 125,000-word trigram language model in Kaldi.
From 1 s of area 6v activity, naive Bayes classification reached 92% for 33 orofacial movements, 62% for 39 phonemes and 94% for 50 words; area 44 was below 12%.
Offline, an improved language model reduced WER from 23.8% to 17.4%, and testing on sentences closer in time to training reduced it to 11.8%.

Evaluation spanned 8 days (5 vocalized, 3 silent); test sentences were not duplicated in training; final training set had 10,850 sentences, with 260-480 training sentences (41 +/- 3.7 min) collected per day.
evidence.section_or_location: Decoding attempted speech; Fig. 2b caption; Fig. 4c

evidence.statement: Without training data from the evaluation day, WER rose to 30%, showing dependence on daily recalibration.

The authors state that a 24% WER is probably not yet low enough for everyday use, that results need confirmation in more participants, and that generalization to more profound orofacial weakness is open.

en.summary: Large-vocabulary attempted-speech decoding in one participant holds; sensor, decoder and LM are now field standard, but the spiking attribution and cross-study ratios outrun the evidence.
en.sensor: Four intracortical microelectrode arrays (areas 6v and 44)

en.speaker: Speaker-dependent

en.limitations: Single participant, daily recalibration, researcher-operated; 24% WER judged insufficient for everyday use by the authors.

title: A high-performance neuroprosthesis for speech decoding and avatar control
expert_take_short: Text, voice and avatar from ECoG in one participant hold as a demonstration; sensor and decoder are standard, and an LM trained on the test pool inflates the text result.
expert_take_long: The paper changed the sensor (M05, 253-electrode high-density ECoG), the decoders (M06, CTC recurrent networks for phones, HuBERT units and gestures) and the output (M08, text, synthesized voice and avatar). M05 and M06 are standard, and the text result trails the [concurrent] intracortical system, which reached a similar error on a vocabulary about 120 times larger [@willett2023] (inference). M08 is the real departure but the weakest evidence: listeners got 54.4% of words wrong on the 1,024-word set, and the real-time avatar is animated from decoded audio. The strongest confound is the language model (M07), trained on the sentence pool that contains the test sentences. Speed, synthesis and personalised-voice claims rest on one participant, one model and comparisons across vocabularies and reference voices.
expert_true_value: Shows that a non-penetrating ECoG array can support multimodal (text, voice, face) decoding from silent attempted speech at high speed, extending the SSI output space beyond text.
canon_before: Moses et al. (2021) decoded 50 words at 15 words per minute with ECoG in anarthria; speech synthesis from ECoG had been shown offline in able speakers (Anumanchipalli 2019).
delta_from_canon: Higher-density 253-channel ECoG, phone-level CTC decoding with a 1,024-word real-time vocabulary, unit-based speech synthesis and facial-avatar decoding in one system.
position_in_field: ECoG counterpart to Willett et al. (2023); key evidence that silent attempted speech in severe paralysis can drive text and voice outputs.
practical_value: Useful blueprint for multi-output communication BCIs and for discrete-unit speech synthesis without ground-truth audio from the user.
axes_moved: Speed (78 wpm), vocabulary for real-time ECoG decoding, synthesized speech and avatar outputs, stability of a frozen classifier across sessions.
axes_unresolved: Synthesized-speech intelligibility for general vocabulary; multiple participants; independent daily use; closed-loop feedback.
axes_regressed: Synthesized speech is far less intelligible than text output on general sentences (median perceptual WER 54.4% vs text WER 25.5%).
technical_limits: Phone-level CTC with 5-gram LM; synthesis via HuBERT units and vocoder. Coverage limited to one array; authors call for denser and broader coverage.
evaluation_limits: Single participant. AAC phrase-set results are offline; general-vocabulary offline result uses a 39,378-word vocabulary. Avatar evaluated perceptually and by correlation with healthy speakers. Text says 13 days of data collection in Results versus 14 in Discussion.
deployment_limits: Percutaneous connection, laboratory sessions, no closed-loop feedback during decoding; personalized voice applied offline.
scope_limits: Read the author-manuscript full text (eScholarship PDF) via automated extraction; about the last 11% of the text (likely late Methods/references) was not read; Extended Data and Supplementary Table values not checked. No independent reproduction.
task: Decode silently attempted sentences into text, synthesized speech and avatar facial movements.
input_modality: High-density electrocorticography (ECoG) during silent attempted speech.
sensor_hardware: 253-channel high-density ECoG array (3 mm spacing), subdural over left middle superior/middle temporal gyri, precentral and postcentral gyri.
body_site: Brain (left sensorimotor and temporal cortex surface).
output_type: Text, synthesized speech audio, avatar facial animation, discrete expression/movement labels.
vocabulary_type: 1024-word-General sentence set (real time); 529- and 50-phrase AAC sets (offline).
vocabulary_size: 1,024 words (general set); 39,378-word vocabulary offline; 529 and 50 phrases.
metrics: Text, 1024-word-General real-time: median WER 25.5% (99% CI 19.3-34.5), PER 18.5%, CER 19.9%, 78.3 wpm. Offline 39,378-word vocabulary WER 27.6%. 529-phrase-AAC WER 17.1% (89.9 wpm); 50-phrase-AAC WER 4.92% (101 wpm). Synthesis MCD 3.45/4.49/5.21 dB and perceptual median WER 8.20%/28.2%/54.4% for 50/529/1024 sets. Avatar forced-choice accuracy 85.7%/87.7%/74.3%; articulatory movement classification 87.8%; nine-way emotion 74.0%. Frozen NATO code-word classifier 96.8% over 19 later sessions.
evaluation_mode: Real-time text, synthesis and acoustic-avatar decoding; offline simulations for AAC sets, direct avatar, vocabulary scaling and electrode exclusion.

evidence.statement: Participant is 47, with quadriplegia and anarthria from a pontine infarct in 2005; she attempted to silently speak sentences without vocalizing, which the authors distinguish from imagined speech.
A 253-channel high-density ECoG array with 3-mm spacing was placed subdurally over left temporal, precentral and postcentral cortex.
Real-time 1024-word-General decoding reached median WER 25.5% (99% CI 19.3-34.5), median PER 18.5% and CER 19.9% at 78.3 words per minute.
Offline, the 529-phrase-AAC set reached 17.1% WER at 89.9 wpm and the 50-phrase-AAC set 4.92% WER at 101 wpm.

Text decoder: 1D convolution plus 4 bidirectional GRU layers predicting 39 phones plus silence with CTC, decoded with a 5-gram KenLM; speech synthesis predicts 100 HuBERT discrete units with CTC and vocodes them.
Synthesized speech MCD was 3.45, 4.49 and 5.21 dB and perceptual median WER 8.20%, 28.2% and 54.4% for the 50-phrase, 529-phrase and 1024-word sets.
Avatar forced-choice perceptual accuracy was 85.7%, 87.7% and 74.3%; six-way articulatory movement classification median 87.8%; nine-way emotional expression 74.0%.
Training used 9,506 sentence trials (about 1.6 h per day) over 13 days; a NATO code-word classifier frozen at day 40 averaged 96.8% across 19 later sessions.
Single participant; the authors call for validation in other individuals, note closed-loop feedback was not provided and that denser, broader coverage is needed.

en.summary: Text, voice and avatar from ECoG in one participant hold as a demonstration; sensor and decoder are standard, and an LM trained on the test pool inflates the text result.
en.sensor: 253-channel high-density ECoG array over sensorimotor and temporal cortex
en.task: Silent attempted speech to text, speech synthesis and avatar
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Real-time median WER 25.5%, PER 18.5%, 78.3 wpm; 50-phrase set WER 4.92% (offline)
en.limitations: Single participant; AAC results offline; synthesized speech on general sentences has 54.4% perceptual WER; lab-based use.

title: Neuroprosthesis for decoding speech in a paralyzed person with anarthria
expert_take_short: Sentence decoding from a person who cannot speak holds for 50 words and one participant; the decoder is standard, and an LM restricted to the test vocabulary drives the gain.
expert_take_long: The paper changed who is decoded (M04, a participant with anarthria and a chronic implant) and moved a closed-vocabulary pipeline from speaking epilepsy patients into that setting (M06, M07); each component is standard for 2021 ECoG work, and the advance is the population, not the decoder. The main claim, sentences decoded from a person who cannot speak, holds for 50 words and one participant at 25.6% median WER. The strongest overreach is the language model: it was trained only on sentences built from the same 50 words as the test set, so the drop from 60.5% to 25.6% WER measures a closed-world prior. The no-recalibration claim rests on a post hoc offline analysis of isolated words, not on real-time sentence use. Against today the decoder is far behind: 99.6% accuracy on 50 words after 30 minutes of data [@card2024] ([later]), where this paper used 22 hours.
expert_true_value: Clinical proof of concept that attempted-speech cortical signals persist and are decodable into sentences long after anarthria onset, setting the baseline later ECoG and intracortical systems improved upon.
canon_before: Speech decoding from ECoG had been shown in epilepsy patients who could speak; decoding in people who had lost speech was unproven.
delta_from_canon: First real-time sentence decoding in anarthria using speech detection, word classification and a language model, with long-term stability analysis over 81 weeks.
position_in_field: Foundational clinical ECoG speech neuroprosthesis; predecessor of Metzger et al. 2023.
practical_value: Establishes feasibility and a stability argument for chronic ECoG; vocabulary and speed are too limited for general communication.
axes_moved: Clinical population (anarthria), real-time sentence decoding, long-term signal stability.
axes_unresolved: Vocabulary size, speed, multiple participants, independent use, false detection rate.
technical_limits: Word-level classification over a fixed 50-word set; sentence accuracy depends strongly on the LM (60.5% WER without vs 25.6% with). High-gamma (70-150 Hz) features only.
evaluation_limits: Single participant; sentence results from 15 blocks / 150 trials; isolated-word results offline without LM; stability analyses post hoc with no multiple-comparison adjustment.
deployment_limits: Percutaneous connector prevented independent daily use; testing at the participant's home with researchers.
scope_limits: Read the author-manuscript full text (eScholarship PDF) via automated extraction; Supplementary Appendix (model layer details, Fig. S5, S10) not read. No independent reproduction.
task: Real-time decoding of attempted words and sentences from a fixed 50-word vocabulary.
input_modality: High-density ECoG high-gamma activity during attempted speech.
sensor_hardware: 128-electrode (16 x 8, 4 mm spacing) high-density ECoG array, subdural over left sensorimotor cortex.
body_site: Brain (left precentral, postcentral, posterior middle frontal and posterior inferior frontal gyri).
vocabulary_type: Closed vocabulary; 50 target sentences built from the same words.
vocabulary_size: 50 words.
metrics: Real-time sentence decoding: median WER 25.6% with LM (95% CI 17.1-37.1), 60.5% without LM, chance 92.1%; median 15.2 words per minute (12.5 correct wpm); 80/150 trials error-free. Offline isolated-word accuracy 47.1% (chance 2%); 98% of attempts detected, 968 spurious detections.
evaluation_mode: Real-time sentence decoding plus offline isolated-word classification and post hoc stability analyses.

evidence.statement: Participant: 36-year-old man with anarthria and spastic quadriparesis after pontine stroke at age 20; 50 sessions over 81 weeks.
A 128-electrode 16 x 8 high-density ECoG array (4 mm spacing) was implanted subdurally over left sensorimotor cortex.
Median real-time sentence WER was 25.6% with the language model and 60.5% without; chance was 92.1%; median rate 15.2 words per minute.
Offline isolated-word classification averaged 47.1% across 50 words (chance 2%) from about 22 hours of data (9,800 trials).
evidence.section_or_location: Results, Word Detection and Classification; Abstract

evidence.statement: Pipeline combines a speech-detection model, a 50-word classifier using 1 s before to 3 s after onset, and a language model via Viterbi decoding.
98% of word attempts were detected, but 968 detections were spurious.
Models performed consistently without daily or weekly recalibration and benefited from data spanning more than a year; these stability analyses were post hoc.
Single participant, 50-word vocabulary, and no independent use because of the percutaneous connector.

en.summary: Sentence decoding from a person who cannot speak holds for 50 words and one participant; the decoder is standard, and an LM restricted to the test vocabulary drives the gain.
en.sensor: 128-electrode high-density ECoG over sensorimotor cortex
en.task: Attempted word and sentence decoding to text
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Median WER 25.6% with LM (60.5% without), 15.2 wpm; isolated words 47.1% (chance 2%)
en.limitations: Single participant, 50-word vocabulary, strong reliance on the language model, spurious detections, no independent use.

title: An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis
expert_take_short: Reaches 2.5% online large-vocabulary WER and 248 h of home use in one participant; rapid calibration is a cross-study claim and the 97.5% conversation accuracy matches the Copy Task figure.
expert_take_long: The paper [@card2024] changes calibration data (M03), array placement (M05) and sustained home use (M13); each is standard by the verdict rules (one participant, no within-participant ablation). Its final Copy Task sessions reach 2.5% online WER on 125,000 words, the lowest online large-vocabulary WER among the topic's ledger candidates (Appendix), against 23.8% for T12 [@willett2023]; the gap crosses participant, placement, language models and months of accumulated data (2.5% by session 15). Rapid calibration holds only as a description: 9.8% WER after about 473 sentences, within one T12 day (inference), is a lower WER at a similar quantity, not less data. The strongest overreach is the abstract's 97.5% accuracy for conversations, which equals 100 minus the Copy Task 2.5% (inference); measured conversational WER is 3.7% in selected sessions. Home use over 8.4 months is the real advance; other users remain untested, as the authors concede.
expert_true_value: Strongest evidence to date (in this set) that an invasive speech neuroprosthesis can be accurate enough and stable enough for sustained, self-initiated daily communication.
canon_before: Willett et al. (2023) and Metzger et al. (2023) reached about 24-26% WER on large vocabularies in research sessions with daily recalibration.
delta_from_canon: Roughly tenfold lower WER on a 125,000-word vocabulary, rapid calibration (usable on day 1-2), and long-term personal conversational use with speech detection from neural activity.
position_in_field: Current reference point for intracortical speech-to-text BCIs aimed at practical home use.
practical_value: Shows that, with 256 electrodes in precentral gyrus, near-usable accuracy is achievable quickly and maintained over months; informs clinical translation.
axes_moved: Accuracy on large vocabulary; calibration speed; months-long personal use; neural speech start/stop detection.
axes_unresolved: Multiple participants; speech rate close to natural conversation; performance as ALS progresses; fully independent setup.
technical_limits: Decoder details (RNN and language-model specifics) are largely in supplementary material not reviewed here; the main text describes 80 ms phoneme decoding with open-source language models.
evaluation_limits: Single participant. Conversation-mode WER computed on 925 sentences with known labels; self-reported accuracy is subjective. The abstract's 97.5% figure is tied to copy-task WER in the main text.
deployment_limits: Percutaneous intracortical arrays; a researcher needed to connect and launch the system; effects of ALS progression not studied.
scope_limits: Read the author-manuscript full text (eScholarship PDF) via automated extraction; Supplementary Appendix (architecture, LM details) not read. No independent reproduction.
task: Real-time decoding of attempted speech to text, read aloud with a personalized TTS voice, in copy and conversation modes.
input_modality: Intracortical neural activity from microelectrode arrays during attempted speech.
sensor_hardware: Four 64-electrode (8 x 8) intracortical microelectrode arrays (256 sites) in left precentral gyrus: two ventral premotor, one primary motor (BA4), one area 55b.
output_type: Text and synthesized speech (TTS in a voice resembling the participant's pre-ALS voice).
vocabulary_type: Closed 50-word set and large open English vocabulary.
vocabulary_size: 50 words; 125,000 words.
metrics: 50-word WER 0.44% on session 1 (after 30 min of data); 125,000-word copy-task WER 9.8% on session 2; 2.5% by session 15; final five sessions 2.5% (95% CI 2.0-3.1) at 31.6 wpm. Conversation-mode WER 3.7% on 925 labelled sentences. 248.3 cumulative hours over 8.4 months, 22,679 sentences, 84 sessions.
evaluation_mode: Real-time copy task and self-paced conversation mode over 84 sessions; offline evaluation of speech detection.

evidence.statement: Participant: 45-year-old man with ALS and severe dysarthria (ALSFRS-R 23); unintelligible to non-caregivers.
Four 64-electrode arrays (256 sites) were implanted in left precentral gyrus: two ventral premotor, one BA4, one area 55b.
On session 1 the 50-word vocabulary reached 0.44% WER; on session 2, the 125,000-word copy task reached 9.8% WER.
Copy-task WER was 2.5% by session 15 and 2.5% (95% CI 2.0-3.1) in the final five sessions at 31.6 words per minute.
Conversation-mode WER was 3.7% (95% CI 3.3-4.3) on 925 sentences with known labels.
The system was used for 248.3 cumulative hours over 8.4 months across 84 sessions, communicating 22,679 sentences, including self-initiated use in 72 sessions.

Phonemes are decoded every 80 ms from neural activity without microphone input and turned into words and sentences with openly available language models; output is spoken by a TTS voice designed to sound like his pre-ALS voice.
The authors note a single participant, uncertain durability as ALS progresses, no data on other disorders, and that a researcher was needed to connect and launch the system.

en.summary: Reaches 2.5% online large-vocabulary WER and 248 h of home use in one participant; rapid calibration is a cross-study claim and the 97.5% conversation accuracy matches the Copy Task figure.
en.sensor: Four 64-electrode intracortical microelectrode arrays in precentral gyrus
en.task: Attempted speech to text with personalized TTS output
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Copy-task WER 2.5% at 31.6 wpm (125k words); conversation WER 3.7%
en.limitations: Single participant; rate well below natural speech; researcher needed to set up; long-term ALS progression effects unknown.

title: Decoding speech perception from non-invasive brain recordings
expert_take_short: Contrastive M/EEG decoding (M06) and subject-layer pooling (M03) were ahead in 2022 and are now standard; tests reuse training participants, and EEG headline and EEG zero-shot claims outrun the data.
expert_take_long: The paper [@defossez2023] changes the decoding objective (M06, contrastive ranking of segments), the training population (M03, 175 participants in one model with a subject layer) and the target (M02, wav2vec 2.0 features). M06 and M03 were ahead: no earlier M/EEG decoder in the ledger ranks open candidate sets against a pretrained speech representation or uses a subject layer (Appendix); the subject layer helps on all four datasets, the contrastive loss on three (Tables 2–3). M02 is standard by cross-modal precedent from lip reading [@afouras2020asr; @ma2021lira]; on Brennan EEG it gains under one standard deviation over a learned Mel encoder. The evaluation (M12) is standard but never tests the subject layer on a new person. The MEG result holds within this protocol; the EEG headline figures, EEG zero-shot words and the parity with invasive decoders do not.
expert_true_value: Strong methodological template for aligning non-invasive brain signals with pretrained speech representations across many subjects; establishes MEG-vs-EEG performance gaps on perception.
canon_before: Non-invasive speech decoding mostly classified a handful of words or phonemes per subject with hand-crafted features.
delta_from_canon: Contrastive alignment with wav2vec 2.0 targets and a shared multi-subject architecture, evaluated as zero-shot retrieval among 1,000+ segments across four datasets.
position_in_field: Key non-invasive perception-decoding reference in the brain section; not evidence for silent speech production decoding.
practical_value: Reusable architecture (later adapted in Brain2Qwerty) and evidence on how much data and subjects matter for non-invasive decoding.
axes_moved: Scale of non-invasive datasets pooled across subjects; retrieval among large candidate sets; contrastive speech-representation targets.
axes_unresolved: Speech production / imagined speech; generative (open-ended) output; real-time use; wearable sensing.
technical_limits: Retrieval over a predetermined candidate set; decoding relies largely on semantic/lexical content; EEG performance is low.
evaluation_limits: Perception only in healthy volunteers. Table 2 values are mean +/- s.d. across three random seeds; text describes them as participant averages. Introduction (1,500 segments) and abstract (1,000 segments) differ; test sets range from 190 to 1,842 segments.
deployment_limits: MEG is not portable and uncommon clinically; real-time decoding not addressed.
scope_limits: Read the published Nature Machine Intelligence PDF via automated extraction; Extended Data figure values (ablations) not inspected. arXiv v2 checked for metadata.
task: Zero-shot identification of the heard 3 s speech segment from MEG/EEG during passive listening.
input_modality: Non-invasive MEG and EEG.
sensor_hardware: MEG (273 and 208 sensors) and EEG (128 and 60 channels) from four public datasets.
vocabulary_type: Natural stories and sentences in English and Dutch; segment retrieval among test-set candidates.
vocabulary_size: Candidate sets of 190 to 1,842 segments per dataset; 175 participants; about 163 hours total (19.2 + 6.7 + 80.9 + 56.2 h).
metrics: MEG top-1 up to 41.3% average, >80% best participant; MEG top-10 up to 70.7% (Gwilliams) and 67.5 +/- 0.4 (Schoffelen); EEG top-10 25.7 +/- 2.9 (Brennan and Hale) and 17.7 +/- 0.6 (Broderick); random-model top-10 0.5-5.3%. Equalized MEG top-10 30.3%/31.7%, still above EEG.
evaluation_mode: Offline, within-dataset held-out segments with a shared multi-subject model; ablations and interpretability regressions.

evidence.statement: Four public datasets: Broderick 2019 EEG (19 participants, 19.2 h), Brennan and Hale 2019 EEG (33, 6.7 h), Schoffelen 2019 MEG (96, 80.9 h), Gwilliams 2022 MEG (27, 56.2 h); participants passively listened to speech.
From 3 s of MEG, top-1 segment identification reaches up to 41.3% on average and above 80% for the best participants.
Top-10 accuracy: MEG 70.7% (Gwilliams) and 67.5 +/- 0.4 (Schoffelen); EEG 25.7 +/- 2.9 (Brennan and Hale) and 17.7 +/- 0.6 (Broderick).
Brain module with spatial attention, participant-specific layer and dilated residual convolutions, trained with CLIP-style contrastive loss to wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53 representations.
After equalizing channels, participants and duration, MEG top-10 dropped to 30.3% and 31.7% but still outperformed EEG (P < 1e-6).
evidence.section_or_location: Results, Is MEG really much better than EEG?

evidence.statement: In Gwilliams, nearly 36% of test words were never presented during training, yet decoding still reached about 40%.
The study covers perception in healthy volunteers; the contrastive objective retrieves from a predetermined set; production decoding and a generative module are left to future work.

en.summary: Contrastive M/EEG decoding (M06) and subject-layer pooling (M03) were ahead in 2022 and are now standard; tests reuse training participants, and EEG headline and EEG zero-shot claims outrun the data.
en.sensor: Non-invasive MEG (208/273 sensors) and EEG (60/128 channels)
en.vocabulary: Natural stories and sentences; 190-1,842 candidate segments
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: MEG top-1 up to 41.3% average; top-10 up to 70.7%; EEG top-10 17.7-25.7%
en.limitations: Perception not production; retrieval from fixed candidates; MEG not wearable; EEG performance low.

title: Speech synthesis from neural decoding of spoken sentences
expert_take_short: 変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（ECoG → 推定した調音 33 次元 → 音響 32 次元の二段 bLSTM）、**M08 出力**（文単位の音声波形）、**M04 利用時の行為**（声に出した文で学習した復号器を、口だけ動かした文に当てる）である。M12（閉じた語群からの聴取書き取り）は付随して論じる。
expert_take_long:
変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（ECoG → 推定した調音 33 次元 → 音響 32 次元の二段 bLSTM）、**M08 出力**（文単位の音声波形）、**M04 利用時の行為**（声に出した文で学習した復号器を、口だけ動かした文に当てる）である。M12（閉じた語群からの聴取書き取り）は付随して論じる。
5 人の MCD 中央値は 5.14〜6.58 dB、二段は直接法より 0.54 dB 良い（P1、全データ。0.2 dB で知覚できる差とされる。いずれも本文確認）。P1 の 101 文の書き取り WER 中央値は 25 語群で 31%、50 語群で 53% である（本文確認）。
最も強い交絡は比較の組み方にある。二段の中間目標には音素ラベルから作った調音位置・様式 18 次元が入り、直接法にはこの学習時の教師がない。層の数（3+3 層と 4 層）と学習率も違う。ただし著者は直接法を二段と同じ 6 層（MFCC を中間層に置く形）でも学習し、4 層のほうが良かったので 4 層を使ったと書いている（方法、本文確認）。比較は P1 一人で、学習の繰り返し回数と乱数種は書かれていない。0.54 dB を「調音を経ること」だけに帰すのは推測にとどまる。著者自身も「十分なデータがあれば二つは収束しうる」と書いている。後続の Le Godais ら [[2]](#ref-2)（後続）は線形法で「直接法と間接法は同等の性能で、直接法がやや有利」と報告した。
神経信号 → 調音 → 音響の二段は、wiki 内の検索では対象より前に見つからなかった（再現率の目安 0.74、既知項目 4/4、別の語での全文検索でも追加なし）。
口だけの発話の MCD は図にしか値がなく、口だけの状態空間の相関の n が本文 38、図 4e 説明 58 と食い違う。聴取試験は閉じた語群で、偶然水準の WER は示されていない。
expert_true_value:
声を失った人の発話補助として、文単位の波形を神経信号から作れることを示した。対象者は発話に障害のない人で、声に出した発話を学習に使っている。声の出ない利用者では、口だけの転用がどこまで効くかが鍵になるが、その値は図にしかない。
後続の研究は、声を出そうと試みる発話で学習する方向（Wairagkar ら [[22]](#ref-22)）に進み、筋電でも調音を中間段に置く試み（Lee ら [[25]](#ref-25)、後続）が続いた。
canon_before:
**M06（調音を中間段に置く復号）**：同じ研究室の Chartier ら [[3]](#ref-3)（同時期、2018-05 オンライン）が、腹側感覚運動野（vSMC）が推定した調音運動を符号化することを示し、その逆推定を対象が中間目標に使った。調音から音声を作る側では、Bocquelet ら [[4]](#ref-4) が EMA 由来の調音を入力に DNN と MLSA で実時間合成し、脳コンピュータインタフェースへの応用を想定していた。ただし入力は神経信号ではない。
神経信号から調音を経て音響を出す二段は、wiki 内の検索では対象より前に見つからなかった（付録A、再現率の目安 0.74、既知項目 4/4）。Saha ら [[5]](#ref-5)（同時期、arXiv 2019-04）は EEG から音韻範疇を中間段にして分類しており、音声合成ではない。

**M08（神経信号から音声を合成する）**：先行は 2 件である。Guenther ら [[6]](#ref-6) は閉じ込め状態の 1 人で、皮質内電極から母音のフォルマントを実時間で復号して音にした。Martin ら [[7]](#ref-7) は発声中の ECoG から聴覚スペクトログラムを線形モデルで復号したが、波形の合成と聴取試験はない。同時期には Angrick ら [[8]](#ref-8)（同時期、bioRxiv 2018-11-27、対象の bioRxiv 版の 2 日前）が ECoG から対数メルスペクトログラムを 3D 畳み込みで復号し WaveNet で波形にした。
対象が足したのは、文単位の波形を作り、それを聴取者に書き取らせた点である。

**M04（声に出した学習を声なしに当てる）**：先行は 6 件ある。Martin ら [[7]](#ref-7) は ECoG で、発声で学習した線形モデルを声に出さない発話に当て、発声音声に DTW で合わせて安静時と比べた。評価の組み方は対象の口だけの評価と同じだが、Martin らの covert は「声に出さずに読む」課題で、口を動かす対象の課題とは行為が違う。EMG では Janke ら [[9]](#ref-9)、Wand ら [[10]](#ref-10)、Janke [[11]](#ref-11) が可聴で学習したモデルを無声 EMG に当てた。Janke の学位論文では EMG→音声の MCD が 5.54 から 6.81 dB に悪化した（本文確認、差 1.27 dB・相対 +23% は査読者の計算）。ただし原著は、可聴の参照が同時収録でないので MCD の妥当性は限られると注記している（6.3 節）。超音波と唇の Florescu ら [[12]](#ref-12)、映像の Petridis ら [[13]](#ref-13) も発声と無声を学習と試験で入れ替えている。

**M12（合成音声の聴取による明瞭度）**：先行は 9 件ある。映像からの再構成では Ephrat ら [[14]](#ref-14) が MTurk で書き取りを、Cornu と Milner [[15]](#ref-15) が語正答率を測った。調音センサでは Hueber と Bailly [[16]](#ref-16)、Gonzalez ら [[17]](#ref-17)（明瞭度最大 92%、本文確認）、Bocquelet ら [[4]](#ref-4)（聴取者 12 人、本文確認）がある。同じ研究室の Bouchard ら [[18]](#ref-18) は声道画像から合成した音声を MTurk で同定させていた。同時期に Akbari ら [[19]](#ref-19)（同時期、bioRxiv 2018-06）が聴取中の聴覚皮質から再構成した数字を 11 人に同定させている（本文確認）。

**継いだ部品**：M01・M05・M11・M13 は Chang 研究室の ECoG 研究の系譜（音読課題、高ガンマ、臨床の留置）、M02 は Chartier ら [[3]](#ref-3) の逆推定、M03 は参加者ごとの学習と早期終了である。
delta_from_canon:
**M06**：二段の利点として著者は、皮質が調音運動をよく表すこと、調音運動が低次元に乗ることを挙げる（考察、本文確認）。状態空間の解析では第 1〜10 主成分で分散の 85%、第 1〜2 主成分で 35% を説明した。参加者間の状態空間の相関は r>0.8（P1・P2・P4）である（本文確認）。
ただし、二段の第 1 段の目標は全員に同じ話者非依存の逆推定から作っている。参加者間でよく似ることの一部はこの共通の写像から来る可能性がある（推測）。直接法との差 0.54 dB は P1 一人・全データでの値で、学習の繰り返し回数は書かれていない。図 1f と図 3 の説明にある「5 回繰り返して同様の結果」が何の繰り返しかは本文から分からない。データを減らした曲線（8 段階、1 区画は約 50 文）も P1 である。

**M08**：MLSA の混合励振で文単位の波形を出し、MCD・スペクトル相関・聴取の三つで評価した。著者は MCD が話者の声質に敏感だと注記している（第 2 段を P1 から P2 へ移すと悪化）。
後続では、Herff ら [[20]](#ref-20)（後続）が単位選択、Chen ら [[21]](#ref-21)（後続）が微分可能な合成器を使い、Wairagkar ら [[22]](#ref-22)（後続）は ALS の 1 人で即時の合成に進んだ。

**M04**：P1 は 10 文を 12 回ずつ、声に出す試行と口だけの試行を交互に読んだ（方法）。口だけの各試行は、直前に声に出した同じ文に DTW で合わせて評価した。本文の「58 sentences」は、口だけの約 60 試行から 2 試行を除いた試行数と読める（推測、除いた理由の記載はない）。結果は「偶然水準より良いが声に出した場合に劣る」で、著者は発声の信号がないためと推測している（本文確認）。
先行の Martin ら [[7]](#ref-7) と比べると、文単位の波形を出した点が新しく、転用という組み方は同じである。EMG の Janke [[11]](#ref-11) の悪化幅（+23%、査読者の計算）と比べる数値は対象の本文になく、比べられない。後続では Gaddy と Klein [[23]](#ref-23)（後続）が EMG で、Komeiji ら [[24]](#ref-24)（後続）が ECoG で同じ転用を基準条件に置いた。

**M12（付随）**：書き取りは、正解語と無作為なテスト文の語からなる 25 語・50 語の語群から選ぶ閉じた課題である。著者は閉じた語群が必要だった理由を本文で述べている。語群の大きさで WER が 31% から 53% に上がること（本文確認）は、語群が結果を大きく左右することを示す。偶然水準が示されていないので、31% がどれだけ偶然から離れているかは読めない。
position_in_field: 神経信号から文単位の音声波形を合成し聴取者に書き取らせた初期の代表例で、調音を中間段に置く二段は wiki 内の検索では先行例が見つからなかった（再現率の目安 0.74）。M04・M08・M12 の個々の要素には先行例がある。
practical_value:
声を失った人の発話補助として、文単位の波形を神経信号から作れることを示した。対象者は発話に障害のない人で、声に出した発話を学習に使っている。声の出ない利用者では、口だけの転用がどこまで効くかが鍵になるが、その値は図にしかない。
後続の研究は、声を出そうと試みる発話で学習する方向（Wairagkar ら [[22]](#ref-22)）に進み、筋電でも調音を中間段に置く試み（Lee ら [[25]](#ref-25)、後続）が続いた。
axes_moved: 神経信号から文単位の音声波形、調音を経る二段、大規模な聴取試験、口だけの発話への転用。
axes_unresolved: 中間段の効果と音素由来の教師の切り分け、P1 以外での比較、開いた語彙での明瞭度、繰り返しによるばらつき。
axes_regressed: なし。
technical_limits: 中間目標は音響からの推定調音と音素ラベル由来の 18 次元で、直接法にはこの教師がない。直接法は 6 層版も試して良かった 4 層を使っている。
evaluation_limits: 直接法との比較と聴取試験は P1 のみで、学習の繰り返し回数は記載なし。書き取りは閉じた語群で偶然水準なし。口だけの発話は 58 試行（10 文の反復と読める）で値は図のみ、状態空間の n が本文 38・図 58 と食い違う。テスト文数も方法と図説明で一部違う。
deployment_limits: てんかん外科の一時的な ECoG、発話に障害のない参加者、オフライン解析のみ。
scope_limits: wiki にある著者稿の本文で読み、刊行版と bioRxiv 版（2018-11）の数値とは照合していない。図の画像と補足資料は未確認。
task: 音読中の ECoG からの文単位の音声合成
input_modality: 高密度 ECoG（高ガンマと低周波）
sensor_hardware: 臨床用の硬膜下高密度 ECoG 電極
output_type: 合成音声（MFCC・F0・有声度から MLSA で波形）
vocabulary_type: 音読した文（MOCHA-TIMIT など）、聴取は閉じた語群
vocabulary_size: 書き取りは 25 語・50 語の語群、単語同定は 325 語
metrics: MCD 中央値 5.14〜6.58 dB、直接法より 0.54 dB 良い（P1）、書き取り WER 中央値 31%／53%
evaluation_mode: オフライン、録音セッションで分けたテスト、MTurk の聴取試験

evidence.statement: 5 人の MCD 中央値は 5.14〜6.58 dB で、P1 では二段が直接法より 0.54 dB 良い。
P1 の 101 文の書き取り WER 中央値は 25 語群で 31%、50 語群で 53%。
二段の中間目標は音素ラベル由来の 18 次元を含み、直接法にはこの教師がない。直接法は 6 層版も試し良かった 4 層を使う。比較は P1 のみ。
口だけの状態空間の相関の n が本文 38、図 4e 説明 58 と食い違い、口だけの値は図にしかない。

en.summary: Two-stage bLSTM decoder maps ECoG during reading aloud to inferred articulatory features and then to acoustic parameters, synthesizing sentence waveforms (median MCD 5.14-6.58 dB in five participants). The two-stage model beat a direct decoder by 0.54 dB in P1, but the intermediate targets add phonetic-label supervision and the decoders differ in depth and learning rate; listener transcription used closed 25/50-word pools.
en.sensor: Clinical high-density ECoG (high gamma 70-200 Hz and 1-30 Hz)
en.task: Sentence-level speech synthesis from neural signals
en.vocabulary: Read sentences (MOCHA-TIMIT and others); closed 25/50-word pools for listener transcription
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Median MCD 5.14-6.58 dB; 0.54 dB better than direct decoding (P1); listener median WER 31% (25-word pool) and 53% (50-word pool)
en.limitations: Decoder comparison and listener tests in P1 only, repetitions not stated; extra phonetic supervision in the intermediate stage (the authors tried a 6-layer direct decoder and kept the better 4-layer one); closed-pool transcription without chance level; mimed-speech values (58 trials of 10 sentences) in figures only, with inconsistent counts; read from the author manuscript (bioRxiv 2018-11 and published versions not compared).

title: An instantaneous voice-synthesis neuroprosthesis
expert_take_short: Closed-loop sentence voice from intracortical arrays holds for one participant; the design is standard, forced-choice and proxy-target metrics overstate intelligibility.
expert_take_long: The paper [@wairagkar2025] changed the training targets (M02, TTS audio aligned to neurally inferred boundaries), the decoder (M06, causal closed-loop synthesis) and the output (M08, voice with intonation and pitch). All three are standard: closed-loop synthesis existed for vowels and unintelligible words, and all results are from one participant. The main claim holds: sentence-level voice from intracortical signals, heard as the user attempts to speak, with acoustic leakage ruled out. Intelligibility is weaker than the headline: 94.34% six-choice matching (chance about 17%, inference) sits beside a 43.75% median open-transcription WER that the authors also report (Fig. 2l). The same group's [later] causal model reaches 5.24% listener WER on this paper's benchmark, offline with simulated real-time inference [@wairagkar2026], so this paper is the closed-loop proof, not the quality benchmark.
expert_true_value: First demonstration that intracortical signals can drive instantaneous, expressive voice synthesis with closed-loop feedback, including from silently mimed attempts, without any ground-truth speech from the user.
canon_before: Speech BCIs decoded text (with optional TTS) at sentence level; direct neural speech synthesis was offline or had large delays.
delta_from_canon: Causal 10 ms-resolution synthesis with audio feedback, TTS-aligned pseudo-targets for an anarthric/dysarthric user, and decoding of paralinguistic features (intonation, emphasis, pitch).
position_in_field: Leading intracortical brain-to-voice result; complements text-based neuroprostheses (Willett 2023, Card 2024).
practical_value: Shows a path to natural conversational turn-taking and prosody that text-to-TTS pipelines cannot provide; pseudo-target method is reusable for SSIs lacking audio ground truth.
axes_moved: Latency (instantaneous, closed-loop synthesis); prosody and pitch control; synthesis from mimed speech; training without ground-truth audio.
axes_unresolved: Consistent open-vocabulary intelligibility; multiple participants; long-term learning effects; home use.
axes_regressed: Open intelligibility (almost 60% of words, per press release) is far below text-decoding accuracy reported for the same participant in Card et al. 2024.
technical_limits: Targets are TTS-derived and aligned at putative syllable boundaries estimated from neural data; decoder modified for session nonstationarities. Quality depends on participant energy and enunciation.
evaluation_limits: Single participant. Main preprint intelligibility metric is a 6-alternative closed-set matching task; open transcription numbers (about 60% vs 4%) and 25 ms latency seen only in a secondary source.
deployment_limits: Percutaneous intracortical arrays; research sessions; long-term practice effects unknown.
scope_limits: Full text read for the bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2024.08.14.607690) via automated extraction, not the final Nature version (publisher page unreachable); published-version figures (almost 60% word intelligibility vs 4%, ~25 ms latency) come from the UC Davis/EurekAlert press release and the Nature abstract. Session counts not verified.
task: Causal, real-time synthesis of the participant's voice from attempted (vocalized or mimed) speech, with paralinguistic control.
input_modality: Intracortical threshold crossings and spike-band power from microelectrode arrays.
sensor_hardware: Four intracortical microelectrode arrays (256 electrodes) in ventral precentral gyrus: ventral premotor (6v), primary motor (M1) and area 55b.
output_type: Synthesized speech audio (Bark cepstral coefficients, pitch, voicing to vocoder), optionally in a cloned own voice.
vocabulary_type: Cued sentences plus self-guided speech, pseudo-words, spelling and interjections; unconstrained synthesis rather than vocabulary-bound decoding.
vocabulary_size: Not applicable (open, unit-free synthesis); 956 evaluation sentences in closed-set listener test.
metrics: Preprint: closed-set 6-alternative listener matching 94.34% mean (median 100%) on 956 sentences; correlation with target speech r = 0.89 +/- 0.04 (attempted) and 0.89 +/- 0.03 (mimed); question intonation 90.5%; word emphasis 95.7%; loud vs quiet 90%; neural processing within 10 ms. Press release (published version): almost 60% of words understood with the BCI vs 4% without; ~25 ms synthesis latency.
evaluation_mode: Real-time closed-loop synthesis across research sessions, evaluated by crowdsourced listener tests and closed-loop paralinguistic tasks.

evidence.statement: Participant T15 is a 45-year-old man with ALS and severe dysarthria, unable to produce intelligible speech, with four arrays (256 electrodes) in 6v, M1 and 55b.

A Transformer-based decoder predicts Bark-frequency cepstral coefficients, pitch and voicing every 10 ms from binned threshold crossings and spike-band power, then a vocoder plays audio with neural processing within 10 ms.
With no ground-truth audio, targets were TTS of the cued text time-aligned to neural activity using putative syllable boundaries; own-voice targets came from voice-cloning TTS.
Fifteen listeners matched each of 956 sentences to one of 6 same-length transcripts with mean 94.34% (median 100%) accuracy.
Mimed (silent) attempts yielded synthesis correlation r = 0.89 +/- 0.03, not statistically different from vocalized attempts (0.89 +/- 0.04).
Closed-loop question intonation reached 90.5% and word emphasis 95.7%; pitch decoding produced distinct low/medium/high levels for melodies.
Listeners understood almost 60% of synthesized words with the BCI versus 4% without it; synthesis latency about one-fortieth of a second.
evidence.section_or_location: UC Davis press release via EurekAlert (published version)

evidence.statement: Single participant; synthesized words still not consistently intelligible; quality depended on participant energy and enunciation; long-term use effects unknown.

en.summary: Closed-loop sentence voice from intracortical arrays holds for one participant; the design is standard, forced-choice and proxy-target metrics overstate intelligibility.
en.sensor: Four intracortical microelectrode arrays (256 electrodes) in ventral precentral gyrus
en.task: Real-time brain-to-voice synthesis with intonation and pitch control
en.speaker: Speaker-dependent
en.key_result: Closed-set intelligibility 94.34%; question intonation 90.5%; emphasis 95.7%; ~60% open word intelligibility (press release)
en.limitations: Single participant; open intelligibility inconsistent; reviewed from preprint plus press release, not final Nature text.

title: Brain-to-Text Decoding: A Non-invasive Approach via Typing
expert_take_short: Executed typing as the decoded action (M04) was ahead for MEG/EEG in 2025; keystroke-locked decoding (M06) and an n-gram LM (M07) are standard, and decoding needs known keystroke times.
expert_take_long: The paper [@levy2025] changes the use-time action (M04): it decodes executed typing of memorized sentences from MEG and EEG, which no earlier MEG or EEG ledger paper does (Appendix), and the result repeats across 20 MEG and 20 EEG participants; that was ahead in February 2025. The decoder (M06) is standard: windows locked to known keystroke times are the field's usual segmentation, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation (Discussion); on the target's dataset, with encoders alone and no language model, the group's [later] asynchronous encoder gives CER 0.59 against 0.39 keystroke-locked, so timing a deployed system would not have carries much of the encoder's accuracy. An independent [later] control shows the aligned windows do not leak labels. The character n-gram language model (M07) is standard and corrects the typists' own errors against the intended sentence, with no language-model-only baseline. The signal is executed finger movement of healthy typists, so the paper demonstrates non-invasive keystroke decoding, not communication for people who cannot move; the two-fold MEG-over-EEG gain compares largely different cohorts.
expert_true_value: Best-documented non-invasive brain-to-text sentence decoding to date in this set, quantifying what MEG and EEG can deliver for typing-based communication.
canon_before: Non-invasive BCIs for text relied on slow evoked-potential spellers or small-vocabulary decoding; sentence-level non-invasive decoding was rare.
delta_from_canon: Sentence-level character decoding from MEG/EEG during natural typing with a conv-transformer-LM pipeline and clustering-based train/test splits.
position_in_field: Non-invasive text-entry neighbour of speech BCIs in the brain section; not a speech or silent-speech interface.
practical_value: Benchmark numbers for MEG vs EEG text decoding and an architecture reusable for production tasks; clinical use for locked-in users remains untested.
axes_moved: Non-invasive sentence-level text decoding accuracy; dataset scale for typing-aligned M/EEG.
axes_unresolved: Real-time decoding; users who cannot move their hands; wearable sensing; speech production.
technical_limits: Requires keystroke-aligned M/EEG segments and full-trial context; supervised training only.
evaluation_limits: Healthy skilled typists; Spanish sentences of 5-8 words; baseline CERs reported only as fold improvements in text; hand-typing error rate given mainly in figures.
deployment_limits: MEG system used is not wearable; not real-time; relies on actual hand movements.
scope_limits: Read arXiv v1 HTML via automated extraction; figure-only values (hand error rate, per-participant curves) not inspected. Venue beyond arXiv not verified.
task: Decode typed sentences (characters) from MEG/EEG recorded during typing from memory.
input_modality: Non-invasive MEG and EEG aligned to keystrokes.
sensor_hardware: Whole-head MEG and scalp EEG (system details not extracted), custom MR-compatible QWERTY keyboard.
vocabulary_type: Spanish declarative sentences of 5-8 words; TF-IDF clustered 80/10/10 splits.
vocabulary_size: 128 unique sentences per session; EEG about 4K sentences (146K characters), MEG 5.1K sentences (193K characters).
metrics: CER: MEG 32% +/- 0.6 average (best 19%, worst 45%); EEG 67% +/- 1.5 (best 61%, worst 71%); MEG > EEG p < 1e-8. Improvement over EEGNet 1.14x (EEG) and 2.25x (MEG). Keyboard-distance vs confusion R = 0.73. Typing errors 3.6-3.9% of keystrokes.
evaluation_mode: Offline, held-out sentence clusters, with linear ridge and EEGNet baselines.

evidence.statement: 35 healthy right-handed skilled typists; 20 recorded with EEG and 20 with MEG (five did both); Spanish sentences of 5-8 words typed from memory without visual feedback.
Brain2Qwerty: convolutional module on 0.5 s M/EEG windows, sentence-level transformer, and a pretrained 9-gram character KenLM.
Average CER was 32% +/- 0.6 with MEG (best 19%, worst 45%) and 67% +/- 1.5 with EEG (best 61%, worst 71%).
Relative to EEGNet, Brain2Qwerty improved CER 1.14-fold with EEG and 2.25-fold with MEG.
Sentences were split 80/10/10 using TF-IDF clustering so similar sentences stay in the same split.
Decoder confusions track physical keyboard distance (R = 0.73, p = 0.02), indicating reliance on motor processes.
Not real-time (needs full trial), requires keystroke-aligned segments, tested only on healthy participants, and the MEG is not wearable.

en.summary: Executed typing as the decoded action (M04) was ahead for MEG/EEG in 2025; keystroke-locked decoding (M06) and an n-gram LM (M07) are standard, and decoding needs known keystroke times.
en.sensor: Non-invasive MEG and EEG during typing
en.vocabulary: Spanish sentences of 5-8 words; 128 per session
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: CER 32% MEG average (19% best), 67% EEG
en.limitations: Typing not speech; offline with keystroke alignment; healthy participants; MEG not wearable.

title: Auto-AVSR: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition with Automatic Labels
expert_take_short: Pseudo-labelling unlabelled AVSpeech and VoxCeleb2 with a public ASR model scales VSR training to 3,448 h and cuts LRS3 visual-only WER to 19.1%, with AV-ASR at 0.9%.
expert_take_long: Auto-AVSR is a data-scaling paper: rather than new architecture, it shows that transcripts from an off-the-shelf ASR model (NVIDIA Conformer-Transducer) are good enough to train lipreading at scale. Adding automatically labelled English subsets of AVSpeech (1,323 h) and VoxCeleb2 (1,307 h) to LRS2/LRS3 brings training to 3,448 h; LRS3 VSR WER falls monotonically from 33.0% (818 h) to 19.1%, and LRS2 VSR reaches 14.6%. AV-ASR reaches 0.9% on LRS3 and ASR 1.0%, where gains saturate. The model is a ResNet-18 + Conformer encoder per modality with MLP fusion and a joint CTC/attention Transformer decoder; a Transformer LM helps VSR only. Noise experiments show the visual stream matters most at low SNR (e.g., white noise at -7.5 dB: 88.9% audio-only vs 24.2% AV). For SSI, the relevance is the visual-only VSR result and the recipe of pseudo-labelling to overcome labelled-data scarcity. Note that 19.1% is not the best prior VSR (ViT3D-CM reports 17.0% with about 90,000 h); the claim is data efficiency. All data are vocalized, frontal 'in-the-wild' broadcast/YouTube speech, so silent-speech lip motion and wearable camera viewpoints are not tested.
expert_true_value: Practical, reproducible recipe showing that automatic labels from public ASR models make large-scale lipreading training feasible with public data only.
canon_before: Best VSR systems depended on large non-public labelled corpora (tens of thousands of hours) or self-supervised pretraining.
delta_from_canon: Uses pseudo-labelled public data to reach competitive VSR and state-of-the-art AV-ASR with 26x less data than the strongest non-public system.
position_in_field: Widely used open baseline for visual and audio-visual speech recognition in the video section.
practical_value: Released-style training recipe and models are a standard starting point for lip-based SSI front-ends and pretraining.
axes_moved: Training data scale via automatic labels; public-data VSR and AV-ASR benchmark performance; noise robustness of AV fusion.
axes_unresolved: Silent (non-vocalized) speech; non-frontal or wearable camera views; non-English languages; speaker-specific adaptation.
technical_limits: Pseudo-labels are noisy; pseudo-label quality does not track LibriSpeech WER, so ASR labeller choice is empirical; ASR performance saturates.
evaluation_limits: Evaluated on LRS2/LRS3 benchmarks only; babble noise shared between training and testing may be optimistic; no silent-speech test set.
deployment_limits: Large models trained on thousands of hours; no latency or on-device evaluation.
scope_limits: Read arXiv v3 PDF via automated extraction; Table 1 column labels were garbled in extraction so its per-column mapping was not used. Code/model availability not verified.
task: Visual-only, audio-only and audio-visual sentence-level speech recognition.
input_modality: Lip-region video and audio.
sensor_hardware: Ordinary video camera and microphone recordings (LRS2, LRS3, VoxCeleb2, AVSpeech).
vocabulary_type: Open-vocabulary English, SentencePiece 5,000 units.
vocabulary_size: Open vocabulary; 3,448 h of training data.
metrics: LRS3 VSR WER 19.1% (3,448 h) vs 33.0% (818 h); LRS3 ASR 1.0%; LRS3 AV-ASR 0.9% (prior AV-HuBERT 1.4%). LRS2 VSR 14.6%, ASR 1.5%, AV-ASR 1.5%. Pink noise -7.5 dB: A 56.8% vs AV 16.2%; white noise -7.5 dB: A 88.9% vs AV 24.2%.
evaluation_mode: Offline benchmark evaluation on LRS2/LRS3 test sets with data-scaling and noise ablations.

evidence.statement: Unlabelled AVSpeech and VoxCeleb2 are transcribed with public pre-trained ASR models (Conformer-Transducer selected) and combined with LRS2/LRS3 for training.
English-filtered AVSpeech contributes 1,323 h and VoxCeleb2 1,307 h; full training set totals 3,448 h.
LRS3 VSR WER decreases from 33.0% (818 h) to 19.1% (3,448 h); ASR from 1.5% to 1.0%.
LRS3 AV-ASR reaches 0.9% WER versus 1.4% for AV-HuBERT; best prior VSR (ViT3D-CM) is 17.0% with about 90,000 h.
LRS2 VSR WER is 14.6% with 3,448 h, compared with 22.6% for VTP.
At -7.5 dB white noise, audio-only WER is 88.9% versus 24.2% audio-visual.
Architecture: ResNet-18 front-ends with 12-layer Conformer encoders, MLP fusion and 6-layer Transformer decoder trained with joint CTC/attention; Transformer LM used only for VSR.
Pseudo-label quality is not correlated with LibriSpeech WER, ASR gains saturate, and babble noise is shared between train and test.

en.summary: Training lipreading and AV-ASR on 3,448 h including ASR-pseudo-labelled AVSpeech and VoxCeleb2 cuts LRS3 visual-only WER to 19.1% and audio-visual WER to 0.9%.
en.sensor: Video camera (lip region) and microphone
en.task: Visual, audio and audio-visual speech recognition
en.speaker: Speaker-independent
en.key_result: LRS3 WER: VSR 19.1%, ASR 1.0%, AV-ASR 0.9%; LRS2 VSR 14.6%
en.limitations: Vocalized broadcast/YouTube speech only; no silent or wearable-view test; pseudo-labels noisy; benchmark-only evaluation.

title: EarCommand: "Hearing" Your Silent Speech Commands In Ear
expert_take_short: Earphone-based SSI that infers silent commands from ear-canal deformation sensed with inaudible in-ear echoes; abstract reports 10.02% WER on 32 word-level and 12.33% on 25 sentence-level commands.
expert_take_long: EarCommand is an early, widely cited earable SSI: an inward-facing speaker emits near-ultrasound signals into the ear canal and an inward-facing microphone captures echoes, from which ear-canal deformation caused by articulator movement during silent mouthing is mapped to commands. Its appeal for SSI is form factor: no camera, no skin electrodes, hands-free, and hardware close to commodity earbuds. The abstract reports a WER of 10.02% for 32 word-level commands and 12.33% for 25 sentence-level commands, and claims robustness across configurations and environmental conditions; press coverage mentions use with masks and in noise but gives no figures. Because the full text (ACM DL) could not be accessed, this review cannot verify the number of participants, user-dependence of training, session/remount handling, signal frequencies, model architecture or how the robustness tests were quantified. As stated, the vocabulary is a closed command set, so the result speaks to command recognition rather than open-vocabulary silent speech. Treat the numbers as author-reported headline results pending full-text review.
expert_true_value: Shows that ear-canal deformation sensed acoustically from an earbud carries enough articulatory information for closed-set silent command recognition, opening the earable SSI direction.
canon_before: Wearable SSIs mostly used skin-contact EMG, cameras or sensors near the mouth; earable sensing of speech-related ear-canal deformation was not established for silent command recognition.
delta_from_canon: Introduces in-ear acoustic sensing of ear-canal deformation as the input modality for silent word- and sentence-level commands.
position_in_field: Representative earable acoustic SSI in the acoustic section; precursor to later earable silent speech work.
practical_value: Attractive form factor for private, hands-free command input on earbuds; practical accuracy and calibration burden unverified here.
axes_moved: Form factor (earphone, no camera or electrodes); new sensing locus (ear canal).
axes_unresolved: Open vocabulary; cross-user generalization; calibration burden; real-time on-device operation; long-term fit variation (not verifiable from abstract).
technical_limits: Closed command sets only; technical details (frequencies, model, training regime) not verified because full text was not accessed.
evaluation_limits: Only abstract-level WERs available; number of participants, splits and robustness conditions unverified. Press coverage reports rounded values (10.2%/12.3%) that differ slightly from the abstract (10.02%/12.33%).
deployment_limits: Prototype earbud with a linked computer per press coverage; on-device performance, latency and power not verified.
scope_limits: Abstract (via ECNU research portal) and secondary press coverage (New Atlas) only; ACM full text not accessible from this environment. All non-abstract details are unverified. title: Deep Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
expert_take_short: 変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（同じ Transformer エンコーダの上で CTC 損失と系列変換損失を並べて比べ、音声と映像を別々の注意で読む復号器を使う）と **M11 評価用の正解**（BBC 放送から自動で作った文単位の公開データ LRS2-BBC）である。残りは前作 WLAS [[2]](#ref-2) の系譜を継ぐ。
expert_take_long:
変えたのは **M06 処理・復号**（同じ Transformer エンコーダの上で CTC 損失と系列変換損失を並べて比べ、音声と映像を別々の注意で読む復号器を使う）と **M11 評価用の正解**（BBC 放送から自動で作った文単位の公開データ LRS2-BBC）である。残りは前作 WLAS [[2]](#ref-2) の系譜を継ぐ。

映像だけの最良は TM-seq2seq で WER 48.3%（外部言語モデルあり）、前作 WAS の 70.4% から約 22 ポイント下がった（表2、本文確認）。
ただし 70.4% の評価条件（言語モデルやビーム幅）は対象に書かれておらず、同時期の同グループ論文 [[3]](#ref-3) の表1 でも「MV-WAS」として条件なしで載っている。70.4% が言語モデルなしの値だと仮定すると、同条件の 49.8% との差は 20.6 ポイント、相対 −29% になる（査読者の計算）。3 か月前の同グループ論文の Transformer は言語モデルありで 50.0% で、対象がそこから足した改善は 48.3% までの 1.7 ポイントである（表1、本文確認）。
しかも前段（3D+ResNet）、事前学習データ（非公開の MV-LRS を含む）、後段の三つが同時に変わっており、寄与の切り分けはない。「新しい前段と後段が 22% 以上の改善に寄与した」（§1）という帰属は強すぎる。

CTC と系列変換の差は言語モデルで大きく縮む。映像だけでは言語モデルなしで 65.0% 対 49.8%（差 15.2）、ありで 54.7% 対 48.3%（差 6.4）である（表2、本文確認）。
音声映像のきれいな音声では 8.2% 対 8.5% で、テスト 6,663 語では二項誤差の目安（1 標準誤差）が約 ±0.34 ポイントあり、差は判別できない（査読者の計算）。乱数種や繰り返しの記載はない。

LRS2-BBC のテストは放送日で分けているが、話者数の記載がなく（表1 は「-」）、同じグループの LRS3 論文 [[4]](#ref-4) は「LRS2-BBC は同じ人物が回をまたいで出やすい」と書いている。前作 WLAS は話者が数千人いるので話者に依存しないと述べるが [[2]](#ref-2)、テストが未知話者の評価であることは保証されない。
expert_true_value:
LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED は、この後の唇読み・音声映像認識の標準ベンチマークになった。TM-seq2seq と TM-CTC は以後の比較表の基準行として繰り返し使われている（付録A の後続文献）。
一方で、LRS2-BBC での数値は、テレビの常連出演者が訓練にもテストにも出うる条件での値である。未知の話者への汎化を言うには、LRS3-TED か話者を分けたテストが要る。
canon_before:
**M06（CTC と系列変換）**：唇読みの文単位認識では、CTC を使う LipNet [[6]](#ref-6) と、注意つき系列変換の WLAS [[2]](#ref-2) が別々に提案されていた。同じ前段の上で両者を並べた比較は、wiki 内の検索では対象より前に見つからなかった（付録A、全文一致の標本 30 本を読んで 0 本、既知項目の再現率は研究単位で 1/1）。
同時期には、同じグループの Interspeech 論文 [[3]](#ref-3) が BLSTM-CTC・全畳み込み CTC と Transformer を LRS2 で比べ、Transformer が言語モデルありで 50% に達していた。対象の TM-seq2seq はこの Transformer と同じ構成（数値と前段の事前学習データは異なる）で、対象が新しく足したのは Transformer 版の CTC（TM-CTC）と音声映像への拡張である（§1「On the content」）。
音声映像の融合は、WLAS の二重注意 [[2]](#ref-2) と、Petridis ら [[7]](#ref-7) の音声・映像の特徴連結＋双方向再帰が先行する。

**M11（実環境の文単位データ）**：LRS [[2]](#ref-2) は BBC 放送から 11 万文を集め、放送日で分割していたが、権利の都合で公開できなかった。LRS2-BBC はその公開版の位置づけである。単語単位では LRW が同じ手順で作られている。

**継いだ部品**：M01・M04（通常の発声を撮った放送映像）、M02（字幕を強制整列し、IBM Watson の認識結果で選別したラベル）、M05、M07、M08、M13 は WLAS の系譜をそのまま継ぐ。カリキュラム学習（§5.2）も前作から継いでいる。対象 §5.2 の「単語から始めて長さを伸ばす新しい戦略を導入する」という文は、WLAS §3.1 の文とほぼ同じである [[2]](#ref-2)。
delta_from_canon:
**M06**：CTC と系列変換を、エンコーダを共有したまま並べた点が対象の中心である。結果は「映像だけなら系列変換が明確に良く、音声があれば同程度、雑音下では CTC が良い」（§6.4）。
映像だけの差は言語モデルで半分以下に縮み（15.2 → 6.4 ポイント）、著者も「言語モデルの利得は CTC で大きい」と書いている（§6.4）。比べているのは損失だけでなく、ビーム幅（CTC 100、seq2seq 35）と言語モデルの重み（α 0.5 と 0.1）も別々に調整した構成どうしである（付録C・D）。
雑音下で CTC が良い（23.6% 対 34.2%）のは一つの雑音種・一つの SNR（0 dB バブル）での結果で、学習と同じ種類の雑音で評価している（§5.3）。

同期ずれへの強さ（図8）は、seq2seq が 1 エポックの微調整でほぼ影響を消し、CTC は 4 エポックでも残る。著者はこれを、二つの入力に別々の注意を使う seq2seq と、二つの符号を連結する TM-CTC の融合方式の差として説明している（§6.3）。損失の違いの効果とは分けられていない。

**M11**：LRS2-BBC は pre-train 195 時間、train-val 29 時間、テスト 0.5 時間で、テストは 1,243 発話と小さい。語彙制限はなく、文は 100 文字か 10 秒で切る（§4、表1）。
自動構築の手順（SSD 顔検出、字幕の強制整列、Watson での選別、音声映像の同期と話者判定）は LRS からの継承である。
話者の分離は管理していない。同時期の LRS3 [[4]](#ref-4) は「TED では同じ話者が繰り返し出ないので重なりは少ない」とし、LRS2-BBC は同じ人物が出やすいと明記している。後続のデータでは、ViCocktail [[8]](#ref-8) がテスト話者を訓練と重ならないよう選んでいる。
position_in_field: LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED は以後の唇読み・音声映像認識の標準ベンチマークになり、TM-seq2seq と TM-CTC は比較表の基準行として使われ続けた。構成要素では M06 と M11 を変え、残りは WLAS の系譜を継ぐ。
practical_value:
LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED は、この後の唇読み・音声映像認識の標準ベンチマークになった。TM-seq2seq と TM-CTC は以後の比較表の基準行として繰り返し使われている（付録A の後続文献）。
一方で、LRS2-BBC での数値は、テレビの常連出演者が訓練にもテストにも出うる条件での値である。未知の話者への汎化を言うには、LRS3-TED か話者を分けたテストが要る。
axes_moved: 公開の文単位ベンチマーク、CTC と系列変換の同条件比較、同期ずれと雑音の系統的評価。
axes_unresolved: 話者の分離、繰り返しによるばらつき、雑音種と SNR の幅、非公開データなしでの再現。
axes_regressed: なし（ただし事前学習に非公開 MV-LRS を使う）。
technical_limits: 前段・事前学習データ・後段が同時に変わり、改善の寄与が分けられていない。
evaluation_limits: テスト話者の重なり未記載、繰り返しなし、雑音は学習と同種の 0 dB バブルのみ、WAS 70.4% の条件不明。
deployment_limits: オフライン評価のみ。学習は GPU 1 枚で 5〜8 日。
scope_limits: LRS2-BBC と LRS3-TED の英語放送・講演映像に限る。
task: 文単位の唇読みと音声映像音声認識
input_modality: 顔（口元）映像と音声
sensor_hardware: 放送用カメラ映像 25 fps、16 kHz 音声
vocabulary_type: 開語彙
vocabulary_size: テスト語彙 1,693（LRS2-BBC）
metrics: WER（映像のみ 48.3%、音声映像 8.2%、雑音下音声映像 23.6%、LRS2-BBC）
evaluation_mode: オフライン、放送日で分けたテスト集合

evidence.statement: 映像のみの TM-seq2seq は LRS2-BBC で外部言語モデルありの WER 48.3%（なしで 49.8%）。
同グループ3か月前の Transformer（言語モデルあり 50.0%）からの改善は 1.7 ポイント。WAS 70.4% は条件不明。
LRS2-BBC のテストは放送日で分割され、話者の重なりは未記載。同グループの LRS3 論文は LRS2-BBC で同じ人物が出やすいと述べる。

en.summary: Landmark AVSR paper that releases LRS2-BBC and compares CTC and sequence-to-sequence Transformers on one shared encoder. Video-only TM-seq2seq reaches 48.3% WER with an LM (49.8% without; the 70.4% WAS baseline has no stated decoding conditions, and the same group's Transformer three months earlier already reached 50.0%). CTC and seq2seq differ little once an LM or audio is added.
en.sensor: Face/mouth video (25 fps, 112 px mouth crop) plus 16 kHz audio
en.task: Sentence-level lip reading and audio-visual speech recognition
en.speaker: Not stated
en.key_result: 48.3% WER video-only (LRS2-BBC, +LM); 8.2% audio-visual clean; 23.6% audio-visual in 0 dB babble
en.limitations: Test speakers may overlap with training (split by broadcast date, speaker count unreported); single runs; matched synthetic babble noise only; pretraining uses non-public MV-LRS; GPU model inconsistent between sections.
